items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Membrane Biology, Beijing Frontier Research Centre for Biological Structure, Tsinghua-Peking Centre for Life Sciences and Center for Life Sciences and Artificial Intelligence, School of Life Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China. sai@tsinghua.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. Following entry into the cytoplasm, the poxvirus core dissociates from the lateral bodies and undergoes expansion, functioning as a compartment for early transcription1. However, how molecules are exchanged between the viral core and the host cytoplasm remains poorly understood. Here, using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging, we determine the structures of the portal complex and its central pore on the vaccinia virus core at 6.7 Å and 4.4 Å resolution, respectively. Guided by structural predictions and experimental density, we identify three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, as the principal components of the pore and construct a structural model of their organization. The pore contains a narrow, positively charged constriction formed by conserved lysine residues in L3, substitutions of which impair viral gene expression and propagation. The dimensions and electrostatic properties of the channel are consistent with a potential role in molecular exchange across the core wall. Together, our findings establish a structural framework for understanding the organization and potential function of the poxvirus portal complex.

items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Evolutionary and Theoretical Immunology, Department of Biology, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM 87131, USA. Electronic address: isalinas@unm.edu.
items.abstract: The ability of vertebrates to conquer land is attributed to innovations in respiration and locomotion. However, land adaptation profoundly reshaped mucosal surfaces such as the skin, the main interface between hosts and the environment. To adapt to land, African lungfish annually remodel their skin, forming a cocoon. Here, we report the discovery of a small pore-forming toxin in African lungfish, Protop-CrTX-A, with no other vertebrate counterpart that is sufficient to drive epithelial morphogenesis transcriptional programs. In free-swimming lungfish, goblet cells secrete Protop-CrTX-A into the mucus. During estivation, this niche is replaced by a mucin-low/basal epithelial niche, adjacent to a granulocyte immune niche that becomes the predominant source of Protop-CrTX-A in the estivated skin. Protop-CrTX-A acts as a reversible switch for skin remodeling, sufficient to convert African lungfish skin between aquatic and terrestrial states. We propose that innate immunity, through its capacity to remodel tissues, was a key driver of vertebrate water-land transitions.

items.title: Paleogenomics illuminates mobility and changing lifeways in Chalcolithic Anatolia
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Middle East Technical University, Ankara, Türkiye; Centre for Palaeogenetics, Stockholm, Sweden; Department of Archaeology and Classical Studies, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden; Department of Health Informatics, Middle East Technical University, Ankara, Türkiye. Electronic address: mehmet.somel@su.se.
items.abstract: Once labeled the "Dark Ages" of Anatolian prehistory, the Chalcolithic period (c. 6000-3000 BCE) was characterized by drastically reduced settlement densities compared with the preceding Neolithic and the succeeding Bronze Ages, a change interpreted as population decline. Using 44 new genomes combined with published data, we find no evidence for a population reduction. The genetic evidence instead suggests that populations in Chalcolithic Anatolia were increasingly mobile and/or growing in size while receiving gene flow from eastern regions (e.g., East Anatolia and the South Caucasus) through a 3,000-year-long admixture process. We propose that genetic and archaeological evidence may be reconciled by hypothesizing the presence of communities with dispersed and mobile lifeways that are mostly invisible to archaeology. These communities also practiced consanguinity at frequencies unobserved in previous periods. Finally, we identify a mid-5th-millennium BCE individual in Central Anatolia carrying ∼10%-30% Pontic-Caspian Steppe-related ancestry, shedding light on mobility between the Eurasian Steppe and Anatolia.

items.title: Echidna: a Bayesian framework for integrative inference of copy number alterations impacting phenotypic plasticity
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biomedical Engineering, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.; Irving Institute for Cancer Dynamics, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.; Department of Computer Science, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.; Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. ea2690@columbia.edu.
items.abstract: The ability of cells to adapt their behavior in response to genetic or environmental changes is a fundamental biological process that drives cellular diversity in both normal and pathological contexts, including in tumor evolution. Copy number alterations (CNAs), which can include large-scale changes in genomic ploidy, play a key role in creating adaptive advantages in evolving cell populations. However, tracing these populations across experiments and disentangling the role of CNAs from other sources of transcriptional variability remains challenging and expensive. Here we present Echidna, a Bayesian hierarchical model that integrates single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk whole-genome sequencing data to enable robust integrative inference of CNAs, jointly across samples and treatment time points, to better understand the impact of genomic events on cellular phenotype. Applying Echidna to patient tumor specimens, we demonstrate its superior performance in clonal reconstruction and derive insights into therapy resistance mechanisms.

items.title: Joint single-cell capture of Cas9 edits and transcriptomes reveals on- and off-target effects on gene expression
items.last_author_affiliation: Integrative Biology Laboratory, Salk Institute for Biological Studies, La Jolla, CA, USA. gmcvicker@salk.edu.
items.abstract: A longstanding barrier in genome engineering with CRISPR-Cas9 has been the inability to measure editing outcomes and their functional effects at single-cell resolution. Here we present Superb-seq, which captures single-cell edits and transcriptome effects by integrating Cas9 editing, T7 in situ transcription and single-cell RNA sequencing. We performed Superb-seq on 35,000 cells from three cell lines. Using seven guide RNAs to target four chromatin remodeler genes in 10,000 K562 cells, Superb-seq detected 5,761 edited cells, all on-target sites and 36 off-target sites. Superb-seq improved estimation of downstream perturbation effects on gene expression compared to Perturb-seq. We compared Superb-seq to 4 bulk off-target detection methods and identified between 6 and 210 edit sites across 3 benchmarking guides. Nineteen off-target edits were associated with differential gene expression, nine of which were cell type-specific. In summary, Superb-seq illuminates the consequences of Cas9 genome editing by connecting single-cell edits with changes in gene expression.

items.title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Modern Biology, Department of Hematology, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China. lupeng.ye@nju.edu.cn.; State Key Laboratory of Pharmaceutical Biotechnology, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China. lupeng.ye@nju.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Abstract Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455–457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100–1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

items.title: High-quality pig pan-genome resources illuminate centromere evolution and enhance genotype–phenotype mapping
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Animal Biotech Breeding, Frontiers Science Center for Molecular Design Breeding (MOE), China Agricultural University, Beijing, China. liujf@cau.edu.cn.; College of Animal Science and Technology, China Agricultural University, Beijing, China. liujf@cau.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Pigs are important agricultural resources and valuable biomedical models, necessitating a high-quality pan-genome to comprehensively capture genomic diversity. Here we present an extensive genomic and phenotypic resource comprising 3 telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genomes and 16 high-quality assemblies. This resource enables the construction of the pig pan-transcriptome and pan-metabolome, thereby enhancing genotype-phenotype mapping. Using 12 Y-chromosome assemblies, we resolved centromere repositioning at basepair resolution, establishing centromeres as unique evolutionary markers. Reconstruction of centromeric three-dimensional genomic architecture revealed their role as structural scaffolds that concentrate chromatin interactions. We identified eEF1A1, a transcriptionally active gene consistently located near chromosome 1 centromeres, as a candidate hotspot for karyotype variation. From a pan-structural variation map, we pinpointed AKR1B1 as a key gene underlying hypoxia adaptation. Moreover, a graph-based pan-genome built from T2T genomes improved heritability capture. Together, this work provides a foundation for studies of centromere evolution, adaptive genetics and precision breeding.

items.title: Integrated QTL mapping and CRISPR screening in pooled iPSC-derived microglia reveals genetic drivers of neurodegenerative risk
items.abstract: Abstract Mounting evidence implicates microglia in neurodegeneration, but linking disease-associated genetic variants to target genes and cellular phenotypes is hindered by the inaccessibility of these cells. We differentiated 261 human induced pluripotent stem cell lines into microglia-like (iMGL) cells in pools with phenotypic (differentiation, phagocytosis and migration) and single-cell transcriptomic readouts. Burden analysis of deleterious variants detected 36 genes influencing microglial phenotypes. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) analysis identified 7,121 eQTL-associated genes and 79 colocalizations across four neurodegenerative disease genome-wide association studies, half of which had limited prior evidence of causality. Integration of eQTL and phenotypic associations highlighted the role of disease-relevant variants, including LRRK2 and TREM2 acting through microglial phagocytosis. A coupled CRISPR screen identified a role for TREM2 in phagocytosis and highlighted the importance of cell type in the directionality of phenotypic effects. By contextualizing variant effects within iMGLs in different inflammatory states, we provide a comprehensive framework for interpreting the function of risk loci in neurodegenerative disorders.

items.title: Evolutionary lineage-specific and heterochromatin-independent repression of transposon-derived sequences
items.abstract: Abstract At least one-quarter of our gene regulatory sequences are derived from transposable elements (TEs). Their rapid evolutionary turnover fuels the innovation of species-specific regulatory networks, yet their activity must be tightly controlled for the integrity of broader gene regulatory programs. Although this is in part achieved through heterochromatin-based repression, notably by KRAB domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (KZFPs) in tetrapods, the regulatory landscape of TEs remains to be fully characterized. Here, we discover that SCAN domain-containing zinc-finger proteins (SZFPs), which originally arose through capture of the sequence encoding a retroviral capsid by a KZFP gene, have expanded their gene repertoires and diversified their DNA recognition specificity in a lineage-specific manner across amniotes. Our comprehensive identification of human SZFP binding sites revealed that they bind regulatory elements derived from distinct TE subfamilies of matching evolutionary ages. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that SZFP binding sites are inaccessible nucleosome-associated chromatin without accompanying heterochromatin marks, H3K9me3 or H3K27me3, and resist opening by pioneer transcription factors such as SOX2 and POU5F1 (also known as OCT4) as well as SWI/SNF-mediated gain of an enhancer-associated chromatin state. These results unravel a rapidly evolving epigenetic machinery responsible for controlling lineage-specific TE-derived regulatory sequences in a heterochromatin-independent fashion.

items.title: Principles and assumptions underlying domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Sydney, Camperdown, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. shila.ghazanfar@sydney.edu.au.; Sydney Precision Data Science Centre, The University of Sydney, Camperdown, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. shila.ghazanfar@sydney.edu.au.; Charles Perkins Centre, The University of Sydney, Camperdown, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. shila.ghazanfar@sydney.edu.au.
items.abstract: Spatial-omics technologies simultaneously measure feature expression and locations within tissues, providing an unprecedented opportunity to study tissue structures. The first key step in analyzing these high-dimensional datasets is identifying biologically relevant clusters, yet the large number of spatial-omics clustering (SOC) methods makes method selection challenging. Here we comprehensively review 47 SOC methods and extract information on 108 variables across 26 groups of method characteristics and applicability. This revealed substantial diversity in the underlying algorithms, affecting the suitability of methods to different tissues and biotechnologies. Based on this, we provide an analytical decision tree to help data analysts select methods based on their data types and research questions, and we highlight knowledge gaps to help bioinformaticians identify new avenues for method development. We thus hope to pave the way for more effective applications in a diverse methodological landscape and guide future method development.

items.title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery
items.last_author_affiliation: Consortium for Biomedical Research & AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), St. Louis, USA. justinreese@lbl.gov.; Division of Environmental Genomics and Systems Biology, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, USA. justinreese@lbl.gov.
items.abstract: Abstract Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer’s blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

Partially functional hypomorphic missense variants in BRCA2 are reduced penetrance pathogenic variants
items.abstract: Abstract Identification of partial loss-of-function (hypomorphic), reduced penetrance pathogenic missense variants (RPPVs) and assessment of the clinical relevance of these variants is needed for improved hereditary cancer risk estimation. Here we show that 70 candidate hypomorphic missense variants in the DNA-binding domain of BRCA2 reduce homologous recombination DNA repair activity and endogenous cell survival, decrease RAD51 foci formation, and increase sensitivity to Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors. The 34 “strong” hypomorphs with greatest effects on function are associated with moderate risks of female breast cancer and later ages of diagnosis than pathogenic variants (PVs), and 14 of these variants can be classified as “likely pathogenic” by integration of functional data into a ClinGen BRCA1/2 variant curation model. In addition, 32% of tumors with hypomorphic variants and corresponding loss of heterozygosity for BRCA2 display homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) compared to 83% of tumors with PVs and 7% with benign variants. These RPPVs represent a class of BRCA2 variants that have implications for the clinical management of carriers.

items.title: Knowledge-guided machine learning deciphers spatiotemporal dynamics in chemical reactor systems
Identification of translation events that drive nonsense-mediated mRNA decay reveals functional roles for alternative RNA isoforms
items.abstract: Abstract The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway targets mRNAs undergoing premature translation termination for degradation. Previously, RNA-seq of yeast lacking NMD revealed that most genes targeted by NMD lack obvious premature termination codons (PTCs). We develop a combined approach using RNA-seq and 40S ribosome profiling to identify cryptic premature termination events that could account for NMD on nearly all these transcripts, including many alternative RNA transcript isoforms associated with annotated genes. Many NMD-targeted transcripts appear to be involved in two-promoter gene regulatory systems and share properties with long un-decoded transcript isoforms (LUTIs). In particular, we show that the DAL5 LUTI regulates expression of the DAL5 protein-coding mRNA in response to changes to environmental nitrogen. Our work expands the functional roles for LUTIs and establishes the importance of NMD in their regulation.

Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
items.abstract: Abstract Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (ε Nd ) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability.

items.title: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects
items.abstract: Abstract Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

items.title: An optimized PanFlu-IOA-based mRNA vaccine targeting hemagglutinin confers broad-spectrum protection against heterosubtypic influenza viruses in mice
A map of multi-omics quantitative trait loci in a Chinese population reveals regulatory variations and disease links
Staggered cryo-plasma FIB milling enables high-throughput cryo-ET
items.abstract: Abstract Cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling combined with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is a crucial technique for studying macromolecules in their native environment. To mill thick samples, plasma ion sources are used. However, the practicality of high plasma currents, which offer the greatest potential for increasing throughput, and their possible damaging effects on the sample have not yet been investigated. Here, we systematically examine high-current xenon plasma-FIB (PFIB) milling and quantify the current-dependent damage in over 4700 tomograms by preparing a total lift-out volume of 9000 µm³. We find that currents of up to 2500 nA can be used in cryo-ET lamella preparations, enabling increased milling speeds and sample volumes that can be examined while maintaining sample integrity. We demonstrate this using a newly developed high-throughput staggered milling routine for waffle-like preparations, in which we achieve high-resolution reconstructions of yeast ribosomes, and for tissue serial lift-outs, enabling a complete experiment within 24 hours. Our results and approach provide a strong foundation for future in situ structural investigations of medically relevant protein complexes in organoids, tissues, or entire organisms.

items.title: Deep strong light-matter coupling in 3D Kane fermions without Dicke criticality
items.abstract: Abstract Deep-strong light-matter coupling is a non-perturbative regime of quantum electrodynamics in which the interaction strength exceeds the frequencies of uncoupled light and matter excitations. Whether a Dicke superradiant phase transition can occur in electronic systems with linear energy-momentum dispersion remains controversial because of the apparent absence of a diamagnetic A 2 term in their low-energy Hamiltonian. Here, we investigate Landau polaritons in a bulk mercury cadmium telluride film hosting Kane fermions coupled to a Fabry-Perot resonator. The ultralow cyclotron mass of Kane fermions and a thermally tunable carrier density enable tuning from weak to deep-strong coupling, reaching the single-mode coupling strength of 1.6 above room temperature. Near the Dirac point (100 K), deep-strong coupling coexists with linear low-energy dispersion. Our microscopic quantum theory and classical electromagnetic simulations are in agreement with measured spectra. We conclude that a diamagnetic A 2 term emerges despite the linear dispersion, preventing a Dicke superradiant phase transition.

items.title: Co-deficiency of RECQL1 and BLM causes replication stress associated with DNA damage and cohesion loss
items.abstract: Abstract The mechanistic basis for chromosomal instability characteristic of RECQ helicase disorders remains poorly understood due to their molecular-genetic complexity. To characterize the genetic interactions of RECQL1 ( also referred to as RECQL or RECQ1) , implicated in RECON syndrome, we performed an RNA interference screen and discovered a functional relationship with BLM , a gene that is mutated in Bloom syndrome. RECQL1/BLM co-deficient cells display pronounced replication stress, DNA damage accumulation, and chromosomal instability. Strikingly, RECQL1/BLM co-deficiency induces sister chromatid separation during metaphase suppressible by depletion of the cohesin unloader WAPL, suggesting that a threshold of replication stress in the genetically co-deficient cells disrupts cohesion. Primary embryonic fibroblasts from transgenic Blm -/- ;Recql -/- mice recapitulate the sister chromatid separation phenotype and heightened replication stress observed for human cells. Our findings highlight the joint roles of RECQL1 and BLM in the replication stress response and their concurrent importance for maintenance of chromosomal stability even in the absence of exogenously induced DNA damage. Furthermore, we elucidated a genetic interaction in which sister chromatid cohesion is synergistically elevated by the loss of two conserved RECQ helicases encoded by genes in which mutations are linked to hereditary diseases that are not associated with sister chromatid cohesion defects. The findings presented provide insights into the genetic crosstalk of two prominent RECQ helicases with established importance in clinical diseases of genomic instability.

items.title: Transforming spinel LiMn2O4 into a Na-layered cathode
items.abstract: Abstract The positive electrode structures of practical sodium-ion batteries are generally confined to polyanionic or layered transition metal oxide frameworks, where the trade-off between specific energy and structural stability limits their application. As a well-established positive electrode structure in lithium-ion batteries, the spinel framework has abundant storage sites for alkali metal ions, but it has received less attention for sodium-ion batteries. Here we show that spinel LiMn 2 O 4 can be transformed into a sodium-ion positive electrode. Electrochemical sodiation drives Mn-ion migration along an octahedral–tetrahedral–octahedral pathway, creating a layered/spinel heterostructure for further sodium storage. Moreover, residual spinel domains inhibit the strain and structural degradation within the layered structure. Consequently, a 26650 cylindrical cell using a LiMn 2 O 4 -derived sodium-ion positive electrode achieves a capacity of 3.85 Ah and retains 95.7% capacity after 900 cycles (1.925 A). This work demonstrates that spinel LiMn 2 O 4 can serve as a viable positive electrode for sodium-ion batteries, and that electrochemical transformation is a feasible approach for creating positive electrode frameworks.

items.title: Structurally guided wavefront neural encoder for broad-range generalizable 3D holography
items.abstract: Abstract Deep learning has advanced computer-generated holography, but learned models remain coupled to fixed wavelengths and distances, limiting generalization. Here we present the structurally guided wavefront neural encoder (SGWN-Encoder), which integrates diffraction physics with neural networks and employs a structural propagation strategy that analytically strips the parameter-sensitive global phase. This reveals a scale-normalized description of diffraction, letting the network learn transferable light-field evolution rules and generalize across propagation distances and visible wavelengths by direct inference. A dataset-free paradigm built on statistically diverse random fields teaches the model the structural mapping from complex amplitude to phase-only holograms instead of external image distributions. Without fine-tuning, a single SGWN-Encoder maintains a distance-averaged RGB PSNR of 31.9 dB and SSIM of 0.91 over the primary 2–200 mm range, retaining reconstruction up to 500 mm. Numerical and optical experiments on full-color 3D scenes establish a physically grounded route toward adaptive holographic displays.

items.title: Focused ultrasound neuromodulation of mediodorsal thalamus disrupts decision flexibility during reward learning
items.abstract: Abstract When learning to find the most beneficial course of action, the prefrontal cortex guides decisions by comparing estimates of the relative value of the options available. Basic neuroscience studies in animals support the view that the thalamus can regulate this activity within and across the prefrontal cortex. We studied a group of patients (n = 37) undergoing unilateral MR-guided focused ultrasound for essential tremor, performing the restless bandit, a reward reinforcement learning task, immediately before and after thalamotomy. Thalamotomy significantly impaired the proportion of switch choices during the task without affecting overall performance. This effect was observed when the task was delivered to co-incide with maximal vasogenic thalamic oedema but not in a control group tested on the same day of their treatment. A reinforcement learning model fitted to the patients’ choices replicated the effect of thalamotomy when the model increased exploitation of the bandits’ learnt value estimate. This shift in the explore-exploit trade-off, manifesting as reduced choice flexibility, co-varied with the pattern of post-operative oedema extension into the mediodorsal nucleus. These findings confirm a causal role of the thalamus and specifically the mediodorsal nucleus in regulating the extent to which value estimates are used to guide decisions and learning from reward.

A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures
items.last_author_affiliation: The Science and Technology Group, Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University, Onna, Okinawa, Japan. yuimaru.kubo@oist.jp.
items.abstract: Abstract Current microwave quantum technologies require the amplification of weak signals with minimal added noise at millikelvin temperatures. To date, this stringent requirement has been met exclusively by superconducting technologies, such as Josephson or kinetic-inductance parametric amplifiers. A fundamentally distinct alternative approach could be offered by masers, the microwave counterpart of lasers, which were predicted as early as the 1950s to achieve quantum-limited noise performance under ideal conditions. However, their dependence on cryogenic operation historically limited further advancement. Here we demonstrate the first-ever non-superconducting, near-quantum-limited maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures utilising nitrogen impurity spins (P1 centres) in diamond. Population inversion is achieved via microwave pumping, exploiting a four-spin cross-relaxation mechanism. We realise a maximum power gain exceeding 30 dB, an added noise of approximately 2.55 quanta above the standard quantum limit, and a maximum 1 dB output compression point of −63 dBm at 6.595 GHz. The ability to operate in strong static magnetic fields of arbitrary orientation may offer a complementary, non-superconducting route for applications such as semiconducting spin-qubit readout, magnetic-resonance spectroscopy, and dark-matter axion searches.

items.title: Lipid droplets amplify inflammasome-driven cytokine secretion in infection and inflammation
items.abstract: Abstract Lipid droplets (LDs) accumulating in infected cells are traditionally viewed as passive nutrient stores exploited by invading pathogens. Here, we show that during infection with virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), but not BCG, host LDs orchestrate protective immune responses by bridging the ISGylation and inflammasome pathways. Proteomic and imaging analyses reveal the selective recruitment of ISGylated proteins together with caspase-1 and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) precursors to the LD surface. Comparative LD proteomics in wild-type and ISG15-deficient macrophages, combined with ISGylome profiling, identify ISGylated proteins as mediators of pro-IL-1β binding to LDs. Functionally, disruption of LD biogenesis in primary human macrophages impairs mature IL-1β secretion and compromises Mtb control. Notably, this LD-dependent amplification of IL-1β release is not restricted to microbial stimuli but also occurs in response to sterile inflammasome activation. Collectively, these findings redefine LDs as immunoactive organelles integrating microbial and danger signals to potentiate inflammasome-dependent IL-1β responses during infection and inflammation.

items.title: Dearomatization and cycloaddition of furans and indoles enable divergent syntheses of spirooxindole alkaloids

items.last_author_affiliation: Institute for Chemical Research, Kyoto University, Uji, Kyoto, Japan. futaki@scl.kyoto-u.ac.jp.; Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyoto University, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto, Japan. futaki@scl.kyoto-u.ac.jp.
items.abstract: Intracellular antibody delivery enables modulation of challenging intracellular targets, including intrinsically disordered proteins, and holds considerable promise for biomedical applications. Here we show that microcondensates composed of engineered IgGs bearing glutamic acid- and tyrosine-containing tag sequences together with a trimeric membrane-permeabilizing L17E peptide [FcB(L17E)3] enable burst-like, rapid intracellular infusion of IgG antibodies under physiological salt and serum conditions. Dynamic membrane remodeling, including filopodia-like protrusions that internalize microcondensates, is visualized by lattice light-sheet and electron microscopy. The recruitment of the intrinsically disordered protein TDP-43 to stress granules is markedly inhibited by treatment with a TDP-43-targeting IgG. Physicochemical factors governing the ability of microcondensates to mediate intracellular IgG infusion are also investigated.

items.title: Brønsted/Lewis acid-catalyzed divergent cascade cyclization of alkoxyallene for the total synthesis of eburnane and aspidofractinine alkaloids
Atomic-level coordination-engineered quantum dots orchestrate mitochondrial energy rescue for diabetic bone regeneration
Mapping redox networks in cardiomyocytes reveals non-overlapping response pathways for cytosolic versus mitochondrial H₂O₂ signaling
items.abstract: Abstract Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are essential redox messengers, yet their effects depend on concentration, localization, and duration. Here, we investigate how compartment-specific hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) production influences cardiomyocyte redox signaling and function. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CM) expressing the H₂O₂ biosensor HyPer fused to D-amino acid oxidase (DAO), we achieve chemogenetic control of H₂O₂ generation in the cytosol, mitochondria, or nucleus. Cytosolic H₂O₂ propagates throughout the cell, whereas mitochondrially generated H₂O₂ remains spatially restricted, reflecting compartmentalized antioxidant buffering. Cytosolic H₂O₂ impairs contractility and relaxation in both 2D and 3D engineered heart tissue models, accompanied by preferential oxidation of Z-disc–associated and actin-binding proteins and by altered sarcomere organization. Antioxidant treatment attenuates these effects. In contrast, mitochondrially produced H₂O₂ is better tolerated and associated with adaptive redox remodeling, with preserved contractile performance that is antagonized by conoidin A-induced inhibition of cytosolic peroxiredoxin activity. These findings demonstrate that the subcellular source of H₂O₂ shapes redox propagation, oxidation patterns, and functional responses, highlighting redox compartmentalization as a determinant of cardiomyocyte performance and stress resilience.

items.title: 4D mitochondrial network assumes distinct and predictive phenotypes through human lung and intestinal epithelial development
items.abstract: Abstract Mitochondria form dynamic three-dimensional networks that exhibit a wide range of morphology and motility depending on cell state, cell type, and cell fate. Isolated phenotypes have been described for individual cell states, but how mitochondrial morphology and motility change across the full course of human tissue development has so far been unclear. Human stem cell-derived branching lung and intestinal organoids mimic developing human organs and make these systems accessible. Here we show, by imaging at key developmental time points from human stem cell through mature organoid tissue with lattice light-sheet microscopy, that mitochondrial networks adopt morphology and motility signatures that vary with developmental stage, that mitochondrial and cellular features can be used to predict developmental stage, and that two-dimensional measurements obscure features resolved only in three dimensions over time, yielding an integrated map of mitochondrial phenotypes across human tissue development.

items.title: Population-level characterisation of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites
items.abstract: Abstract Bacteriophages, viruses infecting bacteria, are abundant in the human gut, but their population-level structure and metabolic associations remain unclear Here we present a foundational characterisation of the gut phageome using deep shotgun metagenomic data in a large population-based cohort ( n = 1,069: TwinsUK). We assembled 116,740 non-redundant vOTUs of which 52.9% were predicted to be temperate and 47.0% virulent. Individuals harboured an average of 3,370 vOTUs, mostly at low abundances, exhibiting structured population-level co-abundance patterns with bacterial species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Blautia wexlerae . Phageome diversity was mostly driven by environmental factors, with modest heritable components. We detected 4 significant vOTU diet associations. Additionally, 6,572 phages were associated with short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, identifying extensive population-level associations between phage-associated genomic variation and microbial metabolites. Over 100 vOTUs encoded auxiliary metabolic genes, while a distinct subset of phages encoded virulence-associated genes, including vacuolating autotransporter toxin (vat) and LPS glucosyltransferases (gtrA, gtrB, gtr) implicated in O-antigen modification and immune invasion, and showed consistent co-abundance patterns with bacterial species previously associated with opportunistic or pathobiont features. These results identify structured population-level associations between phage-associated genomic elements, bacterial communities, and microbial metabolites, motivating future experimental and mechanistic studies.

items.title: Lysine-R2HGylation-C5 identified as a post-translational modification in R2HG-elevated cancers
MyoGen: unified biophysical modeling of human neuromotor activity and resulting signals
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Engineering, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany. alessandro.del.vecchio@fau.de.
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding human motor control requires integrating cortical and spinal activity, muscle mechanics, and electrophysiology, which are typically studied in isolation. We present MyoGen, an open-source framework that unifies spinal circuitry, proprioceptive feedback, musculotendon dynamics, and multimodal electromyography generation. Using data-driven optimization benchmarked against human motor unit recordings, MyoGen produces motor unit population activity matching experimental discharge-rate distributions and variability across muscles. The framework generates decomposable surface and intramuscular electromyography, reproduces beta-band modulation of descending drive and its transformation into force, and implements key sensorimotor loop components. Dimensionality reduction of simulated agonist-antagonist electromyography reveals low-dimensional control manifolds consistent with recordings from able-bodied individuals and those with spinal cord injury. Here, we show that MyoGen provides a physiologically grounded simulation substrate, enabling systematic investigation of motor control principles, benchmarking of signal-processing algorithms, and exploration of experimentally inaccessible sensorimotor interactions.

items.title: Full-circle polychromatic photoluminescence in Mn-doped zero-dimensional metal halide under high-pressure
Constructing radiative dipolar excitons via frontier-state hybridization in 2D perovskites
items.abstract: Abstract Realizing dipolar excitons that simultaneously exhibit strong optical activity and long-range repulsive interactions remains a central challenge in exciton-based nonlinear optics. This challenge stems from the intrinsic trade-off between achieving spatial charge separation, which is necessary for dipole formation, and maintaining sufficient wavefunction overlap to ensure efficient radiative recombination. Here, we overcome this trade-off in the two-dimensional perovskite (AE3T)PbI 4 by leveraging organic-inorganic band-edge engineering to induce frontier-state hybridization, thereby forming bright hybridized dipolar excitons with spatially indirect character and appreciable optical transition strength. These excitons combine an out-of-plane permanent electric-dipole component, room-temperature nonlinear transport consistent with long-range dipole–dipole repulsion, and finite optical transition dipole moments. Beyond addressing a key constraint in dipolar-exciton design, this work establishes frontier-state hybridization as a molecular design principle for constructing optically active, electrically polarized excitons in low-dimensional quantum materials.

items.title: Gut microbiota GABA regulation by intestinal pH osmolality and microbial consumption
items.abstract: Abstract The production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) by the gut microbiota has garnered attention due to its potential role as a driver of gut-brain axis signaling. However, mechanisms regulating microbiota-derived GABA under physiological conditions remain unclear. Here, we identified low pH and high osmolality as promoters of GABA production in the gut microbe Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron by driving changes in the expression of the glutamate decarboxylase system. pH also emerged as a critical factor for enhancing GABA production in a broader set of gut microbes. However, in the cecal microbiota of specific pathogen-free mice and in an ex vivo model of the human colon microbiota, GABA levels did not increase under physiologically relevant acidic conditions. This can partly be explained by microbial GABA consumption. Consistently, reducing cecal pH increased GABA levels in Oligo-MM 12 mice, a gnotobiotic model lacking GABA-consuming gut microbes. Our findings highlight the intricate balance between gut microbial GABA production, consumption, and environmental factors such as pH and osmolality.

items.title: In vivo dynamics of ovulation and oocyte entrance into the oviduct in mice
Directly visualizing the energy level structure of quantum dot molecules
items.abstract: Abstract The orbital, spin and valley degrees of freedom in silicon quantum dots (QDs) support many modes of spin qubit operation. However, it is generally challenging to probe the energy level spectrum over a large parameter space. We demonstrate a spectroscopic technique capable of mapping the energy level structure of a double quantum dot as a function of level detuning, interdot tunnel coupling, and magnetic field. In the one-electron regime, we directly observe the transition from the atom-like energy levels of isolated QDs to molecular-like bonding and anti-bonding states with increasing interdot tunnel coupling. We also resolve the Zeeman splitting of ground and excited valley states in a magnetic field. In the two-electron regime, we gain access to the detuning dependent singlet-triplet splitting. Our work may be extended to a broader class of systems, such as strong spin-orbit materials or proximitized QDs, allowing the direct extraction of various energy gaps.

items.title: Hydroxyl-mediated oxygen anchoring steers CO electroreduction toward ethanol
Leveraging sequence purification for accurate prediction of multiple conformational states with AlphaFold2
items.abstract: Abstract AlphaFold2 (AF2) has transformed protein structure prediction by harnessing co-evolutionary constraints embedded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). MSAs not only encode static structural information, but also contain evolutionary signatures linked to protein dynamics and conformational heterogeneity, which are central to biological function. However, the subtle co-evolutionary signals that bias proteins toward distinct conformational states are often obscured by noise within MSA data and remain challenging to decipher. Here, we introduce AF-ClaSeq, a systematic framework that enriches and purifies state-specific evolutionary signals through iterative sequence classification and selection. By identifying sequence subsets that preferentially encode distinct conformational states, AF-ClaSeq enables robust predictions of alternative conformations across diverse protein systems. Our findings indicate that the accuracy of alternative-state prediction depends more on the purity of the evolutionary signal within an MSA than on sequence depth. Notably, purified sequences encoding specific structural states are distributed across phylogenetic clades and superfamilies, rather than being confined to individual lineages. By extending AF2 beyond single-state structure prediction, AF-ClaSeq provides a promising approach for exploring protein structural plasticity, establishing a foundation for future studies of the sequence determinants underlying conformational switching and allosteric regulation.

items.title: Stepwise transitions unlock three spin states and diverse SHG in a polar Fe(III) spin-crossover complex
items.abstract: Abstract Multifunctional spin-crossover materials are promising for information storage and nonlinear optics, yet stepwise spin-crossover coupled with controllable second harmonic generation switching is hindered by poor thermal stability of non-centrosymmetric lattices. Herein, we report an air-stable polar Fe(III) spin-crossover complex displaying cooling-induced two-step spin-crossover but one-step transition during heating, delivering a wide thermal hysteresis of 75 K (199 K cooling / 274 K heating) via intense intermolecular cooperativity. Sequential phase evolution ( P 1 → P 1 → Pn ) creates three discrete spin configurations with c -axis cell duplication followed by a symmetry-increasing transition to full low-spin phase upon cooling. Second harmonic generation tests verify three separable nonlinear optical states consistent with magnetic responses. Crystal stacking analysis and density functional theory calculations validate that spin ordering-phase transition synergy rearranges molecular dipoles to realize stepwise second harmonic generation modulation. This study offers an original route toward dual spin-optic functional materials for optical storage applications.

items.title: Forced displacement is associated with health service delivery disruption beyond the effects of armed conflict
Facet-dependent anion adsorption for electrolyte-Cu interfacial stability in initially anode-free Li-metal batteries
Improving molecular property prediction with score-based diffusion models
items.abstract: Abstract We explore diffusion-based training as a flexible approach to molecular property prediction in settings shaped by chemical, biophysical, and latent heterogeneity. To address this, we build on score-based generative diffusion models and introduce a conditional diffusion module for predictive tasks, equipped with a joint training and sampling guidance scheme and an optional gated residual mechanism that regulates feature- vs target-driven information flow across noise levels. The module acts as a plug-in learning block for existing molecular encoders, making it complementary to advances in representation learning. Across diverse feature extractors and graph neural networks, diffusion-based training improves over conventional maximum-likelihood objectives on small-molecule regression benchmarks and matches or exceeds strong baselines on multitask regression and classification datasets. It also produces well-calibrated predictive uncertainty as measured by prediction interval coverage, enables confidence-guided ranking, and performs well in challenging settings including activity cliffs and class-imbalanced multitask prediction. Overall, these results position diffusion as a promising representation-agnostic approach for effective molecular property prediction.

items.title: RSM01, an extended half-life RSV monoclonal antibody with a high barrier to in vitro resistance
items.abstract: Abstract Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial infant morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). RSM01 is a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody (mAb) in development for LMICs. In vitro generation of RSM01 resistant mutants has previously been unsuccessful. We systematically assessed the in vitro resistance barrier of RSM01 and the susceptibility of a panel of global contemporary strains to RSM01. Monoclonal antibody resistant mutants (MARMs) were generated by serially passaging triple plaque-purified RSV-A2 and RSV-B1 using HEp-2 cells under pressure from RSM01, nirsevimab, or palivizumab, followed by phenotypic and genotypic characterisation. Moderate resistance was defined as > 3-fold and high resistance as > 30-fold increase in IC 50 compared with parental virus. The susceptibility of contemporary global clinical strains to RSM01 was tested in a neutralisation assay. RSV-A and B strains developed high resistance to palivizumab and nirsevimab, while RSM01 pressure induced moderate resistance. No MARMs demonstrated a fitness advantage. RSM01 neutralised global contemporary strains. In conclusion, in vitro RSM01 resistance was infrequent and moderate and RSM01 had broad activity against circulating strains. The confirmation of the high barrier to resistance of RSM01 is encouraging and provides an alternative should resistance emerge with widespread use of current licensed anti-RSV mAbs.

items.title: Single-cell mass accumulation reveals copiotrophic bacterial growth rates in native seawater
Encapsulating an iron complex within a heme and anthraquinone codecorated capsule for multiphoton C(sp3)−H bond oxygenation
Phenotypic discovery of GABAA receptor-mediated general anesthetics with analgesic activity
items.abstract: Abstract General anesthetics are essential for invasive medical procedures; however, there remains a need for safer agents. Using a bespoke 96-well-plate format platform enabling high-throughput imaging of larval zebrafish behavior, we screen 12,000 compounds and identify an isoxazole chemotype that phenocopies the intravenous anesthetics etomidate and propofol. Its optimization via medicinal chemistry yields an anesthetic that we call nidradine. This anesthetic is efficacious in both zebrafish and mice and lacks the problematic adrenal suppression characteristic of etomidate. Mechanistic studies using electrophysiology and structural biology reveal that nidradine, like etomidate and propofol, is a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA A receptor. Remarkably, behavioral assays in mice demonstrate that nidradine differs from most general anesthetics in that it also produces analgesia at subsedative doses.

items.title: Upcycling of polyolefin and polyester mixtures via a single-atom alloy
Ligand-Mediated Long-Range Interactions Enable Selective Activation of H2O2 for Efficient Water Decontamination
EpiPack: A computational framework for reference mapping and out-of-reference detection for single-cell ATAC-seq data with heterogeneous peak features
Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths
Distinct prelimbic microcircuits control sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Pharmacology, Heidelberg University, Heidelberg, Germany. rohini.kuner@pharma.uni-heidelberg.de.
items.abstract: The microcircuit mechanisms underlying deactivation and altered output of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a common feature of several chronic pain conditions, are poorly understood. Here, using unbiased in vivo longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the mouse prelimbic cortex (PrL), we show that nerve injury induces sensitization of all classes of GABAergic interneurons and a phenotypic switch from unimodal to polymodal responses. Through circuit interrogation, we identified functions for caudal geminal eminence-derived Prox1+ interneurons and revealed that distinct classes of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in the PrL have different functions in promoting neuropathic pain. In addition, we show that the sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain engaged two distinct microcircuits, PV+-Rbp4+ neurons and Prox1+-Cux2+/Ntsr1+ neurons, respectively, to control distinct projection outputs. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for how mPFC guides actions to avoid or overcome pain and how prefrontal deactivation exacerbates neuropathic pain.

items.title: The Drosophila melanogaster Genetic Reference Panel version 3
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute for Human Genetics, Greenwood SC 29646 and Department of Genetics and Biochemistry, Clemson University, Clemson, SC 29634, USA. Electronic address: tmackay@clemson.edu.
items.abstract: Drosophila melanogaster is a leading animal model for biomedical research and quantitative, population, and evolutionary genetics and genomics. The D. melanogaster Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP), containing ∼200 inbred strains with full genome sequences, is a publicly available resource for genome-wide association (GWA) analyses of quantitative traits, systems genetics, and population genomic analyses. Here, we describe the DGRP version 3 (DGRP3), consisting of full genome sequences from >1,000 inbred lines. The DGRP3 harbors extensive genetic diversity, with 8,760,339 molecular polymorphisms including single-nucleotide polymorphisms, insertions, deletions, inversions, tandem duplications, and complex rearrangements. We identified putative damaging variants, loss-of-function genes, and mitochondrial haplotype groups and quantified the microbial composition and numbers of sensory bristles for the DGRP3 lines. We performed GWA analyses for host control of the microbiome composition and sensory bristle numbers, identifying candidate variants and genes for each. The accompanying online tool implements GWA mapping for users' DGRP3 data.

items.title: Condensates increase the frequency of transcription
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Nuclear Organization, Cecil H. and Ida Green Center for Reproductive Biology Sciences, Division of Basic Research, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Department of Molecular Biology, Hamon Center for Regenerative Science and Medicine, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA. Electronic address: benjamin.sabari@utsouthwestern.edu.
items.abstract: While biomolecular condensates have been implicated in activating transcription, investigating the specific contributions of condensates relative to soluble proteins has been challenging. Here, we leverage the concentration dependence of condensate formation to compare the transcriptional activity of condensed and soluble MYOCD, a cell-type-specific transcriptional coactivator. Using single-cell resolution measurements, we find that cells with MYOCD condensates have more target gene transcripts than cells with soluble MYOCD. While transcription can occur in the absence of condensates, it is less frequent and produces fewer transcripts. Both the frequency of active cells and transcriptional output per cell within a heterogeneous population increase sharply above concentration thresholds that promote condensate formation. Mutants that alter the concentration threshold for condensate formation correspondingly shift the MYOCD concentration at which transcription increases. We propose that condensates enhance transcription by coordinating the multiple steps required for gene activation, making an otherwise infrequent event more common.

items.title: The NADHX epimerase NAXE governs PARP1-DNA retention to maintain poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation homeostasis
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Gastrointestinal Translational Research, Peking University Cancer Hospital, Department of Radiation Medicine, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Peking University International Cancer Institute, Beijing Advanced Center of Cellular Homeostasis and Aging-Related Diseases, Institute of Advanced Clinical Medicine, State Key Laboratory of Molecular Oncology, Peking University Health Science Center, Beijing 100191, China; Department of Urology, Peking University First Hospital, Beijing 100034, China. Electronic address: wangjd@bjmu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: PARP1 is a crucial enzyme involved in DNA-damage repair and other biological processes through poly(ADP-ribose) modification (PARylation), but persistent activation can trigger parthanatos. Despite extensive research, the precise mechanisms governing PARP1 activity remain elusive. Here, through multiple CRISPR-Cas9 screens, we identified NAXE, an NADH hydrate (NADHX) epimerase, as a key regulator of PARP1 activity homeostasis. We show that NADHX inhibits PARP1-DNA binding, while NAXE lowers NADHX levels to promote PARP1 recruitment and DNA repair. PARP1 activation, in turn, induces PARylation that binds and inhibits NAXE, forming a negative feedback loop that restrains PARP1 aberrant activation. Notably, knockout of NAXE in mice and C. elegans disrupts PARylation homeostasis, leading to sustained DNA damage and PARP1 activation, ultimately resulting in parthanatos-driven catastrophic neural injury. These findings uncover a metabolite-mediated feedback mechanism that preserves PARylation homeostasis and highlight NAXE as a potential therapeutic target in PARP1-related neurological disorders.

items.title: An image-based CRISPR screen reveals RNA processing control of HP1α condensates
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Genetics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA. Electronic address: ssanulli@stanford.edu.
items.abstract: Heterochromatin protein 1α (HP1α) is a core component of heterochromatin, forming subnuclear condensates whose regulation and function remain poorly understood. Although RNA has been implicated in heterochromatin organization, how RNA influences HP1α localization remains unclear. Here, we develop an image-based CRISPR screening platform to systematically identify regulators of HP1α condensates and identify RNA processing as a central pathway. Perturbations that disrupt RNA processing increase HP1α-RNA interactions and reduce its association with chromatin, leading to loss of silencing. These findings establish RNA processing as a post-transcriptional mechanism that regulates HP1α localization and heterochromatin by altering the composition and nuclear distribution of HP1α-associated RNAs. More broadly, our work reveals functional crosstalk between RNA processing and chromatin organization, providing a framework for how RNA metabolism can influence nuclear architecture and gene regulation.

items.title: Oncogenic histone hyperacetylation drives acute myeloid leukemia through enforced transcription initiation of leukemogenic genes
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Cell and Molecular Biology, The Institute of Cancer Research, London SW3 6JB, UK. Electronic address: alex.radzisheuskaya@icr.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Histone acetylation is tightly correlated with active transcription, yet its causal roles and downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Chromosomal translocations generating fusion proteins involving histone acetyltransferases (HATs) represent a powerful but underexplored system to dissect how dysregulated acetylation rewires transcriptional control. Here, we establish an endogenous mouse model of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) driven by a fusion between two HATs, KAT6A and p300, generated through CRISPR-mediated chromosomal rearrangement. KAT6A-p300 induces aggressive, transplantable AML and confers oncogene addiction. Mechanistically, the fusion establishes broad promoter-associated hyperacetylated domains. This hyperacetylation promotes recruitment and remodeling by the canonical BAF complex, increasing promoter accessibility and stimulating RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription initiation. Fusion formation also redistributes wild-type p300, broadens its chromatin occupancy, and stabilizes its association with fusion-bound loci. Together, our findings establish histone hyperacetylation as a driver of transcription and reveal a direct mechanistic link between aberrant acetylation, chromatin remodeling, and leukemogenesis.

items.title: Dissecting the molecular machinery of CRISPR-associated transposons
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA; Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA. Electronic address: lchang18@purdue.edu.
items.abstract: CRISPR-associated transposons (CASTs) are naturally occurring mobile genetic elements that combine programmable RNA-guided DNA recognition with transposase-mediated integration, enabling site-selective insertion of kilobase-scale DNA without nuclease-induced double-strand breaks. Current structural and biochemical knowledge can be viewed in terms of three functional modules: the transposase module, which performs DNA cleavage and strand transfer; the AAA+ ATPase TnsC, which forms a recruitment and regulatory platform; and TnsD or CRISPR effector-TniQ targeting complexes, which position this platform at selected DNA sites. Here, we synthesize recent structural and biochemical advances in target recognition, recruitment, donor-end pairing, and strand transfer. Comparisons with Tn7 and phage Mu highlight conserved transposase and ATPase functions and system-specific differences in how these components are organized and regulated. We discuss the implications of these advances for engineering programmable DNA-insertion systems and highlight unresolved questions in CAST transposition.

items.title: A cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas reveals intra- and intercellular signaling in Alzheimer’s disease
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Structural Biology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis, TN 38105, USA; Department of Developmental Neurobiology, St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, Memphis, TN 38105, USA. Electronic address: junmin.peng@stjude.org.
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) arises from pathological interactions among diverse brain cell types, but cell-type-specific proteomic changes remain underexplored. Here, we present deep proteomic profiling of sorted or proximity-labeled brain cells from AD mouse models (5xFAD and AppNL-G-F) at multiple ages, quantifying 13,411 proteins in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and neurons, with additional spatial information. We identified 3,028 differentially abundant proteins, most of which were absent in a bulk proteomic dataset, and constructed cell-type-specific networks to define functional modules and hub proteins. Comparison with transcriptomic data revealed that ∼30% of proteomic changes are RNA discordant. Further analyses uncovered cross-cell-type signaling proteins conserved in human AD brains, such as pleiotrophin (Ptn), which is transcriptionally enriched in astrocytes but accumulates in microglia. Importantly, recombinant PTN activates human induced microglia (iMG) cells. Thus, these findings provide a comprehensive cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas of AD models, highlighting novel intra- and intercellular signaling events.

items.title: Noncoding functions of FMR1 transcript in riboregulation of human neurodevelopment
items.last_author_affiliation: Waisman Center, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI 53705, USA; Department of Neuroscience, School of Medicine and Public Health, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, 53705, USA. Electronic address: xinyu.zhao@wisc.edu.
items.abstract: The noncoding functions of protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are largely ignored. Here, we demonstrate an unexpected noncoding role of FMR1 mRNA in human neurodevelopment. A loss of FMR1 and its protein product, fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP), leads to the neurodevelopmental disorder fragile X syndrome (FXS). Neurons derived from FXS patients display hyperexcitability and immature morphology, whereas FMRP knockout (FMRP-KO) neurons that retain FMR1 transcript expression do not. Multi-omics analyses reveal key metabolic differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. Although both FXS and FMRP-KO neurons exhibit reduced mitochondrial respiration, only FXS neurons exhibit elevated glycolysis. We further discover that the FMR1 transcript riboregulates the levels of the glycolytic enzyme lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) by inhibiting the binding of LDHA mRNA to insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (IGF2BP2). Finally, the FMR1 transcript, independent of FMRP, rescues glycolytic and cellular deficits of FXS neurons. Together, these results suggest that FMR1 is a dual-function RNA in human neurodevelopment.

items.title: Professional bodies: How best to promote and support individuals working in human genetics and genomics
Human astrocyte aging couples chromatin closure to focal G-quadruplex accumulation
Integrating hyperspectral phenomics and genome-wide association analysis reveals a ribosome assembly factor regulating wheat grain protein content under drought stress
STRUCT: a statistical approach to detect conserved RNA secondary structures from raw sequencing data without multiple sequence alignment
items.abstract: Abstract Covariation among orthologous sequences is an established evolutionary signal of conserved RNA secondary structures. We present STRUCT (Statistical Testing of RNA Units with Covariation Traits), a covariation-based statistical test that applies to raw sequencing data, bypassing assembly and multiple sequence alignment required by existing covariation methods. Simulations demonstrate false discovery rate control and high power under matched model assumptions. STRUCT rediscovers known HIV structural elements in provirus sequences, identifies conserved rRNA structures, and prioritizes putative viral RNA structures in metatranscriptomics samples. STRUCT offers a novel approach for high-throughput detection of conserved RNA structures and hypothesis generation for viral discovery.

items.title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
Pennycress population genomics reveals a complex global expansion history and local climate-adaptation targets for neodomestication
items.abstract: Abstract Background Field pennycress ( Thlaspi arvense ) is an emerging winter oilseed crop whose life cycle fits between corn-soybean rotations, yielding animal feed and feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel. Results Here we analyze the largest pennycress panel assembled to date, 739 natural accessions spanning four continents, combining genome-wide diversity analysis with multi-year field evaluation. Our genomic data support that pennycress originated in Eurasia and likely underwent a complex history involving multiple introductions and admixture. Scans for selective sweeps among populations between Eurasian and North American identify phenology-related genes, including the MADS-Affecting Flowering ( MAF ) transcription factors and the seed-dormancy gene DELAY OF GERMINATION 1 ( DOG1 ), suggesting possible targets of phenological adaptation. By cross-species climate genome-wide association studies, we detect 10 syntenic peaks, suggesting partly conserved molecular machinery underlying climate adaptation in Arabidopsis and pennycress. Multi-year, multi-location field trials of over 400 accessions in Illinois identify a significant locus associated with green canopy cover, a trait important for biomass, containing a tandem array of Mitochondrial Transcription Termination Factor ( mTERF5 ) genes. Finally, the field trials reveal significant genotype-by-environment interaction, underscoring the need for regional breeding programs. Conclusions Together, these results document worldwide patterns of genetic variation and candidate climate-adaptive genes that can accelerate the neodomestication of pennycress for cultivation in the midwestern United States.

items.title: Osteoclasts Restrict Antitumor Immunity in Dural Metastases
A comprehensive proteogenomic, immunopeptidomic, and metabolomic atlas decodes immunogenicity in cutaneous melanoma
items.last_author_affiliation: National Cancer Institute 36
items.abstract: Abstract Cutaneous melanoma exhibits strong responses to immunotherapy, yet the system-level mechanisms linking mutational burden, genomic alterations, antigen landscapes, post-transcriptional and post-translational regulation, and immune outcomes remain incompletely defined. We profiled 183 cutaneous melanomas using 13 omic layers, including immunopeptidomics, metabolomics, protein ubiquitylation and glycosylation, to construct a holistic view of tumor immunogenicity. Mass spectrometry-based HLA-I immunopeptidomics revealed correlation between tumor antigens and CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Metabolomics revealed distinct ether-linked lipids and mitochondrial metabolic profiles between primary and metastatic tumors. Ubiquitylomics uncovered a subset of tumors associated with worse survival, characterized by high ubiquitylation of the IFN signaling pathway and ubiquitylation-dependent activation of AKT1. Glycoproteomic analyses identified GPNMB glycosylation as a key feature associated with sex-specific survival, linking this signal to a lysosome-associated program and suggesting potential sex-dependent differences in immunotherapy response. This multi-omic atlas of cutaneous melanoma illuminates mechanisms of immune evasion, informing treatment-relevant patient stratification in melanoma care.

items.title: Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity in Children 6 to <12 Years of Age
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, University Medical Center Ulm, Ulm, Germany; DZKJ, partner site Ulm, Ulm, Germany
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Childhood obesity is a chronic, neurometabolic disease with limited options for medical treatments that are efficacious and durable. Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide is approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents and adults, but data for its use in young children are lacking. METHODS: We conducted a phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity. Participants were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or placebo for a period of 104 weeks, after which participants stopped taking semaglutide or placebo for a 7-week washout period. Both groups received counseling for lifestyle modification. The primary end point was the percent change in the body-mass index (BMI; the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) from baseline to week 68. The confirmatory secondary end point was a reduction in BMI category at week 68. RESULTS: Among 167 children who underwent randomization, 112 were assigned to receive semaglutide and 55 to receive placebo. At week 68, the mean percent change in BMI was -13.5% with semaglutide and 2.7% with placebo (estimated between-group difference, -16.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -19.4 to -12.9; P<0.001). The percent change in BMI at week 104 was -9.4% with semaglutide and 8.4% with placebo (between-group difference, -17.8 percentage points; 95% CI, -22.2 to -13.3). At week 68, a reduction in BMI category had occurred in 79% of the participants in the semaglutide group and in 23% of those in the placebo group (odds ratio, 7.8; 95% CI, 3.5 to 17.6; P<0.001), with the BMI below the threshold for obesity (the 95th percentile for age and sex) in 38% of the participants who received semaglutide and in 2% of those who received placebo. Adverse events occurred in 96% of the participants receiving semaglutide and in 93% of those receiving placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most common, occurred more frequently with semaglutide than with placebo, and led to discontinuation in 1 participant in the semaglutide group. CONCLUSIONS: Among children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity, treatment with semaglutide for 68 weeks resulted in a significantly greater mean percent reduction in BMI than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; STEP Young ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05726227.).

items.title: Comparison of high-throughput plasma proteomic platforms in a multi-ethnic Asian cohort.
items.last_author_affiliation: Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore. nilanjana.sadhu@ntu.edu.sg.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Population-scale proteomics is driving precision medicine by enabling systematic drug target identification and robust biomarker discovery. Comparable, well-powered studies across diverse global populations are essential to elucidate shared and population-specific disease pathways. Mass-spectrometry-based and multiplexed affinity-based assays have emerged as complementary, leading strategies for quantifying proteomic variation in large-scale population-based studies. With the objective of performing a comprehensive comparative evaluation of the latest assays for each of these technologies, we compare three leading affinity-based and mass-spectrometry-based proteomic platforms (SomaScan11K, Olink Explore HT, Orbitrap Astral with Seer Proteograph [MS-Seer]) in a multi-ethnic Asian cohort, to inform biomarker discovery and functional genomic studies of global populations. RESULTS: We find limited overlap of 1,740 proteins out of 12,825 total proteins quantified across the three platforms, with modest correlations (0.34-0.10). SomaScan had lower missingness (< 1%) and CV (< 10%), compared to Olink (51%, 23%) and MS-Seer (12%, 19%). The new assays in Olink Explore HT (absent in Explore3072) primarily drove its higher missingness and CV. The number of phenotypic associations varies by trait, while the number of genetic associations (cis-pQTLs at P < 5 × 10-8) are similar for Olink and SomaScan. Protein levels differ between ethnicities, with SomaScan identifying more ethnicity-differentiated proteins than Olink. Finally, SomaScan ANML normalization attenuates biologically relevant associations in our study likely reflecting a limitation inherent to sample-level normalization approaches. CONCLUSIONS: These findings underscore the importance of proteomic platform evaluation and data normalization strategies for application in large-scale, diverse population cohorts.

items.title: Genomic landscapes of natural selection in great apes.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Evolutionary Anthropology, University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria. martin.kuhlwilm@univie.ac.at.; Human Evolution and Archaeological Sciences (HEAS), University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria. martin.kuhlwilm@univie.ac.at.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Great apes are a primate clade with unique biological features. The different species and subspecies have adapted to their respective habitats and followed various evolutionary trajectories influencing their diversity. Hence, studying patterns of natural selection across this clade is an important aspect in understanding their biology. RESULTS: We analyze a curated panel of genomic diversity for bonobos, chimpanzees, eastern and western gorillas, and Bornean and Sumatran orangutans to explore their selection landscapes. A genome-wide screen conducted for recent positive and long-term balancing selection reveals candidate loci potentially related to sensory and immune systems, environmental pressures such as diet or altitude, and reproductive strategies in these species. In addition, the distribution of fitness effects is determined, along with the correlations of distribution of fitness effects across lineages. CONCLUSIONS: We interpret the potential biological meaning of the landscapes of recent positive and long-term balancing selection in our closest living relatives, revealing novel lineage-specific candidate genes and gene categories, as well as recurrent targets across lineages. Our investigation of the deleterious distribution of fitness effects indicates that most non-synonymous mutations fall into either the nearly neutral or strongly deleterious categories, with high correlations between closely related lineages.

items.title: Brassinosteroids improve nitrogen utilization by antagonizing BIN2-mediated SnRK1 activation.
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Life Sciences, The Key Laboratory of Plant Development and Environmental Adaptation Biology, Ministry of Education, Shandong Key Laboratory of Precision Molecular Crop Design and Breeding; Shandong Key Laboratory of Plant Stress Biology and Genetic Improvement, Shandong University, Qingdao, China. baimingyi@sdu.edu.cn.; State Key Laboratory of Microbial Technology, Shandong University, Qingdao, China. baimingyi@sdu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth and development, and is central to increasing crop yield. Brassinosteroids (BRs) and their analogs are widely used in agriculture to enhance crop yields and improve nitrogen utilization, yet the underlying mechanism remains fragmentary. Here, we demonstrate that BR conservatively improves nitrogen utilization by modulating the activity of SnRK1, an evolutionarily conserved regulator balancing carbon and nitrogen metabolism.
