Using Drosophila, we show a novel role for the Ankle2-ballchen (VRK1) pathway in maintaining neuronal resilience and proteostasis. Pan-neuronal and motor neuron reduction of Ankle2 in adult animals shortens lifespan, impairs motor function and accelerates neuronal loss. Lifelong reduction produces more severe phenotypes including an upright wing posture reminiscent of Drosophila Parkinsons disease models. Mechanistically, loss of Ankle2 causes the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins throughout the central nervous system, indicating impaired protein clearance. Ankle2 mutants have reduced proteasome activity with activation of compensatory degradative pathways, supporting this hypothesis. Loss of Ankle2 behavioral and protein accumulation phenotypes are rescued by expression of human ANKLE2, indicating neuronal ANKLE2 function is conserved between flies and humans. Importantly, VRK1/Ballchen reduction also rescues ubiquitin accumulation and behavior phenotypes caused by loss of Ankle2, demonstrating that the developmental Ankle2-VRK1 pathway is preserved and remains functionally important in aged neurons. More broadly, our findings reveal that a conserved developmental ANKLE2- VRK1 pathway is repurposed in aged neurons to maintain proteostasis and neuronal resilience, providing a mechanistic framework linking neurodevelopmental disease genes to age-associated neurodegeneration.

items.title: Gas6 signaling via its cellular receptors is essential for homeostasis in response to endotoxemia and infection
items.corresponding_institution: Bern University Hospital / University of Bern
items.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by infection-induced organ dysfunction and dysregulated host inflammatory responses. Despite advances in supportive care, effective pharmacological therapies remain lacking. Growth arrest-specific protein 6 (Gas6), a vitamin K-dependent ligand of the TAM receptors (Tyro3, Axl, and Mer), operates at the interface of inflammation and coagulation. Here, we investigated the role of Gas6-TAM signaling in endotoxemia and infection in humans and mice. Plasma Gas6 levels increased rapidly during sepsis in patients, during experimental endotoxemia in both humans and mice, and during infection in mice, and these elevations correlated with disease severity and poor clinical outcomes. In both species, circulating Gas6 remained closely balanced with soluble Axl (sAxl), suggesting that much of plasma Gas6 is sequestered in soluble complexes, thereby limiting activation of membrane TAM receptors. In mice, deficiency of Gas6 or individual TAM receptors increased susceptibility to endotoxemia, and Gas6 deficiency additionally heightened vulnerability to bacterial infection. Gas6-deficient mice displayed reduced mean blood pressure, exaggerated cytokine release, altered early leukocyte dynamics, and enhanced macrophage activation. Mechanistically, macrophages secreted Gas6 in response to LPS, and Gas6 acted as an autocrine negative feedback signal limiting inflammatory cytokine production, at least in part through regulation of TLR signaling. Although Gas6 is strongly involved in immune regulation during sepsis, our data do not support a major direct role in coagulation activation. While circulating Gas6 and soluble Mer levels in septic patients were associated with sepsis-induced coagulopathy and impaired thrombin generation, this likely reflects disease severity rather than a causal effect on the coagulation. Consistently, in a murine endotoxemia model, Gas6 deficiency resulted in only minor changes in coagulation markers and did not lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, suggesting that Gas6 primarily reflects systemic inflammation rather than directly driving coagulation abnormalities.

items.title: DNA and H3K4 methylation act cooperatively to protect regulatory elements
items.corresponding_institution: Université Paris Cité, CNRS, Institut Jacques Monod, Paris, France
items.abstract: Histone H3 lysine 4 methylation (H3K4me) is associated with transcriptionally active regulatory elements: H3K4me1 is typically found at enhancers, and H3K4me2/3 at gene promoters. In mammals, the presence of H3K4me can reinforce expression programs, but it might also help protect from epigenetic silencing complexes. To wit, H3K4me antagonizes the binding of the de novo DNA methyltransferase enzymes, which catalyze the repressive 5-methylcytosine (5meC) epigenetic mark. To determine the extent to which H3K4me protects regulatory elements from 5meC deposition - and how this influences genome regulation - we used mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs), which are resilient to the complete absence of 5meC. Employing an inducible dominant negative transgene that globally reduces H3K4me, we assessed the impact in both presence and absence of 5meC. Surprisingly, while ESCs could withstand reduced H3K4me or 5meC, their combined loss led to catastrophic cellular phenotypes in pluripotency and during differentiation. Genomic analyses revealed that H3K4me and 5meC work in concert to protect regulatory elements from Polycomb-mediated silencing. Thus, this work unraveled an unexpected functional cooperation between two epigenetic marks typically viewed as antagonistic in safeguarding transcriptional programs.

items.title: TIP60/KAT5-mediated regulation of apoptotic sensitivity during DNA damage-induced senescence
items.abstract: Cellular senescence and apoptosis are two distinct outcomes to DNA damage. It is unclear what determines the fate decision and the characteristics of senescent cells. Chromatin modifiers are likely candidates, as they can influence the environment for repair of DNA double-strand breaks as well as the transcription of senescent genes. Here we report that the lysine acetyltransferase TIP60/KAT5 is a dosage-sensitive determinant of senescent cell identity in normal human fibroblasts. Although TIP60 is not required for the senescence-associated proliferation arrest of cells after a single dose of 10 Gy of ionising radiation, the resolution of 53BP1 and {gamma}H2AX foci as well as the amplitude of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) as measured by transcript and protein levels of secreted factors is dependent on the levels of TIP60. Furthermore, the sensitivity of senescent cells to apoptosis is also modulated by TIP60 levels. Cells with low levels of TIP60 show reduced p53 output and high levels of the anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and are completely resistant to the senolytic ABT-263. Cells with high levels of TIP60 are modestly more sensitive to ABT-263. These results place TIP60 upstream of the divergence of senescent phenotypes and establish that proliferation arrest and the SASP are uncoupled by the level of a single chromatin modifier. We further identify TIP60 as a candidate determinant of senolytic / senomorphic response and suggest that MCL-1 co-inhibition could be used as a rational addition in contexts where TIP60 levels are low.

items.title: Spindle minus-end microtubule protrusions perturb force balance and delay chromosome segregation
items.abstract: Mitotic spindle function depends on multiple forces that are difficult to measure in cells. In fission yeast, the spindle assembles and elongates within an intact nuclear envelope. Without the kinesin-14/Pkl1, spindle microtubule minus ends detach from the spindle pole body and are pushed beyond it by kinesin-5/Cut7 sliding, forming protrusions that deform the nuclear envelope. We quantified and modeled protrusion dynamics. We found that as protrusions grew, the spindle often shortened, and the extent of shortening correlated with loss of spindle Cut7. Cells with protrusions showed a delay in anaphase onset. A force-balance model can explain fast and slow protrusion length changes, and inferred overlap length at force balance estimated the midzone sliding force density. After laser ablation, severed protrusions retracted and stopped near the cut, consistent with nuclear envelope-driven sliding. The results show the importance of minus-end anchoring for spindle mechanics and how protrusions can probe mechanical coupling between the spindle and nuclear envelope.

items.title: KDM3B enforces a non-mutational ErbB signaling state that sustains cholangiocarcinoma
items.corresponding_institution: Biotech Research and Innovation Centre, Department of Health and Medical Sciences, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.
items.abstract: More than 50% of cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) patients lack druggable mutations, showing broad non-mutational epigenetic perturbations, whose mechanistic insights and clinical benefit remain largely unexplored. Across multiple CCA patient cohorts, we identified prevalent significant upregulation of lysine demethylase (KDM) gene families, with KDM3B emerging as a critical epigenetic dependency for sustaining tumor fitness. KDM3B loss reduced colony formation, proliferation, and migration across intra- and extrahepatic CCA tumor models. Integrated multi-omics linked KDM3B to ErbB activation and downstream PI3K-AKT oncogenic signaling. Mechanistically, KDM3B is bound to the ERBB3 promoter, removing repressive H3K9me2 marks to transcriptionally activate ERBB3, augmenting ErbB receptor activity. Spatial and single cell transcriptomics from patient tumors revealed that high KDM3B-ERBB3 coupling reshapes the tumor niche via enhancing the epithelial-mesenchymal transition crosstalk with neighborhood cells to establish a pro-invasive microenvironment. Pharmacologic inhibition in vivo of the KDM3B downstream ERBB-Akt regulatory axis suppressed CCA xenograft tumor growth. These findings establish KDM3B as a non-mutational epigenetic activator of ErbB-driven signaling, reshaping the tumor ecosystem, and defining the KDM3B-ErbB axis as a vulnerability in CCA.

items.title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark
items.abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front is supported by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.

items.title: Somatic mutation probabilities learned from the DNA sequence
items.abstract: Somatic mutations distribute heterogeneously over genomes, dependent on immediate sequence context, function, and non-genetic factors. Mutations present the foundation for somatic genome evolution towards age-related diseases. Here, we present EAGLE-MUT, a group of DNA language models trained on sparse single base substitution data from esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and melanoma (MELA) samples. In both cancer types, predicted mutation probabilities vary across several orders of magnitude, depending on sequence context. For example, T>G hotspots in EAC localize to A/T-rich ~200 base pair DNA motifs, associated with nucleosome positioning. Coldspots localize to G/C-rich DNA, nucleosome linker DNA, CTCF binding sites, potential origins of replication, and intron-exon boundaries with a transcription strand bias. Fine-tuning EAGLE-MUT for individual patient samples leads to varying mutation distributions relative to genome elements and potential cancer driver mutations. EAGLE-MUT provides new links between DNA sequence, genome function, and stability in individual samples, a foundation for understanding somatic genome evolution, and more personalized strategies for risk-assessment, prevention, and treatment.

items.title: Midkine and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: evidence from Mendelian randomization, multi-omics factor analysis, and single-cell transcriptomics
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal malignancies, in part because its tumor microenvironment actively suppresses antitumor immunity. Midkine (MDK) is a secreted heparin-binding growth factor that is overexpressed in a majority of PDAC tumors, but whether it contributes causally to disease risk and through which cell types it acts have not been firmly established. We combined cis-eQTL Mendelian randomization (GTEx pancreas, n = 328 donors; FinnGen PDAC, 1,252 cases) with multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) of TCGA-PAAD tumors (n = 149), single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), cross-species single-cell RNA sequencing, and DepMap CRISPR dependency screening. Mendelian randomization identified MDK as the only gene passing false discovery rate correction for PDAC risk (inverse-variance-weighted odds ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.19-1.91, p = 6.7 x 10??; FDR = 0.008), with concordant direction across five methods and five independent GWAS. MDK was overexpressed in tumors relative to adjacent normal tissue in an independent cohort (GSE62452, n = 130, p = 5 x 10??), and high expression was associated with shorter overall survival (10.2 versus 21.1 months, p = 0.023). In the MOFA decomposition, MDK localized to a factor characterized by tertiary lymphoid structure gene expression but negative correlation with dendritic cells and macrophages, a pattern consistent with immune exclusion. Single-cell analysis and published functional studies indicated that MDK is produced by cancer-associated fibroblasts and endothelial cells rather than by tumor epithelium, and DepMap data confirmed that MDK is not a cell-autonomous fitness gene. Collectively, these results support a model in which MDK acts through the stromal-immune compartment rather than through tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms, and raise the possibility that MDK blockade could restore antitumor immunity in PDAC.

items.title: One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS): statistical analysis and interpretation of quantitative proteomics data for non-coders
items.abstract: Open-source statistical methods for proteomic differential abundance analysis are well established. Normalization, missing-value handling, and the statistical model must suit the experimental design and change how proteins are called. Together with the frequent need for data reformatting, coding and bioinformatics expertise, these elements limit the bench scientist's analysis of datasets. Here, we present One Stop MS Shop (OSMSS), a no-code R Shiny application that parses Proteome Discoverer, MaxQuant, FragPipe, DIA-NN or Spectronaut search results for user-driven interactive exploration through transformation and differential analysis. Upon import, OSMSS records the experimental design through user questions, selects the analysis workflow, identifies normalization requirements, runs established statistical methods, and records every analytical step in a case-specific methods text. OSMSS supports label-free data-dependent and data-independent acquisition (DDA, DIA) and tandem mass tag (TMT) group comparisons, affinity-purification comparisons, and DIA and TMT phosphosite analyses. OSMSS runs on local devices or servers and provides volcano plots, heatmaps, trend analysis, kinase prediction, pathway enrichment and kinase activity inference. In seven benchmarks, OSMSS performed comparably to matched reference workflows. OSMSS lets bench scientists apply established statistical models and associated tools transparently and without coding, enabling a more informed analysis of their data.

items.title: MeXalign - A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
items.abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality.

items.title: Marker direction and donor structure alter genetic cell-stateprioritization in endometriosis: convergent evidence from single-cell chromatin
items.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify regions of the genome linked to disease, but they do not tell us which cells are involved. Researchers often address that question by testing marker genes from single-cell atlases. We asked how much the answer changes when those markers are defined differently. Reconstructing a published endometriosis analysis, we found that selecting genes with large fold changes in either direction prioritized venous endothelium, whereas selecting up-regulated genes prioritized decidual stroma (the latter was not significant after within-family false-discovery correction). A calibrated benchmark, six-trait control panel, and donor-level checks showed why neither rule can be trusted on its own. In an independent RNA atlas, stromal programs were repeatedly prioritized, although closely related perivascular states remained plausible. We then examined an independent molecular layer: chromatin accessibility in 36,073 nuclei from 12 endometrial biopsies. The initially specified analysis found enrichment of endometriosis heritability in stromal accessible chromatin (z = 4.11, one-sided p = 2 x 10^-5). In a later, more stringent joint model with baselineLD v2.2, the stromal coefficient remained positive (z = 3.83, p = 6.47 x 10^-5) and exceeded the epithelial coefficient (z = 3.68, p = 1.18 x 10^-4). Both effects remained nominally significant when each biopsy was excluded in turn (12/12 analyses). The association was also seen for leiomyoma, and the endometriosis GWAS share participants. Together, these findings support a broad stromal regulatory context for part of inherited endometriosis risk, but do not establish a unique causal cell state or a lesion cell of origin.

items.title: Flux analysis resolves distinct brain uptake and clearance of TfR- and CD98hc-targeting large molecules
items.abstract: Advances in large-molecule delivery across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) by targeting receptors such as transferrin receptor (TfR) or CD98 heavy chain (CD98hc) are shifting the focus from restricted parenchymal access toward brain exposure profiles tailored to therapeutic needs. However, brain concentrations offer only partial insight into delivery mechanisms, as they reflect the net balance of two dynamic processes: flux of molecules entering and leaving the brain, here termed brain uptake and brain clearance, respectively. Here, we establish a generalizable experimental and mathematical modeling framework to resolve these opposing fluxes and demonstrate its application using pharmacokinetic (PK) data from Fc-engineered antibody transport vehicles (ATVs) targeting TfR or CD98hc in humanized knock-in mouse models. First, to directly estimate brain clearance, we engineered anti-ATV antibodies that selectively bind the TV patch to block receptor-mediated brain uptake in vivo. Integrating these measurements with a mechanistic PK model, we then reconstructed brain fluxes of ATV molecules over time across a broad range of receptor affinities. Results demonstrated that TfR-targeting promotes rapid, affinity-dependent brain uptake accompanied by comparatively rapid brain clearance, whereas CD98hc-targeting results in slower brain uptake and prolonged retention. Extending this framework to dual TfR/CD98hc-targeting ATVs suggested that higher observed brain exposure relative to single-receptor formats does not necessarily translate to greater brain delivery: increased exposure was predicted to arise primarily from reduced brain clearance, associated with CD98hc-mediated retention, rather than enhanced uptake through dual-receptor engagement. Together, these results establish a quantitative basis for resolving brain fluxes and engineering brain-targeted biologics for desired therapeutic outcomes.

items.title: Engineered post-transcriptional regulation of Scn10a by Pumilio ameliorates neuropathic pain in mice
items.abstract: Post-transcriptional control of mRNA permeates biology, yet its contribution to sensory neuron physiology and pain remains unclear. The mammalian Pumilio proteins PUM1 and PUM2 (collectively referred to as PUM) are RNA-binding proteins that bind Pumilio response elements (PREs), typically situated in 3' untranslated regions. PUM recruits the CCR4-NOT complex to promote mRNA deadenylation and decay. Several mRNAs that encode voltage-gated sodium channels that regulate action potential generation in pain sensing neurons harbor PREs. Here, we explored whether PUM plays a role in pain signaling. PUM1 and PUM2 were enriched in TRPV1-positive dorsal root ganglion neurons, where PUM2 physically interacted with Scn9a, Scn10a, and Scn11a transcripts, which encode Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9, respectively. Depletion of PUM in sensory neurons produced mechanical hypersensitivity and enhanced inflammatory pain. These effects were reversed by blocking Nav1.8 but not Nav1.7, raising the possibility that repression of Scn10a by PUM can be harnessed using synthetic biology to diminish neuropathic pain. To this end, we generated a chimera comprising the RNA-binding domain of PUM2 and a repressive domain, which we dubbed "super-PUM". Expression of AAV-encoded super-PUM in sensory neurons reduced Nav1.8 abundance, diminished tetrodotoxin-resistant and suzetrigine-sensitive sodium currents, and prevented mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity following spared nerve injury. These results demonstrate that optimization of an endogenous post-transcriptional regulon provides a means to ameliorate neuropathic pain.

items.title: The social conditioned place preference assay is sensitive to drug dose, training regimen, and social context
items.abstract: Beginning in the 1960s, researchers have understood that one of the unique properties of psychedelic drugs is that their effects are modified by the context in which they are taken (also known as their set and setting dependence). To date, 7 different studies have shown that critical period reopening is a shared property across psychedelic drugs, including ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and ibogaine. Moreover, the context dependence of psychedelics effects has been recapitulated for both MDMA and ketamine. Recently, Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026 (PMID: 42972049) have claimed that psilocybin does not reopen the social reward learning critical period, which the authors interpret as a failure to replicate previously published results. Here, we re-analyzed results across three published datasets (Nardou et al., Nature 2019; Nardou et al., Nature 2023; Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026) in order to compare the impact of dose, training regimen, and social context on the social conditioned place preference (social CPP) assay. Our analysis reveals that methodological modifications likely account for Lu and colleagues inability to reopen the social reward learning critical period with psilocybin. Nevertheless, because their results recapitulate previous findings that psychedelics effects are context dependent, they support rather than challenge the growing literature demonstrating that psychedelics reopen critical periods.

items.title: Inactivation of prenyltransferase inhibitors by S-methylation catalyzed by the methyltransferases TMT1A (METTL7A) and TMT1B (METTL7B)
items.abstract: The thiol methyltransferases TMT1A and TMT1B (formerly METTL7A and METTL7B) metabolize thiol-containing compounds, but their substrate range and effects on drug activity remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated whether these enzymes methylate protein prenyltransferase inhibitors and alter cellular sensitivity to these compounds. Mass spectrometry identified several thiol-containing farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyltransferase inhibitors as substrates of both enzymes, whereas other thiol-containing inhibitors showed no detectable methylation. In HT1080 fibrosarcoma cells, TMT1A or TMT1B overexpression conferred resistance to several geranylgeranyltransferase inhibitors and attenuated drug-induced cell-cycle arrest. Pharmacological inhibition of TMT1A with 2,3-Dichloro--methylbenzylamine (DCMB, LY-78335) reversed resistance and restored cell-cycle arrest in TMT1A-expressing cells. These findings expand the known substrate range of TMT1A and TMT1B and support TMT-dependent methylation as a mechanism that reduces the cellular activity of susceptible prenyltransferase inhibitors.

items.title: A single kindred across centuries: patrilineal continuity and a female-mediated increase in the local genetic component of the Lake Onega area at the Kondopoga cemetery
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Bioengineering, Federal Research Center of Biotechnology
items.abstract: We report the first genome-wide ancient DNA data from a medieval population in the territory of the modern Republic of Karelia, Russia: 1240K capture data for 22 individuals from the Kondopoga cemetery on Lake Onega, a churchyard used from the 12th to the 19th century. Combining relatedness estimates, autosomal and X-chromosomal identity-by-descent, uniparental lineages, burial position and archaeological dating, we place eight individuals in a single pedigree spanning five generations, anchored on a founding couple buried in the highest part of the cemetery. Identity-by-descent links almost all the remaining individuals to that couple, indicating that the sample is not a cross-section of a local population but a single kindred, which is the object of this study. Within it, the founding males paternal lineage recurs from the 12th-13th to the 16th century, mitochondrial lineages differ between individuals of the same generation, and autosomal ancestry shifts between generations rather than between archaeological phases. The ancestry of the founders is closest to populations from northwestern Rus and the eastern Baltic, while the Uralic-related ancestry entering the pedigree is best modelled using present-day Finnic groups of the region. The family was patrilineal, and its profile was reshaped by the women who married into it.

items.title: GRASER: haplotype assignment of graph-aligned short reads
items.abstract: Existing read phasing tools operate on reads aligned to a linear reference, where reference bias reduces the information available for haplotype inference and read assignment. Pangenome graphs reduce reference bias, but reads falling within non-reference sequence cannot be surjected to a linear reference, so phasing after surjection reintroduces that bias. Here we present GRASER, which phases graph-aligned short reads against haplotype paths inferred for each individual, using established graph genotyping and statistical phasing to build those paths. GRASER phase uses edges unique to one haplotype path as evidence, so reads are phased directly from graph alignments without conversion to a linear reference. Against true parental haplotype paths, GRASER assigned 22.6 to 24.5% of simulated fragments to a haplotype, and more than 96% of those were placed on the correct haplotype. Inferred haplotype paths reduced the assignment rate by about 4 percentage points. GRASER assigned more fragments than a WhatsHap-based linear-reference workflow in every configuration tested. Applied to whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, GRASER recovered allele-specific methylation at imprinted loci and measured haplotype-resolved methylation within a structural variant.

items.title: Thermodynamically Constrained Encoding Improves Reliability in DNA Data Storage
items.abstract: Synthetic DNA has emerged as a promising storage medium thanks to its exceptional information density and long-term stability. However, sequence-dependent biochemical properties introduced during the encoding process can significantly affect downstream molecular processing and data recovery. Among these properties, the thermodynamic stability of DNA sequences, commonly quantified by the Folding Gibbs free energy ($\Delta$G), can influence amplification efficiency, sequencing coverage, and ultimately decoding performance. In this work, we experimentally investigate the impact of $\Delta$G constraints applied during the encoding stage on DNA data recovery. We compare the reference JPEG DNA, the future image coding standard on DNA, with a $\Delta$G-constrained variant using the same image encoded into synthetic DNA oligonucleotides. Both configurations were synthesized, amplified, sequenced, and decoded under identical experimental conditions. We analyze the relationship between predicted thermodynamic stability, sequencing coverage, and decoding performance to quantify the influence of sequence thermodynamics on the recovery of encoded information. Our results demonstrate that incorporating $\Delta G$ constraints during encoding substantially reduces the proportion of sequences with highly negative predicted $\Delta G$ values and improves sequencing coverage homogeneity, decreases the number of underrepresented oligonucleotides and dropouts, and consistently reduces the sequencing coverage required for successful decoding across three different synthesis providers, thereby reducing sequencing time. These findings provide experimental evidence that thermodynamic sequence optimization represents an effective design strategy for improving the robustness and efficiency of DNA data storage systems.

items.title: Know Thy Neighbour: Benchmarking Protein Language Model Embedding-Based Annotation Reveals Anisotropy Substantially Impacts Retrieval
items.abstract: Functional annotation using protein language models (`pLMs') usually proceeds by transferring the function of a query's nearest neighbour in a reference database. A major drawback is that embedding-based annotation transfer has no null model, i.e. no accepted way to set a cosine-similarity threshold to control false positives. This contrasts with traditional bioinformatics methods, including sequence- and structure-based alignment tools, which rank hits with E-values derived from explicit null models. Here, we benchmark final-layer, mean-pooled embeddings from twelve models against MMseqs2 and Foldseek for remote-homology retrieval on curated datasets based on Swiss-Prot and SCOPe, fixing per-model thresholds at a 1% false-positive rate and probing the score with a ladder of synthetic decoys. On Swiss-Prot, pLMs without retrieval training recover at most 15% of remote homologs at this operating point, against 85% for MMseqs2, and for the ESM-2 and ESM-C families shuffled decoys have higher cosine similarities to their nearest database hits than real remote homologs do. These two pLM families exhibit extreme anisotropy, using fewer than 15 effective dimensions out of 640-2560, and low effective dimensionality is strongly associated with poor performance across models. Applying ZCA whitening, fit on the reference database, to the embeddings sharply raises threshold-free Top-1 superfamily retrieval, e.g. for ESM-2 650M from 59% to 88% on SCOPe, and generally improves remote homology sensitivity at a fixed false-positive rate. As correcting embedding anisotropy requires only the reference database and is compute cheap, it should be considered and tested for any pLM embedding-based annotation task.

items.title: A marine worm oxygen carrier to improve the quality of preserved tumor samples
items.corresponding_institution: Research Center of the University of Montreal Hospital Center (CRCHUM), QC H2X 0A9, Canada
items.abstract: Biobanked tissue samples are essential for cancer research, yet pre-analytical ischemia-hypoxia during tissue handling can compromise tissue or derived models quality, limiting their value for translational research. Here, we investigated whether M101, an extracellular hemoglobin from Arenicola marina, could mitigate, indirectly by providing oxygen, handling-induced ischemia-hypoxia in cancer tissues and subsequent live 3D models. Using prostate cancer PC3 and ovarian cancer TOV-21G XG preserved ex vivo, M101 reduced the emergence of hypoxia-associated markers, including the hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha, and attenuated metabolic stress. In XG-derived micro-dissected 3D tumor models cultured for 8 days, M101 improved tissue morphology, reduced fragmentation, and was associated with higher proliferative activity and lower inflammatory interleukin-6 release. Together, these findings suggest that M101 helps preserve structural and functional features of biobanked tumor models during ex vivo handling. Thus, oxygen carriers could represent a bio-compatible strategy to improve the fidelity of biobanked samples and patient-derived tumor models for precision oncology applications.

items.title: Geometric analysis of postnatal maturational transformations in brain's functional connectome
items.abstract: Birth marks a profound shift in sensory experience, posing a question: does postnatal brain function represent simply a protracted continuation of prenatal developmental programmes or reflect system-level reconfiguration in response to the demands of the postnatal environment? To answer this, we first characterised functional hierarchies of the newborn human brain, separating sensorimotor from visual, unimodal from associative, and parietal from auditory systems. We then implemented a geometric framework to map global transformations that shape functional connectome hierarchies. We show that greater postmenstrual age at birth was associated with emergence of the frontoparietal and salience networks at the tip of the unimodal-associative hierarchical axis; in contrast, greater postnatal age was associated with increasing polarisation of primary perceptual and sensorimotor systems across functional hierarchies. Sex differences in the neonatal connectome recapitulated patterns associated with postmenstrual age at birth and postnatal age, suggesting more advanced maturation of functional architecture in females than in males. Together, the contrasting effects of prenatal and postnatal age support a model of postnatal reconfiguration of brain function, thereby indicating that birth could mark a transition between distinct modes of the functional organisation.

items.title: Harmonizing amyloid PET tracers at the local level: evaluation of regional Centiloid equations
items.corresponding_institution: Research and Early Development (pRED), Hoffmann-La Roche, Basel, Switzerland
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Centiloid (CL) framework standardizes global amyloid-PET across radiotracers. While global scaling remains essential for participant selection, amyloid-targeting therapies require quantifying localized plaque removal. However, applying global equations regionally introduces systematic bias, particularly in subcortical structures where off-target binding alters non-specific background. METHODS: We extended the Centiloid framework regionally and voxel-wise using GAAIN datasets: Level-1 ([11C]PiB) and Level-2 paired [11C]PiB and fluorinated head-to-head cohorts ([18F]florbetaben, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]flutemetamol, and [18F]NAV4694). Level-1 defines the regional Centiloid scale using region-specific intercepts while fixing the global slope. Level-2 calibrates fluorinated tracer uptake to reference [11C]PiB SUVR using linear equations. We compared three slope-intercept models (Global, Regional-Intercept, and Regional) using information criteria and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). RESULTS: Regional-Intercept model was identified as optimal across all four radiotracers. In neocortical regions, Global and Regional-Intercept models showed high agreement across canonical lobes. In deep gray matter, global equations introduced large systematic offsets, with mean absolute conversion errors in the pallidum reaching 27.7 to 45.6 CL. The Regional-Intercept model eliminated this bias, reducing subcortical MAE on average below 15 CL while preserving a unified biological scale. DISCUSSION: Applying global Centiloid equations directly to regions introduces substantial bias in subcortical regions. With the Regional-Intercept model, the same Centiloid value corresponds to the same amyloid concentration across brain regions and radiotracers. This provides a reliable basis for cross- sectional regional evaluation, multi-tracer cohort pooling, tracking regional clearance, and mapping regional progression in clinical research.

items.title: Schizophrenia-Linked 3q29 Deletion Produces Hyperdopaminergic Signaling in the Dorsal Striatum
items.abstract: Dopamine dysregulation has long been recognized as a central feature of schizophrenia (SZ), yet the mechanisms linking genetic risk to dopaminergic dysfunction remain poorly understood. While pharmacological models have historically been used to induce hyperdopaminergic states and recapitulate select clinical features of SZ, these approaches do not model the underlying disease biology. In contrast, genetically informed models enable investigation of dopaminergic abnormalities as emergent consequences of bona fide disease-associated mechanisms. Here, we examined a mouse model of the 3q29 deletion. In humans, this 1.6 Mb deletion is typically de novo and confers a greater than 40-fold increased risk for SZ, representing the single largest known molecular risk factor for the disorder. Using this model, we identified a robust hyperdopaminergic phenotype characterized by elevated evoked dopamine release selectively within the dorsal striatum. Mechanistically, this phenotype appears to arise from a PKC-mediated reduction in dopamine transporter (DAT) availability, impairing dopamine clearance and prolonging dopaminergic signaling. Together, these results establish a direct link between a high-risk SZ mutation and striatal dopamine dysfunction, while also highlighting PKC-DAT signaling as a potential therapeutic target for treatment-resistant neuropsychiatric symptoms associated with 3q29 deletion.

items.title: Parvalbumin interneuron circuit sharpens orientation tuning via the extraclassical surround in cat V1
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology, School of Medicine, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA
items.abstract: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) inhibitory neurons are central to cortical gain control, yet optogenetic studies disagree on whether they sharpen orientation tuning or merely rescale responses. Because this work has been performed almost exclusively in rodents, which lack orientation columns and an orientation-matched extraclassical surround, the contribution of surround circuitry has remained untested. Here we combine cell-type-specific rabies-virus tracing with optogenetics to activate or suppress PV circuits in cat primary visual cortex, and measure single-neuron orientation tuning for stimuli confined to the classical receptive field or extending into the extraclassical surround. Activating PV circuits sharpened tuning progressively with illumination power for classical-receptive-field stimuli, but left tuning unchanged once the surround was engaged; conversely, suppressing them broadened tuning only for surround-engaging stimuli and left classical-receptive-field tuning unchanged. This double dissociation places PV circuitry in the causal path that sets tuning width and identifies surround suppression as the inhibition it supplies: where the surround is not recruited there is little PV-mediated inhibition to remove, and where it is, removing that inhibition widens tuning. PV-dependent sharpening is therefore bounded by the receptive-field architecture through which the population is recruited, not by a fixed property of the PV population itself.

items.title: Dynamic information sharing across frontal-basal ganglia neurons during cost-benefit decision-making and reward pursuit
items.corresponding_institution: Brain Network Dynamics Unit, Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom.
items.abstract: Cost-benefit decision-making requires animals to integrate prospective rewards with the costs of obtaining them and translate these evaluations into motivated action. How population activity is coordinated across the frontal-basal ganglia network during these processes remains incompletely understood. Here, we recorded simultaneously from the anterior cingulate cortex, medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex, dorsomedial striatum, ventral pallidum and subthalamic area in rats performing a cost-benefit decision task. Using canonical correlation analysis, we identified shared population activity across these anatomically distributed circuits and characterised its dimensionality, task-related information and relationship to behavioural sensitivity. The strength and dimensionality of inter-area coupling varied across task epochs and circuit classes, with frontal-basal ganglia interactions exhibiting particularly high dimensionality during reward pursuit. Shared activity represented reward and time on task (trial count) during decision-making, while movement-related information became increasingly prominent during reward pursuit. These representations also depended on subsequent choice: reward was more strongly represented on accepted trials, whereas time on task was more prominent on rejected trials. The strength of inter-area coupling was further associated with behavioural sensitivity across sessions. Stronger coupling between the subthalamic area and the dorsomedial striatum was associated with reduced reward sensitivity. By contrast, communication between the medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex and dorsomedial striatal was associated with reduced effort aversion. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic, circuit-specific organisation of shared neural activity during cost-benefit behaviour and link inter-area coupling to variation in motivated choice. They suggest that distinct communication pathways may contribute to specific facets of motivated choice, with applications to targeted neuromodulation therapies for disorders of motivation.

items.title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
items.abstract: Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection ({beta} = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection ({beta} = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE ({beta} = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction ({beta} = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

items.title: Synthetic diet feeding exacerbates central nervous system autoimmunity in mice independent of weight gain
items.corresponding_institution: German Rheumatology Research Centre (DRFZ), A Leibniz Institute
items.abstract: Consumption of a nutrient deficient diet high in saturated fats and sugar is associated with the increased incidence and exacerbation of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. Efforts to resolve the molecular mechanisms underlying diet-dependent changes to immune responses rely on the use of synthetic diets in mice, often using a standard laboratory chow as control. Critically, it remains unknown whether synthetic diet specific alterations in nutrient and metabolite availability, independent of weight gain and exposure to dietary fats and sugar, can affect the immune response. We reveal that exposure to a synthetic diet, independent of weight gain, is sufficient to alter the immune response, driving increased severity in the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model of central nervous system (CNS) autoimmunity. Mechanistically, synthetic diet feeding leads to systemic reductions in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) abundance, and supplementation of synthetic diet with butyrate mitigates the excessive production of pathogenic T cells, and ameliorates synthetic diet driven increases in EAE severity. Finally, we identify the presence of peripheral Tregs (pTregs) in the CNS of EAE mice, which can arise from shared clonal ancestors as T helper (Th) cells, and reveal that butyrate supplementation increases the proportion pTregs to Th17 cells during EAE.

items.title: Tryptophan catabolism drives AhR-dependent macropinocytosis and tumorigenesis in tuberous sclerosis complex
items.corresponding_institution: University of New England, College of Osteopathic Medicine
items.abstract: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by hamartomatous tumors of the brain, skin, kidney and lung (lymphangioleiomyomatosis, LAM). TSC and LAM arise from biallelic inactivation of TSC1 or TSC2 which drives metabolic reprogramming, including macropinocytic scavenging of extracellular nutrients. To determine which nutrients sustain macropinocytosis, we measured dextran uptake after repletion of individual essential amino acids. Unexpectedly, only tryptophan (Trp) stimulated uptake in TSC2-deficient cells by 2.8-fold compared to amino acid-free medium (p < 0.0001), with no effect in TSC2-expressing cells. Steady-state metabolomics revealed that Trp supplementation raised intracellular Trp by 3.5-fold and lowered kynurenine by 60%. IDO1 inhibition abolished the response, indicating that Trp catabolism rather than Trp itself is the proximal signal. Interestingly, Ido1, Tdo2 and AhR were markedly upregulated in TSC2-deficient cells, and rapamycin repressed Ido1 and Tdo2 but not AhR. AhR was constitutively nuclear in TSC2-deficient cells, and rapamycin or the AhR antagonist CH-223191 returned it to the cytoplasm. Inhibition of IDO1, (Linrodostat), TDO2 (LM10) or AhR (StemRegenin 1, CH-223191) selectively decreased macropinocytosis and proliferation of TSC2-deficient cells. AhR antagonism also depleted glutathione by 70%. In vivo, StemRegenin 1 and CH-223191 reduced tumor volume by approximately 70% and 90% (p < 0.0001), respectively. Additionally, targeting AhR in the TSC2-deficient tumors strongly decreased mTORC1 activity. Collectively, our data identify a Trp-kynurenine-AhR axis that supports macropinocytosis in TSC2-deficient cells, and suggest AhR antagonists as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of TSC and LAM.

items.title: A chemogenetic light-activatable reactive oxygen species generator for precise cell manipulation
items.abstract: The ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) through illumination of photosensitizers provides a powerful means to manipulate cellular function with high spatial and temporal resolution. Here, we present a chemogenetic light-activatable ROS generator based on the FAST technology. By leveraging the heavy atom effect, we engineered chromophores, called ROSgen, that can both fluoresce and produce ROS when bound to FAST variants and exposed to light. Photosensitization is strictly dependent on the addition of the ROSgen, allowing for on-demand activated and targeted photomanipulation. We demonstrate that this chemogenetic light-activatable ROS generator enables to selectively perturb the function of organelles such as mitochondria, inactivate proteins or induce localized oxidative DNA damage, demonstrating its versatility as molecular tool for manipulating cellular processes with high spatial and temporal control.

items.title: Age-dependent downregulation of endothelial lamin A/C impairs mechanotransduction and promotes cardiovascular disease
items.corresponding_institution: Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares (CNIC), Madrid, Spain; CIBERCV, Instituto de Salud Carlos III, Madrid, Spain
items.abstract: Aims: Aging is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated age-associated changes in endothelial lamin A/C expression and the contribution of endothelial lamin A/C loss to cardiovascular dysfunction and disease. Methods and Results: Aging was associated with reduced endothelial lamin A/C expression in human coronary arteries and mouse aorta and heart. We generated an inducible endothelial-specific Lmna knockout mouse model on an atheroprone Ldlr-null background (LmnaKOiEC), which exhibited a 14.6% reduction in median survival. Vascular and cardiac phenotypes were evaluated using vascular reactivity assays, magnetic resonance imaging, blood pressure measurements, echocardiography, histology, nitric oxide assays, and biochemical analyses. LmnaKOiEC mice exhibited increased atherosclerotic burden, impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation, vascular hyperpermeability, arterial stiffening, and hypertension. They also displayed increased cardiac mass, elevated NT-proBNP levels, incipient myocardial fibrosis, and signs of increased cardiac filling pressures despite preserved systolic function, resembling early stages of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Cardiac proteomics revealed inflammatory, profibrotic, and metabolic remodeling, with enrichment of molecular signatures associated with human HFpEF. Mechanistically, aortic single-cell transcriptomics revealed endothelial activation and suppression of the flow-responsive KLF2-NOS3 pathway. Consistently, endothelial lamin A/C deficiency reduced aortic nitric oxide production ex vivo, while siRNA-mediated LMNA knockdown impaired shear stress-induced KLF2 and NOS3 expression in human aortic endothelial cells. Conclusion: These findings identify age-associated endothelial lamin A/C downregulation as a previously unrecognized contributor to cardiovascular aging and disease, and suggest preservation of endothelial nuclear mechanotransduction as a potential therapeutic strategy. Translational Relevance: Our findings identify age-associated endothelial lamin A/C downregulation as a previously unrecognized contributor to cardiovascular aging, linking impaired nuclear mechanotransduction to age-related endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular pathologies, including atherosclerosis, hypertension, and cardiac alterations resembling early HFpEF. These results highlight endothelial lamin A/C and downstream flow-responsive KLF2-NOS3 signaling as potential targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving endothelial function and mitigating age-related cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Catch*ReSeq resolves rare splice isoforms and their host cell states at single-cell resolution
items.abstract: Alternative splicing diversifies the transcriptome and shapes cell fate across development, tissue function, and disease. Single-cell RNA sequencing can link isoforms to cell states, but these methods often lack the throughput and coverage to accurately call splice variants. As a result, rare isoforms are often missed, especially in underrepresented cell types. Here, we present Catch*ReSeq, a targeted enrichment method that yields isoform-resolved readouts linked to host transcriptomes from standard single-cell libraries for the capture of rare isoforms. We found more oligo(dT)-primer cDNA originating from internal A-rich sequences than from terminal polyA tails (80-fold enrichment for simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) and over 6-fold for host transcripts), fracturing cDNA and obscuring isoforms. Catch*ReSeq exploits this fracture to infer each molecule's isoform of origin. In SIV-infected macaque CD4+ T cells, Catch*ReSeq detected up to 13 times as many infected cells as standard 10X and resolved spliced viral isoforms that 10X missed entirely. Splice+ cells carried a translational host program independent of how much virus they transcribed, a distinction invisible to standard single-cell sequencing methods. From macaque and PWH on ART, Catch*ReSeq recovered 13-fold more virus-transcribing cells than 10X, including splice+ cells. We also demonstrated the generalizability of Catch*ReSeq across biological systems by applying it in combination with lineage barcoding to probe alternative splicing in clonally expanded CD4+ T cells, and separately in mouse liver regeneration. As Catch*ReSeq works with archived cDNA and can be redesigned for new targets after the fact, it allows rare isoform profiling on existing biobanked and clinical samples.

items.title: Bounded by compartment, composition and time: efferocytic transcriptional readouts after ischaemic stroke
items.abstract: Background. Efferocytosis after ischaemic stroke is usually inferred from bulk tissue transcripts and condensed into one score, which cannot separate a tissue containing more phagocytes from one whose phagocytes are more active; the gene sets behind such scores also mix clearance machinery with the inflammatory output that follows. Methods. We built a decoupled framework scoring apoptotic demand (DEMAND), clearance machinery (CAPACITY), immunogenic output (OUTCOME) and a brake. We assembled 38 datasets across brain, blood, PBMC and sorted parenchyma, admitted a score only where at least 75% of a program's genes were detected, and tested every claim against expression-matched nulls, lineage proxies and cell-level constraints. Because clearance consumes ATP, supply and demand were scored on one scale under one decision rule. Results. After adjustment for five leukocyte lineages the CAPACITY difference survived in one of three cohorts (+0.473, 95% CI +0.350 to +0.588), fell to +0.014 in the second and was unidentifiable in the third; the unadjusted differences (+0.613 and +0.374) exceeded expression- and detection-matched nulls, so the signal is real, but its compositional share differs by cohort. In matched PBMCs the point estimate was negative and not distinguishable from zero. In the only sorted human parenchyma series, non-microglial myeloid cells made up 0.371 of CD45-positive cells against 0.199 in controls, while every microglial layer fell below its expression-matched floor: it moves the composition boundary without testing capacity. In rodent brain it rose with injury: day 3 in microglia, day 7 in macrophages. Energy supply cleared both gates in eleven of eighteen contrasts and demand in eight, concentrated in entering cells (oxidative phosphorylation +1.512 in infiltrating macrophages at day 3). The two scores ranked samples almost identically ({rho} 0.59 to 0.95), and the one significant gap vanished under the same adjustment. Conclusions. Efferocytic transcripts are a measurement bounded by compartment, composition and time, not a flux assay or a biomarker. Energy supply rises with the work of clearance in the cells that carry it, and can rise in cells that do not engulf, but the two scores move closely enough that no transcript design can show one items.title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
items.abstract: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescence occurs when a cell permanently ceases dividing, halts apoptosis, stops performing its normal functions, and begins secreting chemicals that can induce other cells in its environment to also become senescent. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. This study used novel machine learning algorithms - with guaranteed properties of correctness under broad assumptions - to investigate senescence in human liver tissue by analyzing Visium spatial transcriptomics data. This produced data-driven models of the causes and effects of senescence, both locally and from nearby tissue. This report includes an assessment of whether the data meet key requirements for causal analysis, the transcripts identified by causal analyses as causes and effects of senescence marker genes, and pathway analyses of those gene sets.

items.title: A conserved matrix-centred core links fibrosis across human organs and mouse models
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for Inflammation Research, Institute for Regeneration and Repair, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, United Kingdom
items.abstract: Fibrosis develops in many organs through different initiating injuries, yet repeatedly engages inflammation, stromal activation and extracellular-matrix remodelling. Whether these recurring features represent a conserved disease programme, and whether commonly used mouse models reproduce it, remain unresolved. We developed ScarX, an R/Shiny workflow that analyses organ-resolved bulk RNA sequencing, identifies directional overlap across tissues, and ranks human-mouse conserved signals while retaining organ-restricted results. Public RNA-sequencing datasets representing fibrotic or fibrosis-associated disease in human heart, kidney, liver and lung were compared with matched mouse injury models. Differential expression was estimated independently within each organ using DESeq2, followed by cross-organ intersection, functional enrichment, matched-organ effect-profile comparison and a human-first conserved modulation (HCM) score that gives greatest weight to the breadth and magnitude of human disease change, adds support for same-direction mouse effects and penalises discordance. In human disease, 202 genes increased and 35 decreased in the same direction across all four organs. Mouse models contained 409 pan-organ increases and 46 decreases. After gene-symbol harmonisation, 25 gene-direction signatures were conserved across all four organs in both species. These included AEBP1, CDH11, COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1, COL5A2, COL6A2, EFEMP2, EMILIN1, LOXL1, LOXL2, TGFB2 and VIM. Matched human-mouse effect profiles varied considerably: Spearman rho was 0.42 for kidney, 0.31 for heart, 0.16 for liver and -0.06 for lung. Despite this uneven gene-level fidelity, 62 same-direction pathways were shared across species, led by extracellular-matrix organisation, collagen fibril organisation, cell-substrate adhesion, wound healing and ECM-receptor interaction. The HCM ranking concentrated structural matrix genes near the top but also identified cell-surface, secreted and regulatory candidates. Among the top 500 candidates, 376 carried at least one local tractability annotation. ScarX therefore separates a compact conserved matrix-remodelling core from a much larger organ- and species-dependent response. The results provide a transparent starting point for target and biomarker selection, while also showing why expression conservation alone cannot establish therapeutic dependence.

items.title: Evaluating Language Models as Orchestrators in a Tool-First Biomedical Discovery Platform
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly orchestrate agentic biomedical discovery systems, but cloud deployment raises concerns about inference cost, data privacy, and governance. Small language models (SLMs) that run on-premises are an alternative, provided they orchestrate scientific tools about as well as larger models. We built a tool-first, multi-agent system for scientific discovery in which an orchestrator coordinates six specialized tool systems: differential expression, literature retrieval, pathway enrichment, network-based gene prioritization and knowledge-graph analysis, perturbation signature matching, and structural/druggability assessment. In a tool-first design, specialized tools supply the domain knowledge and computation, so the model's main task is coordination, e.g. choosing tools, passing the right parameters, calling them in the right order, and carrying results across turns. With the tools, prompts, workflow, and benchmark held constant, we compared three orchestrators, Gemma 4 (26B, open-weight and locally deployable), Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5. Evaluation used a custom benchmark of 104 single-turn and multi-turn tests, an LLM-as-judge protocol (groundedness and evidence validity), tool-use accuracy and efficiency metrics, and blind expert review. On single-turn tasks, the three models performed comparably, and reviewers did not rate the SLM below the larger models. In multi-turn tasks, Claude Sonnet 5 showed marginally higher evidence validity, Gemma 4 was weakest when parameters had to be assembled across turns, and all three models struggled with tool ordering on memory-dependent tasks. These differences were illustrated with case studies. Finally, we propose strategies to help SLMs address the multi-turn limitations and support cost- and privacy-aware deployment.

items.title: ProtFlap: Structure-based Deep Learning Prediction of Protein Flexibility from Atomic Energy Networks
items.abstract: Protein flexibility is a key determinant of molecular recognition, catalysis, and regulation, yet remains difficult to characterise at scale. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide detailed descriptions of time-dependent dynamics but are computationally expensive. Although recent AI-based structure prediction methods have substantially improved access to high-quality static protein structures, they inherently lack information regarding the dynamic fluctuations essential for functional understanding. There is therefore a need for scalable, structure-based computational approaches that can infer intrinsic protein flexibility without explicit dynamical sampling. We present ProtFlap, a graph neural network framework for predicting relative residue-level flexibility directly from static protein structures. ProtFlap represents proteins as residue interaction graphs and integrates empirical atomic energy features extracted from a single energy-minimised snapshot with structural and sequence-derived descriptors. Central to our approach is the hypothesis that the local atomic energy network encoded in a frozen protein structure contains sufficient information to estimate structural flexibility. Trained using atomic mobility labels, quantified via normalised root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) derived from short MD simulations, ProtFlap achieves robust and accurate flexibility prediction across diverse protein domains. Feature attribution analysis reveals that van der Waals-related energy terms are the dominant contributors to the prediction.

items.title: ProtCOVER: Family-Aware Conformal Prediction for Variant Effect Predictors on Unseen Protein Families
items.abstract: Protein language models and related variant effect predictors (VEPs) increasingly classify missense variants in proteins evolutionarily distant from those used for calibration. Split conformal prediction over variants is valid for its own target, a random variant dominated by well-studied families, but deployment needs coverage for a variant of a new family. On ProteinGym clinical substitutions with five zero-shot predictors, Mondrian conformal comes within 0.005 of that target for four predictors, yet family-weighted pathogenic coverage is only 0.823-0.873 at a 0.90 target for all five, without any shift. We present ProtCOVER, a conformal procedure that treats homology families, rather than individual variants, as the exchangeable unit. ProtCOVER (i) calibrates at the family level over label-free homology clusters, giving marginal coverage for a new family under family exchangeability; (ii) adapts to descriptor shift by calibrating conditionally on an estimated density ratio of label-free descriptors (sequence similarity, alignment depth and embedding distance; a variant reweights by the ratio instead), with finite-sample family-weighted coverage, valid as computed, whenever the true ratio is a nonnegative affine function of the estimate; and (iii) can abstain at low effective calibration support, which proved no better than random abstention. Under a shift of its descriptors, ProtCOVER's mean worse-class shortfall below the target is 0.000, against 0.010 for group-weighted and 0.029 for hierarchical conformal prediction, with larger sets (about equal at matched coverage); on orphan families and held-out embedding regions it matches group weighting (0.002 against 0.003). In evaluations following pre-registered protocols, every shift-aware method met the target on new ClinVar variants of benchmark proteins, which ESM-1b separated better; on 12,225 proteins outside the benchmark, every method fell short for pathogenic variants with either of two predictors, ProtCOVER and a variant conditioned on the descriptors the least, within the 0.01 margin of group weighting.

items.title: GATA2 SUMOylation Regulates GATA2 Stability to Control Uterine Serous Carcinoma Invasion
items.abstract: Uterine serous carcinoma (USC) is an aggressive uterine cancer subtype that rapidly invades the uterine myometrium and is responsible for 40% of uterine cancer deaths. The molecular mechanisms that underlie this aggressive phenotype are poorly understood. We reported recently that USC tumors with low expression of the zinc-finger transcription factor GATA Binding Protein 2 (GATA2) exhibit aggressive tissue invasion, while retention of GATA2 expression is an independent predictor of 100% recurrence-free and cancer-specific survival in patients with early-stage USC. Here, we explored the mechanism of GATA2 loss in USC tumors that portend invasion. We show that GATA2 in human USC cell lines has a rapid 128-minute protein half-life due to post-translational SUMOylation, which targets GATA2 for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation. Treatment with small-molecule SUMOylation inhibitors, siRNA-mediated depletion of SUMO-2/3, or mutation of GATA2 K222 and K389 increases GATA2 levels and suppresses invasion in USC cell lines and USC tumor spheroids without impacting cell proliferation or viability. Primary USC tumors from newly diagnosed patients show markedly increased SUMO-2/3 levels and upregulation of SUMOylation pathways compared to other uterine cancer subtypes or benign endometrium, and heat-shock mediated induction of USC SUMO signaling leads to a SUMOylation-dependent reduction in GATA2 levels. Our results implicate SUMOylation as a dynamic regulator of USC GATA2 levels and support a model in which stress-related increases in SUMO activity deplete GATA2 to drive USC invasion. Our findings also raise the possibility that small-molecule SUMOylation inhibitors may benefit patients with early-stage USC disease.

items.title: Nicotinamide Riboside Attenuates inflammation in a mouse model of psoriasis
items.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease driven by dysregulated immune responses, in which IL-17-producing T cells play a central role. Nicotinamide riboside (NR), a precursor of NAD+, has recently emerged as a potential immunomodulatory intervention. Previous studies have shown that NR preferentially suppresses Th17 responsiveness in CD4+ T cells from individuals with psoriasis, but whether NR can attenuate psoriasiform inflammation in vivo remains poorly defined. Here, we investigated the effects of NR supplementation in a mouse model of imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform skin inflammation. NR treatment markedly attenuated IMQ-induced splenomegaly and reduced epidermal thickening, indicating an improvement of both systemic and cutaneous inflammatory manifestations. Flow cytometric analysis of skin infiltrates revealed a reduction in inflammatory myeloid populations, including neutrophils and inflammatory monocyte-macrophages, together with a pronounced decrease in dermal TCR {gamma}{delta} and CD4+ T cells. Consistent with these findings, CD4+ T cells isolated from IMQ-treated mice displayed increased IL-17A production following ex vivo TCR stimulation, which was significantly reduced by NR supplementation in a dose-dependent manner. IFN{gamma} and IL-4 responses were not significantly altered by NR in this setting. Furthermore, NR suppressed IL-17A production in Th17-polarized CD4+ T cells, while leaving Th1 and Th2 responses largely unaffected. Together, these findings show that NR treatment attenuates IMQ-induced psoriasiform skin inflammation in vivo and preferentially modulates IL-17A-associated CD4 T-cell responses. The accompanying reduction in dermal {gamma}{delta} T-cell numbers suggests that NR may also influence innate-like T-cell populations involved in cutaneous inflammation, providing experimental evidence for NAD+ boosting as a potential immunomodulatory strategy in psoriasis.

items.title: Conserved Roles of Murine SAMHD1 Isoforms in Replication Fork Dynamics and Nascent DNA Processing
items.abstract: Sterile alpha motif and histidine-aspartic acid domain-containing protein 1 (SAMHD1) is a deoxynucleoside triphosphate triphosphohydrolase (dNTPase) involved in intracellular nucleotide homeostasis, antiviral restriction, and genome maintenance. While human SAMHD1 (hSAMHD1) contributes to DNA replication fork stability and DNA double-strand break repair, the corresponding functions of murine SAMHD1 (mSAMHD1) remain poorly characterized. Here, we generated SAMHD1-deficient murine GL261 glioma cells using CRISPR/Cas9 to investigate mSAMHD1 function in DNA replication. SAMHD1 knockout increased intracellular dATP levels, altered replication fork dynamics, and reduced camptothecin (CPT)-induced nascent DNA degradation, supporting conserved replication-associated functions. RNA sequencing detected transcripts corresponding to all three annotated mSamhd1 isoforms, with isoform 1 predominating, followed by isoforms 2 and 3. To assess isoform-specific functions, individual murine isoforms were expressed in SAMHD1-deficient human HEK293T cells, enabling direct comparison in a SAMHD1-null background. Both major murine isoforms, mSAMHD1 isoforms 1 and 2, localized to the nucleus, exhibited nucleotide-dependent oligomerization and retained dNTPase activity. Notably, both isoforms restored replication fork dynamics and camptothecin (CPT)-induced nascent DNA degradation to levels largely comparable to hSAMHD1. In contrast, isoform 3 exhibited markedly reduced ectopic expression, consistent with its low endogenous transcript abundance in primary murine cells, limiting functional characterization. Together, these findings demonstrate that the two major murine SAMHD1 isoforms retain replication-associated functions of hSAMHD1 despite differences in their C-terminal regions. Furthermore, the established SAMHD1-deficient GL261 cells provide a model for future studies of SAMHD1 function in glioma and its tumor immune microenvironment.

items.title: Pharmacologic IRE1 Activation Rewires Cholesterol Metabolism to Suppress TH17 Differentiation
items.abstract: T helper 17 (TH17) cells are a subset of CD4 T cells that coordinate immune responses against extracellular bacterial and fungal pathogens. Dysregulation of TH17 cell responses drives excessive inflammation and contributes to the development of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, and multiple sclerosis. Here, we demonstrate that pharmacologic activation of the IRE1 signaling arm of the unfolded protein response (UPR) selectively reduces differentiation of TH17 cells without impacting the differentiation of other helper T cell subsets. We show that IRE1 activation suppresses TH17 differentiation by limiting intracellular cholesterol in differentiating TH17 cells through the increased degradation of the rate-limiting cholesterol biosynthesis enzyme HMGCR. Our findings identify IRE1 as a metabolic checkpoint regulating cholesterol biosynthesis in differentiating TH17 cells and demonstrate that its pharmacological activation suppresses TH17 differentiation, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy for limiting TH17-driven inflammatory diseases.

items.title: Revealing the transcriptomic organization of extrasomatic interfaces using SCOUBI
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) generates substantial transcript signal outside segmented cell bodies, which is generally discarded by analysis tools. This is especially problematic for brain ST data, as neuronal mRNAs can be localized far from somata - in axons, dendrites, and synaptic compartments - and up to half of the transcripts in ST data may lie outside cell bodies. Here, we present SCOUBI, a computational framework that identifies axon-dendrite interfaces from extrasomatic RNA in ST data, revealing a hitherto overlooked layer of molecular function in neural tissues. It first partitions extrasomatic space into axon- and dendrite-enriched compartments based on known marker genes, using a neural network trained to maximize marker specificity and inter-compartment communication signals. It then defines interfaces as loci where predicted axonal and dendritic compartments converge and exhibit ligand-receptor colocalization. Applied to mouse brain, SCOUBI creates maps of axonal and dendritic compartments and their interfaces that align with known spatial patterns of neurite and synaptic distribution. It identifies transcriptomic differences between interfaces and the surrounding extrasomatic space, revealing region-specific signatures of neuronal signaling and synaptic plasticity. By comparing interface transcript enrichment with local somatic expression, SCOUBI identifies genes that preferentially localize at sites of intercellular communication rather than simply reflecting nearby cell bodies. SCOUBI reveals interface-associated transcripts beyond established synaptic genes, with molecular signatures reproducible across independent samples and imaging platforms. In summary, SCOUBI transforms a substantial and often-discarded aspect of ST data into an interpretable readout of subcellular organization and neural signaling.

items.title: SLC25A39 loss disrupts mitochondrial redox homeostasis and exposes therapeutic vulnerabilities in glioblastoma
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Metabolism and Systems Science, College of Medicine and Health, University of Birmingham, Edgbaston, Birmingham. B15 2TT. UK
items.abstract: Glioblastoma is an incurable brain tumour characterised by extensive hypoxia and phenotypic plasticity, both of which drive therapy resistance. Mitochondrial glutathione, dependent on the inner membrane carrier SLC25A39, is central to buffering the oxidative stress that hypoxia generates; its regulation and significance in glioblastoma are nonetheless unknown. We find that SLC25A39 expression is hypoxia-inducible and HIF-dependent, enriched in hypoxic tumour niches and heterogeneously expressed within and between tumours. Its loss depletes mitochondrial glutathione, causing oxidative damage to nucleic acids and lipids, mitochondrial hyperfusion, impaired respiration and a compensatory shift towards glycolysis, glutamine catabolism and serine synthesis. SLC25A39-deficient cells grow poorly, yet resist temozolomide while becoming markedly sensitive to navitoclax, an inhibitor of Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, which increases cell killing when combined with radiation and temozolomide. In this work, we identify SLC25A39 as a metabolic vulnerability and candidate stratification marker in glioblastoma.

items.title: Learning predictive latent structure from unclustered neural spike trains
items.corresponding_institution: HHMI, University of California, San Francisco
items.abstract: Neural activity patterns enable perception, thought, and action. A powerful approach to understanding these abilities involves identifying low-dimensional, interpretable latent variables that capture the relationship between activity patterns, the information they represent, and the computations they support. Yet current methods often yield variables that are difficult to interpret and require data preprocessing that limits their accuracy and temporal resolution. Here we introduce Contrastive Prediction of Point Process Observations (C3PO), an unsupervised method that learns a predictive, interpretable latent variable representation directly from continuous time neural spiking without requiring spike-sorting or binning.
