Conclusions and Relevance: In this pooled analysis, seizure recurrence risk after stroke rose gradually, not abruptly at day 7, and differed by subtype. After external validation, subtype-specific risk zones could inform individualized decisions about long-term antiseizure medication.

items.title: Inter-articulatory Timing of Vocalic Tongue Body and Jaw Movements across Talkers with Dysarthria due to Various Neurological Conditions
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Faculty of Medicine and University Hospital Cologne, University of Cologne, Cologne, Germany
items.abstract: Purpose: This study compared inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and jaw across talkers with Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurotypical controls (CON) to identify disease-related differences. The study also explored if a talker's tongue body cycle duration, which serve as a proxy for a talker's habitual speech rate, or a talker's reliance on their jaw, as indicated by their jaw movement amplitude, could predict their inter-articulatory timing patterns. Method: Using three-dimensional electromagnetic articulography, the movements of the posterior tongue and jaw were examined in 24 talkers with PD, 19 talkers with ALS, 18 talkers with HD, 18 talkers with MS, and 34 CON during a sentence repetition task ('Buy Kaia a kite'). The tongue movement during the segment [kai] served as the reference signal (tongue body cycle) for which the phase angle of the jaw reaching the maximum opening position during [kai] was calculated. Tongue body cycle durations were measured as the time between the tongue body movement onset to the tongue body movement offset. The jaw opening amplitude was measured as the relative positional change from the jaw's maximum closing position associated with [k] to the jaw's maximal opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai]. Results: A significant group effect was found for phase angles. Pairwise comparisons showed that talkers with ALS had significantly larger phase angles than talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON, indicating a timing pattern where the tongue reached the target [a] earlier relative to the jaw. No significant differences were found for any other pairwise comparisons. Furthermore, no significant associations were found between tongue body cycle durations and phase angles. A significant association was found between jaw amplitudes and phase angles when considering all talkers [rS(110) = .253, p = .008] and when only considering talkers of the control group [r(34) = .361, p = .036]. Conclusions: Findings suggest that during the production of [kai], tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS differ from those of talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON with the tongue reaching the maximum opening position before the jaw while the opposite pattern was observed for talkers of the other groups. However, the variability in tongue body cycle duration did not significantly contribute to the variability in phase angles and the variability in jaw amplitudes only accounted for 6% of the variability in phase angles across all talkers. Future studies are needed to determine if the observed tongue-jaw timing pattern of talkers with ALS generalizes to other phonetic contexts and determine the underlying factors that contribute to the unique tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS.

items.title: Dual-platform plasma proteogenomics prioritizes GSTA1 and ARG1 as druggable cross-domain targets in cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome
items.corresponding_institution: The First Affiliated Hospital of Shantou University Medical College
items.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome reflects shared pathophysiology across metabolic, renal and cardiovascular systems, yet circulating proteins with causal effects spanning multiple CKM domains remain unclear. We aimed to identify and prioritize cross-domain candidate proteins using an integrative, dual-platform plasma proteogenomic framework. Methods: We combined genetic causal inference, statistical colocalization, single-cell expression mapping, and structure-based druggability assessment. Cis-protein quantitative trait loci (cis-pQTL) instruments were derived from two independent plasma proteomic platforms, UKB-PPP (2,030 proteins with valid cis instruments) and deCODE (1,640 proteins). Genetic causal inference (two-sample Mendelian randomization) was performed against seven CKM-related outcomes across the metabolic (type 2 diabetes [T2D], body mass index [BMI]), renal (estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], chronic kidney disease) and cardiovascular (coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke) domains. Proteins showing false discovery rate (FDR)-significant associations in at least two CKM domains independently on both platforms were prioritized, and cross-platform directional concordance was evaluated as a robustness measure. Prioritized proteins were followed by colocalization, and characterization using single-cell expression, disease-association and druggability resources. Structural and ligand-efficiency analyses were performed for the leading candidate using its co-crystallized inhibitor complex. Results: Proteome-wide analysis yielded 9,734 (UKB-PPP) and 8,837 (deCODE) protein-outcome estimates, with 77.9% two-platform directional concordance. Cross-domain prioritization identified six proteins (ARG1, GSTA1, INHBB, ITIH1, NCAN, SHBG), all acting across the metabolic-renal axis. Colocalization provided strong support for GSTA1 with eGFR (posterior probability of a shared causal variant 0.97) and ARG1 with BMI (0.93). Genetically higher GSTA1 was associated with lower eGFR and higher T2D risk, with kidney expression confined to proximal tubule cells. Genetically higher ARG1 was associated with lower BMI and lower T2D risk, consistent with hepatocyte-restricted expression. Both proteins were small-molecule tractable. For GSTA1, the inhibitor-bound structure (PDB 1GSF) showed a deep, enclosed H-site, and three chemotypes with previously reported low-micromolar potency against recombinant hGSTA1-1 (ethacrynic acid and the dietary flavonols fisetin and myricetin) all exceeded the lead-like ligand-efficiency threshold (0.30 kcal mol-1 per heavy atom). Conclusions: Using dual-platform proteogenomics, we identify genetically supported cross-metabolic-renal candidate proteins in CKM syndrome, with GSTA1 and ARG1 emerging as the most robust, pharmacologically tractable candidates. These findings nominate actionable targets and mechanistic entry points for CKM syndrome.

items.title: Greater medial temporal lobe atrophy is associated with less severe cardiac sympathetic denervation in dementia with Lewy bodies
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Neurology and Gerontoroly, Department of Internal Medicine, Iwate Medical University
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac sympathetic denervation varies in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Our previous neuropathological study demonstrated an association between greater Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and milder cardiac sympathetic denervation in DLB. We investigated whether medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA), a potential marker of concomitant AD pathology, correlates with cardiac sympathetic denervation assessed by 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy in probable DLB. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, we analyzed 162 patients with probable DLB. MTA was assessed by Voxel-based Specific Regional Analysis System for Alzheimer's Disease (VSRAD) Z-scores, and cardiac MIBG uptake by early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios. Associations were examined using Spearman and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and disease duration. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with MIBG-dependent classification, diabetes mellitus or cardiac disease. Results: VSRAD Z-scores correlated positively with early ({rho} = 0.173, P = 0.028) and delayed H/M ratios ({rho} = 0.225, P = 0.004). After adjustment, the association was no longer significant for the early H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.133, P = 0.094), whereas it remained significant for the delayed H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.196, P = 0.013). The adjusted delayed H/M association persisted after excluding 18 patients with MIBG-dependent classification ({rho} = 0.211, P = 0.012) and 40 with diabetes or cardiac disease ({rho} = 0.231, P = 0.011). Conclusions: Greater MTA was associated with relatively preserved cardiac MIBG uptake in probable DLB, particularly on delayed imaging. Consistent with our neuropathological observations, these findings suggest that concomitant AD pathology may contribute to variability in cardiac sympathetic denervation.

items.title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Surgery, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Department of Neuroscience, University of Arizona
items.abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center, Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

items.title: Circulating Apolipoprotein Profiles and Their Associations with Mild Cognitive and Behavioral Impairment in Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.corresponding_institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
items.abstract: Background Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild behavioral impairment (MBI) are overlapping prodromal states associated with dementia risk. Circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) may be linked to cognitive and behavioral changes, but their relationships remain unclear. Objective Examine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos in prodromal dementia. Methods This cross-sectional study included 148 Thai participants aged 60-75 years: 56 cognitively normal controls, 47 with MCI without MBI, and 45 with MBI with or without MCI. We measured ApoA1, ApoA2, ApoB, ApoC1, ApoC3, ApoD, ApoE, ApoH, and ApoJ, five lipids, and APOE genotype, and computed an atherogenic Apo composite (ApoB-ApoC1-ApoC3). Primary analyses used multivariable linear regression of quantitative cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Group comparisons were secondary and served to contextualize the dimensional regression findings. Results Across Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) models, 20.7-28.2% of variance was explained by combinations of ApoH, ApoC3, APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status, age, and male sex (inverse associations), and free cholesterol and education (positive associations). The atherogenic composite was inversely associated with MoCA total, memory index, and delayed recall scores, and with Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) verbal fluency and word list recall. No significant predictors emerged for Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) scores or NPI caregiver distress. All nine Apos differed significantly between groups, with levels highest in MCI, intermediate in MBI, and lowest in controls. Conclusions Circulating Apo profiles differed across controls, MCI, and MBI groups and were more consistently associated with cognitive than behavioral outcomes. ApoH and the atherogenic Apo composite warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of early cognitive dysfunction.

items.title: Exome-wide rare-variant associations vary across disease trajectories
items.corresponding_institution: Massachusetts General Hospital; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Ohio State University
items.abstract: Genetic studies of chronic disease typically collapse longitudinal clinical histories into binary case-control outcomes, obscuring disease timing and differences in genetic association patterns across disease transitions. Time-to-event analysis can preserve this information, but rare-variant analysis of post-diagnosis progression is challenged by sparse carrier-events and extensive censoring. We developed GATE-GENE, a scalable gene-based framework that maintains calibration under these conditions. Across 300 onset phenotypes in UK Biobank (UKB), GATE-GENE identified 107 exome-wide significant germline associations involving 89 genes and 67 diseases. Across 95 multi-state trajectories comprising baseline (T0), an upstream disease state (T1) and a downstream disease state (T2), disease onset (T0[->]T1) and subsequent progression (T1[->]T2) showed limited detectable sharing of rare-variant association signals. Progression showed greater concordance of gene-level association signals with downstream phenotypes (T0[->]T2) when the analyses shared T2 events occurring after T1. Removing overlapping downstream events reduced the median correlation between gene-level association signals from 0.063 to 0.001, after accounting for background correlation. Null simulations reproduced the relationship between event overlap and concordance without genetic effects, whereas additional simulations showed that near-zero concordance could persist despite extensive underlying causal-gene sharing. This attenuation was reproduced across three ancestry groups in All of Us. Cross-biobank meta-analysis identified 12 additional exome-wide significant progression associations beyond three UKB discoveries, although clinical sensitivity analyses suggested that the strongest PKD1 signals largely reflected underlying cystic kidney disease. Together, these findings establish GATE-GENE for investigating rare-variant associations with disease timing and progression, while demonstrating how overlapping clinical events and limited carrier-event information complicate inference about genetic sharing across disease transitions.

items.title: Longitudinal Investigation of Autonomic Symptoms in Biologically Confirmed (SAA+) Parkinson's Disease
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, University of Colorado, Anschutz Medical Campus
items.abstract: Background Autonomic symptoms are common in Parkinson disease (PD) and impact quality of life, with unclear relationship to motor and cognitive progression. Objective: Characterize five-year progression of autonomic symptoms in early PD and their association with motor and cognitive outcomes. Methods We analyzed data from 874 PD participants and 252 healthy controls (HC) enrolled in Parkinsons Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI). Autonomic symptoms were assessed annually over five years using Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's disease-Autonomic dysfunction (SCOPA-AUT); affected autonomic domains were defined as domain subscore >1. Clinical measures included MDS-UPDRS and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Generalized estimating equations evaluated longitudinal changes, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and comorbidities. Results: At baseline, 71% of PD participants reported >1 affected autonomic domain, increasing to 85% among 287 PD participants with 5-year follow-up; HCs reporting >1 affected autonomic domain increased from 40% of participants at baseline to 46% among 145 participants with 5-year follow-up. Gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms were most prevalent in PD. Medication use for constipation and urinary dysfunction increased over time in PD. Cardiovascular comorbidities were common and increased in prevalence in both groups. Greater baseline autonomic symptom burden predicted more rapid cognitive, but not motor decline in PD (p=0.002). Conclusion: Autonomic symptoms in PD are common at disease onset, near universal after 5 years, and associated with faster cognitive, but not motor, decline, driven by those with severe symptoms. The high prevalence and impact of autonomic symptoms in early PD highlights the importance of early assessment and management of these symptoms.

items.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
items.abstract: Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

items.title: Plasma Proteomic Identifies GDF15 as a Candidate Lithium Treatment Response Biomarker in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Secondary Analysis of the LATTICE Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Lithium (Li) demonstrates neuroprotective effects relevant to Alzheimer disease (AD). However, its molecular mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study analyzed plasma proteomic profiles from the Li as a Treatment to Prevent Impairment of Cognition in Elders (LATTICE) randomized clinical trial to identify markers associated with amyloid beta pathology, disease progression, and response to Li treatment. In the LATTICE trial, 80 older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were randomly assigned to receive either low-dose Li carbonate or placebo for two years. Longitudinal plasma samples were analyzed using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120 proteomic panel. Baseline protein levels were compared according to randomized treatment assignment, amyloid beta PET status, and MCI subtype. Analyses included longitudinal changes in protein levels associated with treatment and time, associations between baseline protein levels and subsequent cognitive, functional, and neuroimaging trajectories, and the influence of baseline protein levels on Li treatment effects. Among the 80 participants, 62 had amnestic MCI and 21 were positive on amyloid beta PET. Baseline proteomic differences were more strongly associated with amyloid beta PET status than with randomized treatment assignment. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations were elevated in individuals who were positive on amyloid beta PET and remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Over time, CALB2 and TREM2 exhibited nominal treatment-by-time interactions in the full cohort, while in the amnestic MCI subgroup, CALB2, TREM2, and amyloid beta 40 demonstrated nominal effects. None persisted after multiple-testing correction. GDF15 showed the most consistent associations with CDR Sum of Boxes trajectories and treatment-effect modification that remained significant after false discovery rate correction in the amnestic MCI subgroup, whereas p-tau217 was most consistently associated with hippocampal volume trajectories. Other protein-outcome associations were exploratory. Plasma proteomics identified distinct molecular patterns associated with amyloid beta pathology and the MCI phenotype, along with exploratory evidence of Li-associated protein changes. Plasma GDF15 and p-tau217 emerged as potential markers of clinical progression and treatment-response heterogeneity, warranting validation in larger, adequately powered trials.

items.title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
items.abstract: Background and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

items.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
items.corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

items.title: Hierarchical Graph Learning with Multimodal Distillation for Breast Cancer Survival Prediction
items.abstract: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and DNA methylation can provide complementary information for breast cancer prognosis, yet these measurements may be unavailable for new patients. In this paper, we propose HEAL-Surv, a teacher-student framework that uses both modalities during training to predict five-year net disease-specific survival (DSS) from clinical variables and molecular profiles at inference. An additive Cox teacher integrates all four modalities, using a hierarchical IMC graph encoder to capture local cell relationships and coarser tissue organisation. The student learns from observed outcomes and cross-fitted teacher survival curves, giving more weight to targets that agree across random initialisations. In five-fold cross-validation on 423 METABRIC patients, the full teacher achieved a mean five-year Uno's concordance of 0.723. Removing any modality reduced mean concordance and increased mean Brier-based errors. Relative to the matched student trained on observed outcomes alone, distillation increased mean five-year Uno's concordance from 0.658 to 0.704, with higher integrated and five-year Brier scores. In a separate external evaluation, an IMC-clinical variant trained on METABRIC achieved a five-year Uno's concordance of 0.660 on 265 Basel patients without refitting. These findings support multimodal supervision for improving risk discrimination with fewer inference inputs, while external validation of the student remains necessary.

items.title: Phase I Clinical Trial of Allogeneic Cytomegalovirus-specific T Cells in Combination with Pembrolizumab for Recurrent Glioblastoma
items.corresponding_institution: Queensland Immunology Research Centre and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia; Frazer Institute, University of Queensland
items.abstract: Purpose: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains refractory to immunotherapy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment. Tumour-infiltrating cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells express elevated programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1), suggesting checkpoint-mediated dysfunction may limit T-cell therapy. We evaluated the safety and immunological activity of allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) combined with pembrolizumab. Patients and Methods: In this phase I 3+3 dose-escalation study, recurrent GBM patients received four weekly infusions of CYT-101 followed by pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was safety. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival at 6 months (PFS-6), overall survival at 6 months (OS-6), and immune correlates of response. Results: CYT-101 T-cell therapy demonstrated polyfunctional activity, broad HLA restriction, potent cytolytic function, and diverse T-cell receptor repertoires. Nine patients received study treatment. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached. Only six adverse events were considered treatment-related, and no treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity occurred. OS-6 and PFS-6 were 55% and 11%, respectively, with a median overall survival of 9.1 months. No objective clinical responses were seen. Of the nine treated participants, one had stable disease, five had progressive disease, and three were unevaluable by modified RANO criteria. Immune profiling revealed enhanced global CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell function following CYT-101 therapy, while donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected in six of nine participants, with significant T-cell repertoire remodelling. Conclusions: Allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy combined with pembrolizumab was safe in recurrent GBM, supporting further evaluation of this strategy to overcome immune dysfunction in GBM.

items.title: CONSORTiUM-IO: A Phase 1 Study Evaluating VE800 Plus Nivolumab in Treatment of Select Refractory or Metastatic Cancers
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally.

items.title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
authors: van de Wouw, Y. A. J.
van de Werken, H. J. G.
items.last_author: van de Werken, H. J. G.
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Immunology, Erasmus MC, University Medical Center Rotterdam, Rotterdam, the Netherlands
items.abstract: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

items.title: Feasibility and Psychological Outcomes of a Clinical Meditation Intervention for Patients with Cancer: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Molecular Medicine, Human Genome Center, The Institute of Medical Science, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
items.abstract: BackgroundPsychological care is an important component of cancer care, addressing psychological distress and supporting patients as they cope with illness. Meditation-based approaches, including mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have been incorporated into supportive cancer care internationally. Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho), a meditation method developed in Japan, integrates traditional Buddhist meditation with a contemporary medical care perspective. However, its feasibility and psychological outcomes in patients with cancer have not been sufficiently studied. ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Clinical Meditation intervention and to explore psychological outcomes and participants experiences among patients with cancer who were receiving or scheduled to receive pharmacotherapy at the time of recruitment. MethodsThis single-arm pilot study used a convergent mixed-methods design to evaluate an 8-week program consisting of a 4-week structured phase (1 face-to-face session and 3 brief online group sessions, with prescribed home practice) and a 4-week self-directed phase (1 individual online session, with voluntary home practice). Feasibility was assessed descriptively using retention, attendance, practice frequency, and poststudy feedback. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, fatigue, spiritual well-being (SWB), and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were assessed at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Changes were examined using Friedman tests and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Free-text responses were analyzed thematically and integrated with questionnaire findings at the participant level. ResultsEleven patients were enrolled; 9 (81.8%) completed the 4-week assessment and 8 (72.7%) completed the 8-week assessment. Median practice frequency declined from 5-6 days per week during the structured first month to 3-4 days per week during the self-directed second month (P=.031). Quantitative analyses included 9 participants, of whom 8 completed all 3 assessments; qualitative analyses included 8 participants. SWB and PTG showed significant overall changes (adjusted P=.02 and P=.04, respectively). SWB was higher than baseline at 4 weeks (adjusted P=.012), but the difference was not significant at 8 weeks. PTG was higher than baseline at both 4 and 8 weeks (both adjusted P=.047). No significant changes were observed in anxiety, depression, insomnia, or fatigue. Five themes were identified, encompassing experiences such as relaxation, greater distance from rumination, and meditation as a source of support. Participants accounts generally aligned with increases in SWB and PTG scores, although perceived benefits did not always correspond to changes in all questionnaire measures. ConclusionsThis mixed-methods pilot study suggests that Clinical Meditation may be feasible and acceptable for patients with cancer, although sustaining meditation practice remains challenging. Exploratory increases in SWB and PTG warrant further investigation. Larger controlled studies, comparisons with established MBIs, and deeper qualitative research are needed to evaluate outcomes and clarify the distinctive features of Clinical Meditation.

items.title: Updated outcome of patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection enrolled in phase 2 clinical trials: A report from the Children's Oncology Group
items.corresponding_institution: Dana-Farber / Boston Childrens Cancer and Blood Disorders Center
items.abstract: Objective: Osteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/Methods: This study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. Results: Ninety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. Conclusion: Despite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

items.title: FlahyRecovery is an AI & gene expression based immune profiling biomarker for decision support in precision oncology
items.abstract: Background Accurate characterization of the tumor microenvironment (TME) is crucial for inferring tumor biology, subsequent tumor behavior, and predicting therapeutic response. Current characterization methods are inadequate in capturing the complexity of immune signaling networks, hindering robust clinical decision making. To address this, we have developed FlahyRecovery - an artificial intelligence (AI) and gene expression based immune profiling biomarker, implemented via a supervised classification machine learning model, that integrates response prediction and prognostic insights to personalize treatment design, particularly immunotherapy. Methods Gene expression data of 7424 tumor specimens across 14 cancers was annotated specimen wise into three immune subtypes: Elevated Immunity (Hot) with high cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, Suppressed Immunity (Cold) marked by immune exclusion and stromal dominance, and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) exhibiting mixed features. Following annotation validation, an AI model was trained and tested on the annotated data to classify new tumor specimens into the three immune subtypes: Elevated Immunity (Hot), Suppressed Immunity (Cold) and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) based on the expression of a panel of 1275 genes involved in immune cell signaling and immune signal transduction. Results In a multi-tumor validation cohort (N=1337), the subtyping model showed a sensitivity of 79%, a specificity of 89%, and a one-vs-rest AUC of 0.93. Elevated Immunity tumors correlated with prolonged survival and immunotherapy response, while Suppressed Immunity tumors correlated with treatment resistance and need for combination therapy. Conclusion Artificial intelligence can be effectively used to process tumor biology digitized via next-generation sequencing, to accurately mark the TME from an immunological perspective. Its clinical utility mechanisms andying patients who can benefit from immunotherapies, identifying treatment resistance mechanisms, and informing combination treatment regimes. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Tumor Microenvironment, Next-Generation Sequencing, Subtyping, Algorithm, Metrics, Precision Medicine

items.title: An ingestible, bio-inspired self-powered electrocapsule for in situ ethanol clearance mitigates systemic and neurobehavioral toxicity
Morphogenesis of the muscular ventricular septum is driven by retinoic acid signalling to myocardium
Mpox virus replication and drug resistance in the central nervous system of a man with advanced human immunodeficiency virus at autopsy
items.abstract: Abstract Mpox virus (MPXV) clade IIb caused an outbreak of >100,000 cases globally, with highest disease burden in people living with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), those with CD4 count <200 cells/mm 3 . We performed an extensive autopsy on a fatal case of mpox in a man living with advanced HIV-1, who achieved HIV suppression but poor immune reconstitution despite > 6 months antiretroviral therapy and had progressive necrotizing mucocutaneous mpox disease despite multiple prolonged mpox-targeted therapies. We quantified MPXV DNA across 76 autopsy samples from different anatomical sites and observed a high burden in skin and mucosal tissue and a lower burden in all central nervous system (CNS) tissues tested. However, we detected replication-competent MPXV in multiple CNS tissues and confirmed neuronal and glial cell infection using RNA-scope in situ hybridization. MPXV sequencing from body and brain tissues revealed widespread tecovirimat resistance-associated variants. This case proves that replication-competent MPXV and tecovirimat resistance-associated isolates can infect and persist in the CNS of people with advanced HIV thus informing future therapeutic design.

items.title: Coherence and pairing enhancement in a trilayer cuprate with layer-selective charge order
A revised genome annotation of the model cyanobacterium Synechocystis based on start and stop codon-enriched ribosome profiling and proteogenomics
items.abstract: Abstract Cyanobacteria are important primary producers and popular in biotechnology. Synechocystis 6803 is a model cyanobacterium, yet many coding regions are ambiguous, or have remained undetected. Here, we present a riboproteogenomic analysis combining ribosome profiling with inhibitors that stall ribosomes at translation initiation and termination sites, and proteogenomic re-annotation of its genome. Based on proteogenomics, we report translation of 3055 annotated genes (83%), 3492 based on Ribo-seq (95.2%), and 3,018 supported by both methods (82%). The data suggest additional protein-coding genes and corrections for annotated ones. We validate 15 proteins translated from antisense, intergenic and intragenic loci and provide proteogenomic support for up to 69 additional, mostly small proteins. We identify three genes with ~300 nt long intragenic out-of-frame translons and demonstrate that internal and host translons are translated into interacting proteins. Our data are accessible at https://www.bioinf.uni-freiburg.de/~ribobase/ . They illustrate the enormous value of consolidating genome annotations with integrated experimental data.

items.title: Rhizospheric pH mediated thermo-signalling coordinates root growth under heat stress
items.abstract: Abstract Heat stress events pose a major threat to global agriculture due to elevated air and soil temperatures. While plant roots regulate their growth in response to elevated soil temperatures, they appear to rely on thermosensory mechanisms distinct from those used by shoots. Here, we report pH as a key component of a thermo-signaling mechanism that regulates temperature-dependent root responses via ROS-mediated control of cell cycle dynamics in Arabidopsis thaliana . At moderately high temperatures, alkalization of meristematic and transition zones increases superoxide (O₂⁻) levels, promoting cell division and root growth. Conversely, higher temperatures inhibit growth by increasing acidification and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) accumulation in these zones. Elevating external pH buffers this acidification, reduces H₂O₂ levels, and confers heat resistance. Our data support that this pH-mediated heat resistance is also effective under soil conditions. The heat-induced pH shifts are controlled by plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases (PM-H⁺-ATPases), which are under the control of the kinases TOT3 and TOI5. Our findings reveal an interesting pathway for plant adaptation to heat stress, linking pH, ROS and root thermomorphogenesis, with major implications for improving plant resilience in warming climates.

items.title: Assembly of a renal countercurrent system in a beetle
items.abstract: Abstract Countercurrent exchange describes the crossover of some property between two bodies flowing in opposite direction. Countercurrent circuits, which work more efficiently than concurrent circuits, are common in nature and mimicked in human engineering. An example is the beetle cryptonephridial complex (CNC)—a multi-organ water conservation system which makes key contributions to the water budget in a vast number of species. It is even used by some to harvest water from the atmosphere. The system evolved by a radical reorganisation of insect internal anatomy bringing the renal/Malpighian tubules and rectum into countercurrent configuration, and their isolation in a chamber by an unusual tissue of unknown origin—the perinephric membrane. The CNC is richly supplied with tracheae to meet the high metabolic demands of the system. How the CNC is assembled during development is unknown. Here we characterise CNC development in the model beetle Tribolium castaneum and discover the molecular signals orchestrating its assembly. We find that dynamic crosstalk between the developing precursor cells of the rectum, Malpighian tubules, perinephric membrane, and trachea rely on a single, differentially spliced fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor and two FGF pathway ligands. We also map the origin of the perinephric membrane to a previously uncharacterised population of mesodermal cells, providing clues to its evolutionary origin. This work illuminates the developmental processes underpinning the reorganisation of the insect internal body plan to assemble a natural countercurrent system, one which is fundamental to beetle physiology, ecology and evolutionary success.

items.title: Latent Squamous Plasticity Licensed by Chromatin-State Remodeling Dictates Therapeutic Susceptibility in Cholangiocarcinoma
items.last_author_affiliation: Shanghai Cancer Institute 1 State Key Laboratory of Systems Medicine for Cancer, , Department of Liver Surgery, , Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China.; Renji Hospital 1 State Key Laboratory of Systems Medicine for Cancer, , Department of Liver Surgery, , Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China.
items.abstract: Abstract Adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) has long been considered rare (∼1 to 2%), yet its occurrence portends lethal disease progression. In this study, we identify latent squamous plasticity, a transcriptionally primed yet histology-silent state that is quantifiable by a squamous transition potential (STP) index. Approximately 20% to 30% of patients with iCCA can be classified as STP high and experience ASC-like dismal outcomes. Mechanistically, FOS-like 1 (FOSL1) acts as a plasticity trigger, driving a temporally ordered squamous program by reshaping the chromatin landscape. Additionally, it cooperates with p63 in an enhancer-dependent manner to dysregulate PTGS2/COX-2 expression. The resulting intratumoral prostaglandin (PG) E2 accumulation drives neutrophil-mediated FOXP3-negative type I regulatory T-cell (Tr1) polarization and predisposes STP-high tumors to immunotherapy resistance. Through a drug-repurposing screen, we identify celecoxib as a dual-function agent that counteracts latent squamous plasticity while fostering an immunopermissive state, providing a clinically actionable strategy for squamous-biased iCCA now being evaluated in a phase Ib/II trial (NCT07632235). Significance: Latent squamous plasticity defines a common yet histologically occult high-risk state in iCCA, driven by FOSL1-dependent enhancer reprogramming and coupled to a PGE2-dependent neutrophil–Tr1 immunosuppressive circuit. By integrating STP-based stratification with celecoxib repurposing, this study identifies latent squamous plasticity as a clinically actionable vulnerability to improve iCCA treatment responsiveness.

items.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
items.last_author_affiliation: Early Cancer Institute, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK. jrb75@cam.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Abstract Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

items.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
items.last_author_affiliation: Chemical and Systems Biology Department, Stanford School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA. chistol@stanford.edu.; Stanford Cancer Institute, Stanford School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA. chistol@stanford.edu.
items.abstract: Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase-polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1-4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45-MCM2-7-GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL's activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Physics and Cell Biology, National Institute of Genetics, Shizuoka, Japan. yuta.shimamoto@nig.ac.jp.; The Graduate University for Advanced Studies, SOKENDAI, Shizuoka, Japan. yuta.shimamoto@nig.ac.jp.
items.abstract: Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1-3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

items.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
items.last_author_affiliation: Technology, Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Kensington, Western Australia, Australia.
items.abstract: Abstract A new epoch for direct visualization of accretion dynamics near the event horizon of a black hole began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration synthesized an Earth-sized aperture with millimetre radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image 1–4 of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features 3,5–7 , with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source 8,9 . Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very long baseline interferometry measurements, making interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms and imaging hyperparameters. Here we apply an independent imaging algorithm that we have developed to the M87* dataset that is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with an angular diameter of 42.2 ± 1.5 μas corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 ± 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of approximately 20° from the approaching jet.

UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
items.last_author_affiliation: UCL Queen Square Motor Neuron Disease Centre and Department of Neuromuscular Diseases, UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, University College London, London, UK. p.fratta@ucl.ac.uk.; The Francis Crick Institute, London, UK. p.fratta@ucl.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Abstract TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts 1–8 . Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

items.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Michigan Center for Translational Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. arul@umich.edu.; Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. arul@umich.edu.; Rogel Cancer Center, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. arul@umich.edu.; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. arul@umich.edu.; Department of Urology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. arul@umich.edu.
items.abstract: Abstract Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer 1 , in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP) 2 . Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.

items.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology, The Rockefeller University, New York, NY, USA. mucida@rockefeller.edu.; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, The Rockefeller University, New York, NY, USA. mucida@rockefeller.edu.
items.abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
items.last_author_affiliation: Beijing SHRIMP Center, Institute of Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Beijing, China. wanyushengs@126.com.
items.abstract: The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth's early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada1-3. Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ18O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive εHf(t) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta2, the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin4. Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8-16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740-820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
items.last_author_affiliation: Verve Therapeutics, Inc. (a wholly owned subsidiary of Eli Lilly and Company), Boston, MA, USA. akhera@lilly.com.
items.abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Protein and Nucleic Acid Chemistry, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, UK. jyeeles@mrclmb.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Abstract Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase 1,2 . Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability 3–6 . Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment 4 . In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress 7–10 , but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A 9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.; Department of Chemical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.; Department of Electrical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.; Quantum Information Science Program, Graduate School of Convergence Science and Technology, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH), Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.; POSCO-POSTECH-RIST Convergence Research Center for Flat Optics and Metaphotonics, Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.; National Institute of Nanomaterials Technology (NINT), Pohang, Republic of Korea. jsrho@postech.ac.kr.
items.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) displays, originating from early optical see-through head-mounted systems1, have evolved towards lightweight glasses that seamlessly integrate digital information with the physical world2,3. However, their widespread adoption requires compact optical systems that enable bright, wide-field and comfortable viewing. Diffractive waveguides (WGs) offer a promising approach towards lightweight AR displays yet face inherent trade-offs among field of view (FoV), optical efficiency and eyebox size owing to limited degrees of freedom in light control. Here we show an all-day-wearable AR glass prototype based on spatially varying, interwoven metasurfaces that provide several grating vectors for multidirectional light control. The resulting dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide (meta-WG) achieves a 30° FoV and an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional (2D) eyebox while maintaining an average luminance efficiency of 1,938 nits lm-1 (up to 4,225 nits lm-1) within a 1.5-mm-thick form factor. The prototype produces bright and stable virtual images under outdoor ambient illumination, demonstrating the compatibility of meta-WGs with practical wearable display requirements. By expanding the degrees of freedom for light routing beyond conventional diffractive WGs, our approach provides a scalable framework for balancing efficiency, viewing range and form factor, bringing high-performance AR glasses closer to practical consumer applications.

items.title: Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. ilija.coric@chem.uzh.ch.
items.abstract: Direct arylation of C-H bonds in arenes offers a streamlined alternative to widely used cross-coupling reactions.1 However, native substrates lack the preinstalled functional handles that ordinarily provide both reactivity and control over the site of reaction. Consequently, despite long-standing interest in directly engaging C-H bonds as reactive sites,2-4 the design of general catalysts that deliver high yields across diverse substrate classes while controlling site selectivity remains a challenge.5-12 Here we show that a microenvironment around a prototypical palladium dicarboxylate catalytic site can provide high selectivity for direct arylation of sterically exposed C-H sites, while high efficiency is achieved using an advanced palladium(II) precatalyst and tailored diaryliodonium reagents for selective aryl transfer. The applicability of this system spans from electron-rich to electron-deficient arenes, while electron-neutral benzene, which is often a challenge for C-H arylation, undergoes successive sterically controlled arylations, delivering functionalized polyaryl compounds. In addition to removing the necessity for pre-functionalized substrates, the mild conditions enable direct late-stage C-H arylation and the installation of aryl groups equipped with functionalities that are typically either reactive in traditional cross-coupling catalysis, such as triflates, iodides, and boronate esters, or sensitive to the basic conditions, such as N-hydroxysuccinimide esters. The results emphasize the distinct synthetic value of palladium-catalyzed direct C-H arylation reactions and showcase a catalyst platform that facilitates high yields and control over site-selectivity.

Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
items.last_author_affiliation: Biocenter, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz, Mainz, Germany. edlemke@uni-mainz.de.; Institute of Molecular Biology (IMB gGmbH), Mainz, Germany. edlemke@uni-mainz.de.
items.abstract: Abstract The nuclear pore complex (NPC) regulates molecular traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm 1,2 . Its permeability barrier is formed by intrinsically disordered phenylalanine-glycine-rich nucleoporins (FG-NUPs), whose physical state has long been debated 3–13 . Deciphering how FG-NUPs behave inside living cells is crucial for understanding how NPCs achieve both selective and rapid transport. By combining site-specific labelling with time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy, here we show that FG domains exhibit nanosecond-scale, liquid-like segmental motion in live cells, whereas reconstituted FG condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition in vitro. Experiments and molecular-dynamics simulations further show that importin-β, a principal nuclear transport receptor, and O-linked β- N -acetylglucosamine, a key post-translational modification of FG-NUPs, together stabilize the dynamic FG network. Finely balanced FG–FG and FG–importin-β interactions maintain FG-NUP liquidity and generate a radial organization in which importin-β is enriched near the NPC periphery and extended FG domains remain in the central channel, forming the transport barrier. This organization explains recent MINFLUX observations 14 of rim-biased transport trajectories and is supported here by direct MINFLUX imaging of importin-β in mammalian cells. Together, our results reconcile conflicting models of FG-NUP organization 4,5,7,9,15 and establish a framework for understanding how cellular context tunes intrinsically disordered proteins in health and disease.

items.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, USA.; The Santa Fe Institute, Santa Fe, NM, USA.
items.abstract: Extreme climatic events are increasing in frequency and intensity with climate change1. Their effects on species' distributions and extinction risk remain poorly understood2-9. Most species distribution models rely on long-term mean climate, overlooking potentially important nonlinear effects of extremes. Here we integrate new spatial data on severe drought10, including compounding effects of warmer temperatures, with a comprehensive curated dataset of cactus occurrences (648,316 records) and species distribution models to assess how severe drought alters projected suitable climatic area for 993 species of Cactaceae, a highly threatened family11 that is commonly considered drought tolerant. In 91% of cases, models including severe drought were better supported than mean-climate models. Across emissions scenarios (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5) with 100-km dispersal, including severe drought increased the share of species losing suitable climatic area from 58-61% to 69-72%. The proportion of species projected to lose over a quarter of suitable area increased from 26-43% to 55-58%, and the proportion projected to lose over four-fifths increased from 1-15% to 25-35%. With severe drought, restricting dispersal from 100 to 0 km increased the share losing suitable area from 69-72% to 84-85% across SSPs. These declines reduced regional richness, with five bioregions potentially losing over 25% of species. These findings demonstrate that accounting for climatic extremes can alter assessments of biodiversity vulnerability under climate change. Integrating climatic extremes into ecological forecasting will be critical for assessing biodiversity loss and designing effective conservation strategies across taxa and ecosystems.
