items.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
items.abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

items.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak
items.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

items.title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
items.last_author_affiliation: Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB), Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo.; One Health Institute for Africa (INOHA), University of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo.; Cliniques Universitaires de Kinshasa, Faculté de Médecine, Université de Kinshasa, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo.; Africa CDC, Ethiopia.
items.abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

items.title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Colorado at Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA.
items.abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

items.title: Californians approve controversial $8.4 billion immunology initiative
Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
items.last_author_affiliation: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA.
items.abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

items.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak
items.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

items.title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Ophthalmology, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA.; Smith Cardiovascular Research Institute, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA.
items.abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

items.title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physics, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA.
items.abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

items.title: A trapped catalytic product acts as molecular glue for innate immune signalosome assembly
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Microbial Metabolism, Joint International Research Laboratory of Metabolic and Developmental Sciences, Sheng Yushou Center of Cell Biology and Immunology, School of Life Sciences and Biotechnology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China.
items.abstract: Innate immune systems of living organisms are essential for host defense. Central to these systems is the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, an evolutionarily conserved module. From antiphage systems in prokaryotes to innate immune systems in plants, TIR domains have catalytic activity. However, TIR domains within animal innate immune receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), have been considered as scaffolds for adaptor recruitment. We report that the TLR4 TIR domain possesses an allosterically activated nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) hydrolase (NADase) activity that operates in a single-turnover manner. Its product, adenosine diphosphate ribose, is not released but entrapped as a “molecular glue,” stabilizing a composite catalytic pocket with adaptor TIR domain–containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) to nucleate signalosome assembly. This “produce-and-trap” mechanism represents a signaling mode that integrates enzymatic activity with adaptor function to drive downstream signaling.

items.title: EDITOR’S NOTE on the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals”
items.last_author_affiliation: Editor-in-Chief, Science

items.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution, University of California, San Diego, San Diego, CA, USA.; EFECT, Colombo, Sri Lanka.; Trunks & Leaves Inc., Pittsfield, MA, USA.
items.abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

items.title: Nature’s cellular nuke
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Bioengineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA.
items.abstract: Discovery of an unknown immune cell type and its cytotoxic killing mode.

items.title: Building a cell engineering toolbox
items.last_author_affiliation: Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA.
items.abstract: Biological diversity and deep learning are harnessed for discovery.

items.title: Neurons in a dish are the newest computing machines
items.last_author_affiliation: Washington, D.C.
items.abstract: Brain organoids offer highly efficient processing—if researchers can learn how to harness their power

items.title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE, USA.; Nebraska Center for Materials and Nanoscience, University of Nebraska, Lincoln, NE, USA.
items.abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

items.title: Nicotianamine-driven nickel transport to sink organs underpins maize productivity
items.last_author_affiliation: National Key Laboratory of Plant Design, CAS Center for Excellence in Molecular Plant Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai 200032, China; Shanghai Zhangjiang Smart Breeding Center, Shanghai 201210, China. Electronic address: dychao@cemps.ac.cn.
items.abstract: Nickel (Ni), the last essential trace element identified in plants, has long been enigmatic regarding the genetic basis underlying its homeostasis and its agricultural significance. Using genome-wide association analysis, we identified ZmNAET1 as a key transporter controlling Ni allocation to seeds. Mechanistically, ZmNAET1 mediates nicotianamine secretion and enables nicotianamine-dependent phloem loading of Ni in nodes and subsequent Ni translocation into sink organs. Mutants lacking ZmNAET1 exhibit significant yield penalties, decreased seed germination velocity, and drastically shortened seed longevity. In an irreplaceable role, supplemented Ni fully rescued seed germination and proper vegetative development of the mutants. We show that NAET1-dependent delivery of Ni to urease is essential for amino acid turnover in developing sink organs, revealing an unappreciated role of Ni in yield formation of graminaceous plants. This study uncovers an underestimated requirement for nicotianamine and Ni and opens a new research avenue toward optimizing micronutrient provision for cereal crop productivity.

items.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Health, Seattle, WA 98109, USA. Electronic address: trygveb@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease, yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets spanning eight BG structures, integrating gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling. Alignment across species and to mouse and human whole-brain atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 76 million years. Dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more conserved than D1/D2 receptor or striosome/matrix identity, and striatum (STR) D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neurons have distinct molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features. Cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting, and cell-type-resolved mapping localizes psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk to specific BG cell populations. This work provides a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

items.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA; New York Genome Center, New York, NY 10013, USA; Department of Genetics and Development, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY 10032, USA; Department of Systems Biology, Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, Vagelos Institute for Basic Biomedical Research, New York, NY 10032, USA. Electronic address: bren@nygenome.org.
items.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

items.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Science, Seattle, WA, USA. Electronic address: stephanies@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

items.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer’s disease models
items.last_author_affiliation: Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Neurology, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Bakar Aging Research Institute, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA. Electronic address: andrew.yang@gladstone.ucsf.edu.
items.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

items.title: Stepping (hi)stones: Charting a single-cell multiomic path toward understanding the human brain
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Molecular Neurobiology, Department of Medical Biochemistry and Biophysics, Biomedicum, 17177 Stockholm, Sweden; Science for Life Laboratory (Scilifelab), Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden. Electronic address: goncalo.castelo-branco@ki.se.
items.abstract: In this issue of Cell, two single-cell multiomic atlases jointly profile transcription and histone modifications across different regions of the adult human brain, revealing cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, developmental epigenetic memory, and improved interpretation of neurological variants. These studies establish a framework for understanding human brain cell identity, evolution, and pathology.

items.title: Mapping primate brain aging across cell types, regions, and sexes
From the human genome to the human brain cell atlas
items.last_author_affiliation: University of Texas Health Houston, School of Biomedical Informatics, Houston, TX, USA.
items.abstract: The BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is establishing an evolving reference for neuroscience by integrating cell identities, anatomy, and multimodal evidence across species. In analogy with the Human Genome Project, the BICAN basal ganglia atlas is a model for a federated reference to advance understanding of brain organization, function, variation, and disease.

items.title: Reconstructing developmental and disease progression with sample-level embeddings
items.last_author_affiliation: New York Genome Center, New York, NY, USA; Center for Genomics and Systems Biology, New York University, New York, NY, USA. Electronic address: rsatija@nygenome.org.
items.abstract: Single-cell genomics is transformative for characterizing cellular heterogeneity, but many biological questions require comparing samples rather than individual cells. Typical analyses compare "case" and "control" groups, ignoring sample-level variation within them. Here, we present scSLIDE (single-cell sample-level inference using density estimation), a framework that transforms each sample's single-cell data into a compact profile describing where its cells are distributed in high-dimensional space. By comparing these density profiles, scSLIDE calculates embeddings to characterize variation across samples. We implement scSLIDE in version 6 of our Seurat package and apply it to COVID-19 infection, Alzheimer's disease, and zebrafish embryogenesis. scSLIDE reveals patient subgroups, reconstructs disease trajectories, and identifies coordinated cellular programs across samples. We discover separable axes of infection and severity, a trajectory of Alzheimer's progression, and embryonic "pseudostages" that vary across and within time points. Our results demonstrate how case-control analyses collapse rich biological variation into binary labels and how sample-level embedding represents a powerful analytical alternative.

items.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Neurological Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Weill Institute for Neurosciences, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Anatomy, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Eli and Edythe Broad Center for Regeneration Medicine and Stem Cell Research, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA. Electronic address: tomasz.nowakowski@ucsf.edu.
items.abstract: Rare genetic variants contribute substantially to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the regulatory logic of vulnerable subcortical cells is poorly understood. In a 16p11.2 deletion mouse model, lineage tracing across five brain regions revealed prominent striatal changes. In the human putamen from ASD and neurotypical donors, single-nucleus multi-omics showed transcriptional alterations concentrated in D1 striosome spiny projection neurons (SPNs), affecting synaptic and energy metabolism genes, with altered synapse-supporting programs in astrocytes. Gene regulatory network analysis integrating chromatin accessibility and expression identified EGR1 and EGR3 as key regulators of these programs, with reduced activity in D1 striosome SPNs. Deleting EGR1 or EGR3 in human striatal organoids produced partially overlapping transcriptional changes. These findings establish the striatum as a site of molecular convergence in ASD and provide a multi-omic resource for dissecting subcortical mechanisms.

items.title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas
items.abstract: The NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is developing a standardized, integrated reference framework for classifying and studying brain cell types across human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse. We present a cross-species, multimodal atlas of the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei central to motor control, adaptive behavior, and neurological disease. Built from large-scale single-cell transcriptomic classification and integrated with epigenomic, spatial genomic, multiomic, and developmental datasets, the atlas provides a curated, data-driven taxonomy with standardized nomenclature, extensive phenotypic characterization, and community-informed annotation. Cell types are mapped into species-specific anatomical reference frameworks and linked across species through structural ontologies. Realizing this resource required coordinated standards for tissue acquisition and processing, harmonized donor metadata, anatomical registration, sequencing pipelines, data infrastructure, visualization, mapping tools, and interoperable metadata. The BICAN basal ganglia atlas demonstrates how pipelines and standards can be implemented, validated, and scaled toward a whole-brain human and mammalian cell-type reference.

items.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging
items.last_author_affiliation: Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT, Cambridge, MA 02142, USA; Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA 02114, USA; Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA. Electronic address: emacosko@broadinstitute.org.
items.abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.

items.title: COP1 is a temperature-responsive switch in Arabidopsis
items.last_author_affiliation: Leibniz Institut für Gemüse und Zierpflanzenbau (IGZ) e.V., 14979 Großbeeren, Germany; Institute of Biochemistry and Biology, University of Potsdam, 14476 Potsdam, Germany. Electronic address: wigge@igzev.de.
items.abstract: Temperature is molecular motion, but how living systems sense this is poorly understood. Many responses in plants integrate light and temperature signals, for example, via light receptors and the circadian clock. CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENESIS 1 (COP1) regulates light signaling and is necessary for responding to temperature. We show that COP1 acts as a temperature-dependent switch, becoming activated by a warm temperature-induced conformational change. An intramolecular Val-Pro (VP) motif binds to the active site of COP1 at low temperatures, preventing substrate docking. At warmer temperatures, the VP motif becomes detached, enabling client proteins to bind and be degraded. This discovery explains how plants are able to obtain a precise readout of temperature within a given climate range. Altering the binding of the VP motif is sufficient to adjust the temperature range within which the plant responds. This helps us understand how plants are able to adapt to different climates.

items.title: Spatial and regulatory organization of cell identity across the primate subcortex
items.last_author_affiliation: Princeton Neuroscience Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA. Electronic address: fkrienen@princeton.edu.
items.abstract: Mammalian brain cell identity is shaped by intrinsic factors and external context. We present a spatially resolved transcriptomic and gene regulatory atlas of cell types across all subcortical regions in a primate, the common marmoset. Dense sampling and cross-species integration revealed spatially precise neuronal assemblies, including ones in complex midbrain and diencephalic structures. Chromatin accessibility and transcriptional identity are spatially tuned within and across subcortical structures; spatial gradients within hippocampal subfields are orchestrated by graded transcription factors acting through graded enhancers. The primate-expanded thalamic γ-aminobutyric acid (GABAergic) population shares transcriptional and regulatory syntax with conserved midbrain populations, reflecting an evolutionary adaptation compared with rodents. Similar regional expression across cell types can arise by distinct regulatory architectures, as observed in telencephalic astrocytes and neurons. Conversely, distant cell types can share regulatory programs despite divergent identities: striatal GABAergic spiny projection neurons and telencephalic glutamatergic neurons share a postsynaptic regulatory program despite divergent lineages, regions, and neurotransmitter identities.

items.title: Collaboration across scales: More than the sum of its parts
Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Health, Seattle, WA 98109, USA. Electronic address: trygveb@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

items.title: Single-cell multimodal atlas reveals regulatory programs in the human brain
items.last_author_affiliation: New York Genome Center, New York, NY 10013, USA; Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA; Center for Epigenomics, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA; Department of Genetics and Development, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY 10032, USA; Moores Cancer Center, Institute for Genomic Medicine, School of Medicine, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92037, USA; Systems Biology, Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY 10032, USA. Electronic address: bren@nygenome.org.
items.abstract: Direct measurement of chromatin states together with transcription is essential for understanding how cell-type-specific regulatory programs are established and maintained in the adult human brain. Here, we present a large-scale single-cell multimodal atlas by jointly profiling the transcriptome with active (H3K27ac) or repressive (H3K27me3) histone modifications across 18 adult brain regions. We targeted over 750,000 nuclei spanning 160 cell types and integrated these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, 3D genome architecture, and spatial transcriptomes. This framework resolved chromatin states for over 500,000 candidate regulatory elements, identified enhancer-gene links and regulatory programs, revealed Polycomb-associated ultra-long-range contacts, and uncovered brainwide epigenomic heterogeneity. We further developed a sequence-to-function model to predict cell-type-specific effects of candidate neurological disease variants. Finally, comparative analyses across species reveal conservation in active regulatory programs but divergence in repressive programs. Together, this study provides a comprehensive epigenomic reference for interpreting regulatory principles and epigenetic memory underlying human brain organization and disease.

items.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology, School of Medicine, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Center for Neural Circuit Mapping (CNCM), University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Mathematical, Computational and Systems Biology Graduate Program, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Department of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, School of Medicine, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Department of Computer Science, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA. Electronic address: xiangmin.xu@uci.edu.
items.abstract: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

items.title: Single-cell, multi-region profiling of the macaque brain across the lifespan
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Evolution and Medicine, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA; School of Life Sciences, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA; School of Human Evolution and Social Change, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA; ASU-Banner Neurodegenerative Disease Research Center, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA. Electronic address: nsnyderm@asu.edu.
items.abstract: Brain aging is a complex process with profound health and societal consequences. However, the molecular and cellular pathways that govern its progression, and inter- and intra-individual variation, remain poorly defined. We present a transcriptomic atlas of 5.3 million cells from 582 samples spanning 11 brain regions of 55 rhesus macaques (aged 0.5-21 years). We identify age-depleted and vulnerable neuronal populations and subtle, age-associated compositional differences in glia-detectable only at single-cell resolution. We chart convergent and divergent age-associated molecular signatures across regions and cell types, which include sex-specific signatures that could underlie biases in neurological disorders. These signatures overlap those of Alzheimer's disease (AD), which suggests that aging and AD share molecular roots that emerge at different ages and in region- and sex-specific windows of vulnerability. This work provides a temporal, regional, and sex-stratified atlas of the aging primate brain, offering insights into cell-type-specific vulnerabilities and regional heterogeneity with translational human relevance.

items.title: Sub-second dopamine reinforcement shapes juvenile social play
items.last_author_affiliation: Beijing Institute for Brain Research, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College, Beijing 102206, China; Beijing Key Laboratory of Brain Science and Brain-Machines Interface, Chinese Institute for Brain Research, Beijing 102206, China. Electronic address: liying@cibr.ac.cn.
items.abstract: Juvenile social play is critical for neurodevelopment, yet the neural mechanisms organizing moment-to-moment interactions remain elusive. Using social behavior sequencing (Social-seq)-an occlusion-robust 3D pose estimation and unsupervised clustering pipeline-we found that nucleus accumbens (NAc) dopamine was tightly coupled to sub-second social syllables during naturalistic interactions. In wild-type juveniles, males exhibited a sharper dopaminergic contrast between proactive play and forced submission than females did, consistent with sex-divergent play strategies. In Shank3-deficient autism models, this process was fundamentally corrupted: proactive play-evoked dopamine responses were abolished in males and significantly sign-inverted in females, with male-specific enhancements during non-social behaviors, driving social play deficits. A multi-agent reinforcement learning model parameterized by disrupted, play-related dopaminergic reinforcement values recapitulated mutant phenotypes. Closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of ventral tegmental area (VTA)-NAc dopamine projections, time-locked to proactive play, restored reciprocal play in Shank3-deficient rats. Sub-second dopaminergic reinforcement thus orchestrates naturalistic social behavior, providing a behaviorally contingent interventional framework for neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Conserved striatal mechanisms underlying ASD
A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Human Genetics, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA 90095, USA. Electronic address: cluo@mednet.ucla.edu.
items.abstract: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

items.title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
items.last_author_affiliation: Michigan Center for Translational Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Department of Urology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA; Rogel Cancer Center, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, USA. Electronic address: arul@umich.edu.
items.abstract: Liquid biopsies are one of the few noninvasive procedures for probing disease at the molecular level. They represent a scalable solution to cancer detection and monitoring by capturing tumor-derived signals from circulating biomolecules such as proteins, DNA, RNA, and metabolites. However, these signals are often sparse, heterogeneous, and shaped by genetics, demographics, and comorbidities. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially with multimodal foundation models, have proven capable of extracting signals from noisy, high-dimensional data. Pretraining on large cohorts and integrating complementary modalities may improve sensitivity for tumor signals in blood, though significant clinical and infrastructural barriers remain. This review synthesizes advances in liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence and examines how their convergence can enable enhanced cancer monitoring.

items.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Genomic Analysis Laboratory, The Salk Institute for Biological Studies, La Jolla, CA 92037, USA. Electronic address: ecker@salk.edu.
items.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2+ STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

items.title: Common variation of cell abundances and gene expression in the human striatum
items.last_author_affiliation: Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA; Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Boston, MA, USA. Electronic address: smccarro@broadinstitute.org.
items.abstract: The cellular and molecular bases of inter-individual variation in the human brain are not yet understood, particularly beyond the neocortex. Here, we describe cellular and gene-expression variation in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis of 3.9 million nuclei from 178 adult brain donors. People with more astrocytes, microglia, or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in any one brain region tended to have this property in all gray-matter regions sampled. OPC proportions declined by 40% across ages 30-80 in the cortex and striatum. Age-associated gene-expression changes differed substantially across cell types. Donor age was predicted from RNA-expression patterns with a median absolute error of 6.6 years across cell types. Common genetic variants were associated with the expression of nearly 10,000 genes; these effects were mostly cell-type specific and distinguished striatal from cortical neurons. These open-access data provide a foundation for future studies of human brain variation and vulnerabilities.

items.title: Morphoelectric diversity and specialization of primate striatal neuron types
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Health, Seattle, WA 98109, USA; Department of Neurobiology and Biophysics, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA. Electronic address: briank@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: The basal ganglia are evolutionarily ancient subcortical nuclei that form interconnected loops with the neocortex and limbic system to regulate movement, learning, habit formation, emotion, and motivation. Their dysfunction contributes to major neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet most cellular-level insights derive from rodent studies, leaving knowledge gaps in humans and translationally relevant primate species. To address this, we generated multimodal Patch-seq data linking transcriptomic identity with morphological and electrophysiological properties in the macaque striatum-the input nucleus of the basal ganglia. We found underappreciated diversity among spiny projection neurons (SPNs), including non-canonical types, and variation aligned with functional gradients. Interneurons also exhibited spatial variation and even greater morphoelectric diversity, highlighting their functional modularity. Despite broad evolutionary conservation, we identified primate-specific features and key differences from rodent striatal neurons. By integrating molecular classification with cellular properties that shape network function, our findings provide insights into the functional organization of the primate striatum.

items.title: Harmonized brain ontology and 3D atlases for human, macaque, and marmoset basal ganglia
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Health, Seattle, WA, USA. Electronic address: edl@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: A major goal of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is to create a suite of foundational reference cell atlases and associated standards for human and nonhuman primate brains. Central to this goal is the creation of cross-species-harmonized cellular taxonomies and structural parcellations with formal ontologies that can be mapped onto 3D reference frameworks, bridging neuroimaging and cellular and histological resolutions. We describe an iterative approach, focused initially on the basal ganglia, to co-create structural and cellular ontologies for human, macaque, and marmoset brains and to map and refine structural parcellations into neuroimaging-based common coordinate frameworks. We create a Harmonized Ontology of Mammalian Brain Anatomy (HOMBA) to meet these needs. These references provide the framework for documenting and mapping all experimental sampling in BICAN, allowing analyses of cellular and molecular variation as a function of topographic position and enabling comparisons of cellular, molecular, and neuroimaging-based functional variation across species.

items.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego School of Medicine, La Jolla, CA, USA; Department of Genetics and Development, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY, USA; New York Genome Center, New York, NY, USA; Department of Systems Biology, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY, USA; Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics, Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY, USA. Electronic address: bren@nygenome.org.
items.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

items.title: Advancing multimodal tools to decode organoid complexity
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Bioengineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA. jina.ko@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.; Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA. jina.ko@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.
items.abstract: Organoids are complex, miniaturized three-dimensional structures that replicate key biological features and functions of human tissues and organs. These characteristics make them powerful model systems for investigating tissue and organ development, homeostasis and regeneration; understanding disease mechanisms; and advancing drug development and personalized medicine. To fully harness their potential, it is essential to develop advanced tools capable of comprehensively profiling their intricate composition. In particular, cutting-edge technologies are needed to accurately characterize their genotypic and phenotypic profiles, including DNA, RNA, proteins and physiological functions. In this Review, we examine molecular and functional profiling methods for organoids, providing an overview of emerging techniques, recent advancements, future technologies, key knowledge gaps and challenges, and a framework for multimodal integration of methods. Additionally, we examine current barriers to progress and explore opportunities to refine organoid profiling methods with the aim of deepening our understanding of organoid biology.

items.title: In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics
items.last_author_affiliation: Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, MA, USA. jeffrey.moffitt@childrens.harvard.edu.; Department of Microbiology, Blavatnik Institute, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. jeffrey.moffitt@childrens.harvard.edu.; Department of Pediatrics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. jeffrey.moffitt@childrens.harvard.edu.; Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA. jeffrey.moffitt@childrens.harvard.edu.
items.abstract: Abstract Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

items.title: PANGEA: an integrated cell atlas across diverse biological contexts enables systematic profiling of multicellular responses in human diseases
items.last_author_affiliation: Graduate School of Medical Science and Engineering, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Daejeon, Republic of Korea. jp24@kaist.ac.kr.; SCL-KAIST Institute of Translational Research, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), Daejeon, Republic of Korea. jp24@kaist.ac.kr.; Systems Virology and Spatial Immunomics Group, Center for Virome and Applied Platform, Korea Virus Research Institute, Institute for Basic Science, Daejeon, Republic of Korea. jp24@kaist.ac.kr.
items.abstract: Diseases affect multiple cell types within tissues, but the overall landscape of the multicellular responses in human diseases remains largely unexplored. Here we categorize the multicellular responses of human diseases based on a remapped atlas of human cells, PANGEA, incorporating 12.6 million cells acquired from a pipeline that automatically processes raw sequence files from public repositories. We constructed a hierarchical cell classification framework comprising 32 major cell types and 165 cellular subtypes. On the basis of this annotation framework, we explored an extensive atlas of human cells containing 46.5 million cells from 160 diseases across 48 organs and revealed core archetypes of human diseases repeatedly found across organs. We show that this cell atlas could also serve as a reference for unbiased analysis in spatial transcriptomics, revealing spatial features associated with immunotherapy responses. Collectively, our study provides foundational resources for cell ontologies, enabling cross-tissue comparisons of cellular features in human diseases.

items.title: High school science ambitions
Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Medical Research and Innovation, Shanghai Pudong Hospital, Fudan University Pudong Medical Center, Institute of Science and Technology for Brain-Inspired Intelligence, Fudan University, Shanghai, China. zhiyuan@fudan.edu.cn.; Center for Integrative Spatial-Omics Research, Fudan University, Shanghai, China. zhiyuan@fudan.edu.cn.; Shanghai Academy of Artificial Intelligence for Science, Shanghai, China. zhiyuan@fudan.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Spatial omics technologies provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate how molecular programs are organized within tissues. However, existing analytical frameworks primarily focus on identifying cellular states and characterizing differentially expressed molecular features across these states. The relational spatial organization of molecular features and its dynamics across biological contexts therefore remain largely unexplored. Here we present Gene SPatial Optimal Transport (GeneSPOT), a gene-centric computational framework for characterizing the spatial relationships among genes and quantifying their reorganization across biological conditions. Although gene-centric in design, GeneSPOT generalizes to other molecular features. Across diverse applications, GeneSPOT resolved tissue structures, integrated paired and unpaired spatial multi-omics data, unveiled the spatial convergence of gene programs during embryonic development and identified aging-associated spatial reorganization among genes whose expression did not change significantly with age. GeneSPOT thus complements conventional cell-centric analysis, providing a framework for deciphering how spatial relationships among molecular features are reorganized across biological conditions and over time.

items.last_author_affiliation: Bezos Centre for Sustainable Protein, Imperial College London, London, UK. r.ledesma-amaro@imperial.ac.uk.; Department of Bioengineering, Imperial College London, London, UK. r.ledesma-amaro@imperial.ac.uk.; UKRI Engineering Biology Mission Hub on Microbial Food, Imperial College London, London, UK. r.ledesma-amaro@imperial.ac.uk.; Imperial College Centre for Engineering Biology, Imperial College London, London, UK. r.ledesma-amaro@imperial.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Cellular agriculture promises to reduce the environmental burden and inefficiencies of food systems. The question is no longer whether precision fermentation and cultivated meat production can produce alternative proteins and other food components, but whether they can attain the cost, scale and quality required for broad adoption. We examine cellular agriculture through the interrelated lenses of enabling technologies, food function and manufacturing economics. The field is approaching an inflection point where biological technology development is less important for commercial success than achieving scalable, affordable manufacturing. Key challenges include how products and their functional attributes are designed and how production processes are configured. For precision fermentation, the most compelling opportunities lie in functional approaches to improve taste, nutritional quality, health benefits and formulation rather than in direct imitation of existing foods or ingredients. For cultivated meat production, impact will come first from hybrid and ingredient-based products that capture specific values of cellular ingredients while avoiding the costs of full tissue mimicry.

items.abstract: To elucidate the genetic architecture of the DNA damage response (DDR) network, we conduct unbiased genetic interaction screens using Cas12a. We disrupt 233 DDR genes frequently mutated in cancer and other genetic diseases, either individually or in pairwise combinations, enabling us to assess the phenotypic effects induced by the loss of DDR gene pairs under unperturbed cell growth conditions. We identify high-confidence positive and negative gene-gene interactions, along with connections between previously unlinked DDR pathways. Among the identified genetic interactions, we uncover synthetic lethal interactions between genes encoding the translesion polymerase REV1-Pol ζ complex and the MCM8-MCM9-HROB DNA helicase complex, between Fanconi anemia genes and various mitotic DNA repair genes, as well as between genes encoding the DNA translocase SMARCAL1 and components of the FANCM complex, suggesting opportunities for targeted treatments in tumors carrying mutations in these genes. Collectively, our genetic map of the DDR network identifies synthetic lethal and buffering interactions with therapeutic potential.

items.title: Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture
items.last_author_affiliation: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, USA. aparkin@lbl.gov.; University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA. aparkin@lbl.gov.
items.abstract: Agriculture is both humanity's largest infrastructure and the leading driver of environmental degradation. Many early-stage biotechnologies could mitigate this impact, but their deployability has not been systematically evaluated. We analyze deployability of 77 biotechnologies across eight domains (crops, soils, livestock, watersheds, aquaculture, health and security, food loss/waste and frontiers) by applying a Balanced Readiness Level assessment spanning technological, market, regulatory, acceptance and organizational dimensions. We find that market viability and social acceptance, not technological readiness, represent the primary constraints. High-readiness technologies tend to be 'drop-in', contained, transient and perceived as natural. These characteristics indicate strategies to elevate overall deployability, such as addressing genetically modified organism containment. Assessing the scalability and environmental impacts of biotechnologies for prioritization requires additional quantitative analysis, as shown in a Fermi analysis of microbial fertilizers. We combine our findings into a near- to long-term roadmap for living infrastructure: predictively designed multicomponent biological communities that function as systems at the ecosystem level to enhance food security and environmental resilience.

items.abstract: Abstract Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

items.abstract: Abstract Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans -eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans -acting genetic variation.

items.title: A multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory effects in sheep
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Quantitative Genetics and Genomics, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark. lingzhao.fang@qgg.au.dk.
items.abstract: Characterizing how genetic variants influence genome function and complex traits in livestock is essential for the development of sustainable precision agriculture and comparative genomics. Here, as part of the Farm Animal Genotype-Tissue Expression (FarmGTEx) project, we present the pilot phase of the SheepGTEx resource by analyzing 6,761 RNA sequencing samples from 51 primary tissues in a multibreed sheep cohort. We identify millions of regulatory variants associated with 7 types of molecular phenotypes and fine-map 322,468 primary and 114,017 nonprimary effects, revealing extensive regulatory allelic heterogeneity. We systematically characterize the pleiotropic effects of these variants on molecular phenotypes; assess their context-specific regulation across tissues, breeds, sexes and developmental stages; and explore their evolutionary constraints across mammals. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of SheepGTEx by identifying regulatory mechanisms underpinning 34 complex traits, population divergence between European and Asian breeds and adaptive evolution in sheep over the past 10 millennia.

items.title: A unified framework for defining and analyzing spatial niches in spatial omics data analysis
items.last_author_affiliation: Biostatistics Program, Public Health Sciences Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle, WA, USA. lijy03@fredhutch.org.; Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. lijy03@fredhutch.org.; Department of Biostatistics, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA. lijy03@fredhutch.org.; Department of Genome Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA. lijy03@fredhutch.org.; Department of Statistics, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA. lijy03@fredhutch.org.
items.abstract: The term 'spatial niche' is widely used in spatial omics analyses but is inconsistently defined across studies. We survey the literature and find that it most commonly refers to the following three distinct concepts: (1) a proximity-based neighborhood around an anchor cell or spatial spot; (2) a computationally derived spatial domain comprising spatially proximal spots or cells with shared molecular features; and (3) a biologically grounded ecosystem comprising cellular and noncellular components that support resident cells. We organize existing studies under this taxonomy and distinguish two main analytical roles-niches as spot-level covariates for modeling local context, and niches as spot clusters for within-niche and between-niche compositional and molecular analyses. To reduce ambiguity, we recommend reserving 'niche' for biological ecosystems while using 'spatial neighborhood' and 'spatial domain' for the corresponding computational constructs. We also provide a practical decision framework to help researchers align niche definitions and analytical strategies with the biological questions at hand.

items.abstract: Population-scale single-cell RNA sequencing enables mapping genetic effects on gene regulation at the cellular level (for example, single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTLs)). However, existing sc-eQTL mapping approaches are either not designed for analyzing sparse counts in single-cell RNA sequencing data or become computationally intractable at scale. Here we developed jaxQTL-an efficient pseudobulk sc-eQTL mapping framework using highly efficient count-based models. In simulations, we demonstrated that jaxQTL with a negative binomial model provides calibrated inference while outperforming linear models. In OneK1K data, jaxQTL identified 16% more eGenes than linear models, while running substantially faster than single-cell Poisson mixed effect models. We found that fine-mapped sc-eQTLs are more distal from transcription starting site than those identified in all cells (bulk-eQTLs; P = 1 × 10-4) and more enriched in cell-type-specific enhancers (P = 3 × 10-10), revealing distal regulatory effects that are missed in bulk tissues. Although sc-eQTLs are largely shared across cell types, cell-type-specificity increases with distance to transcription starting site. Finally, sc-eQTLs explain a greater proportion of single nucleotide polymorphism-heritability than bulk-eQTLs across 16 blood and immune-related traits (9.90 ± 0.88% versus 6.10 ± 0.76%) and prioritize disease-associated genes missed by the bulk approach (such as IL6ST), improving, but not closing, the missing link between genome-wide association studies and eQTLs.

items.last_author_affiliation: Montreal Heart Institute, Montreal, Quebec, Canada. guillaume.lettre@umontreal.ca.; Faculty of Medicine, University of Montreal, Montreal, Quebec, Canada. guillaume.lettre@umontreal.ca.
items.abstract: Fine-mapping methods based on summary statistics from genome-wide association studies and linkage disequilibrium (LD) information are widely used to identify potential causal variants. However, LD mismatch between the external LD reference panel and the genome-wide association study population is common and can compromise fine-mapping accuracy. Here we developed Robust SparsePro (RSparsePro), a probabilistic graphical model with an efficient variational inference algorithm, to perform robust fine-mapping in the presence of LD mismatch. In simulation studies with varying degrees of LD mismatch, RSparsePro identified credible sets with consistently higher power and coverage than existing methods. In fine-mapping cis-protein quantitative trait loci and complex trait risk loci, RSparsePro identified credible sets with consistently higher enrichment of variants with potential functional impacts and cross-study and cross-LD-reference-panel replication rates. RSparsePro also identified biologically relevant variants in drug target genes and implicated potential regulatory mechanisms for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol.

items.title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN, USA. borlaug.barry@mayo.edu.
items.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s-1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=-0.46, P<0.001 and r=-0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide's improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496.

items.title: Hemodynamic effects of semaglutide in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Quantitative Health Sciences, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, FL, USA.
items.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide improves symptoms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) through unclear mechanisms. Here, in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 81 patients (47 women) with HFpEF and obesity to semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in invasively measured pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), a direct measure of cardiac congestion, during low-intensity exercise. Additional mechanistic outcomes included other hemodynamic measures and hemodynamic HFpEF remission (defined as normal PAWP under conditions of both rest and exercise at 52 weeks). At baseline, PAWP was 17.5 ± 4.3 mmHg at rest and 31.7 ± 5.2 mmHg during exercise. After 52 weeks, the mean change in PAWP during exercise was -9.8 (95% confidence interval (CI): -11.3 to -8.2) mmHg with semaglutide and +0.9 (95% CI: -1.3 to 3.0) mmHg with placebo (estimated difference, -10.6 mmHg; 95% CI: -13.3 to -8.0; P < 0.0001). As compared to placebo, semaglutide also decreased resting PAWP (estimated difference, -7.1 mmHg; 95% CI: -9.8 to -4.4; P < 0.0001), and semaglutide-treated patients were more likely to experience hemodynamic remission (53.7% versus 7.4%, odds ratio = 14.1, 95% CI: 3.0-134.6, P < 0.001). The results from this trial indicate that, in patients with HFpEF and obesity, treatment with semaglutide reduced left heart filling pressures during exercise and at rest and was associated with hemodynamic HFpEF remission in over half of treated patients. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05371496 .

items.title: An ulcerative colitis taxonomy defined by individual patient-reported response trajectories
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.; Center for Human Immunobiology, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago, IL, USA.
items.abstract: Abstract A barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response-trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor). Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 576 participants linked PRO-defined vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single cell, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics identified vascular inflammation as associated with vedolizumab nonresponse through interactions between SPP1 + macrophages and endothelial cells. In two separate real-world cohorts of 4,981 and 3,854 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anticytokine therapies. These findings define a response-trajectory-based taxonomy that requires prospective validation for clinical utility and applications for selecting vedolizumab combination therapy in UC.
