items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong 999077, China.; State Key Laboratory of Synthetic Chemistry, HKU-CAS Joint Laboratory on New Materials and Shanghai-Hong Kong Joint Laboratory on Chemical Synthesis, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong 999077, China.; Materials Innovation Institute for Life Sciences and Energy (MILES), HKU-SIRI, Shenzhen 518045, China.
items.abstract: Polyradicals in open-shell polycyclic hydrocarbons (PHs) offer access to multiple spin states and hold great promise for spintronics and quantum technologies. Here we report a nonalternant, air-stable tetraradical featuring two fused 7-5-7 rings and a strongly correlated singlet ground state. This molecule displays an exceptional tetraradical character ( y 0 = 1.00, y 1 = 0.89) and exhibits long ambient stability ( t 1/2 = 33 days). Comprehensive electronic structure and magnetic response analyses reveal that the spin topology is governed by both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, with robust electron correlation ( J 1 = +321 K, J 2 = −44 K, and J 3 = −29 K). The unique nonalternant design suppresses hyperfine and vibrational decoherence, giving rise to long spin relaxation and coherence time. These findings demonstrate that embedding nonalternant motifs into PH polyradicals provides a powerful strategy to simultaneously promote molecular stability, spin-exchange coupling, and spin robustness—key features for materials in the rising field of quantum information science.

items.title: Dual-action small-molecule VSP-51-2 ameliorates polycystic ovary syndrome via PPARγ modulation and AKR1C3 inhibition
items.last_author_affiliation: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Molecular Target and Clinical Pharmacology, the State Key Laboratory of Respiratory Disease, The Third Affiliated Hospital & School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou 511436, China.
items.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a prevalent multifactorial endocrine disorder, is inadequately managed by current therapies that fail to concurrently target its core metabolic (insulin resistance) and reproductive (hyperandrogenism) pathologies. We report VSP-51-2, a dual-target lead compound initially engineered as a selective PPARγ modulator that unexpectedly exerts potent uncompetitive inhibition of the androgen-synthesizing enzyme AKR1C3 through a putative allosteric mechanism. In preclinical PCOS models, VSP-51-2 restored regular estrous cyclicity, improved ovarian follicular morphology, enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity, suppressed hyperandrogenism, and did not significantly perturb measured hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis hormonal parameters. Mechanistically, it blocks PPARγ phosphorylation at Ser 273 , thereby enhancing adiponectin secretion and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, and is predicted to bind a putative allosteric pocket of AKR1C3 to constrain androgen biosynthesis. These findings support VSP-51-2 as a preclinical proof-of-concept compound for a dual-target strategy that addresses metabolic dysfunction and androgen excess through a unified molecular scaffold.

items.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Urology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, Hubei 430074, P. R. China.; State Key Laboratory of Materials Processing and Die & Mould Technology, and Hubei Key Laboratory of Bioinorganic Chemistry and Materia Medica, School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan 430074, P. R. China.
items.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

items.title: Comprehensive degron mapping in human transcription factors
items.last_author_affiliation: The Linderstrøm-Lang Centre for Protein Science, Department of Biology, University of Copenhagen, Ole Maaløes Vej 5, 2200N Copenhagen, Denmark.
items.abstract: Gene expression is regulated by the targeted degradation of transcription factors through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Transcription factors destined for degradation are recognized by E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases through motifs termed degrons, embedded within the sequence. In this study, we systematically map degrons in all 1626 human transcription factors. We find thousands of both known and previously unidentified degrons and characterize their sequence properties. Active degrons placed within exposed and intrinsically disordered regions contribute to modulating the abundance of the transcription factors, while the most common somatic mutations that are linked to skin cutaneous melanoma lead to unfolding and exposure of a latent degron buried in the zinc finger structure. We present examples of compartment-specific degrons and demonstrate that variant effects in transcription factors correlate with degron potency. Last, we show that while >60% of all predicted transcriptional activation domains overlap with strong degrons, acidic residues within the remaining transactivating regions counter the degron potency, showing how degrons can shape the transcription factor sequence landscape.

items.title: Reciprocal control of genome instability and RNA processing in cancer: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Oncology and Hemato-Oncology, University of Milan, 20142 Milan, Italy.; Italian Institute for Genomic Medicine, c/o IRCCS, Str. Prov.le 142, km 3.95, 10060 Candiolo (TO), Italy.; IFOM ETS - The AIRC Institute of Molecular Oncology, Milan, Italy.
items.abstract: Genomic instability and dysregulated RNA processing are each recognized as core hallmarks of cancer, but accumulating evidence indicates that they are mechanistically intertwined rather than independent features. Chromosomal instability, mismatch-repair deficiency, and homologous recombination deficiency can reshape RNA splicing, 3′ end formation, and RNA surveillance through changes in gene dosage, DNA damage signaling, and alterations in regulatory elements. Conversely, aberrant splicing, polyadenylation, and RNA modifications can impair DNA repair, perturb mitotic control, and promote replication stress, thereby reinforcing genomic instability. This bidirectional circuit drives clinically relevant phenotypes, including therapeutic resistance, immune modulation, and emergent vulnerabilities that are not captured by DNA-centric biomarkers alone. Here, we present a unified framework for the genome instability–RNA processing axis and its direct clinical implications for cancer diagnosis, treatment stratification, and therapeutic exploitation, highlighting the most actionable mechanistic interfaces and discussing how integrated DNA-RNA biomarkers and rational combination strategies could extend precision oncology beyond static genomic lesions.

items.title: A primordial heavy water reservoir in the outer solar system
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences, UCLA, Los Angeles, CA 90095, USA.
items.abstract: The oxygen (O) isotopic composition of outer solar system ices is believed to be enriched in heavy O isotopes owing to photochemical processes, but evidence for this O reservoir is exceedingly rare in meteorites. Hydrated interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) collected in Earth’s stratosphere that display high densities of solar energetic particle tracks originate from Edgeworth-Kuiper belt objects. Their mineralogy is dominated by hydrated minerals that formed by alteration of anhydrous precursor minerals at low temperatures through reactions with water (H 2 O)–carbon dioxide fluids. The O isotopic compositions of track-rich hydrated IDPs implicate 17,18 O-rich ices as the source of H 2 O involved in their alteration, providing compelling evidence for the presence of a major heavy water reservoir beyond the orbits of the gas giant planets that was largely isolated from inner solar system materials.

items.title: The Azores plume origin of the New England Seamounts chain
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China.
items.abstract: Age-progressive seamount chains are fundamental archives in revealing the past plate motion and mantle convection. However, for a representative example such as the New England Seamounts chain on the North American Plate, both its plume source and its evolutionary trajectory remain debatable. This long-lasting uncertainty is mainly caused by the absence of quantitative high-resolution constraints on plume dynamics and its interactions with multiple plates. Here, we aim to answer this question using data-assimilation–based numerical simulations. We propose that the New England chain and the Corner Seamounts on the North American Plate, the Great Meteor Seamounts on the African Plate, and the Azores archipelago on the Eurasian Plate were created by a single plume—the Azores plume. This plume experienced two stages of motion through time. Subduction-induced sublithospheric mantle flow exerts a dominant control on the spatiotemporal distribution of volcanoes along the track and the geometry of this track, surpassing the influence of plume-plate interaction. The latter primarily affects the continuity of this trans-plate hotspot system. These findings offer a reinterpretation of hotspot-track formation and new constraints on how mantle flow reorganizes across multiple plates.

items.title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
items.last_author_affiliation: Natural Resources Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, 601 Booth Street, Ottawa K1A 0G1, Ontario, Canada.
items.abstract: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

items.title: A single–amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Microbiology, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA.; Global Health and Emerging Pathogens Institute, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA.
items.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

items.title: Reprogramming electron transfer at single-atom Pt sites to break the interference barrier in uric acid detection
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Green Pesticide, International Joint Research Center for Intelligent Biosensing Technology and Health, College of Chemistry, Central China Normal University, Wuhan 430079, P.R. China.
items.abstract: Uric acid (UA) serves as a key biomarker for gout, cardiovascular disease, and kidney dysfunction, yet conventional detection methods relying on H 2 O 2 generation suffer from signal instability and interference from reductive species. Here, we report a uricase-like platinum-nitrogen-carbon nanozyme (Pt-N-C-NH 3 ) that redirects UA oxidation from a two-electron pathway toward a four-electron pathway. By decreasing graphitic nitrogen content, the local electronic microenvironment of platinum sites is modulated, which is associated with a lower calculated free-energy change for the rate-determining absorbed oxygen to absorbed hydroxyl transformation from 1.25 to 0.62 electron volts and thereby promoting oxygen reduction to water. Integrated into a microneedle sensing platform, UA is converted to allantoin for chemiluminescent readout. The sensor exhibits a wide linear range of 50.00 to 1000.00 μM and a detection limit of 15.86 μM, while maintaining 97.57% signal stability against reductive interferents. This work demonstrates that atomic-level coordination engineering enables programmable control over reaction pathways in artificial enzyme systems, thereby facilitating robust biosensing in complex biological environments.

items.title: Dynamic plasmonic imaging of electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for charge-resolved multiplex biosensing
items.last_author_affiliation: Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Intelligent Sensing Technology and Advanced Medical Instrument, Key Laboratory for Biomedical Engineering of Education Ministry, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China.
items.abstract: Multiplexed profiling of diverse biomarkers is essential for precision diagnostics, but remains challenging for label-free sensors because signals typically scale with analyte mass. Here, we present a dynamic plasmonic imaging platform based on electromechanically driven nano-oscillators for multiplexed, label-free quantification of nucleic acids, proteins, and small molecules within a unified sensing architecture. Size-encoded nanoparticles tethered to a plasmonic surface are electrically actuated to oscillate vertically within the evanescent field and tracked by distance-resolved surface plasmon resonance imaging. Molecular binding alters the effective surface charge of each nano-oscillator, modulating the electrostatic-driven forces and changing oscillation amplitude. This charge-to-motion transduction mechanism reduces dependence on molecular mass and enhances sensitivity for low–molecular weight analytes. This platform simultaneously detects microRNAs, proteins, and small molecules spanning a ∼300-fold molecular weight range within a single field of view. We further demonstrate multiplexed profiling of tumor-associated microRNAs in pretreated supernatants from patient-derived breast cancer cells across 24 clinical samples. Dynamic plasmonic nano-oscillators provide a scalable architecture for multiplex molecular diagnostics.

items.title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Environment, Earth and Ecosystem Sciences, The Open University, UK.
items.abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

items.title: Segmented projection image translation for large-area, high-resolution vat photopolymerization
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Radiology, Stanford University, 318 Campus Drive, Stanford, CA 94305-5427, USA.; Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University, 318 Campus Drive, Stanford, CA 94305-5427, USA.
items.abstract: High-resolution projection-based vat photopolymerization (VP) 3D printing enables rapid fabrication of highly detailed polymeric structures. However, expanding the build area traditionally compromises resolution, creating a fundamental trade-off between projected pixel size and printable area due to fixed digital micromirror device (DMD) pixel counts. Herein, we introduce segmented projection image translation (SPIN), a simple implementation strategy that expands the effective projection area by applying controlled orbital translation to an off-axis objective lens within the optical infinity space. In this work, we demonstrate a projection-based VP printer implemented with SPIN that expands the effective build area by 4.8-fold, from a native field of 60.4 square millimeters to an expanded domain of 290.5 square millimeters. The SPIN-enabled printer produces isolated line features as thin as 9.8 ± 2.2 micrometers and fabricates intricate three-dimensional truss structures with features as small as 30 micrometers. These results validate a practical route for extending microscale projection-based VP printing to larger build areas while preserving feature fidelity across stitched exposure fields.

items.title: STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences and Biotechnology, Chungbuk National University, Cheongju 28644, Republic of Korea.
items.abstract: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a pleiotropic cytokine that drives macrophage functions ranging from tissue homeostasis to inflammation, yet how STAT3 specifies these divergent outcomes remains unclear. By integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with selective STAT3 degradation, we show that STAT3 controls IL-6–induced epigenomic remodeling and restrains a latent STAT1-associated interferon program in human macrophages. Graded STAT3 chromatin recruitment scales with locus-specific H3K27ac deposition and transcriptional output across homeostatic and inflammatory programs. STAT3 degradation permits STAT1 recruitment at a subset of regulatory regions and engages a delayed amplification loop that is partially dependent on STING and type I IFN signaling. In severe COVID-19, monocytes exhibit exaggerated STAT3-associated inflammatory signatures together with attenuated STAT1-associated interferon responses, consistent with a skewed STAT3-STAT1 balance. These findings define a framework in which STAT3 calibrates IL-6–induced chromatin output while maintaining pathway fidelity by limiting STAT1 cross-talk.

items.title: A full-hardware edge detection system based on a highly robust dual random number generator
items.last_author_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Brain-Like Neuromorphic Devices and Systems of Hebei Province, College of Electron and Information Engineering, Hebei University, Baoding 071002, P. R. China.; Department of Materials Science and Engineering, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117575, Singapore.
items.abstract: Conventional edge computing hardware at autonomous driving terminals is limited by chip area and power efficiency for complex image data. Recently, researchers have used memristors to construct dedicated hardware systems, achieving advancements in multiple image processing fields such as pattern recognition and edge detection. However, a full-hardware image processing system with anti-interference, low power, and high real-time performance remains challenging. Here, we fabricated a volatile Ag/AlO x /n-Si memristor with exceptional stability and low power. High-resolution electron microscopy visualized Ag conductive filament formation. Integrating two memristors with a logic circuit, we designed a low-power edge detection unit using dual random number hardware computation. Its energy consumption is 92.3% lower than traditional logic circuits, with strong anti-interference. To validate practical use, we constructed a 32-channel parallel full-hardware system with 64 devices, achieving 31.25 frames per second and excellent edge detection. The system exhibits excellent scalability, stability, and anti-interference, offering great potential for edge vision hardware in autonomous driving, safety monitoring, and surgical assistance.

items.title: Symmetry as a common origin of hierarchical emergence and abstraction
items.last_author_affiliation: Sussex AI and Sussex Centre for Consciousness Science, Department of Informatics, University of Sussex, Brighton, UK.; Centre for Complexity Science and Department of Brain Sciences, Imperial College London, London, UK.; Centre for Eudaimonia and Human Flourishing, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK.; XOR Labs, London, UK.
items.abstract: Many systems of interest exhibit nested emergent layers with their own rules and regularities, and our knowledge about them seems naturally organized around these levels. How do such hierarchical structures arise, and why should observers track these hierarchies so closely? This paper proposes symmetry as an answer to both questions. By combining principles from information theory, group theory, and statistical mechanics, it is shown that dynamical processes that are equivariant with respect to a symmetry group give rise to multiple emergent macroscopic levels arranged according to the algebraic structure of the symmetry. The same symmetries shape the Bayesian beliefs of an observer with only partial access to the system, yielding a matching hierarchy of “abstract” beliefs that can be updated autonomously at different levels of resolution. These ideas are illustrated in Hopfield networks, where familiar macroscopic quantities emerge from known symmetries, and in Boolean models of gene regulation, where symmetries are instead found from the dynamics. The computational advantages provided by symmetry are showcased in Ehrenfest diffusion and epidemic modeling, where abstract beliefs enable Bayesian inference over exponentially large state spaces. These results identify symmetry as a sufficient mechanism for hierarchical emergence and—at the same time—for the capacity of abstract beliefs to mirror the systems they track, making feasible inferential problems that would otherwise be intractable.

items.title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Cellular Neurophysiology, HUN-REN Institute of Experimental Medicine, Budapest 1083, Hungary.
items.abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid–releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

items.title: Tracing Neanderthal ancestry patterns through successive population expansions in Europe
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Genetics and Evolution, University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.; Institute of Genetics and Genomics in Geneva (IGE3), University of Geneva, Geneva, Switzerland.
items.abstract: During their expansion from Africa, modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in introgression of Neanderthal DNA into their genomes. This process contributed to a Southeast-to-Northwest gradient of Neanderthal ancestry across Europe. We investigate the population dynamics underlying the emergence and persistence of this gradient through two successive human range expansions. We developed a three-population, layered, spatially explicit simulation framework to track the spatiotemporal evolution of Neanderthal ancestry under a model of interactions among Neanderthals, pre-Neolithic hunter-gatherers, and Neolithic farmers. Our results indicate that the ancestry cline emerged from the interplay between the direction of the initial hunter-gatherer expansion, the northern limit of the Neanderthal range, and strong reproductive isolation, without requiring natural selection. The similar direction of the subsequent Neolithic expansion explains the cline’s persistence and Neanderthal ancestry differences between hunter-gatherers and farmers. These findings demonstrate how spatiotemporal patterns in ancient DNA provide insights into past population dynamics.

items.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
items.last_author_affiliation: The Department of Microbiology and Immunology, The University of Melbourne at the Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity, Melbourne, Australia.; International Collaboration Unit, International Institute for Zoonosis Control, and the Institute for Vaccine Research and Development, Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan.
items.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell. The compounds show exceptional antiviral activity both in vitro and in vivo and protect against influenza illness in ferrets and in mice after a single dose, either therapeutically or prophylactically.

items.title: Visualizing nanoscopic acoustic mode competition in a van der Waals ferroelectric
items.last_author_affiliation: Materials Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL 60439, USA.; Advanced Photon Source, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, IL 60439, USA.
items.abstract: Understanding how low-dimensional ferroelectrics respond to ultrafast excitation at nanoscales is essential for controlling energy flow and mechanical functionality in next-generation polar devices, yet the nanoscopic structural response to ultrafast depolarization remains unresolved, obscuring the microscopic pathways of acoustic decoherence and energy dissipation. Here, we spatiotemporally resolve lattice motion in the van der Waals ferroelectric NbOI 2 using combined ultrafast electron microscopy and diffraction, revealing three acoustic phonons: two transverse shear modes and one longitudinal breathing mode. The transverse mode that shears the layers perpendicular to the in-plane polar axis dominates over that along the polar axis, reflecting anisotropic polarization-strain coupling. Real-space mapping uncovers spatially correlated heterogeneity in mode amplitudes and lifetimes. Regions dominated by a single shear mode exhibit significantly longer acoustic lifetimes than multimode regions, suggesting acoustic phonon–phonon scattering as a major source of decoherence. Our results provide a microscopic understanding of ultrafast depolarization-driven acoustic dynamics and spatially heterogeneous energy dissipation in van der Waals ferroelectrics.

items.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Microbiology and Cell Science, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA.
items.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

items.title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Neuro-Medical Science, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Osaka, Suita, Osaka, Japan.; Department of Molecular Neuroscience, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Osaka, Suita, Osaka, Japan.; WPI Immunology Frontier Research Center, The University of Osaka, Osaka, Japan.; Graduate School of Frontier Bioscience, The University of Osaka, Suita, Osaka, Japan.
items.abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1 -targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

items.title: Photonic entanglement swapping with remote quantum dots
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physics, Sapienza University of Rome, Rome 00185, Italy.
items.abstract: Entanglement swapping is a protocol that details how to create entanglement between previously uncorrelated particles. Its photonic version, mediated by the interference of photon pairs generated by separate quantum systems, finds disparate applications in quantum networks. So far, entanglement swapping with entangled photons from remote systems has been implemented only using probabilistic sources. However, the scaling up of quantum networks requires nonprobabilistic quantum emitters without a trade-off between the degree of entanglement and photon-pair generation rate. Here, we demonstrate photonic entanglement swapping using photon pairs generated by two separate GaAs quantum dots. The emitters are deterministically embedded in hybrid semiconductor-piezoelectric devices that make the entangled photons from two dissimilar quantum dots nearly identical. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated with a fidelity as high as 0.71(2), more than 10 SDs above the classical limit. The experimental data are quantitatively explained by a theoretical model that also suggests how to boost the protocol performance. Our work opens the path to the exploitation of quantum dot entangled-photon sources in quantum repeater networks.

items.title: Nonlinear cooling and control of a mechanical quantum harmonic oscillator
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute for Quantum Electronics, ETH Zürich, Otto-Stern-Weg 1, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland.; Quantum Center, ETH Zürich, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland.
items.abstract: Nonlinearities are a key feature allowing nonclassical control of quantum harmonic oscillators. However, when nonlinearities are strong, designing protocols for control is often difficult, placing a barrier to exploiting these properties fully. In this work, using a single trapped-ion oscillator operated in the strongly nonlinear regime of the atom-light interaction, we show how to generate localized multi (two, three, four, and five)–component Schrödinger’s cat manifolds using a novel form of nonlinear reservoir engineering. We then specifically select Hamiltonians which allow us to perform measurements on these state manifolds. Our work demonstrates the experimental use of high-order nonlinear processes for control of nonclassical states of a quantum harmonic oscillator, opening up a new toolbox which can be applied to bosonic quantum error correction, computation, and sensing.

items.title: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with high-rate symplectic double codes
items.last_author_affiliation: RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing (RQC), Wako, Saitama 351-0198, Japan.; Corporate Laboratory, Toshiba Corporation, Kawasaki, Kanagawa 212-8582, Japan.
items.abstract: High-rate and large-distance quantum codes are expected to make fault-tolerant quantum computing more efficient, but most of them lack efficient fault-tolerant encoded-state preparation methods. We propose such fault-tolerant encoders for two symplectic double codes, [[30,6,5]] and [[36,12,5]]. The advantage of these codes is their compactness, namely, their small code block sizes for their high encoding rates and large distance, allowing for early experimental realization of high-rate codes. Detecting crucial errors during encoding with as few auxiliary qubits as possible, our encoders can reduce resource overheads while keeping low logical error rates compared to more naive methods. Numerical simulations with a circuit-level noise model demonstrate the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed methods. We also develop arbitrary-state encoders that enable the injection of arbitrary quantum states into the code spaces. Combined with basic fault-tolerant operations, they support universal quantum computation. We thus demonstrate that efficient and reliable logical state preparation is achievable even for compact and high-rate codes, offering a potential step toward efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing suitable for near-term experiments.

items.title: CD8 + T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Neuroimmunology and Multiple Sclerosis, University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany.
items.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

items.title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Forensic Medicine, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark.
items.abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

items.title: Weak adsorption, strong consequences: How trace gases control ice growth and quasi-liquid-layer structure
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Earth and Environmental Science, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.; Department of Chemistry, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.
items.abstract: Gases in the atmosphere are often treated as passive background species in cold environments, yet their molecular roles at icy interfaces remain poorly understood. Here, we show how hydrophobic and hydrophilic trace gases can actively reorganize the ice interface and regulate freezing through interfacial stabilization. We find these gases can actively modulate both the kinetics and thermodynamics of the water-ice interface. Using molecular simulations, we find that all gases examined retard ice-front propagation relative to pure water to different extents. This slowing arises from weak but preferential adsorption at the water-ice interface, where gases occupy water-dense interfacial layers and locally suppress ice-like ordering. After freezing is complete, gases do not distribute uniformly across the frozen surface, but partition selectively among multiple adsorption regions across the ice–quasi-liquid-layer (QLL)–air interfacial landscape. Relatively hydrophobic gases exhibit a three-region adsorption pattern, whereas relatively hydrophilic gases occupy only two dominant adsorption regions. Despite these differences, both classes preferentially accumulate near the QLL-air boundary and its immediate outer region rather than the ice-QLL interface. There, gases pair with and compensate for dangling surface bonds (through a surface-passivating effect reminiscent of ligand stabilization), reducing the thermodynamic driving force for premelting and thereby thinning the QLL. These results establish a unified molecular picture in which atmospheric gases are active interfacial modulators of both ice growth and ice structure, with implications for freezing, ice-cloud microphysics, and heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry.

items.title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery, Stanford Medical School, 300 Pasteur Drive, Stanford, CA 94303, USA.
items.abstract: Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in split ends ( spen ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in spen mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in spen mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in spen -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

items.title: Deep learning–assisted electron microscopy for apparent Z-height mapping of atomically dispersed catalysts
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Materials Science and Engineering, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China.; AI for Science Institute, Beijing 100084, China.
items.abstract: Atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer maximal metal utilization and local atomic/electronic structures, yet resolving their actual atomic configurations using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) remains fundamentally constrained by depth ambiguity and complex experimental noise. Existing STEM–machine learning (ML) approaches often rely on ideal simulations or manual annotations, limiting their transferability to realistic ADC images and causing ambiguity between isolated atoms, projected dimers, and small clusters. Here, we develop a physics-informed, domain-adaptive CycleGAN-UNet framework for depth-aware ADC analysis. CycleGAN translates height-labeled simulations into experimental-like images while preserving atomic coordinates and apparent Z-height labels, and a depth-supervised UNet performs simultaneous atom localization and discrete Z-height classification. Support-specific simulations further incorporate support-dependent background contrast, including uniform amorphous carbon (am-C), am-C with local thickness variation, and crystalline supports, thereby improving the applicability of the framework to different ADC imaging conditions. Across diverse metals (Mn, Fe, Cu, Pd, and Pt) and supports (am-C, black phosphorus, and polymeric carbon nitride), the framework achieves high atom detection precision (∼95%) and reliable apparent Z-height classification at ∼2-nanometer binning. By encoding depth-dependent beam broadening features, the framework converts conventional 2D projections into quantitative, apparent Z-height atomic maps. In geminal Pt/PCN catalysts, it resolves the loading-dependent transition from isolated Pt monomers to Pt 2 sites and links these configurations to dehydrogenative aromatization activity. This framework transforms STEM images from projected atom maps into quantitative, depth-aware atomic descriptors for ADC structure–activity analysis.

items.title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Endocrinology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA.; School of Biochemistry and Immunology, Trinity Biomedical Sciences Institute, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland.; Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Princeton Branch, Princeton, NJ, USA.; Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA.
items.abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n = 42), and histology ( n = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

items.title: Electrical spin pumping in exchange-coupled molecules
items.last_author_affiliation: Physikalisches Institut (PHI), Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Karlsruhe, Germany.; Center for Integrated Quantum Science and Technology (IQST), Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany.
items.abstract: Electron spins in single molecules are a promising platform for quantum information processing. However, their practical implementation as qubits requires reliable control at the single-entity level, including an efficient state initialization. Here, we demonstrate the remote, all-electrical spin pumping of the electron spin in single molecules: Using electron spin resonance scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigate coupled pairs of S = 1/2 molecules, where one molecule serves as a readout and pumping unit for the neighboring one. We show that the exchange interaction between them enables angular momentum transfer, which allows for the control of the remote spin state via the direction and magnitude of the spin-polarized tunneling current and the exchange coupling strength. These results establish a general, all-electrical approach for remote spin pumping that is transferable to a wider range of spin-based quantum architectures.

items.title: MAIT cells exacerbate early liver fibrosis by downsizing the intrahepatic regulatory T cell compartment
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Western University, London, ON, Canada.; Collaborative Specialization in Machine Learning in Health and Biomedical Sciences, Western University, London, ON, Canada.; Department of Oncology, Western University, London, ON, Canada.; Division of General Surgery, Department of Surgery, Western University, London, ON, Canada.; Division of Clinical Immunology and Allergy, Department of Medicine, Western University, London, ON, Canada.; Lawson Health Research Institute, London Health Sciences Centre, London, ON, Canada.
items.abstract: Mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells have been paradoxically implicated in tissue repair and fibrosis. However, when and how they modulate fibrogenesis in distinct tissue environments remain unclear. Using the carbon tetrachloride model of liver injury in major histocompatibility complex–related protein 1 (MR1)– and MAIT cell–sufficient and –deficient mice, we identify MAIT cells as early drivers of fibrogenesis. MAIT cells exacerbated hepatocellular injury, myofibroblast activation, and matrix deposition during fibrosis initiation, coinciding with rapid polarization toward a MAIT17 phenotype and induction of a profibrotic transcriptional program. Despite acquiring an exhaustion-associated phenotype, MAIT cells retained their effector functions. Mechanistically, MAIT cells limited hepatic regulatory T (T reg ) cell accumulation, accompanied by reduced Ki-67 and CXCR3 levels in the latter population. Furthermore, in vivo T reg cell inactivation abrogated MAIT cell–dependent differences in fibrosis severity. Together, these findings identify MAIT cells as early orchestrators of fibrogenesis and reveal a previously unappreciated MAIT-T reg axis that can be therapeutically targeted in the early stages of fibrotic diseases.

items.title: High-impulse and reactant-regenerative combustion-based micro actuators
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Electromechanical Engineering, Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics, University of Macau, Macau SAR, 999078, China.
items.abstract: The use of combustibles in micro-actuator technologies enables powerful impulsive actuation capabilities comparable to those of natural organisms. However, the exogenous dependence of fuel limits the development of combustion-based actuators. We present a closed-cycle reactant regeneration strategy wherein the bidirectional interconversion between hydrogen and water achieves real-time fuel replenishment for reactant-regenerative electrolysis and combustion reactions. Based on this, we develop a 1.5-centimeter actuator that generates forces above 20 newtons and operates continuously for >7200 cycles without refueling (a two orders-of-magnitude improvement over existing combustion-based actuators). Experiments confirm its strength and cross-environment versatility for removing obstacles, jetting, and striking via underwater cavitation. These features enable the actuator to be integrated into small robotic platforms, allowing them to reconfigure local surroundings in an active manner.

items.title: Structure of the Chimalliviridae bacteriophage Goslar reveals host recognition and infection machinery
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cellular & Molecular Medicine, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA.; Department of Molecular Biology, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093, USA.
items.abstract: Large-genome bacteriophages (phages) of the Chimalliviridae family have a distinctive life cycle, building compartments inside infected bacterial cells that broadly protect their genomes from host defenses. Here, we use cryo–electron microscopy to determine a structure of the Escherichia coli –infecting Chimalliviridae phage Goslar. We combine manual modeling of 25 structural proteins with AlphaFold structure predictions of an additional three proteins to generate a composite model with 2888 protein chains from 28 different structural proteins, totaling more than 1.4 million amino acid residues. Our structure reveals the architecture of the Goslar capsid, portal, tail, and baseplate, highlighting structural similarities and differences with other tailed phages. Combining our structural data with quantitative mass spectrometry of Goslar virions, we identify several high-copy virion-associated proteins that likely play key roles when injected into host cells upon infection. We also identify a Chimalliviridae -specific family of proteins that form long, flexible filaments anchored at the phage baseplate and which incorporate carbohydrate-binding domains, suggesting a key role in host recognition.

items.title: Prebiotic magnetite enables chirality-magnetic surface feedback
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA.
items.abstract: The emergence of biomolecular homochirality requires both an initial symmetry-breaking event and a mechanism to amplify and preserve a chiral imbalance. Magnetic minerals have been shown to function as chiral agents through the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect and may have enabled homochirality on early Earth, yet the magnetic properties of magnetite formed under realistic prebiotic conditions remain unexplored. Here, we show that magnetite synthesized through two geochemically plausible pathways—UV-driven photo-oxidation and nitrite-mediated oxidation of Fe(II)—produces particles dominated by single-vortex and multivortex magnetic domain states. Magnetic measurements and electron microscopy confirm that these populations differ markedly from the nano-fabricated thin-film substrates conventionally used in previous CISS experiments. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we demonstrate that single-domain and vortex-state grains undergo irreversible, exchange-driven remagnetization when interacting with spin-polarized homochiral compounds. This magnetic irreversibility provides a robust mechanism for storing and reinforcing weak chiral bias, suggesting that prebiotic magnetite could have contributed to the emergence and stabilization of persistent chiral bias on early Earth.

items.title: Real-time complex-valued RF blind source separation via in-physics computing
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Information Photonics and Optical Communications, Beijing. University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, China.
items.abstract: The rise of edge-centric 6G networks demands real-time intelligent processing of heterogeneous radio-frequency (RF) signals. Complex-valued blind source separation (CV-BSS) provides a physical-layer capability, enabling the blind extraction of source components from overlapping RF signals. Here, we demonstrate an integrated photonic vector processor (IPVP) that implements real-time CV-BSS via in-physics computation directly on raw RF signals. The IPVP operates across multiple RF bands up to 24 GHz and achieves blind, in-hardware adaptation to unknown sources and channels via in situ learning. Experiments demonstrate the efficacy of IPVP in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications and multi-band radar interference suppression. The IPVP reduces the EVMs of the two recovered signals from over 50% to 6.18% and 5.3%, respectively, while enhancing the SIR by up to 26 dB. This work demonstrates, to our knowledge, the first photonic processor capable of real-time CV-BSS at RF, highlighting the potential of integrated photonic hardware for ultralow-latency, edge-intelligent signal processing.

items.title: Microscale patchiness controls resource acquisition in populations of foraging bacteria
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Environmental Engineering, Department of Civil, Environmental, and Geomatic Engineering, ETH Zurich, 8093 Zurich, Switzerland.
items.abstract: Chemotaxis, the ability of cells to detect and respond to chemical gradients, allows them to acquire nutrients, seek hosts, or escape toxins. However, directly measuring bacterial foraging in spatially structured nutrient environments has proven elusive. We developed a new approach to investigate bacterial foraging, on timescales from milliseconds to hours, when exposed to nutrient fluctuations and microscale patchiness mimicking realistic ocean conditions. We generated dynamic, patchy, nutrient landscapes in a large microfluidic arena and simultaneously tracked individual cells of the marine bacterium Vibrio anguillarum . Analyzing single-cell nutrient exposure for tens of thousands of cells revealed that the nutrient exposure and distribution of exposure among bacteria depend strongly on the spatiotemporal characteristics of the patchy landscape. Furthermore, bacterial trajectories revealed a progressive decrease of swimming speed counter-balanced by an increase in chemotactic precision, resulting in stable nutrient exposure over time. This work furthers our understanding of bacterial foraging strategies under ecologically relevant conditions.

items.title: H3K9 demethylase KDM3A potentiates interferon signaling and macrophage-driven inflammation in atherosclerosis
authors: Cindy P. A. A. van Roomen
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Medical Biochemistry, University of Amsterdam, Amsterdam UMC, Location AMC, Meibergdreef 9, Amsterdam, The Netherlands.; Amsterdam Cardiovascular Sciences (ACS), Atherosclerosis and Aortic Disease, Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam, The Netherlands.; Amsterdam Institute for Immunology and Infectious Diseases (AII), Inflammatory Diseases, Amsterdam UMC, Amsterdam, The Netherlands.
items.abstract: Macrophages drive atherosclerosis through inflammatory activation programs shaped by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. H3K9 methylation enforces heterochromatin states and represses transcription, whereas removal of this histone modification creates transcriptionally permissive chromatin. Here, we identified KDM3A-mediated H3K9 demethylation to enhance chromatin accessibility at interferon (IFN) signaling loci, thereby promoting IFN production and downstream IFN-dependent transcriptional and chemokine responses. In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, hematopoietic Kdm3a deficiency reduces lesion size, necrotic core formation, and neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, Kdm3a -deficient macrophages show impaired chemokine secretion and reduced neutrophil recruitment both in vitro and in vivo. In primary human macrophages, KDM3A knockdown suppressed IFN responses; consistently KDM3A-dependent gene signatures were enriched in IFN-inducible macrophages within human atherosclerotic plaques, and computational modeling predicted a shift toward more stable plaque phenotypes upon KDM3A inhibition. Together, these findings establish KDM3A as an epigenetic regulator that sustains IFN-driven macrophage activation and promotes progression of atherosclerosis, nominating KDM3A as a potential target for selectively modulating IFN-dependent inflammation.

items.title: GEX1-mediated semigamy induces both maternal and paternal haploids in cotton
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Cotton Bio-breeding and Integrated Utilization, Institute of Cotton Research, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Anyang 455000, China.
items.abstract: How semigamy generates haploids during double fertilization has remained elusive for more than six decades. Here, we identify Gamete Expressed 1 ( GEX1 ) as the gene underlying semigamy and show that it mediates dual-origin haploid induction in cotton. A naturally occurring mutation in GEX1 disrupts normal nuclear membrane fusion during fertilization, resulting in delayed or incomplete karyogamy. Cytological analyses reveal that delayed karyogamy allows the closely apposed but unfused gametic nuclei to undergo independent mitotic divisions, giving rise to maternal haploids, paternal haploids, and chimeric progeny. CRISPR-Cas9–mediated disruption of GEX1 reproduced the characteristic defects in nuclear fusion and enabled both maternal and paternal haploid induction within a single generation. Together, our findings uncover a genetically tractable mechanism underlying semigamy that links nuclear membrane fusion dynamics to haploid formation and establish a versatile strategy for rapidly generating doubled haploids from both parental genomes to accelerate crop breeding.

items.title: When and how particles are removed by drops
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute for Multiscale Thermofluids, School of Engineering, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK.
items.abstract: Particulate contaminants decrease the power output of solar panels and the transparency of windows and are detrimental to microelectronics, where even a single particle can induce a short circuit. Despite substantial research on particle adhesion and self-cleaning, it remains unclear when and how a drop can remove a particle from a surface, thus efficiently cleaning the surface. Here, by combining lattice Boltzmann simulations and confocal microscopy experiments, we show that at least six different scenarios arise from the complex interplay between capillary and friction forces when a drop collides with a particle on a surface. Notably, the capillary force plays a dual role in particle removal: While its tangential component always drives removal, its normal component can also hinder it. We introduce a dimensionless capillary capture parameter that successfully predicts particle removal across a wide range of particle and surface properties. Our results reveal that the design of easy-to-clean surfaces should focus not only on maximizing hydrophobicity but also on minimizing the particle-surface friction.

items.title: Engineering exhaustion-resistance CD19 CAR T cells to address translational barriers for the treatment of cancer and autoimmune disease
items.last_author_affiliation: Precigen, 20358 Seneca Meadows Pkwy, Germantown, MD 20876, USA.
items.abstract: PRGN-3008 is a CD19 CAR T cell designed to overcome key limitations in ex vivo and in vivo CAR T manufacturing, cost, safety, and therapeutic durability. Featuring decentralized overnight manufacturing without ex vivo expansion, PRGN-3008 is engineered using a single nonviral transposon to encode CD19 CAR, membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15) for improved persistence, PD-1–targeting microRNAs to prevent exhaustion, and an inducible safety switch for controlled in vivo elimination. Safety studies showed low vector copy numbers, favorable integration profile, and efficient CAR T ablation upon safety-switch activation. The combined mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation preserved PRGN-3008 polyfunctionality and sustained cytotoxicity across repeated tumor challenges, outperforming nonarmored or singly modified CAR T cells. In xenograft models, overnight-manufactured PRGN-3008 without ex vivo expansion and activation achieved durable tumor clearance, prolonged tumor-free survival, robust antigen dependent expansion, and enrichment of memory T cell phenotypes linked to clinical durability. Notably, PRGN-3008 generated from heavily pretreated patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or lupus nephritis, maintained effector function, resisted terminal differentiation under chronic antigen exposure, and effectively depleted autoreactive B cells in a humanized mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the combination of mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation enhances the expression of genes associated with bioenergetic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, glycolysis, and glutamine utilization, thereby supporting resistance to exhaustion and sustained effector function. Collectively, these data support PRGN-3008 as a clinically translatable, scalable, and controllable CAR T with the potential to expand access to cell therapy across oncology and autoimmune indications.

items.title: Ultrafast Meissner-levitated microrotor
items.last_author_affiliation: Istituto di Fotonica e Nanotecnologie IFN-CNR, 38123 Povo, Trento, Italy.; Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK), 38123 Povo, Trento, Italy.
items.abstract: Levitated mechanical systems offer a powerful and flexible platform for the realization of ultralow-noise sensors and tests of fundamental physics. Here, we report the demonstration of a levitated microrotor, consisting of a magnetic microsphere levitated by the Meissner effect at 4.2 kelvin. The rotor reaches rotation frequencies above 2.3 megahertz (138 million revolutions per minute) while exhibiting an exceptionally low damping rate of 4.75 × 10 −7 hertz. Exploiting the linear dependence of friction on the gas density, we demonstrate high-accuracy absolute pressure sensing over a wide range at cryogenic temperature. Last, we detect the thermal torque noise at intermediate pressure by operating the rotor in synchronized mode, resulting in a first preliminary narrowband search for axion-like dark matter. More broadly, the combination of high rotational speed, low temperature, and low thermal torque noise establishes a previously unidentified regime for precision measurements, with direct implications for the detection of extremely weak forces and fields.

items.title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
items.last_author_affiliation: Gregor Mendel Institute of Molecular Plant Biology, 1030 Vienna, Austria.; Department of Biology, University of Oxford, South Parks Road, Oxford OX1 3EL, UK.
items.abstract: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

items.title: Single-cell profiling of the duodenum during chronic human norovirus infection
items.last_author_affiliation: Caliciviruses Section, Laboratory of Infectious Diseases, Division of Intramural Research, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD 20892, USA.
items.abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of diarrheal disease, yet their pathogenesis remains poorly defined. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing of duodenal biopsies and matched stem cell–derived enteroids from immunodeficient individuals with chronic norovirus infection. Norovirus RNA was detected primarily in enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells, and macrophages, with the highest proportion of viral RNA-positive cells observed among M2 macrophages, followed by late enterocytes. Despite this distribution, late enterocytes produced higher viral yields than differentiated M2 macrophages in vitro. Norovirus infection was associated with the up-regulation of MHC class I-related genes and IL15 in duodenal macrophages and late enterocytes, together with increased IFNG expression by CD8 T cells. Macrophages and late enterocytes up-regulated CXCL9 and CXCL10/11 , respectively, consistent with CD8 and CD4 T cell recruitment to the duodenum. These findings show that noroviruses infect and persist across multiple permissive cell types during chronic infection, resulting in marked dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses that may drive pathogenesis.

items.title: Does government-assisted relocation help households
items.last_author_affiliation: Humphrey School of Public Affairs, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, 301 S 19th Ave, Minneapolis, MN 55455, USA.
items.abstract: Climate change is intensifying floods and storms, leading governments to consider relocating households away from high-risk areas. Yet, there is little evidence on whether such programs reduce risk or improve household well-being. I evaluate the US Federal Emergency Management Agency’s property acquisition (“buyout”) program using nationwide longitudinal records that track households before and after approval. By comparing households facing similar mapped flood risks, I estimate the program’s effects on relocation, residence in high-risk flood areas, and financial outcomes. Households that participate are more likely to relocate outside Federal Emergency Management Agency–designated flood hazard areas and experience short-term reductions in debt and improvements in neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. However, these benefits are concentrated among participants from wealthier and predominantly white neighborhoods, who relocate more quickly and achieve larger reductions in risk. A benefit-cost analysis shows that the program value depends on implementation costs and realized reductions in flood-risk exposure, with benefit-cost ratios ranging from 0.84 to 1.28 across three scenarios. These results show that government-assisted relocation can be an effective adaptation tool, but its social and economic benefits remain unevenly distributed.

items.title: MYC primes a paralog synthetic lethality involving the mitochondrial translocase subunits TIMM17A and TIMM17B and N-Acetylaspartate
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, USA.; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142, USA.
items.abstract: To identify the genes and pathways required for the survival of MYC -amplified cancers, we engineered an isogenic cell system in which transformation is driven by oncogenic MYC . Using a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 library, we identified the mitochondrial membrane translocase TIMM17A as uniquely essential for the survival of MYC-transformed cells. This dependency arises from MYC-driven suppression of TIMM17B , the paralog of TIMM17A . TIMM17A/B is an essential component of the TIM23 mitochondrial protein import complex, and the MYC-induced suppression of TIMM17B creates a strong dependency on TIMM17A . N-acetylaspartate supplementation rescued TIMM17A dependency in MYC -amplified cell lines, highlighting the unique and crucial role of this metabolite in the cell fitness of MYC -amplified cancers. These observations identify a paralog dependency required for the survival of a subset of MYC-driven cancers.

items.title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Pharmacological Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY 10029, USA.; Drug Discovery Institute, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY 10029, USA.
items.abstract: Multiple clinically relevant inborn errors of metabolism occur in lysine degradation, yet the regulation of this biochemical pathway remains poorly understood. The initial rate-limiting step of lysine catabolism is catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS). Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length 400-kilodalton tetrameric AASS enzyme complex with substrates and products bound to both the lysine-2-oxoglutarate (LOR) and saccharopine dehydrogenase (SDH) catalytic domains. We also identified allosteric compounds that modulate the activity of AASS by reacting with cysteine-414 and shifting the pH optimum for biochemical activity. The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Last, targeting allosteric cysteines may be a general strategy for modulating enzyme activity by altering the dynamics of the enzyme.

items.title: An LHX2-DACH1 regulatory innovation drives basal progenitor expansion in the primate neocortex
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Cellular and Organismic Biology, Academia Sinica, Taipei 11529, Taiwan.; Graduate Institute of Medical Genomics and Proteomics, College of Medicine, National Taiwan University, Taipei 10025, Taiwan.
items.abstract: A defining feature of the primate neocortex is an expanded cortical progenitor pool, especially the basal radial glia (bRG), contributing to complex intracortical circuitry underlying higher cognition. Here, a comparative transcriptomic analysis of developing human and mouse neocortical cells identified DACH1 as a transcription factor enriched in human neurogenic RGs. Using both primate ESCs and mouse models, we found an LHX2-DACH1-miR-215-5p program regulating bRG production. DACH1 loss in human cortical progenitors impaired bRG production and shifted neuronal output toward corticospinal neurons, whereas Dach1 depletion in mice had no effect. Conversely, ectopic DACH1 expression in the rodent neocortex induced bRG formation and promoted callosal neuron production. Further, we found that DACH1 is regulated by LHX2 via a primate-evolved enhancer. Introducing this enhancer into mice promoted bRG generation, while its removal in primates impaired bRG production. Mechanistically, DACH1 promotes bRG generation by suppressing miR-215-5p–mediated down-regulation of centromere- and centrosome-related genes. These findings reveal a mechanism by which cortical progenitor expansion shapes the primate cortical connectome for cognitive evolution.

items.title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD + precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biological Sciences, Rutgers University, Newark, New Jersey, USA.; Department of Pharmacology, Physiology, and Neuroscience, Rutgers Biomedical and Health Sciences, Newark, New Jersey, USA.; Center for Immunity and Inflammation, Rutgers Biomedical and Health Sciences, Newark, NJ, USA.
items.abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

items.title: Arbitrarily cuttable and ultrathin MXene structural colors for customizable and wearable multispectral information management
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Flexible Electronics Technology, Key Laboratory of Organic Optoelectronics & Molecular Engineering, Ministry of Education, Department of Chemistry, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, P. R. China.
items.abstract: Structural colors based on natural and artificial microstructures show promising light manipulation. As atomically thick building blocks, Ti 3 C 2 T x sheets have been successfully assembled into the ultrathin, flexible, arbitrarily cuttable, large-size structural colors by the simple and low-cost spray methods based on the lossy thin-film interference. By ordered stacking atomically thick Ti 3 C 2 T x layer by layer at well-organized low–surface tension semidry assemble state, rich colors from yellow to gray with the thickness from ∼22 to ∼154 nanometers of uniform Ti 3 C 2 T x colors are obtained, having the thinnest framework among solution-processed flexible structural colors with similar optical performance. Low-infrared emissivity from room to 300°C temperature and region-selective patterns make highly information-fused and complex visible-infrared (VIS-IR) Ti 3 C 2 T x colors camouflage.
