These included monocyte- and fibroblast-driven inflammation (lung adenocarcinoma), VEGF–TGFβ-mediated angiogenic feedback loops (lung squamous cell carcinoma) and immune-permissive niches promoting antitumor immunity. LuCaS+ offers a clinically anchored single-cell resource to enable personalized, biology-driven therapies in NSCLC.

items.title: The deep learning framework Hist2Prot infers single-cell spatial proteomics from histology to predict biomarkers and clinical outcomes
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Pathology, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA. shanye.yin@einsteinmed.edu.; Einstein Pathology Single-Cell & Bioinformatics Laboratory, Bronx, NY, USA. shanye.yin@einsteinmed.edu.; Montefiore Einstein Comprehensive Cancer Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA. shanye.yin@einsteinmed.edu.
items.abstract: Spatial proteomics enables high-resolution mapping of protein expression within the tumor microenvironment, but its routine clinical application remains limited by cost, technical complexity and restricted tissue coverage. Here we present Hist2Prot, a deep learning framework that generates single-cell spatial proteomic profiles from routine hematoxylin and eosin histology. Trained on approximately 51 million paired cells from a same-section G4X spatial proteomics dataset, Hist2Prot was evaluated in internal test cohorts, independent same-platform G4X cohorts and external cross-platform datasets comprising approximately 72 million additional cells, showing concordance with measured protein profiles and outperforming established baselines. Hist2Prot-derived virtual proteins preserved immune, stromal and tumor cell phenotypes and recapitulated clinically relevant tumor microenvironment organization. Across seven independent patient cohorts comprising 1,774 patients, virtual spatial proteomics improved molecular biomarker, prognostic and immunotherapy response prediction beyond hematoxylin and eosin morphology alone. Hist2Prot enables scalable single-cell computational spatial proteomics from routine histology for precision oncology.

items.title: Natural killer cell inflammatory circuits in antitumor immunity
items.last_author_affiliation: Cancer Immunology Program, Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia. rebecca.delconte@petermac.org.; Sir Peter MacCallum Department of Oncology, The University of Melbourne, Parkville, Victoria, Australia. rebecca.delconte@petermac.org.; Department of Medical Biology, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Victoria, Australia. rebecca.delconte@petermac.org.
items.abstract: Emerging evidence positions natural killer (NK) cells as key initiators of the inflammatory programs required for effective tumor immunity. Beyond direct tumor killing, NK cells trigger early immune responses by recruiting and activating dendritic cells (DCs), thereby enabling downstream T cell activation. However, in established tumors, NK cell-DC communication is often disrupted by metabolic stress and immunosuppressive pathways, leading to immune evasion. Here, we review advances in NK cell-DC cross-talk, cytokine-driven amplification loops and metabolic control of NK cell fitness. We propose that restoring these integrated immune 'circuits' may be key in converting immune-excluded tumors into immunotherapy-responsive states.

items.title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Neurobiology and Neuroscience Institute, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA. marlenecohen@uchicago.edu.
items.abstract: Neurons throughout the brain encode essentially everything, so why have distinct areas? We proposed that areas format different information sources differently, implying their computational role. Here we compared the middle temporal (MT) area, involved in visual motion perception, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), implicated in decision-making and reward. In a task that required monkeys to combine motion and reward information, both regions encoded both motion and reward, but formatted differently. Area MT represented them separably, whereas the dlPFC combined them in a decision-related format. A recurrent network model trained to reproduce that formatting predicted a distinct effect of stimulating those areas. Consistent with predictions, MT stimulation biased choices whereas dlPFC stimulation produced 'winner-take-all' outcomes. Our findings suggest that a modular structure flexibly reformats information to enable complex behaviors.

items.title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism
items.last_author_affiliation: Program in Neurogenetics, Department of Neurology, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. dhg@mednet.ucla.edu.; Center for Autism Research and Treatment, Semel Institute, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. dhg@mednet.ucla.edu.; Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities Research Center (IDDRC), David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. dhg@mednet.ucla.edu.; Department of Human Genetics, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. dhg@mednet.ucla.edu.; Institute of Precision Health, David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA. dhg@mednet.ucla.edu.
items.abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A , and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
items.last_author_affiliation: Mental Illness Research, Education and Clinical Center, Crescenz VAMC, Philadelphia, PA, USA. kranzler@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.; Center for Studies of Addiction, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA. kranzler@pennmedicine.upenn.edu.
items.abstract: Abstract Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Sex-specific meta-analyses revealed 115 independent loci (12 of which were new) among males ( n = 583,066) and 12 loci (2 of which were new) among females ( n = 241,266). Multi-omic gene prioritization analyses highlighted 490 genes associated with MP through their effects on brain-specific and blood-specific regulation. Mendelian randomization analyses showed causal associations between MP and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and C-reactive protein levels. MP variants also showed pleiotropic associations with several brain imaging-derived phenotypes. This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

items.title: Tissue-to-bytes: A digital twin for single-cell omics data integration across BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Neurology, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, Houston, TX 77030, USA; McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, Houston, TX 77030, USA; Texas Institute for Restorative Neurotechnologies, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, Houston, TX 77030, USA. Electronic address: guo-qiang.zhang@uth.tmc.edu.
items.abstract: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) requires coordinated management of scarce human brain tissue resources, standardized metadata, and transparent tracking of tissue-to-data transformations across distributed laboratories and centers. We present the Neuroanatomy-Anchored Information Management Platform (NIMP), a consortium-scale web-based application system developed to coordinate multimodal single-cell omics resource generation and maintain end-to-end provenance throughout the tissue-to-bytes life cycle. NIMP integrates donor registration, anatomical annotation, tissue allocation, sequencing workflows, quality assurance and quality control, and archive-data deposition within a unified data ecosystem infrastructure. Over 3 years of production-strength deployment, the platform has managed BICAN consortium's data and metadata for 762 human donors, 8,449 brain slabs, and 21,781 sequencing libraries across 11 laboratories, collectively supporting generation of more than 18 million single cells. NIMP provides a scalable and reusable platform for provenance-aware resource management, FAIR data generation, and future large-scale atlas and multi-network data coordination initiatives.

items.title: Distinct extraembryonic transcription factors converge on a shared DNA methylation-Polycomb state
items.last_author_affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics, Berlin, Germany; Institute of Chemistry and Biochemistry, Freie Universität Berlin, Berlin, Germany. Electronic address: meissner@molgen.mpg.de.
items.abstract: Extraembryonic tissues and many cancers share unusual DNA methylation landscapes, but how these states arise remains unclear. Here, we use GATA6- and CDX2-driven reprogramming of mouse embryonic stem cells to track genome-wide epigenetic remodeling during acquisition of extraembryonic cell fates. Despite activating distinct transcriptional programs from non-overlapping genomic targets, both transcription factors trigger rapid and genomically synchronized convergence to cancer-like DNA methylation patterns, including simultaneous global DNA methylation loss and de novo methylation of Polycomb-regulated CpG islands. We find that this wave of DNA methylation reprogramming co-occurs with global H3K27me3 redistribution alongside promoter H3K4 methylation loss. Experimental models of cellular senescence, as well as human aging and cancer cohorts, reveal related but progressively more extensive disruption of these same chromatin boundaries. Together, these data define a tractable system for studying coordinated genome-wide transitions between canonical and non-canonical epigenomic states.

items.title: Population-scale integration of spatial omics networks for clinical prediction and biological discovery by SPIN
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biomedical Informatics and Data Science, Heersink School of Medicine, University of Alabama at Birmingham, Birmingham, AL, USA. Electronic address: lgarmire@uab.edu.
items.abstract: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. We introduce SPIN (spatial predictive integration network), which integrates subject-specific, cell-type level, spatially informed co-expression or co-abundance networks for population-scale clinical prediction. Current implementation of SPIN includes three key modules: network construction, molecular-to-clinical prediction by Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning (BSNMani), and visualization & interpretation module. In the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) transcriptomics cohort, SPIN achieved an accuracy of 0.81 for dementia-status prediction and revealed co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance. SPIN also achieved robust survival prediction in a breast cancer single-cell proteomics cohort (C-index = 0.78), identifying two survival-associated spatial proteomic subnetworks. In summary, SPIN is an interpretable tool for spatial-omics-based clinical outcome prediction at the population scale.

items.title: Tracing the evolutionary history of human neocortical regulation
items.last_author_affiliation: Neurogenomics Group, Hospital del Mar Research Institute, Parc de Recerca Biomèdica de Barcelona (PRBB), 08003 Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain.
items.abstract: Anderson et al. extend comparative brain multi-omics across nine mammals and zebrafish, combining sequence conservation and predicted enhancer-gene relationships with functional assays to examine how regulatory elements with different evolutionary histories contribute to brain function and disease risk.

items.title: Q&A with Dr. Philip Awadalla
Leveraging evolutionary conservation to define cell identity
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Experimental Hematology, National Clinical Research Center for Blood Diseases, Haihe Laboratory of Cell Ecosystem, Institute of Hematology & Blood Diseases Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College, Tianjin 300020, China; Tianjin Institutes of Health Science, Tianjin 301600, China. Electronic address: chengtao@ihcams.ac.cn.
items.abstract: Wölbert et al. established a strategy that integrated conserved cell-type-specificity with conservation of transcriptional levels to identify robust signature genes. By leveraging evolutionary conservation as an additional dimension of cell identity, this strategy would facilitate cell identity annotation across species, particularly in non-model organisms and rare cell populations.

items.title: RNA sequencing reveals molecular subtypes across adenocarcinoma, squamous, and small cell lung cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Human Biology Division, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle, WA 98109, USA. Electronic address: eholland@fredhutch.org.
items.abstract: This study combines RNA sequencing data from 1,824 tumors across major lung cancer types to examine how tumor gene expression patterns relate to histologic diagnoses. The resulting reference landscape identifies nine transcriptional clusters, including a neuroendocrine-like adenocarcinoma group and regions with mixed histology. The clusters also show associations with clinical features, genetic alterations, immune characteristics, and survival. An interactive Oncoscape resource allows researchers to explore the integrated data and compare patient tumors with patient-derived xenograft models.

items.title: Genome-wide association study meta-analysis identifies susceptibility loci informing Ewing sarcoma etiology and potential mechanisms of risk
items.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a rare, aggressive pediatric malignancy driven by FET::ETS family fusions (EWSR1::FLI1 in >85% of cases) with no established environmental risk factors. We analyzed 2,014 EwS cases and 10,525 cancer-free controls in a two-stage analysis that combined an international genome-wide association study and a case-parent trio study. The combined meta-analysis identified 18 variants at 14 susceptibility loci (9 novel and 5 replicated) with moderate effect sizes (odds ratios ≥ 1.25). Integrative analyses of the EwS loci revealed enrichment of enhancer-like GGAA microsatellites, with evidence for binding of the EWSR1::FLI1 fusion at most loci. EWSR1::ETS knockdown in EwS cell lines resulted in dysregulated genes at susceptibility loci related to skeletal/muscle development, RNA binding/processing, and chromatin regulation. Our findings provide insights into the inherited component of EwS, highlighting a genetic architecture in which common germline variation with moderate effects interacts with somatic EWSR1::FLI1 fusions to promote sarcomagenesis by dysregulating local genes.

items.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer’s in anterior caudate
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Science, Seattle, WA, USA. Electronic address: jenniec@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

items.title: Multi-omics-constrained kinetic models quantify pathway rewiring and predict metabolic vulnerabilities in BRCA1-deficient ovarian cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Laboratory of Computational Systems Biotechnology, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland; AI center, EPFL, 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland. Electronic address: ljubisa.miskovic@epfl.ch.
items.abstract: Time-resolved, network-wide consequences of cancer metabolic reprogramming remain poorly understood. We built multi-omics-constrained, near-genome-scale kinetic ensembles for isogenic BRCA1 wild-type and BRCA1-mutant ovarian cancer cells. Covering over 2,100 reactions, the ensembles enabled uncertainty-quantified simulations of nutrient, metabolite, and enzyme perturbations. Metabolic control analysis identified 28 enzyme-mediated vulnerabilities; 24 are linked to experimental or approved DrugBank compounds, whereas four lack documented drug associations. Independent DepMap data supported a subset of these candidates. All 28 emerged directly from the mechanistic model structure and multi-omics constraints, with no calibration to known drug targets or cancer-dependency data. Simulations of thymidylate synthase, hexokinase, and triokinase inhibition predicted target- and physiology-specific changes in pathway use, energy metabolism, and a shared ceramide-linked stress response. Mapping predicted enzyme-activity shifts to BRCA1-associated transcription factors suggested regulatory routes underlying differences between the two states. These ensembles provide a reusable framework for time-resolved, mechanistic hypothesis generation across cancers and other diseases. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the supplemental information.

items.title: UC Irvine’s BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) Brain Procurement Program for the Center for Multiomic Human Brain Cell Atlas Project
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA; Center for Neural Circuit Mapping, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA; Institute for Memory Impairments and Neurological Disorders, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA. Electronic address: xiangmin.xu@uci.edu.
items.abstract: High-quality neurotypical postmortem human brain tissue is essential for constructing comprehensive human brain cell atlases, but it is difficult to obtain. Here, we describe the establishment of UC Irvine's Brain Procurement Program, a coordinated multi-institutional pipeline to collect and process neurotypical donor brains for multiomic mapping studies within the National Institute of Health (NIH) BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) consortium. Through partnerships with the Orange County (OC) coroner's office, UC Irvine's Willed Body Program, UC Irvine's Medical Center (UCIMC), and the Children's Hospital of Orange County, we have developed standardized workflows encompassing donor identification, postmortem brain recovery and processing, region-of-interest dissection, neurotypical donor selection, and data management. Our experience demonstrates the feasibility of a community-based, multi-institutional procurement framework while highlighting challenges in recruiting neurotypical donors and ensuring demographic representation reflective of Southern California. We further identify opportunities to strengthen outreach and donation pathways. This program provides a scalable model for advancing population-reflective, high-quality human brain cell atlas efforts.

items.title: ULK1 knockout increases recombinant transcript abundance and improves recombinant membrane protein expression
items.last_author_affiliation: KTH - Royal Institute of Technology, Department of Protein Science, 106 91 Stockholm, Sweden. Electronic address: johanr@biotech.kth.se.
items.abstract: Cell homeostasis depends on pathways balancing degradation and synthesis, including autophagy. Following a previous small-molecule screen, suggesting unc-51-like kinase 1 (ULK1) as a target affecting recombinant protein expression, we generated an ULK1 knockout (KO) Expi293 cell line. The KO cell line increased the expression of a secreted model protein by up to 1.7-fold, and transcriptomic analysis suggested downregulation of key macroautophagy-associated genes despite upregulated productivity-associated stress genes. Transcriptional upregulation of membrane organization and protein localization processes indicated a potential for membrane protein production. Production of three model membrane proteins in the KO cell line yielded up to a 2-fold increase, with the highest increase in the soluble fraction. Transcriptomic analyses suggested an increased recombinant transcript abundance, broader downregulation of autophagy, and weaker stress responses. These findings indicate that autophagy-associated pathways modulate cellular responses to recombinant protein production and point to ULK1-associated pathways for host-cell engineering, especially for enhanced membrane protein production.

items.title: Identification and regulation of an ACC1-associated lipogenic metabolon in liver
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Human Nutrition, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390-9046, USA; Department of Internal Medicine, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390-9046, USA.
items.abstract: De novo lipogenesis (DNL) plays a pathogenic role in triglyceride (TG) accumulation in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Strategies to reduce hepatic steatosis focus on inhibiting enzymes involved in DNL and TG synthesis. Here, we identify a nutrient-responsive, post-translational regulatory mechanism that enhances DNL in mouse liver models and primary rat hepatocytes. Under anabolic conditions, ACC1 interacts with multiple enzymes in the DNL and TG synthesis pathway, supporting the formation of an ACC1-associated lipogenic metabolon. Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy (EM) reveal that ACC1 and associated lipogenic proteins are enriched in lipid droplet (LD)-associated and mitochondria-LD interface regions. In steatotic livers, ACC1-associated lipogenic protein interactions are increased, consistent with enhanced hepatic lipogenesis in MASLD. These studies identify a post-translational mechanism that promotes the spatial coordination of lipogenic enzymes and facilitates substrate channeling to enhance TG synthesis. Disruption of this lipogenic metabolon may provide a therapeutic approach for treatment of MASLD.

items.title: A sequence-encoded promoter-proximal super pause stabilizes an offline RNA polymerase II state
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA. Electronic address: seyvos@mit.edu.
items.abstract: Promoter-proximal pausing by RNA polymerase II is critical for regulating gene expression in multicellular eukaryotes. How nucleic acid sequence and protein factors contribute to pausing remains incompletely understood. We developed gene-specific analysis of transcriptional output (GATO)-seq, which enables massively parallel, temporally resolved, reconstituted transcription in an assay that uses direct RNA sequencing to map 3' ends of nascent transcripts from a library of human genes. GATO-seq identified a "super pause" sequence that potently induces RNA polymerase II pausing and is not relieved by transcription factor (TF) IIS. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of RNA polymerase II on the super-pause sequence revealed a previously unobserved, reversible single-nucleotide backtracked state ("sidetracked"), stabilized by a threonine-lined pocket that limits further backtracking. Together, we introduce a powerful in vitro technique to study transcription regulation and show that nucleic acid sequence encodes pausing propensity and traps sequence-specific offline states, linking sequence to pausing control.

items.title: Promoter-proximal pausing enables transcriptional buffering of RNA polymerase II availability
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Gene Expression, Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Panum Institute, University of Copenhagen, Blegdamsvej 3B, Copenhagen, 2200 Copenhagen N, Denmark. Electronic address: jsvejstrup@sund.ku.dk.
items.abstract: While RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is essential for transcription, the impact of its cellular abundance on gene regulation has been unclear. By titrating RNAPII levels in HEK293 using the dTAG (degradation tag) system, we demonstrate that even modest depletion induces widespread changes in transcription initiation, promoter-proximal pausing, and elongation, along with alterations in splicing, increased transcriptional readthrough, and impaired cell-cycle progression. Interestingly, genes vary considerably in their sensitivity to reduced RNAPII levels. Notably, genes with strong promoter-proximal pausing are largely resistant, effectively buffering RNAPII loss. Moreover, mRNA output is stabilized by increased transcript half-lives under severe depletion. These findings establish RNAPII abundance as a critical determinant of transcriptional regulation, splicing, and termination and identify promoter-proximal pausing as a central buffering mechanism. We propose that the need to buffer RNAPII fluctuations during growth, differentiation, and in response to cellular cues helped drive the evolution of promoter-proximal pausing.

items.title: Nuclear TRiC states captured in situ
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Molecular Sociology, Max Planck Institute of Biophysics, Max-von-Laue-Straße 3, 60438 Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Cluster of Excellence SubCellular Architecture of Life (SCALE), Goethe University, Frankfurt, Germany; Institute of Biochemistry, Goethe University Frankfurt, 60438 Frankfurt am Main, Germany. Electronic address: martin.beck@biophys.mpg.de.
items.abstract: The chaperonin T-complex protein ring complex (TRiC) is an essential protein-folding machine in eukaryotic cells. Although its cytosolic role in folding newly synthesized proteins is well established, nuclear TRiC remains less well described. Here, we combined cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), cross-linking and affinity purification mass spectrometry with AlphaFold3 (AF3)-based structural modeling to examine nuclear TRiC in human cells. We detected intermediates of the TRiC duty cycle in the nucleus and identified several nuclear proteins that bind to TRiC. The respective AF3 models suggest interaction surfaces at the inside of the TRiC chamber. Our findings point toward compartment-specific roles of TRiC and a potential function in maintaining nuclear proteostasis. By data-mining very large datasets, our study establishes that rather low-abundant events can be analyzed by cryo-ET. It thus paves the way toward broader applications.

items.title: The C-terminal tail of the RBR E3 ligase RNF14 defines branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin specificity in ribosomal quality control
items.last_author_affiliation: Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research, 1G Royal Parade, Parkville, VIC 3052, Australia; Department of Medical Biology, University of Melbourne, Parkville, VIC 3052, Australia. Electronic address: lechtenberg.b@wehi.edu.au.
items.abstract: Ubiquitination is a post-translational modification involving the conjugation of polyubiquitin chains to target proteins. Ubiquitin forms at least eight linkage types with specific biological functions. The diversity of this ubiquitin code is enhanced by branched ubiquitin chains, where two ubiquitin molecules are linked to a third ubiquitin via different linkage types. The E3 ligase RNF14 regulates ribosomal quality control (RQC) upon ribosomal stalling, inducing ubiquitination and degradation of translational cofactors eEF1A or eRF1. Here, we show that RNF14 forms branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin in vitro and on eRF1 in human cells. Structural and mechanistic characterization and comparison with the yeast ortholog Itt1 show that the unstructured RNF14 C-terminal tail defines chain-type and branching specificity. Our work reveals a rare example of a single E3 ligase forming specifically branched polyubiquitin and places branched K6/K48 polyubiquitin into RQC pathways, thereby opening research avenues in RQC and the physiological functions of branched ubiquitin signals.

items.title: A lysosomal DRAM1-GLUT1-NADPH axis coordinates glucose sensing with metabolic reprogramming
items.last_author_affiliation: Cancer Research UK Scotland Institute, Garscube Estate, Switchback Road, Glasgow G61 1BD, UK; School of Cancer Sciences, University of Glasgow, Garscube Estate, Switchback Road, Glasgow G61 1QH, UK. Electronic address: kevin.ryan@glasgow.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Perturbed glucose homeostasis is a hallmark of metabolic disease and cancer, and cellular responses to excess glucose are tightly controlled. We report here a lysosomal glucose sensing axis linking the transporter GLUT1 with the lysosomal protein DRAM1. Pathophysiological glucose induces DRAM1 via the MLX/ChREBP transcriptional complex. DRAM1 then binds newly synthesized GLUT1 and promotes its traffic to lysosomes without degradation, reducing surface GLUT1 and acting as a reversible brake on glucose entry. Hexokinase or glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) dehydrogenase disruption weakens DRAM1-GLUT1 complex formation, whereas nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate(NADPH) oxidase (NOX) inhibition enhances assembly, implicating NADPH as a key metabolic signal downstream of elevated glucose. Sequestration of GLUT1 suppresses glucose uptake and glycolysis and rewires metabolism toward glutamine anaplerosis, creating vulnerability to glutaminase (GLS) inhibition. In vivo, Dram1-/- tumors display a glycolytic metabolite profile, consistent with loss of this brake. Together, these data define an mTORC1- and AMPK-independent lysosomal mechanism that protects metabolic homeostasis under hyperglycemic conditions.

items.title: Hierarchical buffering of cellular RNA polymerase II pools maintains transcriptional homeostasis
items.last_author_affiliation: EMBL Australia Node in Single Molecule Science, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW, Australia; UNSW RNA Institute, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW, Australia; Department of Molecular Medicine, School of Biomedical Sciences, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW, Australia. Electronic address: scott.berry@unsw.edu.au.
items.abstract: RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) abundance and transcriptional output are coordinated across diverse conditions to maintain mRNA homeostasis. To determine whether RNA Pol II acts as a limiting factor for transcription, we combined acute perturbations with quantitative single-cell imaging and genome-wide profiling. We find that transcription remains stable across 70%-160% of normal RNA Pol II levels in human cells. This robustness emerges from hierarchical buffering mechanisms operating on distinct timescales. Within tens of minutes of monoallelic depletion of RNA Pol II subunit POLR2A, cells maintain steady transcriptional output by drawing polymerases from a nucleoplasmic reserve pool. However, over hours, cellular RNA Pol II holoenzyme levels also recover, driven by constitutive excess POLR2A subunit production rather than feedback sensing. Together, these results reveal that transcriptional homeostasis in human cells is maintained without feedback regulation of polymerase levels, emerging instead from intrinsic kinetics of the multi-checkpoint transcription cycle and holoenzyme assembly.

items.title: PARP1 hyperactivation uncouples transcription from protein expression through nuclear RNA retention
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biological Chemistry, School of Medicine, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Center for RNA Science and Therapeutics, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA; Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, School of Pharmacy & Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of California, Irvine, Irvine, CA 92697, USA. Electronic address: rbuisson@uci.edu.
items.abstract: The DNA damage response triggers widespread transcriptional changes and modulates protein degradation, yet its role in regulating translation remains largely unexplored. Here, we uncover that hyperactivated PARP1 suppresses global mRNA translation by inducing nuclear RNA retention. Mechanistically, we find that APE1-dependent cleavage of abasic sites drives PARP1 hyperactivation, leading to translation arrest in human cells. Elevated PAR synthesis by PARP1 directly competes with RNA for binding to multiple RNA-binding proteins, disrupting RNA splicing and export and promoting the formation of PARP1-dependent nuclear condensates. As a result, RNA accumulates in the nucleus, reducing the amount of cytoplasmic mRNA available for translation. Moreover, we show that PARP1 hyperactivation inhibits the expression of many DNA damage-induced stress response factors by blocking nuclear export of their mRNAs. Together, these findings reveal an unrecognized role for PARP1 as a post-transcriptional regulator of the DNA damage response, uncoupling gene transcription from translation into proteins.

items.title: Dot1 triggers a conserved ribophagy signal to govern ribosome quality and longevity by methylating Rpl12
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biochemistry and Department of Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic Surgery of the First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, China. Electronic address: yiconglab@zju.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Ribophagy plays a critical role in maintaining ribosome quality, yet how ribosomes are marked for autophagic recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the methyltransferase Dot1/DOT1L as a conserved regulator of ribophagy that generates an "eat-me" signal through methylation of Rpl12, thereby regulating ribosome quality. Under nutrient deprivation, Dot1 methylates Rpl12 at K41 and K48 in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, enhancing its interaction with Atg11 and initiating ribophagy through the TOR-Atg1-Rpl12 signaling axis. In mammals, starvation induces partial cytoplasmic translocation of DOT1L, where it colocalizes with and methylates RPL12. In Drosophila, ribosomes incorporating Gpp (the Dot1 homolog)-methylated RpL12 show strong colocalization with the autophagosome marker Atg8a. Flies carrying methylation-deficient RpL12 mutants exhibit impaired ribophagy, developmental abnormalities, accelerated aging, muscle degeneration, and reduced stress resistance. Collectively, these findings reveal that Dot1-mediated Rpl12 methylation generates a conserved "eat-me" signal that links nutrient availability to ribosome quality control and lifespan regulation.

items.title: RBM33 is a unique m6A RNA-binding protein that regulates ALKBH5 demethylase activity and substrate selectivity
Neutrophils are known by their neighbors in breast cancer
Targeting F. nucleatum with metronidazole plus tislelizumab and fruquintinib in MSS colorectal cancer: A multicenter phase 2 study
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Shanghai Institute of Digestive Disease, Hospital of Digestive Disease, NHC Key Laboratory of Digestive Diseases, State Key Laboratory of Systems Medicine for Cancer, Renji Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China. Electronic address: jingyuanfang@sjtu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Fusobacterium nucleatum has been linked to chemoresistance and immune evasion in colorectal cancer (CRC), but therapeutic strategies targeting this bacterium remain limited. In this multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial (NCT06356597), 33 patients with Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive, microsatellite-stable metastatic CRC received the combination treatment of tislelizumab, fruquintinib, and the antimicrobial metronidazole. The primary endpoint was met, with a median progression-free survival of 6.0 months. The objective response rate and disease control rate were 19.4% and 83.9%, respectively. Grade 3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 30.3% of patients, with no grade 4 or 5 events. Metagenomic analysis showed that metronidazole reduced Fusobacterium nucleatum abundance. Exploratory analyses associated clinical benefit with enrichment of Lactobacillus species and nonresponse with Enterococcus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from responders sensitized germ-free mice to the treatment, which enhanced cytotoxic CD8+ T cell differentiation and reduced terminal exhaustion. These findings support further evaluation of this combination in Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive metastatic CRC.

items.title: A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity
items.last_author_affiliation: MedPacto, Inc., Seoul, Republic of Korea; GILO Institute, GILO Foundation, Seoul, Republic of Korea; Department of Urology, Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, CT, USA; Department of Pediatrics, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland, OH, USA. Electronic address: jasonsjkim@medpacto.com.
items.abstract: Transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) accumulation in the tumor microenvironment (TME) is a major barrier to durable antitumor immunity. We developed fibronectin extra domain B (FN-EDB)-binding peptide (FEBP)-soluble TβRII-Fc (sTβRII), an engineered inhibitor targeting the FN-EDB-rich tumor matrix for localized TGF-β blockade. In fibrotic, immune-excluded tumors, FEBP-sTβRII suppresses TGF-β/SMAD signaling to unleash T cell activation and IFN-γ production, thereby driving feedforward cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)-myeloid reprogramming toward an antigen-presenting state. This coordinated remodeling relieves immune exclusion and converts the fibrotic TME into an antigen-visible ecosystem that sustains robust T cell infiltration and activation. Consequently, FEBP-sTβRII induces T cell-dependent tumor regression, expands effector-memory populations, and elicits long-term, cross-protective antitumor immunity, while minimizing peripheral transcriptional disturbances compared with systemic sTβRII. Together, these findings show that spatially targeted TGF-β blockade overcomes fibrotic immune exclusion to establish durable local and systemic tumor immunity.

items.title: The future of early endpoints for neoadjuvant therapy
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Surgery, University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA. Electronic address: laura.esserman@ucsf.edu.
items.abstract: Early endpoints as surrogates for long-term outcomes are essential for treatment efficacy evaluation. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Conforti et al. report that CPS + EG and Neo-Bioscore scores predict long-term outcomes at the patient level but not at the trial level, highlighting the need for better early endpoints that reliably capture efficacy across trials.

items.title: Decoding neutrophil spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications in breast cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Breast Surgery, Key Laboratory of Breast Cancer in Shanghai, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Shanghai 200032, China; Department of Oncology, Shanghai Medical College, Fudan University, Shanghai 200032, China. Electronic address: zhimingshao@fudan.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Neutrophils are heterogeneous and critical components of the tumor microenvironment, yet their spatial heterogeneity and clinical implications remain poorly understood. We establish large-scale breast cancer cohorts integrating AI-powered computational pathology (n = 1,113) and single-cell spatial omics (n = 104) to investigate the clinical relevance and biological mechanisms underlying neutrophil spatial patterns. Clinical implications were greatest in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC): neutrophil-tumor cell proximity associated with favorable prognosis, while neutrophil-immune cell proximity predicted superior immunotherapy response. Combining these patterns with established biomarkers improved TNBC stratification for prognosis and immunotherapy efficacy. Spatial omics and experimental validation demonstrated that tumor-proximal neutrophils enhanced MHC I expression on tumor cells via inflammatory crosstalk, promoting immune-mediated tumor clearance and improved prognosis. Neutrophils adjacent to immune cells exhibited an antigen-presenting phenotype, augmentable by targeting polyamine metabolism. Our study highlights the functional diversity and spatial heterogeneity of neutrophils and provides a translational strategy with routine computational pathology.

items.title: Antibiotics counteracting tumor-promoting dysbiosis in colorectal cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Centre de Recherche des Cordeliers, Université Paris Cité, Sorbonne Université, Inserm U1138, Metabolism, Cancer and Immunity, Équipe labellisée par la Ligue contre le cancer, Paris, France; Université Paris-Saclay, Inserm US23 AMMICa, Metabolomic Platform, Gustave Roussy, Villejuif, France; Institut du Cancer Paris CARPEM, Department of Biology, Hôpital Européen Georges Pompidou, AP-HP, Paris, France. Electronic address: kroemer@orange.fr.
items.abstract: Antibiotics usually sabotage immune checkpoint blockade. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Jiang et al. report that pulsed, anaerobe-directed metronidazole added to an anti-PD-1 antibody and a VEGF receptor inhibitor achieved encouraging progression-free survival in Fusobacterium nucleatum-positive microsatellite-stable metastatic colorectal cancer, selectively dismantling a pathobiont network without inducing global dysbiosis.

items.title: Glial progenitor-like state is preferentially co-opted in glioblastoma and sustained by POU3F3
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY 10029, USA; Department of Neuroscience, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY 10029, USA. Electronic address: nadejda.tsankova@mountsinai.org.
items.abstract: Oncofetal reprogramming in glioblastoma (GBM) relies on the co-option of still poorly defined pathways that are transiently active during brain development, thereby exposing therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities. To better characterize GBM biology in the context of neurodevelopment, we create an expanded human spatiotemporal multi-omic dataset that resolves both gliogenic and neurogenic lineage fate and assess oncofetal reprogramming at the tumor core and infiltrative margin in both primary and recurrent disease. Analyses reveal the preferential enrichment of a glial intermediate progenitor cell (gIPC)-like state, which is most reminiscent of third-trimester germinal matrix gIPCs, across tumor regions and in recurrence. We uncover EGFR and the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) NRXN1-DT as co-opted gIPC-specific markers, demonstrate NRXN1-DT's clinical utility in GBM diagnostics, and prioritize POU3F3 as a gIPC-like oncofetal driver, confirming its regulatory role in NRXN1-DT enhancer activity, EGFR expression, and maintenance of GBM stem/progenitor-like properties. This study lays the groundwork for future investigations into targeting POU3F3 and other co-opted gliogenic drivers as GBM therapeutics.

items.title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA; Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA. Electronic address: dbautista@berkeley.edu.
items.abstract: Sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

items.title: A consensus spinal cord cell-type atlas across mouse, macaque, and human
items.last_author_affiliation: Allen Institute, Brain Science, Seattle, WA 98109, USA. Electronic address: trygveb@alleninstitute.org.
items.abstract: The spinal cord contains cell types critical for motor, sensory, and autonomic function, many of which are implicated in neurological disease and injury. Yet no shared molecular framework links human spinal cord cell types to the animal models used to study them. Here, we present a cross-species atlas integrating single-nucleus gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and spatial transcriptomics from over one million nuclei spanning cervical to sacral segments in human, macaque, and mouse. Consensus clustering resolves 111 cell type groups replicable across all three species, whose spatial distributions map spinal laminae and nuclei, including Clarke's column. Identity and laminar organization are highly conserved, yet abundance and expression are allometrically scaled, with the dorsal horn being the principal site of divergence, concentrated in neurotransmitter receptor genes and including a primate-specific glycine receptor subunit switch. Sequence models uncover a conserved transcription factor grammar and nominate motifs underlying enhancer-adeno-associated virus (AAV) access to a divergent dorsal horn population.

items.title: Slow-timescale regulation of dopamine release governs recovery of a motivational drive over days
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02215, USA; Center for Neural Science, New York University, New York, NY 10003, USA. Electronic address: xz5184@nyu.edu.
items.abstract: The rise and fall of a motivational state can unfold over many days. We used mouse mating behavior to model how the brain orchestrates such slow-timescale changes in motivation. Male mice become sexually satiated after successful matings, and their motivation to mate recovers over a week. Using deep-brain fluorescence-lifetime imaging in the medial preoptic area (MPOA), we found that tonic dopamine transmission-which regulates mating drive-also declined after mating and gradually re-emerged across several days. Two mechanisms regulated dopamine transmission. First, successful mating transiently reduced the tonic firing of hypothalamic dopamine-releasing neurons, thereby inhibiting dopamine release and mating behavior for 1 to 2 days. Second, these neurons' ability to produce and release dopamine dropped after mating and recovered over the following week, paralleling the recovery of mating drive. Therefore, changes in neuronal firing rate and neurotransmitter composition cooperate to control the early and late phases of motivational dynamics, respectively.

items.title: Neural organoid models of human brain evolution
items.last_author_affiliation: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge Biomedical Campus, Cambridge, UK; Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, Cambridge University, Cambridge, UK. Electronic address: madeline.lancaster@mrclmb.ac.uk.
items.abstract: The human brain has structural and functional differences to our closest living relatives, the other great apes. It is thought that these differences give rise to many of the traits we associate with being human, such as our prodigious capacity to learn and be creative. However, the molecular mechanisms that underpin these differences are mostly unknown. In this review, we describe how neural organoids, an in vitro model of brain development, enable questions of human brain evolution to be functionally investigated in evolutionarily relevant developmental contexts. We discuss new insights at the genetic, cellular, and developmental scales and highlight current challenges in organoid generation, in long-term culture, and in establishing multimodal phenotypic measurements. We anticipate expanding the application of organoid models across Mammalia to help us better define species- and lineage-specific traits and improve our understanding of how complex traits emerge and evolve across developmental and evolutionary timescales.

items.title: Cognitive evaluation of brain organoids and assembloids
items.last_author_affiliation: Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR), Brain, Mind, and Consciousness Program, Toronto, ON, Canada; Collège de France, Université Paris-Sciences-Lettres (PSL), 11 Place Marcelin Berthelot, 75005 Paris, France; Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, INSERM, CEA, CNRS, Université Paris-Saclay, NeuroSpin Center, Gif-sur-Yvette, France. Electronic address: stanislas.dehaene@college-de-france.fr.
items.abstract: The computational abilities of brain organoids and assembloids remain largely unexplored. We propose a hierarchy of assays grounded in cognitive neuroscience and probing representations, memory, and predictive processing, thus enabling causal tests of how architecture and maturation shape emerging computations while providing empirical constraints on debates about organoid consciousness.

items.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Stem Cell & Regenerative Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA; Stanley Center for Psychiatric Research, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA. Electronic address: paola_arlotta@harvard.edu.
items.abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

items.title: Human stem cell neuroscience
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA; Stanford Brain Organogenesis Program, Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute and Bio-X, Stanford, CA, USA; Hoover Institution, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA. Electronic address: spasca@stanford.edu.
items.abstract: In neuroscience, the most relevant human biology has often been the least accessible. Stem-cell-based models, such as organoids and assembloids, are opening ways to generate, assemble, probe, and perturb neural cells and circuits, helping define "stem cell neuroscience." In this issue of Neuron, this and other reviews and commentaries discuss the current state of this emerging field.

items.title: Toward functional oversight of neural organoid research: A report from the 2025 Asilomar Conference
items.last_author_affiliation: Worldview Studio, Menlo Park, CA, USA. Electronic address: brieann@worldview.studio.
items.abstract: In November 2025, an international multistakeholder group convened at Asilomar, California, to address oversight of rapidly advancing neural organoid and assembloid research. This process report documents the convening's design, outcomes, and lessons, and it asks what it will take to turn this momentum into ongoing monitoring and practical guidelines that ensure responsible research without constraining scientific progress.

items.title: Dissociable cerebellar pathways for reach correction and learning
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Physiology and Biophysics, University of Colorado Anschutz, Aurora, CO 80045, USA. Electronic address: abigail.person@cuanschutz.edu.
items.abstract: Sensory feedback can trigger rapid motor corrections, but how self-generated movement errors are corrected and influence subsequent behavior remains less clear. Here, we found that corrective submovements (CSMs), structured, feedback-driven adjustments, occurred either spontaneously or in response to neural perturbations during mouse reaching. Corrections were modestly encoded in the cerebellar anterior interposed nucleus (IntA) along with non-corrective reach kinematic correlates. Closed-loop perturbations directed to red nucleus-projecting neurons were readily compensated for with corrective movements and led to learned shifts in the timing of future submovements, while perturbations to IntA more broadly were not compensated for and produced no learning. Thus, subsets of IntA outputs differentially permit or corrupt accurate corrections and subsequent learning, respectively.

items.title: An astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 axis promotes synapse engulfment in early amyloid pathology
items.last_author_affiliation: UK Dementia Research Institute, Institute of Neurology, University College London, Gower Street, London WC1E6BT, UK. Electronic address: soyon.hong@ucl.ac.uk.
items.abstract: Region-specific synapse loss is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, yet the upstream signals that render synapses vulnerable remain unclear. In a mouse model of amyloidosis, we identify an early astrocyte state that emerges in vulnerable brain regions before widespread plaque deposition and overt gliosis. These astrocytes exhibit bulbous-looking perisynaptic processes enriched in p62 and glycogen, impaired autophagic flux and calcium signaling, and diminished astrocyte-synapse coverage. Rather than exhibiting increased synapse engulfment, bulbous astrocytes show elevated milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 (MFG-E8) and are associated with increased local microglial synapse engulfment. Astrocyte-specific gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that astrocyte-derived MFG-E8 is required for microglial synapse engulfment and acts through microglial β3 integrin signaling. Astrocytic Mfge8 deletion reduces microglial engulfment and synapse loss across amyloidosis models and is associated with reduced amyloid pathology, gliosis, and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings define an astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 signaling axis that contributes to region-specific synaptic vulnerability during early amyloid pathology.

items.title: Unbundling the ethical and social issues in human neural organoid research
items.last_author_affiliation: Robison O. Everett Professor of Law and Philosophy, Duke University, Durham, NC 27707, USA. Electronic address: farahany@duke.edu.
items.abstract: As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. These include interests involved in informed consent, distinct dimensions of consciousness and their implications for welfare, approaches to engaging public concerns, and governance and oversight of both organoids themselves and their uses.

items.title: Advancing brain organoids from disease phenotypes to mechanisms and translation across developmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases
items.last_author_affiliation: Neural Stem Cell Institute, Regenerative Research Foundation, 150 New Scotland Ave, Albany, NY, USA. Electronic address: sallytemple@neuralsci.org.
items.abstract: Diseases of the central nervous system remain among the greatest unmet medical challenges. Human brain organoids provide 3D multicellular systems for investigating neurodevelopmental, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases in a human cellular context. Considering these distinct disease areas together highlights how organoid studies are moving beyond recapitulating disease phenotypes to define molecular and cellular mechanisms and trajectories: when pathogenic changes emerge, how they evolve, which cell types and states drive or resist disease, and how multicellular interactions shape progression. Integrating human genetics with longitudinal, single-cell, multi-omic, and functional analyses provides access to human-specific processes that are difficult to capture in animal models and enables identification of mechanisms and therapeutic targets anchored in human disease biology. Increasingly, well-characterized organoids offer human new approach methodologies (NAMs) for preclinical therapeutic evaluation. Advances in reproducibility, benchmarking, and appropriate validation will be critical to establishing their predictive value and supporting their use in drug development and regulatory applications.

items.title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Cellular and Organismic Biology and Neuroscience Program of Academia Sinica, Academia Sinica, Taipei, 115, Taiwan; Taiwan International Graduate Program in Interdisciplinary Neuroscience, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan. Electronic address: slchiu@gate.sinica.edu.tw.
items.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Structure-guided engineering of eukaryotic Fanzor-ωRNA system enhances in vivo gene editing for dystrophin restoration in a Duchenne mouse model
items.abstract: Abstract Background Eukaryotic Fanzor (Fz) proteins are compact RNA-guided endonucleases homologous to prokaryotic TnpB/Cas12, offering theoretical advantages for single AAV delivery. However, their low editing efficiency and poorly defined specificity in mammals have hindered therapeutic development. Results Here, we perform structure-guided engineering of Spizellomyces punctatus Fanzor1 nuclease (SpuFz1) to enhance its utility for in vivo genome editing and identify several Fanzor variants whose efficiencies are comparable or only slightly lower than widely-used miniature enAsCas12f1 and large-sized SpCas9. We demonstrate that catalytically dead dSpuFz1-v4.2 can be repurposed for CRISPRa-mediated transcriptional activation in a proof-of-concept manner. Genome-wide PEM-seq in mice reveal low translocation frequencies (below 0.05%, much lower than the background threshold set by the PEM-seq protocol), with no detected events attributable to off-target editing. GUIDE-seq analysis also confirms genome-wide low off-target profile for SpuFz1-v4.2 in human cells, with small amounts of off-target editing due to 3’ terminal sequence tolerability. Embryonic mRNA injection efficiently generates mutant mice. Crucially, single AAV9 delivery of SpuFz1-v4.2 in a humanized Duchenne muscular dystrophy model induces targeted exon skipping, restores dystrophin expression to ~ 10% of wild-type levels, and improves muscle contractile force. Conclusions Structure-guided optimization overcomes the activity barrier of eukaryotic Fanzors while maintaining low off-target effect. The engineered SpuFz1-v4.2 retains the hypercompact size necessary for single AAV packaging, establishing a robust platform for in vivo gene editing. This work positions Fanzor by a preliminary proof-of-concept therapeutic study as a viable, miniature alternative to CRISPR-Cas systems for genetic disease intervention and functional genomics.

items.title: Spatial transcriptomics defines segmental and temporal dynamics of pig intestinal epithelium
Short-read sequencing benchmarking with donor-specific assemblies
Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
items.last_author_affiliation: University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland. antti.honkela@helsinki.fi.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The synthesis of anonymized data derived from real-world cohorts offers a promising strategy for regulatory-compliant and privacy-preserving biological data sharing, potentially facilitating model development that can improve predictive performance. However, the extent to which generative models can preserve biological signals while remaining resilient to adversarial privacy attacks in high-dimensional omics contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, the CAMDA 2025 Health Privacy Challenge launched a community-driven effort to evaluate synthetic and privacy-preserving data generation for bulk RNA-seq cohorts. Results Building on this initiative, we systematically benchmark 11 generative methods across two cancer cohorts (~ 1,000 and ~ 5,000 patients) over 978 landmark genes. Methods are evaluated across distributional fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility and empirical privacy risk, with emphasis on trade-offs between vulnerability to membership inference attacks and other evaluation dimensions. Expressive deep generative models achieve strong predictive utility and differential expression recovery, but are often more vulnerable to membership inference risk under the evaluated threat model. Differentially private methods improve resistance to attacks at the cost of reduced utility, while simpler statistical approaches offer competitive utility with moderate privacy risk and fast training. Conclusions Synthetic bulk RNA-seq quality is inherently multi-dimensional and shaped by trade-offs between utility, biological preservation and privacy. Our results indicate that model architecture drives distinct trade-offs across these axes, suggesting that model choice should align with dataset characteristics, intended downstream use and privacy requirements. Privacy risk should also be assessed using multiple complementary attack methods and, where possible, mitigated through formal differential privacy protection.

items.title: G-quadruplex profiling using single-cell CUT&Tag offers insight into the epigenetic landscape of the developing mouse brain
items.last_author_affiliation: Science for Life Laboratory, Department of Medical Biochemistry and Biophysics, Division of Genome Biology, Karolinska Institutet, Tomtebodavägen 23, 17165, Stockholm, Sweden. simon.elsasser@scilifelab.se.; Ming Wai Lau Centre for Reparative Medicine, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm Node, Solnavägen 9, Stockholm, 17165, Sweden. simon.elsasser@scilifelab.se.; Institute for Biology, Universität Freiburg, Schänzlestrasse 1, 79104, Freiburg, Germany. simon.elsasser@scilifelab.se.; Center for Integrative Biological Signalling Studies (CIBSS), University of Freiburg, Schänzlestrasse 18, 79104, Freiburg, Germany. simon.elsasser@scilifelab.se.
items.abstract: Abstract Background G-quadruplexes (G4s) are non-canonical DNA structures that have gained increasing attention for their potential roles in gene regulation and role in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Despite their biological significance, G4 structures have not been studied systematically across tissues and cell types. Results In this study, we employ G4 single-cell CUT&Tag (G4 scCUT&Tag) to characterize G4 landscapes in postnatal mouse brain cells, leveraging single-cell analytical approaches commonly used in scRNA-Seq and scATAC-Seq datasets. Using conventional single-cell omics workflows to process and explore our data, we distinguish distinct cell lineages based on G4 heterogeneity and establish that a subset of lineage-specific genes show unique promoter G4s. Multi-omics integration with scRNA-Seq gene expression profiles, using both a covariance-based technique (canonical correlation analysis) and a transfer learning-based approach, enables more accurate cell-type annotation. These integrations not only reveal correlations between G4 signal and gene expression, but demonstrate that G4 scCUT&Tag enables detailed examination of G4 heterogeneity in complex tissues and supports integrative analysis of G4 profiles with other omics layers, offering new insights into the epigenomic landscapes of the developing brain. Conclusions Our findings establish G4 scCUT&Tag as a framework for investigating the cellular heterogeneity of G4 landscapes in complex tissues and provide a basis for exploring their relationships with gene regulation and other layers of chromatin organization.

items.title: The rise, evolution and future of whole genome projects in Asian populations
AMP Challenge: towards a standardized, community-wide benchmark for AI-driven antimicrobial peptide design
Ultrafast alignment-free detection of viral genome variation with bronko
items.last_author_affiliation: Rice University;
items.abstract: As viral sequencing datasets continue to grow, traditional alignment-based variant calling pipelines are becoming computationally prohibitive. To address these challenges, we developed bronko, an ultrafast alignment-free framework for detecting viral variation directly from sequencing data. The novel computational approach implemented in bronko allows scaling to massive viral sequencing datasets and has four key components: i) a locality-sensitive bucketing function to rapidly identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) relative to reference(s), ii) a direct k -mer count pseudo-mapping approach that approximates a pileup without alignment, iii) a greedy de novo assembly algorithm to reconstruct mutation-dense regions and indels and iv) a streaming-based sliding window outlier test to estimate baseline noise across the genome and precisely differentiate real minor variants from noise. Together, these components yield near-linear computational complexity with respect to sequencing depth, enabling bronko to process thousands of viral samples rapidly on modest hardware. Our results are threefold: 1) On simulated amplicon sequencing, bronko recovers variants with higher precision and comparable recall to existing tools while running up to one to three orders of magnitude faster; 2) bronko generates sequence alignments directly from sequencing data, with SNP content nearly identical to that of whole-genome alignment while also running in a fraction of the time, and 3) applying bronko to longitudinal sequencing data from chronically infected SARS-CoV-2 patients revealed consistent patterns of intrahost diversification and adaptive mutations over time. Altogether, these results demonstrate bronko's potential as a scalable tool for large-scale viral genomic analyses, overcoming longstanding computational barriers for intrahost and interhost characterization of viral variation.

items.title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning
items.last_author_affiliation: Umea University;
items.abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F max of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.

items.title: Derivation of doxorubicin mutational signatures in cancer
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Pediatrics, Emory University School of Medicine, Atlanta, Georgia 30322, USA;; Aflac Cancer and Blood Disorders Center–Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, Atlanta, Georgia 30329, USA;; Winship Cancer Institute, Atlanta, Georgia 30322, USA
items.abstract: Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic agent used for the treatment of solid and hematopoietic malignancies. Doxorubicin acts as a DNA intercalator and inhibits the topoisomerase II enzyme, leading to double-stranded breaks. We hypothesize that doxorubicin mutagenesis leads to a nonrandom pattern of somatic mutations on the genome, termed a mutational signature. We expose cells to doxorubicin using two different methodologies: (1) continuous exposure of a constant dose of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of single-cell clones (previously published methodology) and (2) pulsed exposure of escalating doses of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of a bulk population. We first confirm that the methodologies do not yield differing results through previously published cisplatin-exposed single-cell clone genome data compared with the dose escalation and bulk genome data. We then derive two doxorubicin signatures. The first, SBS-doxorubicin-1, is defined by an abundance of C > A mutations. The second, SBS-doxorubicin-2, is defined by a higher occurrence of T > C mutations. We then assess for the presence of our signatures within the genomes of patients treated with a doxorubicin-containing regimen. Across 10 bulk immune sorted samples from three patients with follicular lymphoma/diffuse large B cell lymphoma, as well as two metastatic samples from one patient with renal medullary carcinoma, we are able to detect both signatures in 83% of samples, with remaining samples harboring either signature. In summary, we experimentally derive two doxorubicin mutational signatures and demonstrate their presence in patient samples.

items.title: Perivascular epithelial remodeling is reflected in circulating cfDNA methylation signals as detection markers for early esophageal tumorigenesis
items.last_author_affiliation: Cancer Hospital of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences 1 Beijing
items.abstract: Abstract Early detection of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is hindered by a lack of noninvasive biomarkers for precancerous lesions. Here, we report a circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation approach for early esophageal neoplasia detection. In prospective community screening, the assay achieved standardized sensitivity of 78% at 79% specificity for the clinically actionable endpoint of high-grade intraepithelial neoplasia (HGIN) or ESCC, with stage-specific sensitivities of 76% for HGIN and 86% for ESCC. Genome-wide methylation profiling reveals HGIN as an early epigenetic reprogramming stage. Integrative spatial and single-cell RNA sequencing reveals pronounced remodeling of the endothelial-proximal epithelial cell population, whose methylation signatures are detected in cfDNA. Guided by these findings, we develop an 11-gene cfDNA methylation panel that shows robust discrimination of early-stage ESCC across three retrospective case-control sets and an independent screening-derived case-control set. Together, these results demonstrate that our cfDNA methylation panel has promising utility for early ESCC detection
