items.title: MACF1 condensates serve as molecular rheostats translating mechanical stress into bone adaptation.
items.last_author_affiliation: Lab for Bone Metabolism, Xi'an Key Laboratory of Special Medicine and Health Engineering, Key Lab for Space Biosciences and Biotechnology, Research Center for Special Medicine and Health Systems Engineering, NPU-UAB Joint Laboratory for Bone Metabolism, School of Life Science and Technology, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi'an, China. qianair@nwpu.edu.cn.; Shenzhen Research Institute, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Shenzhen, China. qianair@nwpu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Bone dynamically maintains homeostasis through mechanotransduction, a process essential for skeletal integrity and frequently disrupted in disease. Yet how bone cells decode mechanical cues into adaptive responses remains poorly understood. Here, we identify MACF1, a cytoskeletal crosslinker and core component of stress granules (SGs), as a mechanosensitive scaffold that undergoes phase separation via its intrinsically disordered region 2 (IDR2). In response to distinct mechanical cues, IDR2-driven condensation promotes the recruitment of PIEZO1, paxillin (PXN), and β-catenin (CTNNB1) into SGs, buffering these signaling molecules from ubiquitination-dependent degradation and sustaining osteogenic fidelity. Moreover, we identify an arginine-mutated IDR2 variant that separates protein interactions from condensate formation, revealing IDR2-driven phase separation as a requirement for MACF1-mediated SG assembly and mechanosensitive protein recruitment. Functionally, bone-targeted delivery of MACF1-IDR2 alleviates mechanical unloading-induced bone loss in male mice. These findings reveal a liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)-mediated mechanism linking mechanical force sensing and transduction to bone adaptation. Together, these findings support a model in which MACF1 condensates act as molecular rheostats that coordinate mechano-responsive cargo sorting under stress and contribute to skeletal homeostasis.

items.title: Bias-reconfigurable barrier photodetectors for integrated broadband sensing and neuromorphic vision.
items.last_author_affiliation: Key Laboratory of State Manipulation and Advanced Materials in Provincial Universities, School of Physics and Technology, Nanjing Normal University, Nanjing, China. phylhw@njnu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Intelligent vision systems demand photodetectors with reconfigurable response to support diverse modalities like high-speed sensing and neuromorphic processing. Here we show a bias-reconfigurable barrier photodetector that enables continuous modulation of response time across 7 orders of magnitude, from 614 ns to 8.28 s. This wide-range tunability is achieved by electrically modulating the interfacial barrier height, which switches the dominant carrier transport mechanism from direct tunneling to barrier-limited thermal excitation and trap-assisted processes. Under low bias, the device functions as a high-speed photodetector, whereas elevated biases extend the response to synaptic timescales, enabling in-sensor neuromorphic computing as a physical reservoir. Notably, the device exhibits a broadband photoresponse from visible to mid-infrared. High accuracy was achieved in complex recognition tasks, such as classifying vehicle acceleration or deceleration. This integration of fast photodetection and neuromorphic computation establishes hardware-efficient paradigms for integrated machine vision, adaptive multispectral sensing, and energy-efficient edge intelligence.

items.title: Fast-charging and durable all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries enabled by pre-embedded solid-solid redox mediator.
items.last_author_affiliation: Beijing Key Laboratory for Theory and Technology of Advanced Battery Materials, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Peking University, Beijing, China. qqpang@pku.edu.cn.
items.abstract: All-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries promise high specific energy and low cost. However, they are challenged by poor rate capability and cycling stability owing to the slow solid-solid sulfur redox reactions. Here, we present fast-charging and durable all-solid-state lithium-sulfur batteries enabled by a pre-embedded solid-solid redox mediator using an amorphous sulfur/iodine nano-eutectic positive electrode. The iodine, intimately homogenized with sulfur owing to carbon mesopore encapsulation, undergoes rapid I2/I- redox reaction, mediating solid-solid sulfur reactions by promoting electron transfer across the boundaries. The iodine within the carbon and on its surface reacts in situ with the sulfide catholyte to form a globally distributed I2/I- nano-network throughout the positive electrode, thereby enabling fast charging. The cell exhibits a specific capacity of 851.9 mA h g-1S/I when charged at 10 C, and 474.7 mA h g-1S/I at a charging rate of 24 C (1 C is defined as 945 mA g-1S/I). The high reversibility of the redox-mediated reaction enables durable cycling for 9,000 cycles over 9 months at 2 C and 2,800 cycles over 17 months at 0.5 C. This strategy represents a perspective for developing solid-state conversion electrodes that are plagued by sluggish reactions.

items.title: ATM promotes nucleolytic processing of reversed replication forks during DNA interstrand cross-link repair.
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA. dsemlow@caltech.edu.
items.abstract: During replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) repair, fork reversal is thought to enable the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway to resolve the ICL through nucleolytic incisions. The resulting regressed arm of the reversed fork undergoes extensive nucleolytic resection that may facilitate completion of replication. Despite the importance of these remodeling events, their regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we use cell-free Xenopus egg extracts and human cells to investigate reversed fork processing during ICL repair by the FA pathway. We find that the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase is activated concomitantly with fork reversal and promotes resection of reversed fork intermediates. ATM enhances chromatin recruitment of DNA2, which acts alongside EXO1 to resect reversed forks formed during ICL repair. Moreover, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) leads to ATM hyperactivation, accelerated reversed fork processing, and accumulation of aberrant end-joining products, implying that PP2A restrains ATM signaling to limit reversed fork resection. Taken together, this work identifies reversed forks as substrates for ATM activation and reveals a phospho-regulatory circuit that controls reversed fork processing.

items.title: pH-responsive manganese carboxymethyl chitosan hydrogel releases pesticide to promote rice tillering and suppress root-parasitic weeds.
items.last_author_affiliation: Engineering Research Centre of Plant Growth Regulators, Ministry of Education, College of Agronomy and Biotechnology, China Agricultural University, No. 2 Yuanmingyuan West Road, Haidian District, Beijing, China. tanwm@cau.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) signaling is an important agricultural target for controlling plant branching and parasitic weeds. Here, based on the SL inhibitor KK094, we describe the design of 32 indole derivatives, of which DK6 exhibits optimal activity. To enhance solubility and bioavailability, we describe a pH-responsive manganese-coordinated carboxymethyl chitosan hydrogel (CMCS-DK6), showing sustained release under alkaline conditions. We demonstrate CMCS-DK6 strongly inhibits germination of parasitic weeds, especially Striga asiatica (IC50 = 1.80 μM), while promoting rice tillering, reducing height, and increasing dry weight. Molecular simulations, along with microscale thermophoresis results, suggest that DK6 binds stably to SL receptors. Transcriptomics reveal DK6 suppresses SL signaling, modulates metabolic pathways, and interacts with hormone pathways to regulate tillering. This work offers a hydrogel delivery strategy and some potential mechanistic implications for improving crop architecture and weed control.

items.title: Periodontal pathogen Tannerella forsythia promotes liver fibrosis via ICAM-1⁺ neutrophil-dependent hepatic stellate cell activation.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Stomatology, The Fifth Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province, China. liqsh26@mail.sysu.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Periodontitis is a key driver in the development and progression of liver fibrosis. Nevertheless, how specific periodontal pathogens contribute to liver fibrosis remains elusive. Here, we identify Tannerella forsythia as the crucial mediator in the link between periodontitis and liver fibrosis, which can translocate to the gut and aggravate liver fibrosis. Mechanistically, Tannerella forsythia promotes the infiltration of ICAM-1+ neutrophils and inflammatory response in the liver via disrupting intestinal barrier integrity. ICAM-1+ neutrophils secrete TNF-α, which activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway in hepatic stellate cells, triggering collagen deposition and fibrogenesis. Conditional knockout of ICAM-1 in neutrophils or global deletion of TNF-α significantly attenuates inflammatory response and liver fibrosis caused by Tannerella forsythia. Taken together, this study identifies an oral-gut-liver axis driven by Tannerella forsythia and provides a prospective therapeutic target for periodontitis-related liver fibrosis.

items.title: Precious metal free tunable manganese oxides for sustainable anion exchange membrane fuel cells.
items.last_author_affiliation: Shanghai Key Laboratory for R&D and Application of Metallic Functional Materials, Institute of New Energy for Vehicles, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, 201804, China. jiwei.ma@tongji.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Eliminating platinum group metals from cathode catalysts in low-temperature polymer electrolyte fuel cells is highly important for addressing the sustainability challenge fuel cell systems face. Here, we propose modifying the electronic structure of Li-intercalated layered Mn-oxide as a cathode catalyst to overcome the activity/stability tradeoff in anion exchange membrane fuel cells. To achieve this goal, we deploy a precious metal free catalyst design strategy involving atomically dispersed p-block metal Sn doped in Li2MnO3, in addition to d-block metals, which has been poorly explored in the research thus far. Operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy and rapid freeze-quench 119Sn Mössbauer methodology are employed to visualize the catalytic dynamics, revealing that part of Mn4+ ions are converted into Mn3+ ions, whereas Sn4+ ions remain unchanged during the oxygen reduction reaction. Under H2/O2 conditions, anion exchange membrane fuel cells employing Li2Mn0.9Sn0.1O3 cathodes achieve peak power densities above 1.0 W cm-2geo and 3.96 W mg-1Pt. This work demonstrates the beneficial modulation of the electronic structure through p-block metal substitution in earth-abundant Mn-enriched oxide materials.

items.title: Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events.
items.last_author_affiliation: Earth Sciences New Zealand, Wellington, New Zealand.
items.abstract: In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

items.title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents.
items.last_author_affiliation: Sociology Department, Data Science Institute, & Knowledge Lab, University of Chicago, Chicago, USA. jevans@uchicago.edu.; Santa Fe Institute, Santa Fe, USA. jevans@uchicago.edu.
items.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have empowered autonomous agents to generate social networks, communicate, and form shared and diverging opinions on political issues. However, our understanding of their collective behaviours and underlying mechanisms remains incomplete. In this paper, we simulate networked systems involving thousands of LLM agents across different backbone models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-V3), in which agents interact through LLM-guided conversations and update their opinions over time, resulting in the emergence of opinion polarization. We discover that these agents spontaneously develop their own social network with properties characteristic of human social networks, such as homophilic clustering. The collective opinions of these LLM agents evolve in ways that exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with social phenomena and mechanisms widely discussed in empirical studies of human behaviour and opinion-dynamics models. This consistency suggests that LLM agents can serve as a valuable synthetic testbed for exploring hypothetical intervention strategies in networked LLM-agent systems. Using this testbed, we further examine the effects of a range of network- and individual-level interventions, such as promoting more diverse interactions and reducing confirmation bias. Overall, this work not only sheds light on subtle opinion dynamics and collective behaviour of LLM agents from a network perspective, but also demonstrates their potential for testing hypotheses about opinion dynamics and intervention strategies.

items.title: SWI/SNF subunit SMARCD1 deficiency promotes clear cell renal cell carcinoma progression via mitochondrial reprogramming.
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Urology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China. 2013tj0589@hust.edu.cn.; Hubei Provincial Clinical Medical Research Center for Minimally Invasive Treatment of Urology, Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, China. 2013tj0589@hust.edu.cn.
items.abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) remains a lethal malignancy driven in part by SWI/SNF dysfunction, yet the mechanistic basis of this link is unclear. We identify SMARCD1, a core SWI/SNF subunit, as a tumor suppressor progressively silenced by DNMT3B-mediated promoter hypermethylation in ccRCC. SMARCD1 loss enables DDX3X binding to the MAFF promoter, leading to transcriptional upregulation of MAFF, which in turn promotes ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the mitochondrial fusion protein MFN1. The SMARCD1-MAFF-MFN1 axis disrupts mitochondrial fusion, reprograms metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation, and enhances metastatic potential. Therapeutically, pharmacological restoration of MFN1 with the FDA-approved immunosuppressant leflunomide reverses mitochondrial dysfunction and suppresses tumor progression in multiple preclinical models. In patient-derived xenografts, leflunomide also potentiates tyrosine kinase inhibitor and immune checkpoint blockade efficacy. These findings establish a direct link between chromatin remodeling defects and mitochondrial dysregulation and highlight leflunomide repurposing as a clinically actionable strategy in SMARCD1-deficient ccRCC.
items.type: Journal Article; Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't

items.title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
items.abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

items.title: A three-factor model can explain symmetry breaking and the n-1 rule during X-chromosome inactivation
items.corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
items.abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is a mammalian gene regulatory process that via chromosome-scale transcriptional silencing, leaves active a single X chromosome per diploid genome complement. The mechanisms that enable cells to select the appropriate number of X chromosomes to inactivate while leaving others active remain unclear. We demonstrate that all known chromosomal counting scenarios during XCI can be accounted for by a three-factor mathematical model that includes (1) Xist, the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) responsible for gene silencing during XCI in eutherians, (2) an X-linked transcriptional activator of Xist, and (3) the autosomally-encoded SPEN, an Xist RNA-binding protein that is essential for gene silencing during XCI. In our model, symmetry between active X chromosomes is broken by stochastic differences in the number of Xist molecules that associate with the X chromosomes at the onset of XCI. Subsequently, integrated positive and negative feedback loops amplify then propagate superstoichiometric assemblies of SPEN complexed with Xist on the inactive chromosome(s), and select for levels of X-linked activator that enable only one X chromosome per diploid genome complement to remain active. Thus, asymmetric propagation of the SPEN-Xist ribonucleoprotein complex may play an essential role in symmetry breaking and chromosomal counting during XCI, independently of or in concert with cis-acting networks of DNA regulatory elements. Our results also have conceptual implications for gene regulatory circuits on autosomes.

items.title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Differ from Controls and Correlate with Aspects of Cognition in Kabuki Syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
items.abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome (KS) and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) are two disorders caused by dysfunctional components of the epigenetic machinery and both result in intellectual disability. Mouse models of both KS and RSTS have seen reversal of cognitive impairment with epigenetic treatments. However, a great need exists for biomarkers in these disorders to improve the likelihood of successful clinical trials. This study aimed to investigate cortical auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in KS and RSTS so that it could potentially be developed into a response biomarker in the future. Methods The amplitude of the N1-P2-N2 complex was measured for passive listening to monotonal auditory stimuli in individuals with KS, with RSTS, and typically developing controls. A standardized cognitive assessment battery was performed and specific subtests were correlated with AEP values. Results Groups differed significantly in P2, N2, and P2-N2 amplitude although RSTS was consistently more different from typically developing controls than was KS. The mid- to late-phase AEP components (P2 and N2) also correlate with cognition within and across these groups particularly with language whereas earlier components N1 and P2 correlate more with measures of executive functioning. Conclusion Late-phase components of AEPs differ in KS and RSTS from each other and from controls. KS and RSTS differ from controls in P2 and N2 amplitude in the same direction and both show a positive correlation between language and P2 amplitude and a negative correlation between language and N2 amplitude. Together they also show an association with N1 and P2 amplitude and executive functioning. Significance AEPs may turn out to be a valuable response biomarker in KS and RSTS individually and together.

items.title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
items.abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

items.title: Neural transformation from image realism to perceived realness
items.corresponding_institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
items.abstract: Humans readily perceive whether a visual stimulus depicts something that could exist in the real world, yet the neural basis of perceived realness remains unclear. Because differences between real and unreal stimuli are ultimately expressed through visual features, realness might be expected to emerge along the ventral visual stream. Contrary to this prediction, we show that perceived-realness representations emerge in higher dorsal visual areas through a transformation of image-realism-related image-feature representations in early visual and early dorsal visual areas. fMRI revealed this representational shift toward intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with IPS patterns predicting perceived realness beyond image features and decision difficulty; source-localized MEG showed that realness coding in IPS peaked later than feature coding in early visual and dorsal visual areas. Together, these findings reveal a transformation from visual features to perceived realness along the dorsal visual stream. This representation may help guide subsequent actions and interactions with the real world.

items.title: γδ T cell-derived IL-17A aggravates experimental epidermolysis bullosa acquisita in response to IL-1β
items.abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a mucocutaneous autoimmune blistering disorder mediated by autoantibodies against type VII collagen and subsequent splitting of the dermal-epidermal junction. Interleukin (IL)-17A promotes the production of chemokines and cytokines involved in neutrophil recruitment and activation, suggesting that IL-17A may contribute to EBA pathogenesis. We aimed to clarify the role of IL-17A in experimental EBA. Using an antibody transfer-induced EBA mouse model, we demonstrate that IL-17A promotes disease development, as pharmacological blockade of IL-17A with a neutralizing antibody ameliorated skin lesions. Gamma-delta ({gamma}{delta}) T cells were identified as the predominant cellular source of IL-17A, supported by the attenuated disease phenotype observed in {gamma}{delta}TCR-deficient mice. In addition, CD4+ T cells and neutrophils contributed to IL-17A production in experimental EBA. Mechanistically, IL-1-beta, rather than IL-23, was identified as a critical mediator of IL-17A production by {gamma}{delta} T cells in vitro, consistent with our in vivo findings. Whereas EBA severity was not reduced in IL-23p19-deficient mice, disease was markedly attenuated in IL-1R-deficient animals. Together, our study provides the first evidence that {gamma}{delta} T cell-derived IL-17A plays a pivotal role in experimental EBA and identifies a previously unrecognized IL-1{beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell/IL-17A axis that expands current understanding of EBA immunopathogenesis.

items.title: A noncanonical function of Dicer fuels self-dsRNA-driven inflammation
items.abstract: Self-derived double-stranded RNA (self-dsRNA) acts as potent triggers of autoinflammation and damage-associated molecular patterns in cancer and infection. However, the upstream processes controlling self-dsRNA homeostasis remain unclear. We uncover a non-canonical role for human Dicer in driving cell-intrinsic immunity to self-dsRNAs that arise from editing or splicing defects, epigenetic deregulation or mitochondrial stress. Dicer loss abolishes type-I interferon induction, PKR activation, and OAS-RNase L activation in response to self - but not exogenous - dsRNA in multiple cell types, including a clinically-relevant hiPSC model of neuroinflammation. Dicer interacts with G3BP1 and LGP2 to regulate self-dsRNA availability and recognition, respectively, independently of miRNAs. As immunostimulatory self-dsRNAs fail to accumulate and activate dsRNA sensors in absence of Dicer, these findings position Dicer as a central regulator of self-dsRNA sensing.

items.title: ER stress-associated IRE1α signalling links impaired QPRT-dependent NAD⁺ biosynthesis to reduced oocyte competence
items.abstract: Oocyte quality is closely linked to metabolic and organelle homeostasis, but the mechanisms underlying naturally occurring differences in oocyte quality remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a link between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired NAD biosynthesis and poor oocyte quality. Poor-grade goat oocytes exhibited profound NAD depletion, accompanied by quinolinic acid accumulation and reduced expression of quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT), suggesting a bottleneck in de novo NAD biosynthesis. Restoring QPRT expression or bypassing this metabolic step improved meiotic maturation. Further analyses revealed altered ER stress signalling, increased IRE1-associated activity and reduced QPRT RNA stability. Recombinant IRE1 processed QPRT RNA in vitro, suggesting a possible link between IRE1 activity and QPRT transcript regulation. Supplementation with nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) restored NAD levels and improved several features of poor-quality oocytes, including calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial membrane potential. NMN treatment also improved early embryonic development, with its beneficial effects involving SIRT6 activity and changes in DNA methylation-associated fluorescence. Importantly, NMN supplementation improved meiotic maturation in poor-grade bovine and porcine oocytes, indicating that this metabolic intervention may have broader relevance across mammals. Analysis of published human oocyte proteomic data further revealed age-associated changes in ER proteostasis and NAD-related proteins. Together, our findings identify ER stress-associated disruption of QPRT-dependent NAD biosynthesis as a potential contributor to poor oocyte quality and suggest that restoring NAD metabolism may offer a strategy to improve the functional properties of compromised oocytes.

items.title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
items.abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.

items.title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Biochemistry, Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen, Germany
items.abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the Saccha-romyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state in vivo. For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

items.title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
items.abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.

items.title: Epigenome-informed Polymer Modeling Reveals Chromosome Folding Landscapes across Distinct Genetic and Epigenetic Contexts
items.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is critical for gene regulation, enabling long-range interactions between genes and distal regulatory elements. Genomic structural variations and epigenetic differences can perturb this organization, contributing to phenotypic variation and tissue-specific gene regulation. Prior studies have assessed the impact of these genetic and epigenetic changes on 3D genome folding, primarily using population-averaged features such as topologically associating domains and loops. However, growing evidence from single-cell and live-imaging studies indicates that chromosomes are highly dynamic and exist as heterogeneous ensembles of conformations. Here, we applied an epigenetic-state-informed polymer modeling framework to generate chromosomal conformational ensembles directly from cell- and tissue-specific epigenomic data. The resulting ensembles reproduced experimental Hi-C maps across cell lines and tissue types. Comparison of these conformational ensembles revealed that, although polymer dynamics were conserved across cell lines, their folding landscapes diverged. These differences arose primarily from cell-line-specific chromatin-state interaction networks and were concentrated in rare, long-lived contacts. Furthermore, modeling a TAD-boundary-disrupting deletion without re-optimizing the model parameters indicated a shift in the chromatin conformational ensemble from predominantly insulated to predominantly fused states. The modeled deletion also selectively strengthened active chromatin contacts and differentially disrupted enhancer contacts involving neighboring genes. Finally, comparison of two tissue types from the same donor revealed epigenetically driven rewiring of chromatin-state interaction networks. These findings establish chromosomal conformational ensembles as a sensitive readout of genome reorganization across distinct genetic and epigenetic contexts.

items.title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating Rx for stone marten and red fox
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for Bioinformatics, University of Veterinary Medicine, Budapest, 1078, Hungary
items.abstract: Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (Martes foina) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund Ry metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that Rx places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio Rx of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats, Rx identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads, Rx and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.

items.title: Learning Strand-Equivariant Tokenizations of DNA with MirrorDNA
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology, Dhaka, Bangladesh
items.abstract: DNA has two strands, and for most regulatory label prediction tasks a sequence and its reverse complement should get same answer. Yet DNA language models are tokenized, trained and tested on one strand at a time. We show that this makes them inconsistent. BPE and $k$-mer tokenizers split 92--100\% of transcription-factor motifs differently on the two strands, and NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA change 25-31\% of their predictions when the test sequences are reverse-complemented. We introduce {\model}, a compact DNA language model with a learned tokenizer that guarantees mirror-symmetric token boundaries across reverse-complement sequences, regardless of its learned parameters. We prove that this symmetry holds through the whole model. As a result, the same model can give identical answers on both strands when the label does not depend on the strand, and can still tell the strands apart when it does, which no strand-blind model can learn. Counting only predictions that are correct on both strands, \model\ more than doubles the MCC of NT-v2, DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA. With 2.3M parameters, it is more accurate than the Caduceus models trained on the same data, and not significantly different from NT-v2 (98M parameters) on Genomic Benchmarks or from DNABERT-2 (117M) on the Nucleotide Transformer tasks. It also stays accurate on inputs sixteen times longer than those it was trained on. The same model trained with reverse-complement augmentation instead still changes about one prediction in ten with the strand, unless its outputs are averaged over both strands. Without any annotation, the tokenizer learns to keep the splice-donor signal \texttt{AGGT} in a single token. Code: https://github.com/NIRJHOR-DATTA/MirrorDNA.

items.title: Automahout: an autonomous image analysis system for cell tracking
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory for Developmental Dynamics, RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research
items.abstract: Cell tracking in time-lapse images is complex image analysis that involves detection, linking and proofreading, often requiring the algorithm to be tuned for every new dataset. We present Automahout, an autonomous agent for the Mastodon/ELEPHANT platform that carries out these operations. It looks at the data and tries existing models; where none fits, it annotates reference cells, trains a detector from those sparse annotations, reviews its output against them and feeds the corrections back until its own stopping criteria are met. It then links, checks the lineage and moves on. On three public datasets, a 2D fluorescence culture, a 2D phase-contrast culture and a 3D embryo, it produced lineages without human input and reached TRA scores of 0.95-0.96.

items.title: scDisentangle: sequential disentanglement for single-cell perturbation response prediction
items.abstract: Predicting the transcriptional response of single cells to perturbation is a central goal of single-cell modeling, with broad application to analysis and experimental design. Existing methods often fail to beat simple baselines and offer little insight into how biological variation is organized. We present scDisentangle, a model that decomposes single-cell expression into observed attributes and a sequence of residual components, generating counterfactuals that preserve source cell identity. scDisentangle outperformed current models and naive baselines on cytokine stimulation, liver infection, and unseen combinatorial genetic perturbations, on which accuracy was largely independent of how closely a response resembled the average perturbation effect. In an immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis cohort, cell-resolved counterfactuals predicted donor-specific intracardiac CD8+ T cell states from peripheral blood. In a castration-regeneration prostate atlas, predictions recapitulated luminal dynamics and progenitor-marker kinetics upon androgen add-back. scDisentangle's coarse-to-fine latent structure aligned with hematopoietic lineage organization, with early levels capturing a less differentiated core progressively refined into cell-type-specific programs.

items.title: RPFace: From biased structural benchmarks to generalizable RNA-protein interface prediction
items.abstract: Modeling protein-RNA complexes with co-folding and docking methods is routine, yet these methods are evaluated on benchmarks whose composition mirrors the deposited structures on which they were trained or tuned, leaving open whether their reported performance reflects true generalization. Here, we focus the evaluation on the region that carries the biological signal: the binding interface. For the first time, we construct and release a fair benchmark that stratifies protein-RNA data into distinct structural and experimental groups, providing a more stringent test of generalization than aggregate averages. On this benchmark, we find that accuracy of detecting the binding site using co-folding methods is concentrated in ribosomal complexes and varies systematically with factors such as experimental modality. For docking methods, it is reliable only when the input conformations are already close to the bound state, and it is inconsistent across RNA classes. Both families of methods fail to transfer to in vivo CLIP experiments. To address this gap, we introduce RPFace, to the best of our knowledge the first model that jointly predicts the binding preference of every protein residue and every RNA nucleotide directly from sequence, requiring no experimental structure, template, or multiple sequence alignment. RPFace combines an ensemble of predicted secondary structures with a multi-modal embedding-enrichment scheme that fuses representations from RNA foundation models and structure prediction models. Unlike existing approaches, it is a very small and fast model that delivers stable performance across structural and experimental conditions, is robust to conformational change, and generalizes to in vivo datasets without extensive pretraining. As a result, RPFace matches the state-of-the-art methods on protein interfaces with no evolutionary information, and outperforms them on RNA interfaces, with the largest gains in zero-shot settings despite using only sequence information. The model, code, and data are available at Github.

items.title: LinearRaccess: linear-time approximation of RNA accessibility without base-pair span limits
items.abstract: Motivation: RNA accessibility is the probability that every nucleotide in a contiguous interval is simultaneously unpaired; it is widely used to predict binding sites for RNA-binding proteins and other RNA-RNA interactions, often in the form of the opening energy, an equivalent measure on a logarithmic scale. Existing tools restrict the maximum base-pair span, discarding long-range base pairs that matter biologically. Others sample structures, introducing statistical variance, or compute accessibility exactly without a span limit, at cubic time cost. No existing method computes the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically in linear time while preserving long-range base pairs. We present LinearRaccess, which computes accessibility directly in linear time via beam-pruned inside-outside dynamic programming with a difference-array aggregation step, without restricting base-pair span. Results: For a sequence of length N and a fixed beam width b, LinearRaccess runs in O(N) time and O(Nb) memory. Against exact accessibility on 12,872 bpRNA-1m(90) sequences of 100-1,000 nt, its median opening-energy error is below 0.001 kcal/mol (0.14 kcal/mol for 700-1,000 nt), and it distinguishes windows of very small accessibility, including 35-nt windows, below the resolution of sampling-based estimates. LinearRaccess analyzes the full 29,903-nt SARS-CoV-2 genome in 419 seconds. Conclusion: LinearRaccess is the first method to compute the accessibility of windows longer than one nucleotide deterministically (without sampling) in linear time without restricting base-pair span. Availability: https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearRaccess, archived at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598502).

items.title: Quantitative live imaging reveals region-dependent medulloblastoma disseminationin the zebrafish brain
items.abstract: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, and relapse is frequently driven by dissemination within the central nervous system. Yet the early dynamics of tumor spread remain difficult to resolve in vivo. Here, we orthotopically transplanted human medulloblastoma cells into larval zebrafish and followed individual xenografts by longitudinal high-resolution confocal imaging. ONS-76 showed particularly robust dissemination, with hindbrain tumors spreading into the developing cerebellum in 81.5% of larvae, more than fourfold the frequency observed for forebrain or midbrain tumors. Disseminating cells extended along brain-surface and leptomeningeal-like regions and frequently associated with cerebral vasculature. Quantitative analysis of tumor area, perimeter, compactness, convex hull area, and fractal dimension captured changes in growth and spatial complexity over time. Dasatinib reduced tumor expansion and dissemination-related features in a concentration-dependent manner, while higher doses revealed host toxicity. These findings establish a powerful in vivo model for resolving medulloblastoma dissemination and therapeutic response.

items.title: stem.MAP: Identification of cell-type-specific protein complexes in mammalian embryonic stem cells.
items.abstract: Protein complexes carry out critical functions during development. Mapping cell-type-specific protein complexes in early embryogenesis is essential for uncovering the molecular mechanisms of embryonic development. We unfortunately currently lack a catalog of protein complexes specific for embryogenesis including embryonic stem cells. Here we develop a proteomics-based machine learning workflow to predict protein complexes present in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC). Our method integrates data from a cell-type agnostic protein complex resource with co-fractionation mass spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments on mESC. Our resource, stem.MAP, identifies 3,986 complexes encompassing ~133,000 unique interactions, and 8,616 proteins. stem.MAP captures variant complexes critical for stem cell function including the PRC2, BAF and NuRD complexes. stem.MAP also discriminates mutually exclusive interactions specific to embryonic stem cells (e.g. Eif4ebp2 - Eif4e). Finally we observe 1,388 high confidence stem.MAP interactions found only in mESC CF-MS data, many with support from AlphaFold modeling and a gastruloid coregulation network. We make stem.MAP protein complexes available through our web resource: stem.proteincomplexes.org. We anticipate stem.MAP will be beneficial to the study of early development and we expect our proteomics-based machine learning workflow to be applicable to the creation of any context-specific protein interaction network.

items.title: Beyond Terrestrial Carnivores: Olfactory Bulb Anatomy in a Semi-Aquatic Mammal
items.abstract: The organization of the olfactory systems remains poorly understood in mustelids, particularly in lutrines adapted to semiaquatic environments. This study provides the first detailed anatomical, histological, lectin-histochemical, and immunohistochemical characterization of the main (MOB) and accessory (AOB) olfactory bulbs of the Asian small-clawed otter (Aonyx cinereus). Serial transverse and sagittal sections were examined using Nissl and Tolivia staining, a panel of lectins, and neuronal and olfactory immunohistochemical markers. Macroscopically, the olfactory bulbs were prominent and elongated, although no distinct AOB could be identified. Histologically, the MOB displayed a well-developed laminar organization, abundant mitral and tufted cells, and a clearly defined lateral olfactory tract. By contrast, the AOB was small, located dorsocaudally within the olfactory peduncle, and lacked the canonical lamination observed in many other mammals. Its identification was supported by the selective binding of Ulex europaeus agglutinin and strong Gi2 immunoreactivity in glomerular-like structures, whereas Go labeling was weak. LEA and STA labeled the superficial layers of both bulbs, while VVA and SBA recognized only scattered MOB glomeruli. Neuronal markers, including NCAM, NSE, NeuN, PGP 9.5, and {beta}-tubulin III, confirmed the neuronal nature of the AOB, while calretinin strongly labeled its glomerular structures and projection neurons. These findings reveal a marked contrast between a highly developed MOB and a small, poorly laminated but neurochemically differentiated AOB. This organization indicates that the vomeronasal pathway is retained in A. cinereus, although in a structurally reduced form, and provides a comparative basis for investigating chemosensory evolution in semiaquatic carnivorans.

items.title: Distinct lifespan trajectories of cortical intrinsic timescales and neural oscillations
items.abstract: The brain integrates information over time through the persistence of neural activity, yet how this persistence changes across the human lifespan and the mechanisms underlying these changes remain unclear. Using resting-state magnetoencephalography from three independent cohorts (n = 1,156; ages 6-88 years), we systematically examined lifespan changes in neural temporal dynamics, focusing on cortical intrinsic timescales and alpha oscillatory frequency. We found that cortical intrinsic timescales shortened from approximately 29 ms in childhood to 9 ms in late adulthood, with the steepest decline occurring before age 30. This compression was reproducible across cohorts and observed in all cortical regions, while the sensory-to-association hierarchy of timescales remained preserved throughout life. By contrast, alpha frequency followed a distinct trajectory, peaking in early adulthood before declining after midlife. Individualized corticothalamic models linked timescale compression to stronger intrathalamic inhibition, whereas increased conduction delays partly accounted for alpha slowing. Further network simulations indicated that intrinsic timescales primarily reflect collective network dynamics rather than single-neuron kinetics. Together, these findings reveal distinct lifespan trajectories of neural persistence and oscillatory rhythms, implicating collective corticothalamic dynamics in the temporal organization of the human brain across development and ageing.

items.title: Single-cell multi-omics identify OTP and NOVA1 as regulators of leptin action in hypothalamic feeding circuits
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Anatomy and Neurobiology, University of California Irvine School of Medicine, Irvine, CA, USA
items.abstract: Leptin acts directly and indirectly on multiple neuronal populations to regulate feeding and numerous other physiologic functions. However, our understanding of how a single circulating signal coordinates diverse neuronal populations across multiple circuits is limited. To further elucidate how leptin reshapes molecular states in its direct and indirect neural targets, we combined time-resolved single-nucleus transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility profiling to map leptin-induced transcriptional and chromatin state changes across individual neurons in two key hypothalamic nuclei: the arcuate nucleus (ARC), which contains the majority of leptin receptor (LepR) neurons, and the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH), an established downstream target of ARC LepR neurons. We found that leptin treatment of leptin-deficient ob/ob mice does not alter neuronal identity, but instead induces coordinated, cell-type-specific transcriptional and regulatory state changes that propagate hierarchically from the ARC to downstream PVH neurons. Integrating RNA velocity, cis-regulatory analysis, and cell-cell communication inference revealed that leptin modulates hypothalamic circuit architecture by selectively strengthening specific interactions while pruning broadly distributed, low-specificity signaling. Although leptin broadly activated STAT3 signaling across LepR neuronal subtypes, integrated multi-omic analyses revealed that activation of STAT3 engages distinct downstream regulatory programs in different neuronal populations, often with opposing physiological functions. Functional analyses identified the homeobox transcription factor OTP, a leptin-responsive regulator selectively induced in AGRP neurons, as a critical mediator of leptin-mediated inhibition of hunger-promoting AGRP neuronal activity and feeding. In parallel, unbiased analysis of PVH neuronal state transitions shows that NOVA1, an RNA-binding protein primarily expressed in inhibitory neurons, is regulated by leptin and alterations of NOVA1 expression bidirectionally control food intake and body weight. Together, these findings define a multi-layered regulatory framework through which leptin regulates hypothalamic feeding circuits to control energy balance.

items.title: Early AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement preserves cerebellar structure and motor function in the shaker rat model of Christianson syndrome
items.abstract: Christianson syndrome (CS) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorder caused by SLC9A6 loss of function, resulting in NHE6 deficiency and epilepsy, intellectual disability, cerebellar atrophy, and ataxia. Following on our prior gene replacement therapeutic development, we preclinically evaluated AAV9-mediated SLC9A6 gene replacement in the context of promoter selection, dosing, and treatment timing. Intracerebroventricular delivery of neuronal-targeted gene replacement at 1 x 10^11 vector genomes (vg) produced substantial improvements in motor coordination and preserved cerebellar volume, quantified through structural MRI. Early postnatal treatment prevented the development of gait ataxia throughout the longitudinal assessment period, statistically indistinguishable from wildtype controls, with molecular analyses demonstrating restored NHE6 expression and preservation of cerebellar markers. Interestingly, later treatments at timepoints corresponding to early neurodegenerative stages yielded strong initial effects, but these effects were largely lost over time, with half-life modelling demonstrating the need for early treatment. This conflicted with more persistent motor benefit shown in prior work with an engineered capsid, suggesting the need to consider the interaction between treatment timing and capsid-specific tropism and/or persistence. Finally, we built models capable of accurately predicting motor coordination from several protein markers. These findings will impact therapeutic development for CS, with relevance across neurodevelopmental genetic disorders.

items.title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
items.corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
items.abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006-0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each persons earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.

items.title: Temporal Structure in Resting-State fMRI under Marginal and Cross-Spectral Surrogate Controls
items.corresponding_institution: PowerMechaniX LLC, Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
items.abstract: Resting-state functional MRI is commonly analyzed using correlations between regional signals and their frequency spectra, which characterize average connectivity and spectral properties but may miss other aspects of temporal organization. Measures of temporal complexity offer complementary information about the recurrence of signal patterns, how fluctuations vary across timescales, and signal roughness. These properties may reveal disease-related alterations in brain activity, offering opportunities for biomarker discovery and insights into mechanisms of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here we examined sample entropy (SampEn), multifractal de-trended fluctuation analysis (MFDFA), and Higuchi curve shapes in 732 scans from 270 ADNI participants, including cognitively normal individuals, people with mild cognitive impairment, and people with dementia. Using the seven Yeo resting-state networks (Yeo-7), we compared recordings with randomized signals preserving either each networks amplitude distribution and approximate spectrum (IAAFT), or the complete cross-spectrum across networks. If these properties fully explained temporal complexity, real recordings should resemble their randomized references. We therefore counted how often each real recording was the strongest outlier among itself and 20 references. This occurred in 21.7%, 12.7%, and 44.2% of 5,124 network-visits for SampEn, MFDFA, and Higuchi, versus 5.5%, 5.1%, and 6.3% in surrogate-only controls. Cross-spectrum-preserving references yielded 39.8%, 17.5%, and 49.8%. Simulations showed that changes in sampling or signal processing, including abrupt changes in signal amplitude, can produce similar differences without changing the underlying dynamics. The measures showed repeatability across visits but did not improve retrospective prediction of changes in Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores. These findings identify temporal features not reproduced by the tested spectral controls and provide a basis for evaluating their potential as disease biomarkers.

items.title: An expansive internal chemosensory system in the insect abdomen implicates Gustatory Receptors in diverse aspects of interoception
items.abstract: Taste and olfactory receptors are gatekeepers that convey chemical information about the external environment. Their role in chemosensory systems has been extensively studied in several model system, which established their role in triggering discrete behavioral as well as physiological responses related to feeding and social interactions. Over time, cases of chemoreceptors expressed internally in organs not linked to the external chemosensory systems of taste and olfaction have been reported. Here, we present the existence of a complex internal chemosensory system in the abdomen of Drosophila melanogaster. We show that the adult fruit fly harbors a complex internal chemosensory system, composed of about 80 to 100 abdominal chemosensory neurons (ACSNs) expressing approximately 20 different Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes, including all sugar receptor and several members of the less conserved bitter receptor genes. The cells expressing specific Gr genes are stereotypically arranged along the entire circumference of the abdominal body wall, in proximity of muscle and fat layers. The ACSN fall into at least nine different subtypes based on co-expression analysis, projection trajectories into the Abdominal Ganglion (AG) and location of cell somata. Identification of different subpopulation of ASCNs expressing discrete combinations of Gr genes indicates that these receptor complexes have new, previously not considered roles in interoception, including monitoring of different nutrients, detection of cell metabolites and their byproducts and chemicals associated with pathogens.

items.title: A reporter mouse model to map RIG-I expression and function in vivo
items.abstract: The cytosolic RNA sensor RIG-I is a critical component of the innate immune response to RNA viruses, yet few tools exist to track RIG-I in vivo. Herein, we report the development of a RIG-I reporter mouse, termed RIG-ImScar, that enables fluorescence imaging and tractable immunoprecipitation of RIG-I in vivo. These mice revealed enrichment of RIG-I expression in circulatory, lymphoid, and mucosal tissues and broad expression across immune cell types. RIG-I itself is upregulated in response to IFN. To distinguish RIG-I sentinel cells, which are programmed to express RIG-I at steady state, from IFN-responder cells, we crossed RIG-ImScar mice with Mx1GFP mice. Blocking IFNAR with a monoclonal antibody showed that basal RIG-I expression in immune cells was largely independent of type I IFN signaling, although Ly6Chi monocytes required IFNAR for RIG-I expression. To probe functional responses in vivo, we intranasally administered a RIG-I-specific agonist, SLR14. Mapping RIG-I expression across the lung identified alveolar macrophages as a critical RIG-I sensor cell population, and depletion of alveolar macrophages, but not neutrophils, slightly impaired lung IFN responses. Together, these findings support the use of the RIG-ImScar model to probe RIG-I dynamics in vivo and predict functional sensor cell populations across tissues.

items.title: The mycotoxin zearalenone couples secondary metabolism to N-acetylglucosamine catabolism
items.abstract: Fungal secondary metabolites are often viewed as terminal products of specialized metabolism, yet how their production influences the physiology of the producing organism remains poorly understood. Here, we show that zearalenone (ZEA) production is functionally coupled to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) catabolism in Fusarium graminearum. Transcriptome profiling of a ZEB2-overexpressing strain revealed enrichment of GlcNAc metabolic functions, and exogenous ZEA induced key catabolic genes independently of Zeb2. Among pathway components, NAG, encoding GlcNAc-6-phosphate deacetylase, was critical for GlcNAc utilization, and its loss caused severe GlcNAc-dependent growth inhibition. Genetic impairment of NAG was poorly tolerated under elevated ZEA pathway activity. Conversely, NAG overexpression increased tolerance to exogenous ZEA and alleviated the growth defect associated with ZEB2 overexpression. Together, these findings reveal a functional connection between secondary metabolite production and primary nutrient metabolism and suggest that ZEA-associated metabolic remodeling contributes to the fitness of the producing fungus.

items.title: The long noncoding RNA FOSIL shapes the dynamics of FOS induction
items.abstract: Immediate-early genes require rapid, transient, and precisely tuned transcriptional activation in response to extracellular signals, yet how this kinetic precision is achieved remains poorly understood. We characterize FOSIL (LINC01220), an inducible lncRNA locus downstream of FOS. Depleting FOSIL RNA delays heregulin (HRG)-induced FOS mRNA and protein accumulation and prolongs the response, indicating that FOSIL sharpens both the onset and the shutoff of the induction wave. Capture Micro-C maps show that FOSIL depletion weakens the chromatin boundary between FOS and FOSIL and increases local compaction across the pre-assembled FOS-FOSIL neighborhood during serum starvation, demonstrating that basal FOSIL production maintains a locally insulated, poised conformation prior to signal arrival. Upon HRG stimulation, FOSIL depletion blunts the rapid movement of the locus toward nuclear speckles, diminishes early speckle-proximal FOS transcription, and extends late firing at speckle-distant alleles. At single transcription active sites, nascent FOSIL activity correlates with closer speckle proximity and higher FOS output, and activating the endogenous FOSIL promoter by CRISPRa, but not supplying FOSIL RNA in trans, enhances both speckle association and FOS induction. Together, these findings support a mechanism where endogenous FOSIL activity coordinates pre-stimulus chromatin folding with dynamic nuclear speckle positioning to fine-tune the onset, amplitude, and resolution of immediate-early gene expression.

items.title: PARP1-mediated PARylation of SPRTN restrains its DNA-protein crosslink repair activity
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Texas at Austin
items.abstract: SPRTN is a DNA-dependent metalloprotease that resolves DNA-protein crosslinks, but how its activity is restrained on chromatin remains unclear. Here we show that SPRTN is PARylated in a PARP1- and HPF1-dependent manner. Mass spectrometry datasets identify seven modified residues in the C-terminal region, and substituting them (SPRTN-PARless) strongly reduces PARylation. The Nudix homology domain is required for SPRTN to interact with PARP1 and for efficient PARylation. SPRTN-PARless accumulates faster and to higher levels at laser-induced DNA damage than wild-type SPRTN. PARylation reduces single-stranded DNA binding of both cell-derived and purified SPRTN, and PARG treatment reverses this effect for cell-derived protein. SPRTN-PARless shows increased autocleavage and accelerates clearance of camptotheci-induced TOP1 cleavage complexes. These findings suggest that PARylation acts as negative feedback on SPRTN after its PAR-dependent recruitment, restraining its DNA engagement and proteolytic activity.

items.title: RhoGEF Solo regulates cell density-dependent keratin remodeling and desmosome maturation
items.abstract: Desmosomes (DSMs) are specialized cell-cell adhesion structures that anchor keratin intermediate filaments and play a crucial role in maintaining the mechanical integrity of epithelial tissues. Keratin filaments associate with DSMs in two characteristic patterns: radial spokes extending from DSMs into the cytoplasmic keratin network and circumferential rims connecting neighboring DSMs. Solo is a Rho-guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RhoGEF) involved in cellular responses to mechanical stress and keratin network reorganization. Here, we investigated the role of Solo in regulating keratin-DSM interactions in response to cell density. The number of radial keratin spokes at cell-cell adhesion sites was markedly reduced at high cell density, concomitant with increased Solo localization at these sites. Conversely, Solo knockout (KO) increased the number of radial keratin spokes. Expression of wild-type Solo, but not a GEF-inactive Solo mutant, rescued the increase in radial keratin spokes in confluent Solo-KO cells, indicating that Solo RhoGEF activity is required for this regulation. Inhibition of actin polymerization or ROCK activity also suppressed the reduction in radial spoke density. Furthermore, expansion microscopy and electron microscopy revealed that DSMs in Solo-KO cells remained small and immature even under confluent conditions. Solo was also partially required for the localization of plakoglobin (PG), a core DSM protein, whereas PG-KO markedly increased the number of radial keratin spokes. These findings suggest that increased cell density promotes DSM maturation accompanied by a reduction in radial keratin spokes, and Solo contributes to both processes, potentially through facilitating PG localization at DSMs and regulating Rho-ROCK-dependent actin cytoskeletal remodeling.

items.title: Endothelial Cell Specific Thioredoxin 1-Dependent Signaling in Oxygen-1 Induced Retinopathy
items.corresponding_institution: University of Oklahoma Harold Hamm Health Campus
items.abstract: Purpose: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of childhood blindness, characterized byoxidative stress and dysregulated angiogenesis in preterm infants with immature antioxidant systems.This study aimed to investigate the specific role of endothelial cell-specific thioredoxin 1 (TXN1), a crucial oxidoreductase, in oxygen-induced retinopathy, hypothesizing that the absence of endothelial TXN1 directly impairs angiogenesis and exacerbates hyperoxia-induced injury. Methods: We generated tamoxifen-inducible, endothelial cell-specific Txn1 knockout mice (Txn1-iECKO) and utilized the oxygen-induced retinopathy (OIR) model, exposing litters to 85% oxygen from postnatal day 7 (P7) to P12. Retinal vascular morphology during vaso-obliteration and neovascularization phases, endothelial cell proliferation, and apoptotic cell death were assessed. Furthermore, human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs) with TXN1 knockdown were subjected to hyperoxic conditions, followed by comprehensive gene expression profiling using RT2 Profiler PCR arrays and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Results: Deletion of endothelial Txn1 significantly enhanced vascular regression during the hyperoxic vaso-obliteration phase at P12 and markedly exacerbated pathological neovascularization at P17. Txn1-deficient retinas exhibited significantly impaired endothelial cell proliferation during the vaso-obliteration phase, while apoptotic cell death remained unchanged. Transcriptomic analysis of TXN1-deficient HRMECs under hyperoxia revealed an enhanced activation of NRF2-mediated oxidative stress response pathways. Conclusions: These findings identify endothelial TXN1 as an essential and oxygen-dependent regulator of vascular development in ischemic retinopathy, primarily influencing endothelial proliferation and redox signaling. This suggests TXN1's crucial protective role and highlights its therapeutic potential to mitigate ROP progression by modulating endothelial cell responses to oxidative stress.

items.title: High piRNA abundance is a hallmark of evolutionarily persistent piRNA-producing loci.
items.corresponding_institution: Josep Carreras Leukemia Research Institute (IJC), Ctra de Can Ruti, Camí de les Escoles s/n, Badalona, Barcelona 08916, Spain.
items.abstract: PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) silence transposons in the germline, and the loci that produce them diverge rapidly between species. Yet, some loci retain both their genomic location and their piRNA production across large evolutionary distances, and the basis for this conservation is unclear. To identify the features that distinguish these persistent loci, we compared piRNA production at orthologous loci in three closely related mouse species, contrasting loci that produce piRNAs in all three species with those that do so in only one. Transposon content and UTR features, often linked to piRNA production, did not distinguish the two groups. Transcription extending beyond gene ends (readthrough) was more frequent at conserved loci, but did not explain conservation once the amount of piRNAs produced was taken into account. Instead, we found that the conserved loci are those that produce the most piRNAs. The same association holds true in human and two other primate species. We speculate that most piRNAs expressed in testis are tolerated molecular noise, and that only the highly expressed minority are likely to be functional.

items.title: Application of metagenomic sequencing to improve sessile serrated lesion detection using the faecal immunochemical test
items.corresponding_institution: Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute, College of Medicine and Public Health, Flinders University, Adelaide, SA, Australia
items.abstract: Most population colorectal cancer (CRC) screening programs use the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), which quantifies occult haemoglobin in faeces and has proven to be effective in detecting and reducing CRC incidence and mortality. Sessile serrated lesions (SSLs) account for up to 30% of sporadic CRC, yet FIT has low sensitivity to detect them. Faecal microbial biomarkers may improve their detection, but FIT samples have not previously been used to study the SSL microbiome. We asked whether FIT samples preserve the faecal microbiome as accurately as fresh collection, and whether they can reveal a microbial signature of SSL. We first reanalysed a published dataset of paired FIT and fresh faecal samples from the same participants. Donor identity explained 63.5% of compositional variance compared with 16.7% for collection method, indicating that FIT preserves the donor-specific signature on which biomarker discovery depends. We then generated shotgun metagenomes from FIT samples of 24 adults scheduled for diagnostic colonoscopy, twelve with at least one clinically significant SSL and twelve with no neoplasia (NN) and compared each group with a published fresh faeces cohort matched on colonoscopy outcome. Collection method explained 6.3% to 7.6% of variance, and no individual species was significantly differentially abundant between methods. Between SSL and NN FIT samples, community structure did not significantly differ, and conservative differential abundance analysis returned no results. More permissive count-based models suggested a depletion of fermentative commensals in SSL. Functionally, SSL samples encoded significantly fewer KEGG orthologs and less polyamine biosynthesis capacity, while orthologs carried by several Bifidobacterium species were more abundant. Many depleted functions reflected Enterobacteriaceae gene content concentrated in a few control samples. No single feature was diagnostic on its own. A multi-feature signature, confirmed in larger cohorts and applied to samples that screening programs already collect, may increase the detection rate of SSLs.

items.title: Learning interpretable compositional features associated with continuous covariates
items.corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
items.abstract: Compositional variation as a function of continuous covariates, such as time, presents challenges for learning interpretable features and accounting for their construction in subsequent inference. Motivated by temporal change in isoform usage in genomics, we introduce IsoVita, a statistical framework integrating covariate-informed balance learning designed for compositional data with complementary tests for abrupt and gradual compositional variation. IsoVita estimates a dominant covariate-dependent direction in the log-ratio coordinates and approximates it as a log ratio of their geometric mean proportions between two learned component groups, linking statistical evidence to explicit component membership. Change point and spline tests evaluate this interpretable feature, while a selection-aware permutation procedure repeats feature construction and testing under each permutation. In transcript-level simulations, IsoVita maintained low empirical false discovery proportions with power to detect differences and change point accuracy improving as temporal signals strengthened. However, the performance depended on trajectory shape and study design. Applications to two human brain bulk RNA-sequencing datasets identified widespread temporal variation in isoform composition while retaining transcript-level interpretability. IsoVita integrates interpretable compositional feature learning with inference along continuous covariates, with potential applications beyond transcriptomics. IsoVita is available as a PyPI package (https://pypi.org/project/isovita).

items.title: Plate design confounds donor variation and model evaluation in single-cell perturbation screens
items.abstract: Single-cell screens of immune cells from many donors are used to study why individuals respond differently and to benchmark response models. Each donor-perturbation combination typically occupies one well, controls are grouped, and donors share one layout, so technical effects can look biological. Using a 90-cytokine screen, two compound screens, four cohorts and simulations, we show that well effects explain most replicate-control variation in abundant cell types, controls carry a shared offset, and identical control wells differ by hundreds of differentially expressed genes at a standard threshold, about as many as two receptor-negative proteins do. Negative controls, design-aware estimators and perturbation-specific evaluation change the interpretation of four recent analyses. A deep-learning model that scores below a perturbation-agnostic predictor under standard evaluation outperforms a simple baseline on perturbation-specific differences in two of three cell types (significantly in one with stricter controls), but predicts less well the component shared with inert wells.

items.title: U-statistics-based Pairwise Discordance Regression for Joint Mean-Variability Inference in Longitudinal Studies with Missing Data
items.abstract: Longitudinal studies are central to scientific inquiry across disciplines; yet, statistical analyses have predominantly focused on mean trajectories while treating variability as a secondary or nuisance component. Increasing evidence suggests that temporal variability and heterogeneity themselves encode critical scientific information, particularly in studies with repeated measurements, heterogeneous populations, or rich covariate structures. The classical mixed-effects and location-scale model family represents variability through latent variable components but relies on strong parametric assumptions and often requires numerical approximation or computationally intensive estimation.
