Expanding the scope of behavioral analysis increased the proportion of ST rats in both early and late PCA training. Rats also increased the time spent interacting with the food cup during the inter-trial interval across extended PCA training. All rats were sensitive to satiety-induced reward devaluation, regardless of sex or devaluation condition. This study helps establish a PCA method optimized for Long-Evans rats with relevance for identifying PCA phenotypes contribution to dysregulated behavior in the context of chronic stress and obesity.

items.title: Walking delays auditory processing in humans alongside a global shift in aperiodic neural activity
items.abstract: Natural sensory processing unfolds during movement, yet human electrophysiology is usually measured under enforced stillness. Here, we used mobile EEG to test whether walking changes the timing of auditory processing. Thirty adults listened to lateralised pure tones while walking freely or standing. Walking led to a delay in auditory N1 latency (< 10 ms). Control analyses ruled out the possibility that the N1 delay was contaminated by foot strike related noise in EEG. Multivariate decoding further indicated a later emergence of sound location information during walking in the subset of participants with reliable decoding in both states. Walking also produced a scalp wide decrease in the aperiodic exponent of neural responses. A larger global exponent decrease was associated with a larger N1 delay across participants. Together, these findings show that natural walking reorganises the temporal dynamics of human auditory processing and link early sensory slowing to a global change in ongoing cortical state.

items.title: Neonatal NMDA receptor blockade disrupts prefrontal cortical regulation of social affective behavior: implications for schizophrenia
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory of Psychology and Behavioral Neuroscience, University of Tsukuba
items.abstract: Developmental N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAr) hypofunction has been implicated in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia, including cognitive and emotional deficits. However, the neural circuit mechanisms linking developmental NMDAr hypofunction to social affective impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated schizophrenia-related social affective dysfunction induced by neonatal exposure to the NMDAr antagonist MK-801 and examined the contribution of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a key hub for socio-cognitive function. Sprague-Dawley rat pups received subcutaneous injections of saline or MK-801 (MK-Low: 0.2 mg/kg; MK-High: 0.4 mg/kg) during the neonatal period. In adulthood, social affective behaviors were assessed using the Social Affective Preference (SAP) and Social Interaction (SI) tests. MK-801-treated rats, particularly the MK-High group, displayed impaired social affective responses, characterized by reduced preference for and investigation of distressed conspecifics. These impairments were ameliorated by chemogenetic inhibition of pyramidal cells in the mPFC, whereas activation of these neurons disrupted social affective behavior in naive rats. Histological analyses revealed reduced parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PVIN) density in the mPFC of MK-801-treated rats. Consistent with the involvement of PVIN dysfunction, selective activation of mPFC PVINs alleviated social affective deficits in MK-801-treated rats. These findings identify impaired PVIN-mediated inhibitory regulation within the mPFC as a circuit mechanism underlying social affective dysfunction following neonatal NMDAr blockade, providing insight into the pathophysiology of schizophrenia-related social impairments.

items.title: A Framework for SPICE MRSI Reconstruction Posterior Uncertainty Quantification
items.abstract: Purpose: Low-rank reconstruction methods such as SPICE substantially improve Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) reconstruction quality. However, SPICE does not provide an estimate of reconstruction uncertainty. A framework for posterior uncertainty estimation in SPICE reconstruction is proposed, hereafter referred to as the framework. Theory and Methods: A Laplace approximation is used to estimate the covariance of the reconstructed spatial coefficients. This covariance is propagated through the spectral basis and spectral fitting to obtain metabolite concentration uncertainty. Matrix-free Hessian--vector products and voxel-wise conjugate-gradient estimation are used to avoid explicit construction or inversion of the full Hessian, making the method tractable. Results: Validation using repeated in vivo 7 T MRSI acquisitions showed that the estimated posterior uncertainty exhibited spatial and spectral patterns similar to those of empirical repeated-scan uncertainty. Experiments further demonstrated how spatial regularization and k-space undersampling affect the estimated uncertainty. Conclusion: The framework provides a practical framework for uncertainty quantification when using SPICE reconstruction of MRSI. It could be adapted to other regularised low-rank reconstruction methods.

items.title: Curved geometry shapes the observability of hippocampal oscillations
items.abstract: Curved neural architectures reshape the spatial distribution of field oscillations, complicating the identification of their underlying generators. To test these principles experimentally, here we resolve the paradoxical poor expression of theta oscillations in the hilus of the folded dentate gyrus (DG), a region that otherwise exhibits some of the largest FPs in the brain. Using laminar recordings across both hippocampi and computational modeling, we show that theta is locally masked by cancellation of phase-coherent contributions. Theta generators in CA1 and DG produce volume-conducted fields that, due to the curved geometry of the DG, exhibit opposite dipolar orientations in the hilus, leading to regional cancellation. In contrast, beta and gamma generators are only weakly coordinated across hippocampal regions and therefore remain prominently expressed despite the same geometry. These results demonstrate that theta amplitude, local observability, spatial segregation and apparent translocation emerge from the interplay between geometry and temporal coherence among distributed generators, with tissue geometry acting as a spatial filter for coherent activity.

items.title: TGF-b/TIF1g signaling restrains CD8+ T cell expansion while preserving cytotoxic competence
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto de Fisiologia Celular, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico
items.abstract: Transforming growth factor b exerts complex and often opposing effects on CD8+ T cell biology, yet the molecular mechanisms that distinguish these functions remain poorly understood. Here, we identify TIF1g (TRIM33) as a critical signal threshold regulator that couples TGF b signaling to CD8+ T cell activation and cytotoxic function. In the presence of TGF b, TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells bypass canonical suppressive signals and acquire a transcriptional program characterized by enhanced activation and proliferation. Despite this hyperactivated state, TIF1g deficient cells fail to acquire full effector function, exhibiting markedly reduced Granzyme B and Perforin expression under TGF b signaling. We confirmed this functional uncoupling in vivo using a secondary Listeria monocytogenes challenge model, in which TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells underwent robust expansion yet failed to efficiently control bacterial infection because of impaired cytotoxic activity. In a lymphopenic homeostatic proliferation model, TIF1g deficiency disrupted cellular quiescence, leading to excessive proliferation and spontaneous effector differentiation. Consistent with these findings, loss of TIF1g accelerated B16 melanoma growth and was associated with reduced Perforin expression in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells. Together, these findings identify TIF1g as a key regulator of TGF b mediated CD8+ T cell responses, uncoupling activation from cytotoxic differentiation and revealing a mechanism by which TGF b independently regulates proliferative and effector programs.

items.title: Genomic features and instability of linezolid resistance in vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecalis ST525
items.corresponding_institution: ALERTA Laboratory, Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Internal Medicine, Federal University of Sao Paulo (UNIFESP)
items.abstract: This study investigated the mechanisms of oxazolidinone resistance and genomic background in clinical ST525 Enterococcus faecalis isolates, a poorly characterized lineage reported in Brazilian hospitals as either vancomycin-resistant (VRE) or linezolid- and vancomycin-resistant (LVRE). Five LVREfs from intensive care unit patients (linezolid MICs, 8-32 mg/L; vancomycin MICs, >256 mg/L) carried only G2576T and G2505A (in three of four rrl copies) as known linezolid resistance determinants, despite variable linezolid MICs. During serial in vitro passages without antibiotic pressure, isolates with initial MICs of 8-16 mg/L exhibited progressive MIC reductions accompanied by reversion of mutant to wild-type rrl copies, whereas the isolate with an initial MIC of 32 mg/L maintained high-level resistance without reversion. Additional domain V substitutions emerged during MIC decline, while growth kinetics remained broadly similar. Whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate (LVREfs L7) revealed a ~2.8-Mb chromosome enriched in mobile genetic elements (~8.6%), lacking a functional CRISPR-Cas system. A plasmid-borne prototype Tn1546 carrying vanA, devoid of internal insertion sequences, was found inserted into a Tn3-family transposase gene, a platform not typically associated with vanA mobilization. Together, these findings indicate that ST525 LVREfs, whose genomic features are consistent with long-term persistence in hospitals, may pose a challenge to routine susceptibility testing. A single mutational mechanism can yield variable linezolid MICs, and the ratio of mutated vs wild-type rrl copies can become heterogeneous in the absence of antibiotic pressure, without correlating directly with these values, contrary to the well-documented copy number-MIC correlation.

items.title: Transition Fibers Play a Central Role in Import of a Glucose Transporter into the Flagellar Membrane
items.abstract: Leishmania parasite promastigotes have a motile flagellum that encompasses a variety of integral membrane proteins, but how such proteins traffic selectively to the flagellum is largely unknown. The flagellar-specific glucose transporter, GT1, binds to the KHARON protein via the transporter hydrophilic amino terminal domain, and KHARON is essential for trafficking of GT1 from the flagellar pocket membrane at the base of the flagellum into the flagellar membrane. A major objective of this study was to determine the mechanism whereby KHARON transports GT1 into the flagellar membrane. We have determined that KHARON is a novel component of the transition fibers that project from the basal body at the base of the flagellum toward the flagellar membrane. We propose that KHARON binds GT1 at the transition fibers and then transfers it to intraflagellar transport (IFT) trains as they enter the flagellum at this site. The IFT trains, associated with the membrane tethering protein TULP, then move GT1 through the transition zone filter into the body of the flagellum. These results provide evidence for a role for transition fibers in transport of membrane proteins into flagella.

items.title: Breaking the bottleneck: semi-automated quantification of actin filament dynamics
items.abstract: Actin reconstitution assays visualized by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy have been crucial for defining mechanisms of filament assembly, disassembly, and higher-order organization. Yet quantitative analysis remains slow, labor-intensive, and subject to investigator bias. We developed SMAUG (Single filament Measurement and Analysis Using a GUI), a semi-automated image analysis interface that extends TSOAX filament segmentation and tracking with user-verified trace analysis of time-lapse TIRF images. SMAUG generates kymographs and quantifies filament nucleation, elongation, pausing, junctions, and filament-associated fluorescence while retaining measurements at the individual filament level. We tested the approach across actin reconstitution assays producing concentration-dependent polymerization, formin-stimulated elongation, capping-induced arrest, Arp2/3 branching, and fascin-mediated bundling. SMAUG reproduced manual measurement while reducing analysis time and revealed where dense networks and bundled filaments require user validation. Together, TSOAX and SMAUG provide a semi-automated approach for quantitative analysis of actin filament dynamics.

items.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

items.title: TailEnrich enables discovery of dysregulated genes through disease sample enrichment testing
items.abstract: Identifying differentially expressed genes is fundamental to elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying complex diseases. However, in complex disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), the genes exhibiting dysregulated expression may vary among patient subsets, reflecting the heterogeneity of the underlying pathological processes. Consequently, pathogenic genes are profoundly dysregulated in only a subset of patients. Conventional differential expression tools, such as DESeq2 and edgeR, are primarily designed to detect population-level expression shifts and may have limited power to identify subgroup-specific dysregulation. To overcome this limitation, we developed TailEnrich, a novel computational method that discovers dysregulated genes within patient subsets. TailEnrich independently tests the extreme left (downregulated) or right (upregulated) tails of a gene's expression distribution for disease sample enrichment. We quantify this enrichment using a new metric, i.e. the PE (Percentage of Enriched disease samples) score. On simulated datasets, TailEnrich demonstrates markedly improved accuracy over DESeq2 and edgeR in identifying dysregulated genes specific to patient subsets. Applied to AD gene expression data, TailEnrich uncovers a distinct, biologically relevant set of genes within key pathological pathways that are missed by mean shift-based approaches. TailEnrich provides a novel method for identifying dysregulated genes, and readily extends to other omics data including genomic variants and proteomics to uncover pathogenic genes in complex diseases.

items.title: Organotchi: an open-source tool for the automated segmentation, morphological characterization, and longitudinal tracking of organoids
items.corresponding_institution: Zoological Institute, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Germany; Institute of Biological and Chemical Systems - Functional Molecular Systems, Karlsruhe I
items.abstract: Neural organoids are three-dimensional stem cell-derived models widely used to study brain development and model disease. Brightfield imaging offers a non-invasive readout of their growth and morphology, and recent advances have made automated organoid segmentation from such images increasingly attainable. Yet existing tools largely leave morphological characterization, quality assessment, and comparisons between conditions to manual or ad hoc analysis. Here we present Organotchi, an open-source tool that integrates automated segmentation with longitudinal morphological analysis of neural organoids. Organotchi quantifies ten morphological features, including area, perimeter, and eccentricity, and tracks cystic structures over time, reports variability within and between batches, and flags outlier organoids and segmentation failures, supporting objective organoid characterization and enhancing downstream analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply Organotchi to disease modelling, pharmacological perturbation, and protocol optimization in neural organoids. One use case assesses drug response in breast cancer spheroids, demonstrating its use beyond its development domain.

items.title: Creation of genomic chimeras via megabase scale genome expansion
items.abstract: An organism's physiology is controlled by its genomic content. Building genomic chimeras would enable melding of the diverse functions and properties of life. However, prior arts in genome synthesis are limited to reconstituting pre-existing functions within a singular genome rather than combining diverse genomic functions across multiple distinct genomes. Existing methods are also prohibitively expensive, labor intensive, and time consuming, and thus fundamentally not scalable for creating large synthetic chimeric genomes. To address all these limitations, we invented Additive Conjugative-CAST Engineering (ACE) combining conjugation with CRISPR-associated transposition (CAST) to deliver and integrate up to half a genome per step from a donor cell into a precisely defined position in the recipient's genome. We have demonstrated ACE's capability to integrate at least a 2-megabase donor genomic segment in a single step and at least 3 megabase in two consecutive steps. Importantly, we confirmed ACE's generality through the creation of multiple genomic chimeras across species, genus, and at least order barriers. With ACE, we further demonstrate such chimeric organisms, or what we call genome expanded organisms (GEOs), can be stably forged from at least three starting bacterial strains, and can be stably maintained to express all their acquired genomic parts in a single chimera. ACE offers a new paradigm of creating artificial lifeforms to combine desired properties and potentially create novel functions beyond the constraints of nature. ACE also offers a unique perspective to probe unexplored plasticity in genome architecture and expression patterns of novel, massively expanded genomes.

items.title: TACO: An open, interpretable model for microsecond-scale TCR specificity prediction
items.abstract: Predicting antigen-induced T-cell activation from T-cell receptor (TCR) and peptide sequence remains difficult for TCRs and peptides not represented in training data. We present TACO (T-Cell Activation from Chemistry and Orientation), an open statistical model for predicting TCR specificity against HLA-A*02:01-presented peptides. TACO takes as input the peptide sequence and six TCR CDR loop sequences. Learning from binary activation labels, TACO selects a single canonical orientation of the CDR loops over the peptide and learns five amino-acid contact-potential matrices as well as two peptide-exposure profiles.The orientation is fixed and does not require experimentally determined or predicted structures. We evaluate TACO on held-out peptides separated by Levenshtein distance at least four from all training and validation peptides, limiting near-neighbor shortcut learning. TACO achieves AUROC 0.67 on a large held-out activation dataset and 0.68 on IMMREP25 HLA-A*02:01, exceeding the open structure-based models evaluated here and matching the reported AlphaFold3-TCRdock result. The model has 2,019 fitted parameters, retains most within-peptide ranking signal with TCR$\beta$ sequence alone, and reaches 406,000 TCR--peptide predictions per second on CPU. This throughput enables computational evaluation of large TCR-peptide search spaces. We show its potential use for prioritizing candidate target peptides from large peptide libraries, reducing the search space for downstream experimental investigation. TACO fitted parameters also expose candidate physicochemical patterns that can be inspected directly. We release TACO's parameters and complete training, evaluation, and inference code.

items.title: Rapid, accurate, and memory-frugal sub-gene-level quantification of probe-based, multiplexed single-cell data
items.abstract: Probe-based, multiplexed single-cell assays enable accurate transcriptome profiling while processing multiple samples in parallel. Their predefined probe sequences and additional sample barcodes introduce computational requirements that differ from those of poly(A)-based assays, for which many existing single-cell quantification tools were developed. We extend simpleaf to enable efficient demultiplexing and quantification of probe-based single-cell libraries. A new, cache-friendly dictionary specializes lookup to small probe references, while a shared thread budget balances parallel decompression and mapping. We extend RAD and downstream tools with reusable sample-scoped correction plans and external-memory collation of hierarchically barcoded data, retaining probe identities through quantification to enable rapid mapping and quantification with a small working memory budget. Across five 10x Genomics Flex datasets comprising 44 samples, simpleaf had the shortest runtime and lowest peak memory use of the three tools on every library, while producing gene-expression estimates, cell clusters, and marker genes concordant with cyto and Cell Ranger. Compared with cyto, simpleaf was on average 2 times faster and used approximately one-thirteenth as much memory. simpleaf also exports probe-level quantification results, allowing a range of analyses at sub-gene resolution. Here, we show that individual probe counts reveal expression changes obscured by gene-level aggregation, identify the transcript groups contributing to gene-level changes, and provide insight into splicing dynamics across cell types. These results demonstrate the computational and biological value of retaining probe-level information in multiplexed singlecell analysis.

items.title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell perturbation data by optimizing causal reach of latent mediator dynamics
items.abstract: Resolving the causal structure of gene regulatory networks is central to understanding cellular regulation. Pooled CRISPR screens with single-cell RNA readouts measure the transcriptional consequences of many interventions in parallel, providing a powerful resource for causal discovery. Combinatorial designs that perturb multiple regulators per cell increase throughput and can reveal responses that single-gene perturbations do not. However, inferring causal gene networks from these experiments remains challenging because gene regulatory interactions are nonlinear, dynamic, and often involve feedback. Thus, attributing the combined effect of several perturbations to individual regulators remains difficult. Additionally, transcriptional regulation is ultimately carried out by proteins, while single-cell perturbation datasets generally measure only RNA levels. Existing methods often simplify regulatory dynamics or rely on assumptions that conflict with gene regulation, such as acyclicity. Moreover, current evaluation practices usually rely on expression prediction error, which is readily computable in real datasets, but does not necessarily reflect graph quality. A complementary metric is needed to assess inferred regulatory connections using observed perturbation responses in real data. To address these challenges, we present CausalODE, a differentiable framework for learning causal graphs from single-cell perturbation data. Our approach incorporates three central insights to improve upon previous methods. First, genes that are differentially expressed when a gene is perturbed should be downstream of the target gene in the regulatory network; we quantify this property with a metric we term causal reach. Second, causal interactions involve transient cellular responses in RNA transcription, splicing, and degradation. Third, gene regulatory interactions are mediated by proteins, whose levels are not directly measured in single-cell RNA-seq experiments. Building on these insights, CausalODE learns a graph that optimizes the causal reach metric, captures transient cellular responses to perturbation, and explicitly models the latent dynamics of protein levels. Together, these components allow nonlinear responses, feedback loops, and time-lagged regulation. Across simulated Perturb-seq datasets with different sparsities and graph structures, CausalODE improves AUPRC and precision among top-ranked edges compared with baselines and competing methods, while achieving competitive AUROC. We introduce a metric to evaluate the causal reach of inferred graphs on real data by measuring how well the graphs explain differentially expressed genes in single-cell perturbation experiments. Using this metric, CausalODE outperforms the strongest competing method or baseline by approximately 60% on the CaRPool-seq knockdown dataset and 80% on the Norman et al. activation dataset. Its top-ranked edges generally show greater enrichment for high-confidence evidence from cell-type-matched ChIP-seq, CollecTRI, and regulatory STRING than those of other methods. The inferred graphs also distinguish non-additive from approximately additive genetic interactions in held-out perturbation pairs. Finally, ablation analyses show that optimizing causal reach improves performance on held-out perturbations, and the learned latent regulator activities track simulated protein dynamics, with median temporal correlations ranging from 0.79 to 0.99.

items.title: Multi-scale place fields provide a predictive basis for hierarchical control
items.abstract: Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit unimodal spatial selectivity in small enclosures, but express multiple, irregularly spaced fields in environments of naturalistic scale. However, existing predictive-map theories of the hippocampus do not scale well to large environments and do not account for these heterogeneous place field characteristics. Here, we introduce the factorised hierarchical successor representation (fHSR), a predictive map that supports hierarchical control using subgoal-directed subroutines. We show that the fHSR allows efficient generalisation across tasks, scaling favourably with environmental size, and it reproduces key statistical and topological characteristics of multi-scale CA1 place cell activity in rats and bats. Analyses of experimental data further confirmed a novel prediction of the fHSR: population firing rates exhibit spatial periodicity with a characteristic wavelength independent of environmental size. These results identify the integration of hierarchical control and predictive representations as a normative principle that unifies efficient navigation with the spatial organisation of hippocampal activity.

items.title: A biological light sheet links cellular voltage to mesoscopic brain dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
items.abstract: Membrane voltage is the fundamental currency of neural computation, yet cellular-resolution voltage imaging of large neuronal populations in vivo remains limited by trade-offs among imaging speed, field of view, and optical sectioning. We overcome this challenge by encoding a biological light sheet in the brain: Selective Plane Expression (SPress) restricts fluorescent indicator expression to a user-defined, 20-m-thick plane, suppressing background at its source. Following one-time two-photon photoactivation, SPress enables standard widefield microscopes to capture high-contrast kilohertz voltage dynamics from hundreds of densely labeled neurons across millimeter-scale cortical sheets and columns in vivo. These recordings reveal mesoscopic subthreshold waves that flexibly reorganize population-wide spike timing, together with cellularscale wavefront microstructure that preserves stereotyped local recruitment biases. By shifting optical sectioning from instrumentation to gene expression, SPress makes kilohertz cellular resolution voltage imaging accessible across mesoscopic scales.

items.title: RadMultiBench: A Reproducible Dual-Task Benchmark Exposing the Limits of Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models Across Thoracic and Breast Imaging
items.abstract: We present RadMultiBench, a multimodal benchmark of 6,148 medical images paired with expert radiological impressions across five categories--Breast Cancer, Lung Benign, Lung Malignant, Pneumonia, and Tuberculosis--targeting two core clinical tasks: automated report generation and disease classification. To enable reliable, repeatable experimentation, we provide a reproducible pipeline for data ingestion, de-identification, split management, and standardized reporting of text and classification metrics, facilitating dataset versioning and continuous benchmark testing. We compare three architectures: (1) a classical CNN-RNN with Bahdanau attention (ResNet-LSTM), (2) a general-domain vision-language (V-L) prefix-projection model (CLIP-GPT), and (3) a domain-specific V-L prefix-projection model (BioViL-T). Results reveal a sharp performance divide: the ResNet-LSTM attains near-perfect classification (99.5% accuracy) and is the only model to generate coherent reports (BLEU-4 = 0.021), whereas both prefix-projection models catastrophically fail generation (BLEU-4 [≤] 0.0001); moreover, the domain-specific BioViL-T also fails classification (11.5% accuracy). From a data-engineering angle, the pipeline is productionizable with lineage, feature registries, and continuous integration to guard against silent regressions when updating models or data; from a data-science angle, the benchmark provides baselines and analyses that foreground feature alignment and architectural suitability as first-order concerns, inviting ablations on multimodal objectives, retrieval-augmented encoders, and uncertainty-aware decoding. Overall, RadMultiBench highlights that state-of-the-art status in general V-L domains does not translate automatically to high-stakes clinical tasks, and it furnishes the tooling and evidence base needed to develop robust, clinically viable multimodal systems.

items.title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
items.abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Furthermore, even when a neuron's place fields changed location, they tended to remain at the same branching level of the binary tree, reflecting the local geometry of the maze. In return sessions where the neural tuning for branching level was preserved more accurately, the mouse explored the environment more efficiently. Population patterns were best preserved near the reward location, and more reliable neural activity there accompanied earlier direct runs to the reward. With repeated experience, spatial representations changed less, both within a visit and across the long absences. A brief experience thus left selective hippocampal traces that survived months of absence despite drift, grew more durable with each return, and were correlated with memory in navigation behavior.

items.title: Neural Bases for Working Memory of Natural Sound Textures
items.abstract: Holding sound objects in mind is critical to understanding the sound world around us. Auditory texture perception is thought to rely on extracting statistical properties of sounds over time, raising the question of how encoding duration influences subsequent maintenance of auditory texture information. We investigated this question using behavioural performance and fMRI while participants performed two delayed match-to-sample tasks: a texture discrimination and a comparison loudness discrimination task. In the texture task, participants judged whether two sequentially presented sounds belonged to the same texture type, whereas in the loudness task, participants judged whether the sounds, drawn from the same texture type, had the same loudness. Stimuli were presented for either 0.1s or 2s. Discrimination sensitivity increased with duration in both tasks, but more strongly for texture discrimination. fMRI analysis revealed distinct effects of duration on univariate and multivariate activity in the auditory cortex and medial temporal lobe (MTL) during maintenance. We found no univariate duration effect in the auditory cortex during maintenance, but multivariate patterns encoded texture category more strongly for longer stimuli, regardless of task. In contrast, MTL activity was modulated by sound duration in both tasks, but there was no effect of duration on texture category decoding. There was a task effect in MTL where multivariate patterns in posterior hippocampal and parahippocampal regions distinguished texture from loudness tasks following 2s stimuli. Together, these findings show effects of duration on sound texture representations during maintenance and that MTL representations reflect the behavioural context in which that information is maintained.

items.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neuroscience, Brown University, Providence, RI, USA
items.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca2+) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

items.title: Motivation-dependent communication between cortex and brainstem
items.abstract: Neurons in the medullary brainstem exhibit movement-related patterns of activity, but the neuronal population codes that specify distinct actions, and the mechanisms by which cortex may shape these codes as a function of motivational state, remain unclear. To explore whether coupling between cortex and medulla depends upon motivational context, we trained mice to make both pre-reward "appetitive" licks that served to trigger water availability and rapidly attenuated with satiety, and "consummatory" licks, which occur post-reward release and more slowly attenuated with satiety. Simultaneous recordings from secondary motor cortex and motor medulla revealed that medullary activity was more time-locked than cortical activity to individual licks and exhibited a phase-based population code that encoded lick direction. Correlations between cortex and medulla were stronger during appetitive licks than during consummatory licks, with causal dependency established by optogenetic intervention and supported by multi-region recurrent network models. Population codes underlying behavior shared across the central nervous system, exemplified by cortico-medullary coupling, thus may depend upon the motivational context underlying action.

items.title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2-related disorders
items.abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1, finding ~50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis
items.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 (Ntsr1)-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1Cre;Thflox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Preliminary analysis of the microbiome was consistent with an obesity-resistant gut profile. Together, these findings indicate that the feeding phenotype is diet- and experiment-dependent and that DIO resistance is not explained by increased energy expenditure, activity, thermogenesis, or detectable changes in fecal energy or fat content.

items.title: Preferential Isoform Usage and Isoform Switching in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Patients with Distinct Autoantibody Profile
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Institute of Science, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India
items.abstract: RNA sequencing has advanced our understanding of molecular heterogeneity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), yet most studies have focused on differential gene expression (DGE), which overlooks transcript-level complexity. Alternative splicing and polyadenylation generate multiple isoforms from a single gene, and their dysregulation may contribute to autoimmune pathogenesis, including through the production of non-canonical isoforms with potential autoantigenic properties. To explore this underexamined dimension, we analysed differential isoform usage (DIU) and major isoform switching (MIS) across SLE subgroups stratified by autoantibody profile: anti-dsDNA+, anti-ENA+ and anti-dsDNA+ENA+. Subgroup-specific DIU and MIS events were enriched in RNA-binding and transcription-related functions. In the anti-dsDNA+ subgroup, the T-cell receptor adaptor GRAP2 showed isoform switching accompanied by expansion of a non-coding retained-intron transcript. In the anti-ENA+ subgroup, IGHM switched from the membrane-bound to the secretory form, consistent with an antibody-secreting cell signature; NACA, a reported IgE autoantigen, showed isoform switching; and BRI3, linked to TNF--induced cell death, switched toward its protein-coding transcript. In the anti-dsDNA+ENA+ subgroup, TNFAIP2, a TNF--induced gene, showed isoform redistribution with loss of a uORF-containing transcript. These findings highlight isoform regulation as a distinct, subgroup-specific and functionally relevant layer of transcriptomic dysregulation in SLE.

items.title: Tools for genetic mapping and gene identification in Caenorhabditis briggsae
items.abstract: The nematode Caenorhabditis briggsae serves as an important companion species for Caenorhabditis elegans for comparative studies. Because C. briggsae exhibits androdioecious reproduction and ease of laboratory culture similar to C. elegans, it has long been used for genetic studies in cross-species comparisons of mutant phenotypes to uncover the evolution of gene function. Here, we provide an updated toolkit for C. briggsae genetic experiments, leveraging the resource of recently improved C. briggsae genome sequence assemblies with variant mapping tools and gene identification methods. We identify and validate a set of indel variants between CGC2 (AF16) and two divergent strains, HK104 and VX34. We then use these variants to genetically map 10 previously isolated mutations and identify the impacted genes using high-throughput sequencing. We combine these new genes with others curated from the literature into an updated map with 73 genes, providing an enriched resource for C. briggsae genetic studies.

items.title: TestNet-PA: Sampling-Zero-Aware Inference of Microbial Presence-Absence Networks
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biostatistics, School of Public Health, Peking University, Beijing, 100191, China
items.abstract: Microbial presence-absence networks, also referred to as co-occurrence networks, characterize patterns of coexistence and incompatibility among taxa. However, sequencing-based presence--absence analysis can be compromised by pervasive 'sampling zeros' in microbiome data, causing widely used methods such as Fisher's exact test to identify spurious co-occurrence dependence. To our knowledge, no existing method is designed to account for sampling zeros in this setting. We introduce TestNet-PA, a method for testing pairwise microbial co-occurrence dependence. TestNet-PA models each observed zero as arising from a mixture of 'structural' and 'sampling' zeros, with the mixing probabilities governed by library size and relative abundance. Because the relative abundance underlying an observed zero is unobserved, we impute it by borrowing information from other samples. We then construct a quasi-likelihood and develop an EM algorithm to infer dependence between the underlying true presence--absence statuses. Extensive simulations based on real gut, vaginal, and oral microbiome data templates showed that TestNet-PA consistently controlled the FDR while maintaining good sensitivity. By contrast, Fisher's exact test generally yielded inflated FDR. Analyses of the three real microbiome datasets further illustrated how accounting for sampling zeros can affect the inferred co-occurrence networks.

items.title: Generative Models for Novel Enzymatic Reactions: How Far Do They Go?
items.corresponding_institution: Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai, India
items.abstract: Enzyme function prediction is a long-standing problem in biology, and deep learning methods have recently become popular to improve performance on this task. While most of these models focus on classifying enzymes or mapping them to known reactions, predicting unknown biochemical reactions remains underexplored. Here we thoroughly examine an approach that generates reactions absent from the training data from the enzyme alone. Existing methods such as BLASTp or CLIPZyme cannot, by design, output reactions that are absent from their training data or were not supplied at inference. The closest prior model, RxnPred, reports high fingerprint-similarity scores on held-out enzymes, a less stringent criterion than exact recovery, but fails to recover the correct answer on unseen reactions. We present a structure-conditioned generative model that outputs a complete reaction, reactants and products, and evaluate it on EnzymeMap_x, a reaction-disjoint benchmark in which no test reaction appears in training, under exact, stereo-respecting scoring. On this benchmark, within 400 sampled candidates, the model generates the complete, correct reaction for 25.0% of the subset of test enzyme--reaction pairs whose reaction is a new combination of metabolites seen in training. Surprisingly, it also correctly generates a few reactions composed of metabolites it has not seen in training (1.6%), though their embeddings are present in the vocabulary. With a lower budget, re-ranking places the correct reaction first for 5.6% of pairs and in the top ten for 12.4%, when the reaction is assumed not to be already known (0.2% and 8.1% without that assumption) along with confidence scores. Assessed more leniently, the model produces at least one correct reaction known for the enzyme (usually memorised from training) for 71.2% of test pairs. Going further, without any retraining, a sequence-only model given the reactants as well as the enzyme produces the correct product set for 9.5% of pairs within five candidates, without re-ranking. We also present head-to-head comparisons on these tasks with BLASTp, DIAMOND, RxnPred and Horizyn. Structure conditioning improves fingerprint similarity on homology-stratified splits, but a matched sequence-only ablation at the best configuration finds no measurable effect on exact recovery. Data coverage and chemical initialisation of the vocabulary seem to matter more than encoder geometry.

items.title: Integrative Multiomics Analysis of the Angiogenesis-EMT Interface in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.abstract: Angiogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) are key hallmarks that contribute to the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but whether the two programs vary simultaneously across tumors and how much of this reflects tumor composition remain unclear. We scored predefined, non-overlapping 20-gene angiogenesis and EMT signatures with a rank-based method in 342 primary oral cavity tumors from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA-OSCC). The two programs were strongly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.809, P = 2.7 x 10^-80), and 2,396 bridge genes were associated with both programs across the transcriptome. The bridge genes were enriched in pathways associated with focal adhesion and extracellular matrix-receptor interaction. In the cellular case, fibroblast and endothelial marker scores were prominent and correlated with the program scores. The coupling was attenuated but remained positive after joint adjustment for tumor purity and stromal and immune scores (partial rho = 0.406) and with an epithelial-restricted EMT score (rho = 0.710). Further correlation was performed with a partial EMT (pEMT), which shows a significant positive correlation (rho = 0.59) and an inverse correlation with tumor purity (rho = -0.70). 146 final gene candidates were found using multi-omic evidence and candidate-level testing on the external cohort GSE30784; after adjusting for inferred cell fractions, 101 of these candidates supported the dual program. For thorough characterization, three candidates with an emphasis on OSMR, MICAL2, and LHFPL2 were chosen. Additional CPTAC data were used to confirm protein-level support, which was strongest for MICAL2. No significant connection was seen between the Interface score and overall survival (hazard ratio per 1-SD increase, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.78-1.08). These results describe a coordinated angiogenesis-EMT transcriptional state in OSCC that is attenuated but retained after accounting for tumor composition, and nominate candidate genes for experimental study.

items.title: Hub labeling makes exact distance calculation practical for large human pangenome graphs
items.abstract: Pangenome graphs are now a standard reference representation, and tools built on them depend on fast minimum-distance queries between graph positions, for example, when clustering seed matches during read alignment. The baseline distance index, previously used by the vg toolkit, answers such queries based on a decomposition of the graph into nested subgraphs called "snarls". Within each snarl, the index uses a dense all-pairs distance matrix. Because such a matrix is quadratic in a snarl's number of children, the large, complex snarls that often occur in many pangenome graphs dominate the overall index size. This means whole-genome graphs can be impractical to index. To mitigate this, the baseline distance index does not fully index the largest snarls, and thus cannot itself answer certain queries involving them. We replace the dense matrix with a hub labeling for snarls above a size limit. Because hub labeling and associated methods are defined for directed graphs, we introduce a directed representation of a snarl's bidirected internal "net graph", whose shortest path lengths are the net graph's minimum walk lengths. Hub labels are built using pruned landmark labeling, ordered by a contraction hierarchy. On four human chromosome pangenomes, our hub-labeling-based distance index indexes every snarl in 0.9 GB to 3.0 GB at a snarl limit of 500, an estimated 28x to 119x less space than dense distance matrices would need for those snarls with more than 500 children, and supports the 3-18.6% of node-to-node queries that the previous index cannot answer by itself. On the queries both indexes can answer, query time distributions broadly overlap. We explore the snarl limit parameter space and are able to build indexes under 50 GB for four human whole-genome pangenomes in under 6 hours, where we estimate dense matrices could have required multiple terabytes.

items.title: Label-free flow operators and stability operators from single-cell time courses: what local dynamical operators can and cannot identify
items.abstract: Local Jacobians of single-cell dynamics are used to locate unstable cells along trajectories, but what they identify from measured data has rarely been tested against independent truth. We present scJDO2, which separates two per-cell operators by the time information they require: a score operator, the Hessian of a score-matched log density, available from any snapshot; and a flow operator, the Jacobian of a drift fitted to a measured velocity, here estimated label-free from a sampled time course by entropic optimal transport. Both are summarized in a shared operator space of magnitude-free descriptors, with the invariance of each stated, and evaluated with pre-registered tests. On synthetic data calibrated to six real datasets, the flow operator from the time course alone separated fate-bifurcation cells from committed cells on held-out seeds (AUC 0.89-1.00) with a-priori settings; tuning on development seeds overfit. On LARRY lineage-traced hematopoiesis, its fitted drift predicted the clonal displacement of barcoded cells beyond population movement (Spearman 0.56, permutation p < 0.001; 0.50 after removing the mean shift) and a held-out sampling day better than mean-displacement and no-movement baselines (energy distance 0.69, 95 % CI 0.66-0.73, vs 0.87 and 0.88); lineage thus validates the velocity, not {lambda}. Mini-batch transport reproduced dense transport (velocity cosine 0.9998) and scaled to all 130,887 cells (transport 5 min and 2.5 GB; drift fit and Jacobians 21 min and 1.3 GB). On an independent simulator it detected two of three bifurcations and two of three cycles and never reported instability on linear trajectories. Several readings failed. Neither operator recovers the values of the true Jacobian; the flow operators leading eigenvalue ranks branching cells empirically. The flow operator depends on the transport metric and inverts on Factor Analysis. Operator archetypes isolated bifurcation cells but did not outperform expression clustering and were unstable across fit seeds. The score operator did not predict CRISPRi knockdown responses or sister-cell fate coherence. A confirmatory test of transition timing could not be constructed, and diffusion is not identifiable at typical sampling intervals. The released software reports these diagnostics.

items.title: Multimodal cellular context enables molecular phenotyping from single-molecule trajectories
items.abstract: Single-molecule tracking (SMT) provides direct measurements of molecular dynamics in living cells, but motion alone rarely specifies the underlying biological process, without accounting for the cellular environment in which that motion occurs. Here, we present MIST (Multimodal Interpretation of Single-molecule Trajectories), a framework that brings the paradigm of image-based profiling to single molecules by integrating trajectory dynamics, emitter properties and cellular context into a common, reusable phenotype space. Using a reference panel of nine proteins in live Escherichia coli, we show that multimodal context more than doubled protein-specific information relative to trajectory features alone, a gap that learned trajectory representations did not close. MIST allowed de novo identification of shared transcription-translation phenotype at the nucleoid periphery. A fixed reference space detected effects of previously uncharacterized MukB ATPase mutations without retraining. MIST provides an interpretable and extensible framework for comparing proteins, mutants and conditions within a common space of molecular phenotypes.

items.title: Brief visual oddball events evoke CSF flow in the spinal canal
items.abstract: The measurement of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow with fMRI, made possible by exploiting edge artifacts of spin saturation when the bottom acquisition slice lies in a CSF reservoir, allows researchers to investigate an aspect of brain health that has been increasingly linked to cognitive aging and neurodegenerative disease via its role in glymphatic clearance. The initial demonstration of this technique used the fourth ventricle, but recent reports show it can also be done when the bottom acquisition slice lies in the spinal canal in the foramen magnum. We present a method to automatically identify the spinal canal without manual tracing, and measure CSF flow with high confidence using multi-echo acquisition to separate out BOLD-like and non-BOLD-like signal components, along with physiological regression to improve signal to noise ratio. Using these methods we found that CSF flow correlated with decreases in BOLD activity in 70 adults aged 19-76. We further found that brief, infrequent salient stimuli (visual oddballs, requiring a button press) were capable of provoking measurable CSF flow.

items.title: Human organoid screen links transient translational modulation to progenitor progression in corticogenesis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, 94305, USA, Stanford Brain Organogenesis, Wu Tsai Neuros
items.abstract: Human pluripotent stem cell-derived models are increasingly used to recapitulate aspects of human corticogenesis, including the emergence of diverse cortical cell types and their progression through developmental states. These systems offer an opportunity to dissect the molecular mechanisms regulating transitions between cell states, but methods for perturbing them systematically at scale remain limited. Here, we developed a semi-automated culture and high-throughput arrayed screening platform for human cortical organoids. Using a library of 1,280 small molecules designed to systematically target major signaling and regulatory pathways, we screened for modulators of EOMES, which encodes for the transcription factor TBR2, and identified Emetine, an inhibitor of translation elongation, as the top hit. The effect of Emetine on cortical cell-state progression was reproduced across human pluripotent stem cell lines, non-human primate cortical organoids, and primary human cortical tissue but not broadly across translation inhibitors. Moreover, transient exposure resulted in a shift from dividing radial glia towards cortical glutamatergic neurons. Mechanistically, nascent-proteome profiling revealed an early and coordinated remodeling of newly translated proteins that preceded detectable transcriptional changes, placing translational regulation upstream of the ensuing cell-state transition. Together, these findings highlight a role for specific translational inhibitors in promoting cortical cell-state progression and establish a scalable platform for systematic perturbation and discovery in human neural organoids.

items.title: Therapeutic Potential of Melatonin, Erythropoietin, and TRPV4 Antagonism in a Preclinical Model of Genetic Hydrocephalus
items.abstract: Symptomatic hydrocephalus is a neuropathological disorder of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) homeostasis characterized by abnormal accumulation of CSF and progressive ventricular enlargement. Current treatment relies primarily on surgical CSF diversion, which is invasive and associated with substantial rates of treatment failure and surgical revisions. Congenital hydrocephalus can be caused by genetic pathologies; for example, a point mutation in the Meckel-Gruber type 3, Tmem67, gene produces a congenital hydrocephalus phenotype in rats, characterized by progressive ventriculomegaly. Here, we evaluated a combinatorial cocktail therapeutic strategy consisting of erythropoietin (EPO), melatonin (MLT), and the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) antagonist, RN1734 (RN), in the Tmem67-- rat model of congenital hydrocephalus. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated marked progression of ventriculomegaly in untreated Tmem67-- rats between postnatal (P) 7 and P15. RN1734 and EPO+MLT+RN1734 (triple therapy) from P7-P14 prevented further ventricular expansion. Hydrocephalus is associated with structural disruption of the periventricular white matter (WM) and ependymal lining (EL), accompanied by regionally increased TLR4 and NLRP3-associated inflammatory signaling. EPO+MLT, RN1734, or triple therapy differentially attenuated these inflammatory responses. The triple combination reduced both TLR4 and NLRP3 protein abundance within the affected periventricular region and ameliorated the structural alterations. These findings support a combined therapeutic approach that addresses ventricular pathology, inflammation and periventricular structural consequences of congenital hydrocephalus.

items.title: Developmental interactions between oscillatory and spontaneous neural activity support improvements in inhibitory control from adolescence into adulthood
items.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period of development marked by improvements in cognitive control driven by maturation of executive brain systems. Neural mechanisms supporting inhibitory control (the ability to suppress a prepotent response in favor of generating a goal-directed response) mature into adulthood in parallel with refinements in frequency-specific neural oscillations and broadband spontaneous activity, supporting more accurate and reliable performance on response inhibition tasks, such as the antisaccade oculomotor task. Prior work has established that the maturation of neural circuitry contributes to age-related decreases in spontaneous activity, supporting higher-fidelity transmission of task-relevant activity, such as frequency-specific neural oscillations, which are crucial for antisaccade performance. Using longitudinal electroencephalography (EEG) data from 146 participants (72 F, ages 10-34, 253 total sessions) collected while participants performed an antisaccade task, we sought to understand the interplay between frontal oscillatory and spontaneous activity during cognitive processing and how it supports developmental improvements in inhibitory control. We found that spontaneous activity decreased developmentally during the preparation of an inhibitory response, and that this was associated with reduced trial-to-trial variability in response latency, indicating that reductions in spontaneous activity may increase the reliability of inhibitory control processing. Furthermore, performance-related decreases in broadband spontaneous activity were associated with the suppression of preparatory high-beta oscillations in an age-dependent manner, such that this relationship became more pronounced through development. Together, these results illustrate how developmental enhancements in the coordination of frequency-specific oscillations and spontaneous activity during inhibitory response preparation support developmental improvements in inhibitory control, providing a potential mechanism through which inhibitory control becomes more accurate and reliable from adolescence into adulthood.

items.title: Homeostatic fibroblast niche collapse in clinically uninvolved skin marks a pre-fibrotic stage of systemic sclerosis
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Heterogeneous clinical presentation and polygenic risk complicate our understanding of disease mechanisms and the path to effective therapy. Single-cell analyses have revealed substantial transcriptional diversity in skin, but disease-associated reprogramming remains poorly defined. To address this, we performed high-resolution spatial transcriptomic profiling of paired clinically uninvolved and clinically affected scleroderma donor skin alongside healthy controls. We identified a continuum of cellular, molecular, and spatial changes to the stroma that were already evident in clinically uninvolved tissue yet remained distinct from the broader and more advanced changes in paired fibrotic biopsies. Uninvolved skin was comparable to healthy tissue by clinical and histopathological assessment, but distinguishable by the numerical reduction, transcriptional reprogramming, and spatial isolation of LGR5+SCARA5+PI16+ progenitor fibroblasts. In parallel, the dermal vascular smooth muscle compartment shifted from a contractile to a synthetic, activated state, suggesting reprogramming that begins before overt fibrosis. Cell neighborhood analysis revealed that progenitor fibroblasts occupy dense stromal niches in healthy skin that collapse in clinically uninvolved tissue, replaced by isolated, disease-associated fibroblast populations. These data indicate that clinically uninvolved skin occupies an intermediate stage along the pathologic continuum of scleroderma, establishing a framework for strategies to allow early diagnosis and preserve homeostatic fibroblast niches before irreversible tissue remodeling and fibrotic commitment.

items.title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells
items.abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate therapeutics regimens of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2, encoded by EPAS1) but not HIF-1 in NK cells. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2 was not dependent on limited oxygen availability. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2 protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2 transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2/HIF-1{beta} heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolism. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1{beta} independent, HIF-2 pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2 to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.

items.title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
items.abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

items.title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
items.abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.

items.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
items.abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

items.title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
items.corresponding_institution: Fuller Evolutionary Biology Program, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, 159 Sapsucker Woods Road, Ithaca, NY 14850, USA
items.abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.

items.title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
items.abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

items.title: Generative 3D Spatial Reconstruction of Cellular Organization from Single Cell Expression
items.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles cellular states at scale but removes their three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization. Reconstructing this organization requires recovering not only individual cell positions but also the physical size, geometry, and neighborhoods of an entire tissue. Existing methods either map cells onto measured spatial references or reconstruct two-dimensional sections independently, leaving the joint reconstruction of a new 3D specimen unresolved. Moreover, predicting the average plausible position of each cell can reduce per-cell error while compressing tissue geometry. We introduce ORBIS, a generative framework that jointly reconstructs whole 3D specimens from single-cell gene expression without requiring a spatial reference at inference. ORBIS learns spatial organization through flow matching in a shared physical coordinate frame, using training views sampled from sparse serial sections, tissue blocks, and whole specimens. At inference, a shared spatial state is iteratively updated through dynamically regrouped windows, enabling the generation of millions of cell positions without independently reconstructing and stitching tissue regions. We evaluate physical size, cell-population shape, per-cell placement, and neighborhood organization separately to distinguish accurate tissue geometry from low per-cell error. Across eight held-out specimens spanning whole mouse brains, thick brain blocks, and Drosophila embryos, ORBIS achieves lower cell-population shape error than all five evaluated baselines on every test and reconstructs specimens containing up to 3.7 million cells. On a single GPU, ORBIS samples million-cell brains in 0.9-2.8 minutes, approximately 38 times faster than the sampler of LUNA-3D, our 3D extension of the state-of-the-art generative spatial reconstruction method LUNA. On two held-out brain tests, sampling reduces size error by 3.3-fold and shape error by 1.8-fold compared with a single-call variant. On an independent dissociated single-cell brain atlas, ORBIS returns on average 37.9% of each region's cells to their dissection region across 23 regions, compared with 28.5% for LUNA-3D.

items.title: Bioprocess Modeling Made Easy With Hybrax
items.abstract: Hybrid models that embed neural networks in ordinary differential equations are increasingly popular in bioprocess modeling, but they are challenging to set up. Much of the effort goes into the code around the model: wet-lab data must be imported and pre-processed, feeds and sampling must be accounted for in the balance equations, and a training loop with cross-validation must be set up. Researchers usually write this code from scratch for each project. In addition, no widely adopted format for bioprocess data exists, and datasets are mostly published in bespoke spreadsheets or not at all. As a result, models and datasets from the literature are difficult to reproduce, reuse, or compare.We present Hybrax, an open-source Python framework that addresses these problems. It combines a flexible format for bioprocess data with a customizable end-to-end training pipeline for mechanistic and hybrid models. Hybrax derives the transport terms in the process dynamics automatically and provides the utilities needed for training, so that researchers can focus on developing the model itself. It also facilitates model sharing and reproducibility: each training checkpoint contains the model parameters, code, configuration, and training data required to run the model or retrain it from scratch. We demonstrate Hybrax by re-implementing two models from the literature, one trained on real-world E. coli data and one on synthetic HEK293 data, with performance comparable to the original models. Hybrax is available at https://github.com/hybrax/hybrax.

items.title: Network analysis of mouse brain proteomes resolves molecular and cellular endophenotypes of aging and Aβ pathology
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, 32610, USA
items.abstract: Aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology exert both shared and distinct effects on the brain, yet their relative contributions to molecular alterations remain poorly defined.
