Here we performed tandem mass tag proteomics across the lifespan in wild-type and 5xFAD mice and integrated these data with human brain proteomic networks to resolve aging- and amyloid-beta (A{beta}-associated molecular programs. We quantified 8,535 proteins and identified 51 co-expression modules representing neuronal, mitochondrial, glial, vascular and proteostatic pathways. Aging emerged as the predominant driver of proteomic remodeling, with widespread alterations in RNA metabolism, protein translation, and neuronal pathways occurring independently of A{beta} pathology. In contrast, A{beta} selectively modified a subset of age-dependent processes, including suppression of mitochondrial ATP biosynthetic machinery and amplification of astrocytic and microglial activation states. These key aging and disease-related molecular signatures were highly conserved in human AD brain proteomes. Together, our findings establish aging as the primary determinant of brain proteome organization while revealing specific mechanisms through which A{beta} pathology reshapes age-associated biological processes. Our results also highlight molecular mechanisms of human aging and AD pathology that can be modeled in mouse models.

items.title: Broad Cognitive and Motivational Enhancement through M4-Selective Muscarinic Modulation
items.abstract: The muscarinic M4 subtype of acetylcholine receptors is part of agonist compounds considered treatment options for Schizophrenia and Alzheimers disease, but how M4-subtype selective modulation affects cognition and motivation is largely unknown due to dose-limiting side effects, a scarcity of receptor-selective compounds, and missing multi-domain assessments of cognition. Here, we surmount these constraints by utilizing a M4-selective positive allosteric modulator (PAM) to assess in nonhuman primates a broad array of endpoints spanning motivational effort control and multiple executive function domains. We found broad dose-dependent performance improvements of set shifting indexing cognitive flexibility, visual search indexing selective attention, antisaccade performance indexing inhibitory control, visuospatial maze learning, and temporal order serial object learning, while working memory span was non-systematically modulated. In addition, the M4 PAM reduced effort avoidance in an effort-based choice task documenting a pro-motivational effect. Task-composite performance scores showed pro-cognitive effects across multiple doses and an effective dose range for individual subjects in the absence of adverse dose-limiting cholinergic side effects. Together, the broad pro-cognitive and pro-motivational multi-task profile of M4 PAM modulation suggests that the M4 receptor is a master regulator of executive cognitive functioning, possibly acting on domain-general neural processes across the prefrontal-striatal circuits.

items.title: Sex-dependent and region-specific morphological adaptations in astrocytes following early-life stress
items.corresponding_institution: University of Montreal Hospital Research Centre (CRCHUM)
items.abstract: Astrocytes are structurally heterogeneous, with cell morphology providing a valuable readout of experi-ence-dependent plasticity. Despite this, single-cell reconstruction including complete cellular territories remains challenging to compare across brain regions and experimental groups. We used unilateral retro-orbital delivery of PHP.eB-GfaABC1D-eGFP as a practical method for sparse astrocyte labeling and ap-plied it to evaluate regional, sex, and early-life-stress comparisons in the mouse amygdala. Systemic vi-rus delivery to broadly target astrocytes across the brain produced eGFP-positive cells throughout cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and amygdala with spatially isolated cells suitable for intensity projection, three-dimensional surface reconstruction, filament tracing, and Sholl analysis. In naive females, we report relatively homogenous morphological features between lateral amygdala and basal amygdala. In naive males, basal amygdala astrocytes had greater volume and a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, while surface area, soma diameter, territory, and arborization measures did not differ significantly. Interestingly, early-life stress produced sex-specific morphological responses in the basal amygdala. Females showed increased perimeter, area, and Feret diameter without significant changes in three-dimensional volume or resolved filament measures. Males instead showed reduced surface area and volume, with no significant changes in projected territorial dimensions, soma diameter or resolved filament measures. S100{beta}-positive cell density was unchanged in the displayed regional and stress comparisons. These findings es-tablish systemic sparse eGFP labeling as an efficient route to single-cell astrocyte morphometry and re-veal a sex-dependent and region-specific dissociation between territorial expansion and three-dimensional volumetric contraction after early-life stress.

items.title: Measuring neuronal input-output operations in vivo with random access projection microscopy
items.corresponding_institution: Allen Institute, Neural Dynamics, Seattle, WA
items.abstract: Neurons transform thousands of synaptic inputs into spiking output, and understanding this transformation requires measuring many submicron synapses at millisecond timescales in vivo. Here we present SLAP2, a two-photon random access projection microscope with no per-target access time cost, yielding over 5-fold faster imaging than existing methods, and performant real-time hardware motion correction. Flexible scanning modes enable measurement of hundreds of synapses at ~200 Hz, >800 synapses volumetrically at 50-100 Hz, and compartment-resolved dendritic voltage at 2-10 kHz in behaving mice. Simultaneous dendritic glutamate and somatic calcium imaging in visual cortex pyramidal neurons revealed nonlinear input-output amplification of stimulus onset and preferred stimulus orientation responses. Amplified features are associated with spatially organized inputs and stronger trial-to-trial coupling between synaptic activity and somatic output. These measurements establish SLAP2 as a powerful tool for recording intricate patterns of subcellular fluorescence dynamics in behaving animals.

items.title: Real-time detection of N2 and N3 sleep from scalp and intracranial EEG
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Chicago
items.abstract: Sleep rhythms such as slow oscillations and spindles arise predominantly during N2 and N3 sleep (N2+N3). Closed-loop stimulation targeting these rhythms is a promising strategy to enhance memory. Such stimulation requires online sleep stage classification. Conventional staging labels completed 30-s epochs using past and future data and cannot support online staging. We developed a causal tracker that, every 2 s, estimates the current stage from the preceding 10 s of scalp or intracranial EEG. We also evaluated a simulated rule that permits stimulation after three consecutive estimates indicating N2+N3 sleep. In six adults with drug-resistant epilepsy with simultaneous scalp EEG and stereo-EEG, real-time N2+N3 discrimination remained close to offline scoring of the same recordings (scalp AUC 0.953 versus 0.958). Thalamic channels alone reached AUC 0.934 and exceeded mesial temporal channels in every patient, and scalp plus thalamus performed best (0.967). The scalp tracker, retrained in 28 healthy adults, reached 0.976. When patients transitioned into N2+N3 sleep with stimulation initially disabled, the rule permitted stimulation within 5 min in 63-73% of transitions, with a median delay of 42-64 s among those detected. After leaving N2+N3, stimulation was disabled after a median of 19-22 s. The rule also switched on incorrectly 1.4-1.8 times per hour outside N2+N3 and remained active during 28-31% of REM in patients, compared with 2% in healthy adults. These findings show that both scalp and thalamic EEG can support real-time N2+N3 detection and inform when stimulation is permitted. Translationally, implanted thalamic leads, increasingly used for neuromodulation in epilepsy, could support sleep-stage-dependent stimulation without scalp EEG, while scalp EEG might be used for noninvasive neuromodulation. Closed-loop systems should be evaluated not only by sleep-stage classification accuracy but also by how reliably and promptly they enable and disable stimulation.

items.title: Generalizable sex differences in functional brain organization follow the cortical hierarchy in youth
items.corresponding_institution: Penn Lifespan Informatics and Neuroimaging Center (PennLINC), University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.; Department of Psychiatry, Perelman School of M
items.abstract: It remains unknown if sex differences in human functional connectivity follow a generalizable overarching principle. Here, we tested whether sex differences in functional connectivity during childhood and adolescence are organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a cortical hierarchy spanning unimodal sensorimotor to transmodal association cortex. We analyzed four large-scale, independent datasets of youth ages 5-23 years (total N = 3,355). Across datasets, males showed greater connectivity between functional networks, whereas females showed greater connectivity within networks, most prominently within the default mode network. More broadly, the sensorimotor and association ends of the S-A axis were more segregated in females and more integrated in males. This difference extended to macroscale cortical organization: the cortical hierarchy was expanded in females relative to males along the principal gradient of functional connectivity. Together, these findings identify the S-A axis as a generalizable organizing principle of sex differences in functional brain organization during youth.

items.title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
items.abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.

items.title: Multi-omics integration reveals candidate genes and molecular mechanisms associated with resistance to sugarcane smut
items.abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum (Syd.), is one of the main diseases affecting sugarcane and is capable of causing severe yield losses in susceptible varieties. Given the limitations of classical breeding, mainly due to the genetic complexity of sugarcane cultivars, molecular and omics approaches have gained increasing prominence for studying the genetic basis of traits such as disease resistance. In this context, we investigated sugarcane resistance to smut through the integration of association mapping methods and transcriptomics. A panel of 155 genotypes was genotyped with 33,335 SNP markers and inoculated with S. scitamineum generating three phenotypic variables. These data were jointly analyzed through genome-wide association analyses to identify marker-trait associations. In addition, transcriptomic analyses were performed using publicly available datasets from four studies evaluating sugarcane responses to smut. The integration of these multi-omics data enabled the identification of candidate genes involved in structural reinforcement, immune signaling, redox homeostasis, genome maintenance, and cellular adaptation. These findings provide valuable molecular resources for functional validation and breeding strategies aimed at developing sugarcane cultivars with enhanced smut resistance.

items.title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
items.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.

items.title: Development of a Pan-Proteome Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Nipah Virus Using Reverse Vaccinology and Immunoinformatics Approaches
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Microbiology, Jagannath University, Dhaka
items.abstract: Nipah virus (NiV) is a high-consequence zoonotic pathogen for which no licensed human vaccine is currently available. This study applied a consensus-guided pan-proteome immunoinformatics framework to design and prioritize a multi-epitope vaccine candidate using sequence information from all nine NiV proteins. A total of 901 NiV protein sequences were retrieved, of which 842 passed quality filtering and were processed through clustering, multiple-sequence alignment, and protein-specific consensus generation. Consensus-derived fragments were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte, helper T-lymphocyte, and B-cell epitopes, followed by multi-criterion filtering based on antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservancy, class-specific immune-response properties, and human-proteome similarity. Ten epitope-selection strategies were combined with two adjuvant candidates and three construct architectures to generate 60 vaccine constructs. Shortlisted candidates were subsequently evaluated for physicochemical properties, HLA population coverage, structural characteristics, conformational B-cell epitopes, TLR3 docking, molecular dynamics, immune-response simulation, and expression-oriented optimization. VC033_V6_BD_L03 construct was prioritized as the lead candidate and showed combined predicted population coverage of 99.78% worldwide and 99.96% in South Asia. Docking against human TLR3 structure 1ZIW yielded a ClusPro score of -1624.8. During a 100-ns molecular-dynamics simulation, the complex underwent early conformational reorganization followed by lower late-phase structural variation and persistent interchain hydrogen bonding. MM/GBSA analysis yielded a mean interaction-energy estimate of -20.52, 15.42 kcal/mol. C-ImmSim predicted coordinated humoral and cellular responses, while codon optimization generated a 1,539-bp expression sequence compatible with virtual cloning into pET-28a(+). These analyses prioritize VC033_V6_BD_L03 as a consensus-derived, pan-proteome NiV multi-epitope vaccine candidate for experimental evaluation of expression, immunogenicity, safety, and protective efficacy.

items.title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
items.abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

items.title: Deducing splicing events from transcript sets with splicelogic
items.abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing captures a greater proportion of full-length transcripts, enabling more accurate isoform identification, discovery of novel isoforms, and more precise differential transcript usage analysis. However, comparing transcripts, whether between conditions or between sets such as novel and annotated isoforms, yields complex isoform changes that are hard to manipulate, summarize, and visualize. This is compounded by vertical integration of some tools, where downstream analysis depends on the specific output of a particular upstream tool. To address this gap, we have developed splicelogic, an R/Bioconductor package that makes transcript-set comparisons biologically interpretable by turning them into discrete splicing events, such as exon skipping, alternative splice sites, intron retention, and alternative transcription start and end sites. We designed splicelogic to integrate easily with existing RNA-seq workflows and tools. The splicelogic functions are modular, readable, and extensible, making it easy for users to adapt core logic to their own custom scientific questions or novel splicing definitions. By obtaining interpretable splicing events from transcript changes, splicelogic enables downstream analyses, including annotation of RNA-binding protein recognition sites, alongside summary statistics and visualization. The splicelogic package is publicly available and distributed through Bioconductor.

items.title: Coarse-graining genome-scale metabolic models for dynamic, multi-scale simulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in gel environments
items.abstract: Microbial communities are shaped by coupled interactions between microenvironment conditions and the intracellular adaptations that emerge in response external metabolic cues. For pathogenic microbes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these interactions can rapidly generate heterogeneous sub-populations that exhibit adaptations for sustaining host infection and resisting antibiotic treatment. Technological strides in -omics data collection, combined with robust computational tools like genome-scale metabolic models (GEM) for predicting cellular metabolism, have yielded promising multi-scale depictions of microbial population development in simulated spatial environments. These multi-scale model simulations help establish and evaluate mechanistic contexts for how infection-enhancing behaviors might emerge in the population or be influenced by variable perturbations in the biological system. However, the number and rigorous tuning of parameters influencing the connections between intracellular-extracellular events pose barriers when shaping simulations to different in vitro systems of interest. In this work, we present a genome-scale, metabolism-informed continuum model (GEM-CM), a computational framework for coupling a reaction-diffusion model to a surrogate GEM representation that generates metabolic rate predictions informed by flux balance analysis outputs. A key feature of GEM-CM is its application of random forest regression, or ensembles, to coarse-grain the interface connecting the GEM and reaction-diffusion models down to a small set of input metabolites methodically chosen through the random forests evaluation of feature importance. To demonstrate GEM-CMs utility, we evaluated simulation predictions against P. aeruginosa PA14 populations radially propagating in low weight percentage agar gels. In addition to biomass growth, we simulated PA14 populations producing the cytotoxic secondary metabolite pyocyanin (PCN). GEM-CM could capture PA14 growth dynamics in agar gels when ensembles were provided with three carbon source inputs describing the simulated growth media. Bacterial motility parameters and the random forest ensemble allowed GEM-CM simulations to accurately predict spatial biomass distributions for PA14 populations over time and probe their PCN production dynamics. Ensembles also demonstrated robust performance for single gene knockout conditions with GEM-CM simulation accurately capturing the partial or total biomass and PCN inhibition observed in transposon mutant screenings. When evaluating transposon mutant population development, the GEM-CM framework additionally suggested that metH may be a promising target to inhibit the spatial propagation of PA14. This works proof-of-concept applications illustrated GEM-CM utility as an early stage multi-scale modeling tool for interrogating in vitro metabolic behavior in microbial populations.

items.title: No Evidence of an Effect of a Single Mirror Visual Feedback Session on Subsequent Motor Imagery
items.corresponding_institution: Neurocognition and Functional Neurorehabilitation Group, Department of Psychology, University of Oldenburg, Oldenburg, Germany
items.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) and mirror therapy, based on mirror visual feedback (MVF), are recommended as adjuncts to conventional therapies for upper limb rehabilitation after stroke. Both approaches activate sensorimotor cortical networks despite the absence of overt movement, and their concurrent application has been associated with enhanced neural activation. The present study investigated whether a single session of MVF modulates subsequent kinesthetic Motor Imagery (kMI)-related neural activity. EEG data from 38 healthy participants (MVF: n = 18; sham: n = 20) were analyzed in a mixed pre-post design. Participants performed kMI before and after either an MVF or sham intervention. Analyses focused on mu-band (8-12 Hz) event-related desynchronization (ERD) and its hemispheric lateralization. Although kMI reliably elicited stronger contralateral than ipsilateral mu ERD, MVF did not significantly affect subsequent kMI-related mu ERD or its hemispheric lateralization. These findings suggest that previously reported facilitatory effects of MVF on MI may be more closely related to concurrent application than to immediate aftereffects, while potential effects of repeated MVF exposure on subsequent MI remain to be investigated. These findings provide a foundation for future studies investigating how MVF and MI can be combined to optimize upper-limb stroke rehabilitation.

items.title: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
items.abstract: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

items.title: Increased Cognitive Load Expands, Stabilizes, and Aligns Visual Representation Across the Human Brain
items.abstract: Cognitive load refers to the mental effort required to perform a task. While previous research has extensively examined its detrimental effects on neural and behavioral performance, much less is known about how the brain actively adapts to heightened demands. Across two fMRI experiments involving visual n-back tasks, we identified several fundamental properties of this adaptive process. First, higher load enhanced and expanded visual representations beyond localized visual regions, leading to widespread visual coding. At the global scale, heightened load promoted cross-regional coordination by increasing representational alignment and strengthening information encoded in interregional functional connectivity patterns. Beyond facilitating stronger visual representation, increased load also reduced neural pattern variability, which led to more stable information coding. Finally, load was encoded independently of other task-relevant information as a separate brain state, supporting its overarching role in guiding visual processing. Together, these findings revealed that the brain adapts to heightened cognitive demands by globally reorganizing neural processing to support flexible cognition.

items.title: Confidence: Its Measurement, Relation to Behavior, and Neural Representation
items.abstract: Confidence (certainty/uncertainty about one's own decision) has attracted considerable attention in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. Yet its relation to behavior remains unclear: Some treat confidence as a cause of behavior whereas others view it as a state controlled by environmental variables. The unobservable nature of confidence makes its measurement validation and analyses difficult. To tackle these issues, we developed a novel procedure combining a decision-making task, risk choices, and a post-task open-ended questionnaire. Point-gain/loss amounts for correct/incorrect decisions varied depending on choices between high-risk/high-return and low-risk/low-return. In the questionnaire, 90% of 16 participants reported feelings interpretable as certainty/uncertainty when making those risk choices despite no instruction about confidence, whereas 8% did so when the choices led to identical outcomes/returns. This suggests confidence is a state controlled by environmental contingencies rather than a cause of behavior. We also decoded changes in the state from electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging.

items.title: Deprivation of dietary fiber promotes low-grade neuroinflammation and anxiety-like behavior in mice
items.abstract: Background: Intestinal health is an important determinant of brain function in that an array of gut perturbants, especially those targeting microbiota, influence behavior. Fermentable dietary fiber nourishes gut microbiota and, consequently, promotes gut health. We hypothesized that depriving mice of fermentable dietary fiber would impact their brain and behavior. Methods: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed standard grain-based chow (GBC), a compositionally defined diet (CDD) which mimics macronutrient content of GBC but lacks fermentable fiber, or CDD supplemented with the fermentable fiber inulin (CDD+INU). Mice were subjected to behavioral testing 6-8 weeks later followed by analysis of the gut brain axis. Results: Relative to GBC-fed mice, CDD-fed mice exhibited low-grade gut inflammation and a reduction in open-field center exploration, signaling heightened anxiety-like behavior. CDD+INU fully reversed these abnormalities arguing they were a consequence of fiber deprivation. Analysis of the gut microbiome and serum metabolome showed that CDD+INU increased oxidative phosphorylation and immune suppressive metabolites. Flow cytometric and transcriptomic analyses of the brain revealed an array of pro-inflammatory alterations in myeloid cells, CD4+ T-cells, microglia and astrocytes in mice fed CDD but not CDD+INU. Most notably, microglia and astrocytes from mice fed CDD, but not CDD+INU, displayed reduced mitochondrial respiration and greater glycolytic activity. CDD, but not CDD+INU consumption also reduced the abundance of oligodendrocytes and neurons, and increased hippocampal pro-inflammatory gene expression. Conclusions: Deprivation of fermentable fiber results in coordinated changes in brain immune composition and glial metabolic state that is associated with increased anxiety-like behavior.

items.title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center
items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8 T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape. Together, our results establish the preclinical efficacy and safety of 3DL2CART-cell therapy and support its clinical translation. This approach may offer a targeted alternative to pan-T-cell-directed CAR T-cell strategies for patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous and systemic TCLs, addressing a critical unmet clinical need.

items.title: Galectin-9 drives thrombo-inflammatory circuits initiating venous thrombosis
items.abstract: Background: Venous thromboembolism is increasingly recognized as a thrombo-inflammatory disease, yet the pathways linking inflammation to venous thrombus initiation remain incompletely defined. Galectin-9 (Gal-9), a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin elevated in inflammatory disorders, has no defined role in venous thrombosis. Methods: Using plasma from patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT), Gal-9-deficient mice, an inferior vena cava stenosis model, intravital microscopy, microfluidics, and ex vivo platelet and neutrophil assays, we assessed the functional contribution of Gal-9 to venous thrombosis. Results: Plasma Gal-9 was elevated in DVT patients, correlated with D-dimer at presentation, and declined over 3-month follow-up. Gal-9 deletion did not alter hemostasis but markedly impaired thrombus initiation, with reduced platelet and neutrophil recruitment to the vessel wall and reduced intra-thrombus neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. TNF-/IFN-{gamma}-stimulated endothelial cells upregulated Gal-9 and promoted platelet adhesion and fibrin(ogen) deposition, which Gal-9 neutralization partially reversed. Under venous shear, immobilized recombinant Gal-9 potentiated platelet activation and thrombus formation, particularly alongside collagen, whereas Gal-9 inhibition suppressed these responses. Gal-9-activated platelets promoted NETosis and shifted thrombus composition toward a NET-rich inflammatory phenotype. Conclusions: Gal-9 is a previously unrecognized driver of venous thrombo-inflammation, linking vascular inflammation to platelet activation, NET formation, and thrombosis. Genetic deletion attenuated these responses in vivo, and antibody-mediated Gal-9 neutralization suppressed platelet activation and thrombus formation in vitro, identifying the Gal-9 glycan-binding pathway as a therapeutic target that disrupts thrombosis without impairing hemostasis.

items.title: Establishing an ex vivo platform for molecular profiling of skin structural cells using frozen human skin biopsies
items.abstract: Skin structural cells, including keratinocytes, melanocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, play critical roles in the development of chronic inflammatory skin disease. Inflammatory stimuli induce transcriptional reprogramming and epigenetic changes in skin structural cells, which contribute to disease pathogenesis. Although two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) skin culture models have been widely used to investigate inflammatory responses in skin structural cells, ex vivo systems that maintain skin structure and cellular composition remain limited. To address this gap, we explored using frozen skin biopsies as an experimental platform to study the responses of skin structural cells to inflammatory stimuli. Using a simple air-liquid interface culture method on permeable Transwell inserts, we showed that viable skin structural cells that retain cell-type-specific transcriptional profiles can be recovered from frozen skin biopsies after prolonged in vitro culture. Stimulation with IFN-{gamma} induced robust transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes that were largely resolved after stimulus removal, with transcriptional responses to secondary stimulation comparable to the primary stimulation. Treatment of cultured skin biopsies with histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors effectively altered global histone modification levels, but did not substantially affect the transcriptional resolution of IFN-{gamma}-induced responses. Collectively, these findings establish cryopreserved human skin biopsies as a scalable ex vivo platform that enables mechanistic studies of inflammatory responses of multiple populations of skin structural cells.

items.title: Onsite fixation preserves phosphoprotein profile in human whole blood
items.abstract: Phospho-flow cytometry is increasingly used as a pharmacodynamic readout of kinase-pathway activity, including in JAK inhibitor trials. Phosphoprotein states are intrinsically labile ex vivo and are further altered by conventional workflows, which typically involve PBMC isolation, cryopreservation, and transit times of hours to days before measurement. Here, we fix whole blood at collection and quantify six phosphoproteins by mass cytometry, benchmarked against matched cryopreserved PBMCs. Unlike PBMCs, whole blood retained neutrophils, ~75-80% of which were pSTAT3-positive at baseline. Basal pSTAT3 was also markedly higher in whole blood monocytes (~41% positive vs. ~9% in PBMCs), whereas T, B, and NK cells differed by less than 1 percentage point. Stimulation produced subset-specific phosphorylation patterns that were retained after 6 weeks of storage. Because fixation does not require centrifugation and retains neutrophils, samples can be fixed at collection sites without on-site processing laboratories and analyzed centrally in batches.

items.title: SARDINE unlocks EWAS summary statistics for large-scale epigenetic biomarker analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biostatistics and Medical Informatics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, USA
items.abstract: Epigenetic clocks are increasingly used to study biological aging, yet their interpretation and utility remain uncertain. Meanwhile, the growing wealth of epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) summary statistics remains largely untapped for evaluating these biomarkers. Here, we introduce SARDINE, a statistical framework that estimates epigenetic clock-phenotype associations using EWAS summary statistics, clock weights, and reference methylation covariance, without individual-level data. SARDINE accurately reproduced individual-level association estimates across 38 epigenetic biomarkers and four phenotypes in 15,677 individuals. Applying SARDINE to diverse EWAS datasets revealed substantial heterogeneity in biomarker associations with aging, diseases, and lifestyle factors. By transforming CpG-level EWAS results into interpretable biomarker-level associations, SARDINE unlocks a largely underutilized data resource and establishes a scalable paradigm for systematic biomarker evaluation and discovery in aging research.

items.title: Isoform diversity as a complementary dimension of gene expression
items.abstract: Most human genes produce multiple mRNA isoforms through alternative splicing and alternative transcription start and end sites. Isoforms of the same gene can differ in function, and their relative abundance varies between tissues and conditions. However, gene expression analysis is often restricted to the gene level, masking its diversification into mRNA and protein isoforms with potentially distinct functionality. Here we show, using an adaptation of Shannon evenness applied to 4,814 GTEx samples from 25 tissues, that isoform diversity constitutes a distinct dimension of gene expression, complementary to gene-level abundance and whole transcriptome diversity. Isoform diversity separated tissues based on non-differentially expressed genes and changed with age in a gene- and tissue-specific manner, most strongly in the brain and often without changes in overall gene expression levels. During neuronal differentiation, it increased most notably in RNA processing and splicing genes. Our results suggest that isoform diversity represents an independent dimension of gene expression and may help explain functional differences between tissues and cell states that are not captured by analyzing expression levels alone.

items.title: Hierarchical Temporal Transformer for Cancer Grade Prediction and Cross-Cancer Transfer Learning from Pathology Reports
items.abstract: Background: Language models for cancer reports usually read one document at a time and are tested on tumour types seen in training. Continuous-time sequence models address the first gap, but whether they use visit timing, not just order, is seldom tested. Methods: We developed the Hierarchical Temporal Transformer (HTT), which encodes reports with adapted BiomedBERT and reads the sequence with a cancer-type-conditioned temporal transformer. We evaluated it against best-possible AUROC ceilings on two synthetic benchmarks, one with the label stated in the text and one recoverable only from tumour sizes and visit intervals (ten seeds). Diagnostics led to an interval-aware time code (HTT-IA). On 4,786 TCGA pathology reports in 14 types, three types were withheld, and a text-only HTT was compared with a survival model. Results: On the phrase benchmark HTT reached AUROC 0.931 +/- 0.012 against 0.913 +/- 0.007 for a last-report baseline (+0.018, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.050); dates cannot raise the ceiling there. On the growth benchmark the initial time code scored 0.790, equal to a no-time model (0.787), whereas HTT-IA reached 0.843 (+0.053, 0.026 to 0.082) against ceilings of 0.894 without and 0.979 with dates. On unseen tumour types HTT reached 0.925 +/- 0.007, equal to in-distribution performance and to a single-report baseline. Text-only macro C-index was 0.592 (CALM 0.626-0.652). Conclusion: Cross-type transfer is carried by the pre-trained encoder. Visit timing is used only when the data make it identifiable and the time code is on a clinical scale. Ceilings, order-only ablations and re-dating probes are inexpensive checks for such models.

items.title: scCircaSim: A Circadian Simulator for Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Cardiac Ultrasound, The Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University, Qingdao, China
items.abstract: Motivation: Simulated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets that capture circadian dynamics while providing known ground truth remain scarce, limiting systematic evaluation of circadian analysis methods. Results: We developed scCircaSim to generate circadian single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from a single-time-point reference. The framework combines phase progression with reference-derived network propagation of anchor gene rhythms and incorporates neighborhood effects for spatial simulation. Outputs retain reference heterogeneity and provide known cell or spot phases, rhythmicity labels, and gene-level mesor, amplitude, and phase values. Validation showed retention of reference structure and recovery of specified temporal patterns. Benchmarks of four cell phase inference methods and three rhythmic gene analysis methods revealed differences in phase accuracy, rhythmicity detection, and parameter recovery. scCircaSim supports reproducible method evaluation and preliminary experimental planning. Availability and Implementation: scCircaSim is implemented in R and available at https://github.com/Liwei-DynamicsLab/scCircaSim.

items.title: Toward space-optimal approximate colored indexes at scale
items.corresponding_institution: Univ. Lille, CNRS, Centrale Lille, UMR 9189 CRIStAL, F-59000 Lille, France
items.abstract: Searching current petabase-scale sequence repositories requires indexes that combine compact storage with high query throughput. Although exact colored indexes retain complete sequence information, their construction and storage costs can become substantial for highly diverse collections. Indexes based on approximate membership query (AMQ) filters offer a compact alternative with fast construction and queries. Being hash-based, these indexes support different seeding schemes without structural changes, while sampling can reduce storage requirements, construction time and query time by an order of magnitude. Within the AMQ framework, querying many independent filters causes scattered memory accesses, reducing throughput. This motivates interleaved filters, which address this weakness by storing filter slots contiguously by position, enabling cache-friendly access and simultaneous membership queries. However, existing implementations face a trade-off between guaranteed construction and space-efficiency. Here, we introduce a new indexing framework based on interleaved ZOR filters, fingerprint-based structures with guaranteed construction that require only approximately 1% more space than the theoretical minimum for AMQ. To exploit redundancy between genomes, we introduce a color-preserving merging mechanism that extends fingerprints with membership bits, allowing multiple genomes to share a filter while retaining their individual identities. Together with a lightweight, sketch-based layout planner, this mechanism yields a compact index structure that accommodates collections with widely varying genome sizes and degrees of similarity. Our third contribution extends the AMQ framework beyond contiguous -mers through a low-density minimizer scheme alongside efficient implementations of sensitive seeds, including gapped -mers and randstrobes. We implement these methods in Zindex, a parallel, SIMD-accelerated Rust index that scales to millions of genomes while supporting diverse seeding and sampling schemes. Zindex indexes the latest RefSeq release of 564,401 assembled genomes in under 22 hours, producing a 289.5 GB index. It further scales to all 2,763,297 genomes of AllTheBacteria, producing a 406.3 GB index in four days with a peak memory footprint of 43.8 GB. Availability. Zindex is available at https://github.com/Malfoy/Zindex

items.title: MOCHI enables systematic identification of candidate independent intronic transcriptional signals from short-read RNA-seq data
items.abstract: Standard short-read RNA-seq analysis pipelines quantify expression over annotated exons and disregard signals mapped to introns, thereby missing independently transcribed intronic RNAs. Existing strategies depend on annotation, biologically crude whole-intron quantification, or subjective, low-throughput manual genome-browser inspection. We present MOCHI (Mapping of Cryptic Hidden Intronic Transcripts), a framework that couples reference-independent, k-mer-based signal discovery with reference-guided genomic interpretation and a custom multi-step filtering module to systematically curate potential independent intronic transcription units from strand-specific short-read RNA-seq data. On two simulated datasets, MOCHI recovered annotated sense-intronic long non-coding RNAs removed from the reference and distinguished them from intronic signal confounders. Across paired ribosomal RNA-depleted and poly(A)-selected libraries from ten cancer cell lines, MOCHI curated candidates whose host introns are strongly enriched for a transcription-initiation signal. Candidate expression is largely uncoupled from host-gene exons, and their genomic features resemble those of annotated long non-coding RNAs. In ten matched cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, candidates were detected in tumor samples, and a subset was associated with overall survival after adjustment for age and host-gene expression. Consequently, MOCHI extends the transcriptomic landscape that can be mined from existing short-read RNA-seq data and provides a curated resource of candidate intronic transcripts for downstream analyses.

items.title: LeadWeaver: Topology-Aware Masked-Lead Modeling for Robust 12-Lead ECG Diagnosis
items.corresponding_institution: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)
items.abstract: Clinical electrocardiography is organized as a structured set of correlated leads, yet most neural ECG classifiers assume that all twelve leads are present, correctly ordered, and acquired under the same device conditions at training and deployment. We propose LeadWeaver, a topology-aware ECG representation model designed for diagnosis under missing, corrupted, or device-shifted leads. LeadWeaver represents each lead as a temporal token stream, couples leads through a fixed-plus-learned physiological lead graph, and performs masked-lead latent completion rather than waveform synthesis. A reliability router estimates which observed leads should dominate each diagnostic decision, while a consistency objective aligns complete-lead and incomplete-lead predictions. We evaluate the model on PTB-XL and CPSC-style settings using complete-input diagnosis, arbitrary missing-lead subsets, lead corruption, cross-dataset transfer, calibration, and selective prediction. The central hypothesis is that robust ECG diagnosis requires explicitly modeling both inter-lead topology and uncertainty about unavailable evidence, rather than treating missing channels as zero-valued inputs.

items.title: Phase-locked dual-band vibration bursts strengthen anti-kindling by vibrotactile coordinated reset stimulation in a spiking network model
items.abstract: Parkinsons disease and related movement disorders are accompanied by pathologically synchronized neuronal activity in cortico-basal ganglia circuits. Coordinated reset (CR) stimulation was derived computationally as a means of suppressing such activity at its source, by resetting the phases of the subpopulations of a synchronized network at staggered times. Under spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), the resulting decorrelated firing depresses excitatory coupling and establishes a weakly coupled, desynchronized state that outlasts stimulation, a process termed anti-kindling. Sustained post-stimulation benefit has been demonstrated for electrical CR stimulation in parkinsonian primates and in proof-of-concept patient studies, and vibrotactile CR (vCR) stimulation realizes the same principle non-invasively through bursts of fingertip vibration. The deployed vCR protocol employs a carrier frequency of 250 Hz, which preferentially recruits Pacinian afferents. Because Pacinian receptive fields extend substantially beyond the stimulated digit, inputs originating at adjacent fingertips converge on overlapping regions of the target population, which degrades the spatial separation on which CR depends. Here we examine whether the spectral composition of the individual burst, independent of the stimulation schedule, governs the magnitude of anti-kindling. In a Hodgkin-Huxley network with STDP, driven through a two-channel model of fast-adapting afferents, a dual-band burst superimposing a 30 Hz component on the 250 Hz carrier yielded the lowest post-stimulation coupling among eleven vCR patterns, at one third of the carriers drive power. Recruitment of focal Meissner afferents by the 30 Hz component restricts part of the drive to the stimulated subpopulation, and phase locking of that component to the burst envelope generates post-burst pauses that reset the phase of the stimulated neurons. Spectral composition therefore determines both the spatial selectivity of vCR stimulation and its capacity for phase resetting.

items.title: Seed Amplification Assay-Based Detection of Alpha-Synuclein Aggregates Outperforms Immunohistochemical Analysis in the Intestinal Mucosal Biopsies of Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy Participants
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether an -synuclein (-Syn) seed amplification assay (SAA) detects seeding-competent aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies, differs by gastrointestinal region, registers pathology more frequently than immunohistochemistry (IHC), and associates with Parkinson disease (PD) diagnosis, disease duration or severity. Design: This cross-sectional, proof-of-concept diagnostic accuracy study analyzed duodenum, ileum, and sigmoid biopsies from PD participants, age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC), plus exploratory multiple system atrophy (MSA) subtypes [parkinsonian (MSA-P) and cerebellar (MSA-C)]. Ileal and sigmoid PD and HC biopsies were assessed using proteinase K-resistant phospho-Ser129 IHC. SAA positivity was evaluated against clinical and biological measures. Results: In PD, SAA detected seeding competent -Syn aggregates with high observed specificity (97.5-100%) and region-dependent sensitivity (18/37, 48.65% in ileum and 36/56, 64.29% in sigmoid). Sigmoid SAA positivity increased significantly with PD disease duration (40.00% at 10 years), independent of motor severity, whereas ileal positivity remained stable across disease stages. In 37 paired sigmoid biopsies, SAA detected -Syn aggregates 2.8-fold more frequently than IHC. Sigmoid seeding activity was detected in all five MSA-P, but not in two MSA-C. IHC did not detect aggregates in any MSA. Conclusions: In PD, -Syn SAA detected seeding-competent -Syn aggregates in endoscopic mucosal biopsies with high observed specificity, moderate sensitivity, and approximately 2.8-fold higher detection rate than IHC in sigmoid. Positive SAA in MSA patients supports GI involvement across synucleinopathies. SAA detection in PD differed by intestinal region and disease duration, supporting further validation of intestinal SAA as a PD biomarker.

items.title: Concussion decreases brain signal variability
items.abstract: Sports-related concussion represents a major public health concern, with millions of cases diagnosed annually. Despite significant methodological advances in functional brain imaging, a clinically meaningful neuroimaging biomarker of concussion has yet to be established. This may be due in part to a reliance on traditional measures. For example, approaches examining mean activation across trials reduce responses to a single measure of central tendency and therefore fail to capture important individual differences. In contrast, blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) variability offers a promising new approach to measuring brain function, Specifically, it captures individual differences in the temporal variability in the BOLD signal over time. Further, it is sensitive to neural, vascular, and neurovascular coupling changes that accompany concussion. We collected baseline (prior to injury) and post-concussion (within 48 hours of injury) neuroimaging data in 56 collegiate athletes. Within this longitudinal dataset, we investigated changes in BOLD variability across multiple spatial scales. In addition, we examined their relationships with self-reported symptoms and cognitive performance. As expected, symptoms increased following concussion while computerized cognitive performance declined. BOLD variability decreased from baseline to post-concussion, particularly in the somatomotor and language networks. Moreover, changes in BOLD variability were related to changes in symptom reporting and cognitive performance. Together, these findings advance our understanding of how concussion affects brain function and highlight BOLD signal variability as a promising biomarker to aid ongoing efforts to improve the diagnosis and treatment of sports-related concussion.

items.title: Neurons entrain and shape an intrinsic arteriole rhythm that distributes blood across the cortical mantle
items.abstract: The cerebral arteriole network distributes blood across cortex through branches whose diameters oscillate near a frequency fvaso ~ 0.1 Hz. We asked whether the spatiotemporal pattern of these vaso-oscillations reflects neuronal entrainment of an intrinsic vascular oscillation. Three findings support this: First, suppressing endothelial hyperpolarization left resting-state oscillations intact but weakened the vascular response to neural activity, showing that vasomotion originates within the arteriole network rather than following neuronal drive. Second, arterioles amplify sensory drive selectively rather than faithfully: neural activity near 0.1 Hz is resonantly enhanced to form a strong peak in the vascular response. Third, neuronal frequency sets spatial reach, and areas compete: when two neighboring cortical areas are driven simultaneously, the one nearer fvaso captures more vascular territory. Neurons therefore entrain an intrinsic vascular rhythm and stimulation frequency governs how vasomotion distributes blood, shapes functional brain images, and may influence interstitial fluid transport.

items.title: SNAzzy: an image processing pipeline for investigating global Synchronous Network Activity
items.abstract: Genetically encoded fluorescent indicators are powerful tools for monitoring biological processes in live samples (Lin and Schnitzer 2016; Nakai, Ohkura, and Imoto 2001). When combined with a large field of view, a single time-lapse recording has the potential to capture many specimens, facilitating high-throughput data collection. However, this approach generates large, multidimensional datasets that are challenging to process and analyze. We present SNAzzy, a Python package for studying synchronous network activity (SNA) in Drosophila embryos via high-throughput microscopy. SNA is a hallmark of developing nervous systems (Wu, Kourdougli, and Portera-Cailliau 2024; Blankenship and Feller 2009; Akin and Zipursky 2020), often studied using genetically encoded calcium indicators to monitor neural activity in vivo. SNAzzy processes and analyzes time-lapse datasets taken from live samples using fluorescent widefield microscopy. Each dataset contains dozens of individual specimens in the same field of view and thousands of time points. The software offers individual specimen cropping for optimization of storage and processing, adaptive regions of interest for quantification of fluorescence and changes in morphology over time, a custom peak detection algorithm, and a graphical user interface for data visualization, curation, and dataset comparison. The code is available at https://github.com/ACRLab/snazzy.

items.title: Probing EEG Foundation Model Attention Maps for Lightweight Interpretable Emotion Recognition
items.corresponding_institution: Neuroengineering and Brain-Computer Interfaces Research Infrastructure, University of Patras, 26504 Patras, Greece
items.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) trained on EEG signals promise subject- and dataset-independent pipelines for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications, but have yet to consistently outperform task-specific architectures, and their large representations are costly to compute and store. As a means of advancing the understanding of the Foundation Models' inner mechanisms, we propose a lightweight alternative that exploits the self-attention mechanism of REVE, a pretrained EEG FM, to derive features similar to weighted Functional Connectivity (FC) without any fine-tuning. Inspired by kernel-based FC matrices, we aggregate the raw first-layer attention weights of a single head over the full duration of dataset trials into weighted channel-to-channel adjacency matrices. These matrices replace standard encoder representation vectors as classification features, substantially reducing computational cost. We further introduce a label-free, symmetry-based criterion, motivated by the emergence of near-symmetric attention patterns in trained encoder-decoder transformers, ranking attention heads by how much discriminative information they carry. Classical machine learning classifiers are then trained on the single most informative head's attention-derived FC matrix and achieve balanced accuracy and F1 scores on the SEED-IV emotion-recognition dataset that are competitive with several fully fine-tuned state-of-the-art EEG Foundation Models, requiring at least two orders of magnitude fewer calculations than the standard use of the encoder. Subsequent cortical region analysis revealed a significant over-representation of frontal region connections by ranking the most discriminative FC matrix connectivity edges, validating our methods as consistent with prior affective-computing literature. These results suggest that interpretable, computationally inexpensive linear probing of attention maps is a viable route to deploying EEG Foundation Models in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Microglial AhR Drives Sex-Biased Amyloid Pathology
items.corresponding_institution: Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III, Madrid, Spain; Unidad de Investigacion Neurovascular, Depto. Farmacologia y Toxicologia, Faculta
items.abstract: Microglia integrate local and systemic signals that can modify their response to amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), but the molecular pathways connecting these signals to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a sensor of microbiota- and host-derived metabolites, as a microglial regulator of amyloid pathology. Sustained administration of the AhR agonist indoxyl-3-sulfate (I3S) exacerbated cortical A{beta} deposition and plaque-associated neuritic damage in APPNL-F mice. Conversely, constitutive AhR deficiency reduced amyloid burden, promoted plaque compaction, and preserved behavioural performance, whereas inducible deletion of AhR in microglia was sufficient to reduce plaque accumulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that AhR loss reprogrammed microglia toward phagolysosomal and A{beta}-recognition states and enhanced microglial A{beta} uptake, with markedly stronger effects in females. APPNL-F mice also exhibited sex-dependent remodelling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Circulating indole-3-aldehyde (IAld) robustly activated AhR and was associated with cortical amyloid pathology. AhR-activating bioactivity was increased in mouse serum, cortex and faecal extracts and was higher in serum from the COGNIBIO12 analytical subcohort than in independently recruited cognitively unimpaired H2H participants. Among amyloid-positive patients, higher serum AhR bioactivity was associated with lower CSF A{beta}42 concentrations. Together, these findings identify microglial AhR as a metabolically responsive regulator linking systemic ligand availability, biological sex, and microglial control of amyloid pathology.

items.title: Analysis of reproductive traits associated with lipoprotein(a) deficiency in participants from the Pakistan Genome Resource
items.abstract: Aims. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of LPA-targeting therapies that markedly lower circulating Lp(a). Because LPA?the gene encoding apolipoprotein(a)?is absent in most model organisms, preclinical studies have limited value for assessing effects such as reproductive safety. Therefore, naturally occurring human LPA ?knockouts? were analyzed to evaluate reproductive outcomes of on-target Lp(a) lowering. Methods and Results. Individuals carrying high-confidence LPA loss-of-function (LoF) variants which reduce Lp(a) in a gene-dosage?dependent manner within the Pakistan Genome Resource were identified. LoF variants showed no depletion of homozygotes relative to Hardy?Weinberg expectations. LPA LoF associations with fertility-related traits (ever having a child and number of children) under additive and recessive models were assessed using regenie-based burden testing, including sex-stratified analyses, and no significant associations were observed. A recall-by-genotype study of female LoF homozygotes alongside heterozygous and non-carrier family member controls was performed, surveying reproductive histories and offspring outcomes. Across 107 pregnancies and 87 children in 19 homozygous LoF women, rates of miscarriage, maternal complications (including preeclampsia, hypertension, and gestational diabetes), delivery complications, neonatal intensive care admission, birth defects, and child health problems were comparable across genotypes with no statistically significant genotype?outcome associations. Conclusions. These genetic and by-genotype analyses indicate that complete lifelong LPA deficiency due to high-confidence LPA loss-of-function variants is not associated with overt adverse maternal fertility, pregnancy or child health outcomes. These findings offer human genetic reassurance regarding reproductive and developmental safety in the context of sustained Lp(a)-lowering, with implications for long-term therapies targeting Lp(a).

items.title: How mutation rate evolves: Gene expression shapes genome-wide mutation rates in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans
items.abstract: Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription- coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.

items.title: Measuring American black bear genetic load in fixed structural variants and runs of homozygosity
items.abstract: Populations living in geographically isolated regions are expected to have reduced gene flow, increased genetic drift, and elevated levels of inbreeding, influencing both genetic load and possibly the distribution of structural variants. The American black bear (Ursus americanus) is widely found across Ontario, Canada, where populations inhabit diverse landscapes ranging from relatively intact contiguous forested landscapes to isolated regions such as the Saugeen Peninsula. Here, we investigated the population genomic history across five Ontario black bear populations using a combination of short-read (SR) and long-read (LR) sequencing data. We compared population genetic metrics including nucleotide diversity ({pi}), Tajimas D, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and genome-wide structural variants (SVs) to assess population health and identify signatures of isolation. Our results showed that the isolated Saugeen Peninsula population is genetically distinct and exhibited reduced nucleotide diversity, greater ROH and SV abundance compared with mainland populations. The population also showed elevated genetic load in all genomic features, suggesting increased exposure of deleterious variation that are expressed in ROH and population specific SVs. We further discuss the integration of ROH, SVs and genetic load in conservation assessments.

items.title: Genome-wide Analysis of the VQ Gene Family and Expression Profiling in Sorghum bicolor
items.corresponding_institution: Shandong Expressway Urban and Rural Construction and Development Co., Ltd.
items.abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts agricultural productivity, making the stress-tolerant sorghum an ideal model for studying crop adaptation. VQ motif-containing proteins are plant-specific transcriptional co-regulators vital for stress responses, yet their roles in sorghum remain underexplored. Here, we identified 35 VQ genes in sorghum, classifying them into seven subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis indicated that the family's expansion was primarily driven by segmental duplication. Notably, synteny analysis revealed a lack of collinearity between sorghum and Arabidopsis VQ genes, suggesting significant functional divergence during monocot evolution. Expression profiling showed distinct patterns among VQ members, with SbVQ34, SbVQ39 adn SbVQ40 significantly upregulated under salt stress. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted SbVQ39 as a potential key regulator in sorghum salt tolerance. This study provides novel insights into sorghum's salinity tolerance mechanisms and establishes a foundation for utilizing VQ genes in breeding salt-tolerant crops.

items.title: Somatic Structural Variant Discovery from Tumor Specific Strings Computed Against a Draft Composite Germline Reference
items.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) are among the most clinically relevant genomic alterations in cancer. However, their accurate detection remains challenging due to complex genomic rearrangements, repetitive genomic regions, difficulties in distinguishing somatic variants from germline variation and sequencing artifacts, and limited sequencing support for low-frequency events. Existing mapping-based somatic SV callers are susceptible to alignment ambiguities in repetitive regions and near complex SV breakpoints, while approaches relying on comparisons of independently generated tumor and normal variant callsets may propagate errors from both callsets. Building on the concept of specific strings, previously applied to germline SV discovery, we introduce VESPA-SS, a novel approach for detecting somatic SVs from paired tumor-normal long-read whole-genome sequencing data. VESPA-SS directly extracts somatic SV signals using specific strings computed from tumor reads against a Draft Composite Germline Reference, without requiring initial read mapping or a high-quality germline assembly. These signals are subsequently clustered and refined through consensus sequence generation and alignment-based procedures to identify somatic SVs. Evaluation on real PacBio HiFi datasets demonstrates that VESPA-SS outperforms state-of-the-art somatic SV callers, achieving F1 scores exceeding 0.92 and 0.90 on the well-characterized HG008 and COLO829 cancer cell lines, respectively, compared with the highest F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.85 achieved by the evaluated methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of specific string based signal extraction for accurate somatic SV discovery and establish a new computational paradigm for identifying complex genomic alterations in cancer. VESPA-SS is freely available at https://github.com/dcmonti/VESPA.

items.title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
items.abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

items.title: Sex-specific dynamics of activity-dependent regulation of synaptic CaMKII
items.abstract: Similar behavioral outcomes in males and females can mask substantial differences in the mechanisms underlying neuronal function. However, to what extent sex influences the abundance and activity-dependent changes of proteins that govern neuronal plasticity remains poorly understood. Here we investigated sex-specific regulation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), an evolutionarily conserved regulator of synaptic stability and plasticity in fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. We find that the steady state levels and activity-driven changes in CaMKII protein differ between female and male at both third instar larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ) and in adult fly mushroom body (MB). These sex-specific differences are downstream of the sex determination pathway, implicating somatic sex identity in the regulation of CaMKII abundance and its activity-dependent dynamics. Despite the differences in CaMKII levels between female and male flies, we observed no impairment of plasticity in either sex. Overall, our findings reveal sex-dependent regulation of both steady-state and activity-dependent levels of a highly conserved neuronal plasticity-associated protein across distinct neuronal contexts and development stages. These results further support the idea that females and males can achieve similar behavioral outcomes through different molecular mechanisms. Growing evidence that sexually dimorphic molecular responses contribute directly to sex differences in vulnerability to stress and disease underscores the importance of identifying these mechanisms and understanding their consequences.

items.title: Stochasticity in Metabolism: Oxidative Stress Response Phenotypes As Emergent Consequences of Network Topology
items.abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are ubiquitous yet elusive due to their reactivity and short half-lives, making simulation essential for mechanistic insight. Traditional ROS modeling has been confined to small ODE frameworks limited by kinetic-parameter scarcity. Here, we recast ROS dynamics as a flux-balance analysis (FBA) optimization problem using COBRA and CPLEX, augmenting the Escherichia coli iJO1366 genome-scale model with 84 spontaneous oxidation, 14 redox, and 9 detoxification reactions, targeting three ROS species: hydroxyl radicals, superoxide, and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). We also formalize five fundamental rules of oxidation biology in the form of mixed-integer linear constraints, allowing us to dynamically incorporate reaction rate constants and let complex behavior emerge from first principles. Among these phenomena is the bimodal killing pattern under H2O2 stress, first announced over 40 years ago and never computationally recapitulated until now. We observe it by stochastically sampling our models with GapSplit, simulating bet-hedging and partitioning solutions into growers, persisters, and non-survivors. In our simulations, this killing effect arises solely from the metabolic network topology during random exploration of alternative metabolic configurations. The conservation of steady state creates a stochastic bias for detoxification when central carbon metabolism reaches its metabolic capacity to deal with ROS, causing the famous survival recovery phase. The recovery phase is thus part of Mode 1 metabolism, characterized by spare detoxification capacity and fulfilled by the Ahp reaction in E. coli. Mode 2 has no spare detoxification. We anticipate this to be an overlooked universal principle.

items.title: Tree shrews combine panoramic vision with an expanded oculomotor repertoire
items.corresponding_institution: Cornell University & Howard Hughes Medical Institute
items.abstract: Mammals differ in how they redirect gaze. Primates shift and hold gaze with rapid, precise eye movements that can be decoupled from the head. In lateral-eyed mammals studied to date, gaze is organized around the head: saccades are coupled to head rotation in freely moving animals and typically accompanied by attempted head movements even under head fixation. These observations suggest a trade-off: animals that keep a panoramic field give up the precise, eye-driven control of gaze typical of frontal-eyed animals. But because lateral eyes and head-centered gaze co-occur in every lateral-eyed species studied, it is unknown whether one follows from the other. Here we test this in the tree shrew, an arboreal mammal with laterally placed eyes. Using real-time eye tracking in head-fixed animals, we find that tree shrews saccade frequently under head fixation and that most saccades occur without detectable attempted head movement. Tree shrews make visually evoked saccades, along both the horizontal and vertical axes of the visual field, toward targets. They can also fixate on visual targets. Using widefield calcium imaging, we show that visual cortex over-represents the central visual field. Lastly, we show that extraocular muscles that move the eyes contain specialized nerve endings found in frontal-eyed species. Based on this suite of evidence, we conclude that lateral eyes do not preclude eye-driven gaze control. The two are separable dimensions of visual system design, a combination that may suit animals whose locomotion routinely points the head away from where they need to look.

items.title: Small RNA-mediated genomic silencing promotes telomere stability in the absence of telomerase in C. elegans
items.corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
items.abstract: We previously found that small RNAs with perfect homology to (TTAGGC)n telomere repeats are very rare. Here we use long read sequencing to reveal that most N2 wild type C. elegans strains have few telomere mutations at 5 prime ends of telomeres, where the telomeric lncRNA TERRA is transcribed.
