Notably, allergen incorporation reversed the relative ability of the two antibodies to neutralize IgE-Fc[epsilon]RI interactions and remodelled Fc[gamma]R binding. Thus, immune-complex composition is a determinant of therapeutic antibody function.

items.title: ATF3 Preserves Macrophage Cholesterol Homeostasis during Metabolic Stress
items.abstract: Background: Macrophages must coordinate immune activation with maintenance of cellular cholesterol homeostasis, yet the transcriptional mechanisms integrating these processes remain incompletely understood. Activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) suppresses inflammatory and interferon responses and has been implicated in macrophage lipid metabolism, suggesting a role in coordinating immune and sterol-responsive transcriptional programs. Methods: Wild-type and ATF3-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages were analyzed by bulk RNA sequencing following Toll-like receptor stimulation and under conditions of sterol loading or depletion. Cholesterol content, cytokine production, and sterol-responsive gene expression were quantified. Human metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) datasets and Kupffer cell-specific ATF3 knockout mice were used to assess disease relevance in vivo. Results: ATF3 deficiency enhanced inflammatory and interferon-responsive transcriptional programs while suppressing a sterol-responsive gene module enriched for SREBP2 target genes. This phenotype was conserved across diverse Toll-like receptor stimuli and accompanied by persistent Ch25h upregulation. Despite exhibiting elevated cellular cholesterol, ATF3-deficient macrophages retained transcriptional responsiveness to sterol loading and depletion while demonstrating reduced induction of SREBP2-dependent genes across conditions. IFNAR blockade reduced interferon-responsive gene expression but did not normalize Ch25h or sterol-responsive gene expression. In contrast, CRISPR-mediated reduction of Ch25h partially restored sterol-responsive gene expression in inflammatory ATF3-deficient macrophages. In human MASLD, hepatic ATF3 expression positively correlated with disease severity. In mice, ATF3 was preferentially induced in Kupffer cells during metabolic stress, and Kupffer cell-specific deletion of ATF3 increased liver injury and Kupffer cell lipid accumulation. Conclusions: ATF3 supports sterol-responsive transcriptional programs while restraining inflammatory activation in macrophages. ATF3 loss results in elevated cellular cholesterol, impaired SREBP2-dependent gene expression, and persistent derepression of Ch25h, which contributes to but does not fully explain the sterol phenotype. These findings identify ATF3 as a coordinator of macrophage adaptation to inflammatory and metabolic stress and support a protective role for Kupffer cell ATF3 during metabolic liver disease.

items.title: A cohesin acetylation complex that recognises nicked DNA
items.abstract: Eukaryotic DNA replication products are held together by cohesin to enable their faithful inheritance during cell division. The establishment of stable sister chromatid cohesion requires replication-coupled acetylation of two conserved lysines on the cohesin Smc3 ATPase head. Here, we use AlphaFold 3 to predict the existence of a budding yeast cohesin acetylation complex, consisting of the replication protein PCNA, the cohesin subunit Pds5 and the Eco1 acetyltransferase. The predicted complex specifically contacts nicked DNA, a replication fork determinant that controls acetylation. Furthermore, cohesin engagement results in predicted conformational adaptations that bring acetyl-CoA in striking distance of the Smc3 target lysine. We perform biochemical and genetic experiments that confirm anticipated features of this reaction trajectory. Related cohesin acetylation complexes are predicted to form in other eukaryotes, including humans. Our study combines AI-assisted structure predictions and wet-bench experimentation to reveal the likely mechanism of replication-coupled cohesin acetylation during sister chromatid cohesion establishment.

items.title: HIF1A-AS2 Regulates Hypoxia-Driven HIF Isoform Switching in Human Endothelial Cells
items.abstract: Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are central regulators of cellular adaptation to low oxygen, with a well-documented transition from HIF-1 to HIF-2 signaling during prolonged hypoxia. Here, we investigate the role of a natural antisense transcript of HIF1A, HIF1A-AS2, in modulating this transition in human endothelial cells (ECs). Genome-wide expression profiling revealed a strong hypoxia-induced upregulation of HIF1A-AS2 that coincided with a marked reduction in HIF1A mRNA levels, whereas EPAS1 remained stable. Interestingly, this negative correlation was consistent across multiple EC types and supported by silencing experiments which demonstrated that both HIF-1 and HIF-2 contribute to HIF1A-AS2 induction. Knockdown of HIF1A-AS2 partially restored HIF1A expression and increased HIF-1 protein and functional activity, as evidenced by elevated VEGFA and GLUT1 expression. Genomic analysis identified HIF-1 and HIF-2 binding motifs upstream of HIF1A-AS2, supporting the dual regulation. Furthermore, cancer tissue analysis revealed frequent downregulation of HIF1A-AS2, correlating with elevated HIF1A and EPAS1 levels. These findings suggest that HIF1A-AS2 acts as a hypoxia-responsive regulator that limits HIF-1 signaling and facilitates the HIF isoform switch, and suggests implications for endothelial adaptation, angiogenic signaling, and vascular remodeling under chronic hypoxia.

items.title: The yeast Gcn2 protein kinase mediates P-body formation both through its activity with eIF2α and with non-canonical substrates
items.abstract: P-bodies (PBs) are control hubs for RNA processing and storage that form when translation initiation is inhibited, including during stress. In yeast, Gcn2 is the sole eIF2 alpha kinase that inhibits translation initiation in response to diverse stresses. We show that PB formation depends strongly on Gcn2 during amino acid starvation but only partially during oxidative stress. Constitutively active Gcn2 also induces PB formation in unstressed cells. Surprisingly, PBs are still constitutively formed in a gcn3 mutant strain that is insensitive to eIF2 alpha phosphorylation suggesting that Gcn2 also promotes PB formation independently of eIF2 alpha phosphorylation. Analysis of several putative Gcn2-substrates involved in RNA metabolism identified several proteins required for Gcn2-mediated PB formation. Among these, Smu2, which was not previously implicated in PB formation, localises to PBs and is required for stress-induced coalescence of mRNA granules into PBs. Together, our findings indicate that Gcn2 promotes PB formation via two complementary routes: eIF2 alpha phosphorylation, which generates untranslated mRNAs, and Smu2-dependent maturation of mRNA granules into PBs.

items.title: A PTN-Rich MSC Subtype Promotes Cartilage Repair in End-Stage Knee Osteoarthritis
items.abstract: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy for end-stage knee osteoarthritis (KOA) shows inconsistent efficacy, and whether MSCs retain cartilage repair capacity in the inflammatory joint remains unclear. Using single-cell RNA sequencing of human Kellgren-Lawrence grade (G ) and (G ) KOA joint tissues and exogenous MSCs, we found that pleiotrophin (PTN) signalling shifts from MSC-chondrocyte crosstalk to chondrocyte-dominated autocrine signalling, with PTN exhaustion and elevated cluster of differentiation 74 (CD74) in G cartilage. We therefore identified and sorted a PTN-rich CD74-low placenta-derived MSC subtype and evaluated it in a murine KOA model and in co-culture with patient-derived chondrocytes. This subtype enhanced cartilage repair, upregulated SOX9, and suppressed MMP13, CD74, IL-6, and IL-1{beta}, potentially through CD74 suppression and reduced NF-{kappa}B signaling. These findings provide a basis for functionally defined, stage-matched cell therapy tailored to the pathological microenvironment of end-stage KOA.

items.title: Junction-level imaging and modeling of transient leaks in epithelia predicts a dynamic tight junction strand network
items.corresponding_institution: Biosciences Unit, Faculty of Medicine and Health Technology, Tampere University, Tampere, Finland
items.abstract: Epithelial tight junctions restrict paracellular permeability, but how small solutes leak through the barrier is not fully understood, because permeability is usually measured globally. Here, we combined fast zinc-based barrier imaging (ZnUMBA) with computational modelling of the dynamic tight junction strand network to study transient leaks at single bicellular junctions in MDCK II cells. Leaks were short-lived, with a median duration of 17 s in wild-type cells, and occurred in all cell lines studied, including ZO-1 knockout, ZO-2 knockout, and ZO-1-overexpressing cells. In ZO-2 knockout and ZO-1-overexpressing cells, leaks lasted longer without changes in their frequency or transepithelial electrical resistance (TER). ZO-1 knockout increased the junctional ZnUMBA signal and reduced TER and the number of detected leaks. Simulations showed that stochastic breaking and sealing of tight junction strands is sufficient to explain the observed leak frequencies and durations, and that a single pair of strand break formation and sealing rates reproduces both junction-level leaks and global permeability. Whereas leak frequency mainly reflects the ratio of these rates, leak duration provides independent information on strand sealing that global measurements cannot resolve. Modulating myosin II activity had little effect on leaks, whereas actin depolymerization compromised the barrier. Together, these results link junction-level leaks of ions and small solutes to tight junction strand dynamics.

items.title: Host control and regulation of human anellovirus persistence
items.abstract: Anelloviruses are the most abundant and diverse eukaryotic viruses known to infect humans and can persist throughout our lifetimes. Despite their ubiquity, the host factors governing their physiologic distribution and abundance remain poorly understood. Here, we construct a viral pangenome of 2,023 strains to quantify anellovirus DNA in >1.1 million participants spanning three genetic biobanks. Genome-wide association studies identify 121 loci linked to viral persistence, predominantly via immune regulation by NF-kB signaling. Further, we associate variable anellovirus detection with conditions characterized by immune dysfunction, including lymphoid malignancies. By screening 3.2 petabases of human single-cell sequencing data, we identify myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow as a prominent site of anellovirus transcription in vivo. Finally, Perturb-seq of anellovirus proteins reveals that anellovirus ORF2, particularly from Alphatorquevirus, attenuates TNF-a-induced NF-kB signaling, connecting host genetic variation, cellular context, and viral immunomodulation to characterize the persistence of the eukaryotic human virome's most abundant component.

items.title: A genomic prediction framework for growth traits in black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) breeding programmes
items.abstract: Background Genomic prediction has been applied in livestock, plant and aquaculture species to accelerate genetic gain. However, its application and potential still remain unexplored in farmed black soldier fly (BSF), an emerging globally important insect production species. Due to the diversity of BSF feed sources, selection strategies need to be evaluated across various feedstocks and production environments to aid in building genomic selection into BSF breeding programmes. In this study, 2,083 BSF larvae from the base population were reared on three diets (SYK: Soy-okara, BSG: brewers' spent grain and FVW: fruit and vegetable waste), and 536 from the F7 population were reared on a chicken starter feed diet. Larvae were phenotyped for four growth traits (LBW, larval body weight; LL, larval length; LW, larval width; LSA, larval surface area) and genotyped across 4,680 SNPs. Genomic prediction was evaluated using seven methods under additive (A) and additive-dominance (AD) models, considering across- and within-diet effects, genotype by diet (G x D) interactions, differences amongst reference and test generations, and SNP densities. Results Performance varied across all scenarios, with LBW showing higher predictive ability (PA) among the growth traits. Accounting for dominance generally improved PA. Multivariate models accounting for G x D performed similarly to, or marginally better than, within-diet predictions. Cross-diet prediction was more variable and generally lower than within-diet prediction, showing reduced transferability across untested nutritional environments. Reducing the SNP density from 4,680 to 3,000 SNPs maintained comparable PA; however, PA decreased below 3,000 SNPs. Across multiple generations, predictive performance declined, resulting from reduced genetic connectivity and possible genotype-by-environment (G x E) interactions between the reference and testing populations. Conclusions Overall, these results provide an application-based framework for genomic prediction in BSF in semi- or commercial production settings. Results also highlight the importance of the genetic model, representative reference populations, and appropriate marker densities for genomic selection.

items.title: TideCluster: clustering and classification of tandem repeats for comparative and pangenomic analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Biology Centre, Czech Academy of Sciences, Ceske Budejovice, Czech Republic
items.abstract: Satellite DNA, composed of tandem arrays of relatively short repeated units, is a ubiquitous component of plant and animal genomes. Despite its biological importance, systematic investigation of satellite DNA remains challenging, in part because integrated bioinformatic tools for structured comparative analyses across individual arrays, chromosomes, and genomes are lacking. Here, we present TideCluster, a reference-independent pipeline that converts fragmented tandem repeat detections into genome-wide, interpretable repeat family catalogs. Starting from a genome assembly, TideCluster consolidates detected regions into arrays, clusters arrays by sequence similarity, reconstructs representative monomer consensus sequences, estimates locus-specific periodicity, identifies higher-order repeats, and generates GFF3 annotations. In addition to predefined visualizations, including the chromosomal distributions of satellite repeat families, TideCluster produces information-rich outputs that can be adapted for user-specific downstream analyses. We demonstrate its capabilities using the well-characterized genome of Arabidopsis thaliana and a set of Solanum species with highly diverse satellite repeat complements that vary markedly in abundance and have monomer lengths ranging from a few base pairs to more than 20 kb.

items.title: HERACLES for fast and accurate likelihood-based reconstruction of massive lineages
items.abstract: CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but rely on distances that may not faithfully represent the editing process, introducing biases whose magnitude and direction are unknown. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms: incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction.

items.title: GeneEmbedLLM: Harnessing Large Language Models for Gene Functional Embedding and Association Prediction
items.abstract: Effective and high-quality gene function representations are crucial for bioinformatics tasks. While biological knowledge about genes is inherently textual, encompassing functional descriptions and pathway annotations, current methods often rely on single-source, non-textual data, failing to capture the rich semantic information in multi-source gene annotations. In this paper, we propose GeneEmbedLLM, a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered framework for generating universal, semantically-aware gene embeddings. The proposed approach advances the gene representation learning through multi-source structured text integration from five authoritative databases and attribute-aware attention based on Longformer architecture and contrastive learning. Experimental results on diverse downstream tasks, ranging from molecular interactions and phenotypic dependencies to epigenetic regulation, confirm the validity and effectiveness of our proposed approach, where competitive performance is achieved across all evaluated benchmarks. We further validate the quality of the generated embeddings through comprehensive analyses, including embedding visualizations, intra-pathway similarity assessments, ablation study, and parameter analysis.

items.title: LinearKnot: linear-time ensemble analysis of RNA density-2 pseudoknots under hierarchical folding
items.abstract: Motivation: A pseudoknot is an arrangement of crossing base pairs. Pseudoknots complicate structure prediction and calculations over possible structures (an ensemble). CParty sums structure weights for hierarchical pseudoknots that keep a supplied pseudoknot-free structure (scaffold). Its time is cubic in sequence length. Results: LinearKnot approximates CParty with beam pruning. It combines at most two partial structures in each step and keeps the highest-ranked candidates. At fixed beam width, hairpin length limit, and scaffold search limit, partition functions, minimum-free-energy (MFE) predictions, and representative {gamma}-centroid structures from base-pairing probabilities take linear time in sequence length. Loop profiles give probabilities for pairing and six unpaired loop types, including gaps between crossing stems (PseudoLoop). Window accessibility is the probability that a window is unpaired. For each RNA, we compared each base's distributions over pairing partners (including the unpaired state) and structural contexts with exact probabilities and averaged their total variation (TV) distances over bases unpaired in the scaffold. At width 200, the 90th percentiles of these RNA averages among 300-399-base RNAs were 0.0015 for pairing and 0.0017 for contexts. At width 100, LinearKnot completed partition functions for all 107 real RNAs through 29 kilobases. Under our settings, CParty completed RNAs up to about 1 kilobase and was faster on them. For the RNAcentral long non-coding RNA URS00023A4DB9 (29,106 nt), partition-function, pairing-probability, and MFE calculations at width 100 took about 7 minutes and 3.22 GiB. We compared free energy and pairing probabilities before and after each increase in beam width and local limits. These changes generally became smaller at larger widths. At width 200, the calculations for URS00023A4DB9 took about 20 minutes and 5.68 GiB. In rat telomerase RNA, a four-base window next to a pseudoknot was mostly unpaired as part of a PseudoLoop. A pseudoknot-free calculation with the same scaffold gave lower accessibility and placed the window mainly in a hairpin when unpaired. Availability and implementation: LinearKnot provides the linearknot command at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnot. Experiment scripts and data are at https://github.com/TakumiOtagaki/LinearKnotExperiments.

items.title: RabbitCD-HIT: Distributed High-Sensitivity Greedy Incremental Clustering for Billion-Scale Protein Sequences in Hours
items.abstract: We present RabbitCD-HIT, a scalable distributed high-sensitivity greedy incremental clustering tool for ultra-large protein sequence datasets. It fully exploits cluster resources to enable efficient billion-scale clustering. RabbitCD-HIT clustered the March 10, 2026 NCBI nr snapshot (1.02 billion sequences; 487 GB FASTA) at 90\% identity within 5 hours on 64 nodes; the resulting representatives and cluster assignments are released as a public database resource. On a 256-core server, RabbitCD-HIT achieved a 2.1$\times$--6.6$\times$ speedup over CD-HIT with identical results under matched settings. Our approach addresses performance bottlenecks of traditional greedy incremental algorithms and provides an effective solution for large-scale protein sequence clustering.

items.title: Extracting and Updating Compact Colored k-mer Indexes
items.abstract: Colored k-mer indexes record, for every k-mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k-mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3,682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k-mers and 12,733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis, with 180,094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k-mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops.

items.title: π-SPECFormer: A Mass Spectrometry-based Foundation Model for Decoding the Dark Proteome
items.abstract: In mass-spectrometry-based proteomics, a substantial proportion of acquired spectra remain unidentified, concealing a vast reservoir of biological variations commonly termed the "dark proteome", potentially obscuring sequence mutations, non-canonical peptides and post-translational modifications. Existing deep-learning methods largely rely on supervised training with peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs), limiting their ability to learn from the much larger pool of unannotated spectra. Here we introduce {pi}-SPECFormer, a mass-spectrometry foundation model pre-trained on 291 million spectra through a two-stage framework that combines self-supervised and PSMs-guided representation learning. {pi}-SPECFormer transfers effectively to de novo peptide sequencing, spectrum clustering and modification detection, consistently outperforming task-specific baselines. When applied to proteomic profiles from 103 individuals with lung adenocarcinoma, the model identified nine high-confidence mutated peptides, including six that were absent from the reference databases. {pi}-SPECFormer thus enables unbiased decoding of molecular complexity beyond the boundaries of the canonical proteome.

items.title: BEHAV3D-Explorer enables natural language-assisted profiling of 3D cellular dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Biomedical Research Sols-Morreale (IIBM), Spanish National Research Council (CSIC)-Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
items.abstract: Obtaining quantitative measurements from live 3D microscopy remains difficult to implement across research settings, particularly without profound image-analysis expertise. We present BEHAV3D-Explorer, an interactive, user-friendly platform that uses natural-language guidance to help users select analysis strategies, tune parameters and configure workflows. BEHAV3D-Explorer enables time-resolved behavioral classification and integrates it with morphological, interaction and functional analyses, thereby connecting dynamic readouts to yield interpretable results across imaging applications.

items.title: Nutrient Availability as a Driver of Transcriptome Reprogramming in Osteosarcoma
items.abstract: Background: Gene expression in mammalian cells is intricately regulated by environmental and metabolic cues. Among these, nutrient availability represents a key feature of the tumor microenvironment and has recently emerged as a potent modulator of oncogenic signaling networks. In this study, we employed a cell-line model of osteosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive bone malignancy affecting both humans and dogs. We demonstrate that altering the concentration of a single nutrient can profoundly reprogram gene expression in osteosarcoma cells, revealing a previously underexplored phenomenon: nutrient-dependent gene regulation. This finding highlights potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention and underscores the broader implications of metabolic regulation for personalized medicine and nutrition. Methods/Results: We performed bulk RNA sequencing of an established osteosarcoma cell line cultured under varying concentrations of two key nutrients, glucose and glutamine. Differential gene expression analysis revealed a pronounced nutrient-dependent transcriptional response. The identified genes were functionally associated with pathways involved in cancer, development, nervous system regulation, metabolism, cellular signaling, and immune responses. We identified seven distinct expression patterns, one of which exhibited a striking correlation with cell growth rate and resembled a FOS-like transcriptional signature. Notably, the proto-oncogene FOS was among the identified genes and displayed a strong growth-rate-dependent expression pattern. Conclusion/Impact: Our findings demonstrate that modulation of nutrient availability profoundly reshapes the gene expression landscape of osteosarcoma cells, revealing nutrient-responsive targets with potential therapeutic relevance. This work expands our understanding of metabolic regulation in cancer and suggests that nutrient-based interventions may provide a controllable means of influencing tumor progression. Beyond oncology, such approaches may also have broader implications for developmental biology, autoimmune disorders, and nervous system function. More broadly, this study highlights the potential of metabolic interventions as a strategy for targeted modulation of gene expression programs.

items.title: Testing and training geometrical knowledge in baboons through a conceptual categorization task
items.abstract: Sensitivity to geometric regularity has been proposed as a signature of human cognitive singularity. Baboons can detect an intruder shape among quadrilaterals but, unlike humans, show no advantage for regular shapes such as squares and rectangles, suggesting they are not sensitive to geometric regularity. Here we asked whether, with symbolic training, baboons may show an enhanced attention to geometric features and their compositions. Using a symbolic match-to-sample task with frequent introduction of new generalization stimuli, we trained baboons and human controls to categorize stimuli as representing a given concept (A) or not (not-A) across two non-geometric domains (image category and line color) and three geometric domains (line perpendicularity, parallelism, and length equality). Baboons learned to perform above chance with all categories and generalize them to novel positive and negative exemplars (except for length equality). These findings provide evidence that baboons can extract geometric properties and associate them to arbitrary symbols. Crucially, this explicit geometry training did not result in the emergence of human-like performance in the quadrilateral intruder task: overall performance improved uniformly across shapes, but the geometric regularity effect failed to emerge. Thus, in baboons, recognizing individual geometric properties is insufficient to trigger the compositional perception of shapes that characterizes human cognition.

items.title: Projection-specific filtering of delta-theta input by layer 5 neurons in mouse secondary visual cortex
items.corresponding_institution: INSERM, INMED, Aix Marseille Univ, Marseille, France
items.abstract: Delta- and theta-band oscillations are thought to coordinate cortical activity and to convey top-down signals, but how the different output neurons of a cortical area transform such rhythmic input is less well understood. Layer 5 contains two projection classes, extratelencephalic (ET) and intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, which carry different information to different targets. Here we asked whether they also differ in how they process slow rhythmic input in the delta-theta range. We combined whole-cell recordings in three stimulus regimes in mouse medial secondary visual cortex (V2M) with local field potential (LFP) recordings in awake mice. With small inputs, IT cells summated strongly and acted as low-pass filters, whereas ET cells resonated at low frequencies, forming moderate-resonance (ET1, about 3 Hz) and high-resonance (ET2, about 5 Hz) subgroups. With large inputs, ET cells amplified depolarisation more than hyperpolarisation, at similar resonance frequencies. When driven to fire by a 4 Hz sinusoid at threshold, cells of all classes fired at a similar phase and kept it nearly constant across cycles. In awake mice, visual stimulation increased deep-layer LFP power across about 1-6 Hz, a band that spans the mean ET1 and ET2 resonance frequencies. Thus, the two output classes of layer 5 in V2M filter slow rhythmic input differently, but once firing, they show no detectable difference in spike timing.

items.title: SAMP1/TMEM201 protects alveolar type 2 cells from DNA damage-associated senescence and restrains pulmonary fibrosis
items.corresponding_institution: National Center for Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Italian National Institute of Health
items.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive interstitial lung disease in which repetitive injury to the alveolar epithelium and senescence of alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells drive persistent myofibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition. Inner nuclear membrane (INM) proteins organise nuclear architecture and participate in the DNA damage response, but whether they influence epithelial senescence and fibrogenesis is unknown. Here we identify SAMP1/TMEM201, an INM protein that binds lamin A/C, emerin and LINC-complex components, as a compartment-selective protector of AT2 cells. In the bleomycin model of pulmonary fibrosis, SAMP1 was reduced in AT2 cells but unchanged in lung fibroblasts. AT2 cell-specific deletion of Samp1 (Sftpc-Cre^ERT2^; Samp1^flox/flox^) aggravated fibrosis at day 21, with higher Ashcroft scores and increased pulmonary Tnfa and Acta2 expression, whereas intratracheal delivery of AAV6-CAG-Samp1 before bleomycin attenuated both histological fibrosis and these transcriptional responses. In primary AT2 cells analysed immediately after isolation without in vitro stimulation, SAMP1 loss was accompanied by reduced 53BP1 protein, comparable gammaH2AX levels, and upregulation of the senescence-associated and profibrotic markers p16^INK4a^ and PAI-1. These findings define a SAMP1-AT2 senescence axis that constrains pulmonary fibrogenesis and suggest that preserving INM-dependent genome surveillance in the alveolar epithelium may offer an epithelium-directed therapeutic strategy for IPF. Because DNA damage signalling was assessed only under baseline conditions, the data establish an association with altered DNA damage signalling rather than a definitive defect in lesion repair.

items.title: Genome-scale modelling and stable isotope tracing reveal dynamic metabolic reprogramming in a human cardiac hypertrophy model
items.abstract: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is associated with metabolic remodelling; however the temporal dynamics of this remodelling remain poorly defined in human cardiomyocyte systems. Here, we combined transcriptomic profiling, genome-scale metabolic modelling and stable isotope-resolved metabolomics (SIRM) to map the metabolic consequences of endothelin-1 (ET-1) stimulation in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). Integration of RNA sequencing data obtained after 8 and 48 hours of ET-1 treatment with the Human2.0 genome-scale metabolic model predicted time-dependent remodelling, characterised by progressive increases in glycolytic flux, enhanced glucose carbon entry into the TCA cycle, and a decrease in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Computational flux predictions were independently confirmed by extracellular flux analysis and 13C-substrate tracing, with concordance between modelled and measured fluxes. Extracellular flux analysis showed increased glycolytic capacity and mitochondrial respiration after 48 hours, with greater sensitivity to inhibition of mitochondrial pyruvate transport. Glucose tracing revealed increased 13C enrichment of glycolytic, pentose phosphate pathway, serine-glycine and TCA cycle metabolites, consistent with altered glucose-derived carbon allocation. Increased m+3 labelling of selected TCA-related metabolites was compatible with pyruvate anaplerosis, although pathway-specific fluxes were not resolved. In three-dimensional engineered heart tissue (EHTs) treated with ET-1 for 7 days, increased hypertrophic marker expression was accompanied by a blunted inotropic response, and metabolomics showed similar changes in metabolite abundance and glucose-derived labelling to 2D cultures. These findings support hiPSC-CMs and EHTs as complementary platforms for studying early metabolic remodelling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy and provide an integrated framework linking model predictions to functional and isotope-tracing measurements.

items.title: A largely shared genetic architecture underlies Saccharomyces cerevisiae persistence across different mouse host genotypes
items.abstract: The extent to which interactions between microbial and host genotypes shape opportunistic pathogen persistence within hosts is an important open question. To assess the contribution of these interactions to persistence, we used Saccharomyces cerevisiae , a genetically tractable model for studying opportunistic fungal persistence in mammalian hosts. A pooled panel of barcoded haploid segregants from a cross between a laboratory strain and a clinical isolate, together with both parents, was introduced intravenously into seven genetically diverse mouse strains. We measured the relative persistence of segregants in mouse brains and livers using barcode sequencing. Persistence showed transgressive segregation in both organs. On average across the two organs, yeast genotype explained 45.2% of the variance in segregant persistence, whereas yeast genotype-by-host genotype interactions explained only 2.9%. Linkage mapping showed that loci detected in more host genotypes generally explained more phenotypic variance than those detected in fewer host genotypes. At some loci, genetic variation correlated with increased yeast persistence across multiple organs (general loci) while at others increased persistence in one organ came at the cost of decreased persistence in another (antagonistic loci). General loci contributed disproportionately to brain persistence, whereas liver persistence reflected contributions from both classes. The clinical parent showed greater persistence than the laboratory parent in every host-organ combination, and the additive effects of detected loci predicted the direction of this advantage. Overall, this work shows that in this system, relative microbial persistence is polygenic, with a strong additive component and only a very small contribution from microbial genotype-by-host genotype interactions.

items.title: Genomic signatures of long-term selection in the Langhill dairy herd: the power of a five-decade experiment for sustainable dairy cattle breeding
items.abstract: Background Selective breeding has transformed dairy cattle productivity, but the genomic consequences of long-term directional selection - what it costs in diversity and where in the genome it acts - are hard to quantify because contemporaneous control populations are rare. The Langhill experiment, established in 1973, is one of the world's longest-running dairy cattle selection trials with a designed control line kept under common management. We used this resource population to ask what five decades of bull selection have cost in genetic diversity, where in the genome selection has acted, and whether complementary scans converge on the loci under selection. Results We genotyped archived blood samples from 1,126 cows of two genetic lines: a Select line sired by bulls in the top decile of UK genetic merit for milk fat-plus-protein yield, and a Control line sired by bulls of average merit. The Select line showed the expected gains in every yield trait. Inbreeding accumulated at the same annual rate in both lines, and effective population size, estimated from that rate, was approximately 33. Linkage disequilibrium was higher in the Select line at every marker distance from 2 to 300 kb. Autozygosity was 24.7% higher in the Select line than in the Control line (0.078 versus 0.063), a difference robust across four calling parameter sets and two independent callers. The excess was confined to runs of homozygosity longer than 2 Mb; shorter runs did not differ between lines, confirming a shared founder base and placing all divergence after the lines were split. It did not arise from a numerically narrower sire pool: the Select line used more sires (79 versus 72), each with fewer daughters, yet its cows were three times more related to one another. Twenty-eight regions across thirteen chromosomes showed strong differentiation; intersecting five scans identified a four-method signal on chromosome 21 spanning the SERPINA gene cluster and sixteen three-method regions, including chromosome 3, with haplotype and diversity statistics agreeing on the line carrying the signal in fourteen of seventeen. Autozygosity itself did not localise to any region. Conclusions Selection left two genomic footprints: diffuse, recent inbreeding accumulated through the narrow ancestry of the elite sire pool, and localised differentiation at specific loci. Runs of homozygosity index only the first process; the second is captured by frequency- and haplotype-based differentiation scans. Because the cost of inbreeding is incurred through ancestry rather than the number of bulls used, mating schemes that constrain the rate of co-ancestry would be preferable to simply managing the number of sires selected and used.

items.title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Genetics, Luiz de Queiroz College of Agriculture, University of Sao Paulo, Piracicaba, SP, Brazil
items.abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.

items.title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
items.corresponding_institution: Argaly, Montmelian, France and Centre de Recherche sur la Biodiversite et l'Environnement (CRBE), UMR 5300 CNRS, IRD, INP, UT, Toulouse, France
items.abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.

items.title: Bioinformatic pipeline for functional inference of Rickettsia akari hypothetical proteins reveals virulence-associated and effector candidates
items.corresponding_institution: Biomedical Research Center Slovak Academy of Sciences
items.abstract: Background Rickettsia akari, the causative agent of rickettsialpox, is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a highly reduced genome encoding numerous hypothetical proteins (HPs) of unknown function. Many of these HPs are expressed during host-cell infection, yet their roles in bacterial physiology and potential contribution to virulence remain unclear. Methodology/Principal Findings We performed an integrative in silico characterization of 54 R. akari HPs previously identified by mass spectrometry in purified bacterial cells. Using a benchmarked computational workflow, we predicted their physicochemical properties, subcellular localization, putative secretion signals, protein folds, potential interaction partners, and evolutionary conservation. Most HPs were predicted to be thermostable. The majority of HPs were predicted to be cytoplasmic (37.00%) or membrane-associated (29.63%). Predicted features associated with the type IV secretion system were more frequent than those associated with type I secretion. Network and structural analyses identified candidate HPs with features consistent with potential roles in outer membrane assembly, host-cell interaction, and immune modulation, including predicted peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerases, oxidoreductases, methyltransferases, and putative E3 ubiquitin ligases. Several HPs were predicted to be antigenic and showed conservation across multiple rickettsial genomes. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis supported the plausibility of selected predicted protein-protein and protein-ligand interactions. Evolutionary analyses indicated predominant purifying selection among the analyzed HPs. A8GP20 showed elevated sequence divergence and warrants further investigation as a potential effector candidate. Conclusions/Significance Our findings prioritize A8GPG8, A8GP63, A8GNV4, A8GMM8, A8GM41, A8GMJ7, A8GMI5, A8GP20, A8GN23, A8GMB4, A8GM08, and A8GM39 as promising candidates for experimental validation of their predicted functions and potential roles in R. akari biology and pathogenicity. This work provides an integrative and reproducible bioinformatic framework to guide functional discovery in R. akari and related neglected intracellular pathogens, and identifies candidate proteins for future studies of rickettsial pathogenesis, antigen discovery, and therapeutic target development.

items.title: Serotonin Reuptake Inhibition Reduces NMDAR-Associated Reward Liability Without Compromising Rapid Antidepressant Efficacy
items.corresponding_institution: State Key Laboratory of Drug Research, Shanghai Institute of Materia Medica, Chinese Academy of Sciences
items.abstract: Ketamine has changed the treatment landscape for depression by providing rapid antidepressant effects, yet its clinical utility remains limited by psychotomimetic effects and abuse potential. It remains unclear whether rapid antidepressant efficacy can be dissociated from mesolimbic dopamine activation and its associated reward-related effects. Here, we show that the serotonin reuptake inhibitor escitalopram, by enhancing serotonergic signaling, attenuates S-ketamine-induced dopamine (DA) release in the nucleus accumbens (NAc). Inspired by this finding, we designed and evaluated VV147 by incorporating SERT inhibition into NMDAR antagonism to reduce the reward-related liability of NMDAR blockade. Unlike S-ketamine, VV147 did not increase NAc dopamine signaling but retained rapid antidepressant effects in chronic stress models of depression. Together, these findings suggest a potential dissociation between rapid antidepressant efficacy and acute dopamine activation, providing a possible strategy for developing rapid-acting antidepressants with reduced dopamine-related reward effects.

items.title: The mouse midbrain periaqueductal gray is organized into target-specific output populations
items.corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute for Brain Research
items.abstract: How brains select between behaviours and coordinate their execution is a central question in neuroscience. The vertebrate periaqueductal gray (PAG) controls a remarkable range of instinctive behaviours, from escape and freezing to hunting, vocalization, and micturition. Its columnar organization, the classical framework for mapping these functions, cannot explain how one region controls so many, often mutually exclusive, behaviours. To determine how PAG output is organized, we generated a whole-brain, column- and cell-type-specific synaptic projection atlas of the mouse PAG, showing distinct dorsal and ventral outputs and dense within-PAG connectivity. Retrograde tracing from four motor-related target regions identified segregated PAG populations, biased towards, but not confined to, individual columns. Channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping showed that one such population, projecting to the cuneiform nucleus, provides substantial local collaterals, positioned to shape ongoing PAG activity. These findings uncover a modular output architecture that extends the columnar framework, offering a circuit logic for how one brain region produces diverse behaviours.

items.title: Transcriptomic and Metabolomic Analysis of the Caudate and Putamen in ADHD
items.corresponding_institution: State University of New York at Buffalo
items.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly heritable, heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that typically manifests in childhood; however, transcriptomic studies have inadequately accounted for age of onset and subtype, with cohorts largely comprising of adults. To address this gap, we established a stringently phenotyped ADHD cohort (up to 19 years; clinically diagnosed combined and inattentive-type ADHD) and integrated postmortem caudate and putamen bulk RNA-seq, LC-MS metabolomics, MEGENA gene co-expression analysis, and cross-study comparison. We identified 279 up- and 35 downregulated DEGs in the caudate and 110 up- and 89 downregulated DEGs in the putamen. The combined caudate-putamen metabolomic analysis revealed dopamine dysregulation (1.68-fold reduction) and dysregulation of four additional metabolites. Enrichment analysis revealed shared molecular signatures involving immune responses, ATP metabolism and calcium ion-dependent signaling, with region-specific differences in the direction of alteration. Neuronal homeostasis, and protein stress showed suppression in the putamen, along with activation of neurotransmitter reuptake, whereas CSF circulation and ECM organization were activated in the caudate, with suppression in CNS myelination, and signs of ventricular perturbations. MEGENA identified 26 ADHD-associated caudate modules and 33 putamen modules. These modules captured canonical synaptic and neuronal-circuitry pathways alongside cellular differentiation, metabolism, and cell-survival processes. FGD1 emerged as a candidate caudate hub gene among the neuronal modules. Cross-study comparison analysis suggested that molecular alterations in ADHD may be age-dependent. Additionally, assessing levels of 76 potential risk genes identified by a large ADHD GWAS study one ARTN exhibited dysregulated levels in putamen and none in caudate. Together, these findings reveal brain-region-specific molecular dysregulation in ADHD across pathways extending beyond canonical neurotransmission to immune, differentiation, and energy-metabolic processes, along with novel evidence of perturbations in the understudied lateral ventricles.

items.title: Ogg1 regulates context-dependent glial states in Alzheimer's disease
items.corresponding_institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Oxidative DNA damage is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), but whether Ogg1, a key enzyme in oxidative DNA repair, contributes to disease pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we show that Ogg1 exerts opposing effects under physiological and disease conditions. Ogg1 deficiency impaired memory and induced glial transcriptional alterations under physiological conditions, whereas in APP/PS1 mice it improved memory, reduced amyloid burden and attenuated AD-associated glial remodeling. These effects occurred without changes in global 8-oxo-dG levels and were accompanied by changes in chromatin accessibility and gene expression, supporting a non-canonical role for Ogg1 in transcriptional regulation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics revealed strong transcriptional responses to Ogg1 deficiency across all major glial cell types and showed that Ogg1-dependent glial transcriptional programs are strongly conserved in human AD. These findings identify Ogg1 as a context-dependent regulator of glial cell states and reveal an unexpected role in AD-associated glial remodeling.

items.title: Automatic orofacial behaviors remap within cortical substrates for voluntary motor control in freely moving primates
items.abstract: Orofacial behaviors, like yawning and emotional facial expressions, involve phylogenetically conserved subcortical circuits. Yet, their context-dependent modulation in primates suggests overlooked cortical contributions. Here, we wirelessly recorded from 640 ventral motor and premotor sites in two freely moving macaques during spontaneous orofacial actions combining automatic and voluntary components to varying degrees (yawning, threat, bite, drink). We identified coupling between synaptic input (local field potential) and spiking output in 169 spatially distributed sites during yawning, while threat display was sparsely represented. Yawn-related sites exhibited an early beta-band suppression followed by high-gamma power enhancement. Of 401 isolated single neurons, 95 (predominantly putative medium-sized pyramidal cells) encoded yawning, mostly together with voluntary biting and drinking actions. No modulation was found during the observation of yawning by conspecifics. Yawn-related units either switched or maintained their mouth opening/closing tuning across yawning and more voluntary actions, suggesting counteracting and synergistic downstream influences on yawning motor control. In contrast, threat-related units predominantly preserved their opening/closing tuning during biting and drinking. Head-free intracortical microstimulation of sites hosting yawn-related units preferentially evoked localized mouth and face movements, supporting their causal role in orofacial motor control. Finally, projecting neural activity into a low-dimensional manifold showed that voluntarily controlled and largely automatic behaviors engaged distinct population dynamics while preserving the discriminability of individual orofacial displays. These findings reveal that cortical substrates of voluntary motor control can be recruited to shape otherwise automatic orofacial displays.

items.title: Visual capture of the head-direction signal in a rat model of Fragile X Syndrome
items.abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a common inherited monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability (ASD/ID), conditions frequently associated with altered sensory processing and multisensory integration. However, the circuit mechanisms underlying these alterations remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the integration of visual and self-motion information in the head-direction (HD) system in a rat model of FXS (Fmr1-/y rats). Using high-density silicon probes, we recorded neuronal activity in the postsubiculum (PoSub), a cortical hub of the HD system, while adult Fmr1-/y and wild-type (WT) rats experienced repeated rotations of a visual landmark. In WT rats, the HD signal only partially followed landmark rotations, consistent with weighted integration of visual and self-motion information, and visual landmark control progressively weakened across repeated cue conflicts. In contrast, the HD signal in Fmr1-/y rats closely followed landmark rotations and failed to show experience-dependent recalibration. This enhanced visual capture was accompanied by reduced angular head velocity tuning in PoSub neurons, indicating weakened representation of self-motion information. Together, these findings reveal an altered balance between visual and self-motion inputs to the HD system in a rat model of FXS and identify a possible circuit-level mechanism through which sensory integration of vision and self-motion may be disrupted in ASD/ID.

items.title: A Common Recognition Architecture Across Memory Scales
items.abstract: Recognition decisions occur across memory episodes that vary vastly in scale, from compact single-item episodes to extended experiences involving hundreds of items. To test how memory scale shapes the neural mechanisms underlying old/new judgments, we recorded EEG while participants performed a recognition memory task across set sizes ranging from 1 to 128 items (spanning 2 to 256 recognition judgments). Classic electrophysiological signatures of recognition, including frontal and parietal old/new effects, persisted continuously across set sizes. Furthermore, multivariate neural classifiers trained on small memory scales generalized robustly across set sizes. Rather than revealing distinct neural formats, increasing memory scale produced systematic, continuous shifts in the timing and strength of a shared recognition response: signals emerged progressively later and weaker at larger memory scales. Temporal-alignment and cross-correlation analyses demonstrated that responses across scales followed a common waveform trajectory, with timing shifts propagating into motor response preparation. Finally, individual difference analyses revealed that this common recognition format exhibits scale-dependent behavioral relevance, tracking working-memory capacity at smaller scales and long-term memory performance at larger scales. Together, these findings demonstrate that recognition signals share a common neural format across scale while changing dynamically in timing, strength, and behavioral relevance, providing evidence for convergence onto a shared recognition architecture.

items.title: Bayesian Modeling of Context-Specific Goal-Directed and Habitual Control in Sequential Decision Making
items.abstract: It is an open question how context-specific habits develop alongside goal-directed planning. We examined action sequence repetition, contingency change, and context switching using a three-step optimization task with interleaved planning and habit contexts. During an initial acquisition phase, optimal sequences varied in the planning context but remained constant in the habit context. When contingencies changed, the original habit sequence became suboptimal and another became optimal. Action sequence repetition improved response speed and optimal-choice performance in the habit context relative to the planning context. Following the contingency change, both advantages initially reversed. Optimal-choice performance in the habit context subsequently recovered but did not significantly exceed that in the planning context, while responses remained slower in the habit context. Context switches reduced optimal-choice performance in both directions, with additional slowing when switching from habit to planning. The Bayesian contextual control model captured choice patterns through learned action sequence priors, goal-directed evaluation, and context inference. Allowing a context-stability bias to vary across participants did not improve model performance. These findings suggest that sequence repetition facilitates performance under stable contingencies while impairing adaptation to change.

items.title: Photomechanical engineering of immunogenic whole-cell vaccines by laser-induced vapor nanobubbles for bladder cancer prophylaxis
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Advanced Chemistry of Catalonia (IQAC-CSIC)
items.abstract: Whole-cell cancer vaccines can provide broad tumor-antigen repertoires, but their efficacy depends on manufacturing methods that inactivate tumor cells while preserving immunogenic danger signals. Here we show that laser-induced vapor nanobubbles (VNB) generated from dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles provide a drug-free photomechanical route to engineer immunogenic whole-cell vaccines against bladder cancer. Using MB49 murine urothelial carcinoma cells, we established VNB conditions that induced rapid tumor-cell killing together with calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release. Rapid cell killing and calreticulin exposure were also reproduced in the molecularly distinct UPPL1541 bladder cancer model, supporting the generalizability of the early photomechanical response across bladder cancer cell lines. Vaccination with VNB-killed MB49 cells reduced tumor incidence and growth after subcutaneous challenge and enhanced splenocyte-mediated antitumor activity against MB49 cells. In an orthotopic bladder cancer model, vaccination prevented MRI-detectable tumor formation and was associated with marked early bladder enrichment of CD8 T cells and inflammatory monocytes. A single administration of the VNB-generated vaccine preparation showed no evident local or systemic toxicity during seven days of follow-up. These findings provide proof of concept for an externally triggered, drug-free manufacturing approach in which short laser irradiation induces rapid photomechanical killing of tumor cells on demand, generating immunogenic whole-tumor-cell vaccine preparations for further evaluation in therapeutic, post-resection and tumor-derived settings.

items.title: Circulating CD4 regulatory T cells are broadly preserved in Parkinson's disease despite altered HELIOS expression
items.abstract: Background Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are an important component of adaptive immune regulation and have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), with previous studies suggesting altered Treg proportions, phenotype and, in some cases, function. However, existing studies have been limited by variable phenotyping approaches and a lack of detailed functional assessment. Given the growing interest in Tregs as potential therapies in PD, better understanding of their phenotype and function in the disease is important. Methods Circulating FOXP3+ Tregs were characterised in individuals with PD and age-matched healthy controls (HC) using a 24-colour spectral flow cytometry panel. Treg suppressive function was assessed by their ability to inhibit proliferation and cytokine production by polyclonally stimulated autologous T effector cells in vitro. Treg lineage stability was assessed by analysis of FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. Results The proportions and phenotypic characteristics of circulating CD4 Tregs were broadly similar between individuals with PD and HCs, as were Treg suppressive function and FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. However, naive CD4 Tregs from individuals with PD showed reduced HELIOS expression, with a similar but non-significant trend in FOXP3 expression. Reduced HELIOS expression was also observed in the CD8 naive Treg compartment. Conclusions Major quantitative or functional abnormalities in circulating Tregs do not appear to be a dominant feature PD. However, reduced HELIOS expression in naive Tregs suggests more subtle phenotypic alterations that warrant further investigation. The broadly preserved suppressive function is reassuring for therapeutic approaches aimed at increasing Treg numbers, although it will be important to establish that expanded Tregs retain a stable phenotype and suppressive function in inflammatory and tissue environments.

items.title: Tfcp2l1 recruits Thrap3 to sustain ESC self-renewal via Jmjd1c exon-5 splicing and DNA repair choice
items.abstract: How embryonic stem cells (ESCs) maintain genomic integrity while sustaining self-renewal remains poorly understood. We find that transcription factor CP2-like 1 (Tfcp2l1) recruits Thrap3 in mouse ESCs, where this complex maintains RNA polymerase II activity and promotes transcription of Tfcp2l1 target genes. In addition, Thrap3 supports mESC self-renewal. Interestingly, knockdown of either Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 induces highly overlapping alternative-splicing changes, including reduced inclusion of exon-5 in Jmjd1c. Further studies reveal that skipping of Jmjd1c exon-5 weakens the association between Jmjd1c and Mdc1, accompanied by elevated Mdc1-associated dimethylation, leading to reduced Mdc1 and Rnf8 interaction and diminished K63-linked ubiquitin signalling. These alterations impair chromatin recruitment of the Rap80 and Brca1 repair complex and increase Rad51 foci formation, indicative of a shift in DNA repair pathway preference. Accordingly, loss of Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 results in accumulated DNA damage, hypersensitivity to genotoxic stress, compromised ESC self-renewal and enhanced apoptosis. Similar phenotypes can be recapitulated in human ESCs. Together, our findings provide new insights into how ESCs coordinate genome maintenance with self-renewal.

items.title: Quantitative trait loci mapping identifies genetic loci modifying MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
items.abstract: Increasing evidence has shown the role of genetic background on the penetrance of monogenic diabetes. A missense mutation of the pancreatic {beta}-cell-enriched transcription factor MafA co-segregates with diabetes (MafA-MODY) and non-syndromic insulinomatosis. We recently investigated the effects of genetic background on MafAS64F-driven dysglycemia in genetically diverse mice harboring this mutation. Here we leveraged the effects of genetic background on phenotypic penetrance to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) potentially modifying glycemia in response to this variant. We investigated MafaS64F/+ mice from an F2 intercross of the C57BL/6J and SJL/J genetic backgrounds through oral glucose tolerance testing at 4, 5, 6, and 8 weeks of age to evaluate glucose tolerance and glycemic trajectory. All F2 mice were genetically monitored for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between the C57BL/6J and SJL/J backgrounds, allowing us to identify modifying loci on 6 chromosomes (2, 126 Mbp; 3, 59 Mbp and 103 Mbp; 7, 47 Mbp; 11 45 Mbp; 13, 4 Mbp; and 16, 85-97 Mbp), containing 172 candidate genes. For example, known MODY genes Abcc8 (Sur1) and Kcnj11 (Kir6.2) are within the QTL region on chromosome 7 and contain polymorphisms between backgrounds that may impart combinatorial effects on the phenotypic penetrance of MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia

items.title: Overlapping enhancer activity robustly regulates rax expression during ocular development in zebrafish
items.abstract: Vertebrate eye development relies on the tightly regulated yet highly dynamic spatiotemporal expression of eye field transcription factors that coordinate developmental programs required for the formation of a functional eye. The gene rax is among the earliest expressed eye field transcription factors and is specifically associated with ocular-fated tissue. It encodes a transcription factor that is essential for optic vesicle evagination, the precursor to the optic cup and retina. Although the developmental functions of rax are well characterized, the cis-regulatory elements that control its expression remain poorly understood. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio), I identified five novel ocular enhancers and demonstrate that they drive similar spatiotemporal expression patterns as rax at three key stages of eye development. Furthermore, I performed an in-depth characterization of two enhancers and demonstrate that they exhibit substantial transcript-level overlap with endogenous rax expression during development. Additionally, through the generation of enhancer deletion lines, I further demonstrate that the gene regulatory network (GRN) controlling rax expression is largely robust to individual and combinatorial enhancer perturbations. However, perturbation of this regulatory network can result in rax-associated ocular abnormalities, including microphthalmia and anophthalmia. Together, these findings highlight the importance of studying developmental ocular enhancers to better understand the functions of noncoding genomic regions and provide insight into potential causes of unexplained congenital eye disease.

items.title: Pseudo-observations of longevity improve detection of resilience-associated genes in the Radiation Late Effects Cohort of rhesus macaques.
items.corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in IBSP, PDGFD, and LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals' intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.

items.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biosciences, University of Oslo
items.abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

items.title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
items.abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

items.title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
items.abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

items.title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
items.abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
items.abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.

items.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
