items.corresponding_institution: Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit, Faculty of Tropical Medicine, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand
items.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

items.title: Population Genomics of the Bovine Sialic Acid Network Reveals Functional and Evolutionary Diversity Across European and South African Cattle Breeds
items.abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

items.title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
items.abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions. Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

items.title: PEEK: integrated primer design for silent-mutation and restriction-site engineering, validated in silico and by whole-plasmid sequencing
items.abstract: Motivation: Silent introduction of restriction sites, direct site insertion, and verification of the result are routine operations in molecular cloning, yet they are typically distributed across separate tools built on inconsistent thermodynamics. Primer design is itself mature and heavily validated; the gap is not accuracy in principle but integration, together with the absence of any explicit account of why one synonymous edit should be preferred over another. Because melting temperature (Tm) gates which primers a tool will accept, any unified tool must first be shown to compute Tm correctly against an external standard, and then shown to produce the edits it proposes. Results: PEEK, a web-based toolkit, unifies silent-mutation discovery, restriction-site insertion, and amplification and screening primer design built on a single thermodynamic model of primer melting temperature (Tm). PEEK's silent-mutation engine identifies the smallest set of synonymous changes required to form a restriction site at a specific position, and ranks the options by codon usage, local mRNA folding, and edit size. Predicted melting temperatures closely matched those of the NEB Q5 Tm Calculator across 17 primers of varying length and GC content (Pearson R^2 = 0.9995, mean absolute error 1.32 C) without any fitted correction, and annealing-temperature (Ta) recommendations exactly matched NEB's rules. In independent trials, a total of 15 silent-mutation designs were translationally silent and contained the intended restriction site. Experimental validation was performed by installing a KpnI site into a 9.9 kb lentiviral CAR plasmid using both a silent-mutation primer and an insertion primer. Whole-plasmid sequencing confirmed that each primer introduced exactly the designed changes, with no off-target differences across the construct and no change to the encoded protein. Availability and implementation: PEEK runs at https://peekbiology.com and requires no registration. Source code, documentation, and test data are available at https://github.com/nkura-arch/PEEK-Protein-Engineering Efficiency-Kit. Implemented in Python 3.11 with Flask, Biopython, and ViennaRNA. Contact: nathan.singh@wustl.edu

items.title: Contrasting within-donor gene covariation identifies disease-associated cells and genes in case-control single-cell studies
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics, Department of Medical and Molecular Genetics, Indiana University School of Medicine
items.abstract: In case-control single-cell studies, disease often affects only a subset of cells of a given type within each patient. Comparing all cells from patients with all cells from control donors therefore dilutes disease signals, while donor variation and recorded or unrecorded batch effects can be confounded with disease status. We present IDC (Identification of Disease-associated Cells), which uses this cellular heterogeneity as signal. A mixture of affected and unaffected cells creates coordinated variation among disease-associated genes within each patient, whereas shifts shared by all cells of a donor leave this within-donor covariance unchanged. IDC therefore contrasts within-donor gene-gene covariance between patients and controls to learn disease-associated expression programs without batch labels, then applies positive-unlabeled learning to score each cell's disease-like state and estimate each donor's disease burden. IDC also computes, in closed form, gene contribution scores and leave-gene-out cell scores that exclude each tested gene, enabling within-donor differential expression testing and cross-donor meta-analysis without retraining. In simulations, IDC identified affected cells and estimated donor burden more accurately than deep generative and label-refinement methods, remained robust to strong unrecorded batch effects, and detected differentially expressed genes more sensitively than case-control pseudobulk methods while controlling false discoveries. In human pancreatic islets and prefrontal cortex, disease burden in held-out donors separated type 2 diabetes (T2D) from non-diabetic donors in beta cells, and late-stage Alzheimer's disease (AD) from non-AD donors in astrocytes and inhibitory neurons, while placing prediabetic and early-AD donors at intermediate levels. Genes with the highest IDC contribution scores were more strongly enriched for the KEGG T2D and AD pathways than case-control pseudobulk rankings, and within-donor testing revealed coordinated metabolic, cell-adhesion and synaptic changes along the inferred disease axis.

items.title: Unveiling immune targets via TriStageHLA: high-throughput screening of peptide presentation, peptide-HLA binding, and immunogenicity
items.abstract: High-throughput screening of HLA class I epitopes underpins neoantigen vaccine design, T cell therapies, and pathogen immune monitoring, yet proteome-scale prioritization remains challenging under severe class imbalance. We present TriStageHLA, a compact three-stage framework that decomposes epitope discovery into peptide-only screening (PRE), allele-specific binding/presentation prediction (BIND), and immunogenicity prediction (IM). PRE performs early pruning via a LoRA-adapted ESM-2 classifier; BIND integrates quantitative binding affinity and eluted ligand data with a dual-branch architecture combining global cross-attention and local motif extraction; IM is fine-tuned on curated human T-cell assay data with a decoupled LoRA head. Trained on IEDB-derived datasets with per-allele balancing and allele-discordant supervision, TriStageHLA-BIND achieves AUROC of 96.2% and AUPRC of 95.2% on combined BA/EL evaluation, while TriStageHLA-IM reaches AUROC of 81.4\% and AUPRC of 73.8\% on held-out immunogenicity data, improving over the strongest immunogenicity baselines ImmuneApp (70.7% / 63.6%) and BigMHC-IM (60.1% / 51.5%). With substantially fewer trainable parameters than prior models, TriStageHLA enables efficient, calibrated epitope prioritization across binding, presentation, and immunogenicity. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/SkywalkerLuke/TriStageHLA.

items.title: AOPTK: Open-Source Software for AI-Assisted Toxicological Literature Analysis
items.corresponding_institution: RECETOX, Faculty of Science, Masaryk University, Kotlarska 2, 611 37 Brno, Czech Republic
items.abstract: Motivation: Toxicologists today face a challenge: although vast amounts of data describing how chemicals affect human health are available across scientific publications and regulatory reports, much of this information remains underutilized because extracting and interpreting evidence across thousands of studies is impractical to perform manually. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), provide new opportunities to automate toxicological literature analysis. Results: Herein, we present the Adverse Outcome Pathway Toolkit (AOPTK), an open-source Python package for AI-enhanced analysis of toxicological and biomedical literature. AOPTK supports (i) automated literature retrieval from databases such as PubMed Central and Europe PMC, (ii) direct processing of full-text articles in PDF format, and (iii) LLM-assisted analysis tools to identify chemicals and extract their relationships to biological effects under user-defined conditions. We demonstrate its utilities through a case-study identifying potential non-genotoxic carcinogens based on their ability to inhibit gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC). The LLM-enhanced analysis achieves 81% agreement with an expert-curated inhibitor list and 95% accuracy in predicting inhibition versus no inhibition when analysing the same subset of 86 publications. Automated retrieval and analysis of 1 124 publications from PubMed Central further demonstrated the feasibility of applying AOPTK to large-scale literature analyses. Availability: The package is developed open source on GitHub, disseminated through PyPI and Bioconda and releases are archived on Zenodo. Individual tools are available in the Galaxy platform for accessible data analysis with user-friendly, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) and end-to-end workflows provided via WorkflowHub. The tools are available on usegalaxy.eu and usegalaxy.cz and are developed open source on GitHub.

items.title: scHiR learns joint cellular representations from paired single-cell transcriptome and 3D genome data
items.abstract: Simultaneously sequenced scRNA-seq and scHi-C technologies provide matched measurements of gene expression and three-dimensional (3D) genome organization within individual cells, offering complementary insights into cellular state. However, integrative analysis remains challenging due to the heterogeneous structures and characteristics of these modalities. To realize the full potential of such data, we need effective computational methods to learn joint cellular representations. Here, we present scHiR, a framework based on a hyperspherical variational autoencoder (S-VAE) for learning co-embeddings from paired gene-expression profiles and chromatin contact maps. The framework facilitate downstream analyses such as cell clustering, fine-grained cell-state characterization, and developmental trajectory inference, while modality-specific decoders enable the signal recovery of input profiles. We evaluated scHiR across six paired datasets generated by HiRES, GAGE-seq, and LiMCA. scHiR captured cell-type-specific information and achieved improved clustering performance compared with representative single-omics methods. It was also capable of resolving fine-grained subclusters and revealed discordant and distinct cellular profiles. In developmental biological datasets, scHiR preserved trajectory-related structure and improved pseudotime in agreement with known developmental progression. Finally, scHiR generated reconstructed transcriptomic and chromatin contact profiles with reduced noise, enhanced cell-type-related signals, and improved recovery of held-out chromatin contacts. These results demonstrate that scHiR provides an effective method for learning joint cellular representations from paired scRNA-seq and scHi-C data.

items.title: PyTorch Frustratometer: An Ultra-fast, Parallelized Tool for Proteome-Scale Local Energetic Frustration Analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Evolutionary Systems Biophysics Group, Life Sciences Department, Barcelona Supercomputing Center, Barcelona, Spain
items.abstract: Most natural protein sequences fold into well-defined three-dimensional structural ensembles, satisfying interactions that have been shaped over evolutionary timescales. The principle of minimal frustration states that most native interactions are energetically more favorable than alternative non-native ones, resulting in a funnel-shaped folding energy landscape. The FrustratometeR tool measures how the energetics of a residue or contact compares to decoys with different amino acid identities or configurations. Contacts are classified as minimally frustrated when these are more stable than random alternatives, highly frustrated when less stable, or neutral when energetically indistinguishable from them. Clusters of highly frustrated interactions are often evolutionarily conserved and are typically associated with functional regions. Therefore, identifying and quantifying local frustration can provide insights into both protein stability and function. Here we present a PyTorch reimplementation of FrustratometeR that accelerates conventional frustration calculations by 70-13,000x on a single GPU, depending on chosen frustration mode and protein size, with substantially larger gains for exhaustive mutational scanning, enabling proteome-scale local frustration analysis. We benchmark against the original algorithm on the CATH v4.4 S40 dataset and show near-identical results across all three frustration modes and mutational scanning. Source code is freely available at https://github.com/ParraLab-ESBG/pytorch-frustratometer.

items.title: Glycolysis and interferon transcription in melanoma immunotherapy
items.abstract: Glycolysis and interferon signalling have both been associated with responses to PD-1 blockade, but their joint transcriptional relationship with treatment outcome remains uncertain. We examined whether a state with high glycolysis and low interferon- response was associated with reduced disease control in melanoma. Fixed Hallmark gene sets were scored by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis in GSE91061, GSE78220 and an additional Liu cohort. Disease control analyses included 47, 26 and 100 patients. Conditional odds ratios for the joint state were 6.06 (exact 95% confidence interval, 1.04 to 65.61), 0.35 (0.026 to 3.11) and 1.03 (0.39 to 2.73), respectively. Holm-adjusted P values for the two initial comparisons were 0.073 and 0.365. The additional exploratory P value was 1.000. Continuous models and analyses that omitted each patient in turn did not provide consistent evidence of an adverse association. IFN scores were negatively correlated with DNA-derived tumour purity in 102 patients (Spearman {rho} = -0.671). Among 40 patients with paired biopsies, disease control was associated with higher on-treatment IFN scores after baseline adjustment, although the paired subset had lower baseline glycolysis than patients without paired profiles. In patient-level single-cell analyses, the baseline CD8 T cell correlation weakened when an alternative rank score used a common gene background. The defined joint state was not consistently associated with poorer disease control across cohorts. Bulk IFN scores were related to tumour purity, and cellular correlations were sensitive to scoring choices. These transcriptomic results do not measure pyruvate concentration, glycolytic flux or STAT1 pyruvylation.

items.title: Choice of annotation data significantly impacts automated reconstruction of genome-scale metabolic networks
items.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models are valuable tools for studying metabolism in many applications, such as metabolic engineering or understanding human disease. However, curated models are available for only a limited number of organisms, and generating high-quality models for additional organisms remains a challenge. To help address this challenge, several software tools have been developed that can produce draft models in an automated fashion, but the quality of these draft models lags behind manually curated ones. Thus, there is still a need to improve these tools. Previous work has focused primarily on developing better methods for each step in the reconstruction process, such as gene annotation and gap-filling. Here, we focus on the data that underlies these methods, such as known connections between protein sequence and function. We find that changing the source of reconstruction data has a substantial impact on the contents and predictions of generated models. In fact, the source of data can have a bigger impact than the choice of reconstruction method. Additionally, we show that the reconstruction process is sensitive to the accuracy of gene annotations in the reconstruction data. Finally, we demonstrate the importance of having functional annotation data from an organism that is closely related to the one for which a model is being built. These observations highlight the importance of reconstruction data and identify principles that should be considered when selecting data for reconstruction tools.

items.title: Calibrating developmental dynamics from single-cell atlases: lineage paths outrun least-action routes
items.abstract: Single-cell atlases infer developmental dynamics from destructive snapshots, yet how far realized lineage paths depart from such inferred dynamics has never been measured with controls. We introduce LADD (Least-Action Developmental Dynamics), a measurement framework that learns a stochastic developmental vector field from time-series single-cell RNA-seq and computes minimum-action and minimum-time paths, together with a three-layer calibration protocol that separates genuine path deviation from the generic cost of centroid measurement, and we compare its forecasting component with optimal-transport and flow-matching methods. In the lineage-resolved Caenorhabditis elegans atlas, the raw action ratio of observed lineage-centroid trajectories to optimal paths is 3.79, yet forward-simulated ensembles of the learned model itself score 2.07, leaving a genuine excess of about two-fold. In zebrafish (Danio rerio), the observed ratio sits entirely at the model's floor. Three mechanisms that could explain the residual deviation (detours, flow-opposition, and fate-map complexity) are each excluded; what remains is speed, with lineages moving 30-43% faster along the learned flow. We report validity boundaries for temporal resolution, cross-species comparison, and energetic interpretation, delimiting where action-based trajectory comparisons are meaningful.

items.title: Low-fidelity simulator selection for multi-fidelity inference of epithelial vertex models
items.abstract: Vertex models link cell division, neighbour exchange, and intercellular forces to epithelial tissue form through parameters such as junctional line tension and perimeter contractility. Bayesian inference of these parameters from data quantifies their uncertainty, but for stochastic models of proliferating tissues it requires many costly simulations. Multi-fidelity simulation-based inference reduces this cost by training on many runs of a cheaper, less accurate ('low-fidelity') simulator before refining with a few full ('high-fidelity') runs. Low-fidelity versions can be constructed in several ways, for example by stopping simulations early, coarsening the timestep, or averaging fewer replicates, but it is unclear which to choose before committing to costly training. To address this, we introduce PRISM (Paired Ranking Index for Simulator Matching), a screen that compares each candidate with the full simulator on paired runs, scoring agreement in cell-packing statistics against cost. For a vertex model of a proliferating tissue, PRISM flags stopping early as unreliable before training; once trained, this choice can produce confidently wrong parameter estimates. By contrast, a coarser timestep, within the range tested, is cheap and accurate; while fewer replicates are accurate but too costly. Using a screened low-fidelity simulator, multi-fidelity inference outperforms approximate Bayesian computation and neural-network inference trained on full simulations alone, at matched cost and with well-calibrated uncertainty. The same pattern recurs for a second vertex model fitted to published Drosophila pupal-wing imaging data, although there stopping halfway proves safe. Together, our findings suggest that which approximations are safe depends on the model, and that screening them before training makes multi-fidelity inference of tissue mechanics practical.

items.title: Pre-synaptic facilitation of corticospinal output improves dexterity and finemotor control after stroke
items.abstract: The corticospinal tract (CST) is a neural pathway that supports skilled use of the arm and hand. Lesions of corticospinal axons result in muscle weakness, deficits of gross motor function, and loss of proximal and distal dexterous control for which effective treatments are still lacking. Here we exploited excitatory connections from motor thalamus to primary motor cortex to potentiate surviving descending signals and restore volitional arm and hand control in three monkeys with corticospinal tract lesion, using deep brain stimulation. Stimulation targeted to thalamocortical projections facilitated upper-limb movements, enabling monkeys with arm and hand paralysis to perform unconstrained 3D reach and fine dexterous tasks. Stimulation improved strength, hand gross motor function, and digits control. Electrophysiology suggested that effects were mediated by and more effective when targeting fibers with monosynaptic connection to the corticospinal motoneurons. Stimulation was delivered in continuous with FDA-clinically approved parameters holding realistic promises of clinical translation.

items.title: Human medial frontal neurons represent integrated semantic content and sensory evidence to inform decision-making
items.abstract: Humans can reconfigure how they act on the world from a single verbal instruction. Central to this capacity is the ability to represent what an instruction specifies and to bring that content to bear on incoming sensory evidence. However, little is known about where in the human brain instruction content is encoded, how it combines with sensory evidence to produce a choice, and how this integration relates to behavior. Here, we characterized single-neuron and population responses recorded in the ventral temporal cortex, medial temporal lobe, medial frontal cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex of neurosurgical patients performing a verbal instruction task. On each trial, a written instruction specified which stimulus feature was relevant and whether the correct response was to choose or to reject the stimulus that best matched it, so that the same image pair required opposite responses under different instructions. Only medial frontal populations jointly encoded the instructed task, and the target feature, whereas ventral temporal populations encoded stimulus features along axes that generalized across instruction conditions. Choice representation emerged first in ventromedial prefrontal and then in medial frontal cortex during stimulus presentation, before a motor response could be prepared. Shuffling instruction content selectively degraded prediction of medial frontal population activity, whereas shuffling stimulus identity selectively degraded ventral temporal activity. To ask how these representations could be computed, we trained a vision-language model with separable visual and linguistic streams converging on a recurrent decision module to perform the same task. Its visual embeddings predicted held-out ventral temporal activity and its recurrent activations revealed a task solution space that predicted medial frontal activity, and the strength of this alignment tracked behavioral accuracy. These results identify a cortical hierarchy in which medial frontal circuitry represents the content of verbal goals and acts on a ventral temporal substrate whose representational axes remain stable, and indicate that functional hierarchies discovered in artificial networks can serve as predictive models of human neural circuitry.

items.title: First-in-class -PET radiotracers for GPR39: A platform for noninvasive target engagement imaging in vivo
items.corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Disrupted zinc homeostasis is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. As a key zinc-sensing receptor, GPR39, a G protein-coupled receptor implicated in neurodegeneration, vascular regulation, and neuropsychiatric disorders, represents an emerging target for molecular imaging. However, the lack of suitable positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers has limited the in vivo characterization of GPR39. Quantitative assessment of GPR39 in vivo could improve our understanding of its role in physiology and disease and facilitate the development and evaluation of targeted therapeutics. Here, we introduce [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a PET radiotracer for specific imaging of GPR39. [18F]GPR39 2.1 exhibited excellent serum stability with negligible radiometabolite formation. In vitro cell uptake studies demonstrated a 55-70% reduction in tracer uptake following pharmacological blockade. PET imaging showed rapid brain uptake, efficient blood-brain barrier penetration, and gradual washout. Blockade studies in rats demonstrated significant reductions in brain uptake of up to approximately 90% (p<0.0001) across multiple brain regions. GPR39 specificity was further validated in GPR39 knockout mice, which showed 76% (p<0.002) and 90% (p<0.0002) reductions in brain uptake by PET imaging and biodistribution, respectively. Moreover, 5xFAD transgenic mice exhibited significantly lower brain uptake by PET imaging (40%, p<0.0002) and biodistribution (77%, p<0.002), indicating sensitivity of [18F]GPR39 2.1 to disease-associated alterations in GPR39. Biodistribution studies demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics, while autoradiography further confirmed GPR39-specific binding, consistent with the PET and biodistribution findings. Collectively, these results establish [18F]GPR39 2.1 as a stable, brain-penetrant, and highly specific PET radiotracer for noninvasive imaging of GPR39 in vivo. This work provides a translational framework for investigating GPR39 biology and supports the development of GPR39 as an imaging and therapeutic target in neurological and systemic diseases associated with GPR39 dysregulation.

items.title: Midbrain neurons regulate the production of courtship squeaks in female mice
items.abstract: Animals produce different vocalization types (e.g., contact calls, mating calls) to communicate in different behavioral contexts, but how the brain is organized to enable the production of different vocalization types remains poorly understood. Recent work found that specialized neurons in the midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) regulate the production of ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in female and male mice, but these PAG-USV neurons are not required for the production of broadband vocalizations (squeaks). To identify PAG neurons that may regulate the production of squeaks, we used an activity-dependent labeling strategy (TRAP2) to identify and manipulate PAG neurons that are active in association with the production of courtship squeaks in female mice. Optogenetic activation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons elicits the production of squeaks, while ablation of TRAPed PAG neurons blocks the production of courtship squeaks without altering female non-vocal courtship behaviors. Surprisingly, ablation of courtship squeak-TRAPed PAG neurons did not affect the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Moreover, non-selective PAG ablation, which blocked the production of courtship squeaks in females and USVs in both sexes, attenuated but did not block the production of footshock-elicited squeaks. Our results identify a population of PAG neurons that critically regulates the production of courtship squeaks in female mice and also suggest that a non-canonical, PAG-independent pathway regulates the production of pain-elicited vocalizations.

items.title: Replicable Connectivity and Spectral Alterations of Functional Networks in Major Depression
items.corresponding_institution: Tri-Institutional Center for Translational Research in Neuroimaging and Data Science (TReNDS), Georgia State University, Georgia Institute of Technology, and Em
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is usually characterized in functional MRI through connectivity alone, often in samples too small to resolve its modest effects. Here we applied multi-scale, template-guided independent component analysis to resting-state data from the multi-site MDD-DIRECT cohort and jointly examined the connectivity, spectral content and spatial composition of 105 intrinsic brain networks. Differences between patients and controls were widespread, small and structured: cerebello-subcortical coupling was reduced, subcortical--somatomotor coupling was increased, and spectral power shifted from lower to higher frequencies, most prominently in the thalamus, which also showed the most altered connectivity. Spatial composition differed in every network examined. In a smaller independent cohort, the direction of effect agreed for 95% of significant connections, 78% of significant spectral effects and 77% of the largest spatial-composition effects. Depression therefore alters several distinct properties of intrinsic networks, consistently across cohorts and most prominently in the thalamus.

items.title: Quantifying Excitation-Inhibition Harmony and Its Breakdown during Epileptogenesis in a Spiking Neural Network of the Hippocampal CA1
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Computational Neuroscience and Daegu National University of Education
items.abstract: Epileptogenesis is often linked to disruptions in excitation-inhibition (E-I) balance, yet its quantitative characterization remains limited. Understanding and quantifying this E-I balance could enable earlier diagnosis and targeted treatment of epilepsy. We investigate competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown using a biologically grounded spiking neural network model of hippocampal CA1 that incorporates two structural pathological mechanisms: pyramidal cell (PC) axonal sprouting and loss of inhibitory interneurons. As recurrent excitatory connectivity increases via PC axonal sprouting or inhibitory interneuron populations decline through interneuron loss, the network undergoes sequential transitions from a healthy phase (HP) to an interictal pathological phase (IIP) and finally to an ictal pathological phase (IP). At the input level, we introduce the competition degree, Cd (= SE / SI), as the ratio of the strengths of excitatory (SE) to inhibitory (SI) synaptic inputs to PCs, to quantify their competitive E-I harmony. As an input-side indicator, Cd remains near 2.6 in HP, exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump to ~ 60 at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter. At the output level, the corresponding output-side measure, the population-averaged mean firing rate (MFR) of PCs, , also exhibits a discontinuous, abrupt jump from ~ 4 to ~ 200 Hz at the HP [->] IIP transition and rises further thereafter, indicating progressive pathological hyperexcitability. Together, these results establish a cause-and-effect framework linking the input-side indicator Cd (cause) to the output-side measure (effect). Accordingly, Cd may serve as a potential quantitative biomarker of competitive E-I harmony and its breakdown, providing a computational causal framework that links structural pathological mechanisms to epileptogenic state transitions and offering potential for translation into diagnostic tools and therapeutic applications.

items.title: An anatomical and day-night atlas links cochlear immunity to adjacent bone marrow
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Medical University, Zhanjiang 524000, Guangdong, China; Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory
items.abstract: The cochlea lies within marrow-bearing bone. How this neighbouring marrow relates to cochlear immunity and daily physiology remains poorly resolved. We profiled 160,643 cells from mouse cochlea and adjacent temporal-bone marrow at six times of day, with rhythm inference calibrated for one pooled sample per time. Three-dimensional confocal reconstruction mapped vascular connections between marrow and cochlea and localized neutrophils along this interface. Neutrophils also occupied healthy cochlear fluids. Parabiosis findings were consistent with a local marrow contribution to cochlear immunity. Structural cochlear cells maintained synchronized, light-entrained clocks. Cochlear neutrophil programmes aligned with circulating neutrophils and opposed those in marrow, with independent flow cytometry supporting daily changes in immune composition and CXCR4. A shared night-associated heat-shock programme was attenuated after noise in an independent cohort. These anatomical and temporal data provide a reference for testing local marrow supply and the origins of cochlear immune rhythms.

items.title: Targeting distinct neuronal populations with AAV vectors reveals neurogenesis-associated anxiolytic effects of JNK inhibition
items.corresponding_institution: Turku Bioscience Centre, University of Turku and Abo Akademi University
items.abstract: c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) regulates stress responses and affective behaviour, but the neural populations mediating these effects remain unclear. Here, we delivered a nucleus-targeted JNK inhibitor to the mouse brain using blood-brain barrier-crossing adeno-associated virus vectors with distinct cellular tropisms. JNK inhibition produced strikingly different behavioural outcomes depending on the neuronal populations targeted. Only AAV-PHP.eB-hSyn1-mediated delivery reproduced the previously reported anxiolytic phenotype, whereas AAV.CAP-B10-hSyn1 increased locomotor activity and depressive-like behaviour and AAV.CAP-B10-mDlx reduced locomotion while enhancing object recognition memory. The anxiolytic response was accompanied by reduced hilar mossy cell abundance and an approximately two-fold increase in doublecortin-positive newborn granule neurons in the dentate gyrus. Notably, this phenotype mirrors our previous findings following selective JNK inhibition in adult hippocampal progenitor cells, implicating the neurogenic niche as a convergent substrate for anxiolytic responses to JNK inhibition. Proteomic analysis of plasma extracellular vesicles revealed widespread alterations in metabolic and inflammatory proteins upon JNK inhibition, despite neuron-restricted transgene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that the behavioural and systemic consequences of JNK inhibition depend critically on the neural populations targeted and identify hippocampal neurogenesis-associated circuits involving mossy cells as candidate mediators of JNK-dependent anxiety regulation.

items.title: Changes in anterior cingulate connectivity associated with response to antidepressant treatment for major depressive disorder
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Research, McLean Hospital, Belmont, MA, USA/University of California Irvine
items.abstract: Background: Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) involving the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the hippocampal formation has been implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD) and antidepressant response. However, it remains unclear whether connectivity changes in distinct ACC subdivisions and hippocampal formation reflect general antidepressant effects or are specifically associated with clinical improvement. Methods: Forty-one, unmedicated adults with MDD underwent functional MRI before and after 8 weeks of sertraline or bupropion treatment. Seed-based rsFC analyses examined subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), dorsal ACC (dACC), and hippocampal formation connectivity. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether connectivity change was associated with treatment response, remission, and dimensional improvement in depressive symptoms. Results: Thirty individuals (73.2%) responded to treatment and 26 (63.4%) achieved remission. Overall, rsFC decreased pre- to post-treatment between (1) dACC and pgACC (but not sgACC and hippocampal formation) and (2) cortical regions primarily involving default mode and frontoparietal networks. When considering treatment response, differences in sgACC and pgACC connectivity with temporal and inferior frontal regions emerged (increased in responders vs. decreased in non-responders). Remission was similarly associated with increased sgACC connectivity with temporal and prefrontal regions, and increased sgACC connectivity with temporal cortical regions related to greater reductions in depressive symptoms. Conclusions: Antidepressant treatment was associated with distinct patterns of ACC connectivity change, with general reductions in dorsal and pregenual connectivity but increases in subgenual and pregenual connectivity associated with favorable clinical outcomes. Findings suggest that changes in sgACC/pgACC connectivity are particularly relevant to antidepressant treatment response. Keywords: Major depressive disorder; Resting-state functional connectivity; Anterior cingulate cortex; Antidepressant treatment; Treatment response; Subgenual anterior cingulate cortex.

items.title: Distinguishing evidence accumulation from choice confidence in neural signatures of perceptual decision making
items.abstract: Human electrophysiology research has identified the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) as an apparent neural correlate of sensory evidence accumulation during perceptual decision-making. The CPP has also been shown to closely scale with subjective confidence. Coupled with the fact of its domain-generality and lack of choice selectivity, this observation raises the possibility that the CPP might in fact trace subjective confidence rather than cumulative evidence, two quantities that are closely correlated in most experiments. To disentangle confidence from cumulative evidence, we used predictive cues with 80% validity to manipulate prior expectations of participants during a contrast discrimination task while recording electroencephalography (EEG). At the time of decision termination, confidence is expected to reach a higher level for validly cued versus invalidly cued choices, whereas the opposite would be expected of a cumulative evidence signal due to biased decision starting points. As expected, valid cues led to faster, more accurate and more confident responses compared to invalid and neutral cues. At the neural level, cues produced systematic increases in preparation of the expected action prior to evidence onset as indexed by premotor mu/beta activity, consistent with cue-biased criterion adjustments. The pre-response CPP amplitude was significantly reduced for validly cued choices and the effect remained even when matching for confidence. Together these findings suggest that the CPP is not a direct read-out of subjective confidence, but an evidence accumulation signal that contributes to both decision formation and confidence estimation.

items.title: Mapping and longitudinal imaging of potentiated synapses in the mouse hippocampus using SynActive-eGRASP
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Padua (DSB), Padua, Italy
items.abstract: Identifying individual synapses that undergo long-term potentiation following learning at specific circuits remains a major challenge in neuroscience. To address this problem, we developed SA-eGRASP, a genetically encoded reporter that combines SynActive (SA) targeting with enhanced GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (eGRASP). SA drives the expression of the postsynaptic half of eGRASP at potentiated spines via the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of the immediate-early gene Arc, thus enabling selective labeling of individual synapses that are both structurally connected and have undergone potentiation through transsynaptic GFP reconstitution. Here, we validated SA-eGRASP and combined it with high-resolution optical imaging to generate a detailed map of hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses subjected to potentiation following contextual fear conditioning in mice. The high signal-to-noise ratio of SA-eGRASP, allowed us to track individual potentiated dendritic spines over the course of several days, to investigate the long-term dynamics of CA3-CA1 potentiated dendritic spines, and to study the selective potentiation of a subset of spines upon experience. SA-eGRASP paves the way to the investigation of synaptic engrams by enabling longitudinal, circuit-specific investigation of synapses potentiated during learning in mice performing naturalistic behaviors.

items.title: Structural evolution of Fcα/μR-mediated antibody recognition
items.abstract: The Fc alpha-mu receptor (Fc/R) is an ancient Fc-receptor sharing common ancestry with the polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR) and binding polymeric IgM and IgA ligands. In several vertebrate lineages, including birds, Fc/R may serve as the sole IgM and IgA Fc receptor; yet its evolution and ligand-recognition mechanisms across vertebrates remain poorly understood. Here, we identify FCAMR expression in duck (Anas platyrhynchos, ap) lymphoid tissues and demonstrate that recombinantly expressed apFc/R ectodomain binds apIgM and apIgA ligands. apFc/R affinity was ~10-fold higher for apIgM versus apIgA and ~10-fold higher than mouse (mm) Fc/R. Cryo-EM structures of apFc/R in complex with pentameric apIgM (3.27 [A]) and tetrameric apIgA (3.57 [A]) showed three Ig-like domains (D1-D3) bound asymmetrically with 1:1 stoichiometry. Comparisons to avian pIgR, which contains four Ig-like domains (D1-D4), revealed overlapping contacts between apFc/R-D1 and pIgR-D1. apFc/R D2-D3 engaged sites similar to pIgR D3-D4, yet formed distinct contact networks. Parallel analysis of a mmFc/R-mmIgM structure (4.13 [A]) revealed mmFc/R's single Ig-domain bound analogous to apFc/R-D1 and to mammalian pIgR-D1, whereas downstream ectodomain regions were not observed. Collectively, the data elucidate PIGR-family mechanisms across vertebrates, providing a foundation for delineating common and divergent functions.

items.title: RCDome: A Multi-Database Human Gene Atlas of Regulated Cell Death
items.corresponding_institution: Universidade Estadual do Norte Fluminense Darcy Ribeiro
items.abstract: Introduction: Regulated cell death (RCD) governs tissue homeostasis, development, and disease, and is executed or regulated by specific genes. Yet for the researcher asking which genes execute or regulate a given RCD form, the answer is rarely simple: gene lists for the same form rarely agree across databases, many associations carry no traceable source, and most have never been systematically checked against primary literature. We built RCDome to answer the most basic question a researcher can ask: where did this gene-RCD association come from, and what is the evidence? Methods: RCDome is a multi-database human gene atlas built through a staged architecture integrating multi-source compilation, literature validation and evidence recovery, mechanistic classification, human-governed ontological adjudication, and web deployment. Five complementary evidence channels (PubMed Boolean search, curated databases, AI-assisted screening, manual curation, and Elicit systematic review) were integrated from 20 public databases into a unified matrix. Sixty-two original name strings were canonicalized into 53 RCD-related entities with curator-adjudicated operational definitions and ontological levels. Gene-RCD associations were systematically evaluated through an independent DeepSeek two-call LLM validation, Europe PMC full-text recovery and deep evidence extraction, an independent Consensus literature-search channel, and GPT-4o arbitration of disagreements. Source-grounding controls rejected extracted evidence not found verbatim in the source document, while the governance contract was enforced as executable code. Results: The compendium holds 22,473 association rows spanning 9,265 unique HGNC-validated genes (21,568 unique gene-RCD pairs). Evidence-first adjudication resolved 5,138 pairs (23.8%) as mechanistically involved; across the 4,775 role-resolved pairs, 225 (4.7%) are executors, 4,455 (93.3%) are regulators, and 95 are markers, revealing a small death-executing core embedded in a vast regulatory network. Under a separate seven-class mechanistic criterion applied to all 22,473 rows, only 3,063 (13.6%) were mechanistically confirmed and 286 (1.3%) were database-only with no verifiable paper trail. Conclusion: RCDome makes the RCD evidence landscape measurable and traceable, showing that AI-assisted curation can be verifiable, human-governed, and explicit about uncertainty. It is delivered as a Shiny web application that lets any researcher query the atlas and inspect the evidence behind each association. Availability: RCDome is freely available at https://rcdome.org/ (source code and data at https://github.com/BioCancerInformatics/RCDome).

items.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
items.corresponding_institution: Beckman Research Institute of City of Hope
items.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.

items.title: Regulation of sociality and neuronal development by the translation initiation factor eIF4H1 in Drosophila
items.abstract: Most animal species exhibit some level of sociality. However, whether sociality-related traits evolved independently, or are instead derived from common core mechanisms, remains controversial. Nevertheless, an emerging theoretical framework stipulates that key aspects of how animals interact with their social environments may be regulated by a phylogenetically conserved genetic toolkit. Therefore, we hypothesized that mutations that lead to social deficits in specific human disorders may implicate genes that play conserved roles in the regulation of core social traits across Animalia. Specifically, here we focus on genes associated with Williams syndrome (WS), a rare human multi-system disorder characterized in part by hypersocial cognitive traits. WS is caused by a hemizygous chromosomal microdeletion of 25-28 protein-coding genes. Consequently, it has been hypothesized that haploinsufficiency in at least one of these genes plays an important role in the development and/or function of social neural circuits in humans. Because the Drosophila genome encodes orthologs of 17 of the 28 genes deleted in WS, we reasoned that at least some of them may serve a conserved role in the regulation of social traits across flies and humans, as predicted by the genetic toolkit framework. Using a neuron-specific RNAi knockdown screen, we identified eIF4H1, an ortholog of a highly conserved subunit of the eukaryotic translation initiation complex eIF4F, as a candidate gene for neuronal regulation of sociality in the fly. We show that eIF4H1 expression is predominantly neuronal in the adult fly brain, and that its action plays a differential role in the organization of specific dopaminergic neuron subtypes that are associated with sociality and cognitive functions. These results indicate that eIF4H1 may serve a conserved function in regulating the development of the neuronal circuits that regulate social behaviors, thus supporting the idea of a conserved sociality genetic toolkit.

items.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Differential Exon Usage and Virulence Gene Family Dynamics in Plasmodium falciparum during Severe Malaria
items.corresponding_institution: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology Department of Biochemistry & Biotechnology
items.abstract: Malaria remains a leading cause of child mortality in developing countries, with roughly 610,000 deaths per year. While the disease is caused by five human Plasmodium species, Plasmodium falciparum (Pf ) causes the most severe form. Progression from uncomplicated to severe malaria is characterized by high proliferation of the parasite, severely affecting children under five years old. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain an active area of research. Many multicopy genes have been implicated in Pf virulence. Some of these genes are implicated in cytoadherence, host-cell invasion, immune evasion, sequestration of infected erythrocytes, and antigenic variation. We employed an integrative transcriptomic analysis in this study to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of severe malaria and gene expression patterns, virulence gene dynamics, and the potential contribution of alternative splicing. Results show an overexpression of protein synthesis and ribosomal genes associated with severe malaria. About 86% (n=1865) of all differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were downregulated in severe malaria, and 226 genes exhibited both differential expression and differential exon usage (DEU). Pf virulence genes and antigenic genes such as var (pfEMP1), stevor, surfin, rif (rifin), ptm-2TM, and msp were upregulated in severe malaria compared with uncomplicated malaria, except for rifin. In severe malaria, there was evidence of co-expression and regulation within multigene families, as well as DEU and alternative splicing in virulence genes and antimalarial resistance-related proteins. Pf does not employ a single mechanism for disease progression but suppresses and deregulates nonessential pathways, processes, and genes, which are upregulated virulence genes, DNA replication, mRNA transcription, and protein synthesis. Multicopy genes are co-expressed and regulated to meet the molecular needs of the parasite. The parasite employs alternative splicing and DEU mechanisms for immune invasion and evasion, host-parasite interaction, as well as antimalarial resistance.

items.title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
items.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.

items.title: Ok-k-mer: Selecting k-mer length ensembles for calculating genomic distance
items.abstract: Current methods for computing sequence similarity across large groups of genome sequences tend to do so at the level of k-mers since this is far more efficient than base-by-base alignment. While these methods use default k-mer lengths, recent work shows that the particular choice of k-mer length greatly affects accuracy, and that using multiple values of k can boost accuracy relative to the best single choice of k, particularly when the goal is to estimate genomic distances that reflect true phylogenetic relationships. Here, we introduce Ok-k-mer, a tool to systematically select weighted k-mer length ensembles for pairwise genomic distance estimation, thereby increasing the accuracy of those estimates. Given a phylogenetic tree, Ok-k-mer ranks genome pairs by Jaccard distance across a range of k and uses a progressive search to maximize the Spearman correlation, {rho}, between weighted-average k-mer ranks and branch distances. Across eight Genome Taxonomy Database datasets, Ok-k-mer ensembles improved correlation over standard default k-mer lengths. In the Chlamydiales taxonomy, a three-length ensemble k=(9,17,22) achieved a 23.9% relative improvement over the best single length (k=20) and a 36.7% improvement over a commonly used default of 31-mers. We demonstrate that Ok-k-mer k-mer length ensembles remain stable (i.e. lengths and weights change only moderately) under genome subsampling within a taxonomy but vary across datasets. Ok-k-mer can annotate all subtrees of a phylogeny, which reveals distinct patterns of ensembles reflecting potential differences in genome evolution. Ok-k-mer provides a framework for moving beyond a "one-k-fits-all" k-mer analysis, improving genomic distance estimation in the era of massive-scale genomics.

items.title: Glycine-Proline driven flexibility and interface-dependent conservation of six-residue {Omega}-loops in protein complexes
items.abstract: {Omega}-loops are six- to sixteen-residue, non-regular structural motifs that occur in protein structures, connecting regular regions and forming a well-defined, ordered structural segment. They are functionally important because of their strategic location on the protein surface, where they are often associated with molecular recognition, ligand binding, and catalytic activity. Their non-regular nature enables them to adopt different conformations, which makes them important in protein dynamics and allosteric communication. In this work, we have curated six-residue {Omega}-loops from diverse protein-protein complexes of varying stability and found them to be abundant across all. We identified 1205 hydrogen-bonded and 6518 non-hydrogen-bonded {Omega}-loops, leading to an average of ~1.7 {Omega}-loops per structure. Glycine and proline were the most enriched residues in the loop, with proline preferentially positioned at the fourth position and glycine distributed across multiple positions, supporting their roles in chain reversal and conformational flexibility. Using ProteinMPNN-based sequence-design modelling and Rate4Site evolutionary-rate analysis, we show that {Omega}-loops occupy a relatively constrained sequence space, with interface loops in obligate homodimers and heterodimers more conserved than non-interface loops; the opposite trend was observed in transient and crystal dimers. Mapping known pathogenic and benign mutations onto the {Omega}-loop present in human proteins, together with a case study of the TEM1 {beta}-lactamase {Omega}-loop, further illustrates how small sequence changes within these loops can produce crucial structural and functional consequences, leading to altered enzyme activity and antibiotic resistance. Altogether, we report that {Omega}-loops are not merely connectors of secondary structure but are structurally constrained, evolutionarily significant elements that contribute to protein folding, stability and function.

items.title: Amino acid clustering and epistasis guide sequence-based prediction of phenotype modulation
items.corresponding_institution: Universidad de Buenos Aires, Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales, Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Cientificas y Tecnicas. Instituto de Quimica Biologic
items.abstract: Protein sequences encode the molecular information necessary for their biological function. As functional adaptation often emerges from combined effects of multiple positions, understanding how sequence variation gives rise to functional differences remains a central challenge. Here, we developed an improved strategy to identify phenotype modulating positions and use them to predict phenotypes, by relating amino acid identity to experimentally measured quantitative properties across families. Using family-specific sequence-phenotype datasets, our results show that epistasis plays a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Position specific amino acid clustering further improved performance indicating that key functional information is often captured by broad physicochemical amino acid classes, with hydrophobicity playing a crucial role in phenotype modulation. Our identified phenotype modulating positions involve both proximal and distal sites relative to functional sites. While the former is captured by individual positions, the latter is captured when epistasis is taken into account. Comparison with experimentally identified positions showed partial recovery of known functionally relevant residues, while at the same time revealing candidate positions that may contribute to phenotypic variation. Taken together, these results suggest that quantitative phenotypes are often governed by a network of interacting amino acid residues and may be engineered by a limited amount of sequence modifications. This finding highlights the potential of our framework to deepen our understanding of protein function, evolution, and adaptation, providing new targets for the rational modulation and engineering of protein phenotypes.

items.title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
items.abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

items.title: Realism and resolution: How AI-predicted protein structures differ from experimental structures
items.abstract: Protein structure predictors can recover protein folds with remarkable accuracy, and their models are increasingly used as if they were experimental structures. Yet even for a confidently predicted fold, it remains difficult to judge how faithfully the model reproduces protein geometry. We introduce WhatRes, which assesses a structure from its coordinates on two complementary axes. Apparent resolution estimates the experimental resolution its local geometry most closely resembles. Realism measures how closely that geometry matches experimental structures at the same apparent resolution. Predicted models can score well on apparent resolution while showing systematically less variation in bond lengths and angles than is observed in high-resolution crystal structures. WhatRes reveals this over-idealisation even in high-confidence models.

items.title: mFrag: Integrating External DNA Methylation References Improves Lung Cancer Early Detection by Fragmentomics
items.abstract: Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

items.title: THiRST: Computer Vision Empowered Three-dimensional High-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Analytics
items.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) preserves gene expression within tissue architecture but remains limited to individual two-dimensional (2D) sections, restricting analysis of continuous three-dimensional (3D) structures and cross-section consistency. We present THiRST, a computational framework for reconstructing multi-resolution 3D spatial transcriptomic representations from serial sections. THiRST combines coarse-to-fine morphology-guided registration, spatial matching of ST units, cross-section association of segmented structures, and integration of Visium V2 and high-definition ST. In serial kidney sections, patch-level refinement increased the same-cluster proportions of matched units at adjacent offsets from 63.8% and 65.6% to 70.7% and 70.0%, respectively, while improving expression concordance. The reconstructed correspondences enabled 3D glomerular and object-level expression analysis, with 54.1% of differential genes detected only in 3D. Cross-platform integration further aligned V2 and high-definition measurements in a shared expression space. THiRST demonstrates the feasibility of object-level 3D ST analysis from serial 2D sections and underscores the importance of accurate local registration.

items.title: A Neurocompliant Ionic Conductive Hydrogel Orchestrates Glial and Vascular Remodeling to Mitigate Traumatic Brain Injury
items.abstract: Developing conductive scaffolds for neural regeneration is often hindered by the cytotoxicity and mechanical mismatch inherent to conventional electronic fillers. Here, we report an ultrasoft ionically conductive hydrogel engineered by grafting choline-based bioionic liquids (BIL) onto fish gelatin (FiBGel). Systematic optimization yields brain-mimetic conductivity (0.25-0.68 S/m), elastic moduli (0.6-0.9 kPa), and physiological water content (72-81%). In 3D culture, the matrix drives spontaneous neurogenesis, achieving ~90% MAP2+ neurons with robust calcium signaling, while concurrently supporting endothelial network formation. We report the first intracerebral administration of a BIL hydrogel, demonstrating remarkable biocompatibility and immunomodulation. In a traumatic brain injury model, a single FiBGel dose halves reactive astrogliosis, enhances cortical revascularization, and limits lesion cavity expansion. Leveraging an FDA-recognized micronutrient, FiBGel offers a translatable strategy that integrates neuromechanics, conductivity, immune modulation, and vascular support within one injectable scaffold for minimally invasive treatment of brain injuries.

items.title: One placement, many fields: robust voxel-wise mapping with multichannel TMS
items.corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences
items.abstract: Understanding the human brain at the individual level is central to understanding its function and a prerequisite for personalized therapy. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can map structure-function relationships at high resolution by regressing trial-wise variation in the TMS-induced electric field (E-field) against a response such as motor evoked potentials (MEPs). This requires distinct E-fields across pulses at different cortical locations, which single-coil TMS (sTMS) achieves by physically repositioning the coil (typically supported by neuronavigation software such as InVesalius Navigator; Souza et al., 2018)--increasingly reliant on robotic guidance and capped by the coil geometry. Multichannel TMS (mTMS) instead steers the E-field electronically via independent currents in several coils, opening a design space of high variability without physical repositioning. We adapt determinant-based sequence optimization from discrete sTMS coil-placement sets to the continuous mTMS current space (D-optimal design), identifying pulse sequences whose induced cortical E-fields are as mutually dissimilar as biophysical constraints allow. We benchmarked optimized mTMS sequences against random baselines and optimized sTMS placements in virtual motor mapping across multiple head models, assessing three mTMS array geometries (5-channel planar, 6- and 12-channel spherical), two figure-of-eight sTMS coils, and varying pulse counts, response noise, and cortical depth. D-optimal mTMS currents substantially outperformed random currents and optimized sTMS at matched pulse counts. The gain was modest without noise but increased significantly with it: at the highest noise level, optimized sTMS failed to converge after 100 pulses (~20-22 mm error), whereas all mTMS arrays reached median errors at or below 6 mm. mTMS also recovered deep targets better than sTMS (up to 35 mm skin-cortex distance, versus 25 mm) and performed uniformly across the region of interest. A coil-space scheme based only on the magnetic vector potential, precomputable once per array without per-subject MRI, captured most of the benefit, matching subject-specific optimization at 100 pulses. mTMS thus makes voxel-wise mapping robust throughout a region of interest without coil repositioning.

items.title: Ergodic breakdown of brain dynamics under chronnectome complexity across cognitive states and age
items.abstract: Chronnectome complexity, the extent to which time-varying functional connectivity follows a structured sequence of distinct configurations, contributes to shaping large-scale brain dynamics. However, it remains unclear how this complexity influences the encoding of information that distinguishes resting state and task conditions. In ergodic theory, time averages represent ensemble behavior under ergodicity, which breaks down when dynamics are non-stationary, as when activity moves sequentially between distinct regimes. We hypothesize that this information resides in time-averaged connectivity under lower-complexity conditions but in trajectory geometry under higher-complexity conditions, where brain activity traverses distinct configurations over time, consistent with ergodic breakdown, which we term the \textit{information migration principle}. We formulate this as dynamics-driven multi-class classification and introduce the Brain Dynamics Classifier (BDC), an interpretable data-driven mechanistic model in which a graph neural network embeds dynamic functional connectivity into a latent space and a neural ordinary differential equation learns the vector field governing trajectories through that space. The proposed model derives two complementary representations within a single learned dynamical system, capturing time-averaged connectivity, which is sufficient under ergodic dynamics, and trajectory geometry, which preserves the temporal organization obscured by averaging under non-ergodic dynamics. Our results show high classification accuracy, $97.4\%$ for eight conditions in the Human Connectome Project young adult cohort and $92.2\%$ for four in the aging cohort. To test the information migration principle, we ablated the time-averaged representation and found that trajectory contributions varied with chronnectome complexity, from high for Working Memory to absent for Relational Reasoning, consistent with ergodic breakdown. Including subcortical regions further increased trajectory contributions for affective conditions. In aging, the distinction between higher and lower complexity conditions was preserved, resting-state dynamics became less ergodic with advancing age, and higher fluid intelligence was associated with more ergodic resting-state dynamics.

items.title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction is Part of a Novel Mechanism for Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathic Pain
items.corresponding_institution: Research Institute of Galilee Medical Center
items.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common, persistent complication of cancer treatment, yet the mechanisms sustaining pain remain unclear. Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in chronic pain, but its role in spinal cord dysfunction after chemotherapy, and whether it can be reversed, is unknown. Here, we show that paclitaxel-induced persistent mechanical allodynia was associated with spinal cord (L1-L6) mitochondrial dysfunction 18 days after the last injection, including reduced oxygen consumption and membrane potential ({Psi}m) in the non-phosphorylated state, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and electron transfer capacity. Paclitaxel also increased susceptibility to mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP)-induction, lowering calcium retention capacity at 3, 8, and 13 days after the last injection. Acute ex-vivo paclitaxel exposure had a similar effect, and cyclosporin A, an mPTP blocker, significantly reversed it. Consistent with a causal role for mitochondrial impairment, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT), initiated after allodynia developed, improved oxygen consumption and {Psi}m and progressively enhanced mechanical thresholds. Likewise, intrathecal delivery of healthy mitochondria to the spinal cord attenuated established allodynia in paclitaxel-treated rats and reduced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in other pain models, sciatic nerve crush and capsaicin. These findings identify persistent spinal mitochondrial dysfunction and increased mPTP susceptibility as features of CIPN and support mitochondrial protection as a therapeutic strategy for CIPN and other pain conditions.

items.title: Identifying a neurochemical signature of the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus that predicts individual variability in cue-reward learning
items.abstract: To investigate neurochemical factors that may confer vulnerability to psychiatric disorders, we used an animal model that captures a transdiagnostically relevant neurobehavioral endophenotype. During a Pavlovian conditioned approach paradigm, rats learn the predictive relationship between a lever cue and food reward. A subset of rats, sign trackers, also attribute incentive motivational value to the lever cue. Relative to non sign trackers, STs are more impulsive, have attentional deficits, and show greater reinstatement of drug seeking behavior. The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus is a key neural node implicated in these individual differences. We combined in vivo microdialysis with liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry to quantify 22 neurobiologically relevant small molecules in the PVT before and 24 hours after Pavlovian training.
