What the representation generalizes is a signal family (band-limited oscillatory activity), not the named task. Geometry-conditioned hyperalignment thus yields an inspectable representation, which is generalizable across datasets and, within the oscillatory regime, across paradigms.

items.title: Neural Encoding Geometry of Human Voluntary Visual Selection
items.abstract: Selecting relevant targets from competing alternatives is a core cognitive function. While human visual selection can be tracked with high spatiotemporal precision, it remains unsolved how selected targets and non-selected alternatives are neurally encoded to effectively separate them. Building on recent work revealing the neural encoding geometry underlying target selection in animals, we here examined how the representational format of selected targets and non-selected alternatives evolve over time during human voluntary selection. Initially, selected and non-selected objects showed equal spatially selective neural activity, yet the selected target was represented more strongly after 300-350 ms. Using cross-decoding, we found that selected and non-selected objects are encoded along a shared sensory axis, whereas selected targets are encoded along an additional spatially selective axis. This encoding geometry effectively separates selected targets from non-selected alternatives in neural space. Our results generalized across selection conditions: we found comparable results in instructed and free-choice selection, as well as in delayed oculomotor and covert visual selection. Together, we demonstrate that the human brain selectively encodes targets, but not distractors, along an additional axis, revealing a neural mechanism through which voluntary selection prioritizes behaviorally relevant information.

items.title: A trio of brain networks dynamically orchestrates music recognition
items.abstract: Recognition memory continuously integrates internal representations with sensory information to guide adaptive behavior. Yet most theoretical models conceptualize recognition as the retrieval of an isolated stimulus through a discrete sequence of steps including sensory processing, hippocampal retrieval, and cortical reinstatement. However, in natural settings, perception, memory, and predictions interact continuously within an evolving context to guide adaptive responses. It is unclear how brain networks coordinate the integration of internal and external information during dynamic recognition. Here, we combined intracranial recordings (N = 30) of high-frequency activity (70-160 Hz) and dimensionality reduction to characterize distributed network dynamics during music recognition. We identified three interacting functional networks supporting sensory processing, sensory-memory integration, and decision formation, whose temporal dynamics predicted the timing of behavior. During recognition of memorized sequences, sensory activity progressively attenuated, sensory inputs were combined with mnemonic and contextual information, and decision-related activity evolved toward sensorimotor engagement. Novel sequences disrupted this organization by sustaining sensory responses and accelerating decision-related activity. Sensory and integrative networks communicated bidirectionally. Our findings reveal recognition as a distributed, context-dependent, and goal-directed process emerging from the continuous and bidirectional coordination of large-scale brain networks.

items.title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease.
items.abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10-based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ-brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer's disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (delta ROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

items.title: Mechanism and subunit-dependence of disease-associated lurcher mutation in AMPA-type glutamate receptors
items.corresponding_institution: University of Edinburgh, School of Biological Sciences
items.abstract: AMPA receptors are glutamate-activated neuroreceptors responsible for the majority of fast excitatory neurotransmission in vertebrate brains. Activity-dependent changes in their functional and trafficking properties underpin cognitive processes such as learning and memory formation. In the past 15 years, a number of mutations within AMPA receptor genes have been identified as disease-causing leading to some form of neurodevelopmental delay. Here, we focused on one such mutation called lurcher, resulting from a change of the third Ala in the highly conserved SYTANLAAF motif to Thr. We determined functional consequences of lurcher mutation in homomeric AMPA receptors composed of subunits GluA1 or GluA2. In GluA1 subunit, lurcher mutation has been identified as a hotspot in a large cohort of patients with neurodevelopmental disorders. We confirm previously established lurcher phenotype characterised by slower deactivation and desensitization kinetics as well as more profound block of desensitization compared to the wild-type (WT) homomers. We show that these effects are more pronounced in GluA2 than GluA1 homomers. Lurcher phenotypes are attenuated, but still present, in more physiologically abundant heteromeric AMPA receptors composed of two GluA1 lurcher and two GluA2 WT subunits (GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT). Schild analysis indicates lurcher enhances activity of AMPA receptors by primarily changing the efficiency with which they open their ion channel upon glutamate binding rather than by changing affinity for glutamate. Perampanel, the only widely licensed drug that targets AMPA receptors, is an anti-convulsant that acts as a non-competitive inhibitor. We show it continues to inhibit GluA1 lc/GluA2 WT heteromeric receptors and that its IC50 depends on the auxiliary subunits associated with the heteromers. Specifically, stargazin (TARP {gamma}-2) brings the IC50 for perampanel into the submicromolar range, just like in the WT receptors.

items.title: Deep CyTOF immune profiles of ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis differ with European and African geographical origin
items.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors influence human immunity and modulate responses to infection. Accounting for immune heterogeneity across human populations is critical to the design of novel vaccines and host-directed interventions that would optimally benefit populations experiencing the highest disease burden. Tuberculosis (TB) burden is unevenly distributed across geographical regions and our understanding of the differential immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) across human populations remains limited. Here, we sought to evaluate the impact of geographical origin on ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mtbinfection. We found that peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy African donors exhibited greater control of Mtbgrowth ex vivo than those isolated from European individuals. High-dimensional single-cell profiling of the granulomatous responses by cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) revealed divergent profiles based on the specimens' geographical origin. Monocytes from European donors displayed a pro-inflammatory phenotype - correlating with Mtbgrowth -, whereas PBMCs of African individuals were enriched in activated, cytotoxic T cells - correlating with Mtbcontrol. Reduced inflammatory response in African monocytes following various microbial stimulations was confirmed. Taken together, our comprehensive immune profiling indicates that environmental and genetic factors shape a cytotoxic-regulatory response that promotes bacterial control. Against the current "one-treatment-fits-all" approach, our findings support the use of specimens from intervention-relevant settings to inform the targeted design of TB vaccines and host-directed interventions.

items.title: Identification and localization of bone marrow ILC2s using Id2/Cxcr6 dual-reporter mice
items.abstract: Type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are present in the bone marrow, where their identification and spatial localization remain challenging because of their low abundance and the expression of shared markers by other lymphoid populations. Here, we evaluated the use of Id2YFP/+ Cxcr6GFP/+ dual-reporter mice to identify and visualize bone marrow ILC2s. Using spectral flow cytometry, we showed that both ST2- and ST2 ILC2s expressed high levels of ID2, whereas CXCR6 expression differed between these subsets. However, the ID2 expressing compartments also contained NK cells, NKT cells, conventional T cells and ILC progenitors. Surface marker profiling identified CD25 and ICOS as useful markers for enriching ILC2 populations, with ST2 enabling the segregation of the ST2- and ST2 subsets. Single-cell RNA sequencing further characterized the diversity of Id2 and Cxcr6 expressing lymphoid populations and supported the use of CD5 and NKp46 as exclusion markers. Combining these markers with the dual-reporter system, confocal microscopy revealed YFPGFPCD5-NKp46- cells compatible with an ILC2 phenotype, distributed throughout the bone marrow as isolated cells or within multicellular clusters. Complementary flow cytometric analyses demonstrated that ILC2s accounted for more than 90% of a phenotypically related reporter-positive population after exclusion of major T and NK cell populations, providing additional support for the identification of the cells visualized in situ as putative ILC2s. Together, these findings establish a strategy combining dual-reporter mice, flow cytometry, transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging to investigate the localization and spatial organization of putative bone marrow ILC2s.

items.title: IL13 critically contributes to the antitumor activity of polyfunctional CD4+ T cells driven by constitutively active Stat5
items.abstract: The presence of polyfunctional T cells capable of concurrently producing multiple cytokines correlates with favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cancer. We previously reported that overexpression of constitutively active Stat5a (CASTAT5) confers polyfunctionality on tumor-specific CD4 T cells, enabling durable antitumor immunity following adoptive cell therapy. However, the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor effects of CASTAT5-modified T cells remain unclear. Here, we identify interleukin-13 (IL13) as a critical effector cytokine contributing to the multifaceted antitumor activity of CASTAT5-conditioned polyfunctional CD4 T cells (C5-CD4). C5-CD4 T cells exhibit a prominent T helper 2 (Th2) cytokine profile, accompanied by extensive epigenomic remodeling at the Th2 cytokine loci, as revealed by Hi-C and histone-modification CUT&Tag assays. Neutralization of IL13 diminished the antitumor efficacy of C5-CD4 T cells. Furthermore, targeted Il13 disruption substantially impaired tumor control and was associated with reduced donor T cell expansion and persistence, diminished systemic cytokine and chemokine responses, and attenuated activation of endogenous tumor-reactive CD8 T cells. Nonetheless, IL13 overexpression alone in donor CD4 T cells failed to fully recapitulate the therapeutic activity of C5-CD4 T cells, indicating that IL13 is a critical contributor but is insufficient to account for the full antitumor activity conferred by CASTAT5. Single-cell RNA sequencing associated donor-derived IL13 with increased representation of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells and IL13-signaling in monocytes and macrophages exhibiting tissue-repair-associated transcriptional programs. Moreover, Il13 disruption diminished the therapeutic efficacy of CASTAT5-expressing CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in a mouse B-cell lymphoma model. Reanalysis of a human CD19CAR-T infusion-product dataset further revealed an association between IL13 expression and type 2 cytokine signatures linked to prolonged clinical response, suggesting a potential contribution of IL13 to the efficacy of human CD19CAR-T therapy. Together, these findings uncover an unexpected antitumor role for IL13 and establish it as a critical node linking polyfunctional donor T cells with endogenous immune cells to promote sustained tumor immunity.

items.title: KAT6 and KAT7 actively maintain mitotic chromatin composition and acetylation to preserve developmental competence
items.corresponding_institution: Sanford I. Weill Department of Medicine, Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center,  Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY, USA.
items.abstract: Mitotic bookmarking enables transmission of regulatory information across cell division, yet how active chromatin states are molecularly preserved during mitosis and how they contribute to postmitotic cell fate decisions remain unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the acetyltransferases KAT6 and KAT7 remain chromatin-bound and catalytically active throughout mitosis in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells. Acute KAT6/7 depletion disrupts mitotic histone acetylation and the retention of multiple chromatin regulators with minimal effects on chromatin accessibility. Mechanistically, KAT6/7 bookmark both self renewal and developmental gene loci, where they are required for post-mitotic transcriptional reactivation and priming of lineage-specific programs. Consistently, genes impaired during postmitotic reactivation also fail to activate during neuronal differentiation upon continuous KAT6/7 perturbation, compromising the establishment of the neuronal program and identity. Altogether, our findings identify KAT6 and KAT7 as a cooperative mitotic chromatin maintenance system that couples active histone acetylation to preservation of chromatin composition, transcriptional memory, and developmental competence across cell division, extending the bookmarking function beyond transcriptional memory. These findings also provide a new framework for understanding KAT6/7 function in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.

items.title: The co-evolution of adhesion and F-actin gives rise to hierarchical cellular force generation
items.abstract: Cells --- the basic units of life --- dynamically adhere to their micro-environment, build their F-actin cytoskeleton, and apply molecular-motor generated contractile forces to it in a remarkably broad range of biological processes and physiological functions, in both health and disease. Yet, how these processes are orchestrated over multiple spatiotemporal scales is not fully understood. Using several experimental approaches and a theoretical framework, we show that adhesion assembly, on-adhesion F-actin accumulation and the contractile force itself all follow the same time evolution over tens of minutes, the cellular force timescale, at well-defined adhesion sites. We also show that the F-actin distribution away from the adhesion site features a multiplicative space-time decomposition. Finally, we show that F-actin retrograde flow --- central in the so-called molecular motor-clutch models --- is markedly faster than force generation rates, that it does not slow down over maturing adhesions and that its density drops at adhesion sites. These findings suggest a hierarchical, multi- scale force generation process that is controlled by slow adhesion recruitment, which is accompanied by rapid, bursty linear actin polymerization. The linear F-actin slowly accumulates with adhesion recruitment to form an extended near-adhesion F-actin network to which molecular motors attach and apply elastic-like contraction.

items.title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
items.abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.

items.title: Long-range regulatory sequence models reveal a phylogenetic boundary in vertebrate genome evolution
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Clinical Medicine, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway
items.abstract: Regulatory activity at a locus depends on local sequence and on long-range interactions with sequence further away, but how long each kind of information stays shared between genomes over evolution is unknown. Here we use sequence-to-function models as a comparative assay, training FunFormer, a long-context binary classifier that reads 20 kb, together with an architecture- and parameter-matched control that reads only the central 1 kb, in six vertebrates spanning 435 million years, and measuring what each retains when applied to another genome. Within species, the long-context model outperformed three published 1 kb classifiers by 1.0 to 3.8 percentage points in every genome, a gain that came from context rather than architecture. Across species, its contribution decayed with divergence, was near zero at the amniote split and reversed between 320 and 435 Mya, while local sequence still transferred into fish. Zebrafish and Atlantic salmon, which share their divergence from tetrapods but differ by the salmonid genome duplication, behaved alike, so the reversal is not explained by the salmonid duplication. An in silico flank intervention showed that replacing the flank with GC-matched sequence from the target genome cost 8 percentage points among mammals. When a mammalian model was applied to fish, a flank drawn from the source genome on average performed as well as the target's own flank, so the model drew nothing from the fish flank that an arbitrary source-genome flank did not provide. The long-range information that these models learn therefore stops being shared between vertebrate genomes well before the local information does. The same boundary sets a practical rule for reusing models in species without their own data, where long context helps among close relatives but is a liability across deep splits, and in variant scoring most foreign models matched a native model in data-limited pig but none did in human.

items.title: Gene-level structure of prior knowledge and perturbation responses informs target-level predictability in prior-informed models
items.abstract: Background: Predictive models of transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations increasingly incorporate biological prior knowledge. However, it remains unclear how well prior knowledge reflects each target's perturbation-response relationships and how closely prior-derived measures track target-level predictive performance. Here, we develop a gene-similarity framework to quantify agreement among eight sources of biological prior knowledge and between prior knowledge and co-function or co-regulation relationships derived from six Perturb-seq datasets. Results: In genome-wide and essential-gene screens, prior agreement accounted for 30-47% of the variance in co-function agreement and 35-43% in co-regulation agreement. Agreement with Perturb-seq responses was higher for essential genes, lower for transcription factor and signaling genes, and varied with gene expression characteristics and cellular context. We compared prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity with measures based on the observed test response in tracking target-level predictive performance. Across three prior-informed models, predictions were more accurate for targets whose observed perturbation-response relationships better matched prior knowledge and that were more similar to training perturbations. Notably, prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity, calculated without the test response, tracked relative differences in target-level predictive performance. The strength of these associations varied across models and datasets and, for train-test similarity, across prior sources. Conclusion: Our framework reveals gene- and context-level heterogeneity in how biological knowledge aligns with perturbation responses, and provides an a priori basis for assessing relative perturbation predictability before perturbation responses are measured.

items.title: Parallel transcriptome profiling of soybean cyst nematodes (SCN) during a three-way interaction among SCN, soybean aphids, and soybean
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biology & Microbiology, South Dakota State University, Brookings, SD 57007, USA
items.abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines (Ichinoe) (Rhabditida: Heteroderidae) is arguably the greatest yield-limiting factor for soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) production in the United States. Previous research found that the impact of SCN infestation on yield is exacerbated during concurrent infestations with soybean aphids (SBA), Aphis glycines (Matsurmura) (Hemiptera: Aphididae). Although recent research has characterized the host root transcriptomic response during these infestations little is known about the corresponding in planta gene expression dynamics of either pest. This study examines the transcriptomic expression of SCN in soybean cultivars' roots under single or combined SBA infestations at two different time points: 5 and 30 days post-infestation (DPI). The SCN transcriptomics for SCN-susceptible (S) PI 518671 (Williams 82) cultivar reacted equivalently to both SCN and SCN + SBA treatments. However, transcriptomics in SCN-resistant (R) MN1806CN (H. glycines HG type 0/race 3 resistant) demonstrated an elevated significant expression pattern under the SCN + SBA combined treatment. During the early infestation period (i.e., sampled at 5 DPI), both S and R cultivars reacted similarly, irrespective of treatment conditions. The functional enrichment analysis of 1829 differentially expressed genes/transcripts showed that during the early co-infestation period (5 DPI), SCN genes were significant and mapped towards resistance breakage, whereas in the late stage (30 DPI), the gene flux oriented towards nematode dormancy. Together, these results suggest that SCN activity is amplified when combined with SBA, offering foundational data for molecular breeding to produce SCN resistant soybean cultivars.

items.title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
items.abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

items.title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
items.abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of -0.003 (range, -0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.

items.title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
items.abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

items.title: ProClust provides reliable statistical significance of clusters for single-cell transcriptomic data
items.abstract: Clustering of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is widely used to identify cell populations. However, overclustering can partition a single cell population into multiple clusters, potentially leading to spurious identification of cell subpopulations. Assessing the statistical significance of clusters is therefore needed to support their biological interpretation. We propose ProClust, a statistical test for clustering significance in scRNA-seq data. ProClust defines a single cluster as a log-concave distribution and adopts a projection-based approach to quantify clustering uncertainty through p-values. These projections can also provide interpretable visual evidence for individual clusterings. ProClust merges clusters when there is insufficient evidence to reject the single-cluster null hypothesis, refining an initial overclustering without prespecifying the final number of clusters. Across parametric and PBMC-based semi-synthetic simulations, ProClust avoided false subdivisions under single-population null settings while consistently recovering the underlying population structure across different numbers of true populations. In real scRNA-seq datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, Tabula Muris, and Hydra, ProClust produced clustering solutions that showed overall agreement with reference annotations while retaining supported substructure and merging groups with insufficient evidence for separation. Together, these results demonstrate that ProClust provides a statistically principled and interpretable framework for refining an initial overclustering and distinguishing supported cellular heterogeneity. The ProClust R package is available at https://github.com/Anonym027/ProClust.

items.title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
items.abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

items.title: DaliScope: Distilling Biological Insights from Deep Structural Alignments
items.abstract: Structural similarity searches reveal protein relationships that sequence alignments miss, but treating DALI results as isolated match lists misses deeper connections. We present DaliScope, an interactive Python framework that treats complete DALI target sets as structured populations for systematic analysis of protein structural neighbourhoods. DaliScope combines structural community detection with sequence profiling, Pfam annotation, residue mapping, and 3D visualization, enabling target sets to be subdivided and examined at the residue level. We demonstrate two applications. In a multidomain protein with sparse domain annotation, structural analysis uncovered previously unannotated domains. A structurally anchored HxD...H signature occurred in 697 of 1,093 Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains and in 15 domains lacking Pfam annotation; relaxing the central residue constraint recovered 96% of Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains among the DALI targets. In a second application, a DALI search with transitive closure returned >12,000 hits. Applying an 80% coverage criterion to a conserved structural core reduced this set to 6,708 domain instances, resolved into 23 structural communities. (80% was chosen instead of the default 50% because the GOLD domain has a compact core with short loops.) Many communities were strongly enriched for individual Pfam families while providing structural context for 1,097 targets lacking Pfam assignments. Three-dimensional superimposition revealed structural continuity among related {beta}-sandwich architectures through progressive changes in sheet geometry and auxiliary elements. Together, these examples show how a single DALI query provides a structural anchor for organizing large neighbourhoods, extending interpretation beyond sequence-based annotations, and deriving structurally anchored sequence signatures from defined populations.

items.title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
items.corresponding_institution: Faculty of Applied Sciences, Macao Polytechnic University, 999078, Macau SAR, China
items.abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.

items.title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
items.abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

items.title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
items.corresponding_institution: School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Peking University
items.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

items.title: Parsimonious Creatures: Building Gene Regulatory Networks Robust to Somatic Evolution
items.abstract: For early multicellular life to have formed and maintained cellular organization, preventing loss of controlled cell replication due to somatic evolution was of critical importance, and remains important to this day for control of cancer. We study how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) can be designed to slow the divergence of somatic clonal lineages in the context of early multicellular life. We model the mutation of GRNs within simplified 12-celled organisms we term "parsimonious creatures", who must replicate from a single cell to 12 cells and then prevent replication past 12 cells to maximize fitness. We found two minimal motifs can achieve these goals, but both are prone to breakdown through somatic evolution: The feedforward motif, which is loosely regulating but relatively robust, and the simple step motif, which uses strong interactions and feedback to form memoryless ultrasensitivity, but is fragile. These simple motifs may be duplicated to form redundant networks via one of two structures: averaging redundancy, which averages multiple sources of information, and min redundancy, which adopts the most conservative source. Averaging redundancy uniformly slows somatic evolution, while min redundancy stalls somatic evolution until neutral mutations accumulate. Either may be superior dependent on life history. However, averaging redundancy slowly increases fitness as the network becomes larger, but large min redundancy networks eventually become "paralyzed", increasing the probability of senescence and reducing fitness. These GRN designs are idealized, yet provide imperfect solutions with fundamental tradeoffs, offering insight as to why somatic evolution remains an incompletely solved problem for multicellular life.

items.title: A complete adult Drosophila melanogaster brain tracheolar network
items.abstract: The tracheal system of the fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, is a complex network of epithelial tubules that supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide throughout the organism, with gases entering and exiting through spiracles along the body. While tracheal development and patterning in the embryonic and larval stages have been extensively studied, particularly in the body, much less is known about tracheal and tracheolar organization within the adult brain. To address this gap, we manually traced every tracheole in the brain of a female adult Drosophila using the Full Adult Fly Brain (FAFB) open-access electron microscopy dataset. We reconstructed 117 tracheoles that branch within the parenchyma, terminating in 1,376 endings without forming an interconnected network. Joint analysis of these skeleton reconstructions with volumetric mesh segmentations from the FlyWire connectome revealed that tracheole volume fraction is heterogeneous across neuropils and largely symmetric in overall tracheation between left and right hemispheres. We observe that synapses are not preferentially positioned near tracheoles, and are instead slightly depleted from a region approximately 15 um around tracheoles, relative to other points along the same neurons. We also quantify the relative proximity of neurotransmitter-specific synapses and cables to tracheoles across neuropils. This detailed anatomical description of the tracheolar network establishes a reference for future studies examining how neuronal patterning, activity, and metabolic demand couple with tracheole development and function.

items.title: HMGB1/CXCL12 heterocomplex activates CXCR4 to suppress the ability of Muller glia to become proliferating progenitor-like cells in the chick retina
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neuroscience, College of Medicine, The Ohio State University,
items.abstract: We investigated how High Mobility Group Box 1 (HMGB1) signaling regulates glial reactivity and Muller glia-derived progenitor cell (MGPC) formation in the chick retina. HMGB1 released from stressed cells is known to form a heterocomplex with C-X-C chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to activate C-X-C chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4). HMGB1 is broadly expressed in retinal neurons and glia and is rapidly exported from the nuclei of stressed inner retinal neurons after damage, a process blocked by inflachromene. Stressed or damaged amacrine cells also exported different transcription factors out nuclei. CXCL12 is expressed by amacrine, horizontal, and bipolar cells, whereas CXCR4 is expressed by Muller glia and is rapidly upregulated following damage. CXCR4 agonist or recombinant HMGB1/CXCL12 treatment selectively stimulates mTOR and Jak/Stat signaling in Muller glia in undamaged retinas. Inhibition of CXCR4 signaling, HMGB1 nuclear export, or HMGB1/CXCL12 complex formation potently stimulated MGPC proliferation without affecting neuronal death or microglial activation. In retinas treated with insulin and FGF2, to induce MGPC proliferation independent of injury, HMGB1 remains confined to nuclei, CXCR4 is downregulated, and inhibition of HMGB1 or CXCR4 has no effect. We further demonstrate that microglia are required to maintain CXCR4 expression in Muller glia, and blockade of HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling does not restore MGPC proliferation in microglia-depleted retinas. Together, these findings identify HMGB1/CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling as an injury-induced pathway that limits Muller glia reprogramming and MGPC formation in damaged retinas.

items.title: Pharmaco-genetic evidence of presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction coupled to detrimental DPR secretion in Drosophila Models of C9orf72-linked ALS/FTD.
items.abstract: Hexanucleotide repeat expansions in C9orf72, the most common genetic cause of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), drive neurodegeneration through both loss of gene function and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms, including transcription of repeat RNA and repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs). Both disease mechanisms have been linked to disruption of the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP), though how this contributes to disease progression remains unclear. By expressing toxic C9orf72 repeats in Drosophila melanogaster, we observed presymptomatic lysosome impairment, coupled with largely preserved autophagosome formation. Pharmacological treatment with valproic acid (VPA) partially prevented neurodegenerative and locomotor phenotypes in expressing animals in presence of Mitf, which is required for lysosomal biogenesis. Genetic inhibition of residual lysosomal degradation enhanced neurotoxicity, whereas downregulation of autophagy and secretory autophagy genes suppressed toxicity, uncovering a previously unrecognized contribution of secretion to disease. Consistent with this, in vitro experiments indicated that disabling lysosome function, but not autophagy induction, leads to an increase in neuronal release of autophagy-associated proteins and DPRs, which can be found be uptaken by nearby neurons and glia in vivo. We propose that repeat-driven presymptomatic lysosomal dysfunction, prevented by pharmacologic treatment, promotes secretory autophagy, which, in turn facilitates extracellular release and intercellular propagation of neurotoxic DPRs.

items.title: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil--brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neuropsychology & Psychopharmacology, Faculty of Psychology and Neuroscience, Maastricht University
items.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil--brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. We therefore asked whether the spectrotemporal and directional organization of such coupling can be captured with wearable systems to test their use in naturalistic settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting-state pupil--brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Cross-correlation, mutual information, and Granger causality analyses revealed that pupil--brain coupling displayed clear frequency-dependent organization. Lower EEG frequencies (2-12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger-causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG-to-pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Overall, these findings align well and extend previous evidence on spontaneous pupil--brain coupling, demonstrating that lightweight and movable wearable devices are suitable to characterize spectrotemporal and directional pupil--brain interactions. In turn, these results encourage future fundamental and translational research in naturalistic environments.

items.title: Sensory and Motor Building Blocks of an Extra Robotic Digit Representation
items.abstract: Supernumerary limbs provide a unique opportunity to ask how the brain represents an entirely novel effector within an existing sensorimotor system. Here, we investigated how primary motor cortex (M1) represents a robotic extra digit (the Third Thumb; Dani Clode Design), and how this representation changes with experience. Using fMRI, we compared participants following short-term exposure with participants who had undergone longitudinal Third Thumb training. The device was controlled by the toes but operated alongside the biological fingers, while its sensory consequences were experienced on the hand. Following prolonged experience, greater activity was elicited in the M1 hand area both during Third Thumb control, and in response to its sensory consequences alone. Multivariate analyses showed that the Third Thumb representation became more distinct from its biological toe controller. Pattern component modelling further showed that the representation could be explained by a combination of its constituent motor and sensory patterns, but their relative contributions changed substantially with experience, from toe-dominated following short-term exposure to sensory-dominated following longitudinal training. These findings suggest that M1 can represent a novel effector through flexible recombination of existing sensorimotor representations, with experience altering how these pre-existing resources contribute to the emerging representation.

items.title: Whole-Brain MRSI Metabolic Connectomics Reveals Network Disruptions and Altered Gradient Coherence in Psychosis Risk
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Psychiatric Neuroscience, Department of Psychiatry, Lausanne University Hospital and University of Lausanne, Lausanne, Switzerland; Division of Child
items.abstract: Brain network alterations preceding first-episode psychosis often escape connectomic approaches based on conventional neuroimaging, such as diffusion or functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Whole-brain magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) offers a potentially more sensitive alternative: by mapping neurometabolites across the brain, it enables the construction of metabolic connectomes that may capture very early and subtle disruptions of brain network properties. We combined whole-brain proton MRSI, diffusion MRI, and resting-state functional MRI in a sample of 29 individuals meeting DSM-5 criteria for Attenuated Psychosis Syndrome (APS) or Schizotypal Personality Disorder (SCZT), pooled into a single High Risk for Psychosis (HR) group, and 30 healthy controls (HC) to construct metabolic, structural, and functional connectomes. Network-based statistics identified a significant metabolic connectivity subnetwork with higher connectivity in HR than in HC, whereas no corresponding structural or functional connectivity differences were detected. Nodes of this subnetwork had modestly higher structural strength but were not consistently enriched among structural hubs, and no significant regional abnormalities in individual metabolite concentrations were detected. Eigenmode analysis of metabolic connectivity revealed a low-dimensional organization spanning a posterior unimodal-to-transmodal axis and a transmodal-to-limbic axis. Path analysis revealed higher bilateral energy in HR, indicating reduced coherence along a metabolic gradient that parallels the neurodevelopmental sensorimotor-to-association axis. These findings identify whole-brain metabolic network organization derived from MRSI as a systems-level phenotype of psychosis risk and raise the possibility that it captures altered development of large-scale cortical organization.

items.title: Spatial proteomics on repurposed sequencers reveals early astrocytic remodeling in an ALS mouse model
items.corresponding_institution: New York Genome Center; Columbia University (Biomedical Engineering; Herbert Irving Institute for Cancer Dynamics); Uppsala University (Science for Life Laborat
items.abstract: Spatial proteomics can reveal how disease reshapes cells and their local environments, but extending these measurements across replicated tissue cohorts requires validated antibodies, consistent sample processing and integrated analysis. These requirements are particularly pressing in studies of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where pathology evolves unevenly across spinal-cord regions and disease stages. Here, we established an end-to-end spatial proteomics workflow linking a validated 28-antibody panel to automated fluorescence decoding and imaging on repurposed high-throughput sequencers, followed by multicycle image processing, cellular profiling and probabilistic spatial-neighborhood analysis. We applied it to 70 lumbar spinal-cord sections from nine SOD1-G93A and nine wild-type mice at presymptomatic, disease-onset and symptomatic stages. Spatial neighborhood analysis revealed that the environments surrounding motor neurons were already remodeled at disease onset. GFAP-high neighborhoods expanded in the ventral gray matter, with 43% of motor neurons embedded in these environments in SOD1-G93A mice, compared with 15% in wild-type mice. This early expansion preceded the later decline of non-reactive gray matter and detectable motor-neuron loss. The regional organization of the protein-defined changes shared features with neuronal and astrocytic patterns mapped by spatial transcriptomics in mouse and human ALS. This work enables spatial proteomics across replicated tissue cohorts and identifies localized remodeling of the environments around surviving motor neurons as an early feature of disease in the SOD1-G93A model.

items.title: Evidence-based re-identification: Leveraging appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than trying to prevent them
items.abstract: Naturalistic behavioral neuroscience experiments, in which groups of animals interact in enriched environments over prolonged periods, require each animal's identity to remain correct throughout the recording. Current multi-animal tracking tools assign identities frame by frame without revisiting past assignment decisions. A single, even sporadic, identity swap is therefore likely to persist until the end of the recording. Consequently, error-free tracking results become progressively less likely as recordings lengthen and cohorts grow. Even state-of-the-art multi-object tracking (MOT) methods that leverage appearance cues do so only to make each assignment more robust. This robustness, however, only delays the inevitable as even the most robust assignment process will eventually make a mistake over prolonged recordings. A mistake that will then persist just as it otherwise would have. Here, we introduce evidence-based re-identification, which uses appearance cues to correct tracking mistakes rather than prevent them. This fundamental shift allows the algorithm to build and progressively enrich appearance representations for each tracked subject. Tracking mistakes are then detected by continuously monitoring the evolution of these representations, triggering a correction whenever two representations drift toward one another in a sustained way. On two distinct, minutes-long benchmarks of mice interacting in enriched environments, motion-only trackers (DeepLabCut, SLEAP, ByteTrack) and the appearance-based BoT-SORT-ReID began accumulating identity errors within seconds, whereas ByteTrack paired with evidence-based re-identification remained reliable, outperforming even ByteTrack paired with the marker-based Tailtag system. This reliability was also positively correlated with the accuracy of the appearance extractor, but only when it was used through evidence-based re-identification. Foundation image encoders (CLIP, MegaDescriptor, DINOv3) showed promising out-of-the-box performance yet still required fine-tuning to be effective. Together, these results show that multi-animal tracking algorithms can remain reliable over prolonged periods only if they can reliably recover from tracking mistakes, and that fine-tuning appearance extractors remains essential to doing so.

items.title: Competing routes back to firing shape population hyperexcitability and its selective suppression
items.abstract: Whether a neuron will fire again is fundamentally a different question from whether a quiescent neuron will activate. Even within the same neuron, successive spikes can follow distinct post-spike trajectories, with after-depolarization permitting early return to firing and depolarization block prolonging inactivity. Therefore, we propose that hyperexcitability involves changes in the opportunities to fire again across the spike cycle, and not just from quiescence. The firing hazard makes these opportunities measurable: in whole-cell recordings of midbrain dopamine neurons, the subthreshold voltage trough resolves a non-monotone aggregate firing hazard into physiologically distinguishable components. We represent these components as competing return pathways within a population renewal model and show that they lead to heterogeneous firing patterns within a single neuronal population subject to a common drive. An immediate-return pathway provides an early opportunity to fire by skipping some stages of recovery, and promotes population hyperexcitability independent of quiescent activation. Conversely, a sequestration pathway diverts recently active neurons into a prolonged non-recruitable state, representing depolarization block or use-dependent blockade. Pharmacological selectivity of anti-seizure medications such as phenytoin and carbamazepine arises from the redistribution of neurons among return pathways at every renewal, with fast-cycling pathological regimes providing more opportunities for renewal and eventual sequestration.

items.title: Object features survive motion at saccadic speed but lose their link to specific objects
items.abstract: Saccadic eye movements sweep objects across the retina at high speed, and this motion is routinely omitted from conscious perception. Whether object identity survives such motion is unclear. In two preregistered experiments (N = 20 and N = 19), we asked how object motion at saccadic speeds, while the eyes fixate, affects object continuity in the object-reviewing paradigm (Kahneman et al., 1992; Sasi et al., 2023). Two Gabor patches each carried a digit, then disappeared and reappeared in place, reappeared displaced, or travelled continuously to their new locations; the intervening interval lasted 300 ms or was matched to the mean or peak speed of a saccade. A target digit then appeared in one patch, and participants identified it. At the long duration, we replicated the Object-Specific Preview Benefit (OSPB): responses were faster when the target had been previewed in that same object than in the other one. At saccadic durations, the OSPB disappeared, and adding a distinguishing surface feature in Experiment 2 did not restore it. The general preview benefit, faster responses to any previewed digit than to a new one, persisted at every duration. Object features therefore survive motion at saccadic speed, but their link to a particular object does not.

items.title: Dual CD40/CD28 co-stimulation reprograms the solid-tumor microenvironment to unleash CAR-T and endogenous anti-tumor immunity
items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, owing to poor T-cell persistence, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and cancer immune evasion. Here we describe LACO-Stim (lymphocytes-APC co-stimulator), a chimeric co-stimulatory molecule composed of an agonistic anti-CD40 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) and the CD28 intracellular signaling domain, such that a single molecule activates CD40-expressing antigen-presenting cells while delivering CD28 co-stimulation to the T cell that bears it. Co-expressed with a 4-1BB-based CAR (LACO-CAR-T), it enhanced anti-tumor activity in vitro and achieved durable, complete in most mice, tumor regression rather than transient control in xenograft and immunocompetent models. In immunocompetent hosts, LACO-CAR-T activated dendritic cells, reprogrammed tumor macrophages toward M1-like, antigen-presenting states, and induced epitope spreading with endogenous CD8 T-cell responses against tumor neoantigens. Single-cell transcriptomics and RNA-velocity analysis revealed coordinated immune remodeling: T cells shifted toward a more stem-like, less terminally exhausted state, regulatory T cells declined in frequency and suppressive function, and myeloid cells acquired antigen-presentation programs while excessive inflammatory and suppressive signaling was restrained. LACO-Stim further synergized with anti-PD-1 blockade to control tumor growth. LACO-Stim thus enables CAR-T cells to coordinate intrinsic T-cell reinforcement with extrinsic immune reprogramming, converting an immunosuppressive TME into a de-inflamed (reduced inflammatory signaling), de-suppressed rather than merely armed niche that supports endogenous anti-tumor immunity.

items.title: Epigenetic Mechanisms Inhibit Smad7 and Contribute to Fibrosis in Crohn's Disease
items.abstract: Background & Aims: TGF-beta1 is a central regulator of profibrotic gene expression, extracellular matrix deposition, and the development of intestinal fibrosis in patients with fibrostenotic Crohns disease (CD). Unlike the increased expression of Smad7 in mucosal and lamina propria monocytes, where it impairs Treg function, mesenchymal cells from patients with fibrostenotic CD do not exhibit elevated Smad7 expression and instead display sustained TGF-beta1 signaling. We therefore sought to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the unexpected silencing of Smad7 in fibrostenotic CD. Methods: Subepithelial myofibroblasts (SEMFs) and muscularis smooth muscle cells were isolated from paired normal and affected ileal tissues obtained from the same patients with each Montreal phenotype of CD, as well as from non-CD controls. Gene expression, RNA-binding affinity, transcriptional activity, promoter methylation, protein levels, and the mechanisms that regulate Smad7 expression were evaluated in ex vivo tissues and primary cultured cells. MicroRNA-21 (miR-21) localization was assessed by RNAscope. miR-21-mediated suppression of Smad7 was investigated using antagomiR-21. Smad7 silencing through promoter hypermethylation was confirmed using 5-Azacytidine treatment and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) knockdown. Smad7 lysine acetylation and Smurf1/2-mediated ubiquitination were examined using selective inhibitors and proximity ligation assays. Results: In SEMFs from patients with fibrostenotic CD, aberrant silencing of Smad7 resulted from DNMT1-dependent promoter hypermethylation and pSmad3-driven, miR-21-mediated degradation of Smad7 mRNA. In addition, Smurf1/2 promoted ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of acetylated Smad7 protein. Inhibition of miR-21 with antagomiR-21 restored Smad7 expression and reduced TGF-beta 1-dependent profibrotic gene expression. Likewise, demethylation with 5-Azacytidine or knockdown of DNMT1 induced Smad7 promoter hypomethylation and restored Smad7 expression. Furthermore, modulation of the balance between p300 acetyltransferase and histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) stabilized Smad7 protein by protecting it from degradation. Conclusions: A distinctive pattern of epigenetic silencing and post-translational regulation of Smad7 was identified in patients with fibrostenotic CD. These mechanisms collectively promote unrestrained TGF-beta1 signaling by suppressing Smad7 expression and stability in SEMFs, thereby contributing to the development of intestinal fibrosis.

items.title: Matrix Gla Protein deficiency reveals a previously unrecognized mucosal calcification in the mouse airways
items.abstract: Tracheal calcification is a common finding that is considered to have limited clinical significance when detected most often in elderly individuals. Despite its frequent occurrence, the cellular and molecular mechanisms at the origin of tracheal calcification remain largely unexplored. In this context, we aimed to characterize the development of tracheal calcification, and to determine the role of matrix Gla protein (MGP), a major inhibitor of ectopic calcification whose genetic or pharmacologic deficiency is associated with premature tracheal calcification in humans. We found that wild-type mice undergo an unexpected early physiologic calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings beginning around one month after birth. This calcification progresses in a dynamic rostro-caudal sequence through a process involving terminal differentiation of tracheal chondrocytes. These findings challenge the prevailing view that tracheal cartilage is a permanent hyaline cartilage and instead reveals an early and highly organized physiologic calcification process. Furthermore, our findings further identify MGP as a key regulator of calcification within the respiratory tract. Indeed, MGP deficiency not only markedly accelerates tracheal cartilage calcification through a similar pattern and mechanism but also induces a previously unrecognized calcification of the tracheal mucosa, a lesion absent in wild-type mice. These alterations could partly explain the respiratory manifestations observed in MGP-deficient patients having Keutel syndrome, which include dyspnea, cough, stridor, and recurrent infections, symptoms previously being mainly attributed to calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings.

items.title: Reticulation-Aware Dissimilarities for Phylogenetic Networks
items.abstract: Dissimilarity measures play a critical role in phylogenetics. They help quantify the accuracy of inferences when the ground truth is known, allow comparisons of inferences obtained using different methods, and provide a tool for summarizing sets of phylogenies. A wide array of dissimilarity measures has been introduced for phylogenetic trees over the past half-century, and they vary in their mathematical properties, empirical behavior, and computational complexity. When the evolutionary history involves reticulate processes, such as hybridization and horizontal gene transfer, it is represented by phylogenetic networks. Although the study of phylogenetic network dissimilarity is less established than its tree counterpart, the past two decades have seen an increasing number of measures developed for phylogenetic networks. However, while some have established mathematical properties---for example, metricity on certain classes of phylogenetic networks---none properly separates reticulation disagreement from tree-like disagreement. This is the rationale behind the introduction of the hybrid ancestry error (HAE) measure by Dai and Molloy. The HAE measure, however, is too simplistic to distinguish different reticulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel family of network dissimilarity measures that explicitly account for reticulation differences while being more informative than HAE. We prove that our measures are pseudometrics on rooted binary phylogenetic networks on a fixed taxon set, with two instantiations yielding metrics on binary level-1 networks. Empirically, the measures remain sensitive to reticulation errors as network size grows and respond to changes in hybrid identity and parental placement. Calibration experiments further characterize the measures' behavior under network edits of various magnitudes. Data Availability: The dissimilarities are implemented in the PhyNetPy library, available at https://github.com/NakhlehLab/PhyNetPy. All the data simulated for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23933421. Funding: This work was supported in part by the NSF grants DMS/NIGMS-2153704 and DBI-2420499. Declaration of AI-assisted technologies: During the preparation of this work, the authors used OpenAI's Codex (GPT-6 Astra) and Anthropic's Claude (Fable 5) to assist with editing manuscript text, developing proofs and analysis code, and preparing figures. The authors reviewed and edited the resulting material, verified the analyses, and take full responsibility for the content of this article.

items.title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
items.corresponding_institution: CSIR - North East Institute of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.

items.title: LIGR-Nue for the global mapping of the bacterial sRNA targetome in vivo
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics, School of Life Sciences, University of Hyderabad, Hyderabad 500 046, India
items.abstract: Interactions between regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) and their target transcripts are central for post-transcriptional regulation in bacteria. Based on RNA-seq analysis, we determined the relative abundance of several sRNAs in the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 under photoautotrophic growth conditions and after transfer to darkness. We observed an increase in the abundance of the sRNAs DsiR1 to 58.6% and of CsiR1 to 19% of the sRNA transcriptome after transfer to darkness. We then developed a duplex-directed, transcriptome-wide mapping strategy of RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, called LIGR-Nue, which involves aminomethyltrioxsalen-mediated UV cross-linking, proximity ligation, crosslink reversal, reverse transcription and sequencing. The data were analysed using the RNANUE pipeline for the detection of chimeric reads and mapping, and benchmarked against known targetome data for the sRNAs PsrR1 and NsiR4. Using this methodology, we identified RNA-RNA interactions, such as PsrR1 as a regulator of carbon assimilation, and DsiR1 as a global silencing factor of photosynthesis-associated mRNAs in the dark. This data enables the comprehensive analysis of sRNA functions in post-transcriptional gene regulation. LIGR-Nue is broadly applicable to map RNA-RNA interactions in bacteria.

items.title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Veterinary Biosciences, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland; Department of Virology, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland
items.abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at [≥]99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

items.title: Uncovering cross-signal interactions in single-cell and spatial omics
items.abstract: Individual cells simultaneously encode multiple biological signals in their gene expression profiles, including spatial position, circadian phase, and disease state. These signals can be entangled in complex ways, including circadian patterns that vary along disease progression and cell cycle dynamics that shift along developmental trajectories. While methods to disentangle such signals have been recently developed, characterizing the interaction itself between multicellular signals along with its effects on tissue function, localizing cellular subpopulations which exhibit signal interactions, and identifying potential candidate genes which drive such interactions, all remain major challenges. We present CRISP which characterizes signal interactions in single-cell gene expression data based on the correspondence between the multiple, probabilistic signal-specific projections of the data.
