Across simulations with tunable couplings and four single-cell and spatial transcriptomic datasets, CRISP recovers diverse biological signal interactions and localizes them to informative cellular subpopulations and groups of associated genes; CRISP distinguishes healthy from fibrotic liver samples and localizes the loss of zonation-position coupling to individual fibrotic hepatocytes, resolves the asymmetric coupling of TGF-{beta} response, EMT, and cell-cycle phase to specific cell subpopulations, and flags transcriptionally delayed hepatocytes in Plasmodium liver infection. Beyond quantifying and localizing signal interactions, CRISP can refine existing labels, uncover continuous cellular transitions and reveal condition-associated genes.

items.title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
items.abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

items.title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
items.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

items.title: Temporal Dynamics of Multi-Item Working Memory Maintenance in Human Gaze Patterns and EEG
items.abstract: Maintaining multiple items in working memory (WM) requires the allocation of limited resources, which may involve prioritizing individual items over others. Previous work has suggested that attentional prioritization can vary rhythmically between WM samples, but direct empirical evidence for such temporal fluctuations remains scarce. Here, we recorded eye-tracking and EEG to track the temporal dynamics of multi-item processing while participants maintained up to three object orientations in WM. Whereas EEG encoding was only short-lived, miniature gaze patterns reflected the orientations of all three items throughout the entire WM delay and showed systematic load and serial position effects. Contrary to rhythmic sampling accounts, however, we found no evidence that eye movements alternated between the concurrently maintained items. Furthermore, the strength of WM encoding in gaze was not modulated by frontal theta activity in EEG, suggesting that oculomotor encoding was not directly coupled to rhythmic neural dynamics associated with WM and internal attention. Together, our findings indicate that the oculomotor signature of visuospatial WM processing was rather stably shaped by all of the simultaneously maintained items. The results further corroborate that eye-tracking and EEG provide complementary windows into the temporal dynamics of WM.

items.title: OpenDrive: An Open-Source Microdrive for Large-Scale Neurophysiology
items.abstract: Neuropixels-NHP probes have ushered in a new era of high-density neurophysiology recording in large animal models. Here, we present OpenDrive, an open-source microdrive system designed specifically for acute insertion of Neuropixels-NHPs. OpenDrive combines a custom motorized microdrive, six-drive control console, and software platform. Compared with commercially available options, OpenDrive offers (1) low cost, (2) precise, accurate, and stable probe movement, (3) scalability to many-probe recording, and (4) open-source hardware designs and software. In our experiments, OpenDrive has already supported recordings from thousands of neurons across a variety of cortical and subcortical structures. By lowering technical barriers and enabling community-driven development with OpenDrive, we aim to accelerate Neuropixels recording in large animal models.

items.title: SIFT: Syncmer-Informed Selection of Haplotypes for T2T Imputation
items.abstract: Genome patching improves the completeness of fragmented assemblies by filling unresolved gaps with sequences from reference genomes. Pangenome panels provide diverse candidate haplotypes for this task, but identifying suitable references efficiently becomes increasingly challenging as these panels grow. We present SIFT, a compressed indexing method for selecting reference haplotypes for genome patching with ImpuT2T. SIFT combines closed-syncmer parsing, phrase-level indexing, and pseudo-maximal exact match (pseudo-MEM) queries. Closed syncmers provide a context-independent parsing rule with bounded distances between consecutive selected positions, enabling consistent parsing of reference and query sequences. We demonstrate that two closed syncmers determine the distance at which they can occur consecutively in any string, so that equal substrings of two parses represent identical sequences and no gap sequence need be stored. SIFT indexes the reference parse and its reverse using run-length compressed suffix arrays and adapts the Boyer-Moore-Li search procedure to identify pseudo-MEMs between the reference parse and query parse. It then aggregates matching evidence to identify candidate reference haplotypes for downstream patching. This framework connects compressed sequence indexing with haplotype selection and provides a basis for querying large reference panels at the phrase level. SIFT is publicly available under the GNU license at https://github.com/EddieFerro/SIFT.

items.title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
items.corresponding_institution: Federal Research and Clinical Center of Physical-Chemical Medicine of Federal Medical Biological Age
items.abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

items.title: Enhanced antitumour activity of combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy is associated with reduced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix-remodelling signatures in gastric cancer
items.abstract: Background The combination of PD-1 blockade, HER2-targeted therapy and chemotherapy improves outcomes in HER2-positive advanced gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. However, chemotherapy can independently alter the tumour microenvironment, making the biological effects of PD-1 and HER2 targeting difficult to distinguish. We therefore investigated how PD-1 and HER2 blockade, alone and in combination, affect tumour growth and associated transcriptional programmes. Methods Immunodeficient NOG mice received human PBMCs by tail-vein injection. Three days later, NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells were implanted subcutaneously. Mice were randomised to vehicle, pembrolizumab, trastuzumab, or combination treatment. Tumour growth was assessed, and bulk RNA sequencing was used to identify treatment-associated changes in gene expression, pathway enrichment, and tumour, stromal, and immune cell-associated signatures. Results Combined treatment produced greater tumour growth control than either monotherapy. Trastuzumab-treated tumours showed enrichment of immune activation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and TGF{beta}-associated signatures, whereas pembrolizumab alone produced a limited transcriptional effect. Combination treatment was associated with reduced proliferation, EMT, and stromal-remodelling signatures, alongside increased cytotoxic immune-associated signatures. Expression of extracellular matrix-associated genes, including VCAN, SPARC, POSTN, collagen genes, and FAP, was lower in combination-treated tumours. Complement-related transcriptional pathways were also enriched. Conclusions In this chemotherapy-free model, combined PD-1 blockade and HER2-targeted therapy was associated with greater tumour growth control, enrichment of cytotoxic immune-associated transcriptional signatures, and reduced EMT and extracellular matrix remodelling signatures. These findings provide hypotheses for further mechanistic validation.

items.title: Curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in homogeneous and heterogeneous tumors
items.abstract: During treatment, dosing protocols with identical total dose may favor one schedule over another depending on how exposure is distributed over time. In homogeneous cell populations, Jensen's inequality has been shown to predict whether continuous or intermittent high-dose followed by low-dose is favored, based on the curvature of the concentration-effect function. Scheduling ordering can be performed based on curvature only: concave functions favor continuous dosing while convex functions favor intermittent dosing schedules with a high time-variance. However, tumors exhibit heterogeneous drug sensitivities, and treatment preferentially eliminates drug-sensitive cells, progressively shifting the surviving population toward greater drug resistance. Whether this treatment-induced selection can reverse curvature-based schedule ordering remains unclear. We develop a mathematical framework in which phenotypes share a common concentration-effect function but differ by fixed, nonnegative sensitivity scales. We prove that the ordering of equal-mean schedules is administrated solely by the scalar cumulative treatment effect, that is, by the curvature of the effect function alone. Consequently, baseline heterogeneity and treatment-induced selection can alter the magnitude of treatment response and the composition of surviving cells, but cannot reverse the ordering of equal-mean schedules predicted by the curvature of the single-cell concentration-effect function. This preservation holds across different temporal dosing profiles and repeated treatment cycles. Our work uncovers a general principle that curvature-based schedule ordering is preserved in heterogeneous tumors despite treatment-induced selection toward resistance.

items.title: BAF complexes cooperate with lineage-restricted transcription factors to establish cell-state-specific regulatory programs
items.corresponding_institution: Princess Maxima Center for Pediatric Oncology
items.abstract: BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) complexes are essential regulators of chromatin organization and cell identity. Genes encoding BAF subunits are among the most frequently mutated in human cancer. Yet, how disruption of a single subunit gives rise to distinct tumor states remains poorly understood. Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRTs) provide a compelling model, as they are uniformly driven by bi-allelic loss of the BAF subunit SMARCB1, yet segregate into distinct molecular subtypes. Using integrated multi-omics profiling of patient-derived ATRT organoids and primary tumor tissues, we show that transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes upon SMARCB1 reconstitution are directed by subtype- and lineage-specific transcription factor (TF) repertoires. Genome-wide binding and transcriptomic analyses reveal that SMARCB1 reconstitution enables the lineage-specific TF RFX4 to engage regulatory elements and activate neuronal differentiation programs, partially reprogramming ATRT-MYC toward an ATRT-SHH-like identity. Together, these findings demonstrate that SMARCB1 loss disrupts TF-dependent chromatin priming, revealing that the lineage-specific regulatory output of BAF complexes is constrained by the underlying TF repertoire.

items.title: Combined pharmacotherapy suppress ferroptosis and inflammation after neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage
items.abstract: Neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is a common complication of extremely premature newborns, and results in reduced neurogenesis, white matter injury, cortical atrophy, and subsequent cerebral palsy, learning and memory disabilities. However, the impact of IVH on the hippocampus, an area critical for memory and learning capabilities throughout life, remains relatively unexplored. Using a preterm rabbit pup model that structurally resembles human perinatal brain development, we report, widespread hematoma and iron accumulation in the hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) following IVH. This accumulation is facilitated by the anatomical positioning of the hippocampus within the unidirectional CSF flow pathway and the vulnerability of the immature dentate gyrus vasculature. Sulforaphane (SFN; an activator of nuclear factor erythroid 2 related factor 2 [Nrf2] transcriptional factor and anti-inflammatory pathways) and deferoxamine (DFN; an iron chelator) reduced iron deposition, free hemoglobin, and activated glial cells (sp. astrocytes and microglia), particularly in the DG molecular layer and hilar regions. The attenuated inflammatory responses correlate with decreased ferroptosis-mediated neuronal death, and substantial restoration of the dysregulated gene pathways associated with inflammation, immune activation, and neuronal cell death in the developing hippocampal/DG region. This was associated with a gene profile favoring ferroptotic cell death rather than apoptosis or autophagy pathways. Moreover, we also identified a regional specificity to certain effects as no astrogliosis was observed in hippocampal CA1 to CA4 regions after IVH or when compared with healthy controls. Our study is the first to demonstrate hippocampal hematoma and iron accumulation associated pathologic mechanisms following neonatal IVH. The results provide mechanistic insights into hippocampal injury as well as a therapeutic proof-of-concept for targeting iron toxicity and inflammation in the developing brain to mitigate injury. These results justify extending analyses of injury reversal to long-term postnatal ages and behavior studies to assess therapeutic potential. The study illustrates novel therapeutic interventions that attenuate early mediators of injury that improves recovery of hippocampal/DG formation/maturation and neuroprotection after neonatal IVH. We speculate that these protective effects may prolong donor stem cell survival thus, potentiating benefits of living cellular therapy in the future.

items.title: Reprogramming transcription factor networks with a HOX inhibitor to address Huntington's disease biology beyond mutant huntingtin
items.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG-repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene. Although inherited CAG-repeat length and the underlying somatic instability are key determinants of age at onset, they explain only part of onset variability, suggesting additional disease mechanisms. We applied the Core Coefficient (CC), a transcription-factor (TF) network-decoding technology that quantifies TF functional dominance, to >100 post-mortem neuronal transcriptomes from HD and control brain datasets. Among human TF families, the HOX family is the only family that uniformly exhibits quiescence in controls versus large and significant functional dominance in vulnerable neurons of each HD donor brain we investigated. HOX TFs are already dominant at Vonsattel grade 0 and at inherited CAG-repeat length. The magnitude of HOX CC values correlates with age at onset and increases with disease grade and CAG-Age Product. HOX TFs form a self-sustained pathological unit targeting >4,000 genes implicated in neuronal patterning, identity, stress, signaling, structure, and senescence. In zQ175 mice, abrogation of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein production only transiently attenuates HOX dominance and does not durably eliminate it. COR-H800, a HOX inhibitor, restored TF-network hierarchy toward wild type, normalizing the functional dominance of transcription factors involved in neuronal differentiation, cell-fate determination, and developmental patterning, and improved disease-relevant phenotypes in R6/2 mice. These findings support the direct selective inhibition of HOX TFs to address the aberrant transcriptional state that can persist despite mHTT lowering or somatic instability-targeted therapeutic interventions.

items.title: An LFP-based characterization of population-level heterogeneity during motor preparation & execution
items.abstract: The goal of the present work is to characterize mesoscale heterogeneity of population-level neural activity in the motor areas during motor preparation and execution using high-frequency local field potentials (HF-LFPs). Understanding the distribution of neural activity at this scale is necessary since ensembles of neural populations underlie most behaviors. HF-LFPs have emerged as a promising signal for such analysis due to their stability and relationship with cortical population dynamics. Here we analyzed HF-LFPs in non-human primates performing a reach-to-grasp task. We quantified three complementary aspects of heterogeneity: variance, latent dimensionality, and directional coherence. Heterogeneity varied by region and neuromotor state, and was specific to the motor behavior being implemented, even in regions exhibiting high correlation. In addition, more heterogeneous activity tended to better encode neuromotor states. Namely, regions and neuromotor states exhibiting higher variance and dimensionality yielded superior motor decoding performance. Further analyses involving low-dimensional linear projections of the signals revealed rich intra-region interactions between ensembles of populations. The present work helps establish intra-region heterogeneity as a multi-faceted and informative measure of neural activity, even on small spatial scales. It also establishes HF-LFPs as an effective signal for capturing complex intra-region dynamics, making it a suitable candidate for multi-region, systems-level analysis.

items.title: An application of fNIRS for the prediction of hearing thresholds in sleeping infants: a proof of principle
items.abstract: This study applied a two-component-response modelling approach to fNIRS recordings obtained from naturally sleeping infants presented with auditory stimuli at different sound intensities. We investigated whether the relationship between fNIRS response measures and stimulus intensity could be modelled to estimate individual auditory hearing thresholds. In the normal-hearing group, 75% of infants had threshold estimates for the sound /ba/ within the expected normal-hearing range, with an estimated mean equivalent normal loudness (ENL) of 10.72 dB HL (SD 8.64 dB HL). A case study further explored the potential application of this approach in an infant with hearing impairment, highlighting the importance of reliable responses at lower stimulus intensities and appropriate regression model selection. These findings provide preliminary evidence that cortical haemodynamic responses can be quantitatively related to sound intensity for estimating auditory sensitivity.

items.title: Hippocampal dorsal and ventral CA2 enable social discrimination after acute social defeat
items.abstract: Remembering the valence of conspecifics based on past aggressive compared to non-aggressive interactions is important for proper adaptive social behaviors. How a single naturalistic encounter establishes a lasting memory of the valence of the experience remains unclear. Our recent work shows that the CA2 region in ventral hippocampus, unlike dorsal CA2, is not required for social novelty discrimination but does contribute with dorsal CA2 to promote social aggression. How CA2 contributes to valence-associated social memory across the dorsoventral axis remains unresolved. We developed an acute defeat-associated social threat discrimination memory (AD-STDM) paradigm after which a male mouse preferentially interacted with a familiar non-aggressor male compared to a familiar aggressor male 24 h after a single defeat episode. Chemogenetic inhibition of Avpr1b-expressing CA2 neurons in either dorsal or ventral hippocampus during learning impaired subsequent discrimination. Acute defeat also increased cFos expression in ventral CA2 neurons relative to non-aggressive social interaction. Thus, although ventral CA2 is not required for social novelty recognition memory, it is required for social memory of an aversive social experience, with a relatively greater level of neural activation during aversive compared to non-aversive social encounters. In contrast, dorsal CA2 is required for both non-aversive and aversive forms of social memory.

items.title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA; Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA
items.abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

items.title: Cytotoxic CD4+ exTregs expressing KLRG1 retain immunosuppressive function in cancer
items.abstract: The role of cytotoxic CD4+ T cells in cancer remains controversial, with both pro- and anti-tumor functionality described. Based on a prior observation that putatively cytotoxic KLRG1+ FoxP3- conventional T cells (Tconv) associated with tumor progression, we deeply investigated the phenotype and function of KLRG1+ Tconv in multiple murine tumor models and in human clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) specimens. We found KLRG1+ Tconv have a conserved, highly activated, terminally differentiated phenotype across species. In murine tumors, KLRG1+ Tconv resemble tumor-infiltrating regulatory T cells (Tregs) at both transcriptional and proteomic levels, upregulating a spectrum of exhaustion-related checkpoint receptors, producing IL-10 and granzyme B (GzmB), and silencing expression of IFN{gamma} and TNF. Functionally, KLRG1+ Tconv exhibited immunosuppressive function in ex vivo assays. Using an in vivo Treg fate mapping approach in tumor-bearing mice, we found a subset of KLRG1+ Tconv are derived from Tregs that have lost FoxP3 protein expression. Ex vivo functional assays demonstrated the exTreg component of the KLRG1+ Tconv compartment is responsible for IL-10 production and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. In treatment studies, we found that KLRG1-targeted antibody-mediated depletion was more efficient than anti-KLRG1 blockade at slowing tumor growth and improving survival, with responses associating with depletion of intratumoral KLRG1+ Tconv and Tregs. In sum, our study discovered a novel conserved pathway of CD4+ T cell plasticity, wherein intratumoral, cytotoxic KLRG1+ CD4+ Tconv cells can be derived from Tregs and maintain immunosuppressive function, despite loss of FoxP3, and that KLRG1-targeted depletion may outperform KLRG1 blockade as an immunotherapeutic strategy in cancer.

items.title: Basic-peptide depletion and precursor masking in bottom-up proteomics
items.corresponding_institution: William Harvey Research Institute, Faculty of Medicine and Dentistry, Queen Mary University of London, Charterhouse Square, London EC1M 6BQ, UK; Barts Health NH
items.abstract: Biomarker proteomics studies report protein identities at the canonical precursor level, yet the underlying mass-spectrometry evidence consists of peptides whose physicochemical properties may diverge from the annotated protein. We reanalyzed peptide-level evidence from public datasets with a proteoform-aware pipeline that maps detected peptides to canonical sequences under a five-level confidence taxonomy, computes sequence-derived physicochemical features for precursors, peptides, and detected regions, and tests class-composition bias against digestion-matched backgrounds. Across ten public studies spanning five result-file formats and 70,020 peptide-evidence rows, detected peptides are depleted in the basic isoelectric-point class relative to their own proteins' theoretical tryptic peptides (fixed-effect odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.44-0.46; leave-one-study-out envelope 0.44-0.49). The depletion is absent among fully tryptic peptides (OR 1.06) and concentrates in missed-cleavage peptides (OR 0.62-0.57), is invariant to detected-abundance stratification, and retains its direction under three independent pI-calculator models. Case studies reveal both directions of precursor-centric masking. Two orthogonal validations ground the framework: a digestion-free synthetic-peptide analysis (basic-class odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.76 under standard DDA) and a paired top-down benchmark, in which detected regions recover top-down sequence space (90% of spans overlapped) but do not delimit proteoform boundaries (8% containment). Pipeline, data, and code are public.

items.title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
items.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

items.title: Detection of Maximal Exact Matches in Terabases of Genome Assemblies in Compressed Space and Sublinear Time
items.abstract: Detection of long exact matches between a pair of genomes has historically been a fundamental operation in genomics. Similarly, detection of long exact matches between all pairs of haplotypes in a large panel of genotyping array data or whole-genome sequencing variant calls is a fundamental operation in population genetics. Thanks to various recent pangenome efforts, for the first time, large panels of high-quality genome assemblies are being constructed. Therefore, we propose the intersection of these two approaches: detection of long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in panels of hundreds to thousands of high-quality assemblies. Since these datasets would contain trillions of basepairs, practically detecting all exact matches requires algorithms operating in at most linear time and compressed space. Previous methods such as Mumemto achieve this, but running them on terabase-sized pangenomes still took very large space and long time. Here, we describe more efficient algorithms for outputting all long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in compressed space and sublinear time given a compressed index of the panel. Given the construction of an O(r) space compressed index--a one-time cost that can be done in compressed space and close to linear time with previous work--we describe three algorithms taking O(r) words of memory: (1) computing all supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) in O(r) time, (2) computing all supermaximal exact matches and their occurrences in O(r + occ) time, and (3) computing all maximal exact matches (MEMs) in O(r + occ) time, where r is the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform of the panel of assemblies and occ is the number of occurrences or matches outputted. Our algorithms use 7.5 times less memory than state-of-the-art competitors on a dataset of human centromere assemblies from 625 haplotypes. They are also 20 times faster if index construction time is counted, and 2,500 times faster if index construction is excluded. Finally, we perform an analysis of all-vs-all MEMs in all well-assembled centromeres of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset that reveals multiple novel insights into structural variation in centromeres. For example, we find that the active -satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) array of Chromosome 2 is flanked by a ~200 kbp inversion on one side and a ~200-300 kbp pseudopalindromic sequence on the other. We also detect large segmental duplications in the centromere of every chromosome except Chromosome Y. These segmental duplications range in size from hundreds of kbp to multiple Mbp and occur both in and out of the active -satellite HOR arrays. Our computational results make pairwise MEM analyses possible in pangenomes, while our biological results show they are likely to be useful. Our algorithms are implemented as TeraMEM in the TeraTools suite available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.

items.title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
items.abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.

items.title: Visual object recognition in the fly: the internal representation of a predator drives defensive behaviour
items.abstract: Animals recognize visual objects and respond to them appropriately to survive. This process is thought to unfold in stages: the visual scene is first deconstructed into constituent features, which are then reconstructed into representations of object identity and relayed to motor circuits. Here we define a neural circuit in Drosophila that underlies the visual recognition of a natural predator, the parasitoid wasp, and orchestrates defence. We found that flies exhibit a repertoire of directed defensive actions structured by the wasp's position within the fly's field of view. Expression of these behaviours is driven by visual detection of a conspicuous morphological cue -- the wasp's elongated antennae. A small subset of lobula columnar (LC) visual projection neuron types are required for defence and are activated by constituent visual features of the wasp. Three LC types respond selectively to the wasp's antennae, and relay this information to LC9, which sums antennal- and body-feature signals to form a composite representation of the wasp. Spatial filtering of this representation onto a descending premotor pathway translates the wasp's location in visual space into directed defence. Feature combination followed by spatial filtering may constitute a general mechanism for coupling object identity to context-appropriate action.

items.title: Geometric determinants of time series learning and attractor stability in closed-loop circuits
items.abstract: Skilled volitional behaviours arise from recurrent circuits, which can sustain structured neural activity in the absence of external drive, through internal feedback. But how such autonomous activity is learned and stability maintained in distributed motor circuits is poorly understood. To investigate the relationship between neural representations and learning we compared a cortex-like recurrent neural network (RNN) and a cortico-cerebellar-like circuit with a feed-forward layer (RNN+FFL), both in a closed-loop configuration. RNN+FFL circuits learned periodic target signals that parameter-matched RNNs could not, due to a failure to form attractor states. Decomposing population activity by frequency, rather than variance, separated the task-relevant and task-irrelevant subspaces. Quantifying their geometric arrangement revealed that the feed-forward layer improved learning and stabilised attractor states by increasing the angles within and between these subspaces. Our results show that task-specific representational geometry is a better predictor of periodic time series learning in recurrent circuits than classical global measures such as dimensionality.

items.title: Phase-specific stimulation of prefrontal beta oscillations modulates distinct cognitive processes
items.abstract: Oscillatory phase has been proposed to organize neural information processing, but whether endogenous phase can be leveraged to causally shape human cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) delivered at specific phases of endogenous beta oscillations over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates working memory and response inhibition. Participants received EEG phase-controlled, closed-loop rTMS delivered at either the peak or trough of their endogenous beta rhythm, using each participant's dominant beta frequency (20-30 Hz). A conventional 20-Hz rTMS delivered independently of the beta phase served as an active control. Compared to this control and each other, peak-targeted rTMS improved response inhibition, whereas trough-targeted rTMS improved working memory. Both phase-specific behavioral effects were accompanied by corresponding increases in event-related potentials, which were not observed after conventional stimulation. Across participants, behavioral improvements correlated with stimulation-induced electrophysiological changes. Finally, phase-specific rTMS induced distinct DLPFC network expansions that complemented the behavioral effects: peak stimulation enhanced posterior centro-parietal connectivity for inhibitory control, while trough stimulation expanded anterior prefrontal networks for working memory. These findings provide first evidence that opposite phases of endogenous prefrontal beta oscillations coordinate distinct cognitive and neural processes. This establishes prefrontal beta phase as a causal dimension for shaping executive function and as a target for prefrontal rTMS to modulate cognition and non-invasively probe phase-dependent brain function.

items.title: Evidence of silent nociceptor activation during the formalin test in rats
items.abstract: Background: Abnormal ongoing activity in C-mechano-insensitive (C-Mi) nociceptors is seen in patients with chronic pain. These 'silent' nociceptors are often under-reported in preclinical pain models - precisely because they aren't mechanically sensitive. The formalin test is widely used as a preclinical model of persistent sensitisation characterised by two behavioural phases, where phase 2 is considered to reflect central sensitisation and the role of peripheral afferent drive in its maintenance is disputed. Increased activity in C-mechanosensitive (C-M) nociceptors has been reported during both phases, but the behaviour of C-Mi nociceptors has not been assessed. Methods: Multi-contact microneurography was conducted from the saphenous nerve of male and female rats. An activity dependent slowing protocol was used to segregate C-fibres, and responses to mechanical stimuli were assessed. Formalin- (2.5%) or saline-evoked activity was then assessed during the two test phases. Results: 168 A- and C-fibres were identified with latency tracking, and classified using activity dependent slowing into C-M and C-Mi nociceptors. ADS-classified C-Mi nociceptors were active in both phase 1 and phase 2 (33.3% and 31.0%, n=18 and n=16, respectively). We find no evidence that formalin mechanically sensitises C-Mi nociceptors or alters the ADS profiles of C-fibres. There was no sex specific difference in C-fibre classes or the effect of formalin. Conclusions: These results indicate the presence of ongoing activity in a substantial population of C-Mi nociceptors in a commonly used persistent pain assay that may play a role in the sensitisation that is seen in phase 2 of the behavioural response.

items.title: B cells dominate the heart immune infiltrate during chronic infectious cardiomyopathy
items.corresponding_institution: York Biomedical Research Institute and Hull York Medical School, University of York, York, UK
items.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and spatially resolved multi-omics have revolutionised our understanding of the cellular and molecular niches governing cardiac homeostasis and acute injury. However, the immune-stromal networks sustaining long-term, chronic heart pathology remain poorly defined, largely due to a paucity of physiologically relevant experimental models. Here, through a side-by-side multi-omic comparison of Trypanosoma cruzi-infected mouse models displaying contrasting degrees of chronic myocardial pathology and fibrosis, we define the long-term cellular landscape of the inflamed fibrotic heart. We reveal that class-switched, antibody-secreting plasma B cells represent the predominant immune subset infiltrating the fibrotic myocardium. CellChat intercellular communication modelling identifies plasma cell-fibroblast crosstalk as the strongest immune-stromal interaction in the fibrosis-prone heart, driven by predicted matrix anchoring (CD44-collagen/laminin) and molecular survival axes (App-Cd74, C3-Cr2). Supporting these computational predictions, immunofluorescence and spatial profiling confirm close proximity between plasma B cells and fibroblasts, alongside a striking accumulation of B cells embedded within extracellular matrix-rich cardiac scars. This localised B cell response maintains prominent pools of parasite-reactive and heart-autoreactive antibody-secreting cells despite a lack of detectable parasite signal in their immediate micro-vicinity. Together, these findings identify a matrix-associated plasma B cell-fibroblast niche as a central driver of chronic cardiac remodelling, revealing how persistent tissue scarring can become decoupled from direct local pathogen presence.

items.title: HCMV glycoprotein B, but not the pentameric complex, is a key target of antibody-mediated phagocytosis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pediatrics, Weill Cornell Medicine, New York, NY
items.abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a leading infectious cause of birth defects globally with devastating fetal health outcomes, and there is currently no HCMV vaccine available. Glycoprotein B (gB) and the pentameric complex (PC) are immunodominant HCMV envelope proteins and candidates of interest in vaccine development due to their ability to elicit strong anti-HCMV neutralization responses. Recent evidence implicates non-neutralizing antibody functions in protection from vertical HCMV transmission, but the involvement of gB and PC in these responses remains incompletely understood. We evaluated immune responses against HCMV elicited by a gB protein subunit vaccine with and without PC in a preclinical rabbit study. Despite improved neutralization and inhibition of cell-associated viral spread, the inclusion of PC did not enhance antibody-mediated phagocytosis or Fc{gamma}R activation against HCMV virions or infected cells compared to gB alone. We additionally found a reduction in phagocytosis function by an HCMV hyperimmune globulin when blocked against gB, but not PC, suggesting that gB is a target of phagocytosis-mediating antibodies while PC is not. Given that antibody-mediated phagocytosis but not neutralization has been associated with protection from vertical HCMV transmission, these findings support the continued assessment of gB, but not PC, as a vaccine antigen for the prevention of vertical transmission via non-neutralizing antibodies to reduce the congenital HCMV burden worldwide.

items.title: Structural and functional characterization of polyclonal antibody responses reveals shared and distinct antigenic features of RSV and hMPV fusion proteins
items.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), members of the Pneumoviridae family, circulate widely and are leading causes of hospitalization for acute respiratory infections in infants and older adults. The viral fusion (F) protein in its prefusion (preF) conformation is the primary target of neutralizing antibodies, yet how naturally elicited circulating polyclonal antibodies are distributed across its antigenic landscape remains poorly understood. Here, we combined serological profiling, site-specific antibody competition assays and electron microscopy-based polyclonal epitope mapping (EMPEM) to characterize preF-directed immunity to RSV and hMPV in healthy adults. All donors exhibited detectable preF-binding antibodies that positively correlated with virus neutralization and broadly recognized multiple antigenic sites, consistent with immunodominance patterns predicted by a surface-centric computational model. Despite this overall similarity, the distribution of responses across individual antigenic sites differed between RSV and hMPV. EMPEM analyses revealed consistent targeting of the highly neutralization-sensitive preF apex (site O) in both viruses, alongside less abundant responses against equatorial and upper-middle epitopes (sites II, III, IV and V). We additionally observed antibody-bound destabilized preF, supporting a model in which antibody binding promotes transient opening of the preF trimer and may interfere with the conformational rearrangements required for membrane fusion. Together, these findings highlight apex-directed antibodies as a prominent feature of naturally acquired pneumovirus immunity in adults and reveal both shared and distinct patterns of antigenic recognition that may inform next-generation vaccine design and antibody-based prophylactics.

items.title: Tetravalent dengue mRNA vaccination orchestrates balanced four-serotype immunity with durable memory and protection in mice.
items.abstract: An effective dengue vaccine must establish durable immunity across four dengue virus (DENV) serotypes, evade antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), and overcome immune imprinting from prior exposure. Here, we developed TetprM-E mRNA-LNP, a tetravalent vaccine comprising LNP-formulated nucleoside-modified mRNAs encoding DENV1-4 precursor membrane-envelope (prM-E) antigens, and evaluated its immunogenicity, durability, protection and breath across serotype-specific immune backgrounds. Three immunization strategies elicited neutralizing titers greater than 1:1500 against each serotype. Passive transfer of immune sera conferred 100% survival and reduced viremia after lethal DENV2 challenge in immunocompromised mice. Vaccination induced DENV envelope (env)-specific CD8+T cells and CD4-dependent germinal-center responses. DENV env-binding antibodies persisted for 34 weeks alongside DENV env-specific memory B cells. Vaccine-elicited sera showed no measurable in vitro ADE. Although monovalent priming initially biased antibody responses, TetprM-E mRNA-LNP vaccination broadened neutralization across DENV1-4 regardless of priming serotype. Together, TetprM-E mRNA-LNP elicits broad, durable, and protective immunity despite serologic constraints from pre-existing immunity.

items.title: The antagonism of sex chromosomes and sex hormones dictates outcomes in Th17 cell-mediated central nervous system autoimmunity.
items.corresponding_institution: axe Neurosciences, Centre de recherche du CHU de Québec-Université Laval, Pavillon CHUL, 2705 boulevard Laurier, Quebec City, QC G1V 4G2, Canada
items.abstract: Biological sex traits are shaped by the combined effects of both sex hormones and chromosomes. How these factors interact in sex-related autoimmune diseases, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), has been a subject of intense recent interest. Here, using the Four Core Genotype (FCG) mouse model, in which these two variables can be disentangled, we describe an antagonism between sex hormones and chromosomes that potently influences outcomes in T helper 17 (Th17)-driven progressive central nervous system (CNS) autoimmunity. Male gonadal hormones dampen disease severity, irrespective of sex chromosome complement, by promoting a Wnt/{beta}-catenin signaling program associated with a homeostatic, non-pathogenic Th17 phenotype. By contrast, XY chromosomal complement exacerbates Th17 pathogenicity in a recipient sex-dependent manner; we identify the X-linked molecule SUV39H1 as an inhibitor of inflammatory Th17 cell function. Unexpectedly, we found that hormonally and chromosomally female FCG Th17 cells induced far more severe disease than WT female counterparts despite being genetically identical, pointing to a parental imprinting effect in dictating Th17 cell pathogenicity. These latter investigations uncovered Runx2, a transcription factor previously linked to developmental programs, as a novel negative regulator of the pathogenicity of Th17 cells. Together, our findings establish biological sex as a multilayered regulator of Th17 pathogenicity, revealing distinct and sometimes opposing contributions of hormones, chromosomes, and parental inheritance.

items.title: A G-Quadruplex Containing First Intron Harbors a Functional Polyadenylation Signal in TP53
items.abstract: First introns of mammalian genes are often longer than other introns and may contain regulatory elements, suggesting that they may have roles in gene regulation. We detected a previously unannotated, low abundance intronic transcript, TP53-INT1, using long-read direct RNA sequencing data. TP53-INT1 has low coding potential and terminates within the first and longest intron of TP53. The transcript structure and 3'-end were validated by independent experimental and in silico evidence. We identified a canonical polyadenylation signal upstream of the transcript termination site and demonstrated its functionality using reporter assays. Furthermore, a potential G-quadruplex (G4)-forming sequence was identified upstream of this polyadenylation signal. The G4-forming potential was confirmed using spectroscopic and thermal stability analyses. Complementing the in vitro characterizations, treatment with Pyridostatin, a G4-stabilizing drug, was associated with decreased TP53 expression. Together, these findings characterize a previously unannotated TP53 intronic transcript and reveal a local genomic context combining accessible chromatin, a functional polyadenylation signal, and a potential G4-forming sequence that may influence full-length transcription.

items.title: Sequence context and partner availability specify divergent cell fates from a single transcription factor
items.abstract: Transcription factors drive the gene regulatory networks that control developmental transitions, yet which of their many targets a cell uses remains unresolved. Expressing Cebp, Cebp{beta} or Cebp{delta} identically, alone or with Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and cMyc, gave four outcomes: adipocyte from fibroblasts and neural stem cells, trophectoderm from embryonic stem cells, and myeloid from B cells. Raising Cebp levels changed how many sites it reached, not which sequence it read: clustered motifs maintained somatic enhancers, while spillover onto low-copy sites created de novo enhancers carrying composites of Cebp and cell-type-restricted partners. In fibroblasts, Cebp also redistributed Oct4, Sox2 and Klf4 from early targets, blocking iPSC formation. Supplying the predicted partners rewrote the output: Spi1 redirected Cebp into parallel adipogenic and myeloid programs, via a transient PpargCD45 state using separate enhancers for each; TFAP2C abolished adipogenic conversion. Motif density and partner composites therefore assemble a factor's instructive output in the receiving cell.

items.title: Deciphering the Dynamics of Leukemogenic Transformation from Clonal Hematopoiesis in Congenital Neutropenia
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Oncology, Hematology, Clinical Immunology, and Rheumatology, University Hospital Tuebingen, Tuebingen, Germany
items.abstract: Inherited neutropenia syndromes, severe congenital neutropenia (CN) and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), confer a high cumulative risk of MDS and AML. It is not yet clear which somatic mutations, in which combination, allele frequency and sequence identify patients at high risk. We analyzed clonal hematopoiesis (CH) in the largest representative cohort of inherited neutropenia patients to date - 658 samples from 309 patients - using error-corrected panel sequencing with longitudinal sampling. This was complemented in selected cases by single-cell DNA sequencing and genotyping of single-cell derived colonies. CH was detected in early childhood, affecting 37.7% of CN and 60% of SDS patients. The somatic mutation burden remained essentially unchanged over decades. In CN, CSF3R mutations were dominant across genetic subtypes, while additional mutations were rare and included ASXL1, TET2, and DNMT3A. ASXL1 mutations most frequently co-occurred with CSF3R mutations. Co-occurring CSF3R and TP53 mutations were only found in SRP54-CN and CLPB-CN patients. In SDS, TP53 was the most frequently mutated gene, followed by low-prevalence somatic mutations in DNMT3A, IDH1, PTPN11, and RUNX1. In CN-MDS/AML, RUNX1 and SETBP1 mutations emerged shortly before progression to MDS/AML, and membrane-proximal CSF3R mutations only at the leukemic stage. In SDS, biallelic TP53-mutant clones expanded prior to transformation, and a variant allele frequency (VAF) of dominant TP53 clone above 0.074 discriminated between patients who progressed and those who did not. Peripheral blood reflected bone marrow genotype for most key drivers. Leukemic transformation in inherited neutropenia is therefore not stochastic, but rather follows a defined mutational sequence, initiated in childhood.

items.title: A genetic screen to identify host factors required for commensal bacterial adherence to the gut epithelia
items.abstract: Bacterial adherence to gut epithelial cells likely involves host genetic components. We isolated a gut commensal bacterium, Lelliottia jeotgali, that can robustly colonize C. elegans through attachment to intestinal epithelial cells. Here, we developed a novel screen in C. elegans to identify host genes required for microbiome bacterial colonization. Using transgenic L. jeotgali strain expressing tdTomato, we conducted forward genetic screens in C. elegans to select for mutants that completely lost colonization. We identified multiple allelic mutations in five different C. elegans genes, termed knockout of Lelliottia adherence (kola) mutants, with a near complete loss of adherence. Each of kola-1-5 is uncharacterized and predicted to encode for a secreted or membrane-bound protein. We also identified gly-5, a GalNAc transferase that initiates O-linked glycosylation. Overall, we describe the first C. elegans screen to identify host factors that control microbiome bacterial colonization in the gut.

items.title: CellVocal Attributes Transcriptional Dynamics to Spatial Signalling
items.abstract: Understanding how local signalling shapes cell-state transitions requires linking spatial context to transcriptional dynamics. Here we present CellVocal, a framework that integrates spatial RNA velocity with cell-cell communication to decompose cell-state transitions into intrinsic and communication-associated components and further attribute their contributions to signalling modules and neighbouring sender cells. CellVocal recovered complex trajectories and communication perturbations in simulations and reconstructed coherent dynamics and spatially restricted ligand-receptor programmes across the mouse brain, gut and lung. Further analyses linked inferred NCAM1-NCAM1 signalling to lower cell-cycle-associated RNA velocity during embryonic neurogenesis. In melanoma, inferred local MIF-CD74+CD44 signalling corresponded to a predicted decline in the melanocytic programme. Analysis of acute liver failure identified hepatocyte-derived ANGPTL4-SDC1 signalling in association with acetaminophen-related communication enrichment and predicted matrix-remodelling RNA dynamics. By converting static ligand-receptor maps into velocity-constrained networks of signalling influence, CellVocal provides a general strategy for generating spatially resolved hypotheses about how intercellular communication contributes to predicted transcriptional changes.

items.title: A modified Arrestin1 Slows Retinal Degeneration Across Genetically Distinct Mouse Models of Inherited Retinal Disease
items.abstract: Inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) are a genetically heterogeneous group of disorders caused by mutations in more than 340 genes, limiting the applicability of gene-targeted therapies and creating the need for broader treatment strategies. Photoreceptor dysfunction is a hallmark of IRDs and often results in disrupted retinal metabolic homeostasis, as photoreceptors have exceptionally high metabolic demands and provide metabolic resources to surrounding retinal cells. Consequently, enhancing retinal metabolism has emerged as a promising gene-agnostic strategy for treating IRDs. We previously developed a modified arrestin1 (ArrGG) that relieves arrestin1-mediated inhibition of the glycolytic enzyme enolase1, thereby increasing glycolytic output and slowing retinal degeneration in the RhoP23H/+ mouse model. Here, we investigated the therapeutic potential of ArrGG as a gene-agnostic approach targeting endogenous metabolic enzyme activity across genetically distinct models of IRD. Using two complementary photoreceptor-enriched transcriptomic analyses, we found no widespread, reproducible transcriptional changes following ArrGG treatment. These findings support our hypothesis that ArrGG modulates photoreceptor metabolism without inducing substantial transcriptional remodeling. The therapeutic efficacy of ArrGG was evaluated in three IRD mouse models representing rapid rod degeneration (rd10), cone degeneration (GC1KO), and RPE-associated retinal degeneration (rd6). ArrGG treatment was associated with preserved retinal function and slowed structural degeneration across all three models. Together, these findings support the potential of modulating endogenous metabolic enzyme activity to preserve photoreceptors across genetically distinct IRD models. This work suggests that ArrGG could be a promising gene-agnostic metabolic therapy for slowing retinal degeneration and preserving visual function in inherited retinal diseases.

items.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes
items.abstract: Early and accurate identification of neurodegenerative disorders has notable implications for treatment and quality of life. Whereas neuroimaging-based biomarkers can accurately identify neurodegenerative subtypes, EEG represents a low-cost alternative that could expand access to dementia care. Here, we investigated whether six data-driven EEG latent factors, derived by nonnegative tensor decomposition of clinical EEGs, differ systematically across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative phenotypes. In 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET acquired within one year of each other, factor expression was compared across 14 diagnostic classes assigned by StateViewer, a validated artificial intelligence framework for FDG-PET interpretation. To separate disease-general severity from phenotype-specific topography, each factor was also regressed on a subject-level slowing index. Finally, we related the factors to regional FDG uptake and to neuropsychological performance (n = 98) and assessed their potential utility for single-subject classification. Four factors reflecting neurophysiological oscillations (posterior alpha, Rolandic beta, frontotemporal delta-theta and posterior theta-slow alpha) varied significantly across phenotypes, with attenuation of faster and augmentation of slower rhythms most pronounced in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), dysexecutive Alzheimer disease (AD) and posterior cortical atrophy, whereas factors dominated by eye-movement and muscle artifact showed no robust phenotypic association. Alpha and beta effects were largely attributable to overall slowing, whereas posterior theta-slow alpha became more phenotype-specific after adjustment (eta-squared 0.082 to 0.147), dissociating the Alzheimer disease spectrum from frontotemporal syndromes. The slowing index tracked with an FDG-PET pattern highly associated with DLB across the cohort, irrespective of assigned phenotype (r = 0.51, P 0.8) but poorly discriminated frontotemporal dementia phenotypes canonically associated with 4-repeat tau. Thus, data-driven decomposition of clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artifact into factors that track metabolic phenotype, regional metabolism and cognition, capturing both overall slowing and phenotype-specific patterns. This work informs the further development of scalable, biology-informed EEG-based phenotyping of neurodegenerative disease.

items.title: CoReg, tracking-based motion compensation for in vivo calcium imaging
items.abstract: In vivo calcium imaging enables the observation of neural activity with high spatial and temporal resolution. However, recordings are frequently affected by motion artifacts caused by animal movement, physiological processes, tissue drift, or instability of the imaging setup. These artifacts make signal extraction harder and reduce the consistency of downstream analyses. Current registration methods can correct rigid and non-rigid motion, but often estimate motion from individual frames or image patches and make limited use of temporal information. In addition, activity-driven fluorescence changes can make it difficult to distinguish changes in image appearance from actual motion. Here, we treat motion correction in calcium imaging as a point tracking problem and introduce CoReg, an open-source Python- based software tool with a graphical user interface. We benchmark CoReg against established registration methods using fluorescence imaging datasets from multiple species. CoReg performs competitively with or better than existing approaches across several settings. We further show that its performance is robust to the choice of tracked points, making the method straightforward to apply. CoReg includes implementations of both our method and the evaluated established methods. Our results show that tracking-based registration provides a simple and reliable approach for motion correction in vivo calcium imaging.

items.title: Chronic FMNL2 overexpression is associated with changes in brain histology and exploratory behavior in adult zebrafish
items.abstract: Formin-like protein 2 (FMNL2) has been associated with Alzheimer`s disease and cerebrovascular pathology and regulates gliovascular remodeling following amyloid exposure. However, the consequences of sustained FMNL2 elevation remain unclear. We generated a transgenic zebrafish line expressing human FMNL2 under the her4.1 promoter and examined adult brain histology and behavior under baseline conditions and following acute amyloid-{beta}42 (A{beta}42) exposure. Histological analyses assessed FMNL2 immunoreactivity, overlap between the glial marker BLBP and endothelial tight-junction marker ZO1, synaptic vesicle protein SV2 labeling, and microglial counts. Exploratory behavior was evaluated using the novel tank test and free-movement pattern Y-maze. Compared with uninjected wild-type controls, uninjected FMNL2-overexpressing fish showed higher FMNL2 immunoreactivity, lower BLBP-ZO1 overlap, fewer normalized SV2 puncta, and higher counts of total and morphologically activated microglia. Acute A{beta}42 exposure in wild-type animals produced changes in the same direction across these histological endpoints. No significant additional histological changes were detected following A{beta}42 exposure in the overexpression background. In the novel tank test, uninjected FMNL2-overexpressing fish had a higher composite boldness index than uninjected wild-type controls. These findings indicate that sustained FMNL2 overexpression is associated with histological changes resembling several responses to acute A{beta}42 exposure, together with altered exploratory behavior. They support further investigation of persistent FMNL2 elevation as a contributor to altered glial-vascular organization and cellular responses relevant to Alzheimer`s disease.

items.title: INSULIN MODULATES FOOD VALENCE THROUGH ASTROCYTES
items.abstract: Brain cells involved in assigning affective value (i.e.: valence) to stimuli modulating brain states are not yet fully identified. Since astrocytes modulate brain states, and insulin regulates feeding behavior and exerts its central actions in part through astrocytes, we analyzed the role of the insulin receptor in astrocytes in assigning valence to food. We used the modulatory actions of food on anxiety and fear, as proxies of the affective influence of food on mood. Mice lacking insulin receptors (IR) in GFAP astrocytes (GFAP-IR KO mice) showed increased anxiety and fear in response to food, while control littermates showed the opposite behavior. Since orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) are involved in fear conditioning, and are inhibited by feeding, we determined whether they are involved in mood alterations observed in fear-conditioned fed GFAP-IR KO mice. We observed increased c-fos expression in orexin neurons of these animals, indicating that the lack of IR in astrocytes modifies the response of these neurons to food. Moreover, chemogenetic stimulation of LH astrocytes in fed GFAP-IR KO mice was sufficient to significantly attenuate their fear responses. These findings suggest that astrocytic insulin receptors modulate the responses of hypothalamic orexin neurons to food. We speculate that cellular mechanisms underlying eating disorders may involve insulin modulation of food valence through astrocytes.

items.title: Synaptotagmin 7 differentially regulates synaptic vesicle trafficking at tonic and phasic synapses
items.abstract: Synaptic vesicle (SV) release probability can differ across neuronal subtypes, but the molecular mechanisms establishing such differences remain incompletely understood. In the current study we demonstrate that Synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7), a calcium-sensor regulating SV trafficking, is enriched at Drosophila tonic Ib synapses compared with phasic Is synapses. Loss of SYT7 preferentially enhanced evoked release at Ib terminals, whereas overexpression strongly suppressed fusion at both neuronal subtypes. High-frequency stimulation partially overcomes this inhibition, producing robust facilitation. Ultrastructural analysis revealed that SYT7 overexpression preserved morphologically docked SVs while promoting accumulation of enlarged presynaptic cisternae and redistribution of SV-associated proteins. Conversely, SYT7 loss reduced activity-induced presynaptic cisternae, suggesting an important role in regulating the bulk endocytosis pathway. Together, these findings identify differential SYT7 abundance as a contributor to tonic and phasic synaptic diversity and reveal a role for SYT7 in coordinating SV release and presynaptic membrane cycling.

items.title: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
items.abstract: Gastric interoceptive attention to internal, bodily signals such as hunger, satiety, and fullness are important for regulating feeding behaviors. However, abnormal processing or sensitivity to these can lead to disorders that result in overly restrictive or excessive consumption, highlighting the need for better understanding of the cortical processing of these cues. Specifically, understanding cortical representations of self-perceived gastric fullness have yet to be studied in humans. In this work, we demonstrate that consistently across individuals, the broadband power spectral density of EEG signals, as quantified by the aperiodic exponent, flattens after individuals drink water until fullness. Simultaneous measures of the stomach and heart demonstrate increased vagal drive to peripheral organs. We further find that changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns are associated with changes in the frequency of gastric oscillations. Overall, this suggests that the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker for assessing gastric interoceptive attention.

items.title: Interpreting computational mechanism from multi-area neural recordings
items.corresponding_institution: Emory University & Georgia Institute of Technology
items.abstract: Distilling computational mechanisms from neural recordings requires disambiguating intrinsic dynamics from external inputs. Here, we introduce Dynamically Interacting Systems (DynISys), a multi-compartment dynamical-systems model that infers per-area dynamics and structured inter-area communication from multi-area spiking activity. DynISys combines neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) latent dynamics with injective latent-to-neural mappings to achieve expressive and trustworthy dynamical inference. When applied to simultaneous dorsal premotor (PMd) and primary motor (M1) recordings from a continuous reaching task, DynISys accurately reconstructs neuronal responses without inventing spurious latent features. Analyzing the model's dynamics reveals putative mechanisms for motor planning and execution, with PMd-to-M1 inputs positioning a stable fixed point in M1 that encodes execution dynamics for the upcoming movement, subsequently evoked by external (non-PMd) inputs. Finally, multi-session DynISys achieves consistent latents when fit to neural recordings spanning multiple days. In summary, DynISys allows distillation of multi-area recordings into an interpretable account of distributed neural computation.

items.title: A Complete Three-Dimensional Spiral Ganglion Neuron Map in a Human Adult using a Deep Learning Pipeline
items.abstract: The quantity and distribution of spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) greatly influence speech and hearing ability. Historically, approaches to quantify SGNs from archival human temporal bones (TBs) have utilized only every 10th section to estimate the total SGN count. The current study evaluates a novel deep-learning pipeline for SGN quantification to produce the first complete three-dimensional SGN map of the human cochlea using every tissue section. The reconstruction is based on one adult human cochlea in which all 421 consecutive, 20 um thick, celloidin-embedded sections were H&E stained, mounted and digitized. SGN nuclei were manually labeled in training sections which were subsequently used to create UNet++ models for SGN detection. These models were then applied to all other sections and compared to manual counts by three experienced histopathologists. After quantification, serial sections were aligned and SGNs were assigned percent distances along Rosenthal's canal and characteristic frequencies using a modified Greenwood formula. Models to automatically identify SGN nuclei from digitized tissue sections performed with great accuracy: SGNs were counted in 191 sections with 97% accuracy compared to manual counts. When tissue sections were systematically omitted, counting only every 10th section was determined sufficient to ensure a median inferred total count accuracy of 98%. We present a new, flexible machine learning pipeline for identifying SGNs in digitized human TBs. Further, we show the first full 3D visualization of all 27,880 SGNs in an adult human cochlea, with associated tonotopic maps and basal-to-apical SGN distributions.

items.title: A Glutamate-Neuropeptide Circuit Converts Transient Mate Contact into a Persistent Local Search State in Caenorhabditis elegans Males
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Molecular and Cellular Biology, College of Life Science, National Taiwan University; Department of Life Science, College of Life Science, National
items.abstract: Transient sensory encounters can trigger behavioral states that persist long after the initiating stimulus has disappeared, yet how neural circuits initiate and sustain these states remains poorly understood. Here, we show that brief contact with a suitable mate induces a persistent local search state in male Caenorhabditis elegans, characterized by increased reversals and spatially restricted exploration that continues after mate removal. Transient optogenetic activation of male-specific ray type B (RnB) sensory neurons recapitulates this state, with its magnitude and persistence increasing with stimulation strength. Glutamatergic signaling promotes neuronal responses within the interconnected RnB sensory network and contributes to prolonged activity in downstream LUA interneurons. In contrast, loss of the LUA-derived neuropeptide NLP-13 or its receptor DMSR-2 preserves initial stimulus-evoked neuronal responses but reduces prolonged LUA calcium activity and behavioral persistence. LUA-specific restoration of NLP-13 rescues persistent local search, identifying these interneurons as a functionally important source of the neuropeptide. Together, our findings reveal complementary contributions of glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling to the generation and persistence of behavioral states, illustrating how distinct signaling mechanisms cooperate to transform transient social encounters into prolonged circuit activity and persistent behavior.

items.title: Zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis despite retaining functional RIPK3
items.corresponding_institution: University of Cambridge, Department of Medicine, MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
items.abstract: Organismal development, homeostasis and immunity are facilitated by distinct forms of regulated cell death (RCD). These include conserved apoptosis and necroptosis, a proposed backup antimicrobial defence that requires RIPK3-mediated activation of MLKL and is predicted to be absent in several species lacking MLKL. Zebrafish studies have identified a RIPK3-dependent regulated necrosis that is distinct from necroptosis and is pathogenic in tuberculosis. Here, we experimentally confirm the bioinformatics-based prediction that zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis because they lack MLKL, despite retaining functional RIPK3. We take advantage of the finding that Caspase-8 promotes apoptosis while restraining necroptosis; its deficiency is embryonic lethal in mice unless RIPK3 or MLKL is also inhibited. In contrast, we found that Caspase-8-deficient zebrafish are viable through adulthood without obvious morphological defects. Inhibition of related caspases did not compromise viability, arguing against functional redundancy. Finally, Ripk3 overexpression failed to induce death in Caspase-8-deficient embryos. Our work highlights the zebrafish as a model for exploring RIPK3 and extrinsic apoptosis biology in disease contexts in the natural absence of canonical necroptotic execution.

items.title: ACE-engineered human iPSC-derived neutrophils enhance host defense against multidrug-resistant bacterial infections
items.abstract: Severe neutropenia predisposes patients to life-threatening infections, while donor-dependent granulocyte transfusions are limited by availability and variable cell quality. Here, we engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) to constitutively or inducibly express angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and differentiated them into functional ACE-engineered neutrophils (ACE-iNeu). ACE expression enhanced granulocytic maturation, reactive oxygen species generation, inflammatory cytokine production, and antimicrobial signaling. ACE-iNeu exhibited enhanced bactericidal activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Following adoptive transfer into neutropenic mice, ACE-iNeu significantly reduced circulating and tissue bacterial burdens. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed ACE-associated alterations in adenine nucleotide abundance and developmental and inflammatory pathways.
