items.abstract: TGF-{beta}1 is secreted as a latent complex tethered to the cell surface by milieu molecules such as GARP, and its activation requires direct engagement by integrin-expressing cells. How this interaction converts the latent complex into signaling-competent growth factor (GF) remains unclear. Here we show that contact between GARP/TGF-{beta}1-presenting cells and cells expressing integrin V{beta}6 or V{beta}8 triggers rapid trogocytosis of the latent complex, both in transfected cells and two cancer cell lines that natively express these integrins. Independent labeling of the prodomain, GF, and GARP shows that all three components are co-transferred to the integrin-expressing cell, and a TGF-{beta}1 mutant (RGE) that cannot bind integrins shows little transfer. Using a reporter system that tracks pathway activation in presenting, integrin-expressing, and bystander cells, we find that GF-neutralizing antibodies block downstream signaling more effectively in bystander cells than in the first two cell types that participate in trogocytosis. Blocking cleavage between the prodomain and the GF blocks signaling in bystander cells while still permitting signaling in trogocytosing cell types. Finally, we integrin-expressing cells that have taken up latent TGF-{beta}1 by trogocytosis can activate it and signal to bystander cells after the TGF-{beta}1 cells are removed, indicating that trogocytosis converts integrin-expressing cells into TGF-{beta} signaling relays. These findings identify a role for trogocytosis in regulating the specificity of TGF-{beta}1 activation and signaling, and reveal a novel function of integrins in controlling protein localization.

items.title: Single-cell Transcriptome-Proteome-PTMome(x8)-Metabolome (scTPPM) co-profiling decodes multimodal regulation during mouse oocyte meiosis
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Microanalytical Systems in Department of Chemistry,  Zhejiang University
items.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics technology is crucial for comprehensive characterization of cellular molecular features. Despite recent advances in single-cell multi-omics approaches, co-profiling of nucleic acids, proteins, metabolites, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) within the same cell individuals remains major challenges. Here, we developed a single-cell transcriptome, proteome, PTMome, and metabolome (scTPPM) profiling approach, enabling simultaneous analysis of transcriptomes, proteomes, eight types of PTMs (e.g., phosphorylation, methylation, ubiquitination, O_GlcNAc, acetylation, crotonylation, lactylation, and succinylation), and metabolomes in individual cells. We demonstrated the scTPPM's performance in tumor cell lines and oocyte samples, reaching total identification and quantification of 27,668 genes, 4,847 proteins, 1,508 PTM sites, and 680 metabolites in single mouse oocytes. We profiled previously-uncharacterized dynamic crosstalk among the entire metabolic pathways from metabolic enzyme expression and regulation to metabolite-mediated post-translational modifications during oocyte maturation. In summary, scTPPM provided an effective workflow for multi-omics co-profiling in single cells, enabling multi-layered insights into complex regulatory network.

items.title: A dynamic phosphoproteome reveals stage-specific regulation of cytokinesis in Leishmania
items.abstract: Leishmania parasites undergo extensive morphological and metabolic remodelling during their transition from motile insect promastigotes to non-motile intracellular amastigotes, yet how dynamic protein kinase signalling drives this process remains poorly understood. Here, we present a high-resolution temporal phosphoproteome of L. mexicana promastigote to axenic amastigote differentiation, profiling 16,495 phosphosites on 3,101 proteins across seven developmental time points and identifying 5,795 dynamically regulated sites. This temporal map reveals stage-specific signalling programs, including regulated sites in MPK2 and non-regulated sites in MRK1, protein kinases known to be essential for amastigote differentiation. Using analogue-sensitive (AS) chemical genetics, we show that acute inhibition of either kinase in axenic amastigotes disrupts the spatial coordination of cleavage furrow ingression with nuclear and kinetoplast segregation, revealing essential cytokinesis roles obscured in constitutive gene deletions. Despite generating similar cytokinesis phenotypes, genetic over-expression and cellular localisation analyses demonstrate that MPK2 and MRK1 act through spatially segregated signalling pathways. Time-resolved phosphoproteomics upon MPK2 inhibition places its activity upstream of cytoskeletal remodelling networks. Importantly, we show that the stage-specific requirement for MPK2 is defined by the parasite's morphology: while motile promastigotes tolerate MPK2 inhibition, genetic ablation of flagellar motility sensitises them to loss of MPK2 activity. Thus, flagellar motility acts as a mechanical buffer during promastigote division, explaining why non-motile amastigotes are vulnerable to MPK2 inhibition. Together, our findings provide a systems level framework for Leishmania signalling and demonstrate that cellular architecture and biomechanics dictate protein kinase dependency across developmental stages of the parasite.

items.title: Single Nucleus Profiling Reveals Rewired Tumor-Immune-Stromal Cell Communication in Plasmacytoid Urothelial Carcinoma
items.corresponding_institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
items.abstract: Plasmacytoid urothelial carcinoma (PUC) is an aggressive histologic subtype of bladder cancer associated with worse patient outcomes and therapeutic response compared to conventional urothelial carcinoma (CUC). While recent work has demonstrated metastatic lymph nodes from PUC tumors have an inflamed phenotype, how the tumor microenvironment (TME) and crosstalk between tumor, stromal, and immune cells in primary PUC bladder tumors differs from those in CUC remains poorly understood. The impact of these differences on response to immunotherapy is also unknown. To understand TME differences between CUC and PUC and their impact on cell signaling, we performed single nucleus RNA sequencing on PUC and CUC tumors, as well as Xenium spatial transcriptomics on a mixed CUC / PUC tumor. We identified increased signaling between PUC-enriched, CDH1-low urothelial cells, immunosuppressive lipid-associated macrophages, and SFRP2+/CTHRC1+ fibroblasts in PUC tumors compared to CUC. Spatial transcriptomics identified increased macrophage infiltration in PUC histology and colocalization of PUC tumor cells, immunosuppressive macrophages, and SFRP2+ fibroblasts. Taken together, this study delineates PUC architecture and demonstrates interplay CDH1-low tumor cells, EMT, and immunosuppressive macrophages, identifying possible therapeutic vulnerabilities in PUC.

items.title: An anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis formulation for the in vitro study of oxygen sensitive proteins
items.abstract: Anaerobic microbes harbor unique enzymes and metabolic pathways with potential biotechnological applications, yet these microbes remain difficult to study and engineer. Research is limited by the labor-intensive workflows required to maintain anoxic environments and the lack of genetic tools available for non-model anaerobes. Here, we present an anaerobic cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) platform for the in vitro study of oxygen-sensitive enzymes. This study establishes two methods for conducting anaerobic CFPS, achieving an anoxic environment by (1) sparging with inert gas or (2) lyophilizing to remove oxygenated water. We show the functionality of our anaerobic CFPS formulation by producing oxygen-independent fluorescent protein reporters and a [4Fe-4S] cluster pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) with a specific activity of 5.2 {+/-} 0.3 x 10-4 U/{micro}L cell-free extract. This highly modular platform will allow study of diverse oxygen-sensitive proteins and requires only minor modifications to commonly used CFPS workflows.

items.title: Associative Learning and Memory Erasure in a Synthetic Multicellular System
items.abstract: Learning is a basic form of adaptation that organisms display from neural systems to single cells. In associative learning, the pairing of two stimuli lets one of them evoke the response to the other. Engineering this behavior in a living cell is difficult, because coincidence detection, memory, and conditional readout must be wired into a single regulatory network. Here we build a consortium of five E. coli strains that distributes the operations of associative learning and communicates through one diffusible quorum-sensing signal. The same signal acts as the memory trace. One strain detects the coincidence of the two inputs, a second maintains the memory through positive feedback in the shared medium, a third reads it out on the conditioned stimulus, a fourth reports the unconditioned response, and a fifth erases the memory on command. We show experimentally that the assembled consortium learns the association, since a stimulus that is silent before training evokes a strong response after pairing. Memory is retained through a medium exchange in which both stimuli are removed, and then the conditioned stimulus alone evokes the response. The reporter is not produced without its input. An erase command returns the response to the background. A population model of the consortium accounts for the sequence of responses and gives design rules for writing, retention, and erasure, and a trade-off in storing memory in a shared extracellular signal. Distributing the operations over strains makes each of them separately tunable and testable and provides a route to microbial communities that learn from their history.

items.title: Self-organized criticality in a mammalian RNA-interference circuit
items.abstract: Living systems have been argued to operate near critical points, but their relevance at the cellular level is poorly understood. Critical states allow for a high sensitivity to external inputs and maximal information transfer and display fluctuations at all scales. Critical points are very special, and require the fine tuning of a control parameter, which is hard to reconcile with the robustness of living cells. Self-organized criticality (SOC) proposes that feedback, rather than tuning, brings a system to its critical point. Here we show that RNA interference, in which messenger RNAs compete for shared silencing machinery and so queue for service, together with negative feedback gives rise to SOC in mammalian cells. In a synthetic circuit, a protein repressor whose mRNA competes with the mRNA of a fluorescent reporter that it represses senses the congestion of the queue, closing the feedback loop. Theory and stochastic simulations show that the loop holds the queue near its critical point despite changes in its parameters, and that expression becomes intermittent, with scale-free bursts. Measurements in human cell lines show the predicted power-law distributions of single-cell fluorescence. RNA interference could thus support engineered SOC in animal cells and may also contribute to SOC in natural systems.

items.title: Coarse-tuning to improve a protein foundation model for a domain of proteins: the example of outer membrane beta barrels
items.abstract: Foundation models for proteins have shown great potential in addressing a wide range of challenges in computational molecular biology. State-of-the-art models are trained on large and diverse corpora of protein sequences, enabled by self-supervised training. The models are then used in transfer learning and the embeddings they calculate are used in supervised downstream tasks. We propose a novel focusing mechanism for foundation models, which we call 'coarse-tuning'. In coarse-tuning, we further update the model, using a defined yet unlabeled, dataset to enhance its performance in a specific domain. We demonstrate this approach using Outer Membrane Beta Barrels (OMBBs) - proteins that are found in the distinct biophysical environment of the outer membrane. Our results show that coarse-tuned models outperform the original foundation model when applied to various transfer learning tasks. Additionally, we study the embeddings generated by the coarse-tuned models and compare them to those from the original foundation model, including an investigation of the learned attention matrices via contact map predictions. Our work suggests that a medium-sized dataset (fewer than 100,000 protein sequences) is sufficient to effectively specialize a foundation model to a specific domain, enhancing its utility for domain-specific applications.

items.title: Cortical ER-PM contact sites promote nuclear ER membrane integrity and mitotic nuclear segregation
items.abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) extends from the nuclear envelope through the cytoplasm to the cell cortex, where it contacts the plasma membrane (PM) at ER-PM membrane contact sites (MCSs). We hypothesized that as contiguous extensions of nuclear ER these cortical ER (cER) attachments to the PM might dampen shearing stresses on the nuclear envelope and help orchestrate nuclear ER dynamics. Although individual cER-PM tether proteins promote cER inheritance during mitosis, our findings reveal that removing all cER-PM tethers collectively disrupts nuclear envelope membrane integrity. In yeast {triangleup}-super-tether ({triangleup}-s-tether) cells lacking seven cER-PM tethers, cER detachment causes membrane blisters and nuclear envelope ruptures; however, individual tether deletions or ER stress do not disrupt nuclear containment. Despite the extensive nuclear envelope lesions in {triangleup}-s-tether cells, ESCRT-III (Endosomal Sorting Complex Required for Transport-III)-mediated membrane repair sustains cell viability. The loss of nuclear integrity, however, appears to disrupt genomic repair and promotes spontaneous mutation; separately, nuclear inheritance is also disrupted. Without cER-PM MCSs, cortical actin depolarization and defects in nucleopodia impair mitotic nuclear dynamics and segregation, which triggers a Spindle Position Checkpoint (SPOC) cell-cycle delay. That cER-PM MCSs serve as dual-function hubs for the preservation of nuclear envelope integrity is indicated by two independent mechanisms capable of rescuing the observed nuclear membrane defects: the restoration of phospholipid metabolism or the re-establishment of nonspecific cER-PM contact.

items.title: A novel function of neuroligin 3: Beyond sociality, Regulating lifespan in Drosophila
items.abstract: Neuroligins are conserved postsynaptic adhesion proteins involved in synaptic function and behaviour. In Drosophila melanogaster, Neuroligin 3 (Nlg3) regulates social behaviour, sleep and synaptic architecture. We now report, through analysis of publicly available transcriptomics data, confirmed with RT-qPCR data, that loss-of-function of the nlg3 gene downregulates the expression of longevity-associated genes foxo, hsp70s, and hsp68. Graded genetic manipulation of the Drosophila melanogaster neuroligin 3 (nlg3) gene indeed modulates both social spacing and lifespan. Specifically, reduced nlg3 expression (via heterozygous deletion, or transposable-element insertion) extends lifespan in both sexes, while overexpression or complete deletion shortens it. In contrast, overexpression or complete loss of nlg3 leads the flies to be further apart (increased social distance, or social space), as does RNAi knockdown, while heterozygous reduction of nlg3 expression either lowers or does not alter the flies social space. This work identifies a previously unrecognized link between a conserved synaptic gene, social behaviour, and organismal longevity.

items.title: Sleep promotes neuronal autophagy for intracellular clearance
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Neuroscience, Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai 200031, China.
items.abstract: Sleep is essential for brain health, yet how it maintains neuronal homeostasis at the cellular level remains poorly understood. Here, we show that extended wakefulness selectively suppressed neuronal autophagic flux in the cortex of mice, whereas sleep rapidly restored it, accompanied by a shift in autophagic cargo from mitochondrial components to synaptic proteins. Sleep upregulated ATG7 expression in the cortex, involving both lysosomal degradation and a putative noncanonical secretory route. Moreover, low neuronal activity is associated with efficient flux, as Gq-mediated neuronal activation impaired autophagy and promoted intracellular amyloid-beta; accumulation. Notably, closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of lysosomal acidification, exclusively during sleep, reduced amyloid pathology in 5xFAD mice, whereas wake-targeted stimulation worsened pathology. Together, these findings demonstrate that sleep serves as a physiological gatekeeper for cortical neuronal autophagy, and highlight the importance of brain-state timing for enhancing intracellular proteostasis in neurodegenerative disease.

items.title: An AAV model of tauopathy targeting the mouse dentate gyrus reveals greater trans-synaptic tau spreading with aggregation-prone tau variants
items.corresponding_institution: Paris-Saclay University, CEA, Translational Research Approaches for Therapeutics, Modeling and Imaging of Neurodegenerative Diseases (TREATMIND) and Molecular I
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive memory and cognitive decline, which is strongly correlated with the anatomical progression of tau pathology. Resulting from the intraneuronal aggregation of misfolded tau protein, tauopathy propagates in an anterograde manner between synaptically connected neurons through a prion-like mechanism. While glial cells, particularly microglia, are implicated in this process, the precise mechanisms underlying tauopathy propagation remain poorly understood. A critical unresolved question is whether aggregated or soluble pathologic tau forms mediate this spread. Here, we show in vivo that tau spreading scales with the aggregation propensity of the tau variant expressed. We developed a mouse model using adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene transfer to overexpress distinct tau forms in the dentate gyrus, alongside a reporter gene. This design enabled discrimination between transduced neurons and those secondarily affected by pathology propagation. Leveraging contralateral neuronal projections, we quantified propagation levels. To investigate the role of microglia and of extracellular vesicles, we analyzed microglial morphology in response to different tau forms and measured tau protein levels in extracellular vesicles isolated from injected mouse brains. We first confirmed the presence of vector-derived tau protein in non-transduced neurons, validating our model for studying tau propagation. We then found that aggregation-prone tau variants were associated with a greater number of tau-positive neurons in the contralateral hippocampus than wild-type tau. Additionally, extracellular vesicles from brains injected with aggregated tau contained higher levels of tau protein. Given that insoluble tau aggregates represent the ultimate stage of tauopathy, our findings suggest that propagation occurs at advanced stages of tau pathology, and that extracellular vesicles may contribute to the transfer of pathological tau, although the cellular origin of these vesicles was not determined in this study. Furthermore, our model provides a robust experimental paradigm for exploring therapeutic strategies aimed at inhibiting tauopathy propagation.

items.title: Extending intravitreal retention of CNTF via fusion to the HA-binding protein VG1
items.corresponding_institution: Pharmaceutical Development, Drug Delivery, Genentech, 1 DNA Way, South San Francisco, California 94080, US
items.abstract: Glaucoma is the leading cause of permanent blindness worldwide. Vision loss in glaucoma stems from the loss of retinal ganglion cells (RGC). Ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) has been shown to protect RGCs in pre-clinical models of glaucoma. However, CNTF has a short ocular retention time following intraocular injections due to rapid diffusion. To address this, we developed a fusion protein between CNTF and the hyaluronic acid- (HA) binding G1 domain of endogenous extracellular matrix (ECM) protein, versican (VG1; CNTF-VG1). We hypothesize that a CNTF-VG1 protein will have an extended ocular retention time compared to CNTF due to HA-binding with endogenous vitreous-HA. We demonstrate that CNTF-VG1 non-covalently binds HA with high affinity and is bioactive. We show that the vitreous and thermal stability of CNTF-VG1 can be significantly increased through co-formulation with HA. In an in vivo pharmacodynamic study, we show that VG1 significantly increases the window of neuroprotective JAK/STAT3 pathway activation in un-injured mice (C57BL/6J, female) retina. Finally, we close our work by showing that CNTF is neuroprotective of primary mouse cortical neurons in an acute H2O2 cytotoxicity model. Taken together, our work demonstrates the potential of HA-binding domain VG1 to improve the ocular retention of neuroprotective CNTF following intraocular injection.

items.title: Distinct effects of Atg3 and Atg10 on Autophagosome Formation in Yeast
items.abstract: Autophagosome formation involves two E2 enzymes: Atg3, which conjugates Atg8 to the lipid phosphatidylethanolamine, and Atg10, which conjugates Atg12 to Atg5. Although both are required for autophagy, it is unclear exactly what roles these pathways play in the process of autophagosome formation. We used baker's yeast expressing mutant versions of both Atg3 and Atg10 that reduce, but do not eliminate, their activity to better understand their effects on Atg8 lipidation, autophagic flux, and the size and number of autophagosomes formed during nitrogen starvation. We found that while Atg3 primarily affects Atg8 lipidation and autophagosome size, Atg10 has less of an effect on Atg8 lipidation and primarily controls autophagosome number. This demonstrates that these two enzymes have distinct mechanistic roles in autophagosome formation, and implies an as-of-yet undiscovered function for the Atg12-Atg5 conjugate.

items.title: Tumor vascularization and the nonlinear dynamics of metastatic cancer treated by oncolytic viral therapy
items.abstract: Oncolytic viral therapy (OVT) is an emerging cancer treatment where therapeutic viruses are injected into a patient. Models have been developed which describe the interactions of the virus, tumor and immune system through systems of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Some suggest that an initial phase of treatment with immunosuppressants could improve the efficacy of OVT by preventing the immune system from attacking the oncolytic viruses before they can infect many tumor cells. However, all such models have focused on a single, localized tumor. Here, we model a primary tumor and its continuous metastatic seeding of a secondary organ under simplifying assumptions about tumor vascularization. Bifurcation analysis and simulations reveal regions in parameter space for which immune modulation encourages distant metastasis, leading to the dangerous scenario where the elimination of a primary tumor creates the false impression of a good prognosis. We also suggest that vascular disrupting agents may be useful for treating small tumors while they may promote OVT resistance in larger tumors.

items.title: Simple, static, spiking nonlinearities can account for seemingly complex interactions between visual, motor and cognitive variables in the visual cortex.
items.abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex is driven by the stimulus and modulated by multiple task-related variables, including spatial attention, eye movements, and perceptual decisions. These multiple influences are each typically described as nonlinear interactions such as gain or normalization, raising the question of how these diverse signals can be combined through cellular or circuit mechanisms. Here we address this problem by examining neuronal responses in macaque visual areas V2 and V3 during a visual discrimination task that dissociates spatial attention from motor planning and microsaccadic eye movements. Using a statistical modeling framework, we show that attentional, microsaccade-related, and choice-related influences on neural activity are best explained by a simple additive stimulus-independent input modulation, which manifests as a gain via a spiking nonlinearity. In addition to explaining how interactions between variables might be accomplished mechanistically, this framework also resolves a controversy about the relationship between microsaccades and spatial attention. We find that neither microsaccade direction nor microsaccade-related neural activity accounts for attentional modulation, although these variables are often correlated, leading to apparent interactions. Thus, visual cortex can integrate sensory, motor-related, and cognitive signals through a parsimonious mechanism that preserves stable stimulus representations while supporting flexible, context-dependent modulation.

items.title: PKR drives neuropathology in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome
items.corresponding_institution: Institut de Neurociencies and Department of Cell Biology, Physiology and Immunology, Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona, Bellaterra, Barcelona, Spain
items.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a trigger of innate immune responses, yet whether these responses contribute to neurodegeneration remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a cell-type-specific antiviral program in vulnerable GABAergic neurons of Ndufs4-deficient mice and human brain organoids modeling Leigh syndrome. Despite robust type I interferon responses, genetic ablation of innate immune mediators Ifnar1 or Sting1 fails to ameliorate disease progression. Instead, we identify the double-stranded RNA sensor protein kinase R (PKR) as a critical mediator of mitochondrial neuropathology. PKR associates with mitochondrial RNA, while its genetic deletion or silencing delays neurological decline, attenuates neuroinflammation, and extends survival without restoring mitochondrial respiration. PKR deletion also normalizes JNK signaling without detectable global translational repression, suggesting a noncanonical contribution to disease. Together, our findings reveal PKR-mediated antiviral RNA sensing as a pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial complex I deficiency and highlight PKR as a candidate target for mitochondrial encephalopathies.

items.title: SOX7 and ERG reprograms neuroectoderm into microenvironmentally attuned brain endothelial cells that possess forebrain regional bias
items.abstract: Reliable human blood brain barrier (BBB) models are limited by a persistent problem of cellular identity: many protocols select cells for barrier or transporter properties rather than authentic, regionally specified brain endothelium. Here we show that constitutive expression of the transcription factors SOX7 and ERG converts human pluripotent stem cell derived epithelial barrier-forming cells into bona-fide vascular endothelial cells (SE rECs) whose transcriptome and proteome converge on primary human brain endothelium. Benchmarked against a human adult-brain endothelial atlas, SEr ECs acquire a forebrain-biased regional program stronger than that of permissively (ETS-)reprogrammed or umbilical-vein endothelial cells, reproducibly across biological replicates, although it does not reach the absolute regional identity of in-vivo brain endothelium. At the transcript level, epithelial-derived barrier forming cells (iBFCs) cells score highly on select barrier and transporters genes yet lack endothelial lineage identity, showing that transporter benchmarks alone do not establish endothelial fate. Coculture of SE rECs with astrocytes and pericytes in a two-dimensional neurovascular-unit model as well as a perfused microfluidic device induces mature BBB features and reduces paracellular permeability. SE rECs thus provide a lineage-faithful, organotypically informed platform for modelling the human BBB.

items.title: A short nucleophosmin isoform couples nucleolar remodeling to DNA damage repair during meiosis
items.corresponding_institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey
items.abstract: Nucleoli are nuclear compartments wherein ribosome biogenesis occurs. Observations spanning over a century have demonstrated that meiotic male germ cell nucleoli have unusual morphology and a close association with a large DNA damage repair foci formed around the sex chromosomes termed the XY-body. A mechanistic understanding of this relationship and its impact on ribosome biogenesis has remained elusive. High-resolution microscopy revealed XY-body associated nucleoli have an unusual two-part morphology made up of an XY-body intercalated and an XY-body adjacent part, each marked by different isoforms of the nucleolar protein nucleophosmin. Additionally, the entire structure is transcriptionally inactive and likely derived from autosomal nucleoli. Further, proper formation and maintenance of the structure rely on an interaction between NPM1 and the DNA damage marker {gamma}H2AX. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the XY-body and nucleolus association and reveal unrecognized connections between nucleolar proteins, ribosome biogenesis, and DNA damage repair during meiosis.

items.title: Proteomic analysis of early SASP-associated responses in doxorubicin-treated cardiac fibroblasts
items.corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity is associated with progressive cardiac dysfunction and fibrotic remodeling, processes in which cardiac fibroblast senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype have been implicated. However, the early secretory responses that precede established senescence following doxorubicin (DOX) exposure remain poorly defined. Primary cardiac fibroblasts isolated from healthy rat hearts were treated with varying concentrations of DOX (0-3 M) for 24 hours. Media collected at Day 1 were analyzed by untargeted proteomics, while cell viability, proliferation, and senescence-associated {beta}-galactosidase activity were assessed at Days 1 and 7. Acute DOX exposure reduced cell viability and proliferation at Day 1 without significantly increasing senescence-associated {beta}-galactosidase activity. At Day 7, we observed persistent proliferative arrest and increased {beta}-galactosidase activity with DOX exposure, consistent with delayed senescence. Proteomic analysis of Day 1 conditioned media identified 35 proteins significantly associated with DOX treatment after false discovery rate correction (22 positive and 13 negative associations; P-FDR < 0.05). Functional annotation identified proteins related to extracellular matrix (ECM) regulation, mitochondrial function, cellular stress, cytoskeletal organization, calcium signaling, protease activity, and cell-cycle regulation. Network analysis identified a collagen-centered network (COL1A1, COL1A2, and COL3A1) associated with reduced abundance of ECM proteins and a second network centered on GAPDH, HSPA8, and HSPA9 that included proteins associated with mitochondrial proteostasis, oxidative stress, metabolic adaptation, and structural remodeling.

items.title: Rab7 activation ameliorates impaired lysosome dynamics and mitophagic flux during chronic iron overload
items.abstract: Iron homeostasis is essential for cellular function, yet iron overload is linked to pathologies including cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome. Although excess iron has been associated with impaired autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction, the effects of iron overload on lysosomal dynamics and mitophagy remain poorly defined. In this study, we demonstrate that iron overload disrupts mitochondrial morphology and lysosomal homeostasis, accompanied by iron accumulation in both organelles. While mitophagy is triggered upon iron overload, mitophagic flux is impaired, suggesting a defect in mitophagosome maturation and incomplete clearance. Notably, lysosomes in iron loaded cells were hyper-acidic and degradative, but became enlarged, perinuclear, and less motile, suggesting that altered lysosomal dynamics may contribute to defective mitophagic clearance. Interestingly, pharmacological activation of Rab7 restores lysosomal motility and mitophagic flux under iron overload conditions. It also improves mitochondrial function and cell viability. Together, these findings indicate that iron overload disrupts organelle homeostasis by impairing lysosomal and mitochondrial dynamics, ultimately arresting mitophagic flux due to altered lysosome dynamics and promoting cell death. Targeted activation of Rab7 mitigates these iron-induced effects, providing a potential therapeutic target for iron overload-induced cell death and tissue damage.

items.title: DM4ISL: high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware in silico labeling of fluorescence images via diffusion models
items.abstract: In silico labeling predicts organelle-specific localizations from label-free images, potentially enabling longitudinal and multiplexed live-cell imaging. Here we present DM4ISL (Diffusion Model for In Silico Labeling), a high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware model that overcomes current limitations, such as blurry or structurally inaccurate predictions, by resolving the intrinsic entanglement of biological signal and noise that characterizes fluorescence imaging. DM4ISL leverages the iterative nature of diffusion through a step-wise self-ensemble averaging approach that marginalizes these stochastic fluctuations, preventing the overfitting to noise that typically degrades standard final-step predictions. Benchmarking across six organelles demonstrates that DM4ISL systematically outperforms state-of-the-art architectures in structural fidelity, as confirmed through both pixel-based and application-specific metrics. Furthermore, calculating the standard deviation across intermediate denoising steps generates localized uncertainty maps that automatically detect erroneous predictions at inference time. Providing high-fidelity predictions alongside built-in reliability metrics, DM4ISL offers a robust method for trustworthy, data-driven discovery in cell biology.

items.title: Multimodal protein representations across human brain cell types
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Informatics, Harvard Medical School; Aligning Science Across Parkinson's ASAP) Collaborative Research Network; Broad Institute of MIT a
items.abstract: The central nervous system (CNS) comprises diverse cell types whose molecular context shapes the roles of the proteins they express. Computational models offer a scalable way to study the roles of proteins across human brain cell types, with protein language models and interactome- or single-cell-based models capturing complementary information encoded in protein sequences and cellular network contexts. Human brain tissue is hard to access, so brain cell types make up a small fraction of the atlases single-cell models train on and of the benchmarks used for their evaluation. To capture these complementary sources of information in the CNS, we introduce SEMPER, a multimodal representation learning model that aligns protein language model representations with protein-protein interaction networks from 442 cell types of the adult human brain, giving each protein a sequence-informed representation in every cell type in which its gene is expressed. We show that SEMPER representations predict cell type-specific protein complexes and predict genes essential to the survival of dopaminergic neurons, measured in a genome-wide CRISPR screen. In zero-shot retrieval, SEMPER recovers clinically pursued drug targets for Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis at higher rates than cell type-specific models. To further improve target recovery, we combine SEMPER with a large language model that reasons over protein functional annotations. The combination recovers more targets, with SEMPER providing experimentally derived cellular context that complements literature-based reasoning of the large language model.

items.title: Scalable Multi-omics Diagonal Integration from Self-Mapping
items.abstract: Diagonal integration seeks to align single-cell multi-omics datasets in which distinct modalities, such as RNA and protein, are measured in different cells. Unlike horizontal integration, these datasets lack direct cell--cell correspondences and complete feature mappings across modalities. Leading methods for weak-linkage integration often infer anchor cells between modalities by searching for cross-modal similarities through predefined feature links, then use these anchors to guide alignment. Their required matching or anchor refinement can become computationally burdensome at atlas scale. Here, we introduce a novel self-mapping technique, a mechanism that aligns modalities by mapping each computationally decoded cross-modality omics profile prediction to its own observed inputs. We implement this strategy in SCALEMAP, a scalable, modality-agnostic method for diagonal integration. Across transcriptomic, epigenomic and proteomic benchmarks, SCALEMAP matches or outperforms leading alternatives while requiring substantially less runtime and memory. In large-scale experiments, SCALEMAP integrates more than 1.5 million multi-omic profiles in less than 5 minutes with under 20 GB peak memory, which enables rapid synthesis of massive single-cell multi-omics resources into unified biological representations.

items.title: Transcript-resolved analysis identifies lncRNA carrier architectures and selective nucleolar enrichment in colorectal cancer
items.corresponding_institution: Rosalind Franklin University of Medicine and Science
items.abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) in colorectal cancer (CRC) are commonly characterized at the gene level, obscuring processed RNA architectures and regional localization. In renal cell carcinoma, a processed CRNDE isoform retaining an ultraconserved element (UCE) with a C/D snoRNA-like region promotes pre-60S maturation. Here, we examined CRNDE UCE-region representation and integrated CRC tumor expression and clinical evidence with published HEK293 cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (CLIP) profiles for C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNP) proteins and long-read sequencing to identify retained CLIP-supported regions. CRNDE was upregulated in 49 of 50 paired tumors, and UCE-region signal was detected in 380 of 382 assessable primary tumors, although total CRNDE abundance showed little association with stage or outcome. Processed UCE-retaining CRNDE transcripts were identified in Caco-2 cells. Integration identified 1,714 disease-supported lncRNAs with CLIP overlap; among 576 non-CRNDE candidates, 188 CLIP-supported regions were retained within processed transcripts from 65 loci in both CRC cell models. Region-directed RT-qPCR following pre-ribosome sequential extraction revealed preferential enrichment of selected JPX, DLEU2, and LINC00630 RNA populations in the core nucleolar fraction relative to broader transcript-region measurements in both cell lines. These findings identify retained-region transcript architectures and reveal region-dependent nucleolar enrichment not apparent from broader transcript measurements.

items.title: A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
items.abstract: Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). In the clinically relevant TP53-mutant background-which disables the G1/S checkpoint and forces reliance on ATR-mediated S/G2 arrest-MBD4-LOF lines (n=11 vs n=619 WT) demonstrate pronounced ceralasertib hypersensitivity (Delta LN_IC50 = -1.07, 95% CI [-1.62, -0.41], Cohen's d = -0.74, p2s = 0.0060, BH-FDR q = 0.036; Delta AUC = -0.087, d = -0.89, p2s = 0.0017), with 11/11 leave-one-out (LOO) jackknife iterations retaining two-sided significance (p2s <= 0.014). This genotype-associated dependency remains robust in the unstratified pan-cancer cohort (n=14 vs n=914 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.11], d = -0.50, p2s = 0.0430; Delta AUC = -0.056, d = -0.56, p2s = 0.0259) and after purging microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) lines (n=10 vs n=906 WT MSS; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.91, 95% CI [-1.50, -0.22], d = -0.62, p2s = 0.0307). By contrast, Wee1 inhibition (adavosertib; n=15 vs n=920 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.35, p2s = 0.1667) does not reach statistical significance. (3) Absence of Single-Agent PARPi Sensitivity (Axis 3): While PARP1 transcript abundance strongly governs pan-cancer PARPi cytotoxicity across n=481 cell lines (rho = -0.416, p < 10^-21 across five clinical PARPi), MBD4-LOF tumors (n=19 vs n=1,498 WT) show zero compensatory PARP1 upregulation (median 6.77 vs 6.66 log2[TPM+1], Delta median = +0.11, 95% CI [-0.39, +0.71], p2s = 0.605; TOST equivalence p_TOST = 0.0199 within +/- 0.50 log2[TPM+1]). Direct GDSC2 evaluation of MBD4-LOF (n=8) versus WT (n=478) confirms complete absence of single-agent PARPi sensitization across talazoparib (p2s = 0.973), olaparib (p2s = 0.522), niraparib (p2s = 0.877), rucaparib (p2s = 0.804), veliparib (p2s = 0.538), and the composite 5-drug mean PARPi Z-score (Delta median Z = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.84, +0.60], p2s = 0.841). Under Leave-One-Anchor-Out cross-validation across 12 canonical DDR genes (370 gene-drug pairs), our 5-Layer De-confounded SL-ML Engine achieves an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.9716, AUPRC of 0.8007, and Top-1 accuracy of 82.86%, zero-shot ranking gemcitabine (#1) and ceralasertib (#2) as the top therapeutic dependencies for held-out MBD4 while rejecting all PARP inhibitors (ranks #13, #27, #28, #31). Conclusion: MBD4-LOF tumors exhibit a selective, TP53-potentiated pharmacological dependency on ATR kinase inhibition alongside mechanistic vulnerability to cytidine analogs, but lack both the nicked BER repair intermediates and the PARP1 target expression required for single-agent PARP inhibitor efficacy.

items.title: Transactivation of EGFR by LCK underlies an activity-defined dependency that predicts response to EGFR inhibition in cholangiocarcinoma
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Surgery, Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN 55905, USA
items.abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is an aggressive biliary tract malignancy with limited molecularly guided treatment options. The Src-family kinase LCK is a therapeutic vulnerability in CCA, yet its canonical T-cell substrates are minimally expressed in CCA cells, leaving its downstream effectors undefined. Unbiased proximity labeling in HuCCT1 cells identified EGFR within the LCK signaling neighborhood. LCK depletion or inhibition reduced EGFR phosphorylation, whereas recombinant LCK increased EGFR phosphorylation in a cell-free assay, supporting a noncanonical role for LCK upstream of EGFR. Given the failure of EGFR-directed therapies in unselected CCA populations, we hypothesized that EGFR activity, rather than abundance or mutation status, identifies EGFR-dependent tumors. Among 28 patient-derived xenografts ranked by pretreatment substrate-inferred EGFR activity, the activity score correctly classified afatinib response in all six models tested. An analogous EGFR activity score stratified primary tumors in two human CCA cohorts. Together, these findings identify a therapeutically actionable LCK-EGFR signaling axis and nominate EGFR activity as a functional biomarker to guide tumor selection for EGFR-directed therapy in CCA, warranting prospective clinical validation.

items.title: CCR8⁺ regulatory T cell depletion overcomes immune checkpoint blockade resistance in BRCA2-deficient prostate cancer
items.corresponding_institution: Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA; Division of Hematology and Oncology, Departmen
items.abstract: BRCA2-mutated prostate cancer is an aggressive, genomically unstable subtype, yet how this genomic instability influences tumor immunity remains undefined. We developed an isogenic, immunocompetent model of Brca2-deficient prostate cancer in which BRCA2 loss activated the cGAS/STING pathway and a type I interferon response across multiple cellular compartments, paradoxically leading to an overall immunosuppressed tumor microenvironment. Within this microenvironment, tumor-associated macrophages were interferon-responsive and expressed the CCR8 ligand Ccl8, and there was enrichment of immunosuppressive CCR8 regulatory T cells (Treg). Anti-PD-1 monotherapy was ineffective and instead reinforced this immunosuppressive circuit, leading to expansion of CCR8 Tregs. However, depletion of CCR8 regulatory T cells overcame resistance to checkpoint blockade. Analysis of human BRCA2-mutated prostate cancer showed elevated CCR8 expression, supporting the translational relevance of the CCR8 Treg axis as a potential therapeutic target in a disease largely refractory to immunotherapy.

items.title: S100A4 Is a Targetable Regulator of Immune Suppression in Glioblastoma
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor that remains largely refractory to immunotherapy owing to a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Here, we use mouse models of GBM to identify S100A4 as an actionable regulator of immune suppression and demonstrate that its inhibition converts GBM into an immunotherapy-responsive state. Genetic knockdown of S100a4 in glioma cells reprogrammed the GBM TME, enhancing CD8 T cell infiltration and effector function while promoting maturation of antigen-presenting cells. These changes translated into significant survival benefits across diverse molecular subtypes of GBM. Therapeutically, a novel S100A4/Transferrin Receptor (TfR) bispecific antibody phenocopied S100a4-KD and showed significant therapeutic efficacy, particularly in combination with PD-1 blockade. Notably, BsA+anti-PD1 combination treatment generated tertiary lymphoid-like structures in GBM. Together, these findings establish S100A4 as a targetable driver of immune evasion in GBM and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance to immunotherapy in this lethal disease.

items.title: Neuroblastoma immune microenvironment is characterized by limited T cell infiltration and abundant macrophages expressing targetable receptors
items.abstract: Background & Aim Neuroblastoma (NBL) is a heterogenous pediatric malignancy ranging from low-risk infant tumors to high-mortality stage IV disease. We aimed to characterize the composition and spatial organization of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) across different tumor stages and assess the prevalence of immunotherapeutic targets, particularly focusing on macrophage-directed therapies. Methods Multiplexed immunofluorescence staining was performed on 185 retrospective formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue cores from 39 NBL patients. Four antibody panels targeting a total of 32 proteins were used. Immune and stromal cell phenotypes and their spatial location were identified by single-cell image analysis and correlated with clinical features such as stage, MYCN status, prior treatment, and survival. Results Immune infiltration varied among samples and patients. CD45+ leukocytes comprised a median of 1.8% of all cells (range 0.2-51.0%, IQR 0.8-6.5%), dominated by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs; 31.7% of CD45+ cells), and NK cells (15.6%). Stage IV tumors contained fewer lymphocytes. Chemotherapy shifted the TIME toward a macrophage-dominated, lymphocyte-depleted profile. Rather than segregating into M1- and M2-like subsets, TAMs co-expressed pro- and anti-inflammatory markers: CD40, CSF1R, and CD163 were broadly expressed, Clever-1 was detected on 41% of macrophages, and CD200R was virtually absent. CD47+CD45- cells were enriched in stage IV tumors. In univariate Cox analysis, higher fractions of total CD45+, NK, NKT-like, B, and cytotoxic T cells were associated with improved overall survival. Higher proportion of CD47+CD45- cells predicted worse survival. Blood leukocyte counts did not correlate with intratumoral immune infiltration. Conclusions The NBL TIME was heterogenous. High-risk tumors shared a lymphocyte-depleted, myeloid-skewed phenotype, whereas higher overall immune content predicted better survival. Macrophages were present in all tumors and expressed targetable receptors (CD40, CSF1R, CD163, Clever-1). CD47, enriched in high-risk disease, could also be a candidate macrophage-directed target.

items.title: Methylene blue modulates G3BP1-associated condensation and attenuates Kras-driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesions
items.abstract: Abstract Stress granules (SGs) are dynamic biomolecular condensates implicated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with G3BP1/2 serving as key regulators of their assembly. We combined structure-based screening of FDA-approved drugs with cellular and biochemical assays and identified methylene blue (MB) as a modulator of SG assembly. MB suppressed SG accumulation across multiple PDAC cell lines under arsenite (AS)-induced stress, nutrient deprivation, and heat shock without reducing the abundance of major SG-associated proteins. In reconstituted systems, MB inhibited G3BP1 condensation with or without added RNA and showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower G3BP1-Caprin1 co-immunoprecipitation in cells. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted a potential MB interaction site within the G3BP1 NTF2-like (NTF2L) domain. The G3BP1 V11A/F15A/F33A/F124A mutant retained basal condensate-forming capacity but showed reduced responsiveness to MB compared with wild-type G3BP1, implicating this region in MB-mediated regulation. In Kras-driven KC mice, chronic oral MB administration was associated with reduced pancreatic G3BP1-positive puncta, increased acinar preservation, and decreased preneoplastic lesion burden, epithelial proliferation, and stromal remodeling, without overt abnormalities in the evaluated endpoints. Together, these findings identify MB as a small-molecule probe that modulates G3BP1 condensation dynamics and demonstrate that chronic MB treatment is associated with the attenuation of early Kras driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesion progression in vivo.

items.title: Sense-to-sense changes in bacterial genetic codes: Experimental validation by cell-free translation and native-host proteomics
items.abstract: In the sixty years since the publication of the complete genetic code [1], many variants of the classical codon table [2] have been observed to occur naturally, including both stop codon and sense-to-sense reassignment, but in bacteria the only experimentally validated variants are stop-codon reassignments. Recently, computational analysis with Codetta predicted bacterial genetic codes containing sense-to-sense changes. Using an Escherichia coli cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) system, we tested tRNAs predicted to reassign arginine codons to tryptophan. These candidate CGG-decoding tRNAs from bacteria phylogenetically distant from E. coli restored cyan fluorescence from an sfGFP Y66R reporter in a dose-dependent manner when added to CFPS extracts containing canonical tRNAArg(CCG). Reactions lacking the CGG-to-Trp candidate tRNA remained near background. Reassignment was also observed with firefly luciferase and NanoLuc reporters, in which Trp incorporation restored activity and solubility. Intact-protein mass spectrometry yielded masses consistent with Arg-to-Trp substitution. Deep data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics of Anaerococcus prevotii, a species for which Codetta predicts CGG to code for Trp, revealed six peptides containing Trp encoded at native CGG codons and no peptides containing CGG-encoded Arg, consistent with native CGG decoding as Trp in this organism. Together, these results provide direct functional support for predicted bacterial sense-to-sense genetic codes and establish a cell-free framework for discovering natural tRNAs that expand translational coding capacity.

items.title: Coupling environmental biosensors to inverter circuits in soil bacteria
items.corresponding_institution: Systems Biology Department, Centro Nacional de Biotecnologia (CNB), CSIC, Darwin 3, 28049 Madrid, Spain
items.abstract: Genetic logic gates, such as inverting NOT functions, are routinely designed and optimised for a narrow set of laboratory-standard chemical inputs. This reliance limits their utility in real-world applications, where engineered chassis must navigate complex, niche-specific signals. Focusing on environmental synthetic biology, we engineered four biosensors responsive to ecologically relevant physical and chemical inputs (iron, oxygen, temperature, and light) and systematically coupled them to three repressor-based NOT logic gates (QacR, SrpR, and LitR) to generate 12 composite sensor-gate circuits. To evaluate cross-host robustness, all constructs were benchmarked in two non-model soil bacteria: Pseudomonas putida KT2440 and Pseudomonas protegens Pf-5. Our findings demonstrate that overall circuit performance is non-additive and cannot be predicted simply by summing individual sensor and gate dynamics. While standalone biosensors reliably detected their cognate inputs, concatenation across regulatory junctions introduced non-linearities, emergent dynamics, and host-dependent effects that caused several pairings to deviate unexpectedly from their predicted behaviour. Furthermore, host context directly governed logic execution: P. protegens Pf-5 exhibited superior overall circuit-processing capacity, whereas specific configurations, such as iron-responsive gates, performed better in P. putida KT2440. All 12 constructs are modularly integrated using the Standard European Vector Architecture (SEVA) format, providing a benchmarked toolkit to program complex information processing in real-world environments.

items.title: scCody distinguishes aging-aligned from divergent disease-associated cellular remodeling
items.abstract: Biological aging clocks summarize molecular changes as a single age estimate, but cannot distinguish disease-associated changes that follow healthy aging from those that deviate from it. Here we introduce scCody, a generative framework that learns age-dependent cellular population dynamics from cross-sectional single-cell cohorts using population-level optimal transport and endpoint-consistency regularization. scCody accurately reconstructed cellular populations at unseen ages, recovered age-associated transcriptional changes more effectively than existing generative dynamics models, and enabled donor-age inference without direct age-regression training. Using the learned healthy aging reference, scCody decomposed disease-associated cellular displacement into aging-aligned and orthogonal components. In Alzheimer's disease, selected neuronal populations showed substantial aging-aligned remodeling alongside shared orthogonal changes associated with established pathology signatures. In contrast, COVID-19 exhibited weaker aging alignment and more pronounced orthogonal immune remodeling. Further decomposition revealed patient-level interferon variation associated with symptom duration and increased transcriptional heterogeneity in CD16 monocytes. This framework provides an extension of biological age assessment beyond a single age estimate, distinguishing cellular changes that resemble healthy aging from those that depart from it.

items.title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Texas at Austin
items.abstract: Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.

items.title: The thalamic reticular nucleus provides spatially and temporally tuned inhibition to the lateral geniculate nucleus across species
items.abstract: By proposing a role in spatial attention, Francis Crick piqued interest in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a GABAergic structure that receives input from relay cells projecting to cortex and feeds back inhibition in return. Importantly, predictions of Crick's hypothesis extend beyond attention to suggest that TRN provides selective, localized inhibition to relay cells and, thus, influences sensory processing per se. To ask if this latter role for TRN holds across species, we compared previous recordings from cat with a novel dataset from mouse, focusing on vision. We estimated receptive field size and structure of reticular cells in the visual sector of TRN and of relay cells in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Cells in both nuclei encoded specific visual features and had receptive fields of comparable size within binocular visual space. Moreover, paired recordings from both structures suggested that TRN is able to promote burst firing in dLGN in addition to modulating spike rate. Thus, TRN is not only important for attentional regulation, but is also able to make fine-tuned contributions to early sensory processing.

items.title: Dynamic zonal identity is a functional determinant of liver disease
items.abstract: Liver zonation demarcates functional division of labor within the hepatic lobule, yet how zonal identity is reshaped during disease remains poorly understood. We developed RIZLiver, a Bayesian framework that infers zonal identity from gene expression without spatial coordinates. RIZLiver identified progressive loss of zone-3 metabolic identity with advancing stages of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) across independent patient cohorts. Complementary mouse models reveal that perturbing zonal identity shifts susceptibility to diet-induced metabolic injury, linking zone-3 identity to adaptive lipid utilization through lower case beta-catenin and PPARalpha. CTNNB1-mutated hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) showed an enriched zone-3 and lipid-oxidative phenotype, extending metabolic perturbations beyond MASLD. Pharmacologic reactivation of the zone-3 program shows a therapeutic effect in MASLD. Conversely, interfering with lipid-metabolic addiction in CTNNB1-mutated HCC by targeting PPARalpha; yielded a therapeutic benefit. Our findings identify zonation as a dynamic component of disease phenotype and its restoration as a potential therapy.

items.title: Direct Whole-Blood PCR for Molecular Diagnostics
items.corresponding_institution: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
items.abstract: Outbreaks of Ebola and other viral diseases underscore the need for rapid molecular diagnostics that can be performed directly from blood, yet conventional PCR workflows require sample processing that limits testing in remote settings. Here, we establish an extraction-free workflow for quantitative PCR (qPCR) and reverse-transcription qPCR directly in whole blood. Using 2 uL of blood per reaction, we combine blood-compatible amplification chemistry, RNase inhibition for RNA targets, and longer-wavelength fluorescence detection to address both biochemical and optical interference. We demonstrate detection of hepatitis B virus DNA at 10 copies/uL and RNA from hepatitis C, Bundibugyo, Ebola, and Sudan viruses at 100 copies/uL in blood spiked with viral nucleic acid standards. A portable instrument detected the Bundibugyo target with less than two minutes of hands-on preparation and results within one hour. These findings establish analytical feasibility for simplified blood-based molecular testing and motivate validation using intact viruses and clinical specimens.

items.title: The KAT2 Acetyltransferase PCAF-1 Couples Stress-Responsive Transcription to Proteostasis and Longevity
items.abstract: Aging erodes the capacity of cells to sense stress and maintain a functional proteome. Lysine acetyltransferases can link stress signals to gene expression, but whether boosting the activity of a single acetyltransferase can enhance stress responses to protect the aging proteome and extend healthspan remains unknown. Here we show that increasing the dosage of PCAF-1, the sole KAT2 family acetyltransferase in Caenorhabditis elegans, is sufficient to extend lifespan, preserve healthspan, and reprogram stress-responsive transcription. This program is conserved; mammalian orthologs of PCAF-1-induced genes are enriched among transcripts that decline upon KAT2A and KAT2B depletion. PCAF-1 strengthens inducible stress responses, attenuates the age-dependent decline in proteasomal degradation, and limits protein aggregation in C. elegans models of human neurodegenerative diseases, while preserving motility and survival. Mechanistically, PCAF-1 drives DAF-16/FOXO activation, and DAF-16 is required for both PCAF-1-dependent longevity and for protection against polyglutamine aggregation. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which KAT2 acetyltransferases promote longevity, positioning KAT2s as potential tunable regulators of proteostasis and healthspan during aging.

items.title: Comprehensive engineering of the CasX-Editor to generate a therapeutically optimized genome editor
items.abstract: CRISPR-based genetic modification is enabling curative, one-time treatments, but extending its use to more diseases will require increasing potency at low doses while avoiding unintended genomic modification. CRISPR technologies derive from microbial nucleases, such as Cas9, whose properties evolved for antiviral defense rather than precision editing in human cells. Although these systems can be engineered for greater activity or specificity, improving both properties to meet the challenges of in vivo delivery in large animals remains challenging. Here we used iterative molecular engineering of the Cas12e protein and its guide RNA to produce the X-Editor (XE), a compact nuclease platform that combines robust in vivo activity with exceptional genomic specificity. Screening tens of thousands of protein variants and guide designs and iteratively testing and combining beneficial mutations yielded an enzyme with more than 100-fold higher editing activity in human cells. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed novel inter- and intramolecular interactions driving enhanced function. XE mRNA was delivered to nonhuman primate liver via lipid nanoparticle with guides for two distinct targets. At both targets, XE demonstrated greater editing at lower doses than comparable preclinical data from Cas9-based therapies that are now in clinical testing. No off-target editing was detected for either guide in full specificity assessments performed in primary human hepatocytes at doses tenfold above the on-target effective concentration (EC90). These findings establish that more potent in vivo editing and stringent genomic specificity can be jointly engineered into a naturally compact CRISPR system for delivery using adeno-associated virus (AAV) or lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery strategies. These results provide a new foundation for advanced genetic medicines that demand lower dosing and greatly reduced off-target risk.

items.title: Evaluation of N8-propargyl spermidine as a chemical probe for deoxyhypusine synthase-dependent post-translational modifications
items.corresponding_institution: IMol Polish Academy of Sciences, Warsaw, Poland
items.abstract: Hypusination is a highly conserved post-translational modification generated on eukaryotic translation factor 5A (eIF5A) by the sequential action of deoxyhypusine synthase (DHS) and deoxyhypusine hydroxylase (DOHH). Recently, expanded DHS substrate specificity and DHS-dependent acetylhypusination of receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1) have been proposed based on studies employing N8-propargyl spermidine in click chemistry-based workflows, alongside additional analyses. Here, we used orthogonal approaches to evaluate N8-propargyl spermidine as a chemical probe for protein hypusination and to reassess the evidence for DHS-dependent modification of RIPK1. Protein labeling following treatment of cells with the probe was unaffected by DHS inhibition but was strongly reduced when cysteines were alkylated after metabolic labeling and before initiation of the click reaction, suggesting that probe-associated adducts form through reactions involving free cysteine thiols after cell lysis. Consistent with this observation, analysis of probe-modified peptides localized adducts to cysteine residues, with masses consistent with copper-dependent azide-alkyne-thiol coupling, and detected no lysine modifications corresponding to propargylated hypusine or deoxyhypusine. In a reconstituted enzymatic assay, N8-propargyl spermidine did not support DHS-dependent modification of eIF5A, whereas native spermidine supported robust modification of eIF5A but no detectable modification of RIPK1. Furthermore, our structural study revealed a non-productive binding mode of N8-propargyl spermidine to DHS. These findings challenge the interpretation of widespread chemical probe-derived labeling as evidence for expanded DHS substrate specificity and highlight the need for stringent validation before proposing new hypusination targets.

items.title: Enhancing pancreatic islet cell survival via NMDAR antagonist-driven ROR1 activation as revealed by phosphoproteomics
items.abstract: NMDA receptors (NMDARs) control function and survival not only of neurons, but also of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Since insufficient insulin secretion and beta cell death are key events during diabetes development, targeting NMDARs offers a therapeutic approach. Specifically, the NMDAR antagonist dextrorphan (DXO) increases glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in clinical trials. Furthermore, treatment with DXO or optimized DXO derivatives prevents pancreatic islet cell death upon diabetogenic insults. Nonetheless, the signaling pathways induced by NMDAR inhibition are poorly understood. Here, we use complementary approaches, phosphoproteomics and tyrosine kinase profiling, to demonstrate that DXO and its derivatives rapidly regulate multiple intracellular signaling clusters, including mTOR and ERK signaling, in pancreatic islets. Notably, mTOR inhibition, but not ERK inhibition, is sufficient to negate DXO's protective effects. Further, we show that activation of Receptor Tyrosine Kinase-like Orphan Receptor 1 (ROR1) is a universal event upon NMDAR inhibition in islets. Simultaneous knockdown of Ror1/ROR1 and its paralogue Ror2/ROR2 compromises the viability of both mouse and human islets, highlighting the ROR1/2 signaling axis as a promising avenue for enhancing beta cell survival.

items.title: mRNA/LNP-mediated expression of a ligand-independent Tie2 pathway activator, COMP-Tie2*, enables sustained endothelial stabilization
items.abstract: Activation of the angiopoietin/Tie2 signaling axis is a validated strategy for endothelial stabilization. However, therapeutic Tie2 activation via angiopoietin-1 (Ang1) or Ang1-derived agonists is intrinsically limited due to several mechanism including ligand instability, competitive Ang2 inhibition, Tie2 ectodomain cleavage, VE-PTP-mediated Tie2 dephosphorylation, and ligand-induced receptor degradation. All these inhibitory mechanisms restrict both magnitude as well as duration of therapeutic Tie2 signaling, particularly under inflammatory conditions such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) or sepsis. Here, we describe a novel ligand-independent strategy for sustained Tie2 activation based on engineered membrane-anchored Tie2 variants. By combining intracellular Tie2 kinase domains harboring naturally occurring autoactivating mutations with heterologous membrane-targeting domains, we generated truncated, constitutively active Tie2 variants that bypass extracellular ligand regulation entirely. mRNA-mediated expression of these constructs induced robust and persistent Tie2 autophosphorylation and downstream Akt-FOXO1 signaling in pulmonary endothelial cells, which exceeded COMP-Ang1-mediated activation in both strength and duration. Systemic administration of COMP-Tie2* mRNA using lung-targeted lipid nanoparticles resulted in selective pulmonary Tie2 receptor engagement in vivo. Collectively, these data establish LNP-mediated mRNA delivery of engineered recombinant receptors for intrinsic Tie2 activation as a promising novel approach for endothelial stabilization under inflammatory conditions.

items.title: Culture-Associated Changes in the Human Cardiac Fibroblast Surfaceome: A Proteomic Resource for Cell Surface Marker and Target Discovery
items.abstract: Cardiac fibroblasts (CF) are central to cardiac homeostasis and fibrosis, but the lack of reliable cell surface markers limits their direct isolation, characterization, and selective targeting in human myocardium. Most CF studies use cultured cells, yet how the cell surface changes during culture remains poorly defined. We used mass spectrometry-based surfaceome profiling in five sequential substudies of human CF, spanning failing and non-failing hearts, fresh and cryopreserved myocardium, and laboratory-isolated and commercially sourced cells. Culture was associated with extensive changes in surface protein abundance, which were largest between P0 and P1 and were reproduced in CF from fresh and cryopreserved tissue. These changes included increases in proteins associated with fibroblast activation and matrix production, and changes in proteins used as CF markers and pharmacologic targets. Whole cell proteomics showed that these changes extended beyond the cell surface. Because culture history shapes cultured CF, we examined 30 years of CF literature, revealing widespread use of later, mixed, or unreported passages and incomplete reporting of culture conditions. To aid future studies, we developed CFxplorer (CFxplorer.net), an interactive resource that integrates this literature analysis, passage-resolved protein trajectories, and a Human CF Surfaceome Atlas of 1,577 cell surface N-glycoproteins detected across 234 CF samples, with extracellular peptide evidence and biological and pharmacologic annotations to help prioritize candidate surface markers and targets for validation. Collectively, this study expands the human CF surfaceome, defines how it changes during culture, and shows that the properties of cultured CF should be verified, not assumed, before use in experiments.

items.title: Germ Granule Remodeling Reveals Germline Age in Caenorhabditis elegans
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular Biology, Cell Biology, and Biochemistry; Center on the Biology of Aging; Legorreta Cancer Center; Brown University
items.abstract: Germline aging limits reproductive lifespan, yet quantitative measures of germline age at cellular resolution within intact tissue remain limited. Here, we show that two germline condensates, P granules and Mutator foci, undergo systematic age-associated remodeling in Caenorhabditis elegans, changing in morphology, spatial organization, and mutual associations. From these single-nucleus features, we develop Germ Granule Clock (GG-Clock), an image-based aging clock that accurately predicts chronological age. Intermittent fasting, a pro-longevity intervention, shifts GG-Clock predictions toward a younger germline state, demonstrating the clock's responsiveness to anti-aging interventions. To make the approach broadly usable, we introduce GGProfiler, an open-source tool that automates granule segmentation and feature extraction. Together, our findings establish germ granule architecture as an interpretable, image-based readout of germline aging and provide a platform for quantifying condensate remodeling across genetic and environmental interventions, with potential translation to other systems.

items.title: Defining a hypoxic exposure paradigm for modelling preeclampsia-associated syncytiotrophoblast dysfunction in human blastocyst-derived placental stem cells
items.corresponding_institution: McMaster University, Graduate Program in Medical Sciences and the Department of Pediatrics
items.abstract: Introduction: Preeclampsia (PE) is a hypertensive pregnancy disorder in which placental dysfunction is thought to play a central role. Although hypoxia is widely used to model PE-associated syncytiotrophoblast (ST) dysfunction in vitro, considerable variability in oxygen control conditions and hypoxic exposure paradigms has limited standardization across studies. This study aimed to establish physiologically relevant oxygen control conditions and identify a hypoxic exposure paradigm that consistently recapitulates characteristic features of PE-associated ST dysfunction. Methods: Human blastocyst-derived trophoblast stem cells were differentiated into STs and exposed to physiological (8% O2), atmospheric (21% O2), or hypoxic (1% O2) conditions for 24 or 48 h. Angiogenic and apoptotic marker expression, cell death, and mitochondrial stress were assessed. Results: Compared with atmospheric oxygen, 8% O2 reduced cell death and more closely reflected physiological ST conditions. Acute hypoxia (24 h) induced a robust PE-like phenotype in STs characterized by induction of anti-angiogenic markers, sFlt-1 and sEng, reduced expression of the pro-angiogenic factor PlGF, and increased cell death, apoptotic signalling and mitochondrial stress. Notably, induction of several of these markers was attenuated or reversed following prolonged hypoxic exposure. Conclusions: These findings identify 8% O2 as a physiologically relevant control condition for modelling PE-associated ST dysfunction relative to 21% O2, and demonstrate that 24 h of severe hypoxia more consistently reproduces key molecular and cellular features of PE than prolonged hypoxia. This work establishes a framework for modelling hypoxia-induced ST dysfunction while highlighting the importance of oxygen control conditions and hypoxic exposure duration when modeling PE in vitro.

items.title: Actin reorganization and junctional remodeling in podocyte foot process effacement
items.abstract: Damage to podocytes results in kidney disease affecting millions of patients worldwide. Actin remodelling is a shared feature in podocyte FP effacement occurring after podocyte injury. However, it remains unclear which processes initiate and orchestrate cytoskeletal changes. Here, we show novel insights into actin dynamics during nephrotoxic serum nephritis and other podocyte disease models. Using Lifeact.mScarlet-I reporter expression and STED microscopy in podocytes, we could show distinct actin patterns occurring during FP effacement, independent of damage origin. Additionally, the protein composition of the slit diaphragm changed in a reversible manner. Tight junction proteins ZO-1 and Claudin-5 appeared at the plasma membrane with the onset of proteinuria. The changes in actin and junctional protein assembly during NTS nephritis were reversible as FP effacement disappeared, proteinuria declined and the podocytes recovered. For the first time, we could show with great spatial and temporal detail how the podocyte actin cytoskeleton adapts to insults and that a reversible response in slit diaphragm dynamics leads to a junctional remodelling better suited for upkeeping filtration barrier function.

items.title: Partial reprogramming reveals lineage-specific uncoupling of rejuvenation, function, and recoverability in human cells
items.abstract: Partial reprogramming is therapeutically useful only if cells keep its benefits while recovering their lineage identity and function after the reprogramming factors are withdrawn. Whether the relationship between reprogramming depth and recovery differs between lineages is unknown. Using reversible, traceable Sendai-OSKM, we prospectively isolated intermediate reprogramming states from primary human fibroblasts, cytotoxic T cells, and aortic endothelial cells and followed their recovery.
