Outcomes diverged: fibroblasts kept a reduced DNA methylation age but retained stromal remodeling and incomplete proliferative recovery; T cells recovered only from shallow reprogramming, with enhanced effector function; endothelial cells rapidly recovered identity, kept a reduced methylation age, and markedly improved vascular function. None of this tracked iPSC derivation efficiency. Multiome and knockdown analyses identified TOX as a shared progression dependency, whereas its candidate downstream programs were predominantly lineage-specific. Partial reprogramming involves a lineage-specific tradeoff between rejuvenation and recovery that must be optimized one lineage at a time.

items.title: Fish Metastasis Atlas for the Systematic Analysis of Organ-Specific Dissemination of Cancer
items.abstract: Metastasis is a multifaceted process in which cancer cells must overcome diverse biological barriers to establish secondary tumors and drive disease progression. Different cancers exhibit highly non random, organ specific patterns of dissemination, known as organotropism, which arise from cancer cell plasticity and interactions with the host microenvironment. A major challenge in the field is the lack of approaches that capture cancer cell dissemination at the whole organism scale while maintaining physiological relevance. Here, we introduce an in vivo zebrafish model coupled with a data driven computational framework to systematically map and compare patterns of cancer dissemination. Using patient derived Ewing sarcoma cell lines, global analyses reveal pronounced heterogeneity across individual cell lines, which are further resolved by local metrics that capture region specific colonization frequency and cancer cell visit density. This combined global-local approach identifies recurrent spatial preferences across the fish body and uncovers correlated organ targeting, indicating coordinated and structured dissemination dependent on cancer cell line and disease stage. The framework is robust and adaptable to diverse imaging datasets, providing a scalable platform for studying cancer-microenvironment interactions and spatially organized metastatic behavior for various cancer types as well as genetic and drug perturbations, with potential relevance for personalized treatment strategies.

items.title: The SOX9 C-terminus encodes a transferable cBAF-recruitment module for enhancer remodeling and cell-state control
items.corresponding_institution: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; Harvard Medical School; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
items.abstract: Transcription factors select genomic targets, but how they recruit chromatin remodelers to convert DNA occupancy into cell-state-specific accessibility remains unclear. Here, we identify an intrinsically disordered SOX9 C-terminal module that recruits SMARCB1-containing canonical BAF (cBAF) to stem-like enhancers that open during APC-mutant adenoma formation. Acute, reversible SOX9 degradation displaces cBAF from ~80% of co-bound enhancers, exceeding effects on pBAF and ncBAF, and collapses accessibility and stem-like identity; SOX9 re-expression restores these features. C-terminal truncation preserves DNA binding but disrupts cBAF engagement and chromatin opening. Enforced SMARCB1 docking to truncated SOX9 partially restores cBAF recruitment, accessibility, stem-like transcription, and organoid self-renewal, identifying remodeler recruitment as a limiting effector function. The isolated C-terminus supports higher-order cBAF assembly and, when fused to dCas9 as COMET, redirects endogenous cBAF to targeted loci to open chromatin. Disordered TF regions can therefore encode transferable instructions that deploy specific remodeling complexes to control cell state.

items.title: NPM1::ALK fusion-derived circular RNAs drive aggressiveness in ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma
items.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) derived from the NPM1::ALK fusion have been identified in ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALK+ ALCL), but their functional contribution to disease progression remains poorly understood. Divergent RT-PCR and long-read Nanopore sequencing identified eight NPM1::ALK-derived circRNA variants across ALK(+) ALCL cell-lines, a CRISPR/Cas9-engineered model, and a patient-derived xenograft. The abundance of f-circA23N2 and f-circA26N3, recurrently detected, steadily increased in crizotinib-resistant cell models. Both, highly stable, were predominantly cytoplasmic. Their overexpression in SU-DHL-1 did not affect NPM1::ALK expression, cell proliferation, or cell-cycle, in the absence or presence of crizotinib. circRNA overexpression delayed subcutaneous tumor-growth without altering response to crizotinib. Xenograft analysis disclosed altered immune response pathways and changes in inflammatory and myeloid-recruiting cytokines. RNA-seq deconvolution identified remodeling of the myeloid compartment. Intravenous f-circA23N2 and f-circA26N3 shortened survival with systemic lymphoma dissemination. NPM1::ALK-derived circRNAs appear to be non-cell-autonomous modulators of cytokine signaling and myeloid remodeling contributing to lymphoma dissemination.

items.title: Light power density governs local and systemic responses to photodynamic therapy
items.abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a promising remedy against tumor cells by light activation of a photosensitizer, and its systemic antitumor effects are commonly attributed to immunogenic cell death and the release of soluble damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Here, we show that light power density (mW/cm2), which is often treated as a mere technical parameter, determines whether PDT suppresses distant, unirradiated tumors. At an identical light dose (J/cm2), PDT at a low power density sustained singlet oxygen (1O2) generation in tumors, preserved tumor perfusion, and suppressed both irradiated and unirradiated tumors. PDT at a high power density resulted in reduced 1O2 generation, reduced tumor perfusion, and increased programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in unirradiated tumors without inhibiting their growth. Serum levels of soluble DAMPs did not differ between the two conditions, whereas circulating small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) carried distinct protein cargo. Power density is thus a controllable determinant of the systemic effects of PDT, and circulating sEVs are candidate mediators of these effects.

items.title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
items.abstract: Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI ([≥]30 kg/m2) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m2) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73-0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor-stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

items.title: Loss of CDKN2A remodels Golgi morphology to create a lipid peroxidation vulnerability
items.corresponding_institution: Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program, Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center, The Wistar Institute, Philadelphia, PA, USA & Eppley Institute for Research i
items.abstract: Loss of the tumor suppressor CDKN2A/p16 occurs in ~50% of human cancers, yet no therapies specifically target tumors with complete loss or reduced CDKN2A/p16 expression (hereafter CDKN2A/p16-Low). Identifying selective vulnerabilities in CDKN2A/p16-Low tumors therefore represents a critical unmet need. Here, we identify altered Golgi morphology as a vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanoma. A CRISPR knockout screen revealed that genes associated with Golgi membranes are essential for CDKN2A/p16-Low cell survival. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown in human and murine cancer cells was associated with striking Golgi compaction. CDKN2A/p16 knockdown sensitized cells to pharmacologic Golgi disruption via lipid peroxidation both in vitro and in vivo. Notably, reduced Retinoblastoma-associated protein (RB1) expression did not recapitulate the increased sensitivity to Golgi disruption, supporting a role for non-canonical p16 functions in this vulnerability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized link between CDKN2A/p16-Low status and Golgi remodeling, revealing a Golgi-associated metabolic vulnerability in CDKN2A/p16-Low melanomas.

items.title: Overcoming resistance to KRAS inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutated colorectal cancer
items.abstract: Oncogenic alleles of KRAS drive colorectal cancers (CRC) growth and are associated with worse disease outcomes. Despite potent allele-specific and pan-RAS inhibitors targeting now in clinical test, CRC patients are not experiencing the same therapeutic benefit as patients with other cancers. PI3-Kinase (PI3K) is a direct RAS effector and is co-mutated in about 45% of CRC cases, raising the possibility that frequent oncogenic PI3K mutations contribute to the limited benefit of KRAS inhibition in CRC. Using isogenic colorectal cancer cells engineered to harbor either of the two most common activating PIK3CA mutations, we show that oncogenic PI3K promotes resistance to the pan-RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib (RMC-6236). Global phosphoproteomic profiling revealed that PIK3CA-mutant cells undergo a distinct adaptive response to RAS inhibition, characterized by sustained PI3K-AKT signaling and extensive remodeling of pathways controlling cell-cell adhesion and junction signaling, alongside suppression of apoptotic signaling. Combined RAS and PI3K inhibition overcame this resistance, suppressed signaling through both pathways and induced apoptosis in PIK3CA-mutant cells. Together, these findings identify oncogenic PIK3CA as a determinant of resistance to RAS inhibition in KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer and provide a mechanistic rationale for combined KRAS and PI3K inhibition in KRAS/PIK3CA co-mutant tumors.

items.title: Proton pump inhibitor-associated microbiomes shape systemic host responses
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Experimental Medicine, Kiel University, Kiel, Germany
items.abstract: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) consistently alter the gut microbiome, but the contribution of these changes to systemic effects associated with PPI use remains unclear. Here, we show that PPI-associated microbiome remodelling induces systemic metabolic and transcriptional responses independently of direct drug exposure. Integrating human microbiome and metabolomics data with metabolic modelling, we identified consistent alterations in microbial metabolic functions and host-microbiome co-metabolism. Transfer of PPI-associated microbiota into germ-free mice reproduced key metabolic changes observed in humans, particularly in aromatic amino acid metabolism, and induced additional alterations in systemic lipid metabolism. These changes were accompanied by tissue-specific transcriptional responses in the colon, liver and brain, affecting metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Together, our findings identify transferable metabolic and transcriptional microbiome-mediated signatures that may contribute to the adverse systemic effects associated with PPI use.

items.title: Generalized inference of noise-corrected state variability in single cells
items.abstract: Single-cell omics methods operate at their detection limit and are less conducive to technical controls than mini-bulk approaches, which combine cells of the same type before profiling. To integrate mini-bulk samples with paired split-pool controls more holistically, we built stochprofIC, an algorithm that considers data, noise, and covariates in a distributional-regression framework. We vet stochprofIC with synthetic datasets and compare against an adjusted-variance alternative using mini-bulk data in mouse brains and human breast cancers. The noise-batch corrections provided by stochprofIC enable inference of the single-cell populations comprising the mini-bulk, which are validated repeatedly by RNA FISH in different contexts. We use stochprofIC outputs as input to a systems model of nucleocytoplasmic transport and distinguish heterogeneous trafficking states. Pharmacologic inhibition of a MAP3K11-high state inhibits apoptosis in primary breast-cancer organoids, supporting relevance to phenotypes. By deconvolving changes in location and scale, stochprofIC supports mini-bulking when high-sensitivity and reliability profiles are important.

items.title: Brain proteinopathies associated physiological changes leading to cognitive resilience in Alzheimer's disease
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology has been well characterized, however the molecular mechanisms underlying resilience to the disease remain understudied. With the growing evidence of individuals who are resilient to AD and generation of cross-cohort multiomics data, it has become feasible to understand these mechanisms. In this study, we integrated longitudinal cognitive assessments, regional neuropathology, and matched prefrontal proteomic and metabolomic profiles across donors from two independent cohorts. We identified that asymptomatic AD (AsymAD) brains exhibited amyloid burdens comparable to AD but had fewer compact plaques, lower regional tau burden, and more restricted TDP-43 pathology. Across matched stages of amyloid, tau, and TDP-43 pathology, AsymAD was consistently distinguished from AD by preservation of mitochondrial translation and bioenergetics, synaptic programs, glutamatergic metabolites, and polyunsaturated membrane lipids. Longitudinal cognitive assessments further separated resilient from vulnerable AsymAD individuals despite comparable amyloid and TDP-43 burden, with vulnerability associated with greater neurofibrillary tangle accumulation. Both AsymAD groups retained a prefrontal proteome close to that of cognitively normal individuals, apart from amyloid-associated proteins, whereas mitochondrial, synaptic, and immune changes were largely confined to AD.

items.title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy reshapes the host microbiota immune axis in autoimmune diseases
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Internal Medicine 3, Rheumatology and Immunology, Friedrich-Alexander-Universitaet Erlangen-Nuernberg (FAU) and Universitaetsklinikum Erlangen (UK
items.abstract: CD19 targeted CAR T cell therapy induces profound B cell depletion and clinical responses in autoimmune disease; however, whether it reshapes host microbiota interactions remains unknown. We longitudinally profiled gut microbiome composition and microbiota-specific humoral immunity in 20 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or idiopathic inflammatory myopathy undergoing CAR T cell therapy, alongside 23 healthy controls, using shotgun metagenomics, IgA/IgG-bound microbiota profiling, and PhIP Seq. CAR T cell therapy reshaped microbiota directed humoral immunity, with reduced fecal IgA and serum anti commensal IgA and IgG accompanied by selective remodeling of microbiota-reactive antibody repertoires. This finding was paralleled by selective changes in gut microbial composition, including depletion of Bifidobacterium adolescentis, without uniform depletion of disease-associated pathobionts. Integrated host microbiome analyses identified altered predicted protein protein interactions involving the immunoproteasome and B cell plasma cell pathways, with interactions before CAR T cell intervention being significantly associated with subsequent relapse. Consistent with these findings, taxon specific IgA targeting, but not global diversity of IgA IgG coated microbiota, differed according to subsequent relapse. Lower baseline fecal IgA was also associated with delayed B-cell reconstitution, linking mucosal humoral immunity to immune recovery after CAR T cell therapy.

items.title: Single-cell imaging links antibiotic resistance gene copy number and bacterial host identity
items.abstract: Identifying the in situ microbial hosts of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in complex environments remains a major challenge, as many of these genes are associated with mobile genetic elements. Here, we introduce combined-FISH, which integrates direct-geneFISH for ARG detection with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) for rRNA labelling, thereby enabling the simultaneous visualization and copy number quantification of ARGs in taxonomically identified single cells within microbial samples. Using the sulfonamide resistance gene sul1 as a model target, we designed a polynucleotide probe set covering all non-redundant database sequences of this gene within 5% sequence mismatch. The method was validated using model organisms harboring plasmids with sul1, Escherichia coli K12 J53 with R388 and Acinetobacter defluvii with pOXA58_010030. Combined-FISH enabled quantitative determination of sul1 copy numbers at single-cell resolution, with E. coli harboring 1-8 copies and A. defluvii 1-4 copies per cell. Following plasmid-mediated transfer of sul1 from E. coli to Pseudomonas alloputida, recipient cells typically contained 2-6 sul1 copies, with up to 14 copies detected in individual cells, demonstrating the applicability of the approach for investigating horizontal gene transfer. The method was successfully applied to river biofilm samples containing sul1-harboring bacteria, enabling simultaneous tracking of the bacterial host and its associated ARG within a complex microbial community. Collectively, these results establish combined-FISH as a powerful tool for quantitatively linking ARGs and microbial hosts in situ, and for investigating plasmid copy number and gene transfer at single-cell resolution in technical and environmental systems.

items.title: A Charcot-Marie-Tooth-associated dynamin mutation causes peripheral neuropathy-like phenotypes via Patronin/CAMSAP-dependent microtubule stabilization
items.abstract: Dynamin-2 mutations are associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) neuropathy; however, how these mutations affect neuronal function in vivo remains unclear. Here, we generated a Drosophila model carrying a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of the shi549{Delta}3 mutation, corresponding to the human dynamin-2-551{Delta}3 variant, and examined its physiological and cellular consequences. The shi549{Delta}3 mutants exhibited progressive motor impairment across multiple genetic conditions. At the neuromuscular junction, the mutation caused synaptic overgrowth accompanied by excessive microtubule stabilization, including increased Futsch-positive loop structures and bouton numbers. Genetic interaction analysis revealed that reduction of Patronin, the Drosophila homolog of mammalian CAMSAPs, partially suppressed lethality and motor defects, linking microtubule stabilization to neuronal dysfunction in vivo. Consistently, CAMSAP2 knockdown in mammalian cells attenuated dynamin-2-induced microtubule acetylation, supporting a conserved mechanism. Together, these findings identify dysregulated microtubule stabilization as a key mechanism underlying neuropathy-like phenotypes caused by a CMT-associated dynamin mutation in vivo.

items.title: A novel interaction between MNT and CCDC6: structural insights and distinct roles in cell migration and the DNA damage response
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Biomedicine and Biotechnology of Cantabria. University of Cantabria-CSIC, Albert Einstein 22, 39011, Santander, Spain
items.abstract: MNT is a transcription factor of the MYC-MAX-MXD network whose biological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify CCDC6, a tumor suppressor involved in the DNA damage response (DDR), as a novel MNT-interacting protein. Co-immunoprecipitation and interaction mapping analyses identified a part of the CCDC6 coiled-coil domain and the MNT bHLH-LZ region as major determinants of binding. Structural modelling further identified MNT residues predicted to mediate CCDC6 binding that are also critical for MNT-MAX dimerization. Transcriptomic analyses revealed substantial overlap between the gene expression programs regulated by MNT and CCDC6. Loss of either protein promoted cell migration, whereas MNT and CCDC6 cooperated in the regulation of {gamma}H2AX signalling, cisplatin responses and CCDC6 localization during the DDR. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized connection between CCDC6 and the MYC-MAX-MXD network through its interaction with MNT, revealing an additional layer of regulation within this transcriptional network.

items.title: Synthetic Hibernation Suppresses Osteosarcoma Growth and Protects Normal Tissue from Radiation
items.abstract: Natural hibernation can arrest tumor growth, but whether this effect can be reproduced through repeated pharmacologically induced synthetic torpor (ST) remains unclear. It is also unknown whether the radioprotection conferred by natural and synthetic torpor extends to tumors, potentially compromising radiotherapy. Here, five 5 AMP induced torpor bouts administered every other day, a protocol designed to mimic repeated hibernation cycles (synthetic hibernation), markedly restrained osteosarcoma growth in female C3H/HeNRj mice bearing syngeneic LM8 tumors. Interestingly, growth suppression persisted long after the final torpor bout. When 6 Gy total-body X-ray irradiation was delivered during the second bout, tumor growth control was comparable with irradiation under normothermia, whereas ovarian follicular atresia was lower and remained similar to non-irradiated controls. Together, these findings support synthetic hibernation as a strategy to restrain tumor growth and mitigate normal-tissue radiation injury without compromising tumor control.

items.title: Versatile and Cross-Species Alveolar Type II Cell Isolation Using Humanized Monoclonal Antibody Upifitamab
items.abstract: Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are primary adult alveolar stem cells that maintain healthy alveoli. AT2 cell dysfunction is broadly linked to many lung pathologies from emphysema to fibrosis. Isolation of AT2 cells with high purity is therefore central to diagnostic studies, proteomics, transcriptomics and ex vivo experiments that can lead to future AT2 cellular therapies. Current markers for AT2 isolation exhibit various limitations from species-restrictions (e.g., mouse vs human) to limited AT2 specificity, which creates challenges for flow cytometric gating/sorting and application to magnetic-activated cell isolation. While underrepresented in the literature, these bottlenecks have made AT2 cell isolation inherently difficult and slowed AT2 cell research. Here we leverage surface protein-restricted transcriptomics to identify the sodium phosphate transporter NaPi2b (SLC34A2) as a highly specific AT2 cell marker optimally detected with the humanized monoclonal antibody upifitamab. Upifitamab-based labeling of AT2 cells is compatible with flow cytometric or magnetic-activated AT2 isolation and applies to both mouse and human AT2 cells, thus streamlining protocols and circumventing species-specific nuances. AT2 cells obtained with upifitamab can be cultured as organoids, in monolayers or differentiated to AT1 cells. This simplified AT2 isolation approach should overcome several current barriers while facilitating ex vivo studies on alveolar biology and related therapeutic developments.

items.title: HPV Oncogenes rewire DNA crosslink repair to create a PRIMPOL-dependent therapeutic vulnerability
items.corresponding_institution: CHU de Quebec - Universite Laval Research Center
items.abstract: Cisplatin-based chemoradiation is the standard of care for both HPV-negative (HPV-) and HPV-positive (HPV+) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), even though patients with HPV+ tumors have better treatment responses and a better prognosis. Understanding how HPV status shapes this response could guide alternative strategies that lower long-term toxicity. Using genome-wide CRISPR screens, we show that the genetic requirements for surviving chemoradiation diverge between HPV- and HPV+ HNSCC cells. HPV+ cells tolerate cisplatin-induced interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia pathway, a phenotype recapitulated by expressing HPV16 E6 and E7 in an HPV-negative background. In these cells, DNA damage tolerance depends instead on PRIMPOL-mediated repriming and post-replicative gap filling by translesion synthesis polymerases. Although they recruit BRCA1 normally to double-strand breaks, BRCA1 accumulation at cisplatin-stalled forks is markedly reduced, indicating that BRCA1 function is uncoupled between these two substrates. This tolerance pathway leaves cells dependent on dynamic RAD51 turnover at single-stranded DNA gaps. Depletion of the RAD51 unloading factor FIRRM, or chemical stabilization of RAD51 filaments, selectively kills HPV+ and HPV oncogene-expressing cells treated with cisplatin, and PRIMPOL depletion rescues this lethality. Our findings show that HPV oncogenes rewire the response to crosslink-induced replication stress and identify RAD51 filament dynamics as a therapeutic vulnerability in HPV+ HNSCC.

items.title: Conjugative pilus tip structure reveals convergence in secretion systems
items.corresponding_institution: Univ. Rennes, CNRS, Institut de Genetique et Developpement de Rennes (IGDR) - UMR6290, T4-SECRET Team, 35000 Rennes, France.
items.abstract: Bacteria deploy specialised secretion systems to transfer proteins and DNA into other cells, driving microbial evolution, virulence and the spread of antibiotic resistance1. Among these, type IV secretion systems (T4SSs) are unique in mediating both effector delivery and conjugative DNA transfer via extracellular pili that establish contact with recipient cells2. How these molecular machines couple recipient-cell engagement to the opening of a secretion channel is a central unresolved question across direct-contact secretion systems. Here we present the first high-resolution structure of a conjugative pilus tip from the R388 T4SS. The tip comprises the major pilin VirB2 and the minor pilin VirB5 together with two unexpected components: VirB6, repositioned from the inner-membrane stalk to the pilus apex where it forms a dynamic gate, and KikA, a modular distal adhesin likely involved in recipient-cell engagement. These findings unify pilus biogenesis, entry exclusion and recipient-cell engagement into a single structural mechanism in which VirB6 acts as a gatekeeper that couples tip contact to channel opening, while KikA shapes a pointed adhesin at the apex. By comparing this architecture to the type III and type VI secretion systems, we reveal convergent gating and penetration principles to contact-dependent bacterial secretion.

items.title: A role for TRIP12 in regulating the E3 ligase network under proteotoxic stress
items.abstract: Cellular proteostasis relies on the coordinated action of molecular chaperones and protein degradation pathways to maintain protein folding and turnover. While the roles of chaperones and the proteasome are well established, how ubiquitin E3 ligases contribute to the proteostasis network remains incompletely understood. Here, we analyzed proteostasis in melanoma cells using quantitative proteomics under mild protein folding stress induced by HSP90 and proteasome inhibition. We identified the HECT-type E3 ligase TRIP12 as a proteostasis-responsive factor that was upregulated upon proteasome inhibition. Depletion of TRIP12 led to protein accumulation of a distinct group of epigenetic and transcriptional regulators, suggesting that these proteins may constitute a novel class of TRIP12 targets. Notably, the loss of TRIP12 led to a widespread reduction in the abundance of many other proteins, including components of the proteostasis network, particularly ubiquitin E3 ligases. These changes occurred largely without corresponding mRNA alterations, indicating post-transcriptional regulation. HSP90 inhibition similarly reduced protein abundance and acted in an additive manner with TRIP12 depletion to further destabilize the proteome. Together, our findings suggest that TRIP12 functions as a regulator of the E3 ligase network and proteostasis capacity, and that its loss, particularly under folding stress, causes a reduction of global protein content. These results reveal an unexpected role for TRIP12 in maintaining proteome stability and support the functional interplay between ubiquitin ligases and molecular chaperones in buffering proteotoxic stress.

items.title: Extending Mendelian randomisation to founder-haplotype data in Diversity Outbred mice
items.abstract: Observational associations can reflect confounding or reverse causation, which Mendelian randomisation (MR) avoids by using genetic variation to estimate causal effects. In Diversity Outbred (DO) mice such estimates can be tested experimentally, but applying human summary-data MR, with one scalar association per variant, ignores the differing effects of their eight founder haplotypes. We introduce Founder GLS-IVW, which uses each locus's founder-effect pattern for causal estimation and diagnosis. At Qsox1, it recovered the direction of effect seen in knockout mice, which one scalar coding failed to detect. Across 4,596 trait pairs, scalar and founder analyses disagreed for 29.7%; in seven of eight, only the founder analysis found an effect, using information scalar coding discards. Because exposure and outcome may be measured in different or partly overlapping animals, the method supports two-sample MR across separate experiments. Our R package qtl2mr, built on the widely used R/qtl2, helps prioritise mechanistic experiments.

items.title: Sedimentary ancient DNA expands bioarchaeological evidence and interpretation at Roman Harelbeke
items.abstract: Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) can expand archaeological research by recovering broad biological signals from small amounts of sediment. Here, we apply shotgun sedaDNA metagenomics and target capture (also known as hybridization capture) to disused Roman wells from the vicus of Harelbeke, Belgium, dated to ca. 160-300 CE, and integrate the results with existing bioarchaeological datasets. Moving beyond individual introduced taxa as proxies for Roman influence, we reconstruct community-level profiles spanning consumption-related, synanthropic, and environmental organisms. SedaDNA reproduced most established bioarchaeological signals, including cultivated plants and domestic animals, while also recovering additional environmental taxa that established methods underrepresented. Mitochondrial target capture strengthened selected faunal detections and enabled phylogenetic placement of a pig (Sus scrofa) within the European mitochondrial lineage. The predominance of previously established consumption-related taxa is consistent with subsistence continuity and selective adoption of Roman-introduced resources, although taxon counts alone cannot establish their relative importance. Analytical-effort modeling further indicates that batch-based sedaDNA workflows can provide broad biological profiles at lower cost and time investment than established archaeological methods. Overall, sedaDNA complements conventional bioarchaeology by broadening taxonomic recovery, supporting scalable sampling, and providing a broad-spectrum approach to reconstructing settlement ecology, subsistence, and human-environment interaction.

items.title: Heterogeneous plasticity rules generate diverse structures in recurrent networks
items.abstract: How do local changes at individual synapses give rise to structured recurrent connectivity? Experiments have revealed diverse forms of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) across the brain, making it difficult to predict which circuit structures arise from different rules. We developed an analytical framework mapping excitatory Hebbian, anti-Hebbian, and symmetric STDP rules to directed three-neuron motifs. Individual homogeneous rules generate restricted subsets of motifs, and no single rule produces all motifs. Combining different rules generates motifs inaccessible to individual rules and yields the full motif repertoire. These predictions generalize to larger recurrent networks. The mapping is nevertheless highly non-unique, with distinct rules and parameters producing similar motif distributions, including distributions compatible with experimental connectivity. Thus, circuit structure constrains candidate plasticity rules but does not uniquely identify them. Finally, networks with similar motif distributions can nonetheless differ in their firing rates and pairwise correlations, suggesting that activity may provide an additional constraint on candidate plasticity rules.

items.title: Cell type-specific coexpression networks funnel genetic risk into core genes
items.corresponding_institution: Section of Genetic Medicine, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
items.abstract: Genetic effects on common disease are mediated through many genes in multiple cell types, yet how networks connect genome-wide genetic risk to core disease genes remains unclear. One key limitation is that disease-related gene networks are likely cell type-specific, but these are poorly captured by bulk and pseudobulk coexpression networks. Here we used population-scale single-cell immune transcriptomes to decompose interindividual gene coexpression into cell type-shared and -specific networks, which have nearly opposite properties. Shared network hubs were enriched in constrained housekeeping genes, whereas cell type-specific hubs were dynamically expressed, rapidly evolving, and enriched in cell type-matched enhancers and transcription factors. Specific hubs enriched for immune disease GWAS heritability, Mendelian genes, and drug targets; these enrichments were absent or weak for non-immune disease and shared hubs. Gene-gene network edges enriched for causal trans regulation identified by trans eQTLs and perturb-seq, with shared hubs skewed to upstream regulators and specific hubs skewed to downstream disease-proximal genes. Specific hubs increased the relative success of genetically supported immune drug targets from 1.7-fold to 2.7-fold; for example, the lupus drug target BAFF is a monocyte hub connected to the Mendelian gene TREX1 and interferon-responsive genes. Overall, accounting for shared housekeeping networks reveals that cell type-specific networks funnel genetic risk into downstream and dynamic core disease genes.

items.title: A spatially continuous cell-type atlas reveals multiscale organization of the human cortex
items.abstract: Neuroimaging has increasingly revealed fine-grained spatial heterogeneity within the human cortex, uncovering regional differentiation beyond conventional cortical divisions. However, understanding the cellular architecture underlying these imaging features requires spatially continuous cell-type references that capture both cortex-wide organization and regional specialization. Here, we introduce RIDGE (Regional Integration of Deconvolution with Guided Estimation), a deconvolution framework that anchors multiple regional references to continuous cortex-wide transcriptomic maps, thereby recovering cortex-wide organizational patterns while supporting region-specific cell-type inference. RIDGE reconstructs spatially continuous distributions of 24 major cortical cell types across the human cortex. The resulting maps are robust across analytical pipelines and independent reference datasets, recover established cell-type associations with known cortical features, and recapitulate the canonical primary sensory-allocortical/periallocortical (Pr-Al) axis of cortical cellular organization. At finer scales, RIDGE resolves distinct cellular profiles across default mode, motor, and visual systems, revealing local cellular specialization within each system. By relating these cellular maps to cortical imaging features, we demonstrate their utility for investigating cellular contributions to global cortical organization and regional specialization. Together, RIDGE provides a unified framework and spatially continuous cellular reference resource for integrating cellular architecture with human cortical imaging across spatial scales.

items.title: Parallel enterocyte caspase and cytokine responses couple hypoxia to reoxygenation-dependent intestinal regeneration in Drosophila
items.abstract: Intestinal oxygen availability fluctuates during both normal physiology and disease, yet how the intestinal epithelium adapts to these changing environments remains poorly understood. Using the adult Drosophila intestine, we show that hypoxia and reoxygenation drive distinct phases of an epithelial damage and repair response. Hypoxia induces two parallel responses in largely separate enterocyte populations: an AMPK-p53-dependent response that primes enterocytes for apoptosis, and an independent Upd cytokine response that activates JAK-STAT signaling in intestinal stem cells (ISCs). Despite activation of both pathways during hypoxia, neither apoptosis nor ISC proliferation occurs until oxygen is restored. Upon reoxygenation, enterocyte loss and ISC proliferation proceed together and both are required for recovery of intestinal length. We further show that HIF-1/Sima is dispensable in enterocytes but required in progenitor cells for reoxygenation-induced proliferation. Finally, repeated episodes of hypoxia-reoxygenation shorten lifespan, and this is exacerbated by enterocyte p53 knockdown. Together, these findings indicate that the epithelium adapts to fluctuating oxygen by coordinating damage and repair responses in space and time.

items.title: Genetic ancestry influences the relative expression of ancestral haplotypes within admixed individuals
items.abstract: Allele-specific expression (ASE) reflects differences between the two haplotypes a person carries, but most ASE studies have been done in European-descent samples. Admixed individuals carry haplotypes from different ancestral backgrounds within the same cell, which allows ancestry effects on regulation to be measured directly. We integrated phased whole-blood RNA-seq with local ancestry inference in 779 participants from the MAGENTA cohort, including non-Hispanic White, African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Peruvian individuals. Higher West African (YRI) ancestry proportion was associated with more ASE-positive genes per person, and the association remained after adjusting for age, sex, Alzheimer's disease status, APOE genotype, and the number of heterozygous genes. Peruvian ancestry showed no significant association. A gene-level test of imbalance across population groups found 2,053 of 15,008 genes with significant differences, including the major histocompatibility complex in all four groups. A genome-wide scan of 2,213 1 Mb windows compared people carrying two haplotypes of different ancestries with those carrying two of the same ancestry. It identified 52 non-redundant loci that replicated across all four population groups, containing 201, 60, and 110 ancestry-associated genes under the CEU, YRI, and PEL reference baselines. A haplotype-resolved directional analysis showed no genome-wide advantage for either ancestry. It found locus-specific dominance at 11 loci, and only chr8:2-3 Mb (CSMD1) showed the same direction in more than one population group. Genetic ancestry therefore shapes allelic regulation at global, gene, and locus scales.

items.title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
items.abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. Without training on lineage, clade or drug-susceptibility tasks, MicroDUET identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mpox virus lineages and clades (0.965, 0.975 accuracy), discriminated rifampicin resistance without lineage adjustment (AUROC 0.985), and retrospectively identified an emerging mpox lineage as anomalous (AUROC 0.974). MicroDUET operates 10^3 - 10^4 times faster than single-threaded sequence-based alignments. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

items.title: Affinity-guided design of PDZ-binding peptides in a shared latent space
items.abstract: PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) are short C-terminal sequences that bind PDZ domains and contribute to protein localization and complex assembly. Designing PBMs could modulate these interactions while leaving most of the original protein sequence unchanged. Because PDZ recognition preferences overlap, modulating intended interactions requires considering off-target binding alongside target affinity. Computational PBM design methods generally use sequence-based affinity prediction and structure-based evaluation, but it remains challenging to guide sequence searches toward different binding objectives with a single trained model. Here, we propose a deep learning-based method to design PBMs by analytically formulating single-target, off-target-aware, and dual-target design objectives as directions in a PDZ-PBM shared latent space learned through quantitative PDZ-PBM affinity prediction. In single-target PBM redesign for DLG4-PDZ3, our method identified 100 top-ranked candidates, 84 of which were in the top 1% for experimentally measured interaction fitness in a published mutant library, compared with 64 using an existing method. In single-target de novo design of 10-residue PBMs, our method achieved the highest median in silico binding scores among the compared methods for three of the four PDZ domains tested. In off-target-aware and dual-target PBM design for PTPN3 and SCRIB-PDZ3, off-target-aware design increased between-group score differences within each domain at the cost of lower target-domain scores, whereas dual-target design yielded scores close to those of the respective single-target designs for both domains. Together, these results show that shared latent representations learned from quantitative affinities allow a single trained model to guide PBM design across different binding objectives without retraining.

items.title: Epigenomic circuits shaping cellular heterogeneity in pleural mesothelioma
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive and lethal malignancy with current treatments offering limited clinical benefit. In this study, we utilized single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of patient-matched samples to infer the epigenomic regulation underlying cellular heterogeneity in PM. High-resolution epigenomic profiling suggested transcriptional regulators with putative pro-tumoral roles in mesothelioma, whose function was experimentally tested using genetic perturbations across four PM cell lines. Furthermore, we observed several putative associations between epigenomic circuits and macrophage ontogeny, a sarcomatoid-like neoplastic state, and a fetal-like endothelial cell state. Our analysis also showed similarities between the chromatin accessibility landscapes of exhausted CD8 T and KLRC1 natural killer cells and identified NR4A2 as a potential shared regulator of dysfunction in both lymphocyte subsets. We further identified a state-specific distal enhancer near NR4A2 and experimentally validated its regulation of NR4A2 expression in Jurkat cells. Together, we provide an epigenomic map of PM and nominate candidate transcription factors and regulatory elements for future functional investigation, including their potential relevance to epigenetic editing strategies to limit tumor growth and enhance anti-tumor immunity.

items.title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
items.corresponding_institution: Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Tianjin 300308, China
items.abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. For PcPT6, corresponding to the previously reported PcPT07, removing 40 N-terminal amino acids increased bakuchiol production by 53% relative to the full-length enzyme. We reconstructed bakuchiol biosynthesis in Y. lipolytica and reinforced aromatic precursor synthesis to increase p-coumaric acid supply. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. Following fermentation optimization, titers reached 108.29 mg/L in shake flasks and 6.03 g/L in a 7.5-L fed-batch bioreactor. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

items.title: A Mathematical Model Connecting Appetite-Driven Food Intake to Metabolic Changes across Diet and GLP-1RA Treatments in Mice
items.abstract: Mouse models are widely used to study obesity and the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) on appetite-driven meal responses and eating behaviours. However, connecting these behavioural changes to disease prevention remains limited. One reason is that eating behaviour is often summarised as daily or weekly energy intake, obscuring meal-level dynamics. Here we present a mathematical model of mouse appetite-driven food intake across diets and treatment with the GLP-1RAs semaglutide and exenatide. The model jointly described three studies and passed both qualitative assessments and a statistical {chi}2 test (disagreement<threshold, 348<1111). Predictive performance was subsequently validated using four pre-existing studies and one new study. Finally, the model was used to simulate mouse populations under dietary and GLP-1RA interventions, with predictions showing qualitative agreement with the literature. This work aids preclinical drug discovery, supports mouse study design, and improves understanding of how individual meals accumulate into long-term physiological changes.

items.title: Large language models complement established workflows for mechanistic model construction and refinement in systems biology
items.corresponding_institution: Life and Medical Sciences (LIMES) Institute and Bonn Center for Mathematical Life Sciences, University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany
items.abstract: Mechanistic models provide a framework for describing, understanding, and predicting biological processes, but their development requires an interdisciplinary team with expertise in biology, mathematics, and computation. Here we present Octomod, a multi-agent workflow based on large language models (LLMs) that integrates biological knowledge retrieval, model construction, parameter estimation, and hypothesis testing. Built on established software tools, including AMICI and pyPESTO, and community standards, including SBML and PEtab, Octomod supports model development and refinement through natural-language interaction with a user. The agents' proposals must pass defined checks and the user's decision before they are used. Every input, model, check, and decision is recorded, so that model building remains transparent and reproducible. We applied Octomod to four problems. Three used published data and differ in model size and in how much the user guided the run: Octomod constructed a model that matched a published model without user guidance, supported the interactive refinement of a gene-regulatory model, and built models of cell-cell communication that explained the responses of five immune cell types to different stimuli. In the fourth application, on newly generated and unpublished lipidomics data, Octomod helped to determine which processes the measurements could inform, identify unresolved label fluxes, and reduce a supplied model to those processes. Together, these results show how LLMs can strengthen and complement established workflows for constructing and refining biologically informed models.

items.title: A cortically gated sensory reference to the basal ganglia guides vocal reinforcement learning in songbirds
items.abstract: Songbirds learn to sing by copying a memorized tutor song. Reinforcement learning models of vocal imitation propose that a dopaminergic signal strengthens the cortico basal ganglia synapses whose activity coincides with similarity to the tutor like song. To do so, the circuit must access a representation of the tutor song. Whether such a reference is available within the songbird basal ganglia nucleus Area X, and how it arrives, is unknown. In juvenile male zebra finches that learn to imitate adult courtship songs, we found that lesions of Area X impaired imitation more severely the earlier they were made. Intracellular recordings from Area X in awake juvenile zebra finches showed that the tutor song evokes precise subthreshold depolarizations that inversely scaled with imitation proficiency throughout song learning. Silencing the upstream nucleus HVC reduced these tutor-evoked responses, whereas disinhibiting HVC enhanced them. An inhibitory gate in HVC thus supplies Area X with the temporally aligned tutor reference that reinforcement driven vocal learning requires. These findings uncover a critical missing link in biological reinforcement learning, revealing how the brain structurally routes sensory templates to the basal ganglia to guide the acquisition of complex motor skills.

items.title: Ciliated keratinocytes define a spatially restricted pro-inflammatory state in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Psoriasis vulgaris (Pso) and atopic dermatitis (AD) are characterized by recurrent flares and incomplete disease resolution. Primary cilia are antenna-like sensory organelles that project from the cell surface and coordinate extracellular signaling. Although epidermal ciliated cells are rarely detected in healthy skin and are selectively increased in AD and Pso, their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance remain unclear. Objective: To characterize epidermal ciliated cells in Pso and AD and determine their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance. Methods: We integrated single-cell-resolved spatial transcriptomics with primary cilia immunostaining in healthy skin (n=6), AD lesions (n=10), and paired psoriatic skin before and after phototherapy (n=7 each). Functional analyses using HaCaT cells with increased primary cilia formation included MAPK/NFkB signaling assays, ATAC-seq, and pathway inhibition assays. Results: Ciliated cells were largely restricted to AD and both pre and post treatment psoriatic skin, with KCs accounting for more than 70% of all ciliated cells. Ciliated KCs were predominantly localized to the basal and spinous layers. These cells exhibited disease and stage specific inflammatory programs and formed spatially organized communication networks with surrounding cells, including non ciliated KCs, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and myeloid cells, suggesting a ciliated KC centered inflammation niche. Mechanistically, increased primary cilia formation enhanced MAPK and NFkB signaling and increased chromatin accessibility at inflammatory gene loci enriched for AP1 motifs, even in the absence of stimulation, consistent with a chromatin primed state. Higher residual ciliated KC abundance after phototherapy was associated with subsequent treatment escalation. ERK1/2 inhibition reduced cytokine induced primary cilia formation. Conclusions: Ciliated KCs represent an inflammatory epithelial cell state associated with residual disease activity in AD and Pso. The suppression of cytokine-induced primary cilia formation by ERK1/2 inhibition suggests that inflammation associated primary cilia formation may be modifiable process in persistent skin inflammation.

items.title: Peripheral Immune Cell Shifts Associated With Alzheimer's Disease Vary in Multi-Ancestry Cohorts
items.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is heavily influenced by immune system dysregulation, yet the role of peripheral immune processes--and how these vary across ethnicities--remains understudied. Objective: To investigate ancestry-specific immune alterations in AD by profiling peripheral immune cell proportions using high-resolution deconvolution of whole blood RNA-sequencing data, characterizing disease associated cell types, and identifying enriched biological pathways. Methods: We analyzed whole blood RNA-seq data from non-Hispanic White (NHW), African American (AA), Caribbean Hispanic (CariHISP), and Peruvian (PERU) individuals, balanced between AD cases and cognitively normal controls. Immune cell proportions were estimated using CIBERSORTx and compared using linear models (propeller R package) adjusted for age, sex, and APOE genotypes in case-control models. Cell-type-specific differential expression was performed using CARseq, and pathway enrichment analyses performed using MSigDB gene sets. Results: Baseline immune composition differed substantially across cohorts for multiple innate and adaptive cell types. In a multi-ethnic AD versus control analysis, eight cell types reached FDR significance: AD was associated with decreased proportions naive B cells, CD56dim NK cells, B cells, intermediate monocyte I, and double-negative T cells, alongside significant expansion in neutrophils and non-classical monocytes. Interaction analyses revealed heterogeneous group-specific effects, with the broadest shifts in AA and CariHISP. Pathway enrichment indicated shared heme metabolism, interferon, and oxidative phosphorylation programs across groups, with distinct emphases: broad, strong heme metabolism enrichment and the highest oxidative phosphorylation signal (in myeloid populations) in AA; MYC targets in naive B cells and eosinophils in CariHISP; dendritic cell - and T follicular helper cell - centered interferon, inflammatory, and proliferative programs in NHW; and TGF-{beta} and apoptosis signatures, unique to PERU, alongside the broadest cell-type coverage. Conclusions: Peripheral immune dysregulation in AD is characterized by depletion of lymphoid and intermediate monocyte populations with concurrent neutrophil and non-classical monocyte expansion, and these patterns vary meaningfully by ancestry. These findings underscore the need for population-informed biomarkers and therapeutic strategies in AD.

items.title: MAFB and MAF cooperatively orchestrate human anti-inflammatory macrophage identity via autocrine Interleukin-10
items.abstract: Macrophage lineage identity is governed by intricate transcriptional networks. Although the large MAF basic region-leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors MAFB and MAF are critical regulators of anti-inflammatory programs, their molecular coordination and non-redundant contributions within human macrophages remain poorly defined. Here, utilizing integrated proteomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiling, we demonstrate that endogenous MAFB and MAF physically associate to form a stable heterodimeric complex on chromatin in human M-CSF-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages (M-Mac). Genome-wide CUT&Tag mapping reveals a hierarchical epigenomic architecture in which MAFB acts as the primary global anchor of M-Mac identity, whereas MAF provides localized transcriptional tuning. Mechanistically, both factors directly bind the IL10 locus, but functional IL-10 expression is primarily driven by MAFB. Neutralizing antibody assays reveal that endogenously produced IL-10 establishes an obligate autocrine feedback loop mandatory for both the initial acquisition and the maintenance of the M-Mac anti-inflammatory profile. Functionally, MAFB and MAF exert non-redundant control over core macrophage effectors: MAFB dictates apoptotic cell efferocytosis amd T cell activation, whereas MAF modulates phagocytosis, and acts as a brake suppressing acute pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine hyper-induction. Together, these findings establish a comprehensive molecular blueprint of how MAFB and MAF cooperatively fine-tune human monocyte-derived macrophage identity and functional plasticity.

items.title: A living organism-level model of subcellular architecture across adult life reveals a midlife architectural state shift
items.corresponding_institution: Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health
items.abstract: Many features of subcellular organelle architecture change throughout life and influence aging. However, our understanding of this structural dynamism relies on single cell systems or comparisons between data sets focused on a limited number of organelles or timepoints. To overcome this barrier, we developed Multiorganelle Mapper (MoMA), a C. elegans strain enabling simultaneous imaging of six organelles across all somatic cell types in fully intact, living animals via fluorescence microscopy. We use MoMA to generate an organism-level in vivo map of subcellular architecture throughout adult life to understand how and why organelle organization changes with age. Aging drives a widespread and consistent shift in subcellular architecture throughout the body. Strikingly, most of this remodeling does not accumulate progressively, but emerges abruptly within individuals at midlife, an inflection point we term the midlife architectural state shift (MASS). Through a targeted RNAi screen, we show the MASS is not unique to aging, but instead resembles a generalized reactive state which can be triggered by a range of distinct homeostatic challenges. Finally, we show the MASS both coincides with and can be driven by midlife physiological changes, suggesting that this remodeling may largely reflect a coordinated reaction to the aged organismal state. Together, we present MoMA as a practical approach for visualizing subcellular architecture at organismal scale and demonstrate how it can be used to uncover principles underlying the dynamic regulation of subcellular architecture throughout life.

items.title: A PI3K-RAC1 signaling axis downstream of mutant TIE2 promotes endothelial dysfunction in venous malformation
items.abstract: Background: Activating mutations in the endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase TIE2 are a cause of venous malformations (VMs), primarily through dysregulated PI3K/AKT signaling. However, the downstream mechanisms linking constitutively active mutant TIE2 to enlarged vascular lumens, endothelial dysfunction and VM remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of RAC1 signaling in mutant TIE2 p.L914F driven VM. Methods: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing wild-type TIE2 or constitutively active mutant TIE2-L914F were analyzed using RAC1 GTP pull-down assays, immunoblotting, and endothelial cell (EC) 2D and 3D functional assays. The role of RAC1 was evaluated using the RAC1 inhibitor NSC23766 in vitro and in vivo xenograft model of VM. Results & Conclusions: ECs expressing mutant TIE2-L914F showed increased active GTP-bound RAC1. TIE2-L914F ECs exhibited cytoskeletal changes with enhanced lamellipodia formation and maturation, accompanied by increased migration. Pharmacological inhibition of RAC1 significantly attenuated the aberrant vascular lumen area and migration in the mutant TIE2 ECs. Mechanistically, we showed that RAC1 hyperactivation is PI3K-dependent but not MEK/ERK-dependent. Consistent with these findings, RAC1 inhibition significantly reduced vascular lesion formation in a xenograft model of VM with TIE2-L914F ECs. Our study identifies RAC1 as a downstream mediator of TIE2-L914F driven endothelial dysfunction. These results establish a previously unrecognized PI3K-RAC1 signaling axis in the pathogenesis of TIE2-mutated VMs.

items.title: Assembly-independent measurement of human Yq12 heterochromatin reveals population-scale variation and Yq12-derived RNA in testis
items.abstract: Despite advances in long-read sequencing and telomere-to-telomere assembly, population-scale analysis of large satellite arrays remains challenging. Human Yq12 is a megabase-scale heterochromatic region composed primarily of DYZ1/HSat3A6 and DYZ2/HSat1B repeats, whose near-equal proportions are maintained despite extensive variation in total array length. Here, using complete Y-chromosome assemblies, we developed k-mer-based tools to estimate Yq12 size directly from short- and long-read sequencing data without requiring sample-specific complete assemblies. Across 1,597 males from the 1000 Genomes Project, Yq12 length ranged from ~1 to 52 Mb (mean 26.5 Mb) and varied substantially within and between Y haplogroups. Phylogenetic analyses supported long-term constraint of total Yq12 length near an equilibrium of 26 Mb and strongly coupled evolution of DYZ1 and DYZ2 around near-parity composition. In 303 father-son pairs, fathers had longer estimated Yq12 regions in 70.6% of pairs, while sons more often showed DYZ1:DYZ2 ratios closer to 1:1. Testis Iso-Seq identified transcripts containing DYZ1 and DYZ2 satellite sequences, while single-cell RNA-seq revealed their expression in haploid spermatids. These results establish a scalable framework for studying Yq12 population variation, intergenerational dynamics, and transcription, providing new opportunities to investigate how extreme satellite-array variation relates to Y-chromosome evolution and male germ-cell biology.

items.title: Elucidating Bat SuperImmunity: Insights from the Bent-Wing Bat Genome Assembly and Multi-Omics Analysis
items.abstract: Bats have evolved a range of unique adaptations, including powered flight, echolocation, and exceptional longevity. They have also attracted considerable scientific attention, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic, due to their association with a broad diversity of viruses and their potential role in zoonotic transmission and emerging infectious diseases. Despite hosting numerous viruses, bats often exhibit limited clinical manifestations of infection, suggesting the evolution of distinctive mechanisms of immune regulation and tolerance. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms has become a major focus of current research, with genome-wide analyses providing important insights into the genetic adaptations underlying bat immunity. Nevertheless, the regulatory complexity of bat genomes, particularly the contribution of non-coding RNAs and post-transcriptional RNA editing, remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we present an integrated multi-omic framework for the common bent-wing bat (Miniopterus schreibersii), combining a contiguous chromosome-scale genome assembly with multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling, long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) identification and synteny analysis, endogenous viral elements (EVE) mapping, and same-individual RNA editomic analyses. This study provides a comprehensive resource for investigating genome organization, transcriptional regulation, evolutionary relationships, and post-transcriptional modifications in this species. In particular, it offers an opportunity to explore the potential contribution of non-coding regulatory elements and RNA editing to the molecular mechanisms underlying viral interactions and immune regulation in bats. Collectively, these resources provide a valuable foundation for advancing our understanding of bat genome evolution and the regulatory mechanisms potentially associated with their distinctive responses to viral infections.

items.title: Systematic benchmarks reveal DNA polymerase combinations for high-quality genome assembly
items.corresponding_institution: Senckenberg - Leibniz Institution for Biodiversity and Earth System Research, Senckenberganlage 25, 60325 Frankfurt, Germany; Institute of Cell Biology and Neur
items.abstract: Background: A fundamental challenge in biodiversity genomics is generating long-read sequencing data and high-quality genome assemblies from samples lacking gold-standard flash-frozen tissue, including ethanol-preserved specimens, minimally invasive biopsies, and small-bodied organisms. Amplification-based library preparation enables long-read sequencing of such samples, but assembly quality critically depends on the polymerase used for amplification. Results: We present a systematic benchmark of eleven long-range DNA polymerases for PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly across three taxonomically diverse species: a springtail, a sea slug, and a bat. We show that polymerase choice substantially affects assembly contiguity and gene completeness, primarily caused by polymerase-intrinsic GC-dependent amplification bias and read coverage heterogeneity. Five polymerases consistently produced assemblies with comparatively high contiguity and completeness, with some enzymes outperforming the polymerase currently used in the PacBio Ampli-Fi protocol. Importantly, combining reads amplified with different polymerases frequently resulted in superior assemblies, because polymerases complement each other by covering regions where others drop out. Combining reads amplified with different polymerases, we generated haplotype-resolved assemblies of the ~1 Gb giant springtail and ~2 Gb bat genome and improved the sea slug reference genome. Using the human GIAB benchmark, we further show that optimized amplification strategies improve variant-calling accuracy, highlighting their utility in medical and clinical research. To facilitate polymerase benchmarking across additional taxa, we provide the polymeval pipeline (https://github.com/casparbein/polymeval), which automates the computational workflow. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that optimized amplification-based HiFi sequencing generates assemblies with >1 Mb contig N50 and >90% gene completeness, providing a toolkit to produce long-read genome assemblies from challenging samples.

items.title: msiFlow 2.0: Extending Mass Spectrometry Imaging Workflows with Mass Recalibration, Annotation, Batch Correction, and Visual Quality Control
items.abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) enables label-free, spatially resolved molecular profiling of tissues and cells, providing insights into physiological and pathological processes. However, its large and complex datasets require specialised computational approaches. We recently introduced msiFlow, an open source, end-to-end solution for reproducible and scalable MSI data analysis. Here, we present msiFlow 2.0, a major extension that integrates pixel-wise post-acquisition mass recalibration, automated lipid annotation, batch correction, and visual quality control, together with improved alignment, spatially informed deisotoping, and computational scalability. The workflow was evaluated using four human and mouse MALDI-2 and t-MALDI-2 MSI lipidomic datasets encompassing different biological conditions, sample types, and spatial resolutions. The updated computational mass recalibration and alignment workflow significantly improved mass accuracy of reported m/z values by correcting systematic mass deviations, achieving a mean absolute mass error below 1.5 ppm for independent MS/MS-supported lipid features. The integrated lipid annotation module reduced the number of unsupported candidate lipid assignments, while ComBat correction reduced sample-associated variation and retained separation of tissue compartments. Computational optimisation reduced alignment runtime by approximately 80%. Together, these advances provide an accurate, transparent, and scalable open-source framework for MSI data processing and downstream analysis.

items.title: Propensity-Adjusted AUC under Nuisance-Model Misspecification
items.abstract: Propensity adjustment compares medical-image detector scores within groups with similar measured properties, such as stain or focus. We examine its sensitivity to the nuisance model that forms those groups. Under Gaussian latent-index assumptions and exact linear-index strata, a closed-form correlation gives an exact boundary for adjusted AUC to fall below one half. Quadrature matches 36 simulation cells within 0.008. Inflation and attenuation relative to correct adjustment are empirical findings, not general ordering results. An overlap screen and a self-stratified control introduced for this study miss 140 of 141 simulated cells with absolute error above 0.05: checking the fitted propensity cannot certify completeness of the adjustment set. On real pathology corpora, logistic and boosted-tree models using the same 16 features disagree. Among splits where both pass both checks, mean adjusted-AUC gaps are 0.057 on acid-fast bacilli (AFB), 0.048 on Kaggle, and 0.049 on PCam, over three, five, and three splits respectively. These gaps measure model sensitivity; neither estimate is known to be correct. A controlled colour shift moves adjusted AUC relative to model-specific references in the predicted direction in 78 of 80 label-dependent cells. Broader balance and label-fit diagnostics favour trees without certifying their adjusted AUC. We recommend reporting sensitivity across nuisance models alongside these diagnostics. Reversal relative to known truth occurs in constructed stress tests; its frequency in practice remains unknown.

items.title: Reproducibility and cross-dataset concordance of drug-induced transcriptional responses
items.abstract: Drug-perturbation transcriptomic resources are expanding, but the reproducibility and cross-source consistency of the responses they measure remain critical to their use. We compared six resources using independent replicates, matched-drug analyses, and response decomposition. High agreement in treated expression did not translate into equally repeatable drug-induced changes. Cross-source response concordance was generally limited, including under matched cell and treatment conditions, although some comparisons retained drug-specific information. In Tahoe, a control-expression-only baseline left substantial drug-specific variation unresolved. Measured drug main effects - the average responses across cell lines - provided information for predicting cell-specific interactions, with this relationship retained in a cross-plate validation. Exploratory analyses of structure, target, and external-response representations identified modest signals in selected pipelines. Together, these analyses characterize the reliability and transferability of current perturbation resources and identify prediction of drug main effects as a key bottleneck in the framework examined, motivating shared reference measurements and better recovery of drug-specific responses.

items.title: Regulation of the Epstein-Barr Epigenome by Histone Variant MacroH2A
items.abstract: Histone variants play an important role in regulating chromatin dynamics of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Here, we investigate the role of histone variant macroH2A in EBV chromatin structure, gene expression and copy number control during latent infection. ChIP-seq analysis in EBV+ SNU719 gastric carcinoma and Mutu I Burkitt lymphoma cells revealed that macroH2A was most enriched at repetitive DNA elements, including oriLyt, BHLF1, LF3 and terminal repeat (TR) regions of the EBV genome. MacroH2A depletion in EBV-associated gastric cancer cell line SNU719 led to a small increase in some viral lytic genes and increase in viral DNA copy number. RNAseq transcriptomics after macroH2A depletion identified major perturbations in cellular gene pathways, including beta-catenin/TCF signaling and chromatin remodeling. Depletion of macroH2A during EBV lytic reactivation reduced EBV lytic gene activation, but increased EBV DNA copy number. Previous study demonstrated a colocalization and cooperative binding between histone variant H2A.Z and EBNA1. We now show that depletion of macroH2A causes an increase in both H2A.Z and EBNA1 at oriP and cellular binding sites for EBNA1. We also found that gammaH2AX localizes to oriP and that this depends on macroH2A. Finally, we show that CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of macroH2A increases the replication and episome maintenance of oriP-containing plasmids. Taken together, these findings indicate that macroH2A localizes to the repetitive elements of EBV, including oriLyt, and can function to limit H2A.Z and EBNA1 binding at oriP, which alters DNA damage signaling at oriP and limits episomal replication. These findings provide a novel role for macroH2A in maintaining EBV copy number and genome integrity.

items.title: Local consequences of FMRP loss: cell type-specific mRNA and protein profiles of Fmr1-KO synapses
items.corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute for Brain Research
items.abstract: Brain function relies on billions of neurons interconnected by synapses with unique molecular composition specialized for cell type, brain region, and their role in circuit dynamics. Pathological synaptic dysfunctions - so-called synaptopathies - underlie many neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including Fragile X Syndrome (FXS). While synaptic deficits are well documented in FXS, molecular studies have largely relied on bulk brain homogenates or synaptic fractions, which typically represent ''average'' molecular identities, potentially masking synapse type-specific alterations. To provide synapse type resolution, we use fluorescence-activated synaptosome sorting coupled to RNA-sequencing and mass spectrometry to isolate and profile cortical excitatory and inhibitory synapses of hemizygous and heterozygous Fmr1-deficient mice. We found that full or partial FMRP loss leads to cell type- and compartment-specific molecular remodeling (syndive.org), affecting mRNAs and proteins related to synaptic organization and metabolic pathways. Strikingly, only a minority of dysregulated mRNAs/proteins were shared across excitatory and inhibitory synapses - the substantial majority were uniquely regulated at one subtype. Indeed, FMRP loss often resulted in opposing protein changes in each synapse type. Changes in mRNA or protein abundance were also not well coordinated, consistent with substantial post-transcriptional regulation, including changes to the translational and ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation machinery. For example, our data suggest a disturbed, cell type-distinct coordination of protein degradation via CAND1 as one key consequence of FMRP loss. Furthermore, we observed differences in male (Fmr1-/y) and female (Fmr1-/+) transcriptomes, where, for example, FMRP dosage was coupled to reciprocal regulation of the NDD-risk gene Trpc4 in both synapse types.

items.title: Oscillatory Entrainment Guides Temporal Prediction in Non-Deterministic Continuous Environments, Independent of Bayesian Sequential Learning
items.corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics
items.abstract: Predicting future event timing is essential for human interaction with our environment, and has been established in stimulus streams containing deterministic regularities. However, real-world streams often lack such regularities, leaving it unclear whether and how temporal predictions operate. Here we show that oscillatory entrainment, a mechanism identified for deterministic streams, operates in non-deterministic streams containing substantial temporal jitter. Model simulations revealed divergent dynamics and predicted timepoints between the oscillatory mechanism, which tracked local input regularities, and Bayesian learning, an alternative computational mechanism, which encoded global statistics. Across two speeded detection experiments using mechanism-dissociating streams, human performance was facilitated for targets appearing at oscillator-predicted times in streams with intermediate jitter levels, relative to maximal-jitter streams. Importantly, this effect was decoupled from Bayesian-based prediction and non-specific preparation, and could flexibly adapt to stream rate variations. These findings reveal the parallel mechanisms employed by humans when faced with continuous temporal uncertainty.

items.title: Channel expression aligns with dendritic conductance load in the reinforcing, not compensatory, direction in cortical GABAergic neurons
items.abstract: Neurons could offset the conductance load imposed by their dendrites through channel expression (compensation), or channel expression could move with that load (reinforcement); which arrangement holds in adult cortex is unknown. Writing rheobase as the product of input conductance and an effective-voltage factor turns the question into a sign test.
