In mouse cortical GABAergic Patch-seq neurons, after removal of transcriptomic type and covariates, an out-of-fold channel-gene score co-varies positively with residual input conductance (median Spearman {rho} = 0.32 over 20 cross-fitting splits, n = 493) and with a conductance score predicted from dendritic morphology alone ({rho} = 0.23, n = 483). The association is carried mainly by Sst and Pvalb cells and is close to zero in Vip cells. Its slope on the compensation axis is 0.13, against -1 for compensation and 0 for independence, so the finding concerns direction rather than magnitude: it excludes a population-wide compensation rule without implying strong amplification. Reduced NEURON models show that a compensatory correction is biophysically feasible, and the morphology-derived conductance predictor transfers from mouse to human reconstructions ({rho} = 0.27, n = 128).

items.title: New disease models for investigating SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD) caused by a common heterozygous nonsense SYNGAP1 mutation
items.corresponding_institution: Neuroscience Research Center, Charite-Universitaetsmedizin Berlin, Germany
items.abstract: Mutations in the SYNGAP1 gene cause SynGAP1-related disorder (SRD), a severe neurodevelopmental disorder marked by intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, autism spectrum disorder, and global developmental delay. Studies in mouse models of SRD show that restoration of SynGAP1 expression in adult animals improves memory and seizure threshold, highlighting the disorders potential for successful therapeutic intervention over the entire lifetime. We established an integrated disease-modelling pipeline centered on the recurrent SYNGAP1 c.427C>T, p.(Arg143Ter), nonsense mutation, integrating neuronal and organoid models from patient-derived human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and a humanized knock-in mouse line to investigate mutation-specific disease phenotype across complementary experimental systems. We demonstrate that the c.427C>T mutation leads to a reduction of SynGAP1 protein levels and a corresponding dysregulation of Ras/ERK signaling in human forebrain organoids as well as in the mouse model system. In vivo, mice harboring the c.427C>T mutation show a hyperactivity phenotype that corresponds well to phenotypic features seen in patients such as absence of fear, hyperactive behavior and a strong urge to investigate the immediate surroundings. Taken together, our molecular and behavioral data in the humanized mouse are in line with studies on conventional heterozygous SynGAP1 knockout models, underscoring the relevance of these new disease models for further investigations into disease pathology. Moreover, with the three models described here, we present a translational platform that enables the development and evaluation of gene therapies that target disease-causing single nucleotide variations in the SYNGAP1 coding sequence.

items.title: Differential and Cooperative Immunomodulation by Saponin Adjuvants QS-21 and QS-7 in Human THP-1 Macrophages
items.abstract: QS-21, a triterpene glycoside saponin derived from Quillaja saponaria, is a potent immunostimulatory adjuvant incorporated in several FDA-approved vaccines. QS-7, a structurally related saponin fraction, has been reported to retain immunomodulatory activity with reduced hemolytic toxicity; however, its lower natural abundance has limited its systematic immunological characterization. To address this gap, we systematically compare responses to QS-21 and QS-7 in the THP-1 human macrophage model to resolve their distinct and cooperative contributions to antigen presenting cell (APC) activation. Following cytotoxicity profiling to establish safe and biologically relevant dosing, flow cytometry, proteomics, and transcriptomics were used to delineate the immunological programs engaged by each saponin alone and in combination. QS-7 alone induced minimal upregulation of cell surface activation markers and did not elicit a significant transcriptional signature, yet it drove dose-dependent secretion of a broad panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, revealing a dissociation between these two arms of macrophage activation. Strikingly, co-administration of QS-7 with QS-21 substantially potentiated macrophage activation across all parameters tested, amplifying surface marker upregulation, broadening cytokine and chemokine output to include IL-12p70 and IFN-{gamma}, and markedly expanding the pro-inflammatory transcriptional and pathway landscape induced by QS-21, while concurrently suppressing counter-regulatory lipid-sensing pathways (PPAR, RAR, FXR/RXR) that constrain inflammatory output. Collectively, these findings establish QS-7 not merely as an attenuated analog of QS-21, but as a functionally distinct immunomodulator that recalibrates both the magnitude and regulatory tone of QS-21-driven macrophage activation. These findings show that structurally distinct saponins elicit distinct and complementary macrophage responses, providing a foundation for structure-function studies. Together with synthetic biology and data-driven design, this knowledge can guide the development of new-to-nature saponin adjuvants.

items.title: MERTK and RAC1P29S Drive Melanoma Cannibalism of T cells
items.abstract: Metastatic melanoma cells are cannibalistic, engulfing living and dead lymphocytes, but the molecular mechanisms that drive this behavior, including how they recognize their targets, are unknown. RAC is a Rho family GTPase that plays a key role in F-actin dynamics. RAC1P29S is a hyperactivating driver mutation that is common in melanoma where it promotes proliferation, motility, and therapy-resistance. Here we show that RAC1P29S melanoma cells engulf more Jurkat T cells than an isogenic RAC1WT revertant line. Live imaging captured lamellipodial dynamics and whole-cell engulfment in real time. An inhibitor screen across RAC1P29S and RAC1WT patient-derived lines showed that cannibalism requires the phosphatidylserine receptor MERTK. A RAC1P29S line lacking detectable MERTK was not cannibalistic, indicating that RAC1 hyperactivity amplifies a specific, receptor-mediated response. RAC1P29S lines are sensitive to RAC and Arp2/3 inhibition. We propose a "grip and gulp" model in which MERTK provides the grip and Arp2/3-driven branched actin the gulp.

items.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana L., 1753
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biosciences, University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway
items.abstract: We present a chromosome-level genome assembly for the vascular plant northern dragonhead, Dracocephalum ruyschiana. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 661 Mb and 681 Mb, with 93.6% and 92.5%, respectively, scaffolded into seven chromosomes each - in line with the known karyotype. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 97.9% and 97.8%, combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%, and 38,141 and 38,617 annotated protein-coding genes for hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a high-quality genomic resource for future research and conservation of northern dragonhead, as well as the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, which depends on the plant for reproduction and whose genome assembly is described in a complementary genome note.

items.title: Bloom unifies brain cell representations across modalities and contexts
items.corresponding_institution: Allen Institute, Brain Science, Seattle WA, USA
items.abstract: Multimodal genomic datasets now profile mammalian brain cells across anatomical regions, developmental stages, disease states, and species. Learning shared representations that capture cellular diversity across these heterogeneous observations remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce Bloom, a transformer-based model that represents cells using gene expression, chromatin accessibility, or both. Bloom is trained on 300,000 adult mouse brain cells with paired measurements, randomly sampled with broad-subclass balancing--approximately 100-fold fewer cells than used by comparable pre-trained models. By combining genomic sequence embeddings with randomly sampled multimodal cell views, Bloom outperforms unimodal cell models in resolving brain-wide cell types and in annotation, regression, and label-transfer tasks. Its attention patterns reveal cell-type-dependent associations among genomic loci, including pairs separated by millions of base pairs. These results establish Bloom as a data-efficient framework for integrating multimodal brain cell measurements and generating hypotheses about cell-type-specific genomic relationships.

items.title: Anatomy-preserving rare-subregion correction for pediatric brain tumor segmentation on multiparametric MRI: a BraTS-PEDs 2026 challenge study
items.abstract: Pediatric brain tumor subregion segmentation is strongly imbalanced: whole-tumor anatomy is comparatively stable, whereas enhancing tumor (ET), cystic component (CC), and edema (ED) may be absent or small. We present an anatomy-preserving multi-stage system for BraTS-PEDs 2026 Task 2. A five-fold residual-encoder nnU-Net supplies robust anatomy and calibrated out-of-fold priors. Candidate ET and CC regions are recovered by independent fold agreement and component-level filters. A rare-aware residual adapter then operates only inside voxels labeled non-enhancing tumor core (NETC), using MRI, signed inter-modality contrasts, probability uncertainty, spatial anatomy, and coordinates. Its constrained assembly permits only NETC-to-ET or NETC-to-CC transitions; therefore background, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor are invariant. On 236 out-of-fold cases, the adapter improved CC Dice from 0.223 to 0.253 and CC normalized surface Dice from 0.233 to 0.263, while preserving tumor-core and whole-tumor scores exactly. The frozen Docker submission achieved Dice scores of 0.510, 0.908, 0.144, 0.000, 0.937, and 0.937 for ET, NETC, CC, ED, tumor core, and whole tumor, respectively, on the 91-case challenge validation set. The results show that constrained rare-subtype correction can improve difficult labels without sacrificing strong anatomical predictions, while also exposing persistent domain shift for CC and ED.

items.title: Global effects of the guanine quadruplex binding ligands Pyridostatin and TMPyP4 on microRNA regulation in response to ionizing radiation in HeLa cells
items.abstract: Guanine quadruplexes (G4s) are secondary structures in DNA and RNA that regulate a wide range of biological processes. Small molecules that assist in formation, stabilization or destabilization of G4s indirectly alter the cellular functions governed by these structures. Pyridostatin (PDS) and TMPyP4 are two well-characterized G4-binding ligands that have been shown to modulate various cellular functions, particularly in cancer cells. However, their effects on microRNAs (miRNAs), which are key regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression, remain poorly understood. HeLa cells treated either with PDS or TMPyP4 and gamma radiation were subjected to small RNA sequencing. Analysis results revealed a higher overall small RNA content in PDS treated cells, whereas TMPyP4 treated cells exhibited a greater number of differentially expressed miRNAs following gamma radiation exposure. Target gene analysis of the top differentially regulated miRNAs revealed that molecular functions related to DNA/nucleic acid binding activities of various factors, including RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory region sequence-specific binding activity, were largely affected. Furthermore, KEGG pathway enrichment studies suggested that observed changes may result from alterations in signal transduction pathways in cells treated with G4 ligands and gamma radiation compared to untreated control cells. Additionally, G4 ligand treatment altered the cellular expression levels of histone modifying enzymes, including histone deacetylases and methyltransferases. This finding suggest that the two G4 binding ligands- PDS and TMPyP4 differentially regulate miRNA expression profiles, histone modifying enzymes and associated biological pathways in HeLa cells.

items.title: Multimodal Liquid Biopsy Improves Longitudinal Circulating Tumor DNA Detection in Children with Central Nervous System Tumors
items.corresponding_institution: Bioinnovation and Genome Sciences Division, Translational Genomics Research Institute, Phoenix, AZ, USA; Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, School of
items.abstract: Background: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, but limitations in sensitivity and universally accepted detection criteria remain. We evaluated multimodal ctDNA detection using a novel composite scoring framework integrating mutation, copy number, and fragmentomic analysis in longitudinal plasma and CSF samples from children with CNS tumors. Methods: Tumor, blood and/or CSF samples were collected from pediatric CNS tumor patients. DNA was extracted from plasma, CSF, tumor, and whole blood. All samples underwent targeted and whole genome sequencing. Plasma and CSF samples were evaluated for ctDNA positivity--defined by a composite score [≥]2--utilizing a tri-modal approach of whole genome sequencing for copy number alterations and fragmentomics and targeted sequencing. Results: The cohort included 28 patients: medulloblastoma (39%), diffuse midline glioma (25%), high-grade glioma (18%), pilocytic astrocytoma (11%), and ependymoma (7%). A total of 140 plasma and 27 CSF samples were collected longitudinally. Combining all three modalities identified ctDNA in 70% of CSF and 17% of plasma samples, exceeding rates achieved by any single modality alone. Post-diagnosis plasma ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with worse progression-free and overall survival. CSF demonstrated significantly higher ctDNA signal intensity than plasma across all assay modalities. Conclusions: A multimodal composite scoring approach improves longitudinal ctDNA detection in pediatric CNS tumors. Although CSF remains the most sensitive biofluid, plasma ctDNA reflects disease progression in select patients. These findings support integrated, multimodal liquid biopsy strategies for disease monitoring and highlight the need for prospective validation of standardized detection criteria.

items.title: NRF2-driven thiol metabolism creates a selective vulnerability to selenite
items.corresponding_institution: H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Center and Research Institute
items.abstract: NRF2 hyperactivation caused by mutations in KEAP1 or NFE2L2 occurs in 20-30% of non-small cell lung cancers and confers therapy resistance. Here we show that NRF2-driven metabolic reprogramming creates a selective vulnerability to selenite. NRF2-dependent thiol export promotes the extracellular reduction of selenite to selenide. Our data support a model in which selenide enters cells and reaches mitochondria, where sulfide-quinone oxidoreductase uses selenide and glutathione to generate the selenopersulfide GS-SeH. A four-hour pulse of selenite was sufficient to induce cell death after washout, consistent with a selenium redox cycle that consumes NADPH and regenerates selenide. Within hours, selenite abolished aconitase activity and impaired mitochondrial respiration. The resulting cell death occurred independently of apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis and disulfidptosis. In mice, a selenite-rich diet selectively suppressed the growth of NRF2-hyperactive tumors. These findings identify an NRF2-driven metabolic vulnerability and support further investigation of selenite as a therapeutic strategy for NRF2-hyperactive cancers.

items.title: A neural circuit for stereopsis in the fly
items.abstract: Stereopsis involves combining different views from the two eyes to infer depth, an ability that has intrigued neuroscientists for almost two centuries (Wheatstone, 1838). It enables insects such as the praying mantis to estimate the distance of prey (Nityananda et al., 2018), or primates to fixate objects at different depths (Cumming and Judge, 1986; Rashbass and Westheimer, 1961). While theoretical models for stereopsis have been proposed based on neural activity recordings (Marr and Poggio, 1976; Grossberg, 1983; Ohzawa et al., 1990), we do not have a detailed circuit mechanism for stereopsis founded on neural wiring. Here we achieve this in the fly, Drosophila melanogaster, by analyzing two whole-brain connectomes (Dorkenwald et al., 2024; Berg et al., 2026). Flies have sufficient overlap between the eyes to utilize binocular vision (Kemppainen et al., 2022); however, a circuit that performs stereopsis has not been uncovered in this model system. We show that a cell type that connects the two optic lobes called LC14 (Otsuna and Ito, 2006) forms a recurrent circuit across the brain that is capable of depth estimation. By building a connectome-constrained model, we demonstrate that recurrence is critical for binocular distance tuning in this circuit. Tuning is optimal for the size and distances of social targets (other flies), and we uncover a pathway within the brain specific for binocular vision computations. Silencing LC14 neurons renders this downstream circuitry sensitive to only monocular information and alters distance-dependent courtship behaviors, while activation of LC14 neurons causes flies to slow in response to an illusory object in their binocular visual field. In sum, we predict function from structure, uncovering how the fly brain computes distance from binocular cues, and identify a role for binocular vision in patterning social behavior.

items.title: Ribosome remodeling under glucotoxic conditions impairs beta-cell function
items.abstract: Diabetes develops when pancreatic beta-cells fail to secrete sufficient insulin to meet metabolic demand. Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates beta-cell failure and dysregulates mRNA translation before the onset of endoplasmic reticulum stress, but the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, quantitative mass spectrometry of translating ribosomes isolated from MIN6 cells under control and glucotoxic conditions revealed that sustained high glucose remodels ribosome composition by selectively decreasing Ribosomal Protein Lateral Stalk Subunit P1 (RPLP1) on actively translating ribosomes. Knockdown of RPLP1 in MIN6 cells and in primary islets reduced translation of insulin and impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Depletion of RPLP1 in vivo led to glucose intolerance. Together, our findings indicate that glucotoxicity remodels beta-cell ribosomes, leading to selective mRNA translation impairment and decreased insulin secretion. This previously unrecognized mechanism linking metabolic overload to beta-cell dysfunction suggests that preserving RPLP1 association with ribosomes could represent a therapeutic strategy for maintaining beta-cell function in diabetes.

items.title: Reusing pipettes in Patch-seq: a foundation for automated multimodal profiling
items.abstract: Patch-seq is a technique for single-cell multimodal characterization. It combines whole-cell electrophysiology, single-cell transcriptomics, and morphological reconstruction in single neurons. Patch-seq morphologies are a critical bridge among cell types, genes, physiology, and large-scale connectivity platforms such as EM connectomes and single-cell-resolution projectomes. However, patch-seq experimental complexity and operator dependence limit throughput. Automation could enable scalable Patch-seq but requires procedural adaptations, including detergent-based pipette cleaning, robotic nucleus extraction and collection. The impact of these automations on Patch-seq quality has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we show that each of these modifications preserves or improves key Patch-seq outcomes. Automated nucleus extraction performs comparably to, or better than, expert manual operation, preserving key RNA and morphological metrics. Detergent-cleaned, reused pipettes supported a viable sealing success rate across multiple cleaning cycles and preserved electrophysiological quality and transcriptomic yield without introducing excess contamination. Sonication effectively allows collection of nuclear material without damaging RNA and supports subsequent pipette cleaning and reuse. Enhanced automated sealing and break-in procedures increased throughput regardless of brain region, cell type or species. Together, these results validate the core procedural adaptations required for automated Patch-seq and establish a foundation for high-throughput, standardized multimodal single-cell characterization.

items.title: A Mechanistic Account of Dedifferentiation in the Aging Visual System
items.abstract: To uncover the mechanisms of age-related dedifferentiation, we simulated neural degradation in a computational model of the ventral visual stream. Severing connections or adding noise, whether in inferotemporal cortex (IT) or upstream, reduced IT differentiation, indicating that dedifferentiation need not originate locally. Degrading peripheral V1, which preferentially drove place-selective IT neurons, selectively reduced place differentiation, a candidate mechanism for the stronger place dedifferentiation reported in aging.

items.title: Development of direction selectivity in the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum and midbrain tegmentum
items.abstract: Detecting motion direction is a fundamental function performed by direction selective (DS) neurons. DS neurons in the optic tectum (superior colliculus in mammals) enable the tracking of moving objects. DS neurons of the accessory optic system support reflexive eye / head movements that stabilize gaze during self-motion. By developmental stage 48 (10 days postfertilization), Xenopus tadpoles display visually guided behaviors that require both types of DS neurons. Our previous work has shown that these two regions are not only functionally distinct but also follow different developmental programs. Here we characterized and compared how direction selectivity develops in both visual processing centers. Using in vivo electrophysiological recordings during moving bar visual stimulation, we measured DS synaptic inputs and spiking outputs in both regions across three key developmental stages of the retinotectal projection. Tegmental neurons were direction selective ab initio, and both input and output tuning remained stable across development. Tectal neurons were observed to receive DS inputs early, and their input selectivity also remained stable across development. However, their spiking output grew substantially more DS at the later developmental stage. This was due at least in part to a naturally occurring decrease in intrinsic excitability which preferentially dampened overall spike rates, but especially in response to the non-preferred direction of motion, thereby increasing direction selectivity. These results reveal distinct developmental trajectories in parallel visual pathways. Tegmental direction selectivity is established early and stays stable, whereas tectal output tuning sharpens during development through a decrease in intrinsic excitability.

items.title: Oligodendroglial dysfunction drives parvalbumin interneuron hypomyelination, circuit dysfunction and social deficits in an ASD model
items.corresponding_institution: Achucarro Basque Center for Neuroscience & University of the Basque Country
items.abstract: Altered social behaviour in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) has been linked to disruptions in neural circuit development, with emerging evidence implicating abnormal myelination. Yet how myelin development is affected and how this impacts circuit function remain unclear. Here, using the cntnap2-/- mouse model of ASD, we show that oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) differentiation is transiently impaired during early postnatal development, resulting in delayed myelination in the somatosensory cortex and corpus callosum, altered myelin lipid composition, and impaired sheath wrapping, accompanied by transient microgliosis and increased oligodendrocyte apoptosis. Transcriptomic analysis reveals upregulation of interferon and immune-related pathways alongside downregulation of GABAergic synaptic genes in oligodendrocytes. These alterations converge on disrupted GABAergic interneuron to OPC communication, leading to hypomyelination and impaired maturation of parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons through a non-cell-autonomous mechanism, with selective deficits in PV function, excitation/inhibition balance and gamma oscillations. Early treatment with the promyelinating agents clemastine or pranlukast restores OPC differentiation, myelination, and PV maturation, rescues circuit dysfunction, and ameliorates social deficits and behavioural inflexibility. Our findings establish that transient developmental failure in OPC differentiation drives PV interneuron hypomyelination, linking oligodendroglial dysfunction to circuit-level and behavioural alterations in ASD, and highlight early myelin-targeted interventions as a potential therapeutic strategy.

items.title: The adaptor protein DAB2 cell-autonomously links APOE with disease-associated microglia (DAM)/TREM2 state dysregulation associated with Alzheimer's disease
items.abstract: The neuron-secreted Reelin (RELN) protein and its adaptor DAB1 modify Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk through genetic interaction with APOE4. While RELN and APOE4 exert antagonistic effects on amyloid and Tau pathology in mice, how risk is conferred in the human brain remains unclear. The related adaptor DAB2 endocytoses RELN/APOE receptors and, via LRP8, modulates non-canonical pro-inflammatory signalling in non-neuronal cells. We hypothesised that RELN and APOE signalling directly influence microglial function to modify AD risk. Integrating human brain transcriptomics, a Reln-deficient mouse, and DAB1/DAB2 knock-down in APOE isogenic iPSC-microglia, we found that microglial DAB1/DAB2 pathways were dynamically regulated across the lifespan, with DAB2 dysregulated with increasing amyloid pathology. DAB2 transcriptional networks correlated with disease- and lipid- associated microglial states (DAM/LDAM) linked to networks expressing dementia-risk loci (TREM2, GRN, ACE, SORL1) and associated with endolysosomal and lipid-handling pathways. DAB2- knockdown cell-autonomously shifted microglia away from gene networks enriched in DAM/TREM2 states and towards pro-inflammatory cytokine-responsive states and TNFNF{kappa}B pathways. APOE4/E4 microglia showed elevated APOE and reduced DAB1pY232 under inflammatory stress, and blunted DAB2-knockdown transcriptomic responses, consistent with pathway-level genetic interaction. In vivo, RELN-deficiency reduced microglial ramification and increased CD68. These findings identify DAB2 as a regulator of microglial state transitions and a modifier of dementia-risk networks linking APOE genotype to inflammatory, phagocytic and amyloid-beta clearance pathways relevant to AD.

items.title: Peptide-centric proteomics reveals molecular subtypes of sporadic Alzheimer's disease
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex, age-related disease that continues to increase in incidence worldwide. Although some cases are caused by known pathogenic mutations, the majority of cases are sporadic, with uncertain etiology and commonly complicated by comorbid diseases. To better understand the molecular landscape of AD we constructed a unique brain sample set free from neuropathologic comorbidities. This cohort consists of autosomal dominant AD dementia, sporadic AD dementia, cognitively normal individuals with high AD neuropathologic change - a condition called resilient to AD, and cognitively normal cases with no or minimal AD neuropathologic change. Through quantitative mass spectrometry proteomics we obtain measures of peptides mapping to A-beta; and to tau, capturing differences in the histopathologic burden of disease. Correlations of these peptide abundance differences within sporadic AD dementia cases in the superior and medial temporal gyrus indicate the presence of two separate sporadic AD phenotypes. Additional differences are characterized at a peptide level between sporadic AD dementia and autosomal dominant AD dementia in the inferior parietal lobe and caudate nucleus. These findings indicate both shared and distinct molecular features in AD influenced by cause and age of onset of disease.

items.title: deepTools4: Faster, Scalable, and Modernized Genomic Data Analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Max Planck Institute of Immunobiology and Epigenetics
items.abstract: The deepTools suite is widely used for quality control, summarization, and visualization of high-throughput sequencing data. However, as genomic datasets grow in scale and depth, existing tools often become computational bottlenecks. We present deepTools4, a modernized framework designed for high performance, scalability, and enhanced usability, while maintaining seamless integration with the Galaxy platform. Core functionality has been rewritten and thoroughly benchmarked, achieving substantial computational speed-ups. Visualization tools have been modernized to provide more intuitive, high-quality graphical outputs. In addition, our testing framework has been expanded to facilitate continuous development and ensure robustness. We demonstrate the utility of deepTools4 across diverse epigenomics and transcriptomics datasets, highlighting its ability to summarize genome-wide signals, apply a wide range of common normalization methods, and visualize enrichment patterns. The enhanced deepTools4 framework delivers a faster, more scalable solution for reproducible genome-wide analysis and interpretation across many sequencing modalities. Availability: https://github.com/deeptools/deepTools/

items.title: Learned attraction replaces innate aversion in the evolution of an olfactory response in Mus musculus
items.abstract: The evolution of behavior is typically attributed to changes in innate circuitry, but learning can also drive behavioral evolution. Mus musculus evolved to produce trimethylamine (TMA) and behaviorally approach it, unlike the ancestral response retained by other mammals including Mus caroli. Here we demonstrate that this attraction is not innate but learned, depending on developmental TMA exposure. Whole brain immediate-early gene mapping reveals experience-dependent patterns of activation in response to TMA olfaction. Using activity-dependent TRAP2 labelling, we find that TMA-responsive neurons in the anterior olfactory nucleus are necessary and sufficient for attraction, consistent with a memory engram. Meanwhile, Mus caroli innate aversion is dependent on excitatory neurons in the posterior cortical amygdala. These results demonstrate how innate and learned circuitry both contribute to behavioral evolution in mammals.

items.title: The temporal dynamics of animacy-related neural representations are robust to controversial training
items.abstract: Animal bias refers to the human tendency to prioritise the neural processing of animate over inanimate stimuli, a phenomenon observed across multiple cognitive domains, such as attention, perception, memory, and language. Lookalikes (also referred to as zoomorphic objects), inanimate objects that visually resemble animals, tend to be interpreted as animate regardless of their inanimate identity. We examined whether this animal bias can be modified through learning to understand how experience and plasticity shape visual object representations. We tested whether feedback-based categorisation training in which lookalikes had to be categorised as inanimate could reduce the animal bias. Thirty healthy participants completed three weekly sessions of animacy categorisation training, followed by an EEG recording session during which they performed an animacy task. Repeated-measures ANOVA on behavioural data revealed that categorisation efficiency, measured as the inverse efficiency score, improved both within and across sessions, but there was no evidence that this improvement was specific to lookalikes. Time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis and representational similarity analysis on EEG data obtained after this training showed a descriptively smaller animal bias relative to the no-training dataset from \citet{Chen2023}, but this reduction was not statistically significant in any analysis. Moreover, a significant animal bias was still present in participants who underwent training. Thus, neural reorganisation related to the animal bias is limited even after several training sessions to overcome this bias.

items.title: Functional mapping of synaptotagmin 1 Ca2+ ligands that mediate excitation-secretion coupling in neurons
items.abstract: Synaptotagmin (SYT) 1 is a Ca2+ sensor that triggers rapid synaptic vesicle exocytosis, but how it is activated by Ca2+ remains enigmatic. SYT1 contains two Ca2+-sensing motifs, C2A and C2B. Structural studies have proposed that five acidic residues in each C2 domain mediate Ca2+-binding, but their functional relevance remains unclear. Here, we mutated each of the ten putative ligands and conducted side-by-side comparisons of Ca2+-binding activity and evoked glutamate release. Remarkably, all ten putative ligands are crucial for evoked synchronous release, overturning the view that binding of Ca2+ to C2A is dispensable. Importantly, Ca2+ binding to C2B is essential for synchronization. Furthermore, we report that two new human mutations, corresponding to Ca2+ ligands in C2B, are dominant-negative. Finally, four new crystal structures reveal how the choice of neutralizing substitution differentially alters SYT1 structure and, consequently, function.

items.title: Dopamine reward prediction error signal encodes effort cost as negative reward value
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB2 3EG, UK
items.abstract: All life must balance the economic problem of allocating scarce energy resources to maximize reward. Economic theory proposes that rational (reward-maximizing) decision makers balance the possible benefits from rewards against the cost of efforts for obtaining the rewards. Here we measured how the reward prediction error signal of monkey dopamine neurons reflects the negative value of effort cost (joystick resistance) and compared it with the dopamine signal for the positive value of reward. The animals repeatedly made binary choices between options varying in reward amount and effort to obtain the reward. Midbrain dopamine neurons signaled the negative value of effort cost both at effort-predicting stimuli (as reduction of reward-predicting excitation) and at experienced effort (as inhibition with more effort than predicted and as excitation with less effort). These effort signals contrasted with the opposite signal reflecting the positive value of reward relative to prediction (reward prediction error; RPE). Thus, dopamine neurons code effort cost as negative value opposite to the positive value of reward. In occurring with both stimuli and outcomes, this dopamine signal complies with the formalism of temporal difference reinforcement learning.

items.title: A Dual Effort Choice paradigm reveals pharmacological divergence between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation within the same task environment
items.abstract: Motivation loss is a transdiagnostic symptom, prevalent across neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Current treatments fail to effectively treat this symptom domain, giving it significant clinical importance. The fields of neuroscience and drug development have primarily focused on extrinsic motivation, whereby an animal must perform an action to receive an external food or water-based reward. However, many of our everyday activities are facilitated by intrinsic motivation, where completing an action is inherently rewarding. By utilising tasks focused only on extrinsic motivation, we may miss critical neurobiological and therapeutic differences between motivation types. Previous work has shown divergence in drug effect between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation tasks across a wide range of clinically-used drugs, indicating translationally-relevant differences across motivation domains that warrant further study. Therefore, the aim of this work was first to develop a task capable of simultaneously quantifying intrinsic and extrinsically motivated behaviour within the same task environment. Secondly, to use this task to further investigate this neurochemical divergence by examining a wide range of clinically-relevant drugs within this new task context. Here, we find that a pharmacological reduction in dopaminergic signalling reduced motivation across both extrinsic and intrinsic options within the new task, though this effect was mechanism dependent. In contrast, acute serotonergic and dopaminergic signalling increase produced a more heterogenous pattern, indicating nuanced mechanistic differences even when presented in the same task environment. Therefore, this task provides a new approach for characterising drug effects on distinct forms of motivated behaviour that may go unnoticed using conventional assays.

items.title: Aging limits the reduction of reactive muscle activity to perturbations but spares the retrieval of context-specific patterns with practice
items.abstract: Moving smoothly through a changing environment requires immediate reactive responses to maintain balance at an environmental transition, and learned, context-specific responses to efficiently meet the new environmental demands. People use both the reactive and context-specific responses to adapt to new environment and to re-adapt more rapidly on subsequent re-encounters. While re-adaptation slows with older age, the underlying muscular mechanisms are unknown. We hypothesized that practice would reduce reactive recruitment and increase context-specific recruitment and that both changes would be smaller in older adults. To test this, younger and older adults practiced split-belt walking (one belt faster than the other) over three days. We recorded surface electromyography from 10 muscles per leg and used linear regression to decompose each session's activity into a reactive component (template from naive, early exposure) and a context-specific component (template from practiced activity). Mixed-effects models showed that, with practice, older adults decreased reactive recruitment less than younger adults, particularly in distal muscles, with no strong evidence for an age difference in context-specific recruitment. In sum, with practice, aging limits the reduction of reactive responses to a novel walking context but spares the retrieval of context-specific muscle patterns, suggesting that mobility rehabilitation for older adults could target reactive mechanisms.

items.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction activates a translational stress response that drives diabetic pain
items.abstract: Neuropathic pain is common and debilitating among diabetics. The reactive glycolytic metabolite methylglyoxal (MGO) is strongly associated with painful diabetic neuropathy. MGO triggers pain through activation of the integrated stress response (ISR). The underlying molecular mechanisms are unclear. Here, we show that general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase acts as a conserved sensor that bridges glycolytic and mitochondrial dysfunction to pain hypersensitivity. In human sensory neurons derived from dorsal root ganglion (DRG), MGO increased eIF2 phosphorylation and suppressed global translation. These effects were blocked upon inhibition of GCN2. Unbiased ribosome profiling of mouse DRG revealed that MGO triggered repression of mRNAs that encode components of the electron transport chain. Based on this observation, mitochondrial dysfunction was examined as a potential upstream trigger for GCN2 activation. MGO directly glycated mitochondrial complex I and increased the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Correcting this redox imbalance via expression of a mitochondrial-targeted bacterial NADH oxidase (mitoLbNOX) prevented ISR activation by MGO. In a streptozotocin-induced mouse model of diabetic neuropathy, pharmacological GCN2 inhibition or sensory neuron-specific conditional deletion significantly attenuated mechanical allodynia. Calcium imaging revealed that genetic deletion of GCN2 reduced calcium influx in response to an agonist of TRPA1. Finally, expression of mitoLbNOX using adeno-associated viruses (AAV) in DRG sensory neurons in vivo reduced streptozotocin-induced mechanical hypersensitivity. Our findings demonstrate that GCN2 is a central, conserved driver of translational dysregulation downstream of mitochondrial redox stress in diabetic pain. This work highlights the critical role of mitochondrial function and translational control as key drivers of painful diabetic neuropathy.

items.title: Single-Session HRV Biofeedback Alters Neural Activity but Not Subjective Anxiety
items.abstract: Anxiety and stress are among the most prevalent mental health concerns worldwide, yet barriers to effective treatment remain high. Biofeedback-based approaches offer a promising, low-cost complement to traditional interventions. The present study examined whether real-time heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback enhances the efficacy of paced breathing for reducing state anxiety, and whether self-reported and neural measures of anxiety relief converge. Healthy adults completed a speeded Stroop task for stress induction, followed by a ten-minute paced breathing exercise. Participants were randomly assigned to an HRV biofeedback condition, in which real-time cardiac variability was displayed, or a control condition with the same breathing cue and no physiological feedback. State anxiety was assessed using the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), and neural activity was measured via EEG spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. The Stroop task reliably elevated state anxiety, and paced breathing reduced STAI-S scores equivalently in both groups; HRV biofeedback did not confer additional subjective benefit. In contrast, EEG analyses revealed that the biofeedback group showed increases in delta and bilateral theta power relative to controls, and spatially widespread increases in alpha and beta power. Time-frequency analyses further showed more extensive and sustained spectral modulation in the biofeedback condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between self-reported and neural responses to a brief HRV biofeedback intervention: paced breathing alone was sufficient to reduce acute state anxiety, while HRV biofeedback produced distinct changes in neural oscillatory activity without enhancing self-reported anxiety relief. These results show that subjective anxiety recovery and neural recovery can diverge during acute HRV biofeedback, suggesting that physiological engagement with biofeedback emerges before conscious benefits.

items.title: HUH-tag conjugation enables accessible, site-specific functionalization of DNA origami with signaling-competent proteins
items.abstract: DNA origami enables precise nanometer scale control over the number, spacing, and geometry of biomolecules, making it a powerful tool for dissecting spatially organized biological processes such as receptor signaling. However, functionalizing origami with proteins remains a bottleneck restricting the technology to specialized laboratories. Here we show that viral-derived HUH endonuclease tags, small (~10 kDa) domains that form a covalent phosphotyrosine bond with short unmodified ssDNA, provide a simple and cost-effective route to decorating DNA origami with functional proteins. Using interleukin-1{beta} (IL-1{beta}) as a model ligand, we generated recombinant IL-1{beta}-HUH, achieved efficient site-specific conjugation to unmodified ssDNA within minutes, and coupled the conjugates to a DNA origami pegboard with tunable stoichiometry. IL-1{beta}-functionalized origami triggered ligand-dependent signalling in living cells and allowed visualization of the recruitment of downstream signaling molecules, confirming that HUH-tag conjugation preserves functionality. Because this strategy requires only standard molecular biology equipment and unmodified DNA, it lowers a technical and financial barrier to DNA origami-based experimentation, opening the approach to a broader range of biological questions and laboratories outside the DNA nanotechnology field.

items.title: Metaplasia Orchestrates Tissue Recovery and Immune Remodeling Through CD73 in Chronic Pancreatitis
items.abstract: Chronic inflammatory injury promotes epithelial metaplasia, and progression from metaplasia to dysplasia is a recognized initiating event in carcinogenesis, as metaplastic cells exhibit heightened susceptibility to genetic alterations. In the pancreas, persistent acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) can progress to pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN), yet the mechanisms that determine whether ADM resolves or persists with fibrosis and sustained inflammation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify CD73 as a central regulator of ADM fate, tissue repair, and immune microenvironment remodeling during chronic pancreatic injury. Analysis of previously published single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from chronic pancreatitis (CP) tissues identified enrichment of Nt5e, which encodes CD73, within Hnf1{beta} ADM populations. Hnf1bCreERT2 and CD73fl/fl;Hnf1bCreERT2 mice were treated with caerulein for 4 weeks to induce pancreatitis and ADM prior to tamoxifen-induced deletion of CD73 in HNF1B-expressing metaplastic epithelial cells. Histologic phenotyping and immune profiling were performed using immunohistochemistry and imaging mass cytometry. Metaplasia-specific CD73 deletion exacerbated pancreatic injury and fibrosis, impaired epithelial proliferation and recovery of the acinar compartment, and altered the abundance and spatial organization of inflammatory cells. Ex vivo ADM assays further demonstrated that CD73 loss increased ADM formation and the production of MCP-1 and TIMP-1. These findings identify CD73 as a context-dependent checkpoint linking epithelial plasticity and immune modulation during chronic pancreatic injury and tissue repair.

items.title: Plasmodium vivax relapse reservoirs in Ethiopia: microhaplotype sequencing informs recurrent infection origins
items.abstract: Determining the origin of recurrent Plasmodium vivax infections is critical for quantifying the public health burden of the hypnozoite reservoir, understanding transmission potential, and evaluating anti-relapse antimalarial efficacy. In Ethiopia, P. vivax is a major contributor to malaria burden, but the relative contribution of relapse to recurrent infections remains poorly quantified. We performed microhaplotype genotyping using a panel of 93 genome-wide markers and applied a probabilistic recurrence classification framework to recurrent P. vivax samples collected in two Ethiopian radical cure trials (IMPROV and OPRA). Genotyping was conducted on parasite isolates collected at enrolment and subsequent recurrences, with participants monitored over a 12-month follow-up period (IMPROV: 604 samples from 444 participants; OPRA: 621 samples from 342 participants). Recurrent infections were classified using a Bayesian hierarchical model implemented in Pv3Rs, which estimated marginal posterior probabilities of relapse, reinfection, or recrudescence based on genotyping data and background population dynamics. Priors were structured across biologically motivated time windows reflecting the natural history of P. vivax infection in Ethiopia and anticipated drug efficacy. Recurrences with a probability of relapse (p(L)) [≥] 0.75 were classified as relapses. In the absence of primaquine, probable relapse was the dominant classification for primary recurrent infections in both trials (75.5%; 102/135) and for consecutive recurrent infections within individuals (75.2%; 204/271). Primaquine substantially reduced the proportion of participants experiencing recurrent infections attributable to probable relapse, from 57.3% to 1.7% in IMPROV and from 60.2% to 9.5% in OPRA. Polyclonal infection at enrolment was independently associated with increased odds of recurrence and a higher rate of probable relapse in OPRA, with a consistent but non-significant trend observed in IMPROV. These findings provide direct molecular evidence that the hypnozoite reservoir is the dominant driver of recurrent P. vivax infections in Ethiopia in the absence of radical cure. The marked reduction in probable relapse following primaquine treatment highlights the critical importance of expanding access to safe and effective radical cure strategies in Ethiopia and other comparable high-transmission settings.

items.title: Continuous ancestry profiles from genomes and genealogies
items.abstract: Using a single population label to represent an individual's ancestry may offer convenience, but ancestry is multidimensional, continuous, and reflects contributions from multiple ancestral sources. Here, we demonstrate empirically that ancestry profiles outperform categorical ancestry labels in capturing this complexity. Relatedness among 28,332 genotyped individuals was measured using haplotype painting and ordination and was regressed on regional ancestry proportions from the deep genealogies available for one-third of the cohort. When tested on participants in a validation set, predicted profiles placed 78% of documented ancestry in the correct region, against 48% for the training set average. Giving each participant a single regional label placed only 32% of their documented ancestry correctly, and a perfect classifier naming each person's largest documented region would reach only 38%, because most individuals carry ancestry from several regions. Thus, the continuous profile captures substantially more ancestry than any classification, providing support for representing ancestry as a continuum rather than a label.

items.title: Regional Signals Matter: Rethinking Global Pooling for mRNA Foundation Models
items.abstract: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences. However, existing benchmarks commonly reduce token-level embeddings to transcript-level representations through global mean pooling before fitting a downstream probe. This aggregation does not explicitly preserve the identities of biologically distinct mRNA regions. Consequently, signals associated with short regulatory regions may be diluted, confounding assessments of representation quality with the information preserved by the readout. We introduce an architecture-agnostic, region-aware readout that separately averages embeddings within the 5$'$ untranslated region (UTR), coding sequence, and 3$'$ UTR and concatenates the resulting representations for linear probing. We reproduce mRNABench evaluations for 20 frozen models from 18 families, with a median absolute score difference of 0.0009 across 380 model--dataset--target evaluations published for 19 models, and construct a region-aware benchmark using the same models, tasks, and splits. Relative to global mean pooling, region-aware pooling increases Pearson correlation, averaged across the 20 models, by 11--25\% on translation and stability tasks, with no statistically significant decreases detected for any model on the regression tasks. On classification tasks, relative changes in the area under the precision--recall curve range from $-3\%$ to $+11\%$. Boundary randomization and displacement generally reduce performance, while dimensionality-matched and sequence-composition controls indicate that the gains are not explained solely by increased feature dimensionality, region length, or guanine--cytosine (GC) content. Learned attention pooling approaches region-aware performance only when supplied with one query per region. In silico perturbations reveal stronger sensitivity to upstream AUGs (uAUGs) and their Kozak context, while analyses of endogenous transcripts show approximately threefold greater recovery of length- and GC-adjusted uAUG-associated differences than global-mean probes. Both readouts capture codon optimality. Model rankings averaged over the regression tasks remain largely stable, while within a task models move by several places. Our region-aware benchmark therefore provides a biologically structured and complementary evaluation of mRNA foundation models, revealing regulatory information that is less accessible to linear probes after global mean pooling. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/Sanford-Labs/rnaregionpooling

items.title: Rejuvenation rankings from CRISPRi screens change with the aging cohort and track cell growth programs
items.corresponding_institution: WHO collaborating centre on eHealth, UNSW Digital Health, UNSW Sydney, Australia
items.abstract: Ranking gene knockdowns by how well they reverse an aging expression signature is a common way to find rejuvenation targets, but the stability of these rankings has not been tested. We built TRACE, an open-source set of tests, to score 18,746 knockdown profiles from five CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens in four human cell lines. Rankings built from fibroblasts of 111 donors and from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) fibroblasts were unrelated ({rho} = -0.05). In an exploratory test, the 200 strongest age genes of the first cohort changed in the opposite direction in GTEx ({rho} = -0.55), but this was not significant after correction and shrank when GTEx batch was modeled. Raw scores followed the broad programs inside each signature: strongly for proliferation with the fibroblast signature, weakly for stress with a GTEx-derived signature. Proliferation alone matched the fibroblast scores' agreement with senescence labels. TRACE runs on other aging cohorts and screens.

items.title: Spatial multi-omic profiling of non-autonomous transcriptomic and epigenomic responses to genetic perturbation
items.abstract: Multicellular organisms develop and maintain differentiated cell states through a combination of cell-autonomous and non-autonomous regulatory mechanisms, including signal transduction pathways mediated by ligands, receptors, and kinases. Genetic perturbation through CRISPR pooled screening is widely used to study cell-autonomous regulatory mechanisms, but the challenges of cellular-resolution in situ measurement have limited the study of non-autonomous regulatory mechanisms. We developed Perturb-Tags, a spatial multi-omic technique for pooled CRISPR screening that tags nuclei with spatial barcodes, allowing joint measurement of single-nucleus gene expression, CRISPR guide RNAs, chromatin accessibility, and spatial positions within intact tissue. Perturb-Tags achieves cellular-resolution, unbiased gene expression and multi-omic profiling, and higher sensitivity than previous spatial perturbation approaches. We used Perturb-Tags to systematically perturb ligands, receptors, and all expressed kinases in human embryoid bodies. These experiments revealed extensive non-autonomous gene expression changes after perturbation, including distance-dependent loss of signaling pathway activity upon ligand knockdown, compensatory upregulation of alternative signaling pathways, and responses to receptor and kinase knockdown that vary with cell microenvironment. We also identified changes in the spatial organization of cells with ligand and kinase knockdowns. Finally, we trained a graph neural network to model the combined effects of genetic perturbations on gene expression and chromatin accessibility across an entire tissue. Our work provides a powerful experimental and computational platform for mechanistic studies of non-autonomous regulatory mechanisms across healthy and diseased tissues.

items.title: Batch Correction via Cross-Modal Anchoring
items.abstract: Batch correction is essential for integrating molecular cohorts, yet unimodal correction cannot reliably separate batch effects from biology without explicit covariates. Here we introduce anchor-guided batch correction, a label-free method that uses a comparatively stable paired omic layer to protect biology while correcting a batch-affected assay, requiring no predefined clinical covariates and returning full feature-level profiles. Across seven standard cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas, controlled confounding benchmarks, role-reversed transcriptomic workflows, and simulations, our method removed almost all platform variance in the standard cohorts, outperforming ComBat in biological preservation and CpG recovery under confounding. In the imbalanced breast cancer benchmark, where ComBat collapsed subtype retrieval (AUC 0.37) and attenuated differential methylation recovery (73.2%), anchorguided correction preserved subtype structure (AUC 0.72) and recovered 82.8% of reference CpG signals. Running in three seconds on 1,091 tumours on a single CPU without external training data, cross-modal anchoring offers a fast, practical solution for paired multi-omic harmonization.

items.title: Structural characterization of Posaconazole- parechovirus A3 capsid interaction using molecular simulations and cell infection assays
items.corresponding_institution: Iowa State University of Science and Technology: Iowa State University
items.abstract: Parechovirus-A3 (PeV-A3) is a major cause of central nervous system infections in neonates, associated with meningoencephalitis and neurodevelopmental delays. Yet there are no specific antivirals against PeV-A3 infection. A newer clade of PeV-A3 has emerged post COVID-19, and our preliminary data shows that infants are not immune to the emerging variants, underscoring the need for a focused therapeutic discovery. Posaconazole (POS) is seen to attenuate PeV-A3 entry and infection, but the mechanistic understanding of drug-capsid interaction remains unknown. To this end, we combined mechanistic interrogation of drug-capsid interactions and conformational dynamics, with experimental infection assays. We identify two POS binding sites: a VP0-VP1 interface in the 2009 isolate (US WI-09), and a VP3-VP1 groove in the 2022 isolate (9C-CMKC) and a laboratory-selected POS-resistant variant (US WI-09 POSA P14). Apo simulations showed congruent trajectories of POS: to the VP0 face in US WI-09, and to the VP3 arm in 9C-CMKC and US WI-09 POSA P14. The relative contribution of VP0 to the drug-capsid interaction decreased from 86% in US WI-09 to zero in both 9C-CMKC and US WI-09 POSA P14, indicating a redistribution of binding interactions across capsid subunits. Cysteine or arginine substitutions to VP1 Tyr224 abolished the Tyr224-VP3 anchor. Functionally, 0.3 {micro}M POS inhibited replication of US WI-09 and 9C-CMKC in Vero-P cells but only US WI-09 in receptor-overexpressing Vero-MYADM cells. These findings suggest that POS efficacy depends on binding-site localization near the MYADM-engaging VP0 interface, revealing how emerging PeV-A3 variants may retain drug binding while evading antiviral inhibition.

items.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
items.corresponding_institution: Zero-Noise Lab, Ernst Strungmann Institute of the Max Planck Society, Frankfurt a.M., Germany
items.abstract: High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

items.title: Identifying aligned tensor decompositions across heterogeneous neural datasets
items.abstract: Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

items.title: Excitatory neurons downregulate synaptic proteins before motor onset and glia reduce neuronal support in Huntington disease mice
items.abstract: Background: Huntington's disease burdens protein homeostasis and affects neurons and glia differently across brain regions, but how these two main cell populations respond as the disease progresses remains unresolved. Whole-tissue proteomes mix these cell types and hide how the proteome of each changes. We therefore measured the proteome of each cell type separately at different disease stages. Methods: We metabolically labelled cell-type-specific proteomes in living R6/1 mice and wild-type littermates for 15 days at different disease stages. We examined cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons at 1.5, 3 and 7 months, cerebellar inhibitory neurons at 3 and 7 months, and cortical, striatal and cerebellar glia at 7 months. We combined mass spectrometry with functional enrichment and competitive protein-set tests to understand the differential proteostatic response to mutant huntingtin across disease progression, brain regions and cell types. Differential abundance was tested with a peptide-centric linear mixed model (msqRob, Benjamini-Hochberg q < 0.1), and proteins whose levels varied together in cortical and hippocampal neurons were grouped into modules by weighted correlation network analysis. Results: Hippocampal excitatory neurons showed broader and more coordinated regulation than cortical neurons already before motor onset, whereas the cortical response increased with age and no cortical protein module differed between genotypes before the most severe stage. All three neuronal populations upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) proteins as the disease advanced. Protein folding changed, with more subunits of the chaperonin CCT/TRiC but fewer J-domain proteins and, in excitatory neurons, fewer HSP70 chaperones. At the most severe stage, glia of the three studied regions regulated mainly different proteins, but all increased UPS proteins and decreased key proteins of neuronal support, among them the main glial glutamate transporter GLT-1. Cholesterol-related proteins decreased in cortical and cerebellar glia, and respiratory-chain proteins in striatal glia. Conclusions: Synaptic proteins decreased early in cortical and hippocampal neurons and were not restored at later ages. A later and broader maintenance response coexisted with their continued and increasing downregulation. In this first cell-type-resolved view of the labelled proteome in a Huntington's disease mouse model, progression appears as a change in the coordination of cellular functions, which whole-tissue measurements would dilute.

items.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
items.abstract: Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

items.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychology, University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA
items.abstract: For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many streamlines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test--retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat .

items.title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of 5xFAD mouse brain maps cell-type-specific transcriptional disruption and preferential rolipram rescue in VIP interneurons
items.corresponding_institution: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center
items.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive synaptic dysfunction and inhibitory circuit disruption across multiple brain cell types. Rolipram, a selective phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor that elevates intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), activates proteasome, and produces robust procognitive effects in AD mouse models. Still, the cell-type-specific transcriptional mechanisms underlying these effects remain uncharacterized. Methods: We profiled 29,664 nuclei from 5xFAD and wild-type (WT) mouse right hemisphere across four conditions: WT Vehicle, WT Rolipram, 5xFAD Vehicle, and 5xFAD Rolipram (0.03 mg/kg/day, 30-day subcutaneous osmotic pump) using the Parse Biosciences Evercode WT v3 combinatorial barcoding platform. Nuclei were clustered into 16 annotated cell type populations using Seurat v5. Disease and rescue effects were quantified as log fold changes (LFCs) across all clusters, with Gene Ontology enrichment assessed using clusterProfiler and transcription factor activity inferred using decoupleR. Results: Disease-associated transcriptional disruption was highly cell-type-specific in its magnitude. Among inhibitory subtypes, VIP/Reln disinhibitory interneurons (n = 149 nuclei) showed the most coherent transcriptional disruption: 289 candidate genes were lower in 5xFAD, with Gene Ontology enrichment concentrated in synapse organization programs, including regulation of synapse structure or activity (padj = 1.5x10^-14, 44 genes), regulation of synapse organization (padj = 1.9x10^-14, 43 genes), and postsynapse organization (padj = 1.1x10^-13, 38 genes). This pathway-level specificity was not reproduced in PVALB or SST interneurons. Astrocytes showed loss of cell-adhesion programs (cell-substrate adhesion padj = 2.4x10^-4, 10 genes). Rolipram rescue was preferential: VIP interneurons yielded 72 true rescue genes and astrocytes yielded 42, with the remaining 14 clusters showing substantially fewer. The cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde7b was disease-context-specifically lower in 5xFAD VIP interneurons (LFC -0.53) and restored by rolipram (LFC +0.54), with WT expression unchanged. decoupleR CREB1 activity inference identified reduced CREB1 activity in 5xFAD VIP interneurons with partial restoration in 5xFAD Rolipram, supporting a stepwise transcriptional cascade in which amyloid pathology reduces cAMP, which suppresses PKA and CREB1 activity. This in turn reduces Pde7b transcription, and rolipram reverses this cascade by blocking cAMP hydrolysis upstream. Conclusion: This single-nucleus atlas provides the first cell-type-resolved characterization of rolipram's transcriptional effects in the 5xFAD brain. VIP disinhibitory interneurons emerge as the most transcriptionally vulnerable inhibitory subtype and the preferential site of rolipram-associated rescue, with the Pde7b/CREB1 signaling axis nominating a tractable, disease-context-specific pharmacological substrate.

items.title: The Xist locus on the X chromosome of males regulates cognition and metabolism despite minimal expression
items.abstract: The long non-coding RNA Xist is the master regulator of X chromosome inactivation (XCI) in females, but its functional significance in males, where Xist expression is normally minimal, is unknown. Here we investigated whether the Xist locus influences male physiology and brain function across the lifespan using mice carrying a targeted Xist deletion ({Delta}Xist). Xist deletion produced a small further reduction in the very low, residual Xist signal in aged male hippocampus. Metabolically, Xist deletion lowered fasting blood glucose in old, not young, males, without affecting body weight. In the brain, Xist deletion modestly improved spatial memory at 24 hours in the Morris water maze in young males, with a similar trend at middle age in an interactive place avoidance task, independent of anxiety-like behavior or locomotor activity. This early cognitive benefit did not persist with aging and motor function on the rotarod was unaffected by genotype at any age. Together, these findings indicate that the Xist locus exerts age- and domain-specific effects on male metabolic and cognitive functions despite near-absent baseline Xist expression. These data identify an unexpected role for a canonically female-associated regulatory locus in males and raise the possibility that Xist-associated mechanisms contribute to male brain function and metabolism.

items.title: Daily light exposure differences between extreme chronotypes persist after alignment to habitual sleep timing
items.corresponding_institution: TUM School of Medicine and Health, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany
items.abstract: Purpose: Morning and evening chronotypes may receive light at different clock times, thereby providing differently timed signals to the circadian pacemaker. Prior studies have suggested phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a way that could reasonably counteract timing extremes. Methods: We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from an international cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). We compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc) in clock time and relative to MSFsc using cyclic generalized additive mixed models, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. In exploratory analyses, we tested moderation of these differences by daylength and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing. Results: The modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06-0.40) 9.6-11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc) and 14.0 (5.6-34.8) 0.9-4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R2 (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSFsc-relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSFsc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSFsc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06-6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSFsc contrast. Exploratory weighting by the published PRC gave higher advance-weighted point estimates in extreme evening than extreme morning types; the group difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Extreme chronotypes differ in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSFsc. The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure showed significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

items.title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
items.corresponding_institution: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: Working memory (WM) requires neural circuits to change how they interact as information is encoded, maintained and used. Directional oscillatory interactions in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contribute to memory processing, but how these interactions are spatially organized during verbal WM remains unclear. Here, we analyzed intracranial electroencephalogram and neuronal spiking recorded from the human MTL during a verbal Sternberg task. Theta- and gamma-band activities in MTL showed predominant directionality in the posterior-to-anterior axis during WM encoding, but this direction was reversed to anterior-to-posterior during retrieval. Theta activities reflecting the WM load were more prevalent in left than right MTL, and theta in left MTL coordinated spike timings more strongly. Moreover, interhemispheric interactions showed a predominant left-to-right influence, with posterior-to-anterior interactions enhanced during encoding and anterior-to-posterior interactions enhanced during retrieval. Together, these findings suggest that verbal WM engages a spatially organized MTL network in which the predominant direction of oscillatory interactions changes across task phases.

items.title: Impaired cholinergic modulation of striatal spiny projection neurons in repetitive behaviors associated with TSHZ3-linked autism spectrum disorder
items.corresponding_institution: Aix-Marseille Univ, CNRS, CRPN, UMR7077 Marseille, France
items.abstract: Alterations in central cholinergic systems are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We previously identified TSHZ3 as an ASD-linked gene and provided evidence, from transgenic mouse models, supporting the view that striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) are key players in the core ASD trait represented by repetitive behaviors (RBs). Indeed, conditional deletion of Tshz3 in cholinergic neurons (Chat-cKO model) results in RBs associated with reduced SCIN firing activity and decreased striatal cholinergic tone. Here we tackled the resulting adaptations in the striatal circuitry underlying RBs in Chat-cKO, focusing on the two populations of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) that express dopamine D1 (D1R) or D2 (D2R) receptor. Using patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, as well as behavioral, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we show reduced cholinergic transmission through the muscarinic M1 receptor onto SPNs, with no changes in the functionality or expression of this receptor. Notably, we demonstrate a loss of the differential excitability of D1R- vs. D2R-SPNs. Finally, acute in vivo treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil significantly alleviates RBs in mutant mice. These findings point to dysfunction of SCINs as a pathological and druggable mechanism underlying RBs in Tshz3-linked ASD, and to altered SPN excitability as a critical contributor in the resulting pathophysiological functioning of the striatum.

items.title: Combining non-linear and spectral cardiac variability metrics differentiates rat alcohol drinking with and without challenge
items.corresponding_institution: 1Department of Psychiatry, Indiana University School of Medicine (IUSM), Indianapolis IN, USA. Stark Neurosciences Research Institute, IUSM, Indianapolis, IN, U
items.abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remains a substantial global challenge, with notable individual and sex differences. Heart rate variability (HRV) offers a potential link into the autonomic system underlying alcohol drinking. While simpler, time-domain HRV metrics have been explored, non-linear indicators could provide unique insights into more complex states like compulsive drinking, intake that persists despite negative consequences. We examined heart rate traces from male and female rats during intake of alcohol-only and alcohol+10mg/L quinine, a putative compulsive drinking model. In particular, we re-analyzed previously published findings, but newly focused on several non-linear HRV metrics: the Poincare ratio (possibly reflecting sympathovagal balance) and MultiScale entropy (MSE, perhaps reflecting unpredictability in broader and narrower time windows), along with the previously unexamined spectral HRV metrics (the parasympathetic indictor high-frequency HRV, HF-HRV%). HRV was assessed for the first ~1100 heart beats (~2.5 minutes), to assess HRV correlates of greater alcohol front-loading while having approximately similar amount of data per session. Lower Poincare ratio and higher HF-HRV% were overall related to higher alcohol consumption. In contrast, compulsive drinking, but not alcohol-only, was associated with lower broader-window HRV entropy, which was more pronounced in males. Drinking- and sex-related patterns were further identified using Principle Component Analysis, Ordinary Least Squares, and Linear Mixed Models. Limitations included perhaps being underpowered to detect significant relationships, especially in females.
