Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that combining HRV metrics could represent useful biomarkers for consumption levels during front-loading, which distinguished general intake from compulsion.

items.title: State-Dependent Stimulation for Seizure Termination in a Morris-Lecar Network: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
items.corresponding_institution: HUN-REN Wigner Research Centre for Physics
items.abstract: The efficacy of neurostimulation for seizure termination depends not only on the stimulus itself but also on the dynamical state of the epileptic network. Here, we develop a dynamical-systems-informed reinforcement-learning framework that learns when to deliver a predefined pulse to terminate seizure-like activity. We simulate a sparsely connected network of 100 extended three-dimensional Morris-Lecar neurons. Bifurcation analysis of the single-neuron model identifies bistable regimes and provides a mechanistic basis for considering transitions between resting and oscillatory activity. The learning agent uses semi-gradient Q-learning with tile coding and receives a two-dimensional time-delay embedding of either the population-averaged membrane potential or a derivative-based proxy for extracellular potential. It learns a state-dependent policy that selects between stimulation and no stimulation, without modifying the pulse waveform. Across 30 independently generated test networks, both learned policies markedly reduced median seizure duration compared with trigger-only and state-independent stimulation controls. The two learned policies performed comparably, indicating that the estimated extracellular potential proxy retained sufficient dynamical information for control in this model. These results provide a proof of concept that combining dynamical-systems-based state reconstruction with online reinforcement learning can identify effective stimulation timing for terminating seizure-like activity.

items.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Health and Kinesiology, College of Health, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, USA
items.abstract: Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

items.title: TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction and Clustering From Sparse Evidence For Disease Subtyping and Staging
items.abstract: Chronic progressive diseases often follow heterogeneous courses, with individuals differing in the pattern and timing of biomarker abnormalities. However, observed data are typically sparse and predominantly cross-sectional, with limited follow-up covering only short segments of disease progression. Reconstructing heterogeneous trajectories from such data requires disentangling variation along disease trajectories from subtype heterogeneity while inferring individuals' unknown subtype assignments and disease stages. Existing approaches may confound disease stage with subtype, scale poorly as the number of biomarkers increases, or fail to effectively integrate cross-sectional and longitudinal observations. We propose TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction And Clustering from Sparse Evidence, a probabilistic framework that jointly reconstructs biomarker trajectories and infers disease subtypes and continuous stages. TRACE combines monotonic neural networks for flexible modeling and data-driven clustering of subtype-specific progression trajectories with temporal regularization derived from longitudinal observations when available. All model components are jointly optimized end to end using stochastic gradient descent, enabling efficient and scalable estimation. We evaluate TRACE on semi-simulated MRI biomarker data with known subtype and stage structures and demonstrate its ability to identify clinically meaningful subtypes and disease stages in real-world neurodegenerative disease datasets.

items.title: Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) restrains the maintenance and acquisition of the anti-inflammatory identity of monocyte-derived macrophages.
items.abstract: The Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is an essential environmental sensor bridging metabolic cues with immune regulation, yet its precise role in defining human monocyte-derived macrophage identity remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that AhR functions as a critical transcriptional rheostat that selectively restrains the anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic identity of M-CSF-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages (M-Mac). Integrated ChIP-Seq and transcriptomic profiling revealed that AhR activity is enriched in M-Mac in a MAFB-dependent manner, directly occupying regulatory regions of core M-Mac identity genes, including CD163, LGMN, and IL10. Unexpectedly, siRNA-mediated knockdown and CRISPR/Cas9 ablation demonstrated that AhR primarily functions as a repressor; its deficiency accelerated and exacerbated the acquisition of a "resident-like" (LYVE1+/FOLR2+) and pro-fibrotic phenotype. Functionally, AhR restricted the M-Mac anti-inflammatory response to TLR7 ligation, and limited an overly tolerogenic profile during M-Mac-driven T-cell responses. Pharmacological modulation using the endogenous ligand FICZ and the antagonist SR1 confirmed that AhR activity limits the magnitude of the MAFB-driven program and the autocrine IL-10 signaling axis. Collectively, these findings establish AhR as a fundamental checkpoint that prevents macrophages from acquiring an excessive anti-inflammatory state, thereby ensuring balanced responses essential for tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance.

items.title: Uncoupling Osteoclast Fusion and Resorptive Activity Through Differential Talin1-Rap1 Signalling Pathways
items.corresponding_institution: Institut de Pharmacologie et Biologie Structurale (IPBS), Universite de Toulouse, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, Universite Toulouse III, CNRS, I
items.abstract: Bone remodelling is essential for skeletal growth and repair and depends on a balance between osteoblast-driven bone formation and osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Integrin activation, regulated by Rap1 and Talin1, is critical for osteoclast function by coordinated adhesion and actin cytoskeleton organization. In this study, we investigated Rap1 effectors controlling Talin1 in osteoclasts. RIAM and Lamellipodin (Lpd) are expressed and localise to actin-rich structures, including tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) and podosomes, supporting roles in cytoskeletal organisation and intercellular connectivity. Functional analyses revealed distinct, stage-specific functions. Lpd deficiency impaired early osteoclastogenesis by reducing TNT formation, disrupting precursor fusion, decreasing multinucleation, and lowering bone resorption. In contrast, RIAM deficiency has minimal impact on fusion but significantly reduced resorption activity in mature osteoclasts, indicating a role at later stages. Disruption of the direct Rap1-Talin1 interaction caused broader defects affecting both early and late stages, including reduced TNT formation, delayed fusion, altered multinucleation, and impaired bone degradation. In vivo, only disruption of this direct interaction increased bone mass and reduced osteoclast number and/or activity, whereas RIAM or Lpd deletion had no significantly impact. These results demonstrate that RIAM and Lpd perform distinct but complementary functions and identify the direct Rap1-Talin1 interaction as a central mechanism controlling osteoclast fusion and bone resorption.

items.title: Global mapping of VEGF-A driven changes in the RNA bound phospho-proteome reveals a molecular switch to coordinate angiogenesis in endothelial cells
items.corresponding_institution: Medical Faculty Mannheim, University of Heidelberg
items.abstract: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) serve as upstream master regulators of cellular fate transitions at the post-transcriptional level. RBP-RNA interactions are dynamically regulated by post-translational modifications to coordinate cellular responses. We hypothesised that changes in RBP phosphorylation will play a key role in coordinating angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, in endothelial cells (ECs). Therefore, we used phospho-proteomic analysis of the mRNA bound proteome to identify global phosphorylation changes in mouse cardiac ECs during acute and prolonged VEGF-A stimulation. Of the differentially phosphorylated RBPs, we found that the phosphorylation of serine 199 within mRNA bound Phf6 (PHD finger protein 6) was consistently increased following VEGF-A stimulation. Phf6 phosphorylation at this specific site was sufficient and required to induce a pro-angiogenic phenotype, facilitating a change in Phf6 conformation promoting interaction with distinct RNAs. We show here that Phf6 phosphorylation at serine 199, downstream of VEGF-A, acts as a molecular switch to differentially coordinate a decrease of anti-angiogenic RNAs (i.e. extracellular matrix genes) and an increase in pro-angiogenesis related RNAs, in part by differentially regulating their stability, to promote angiogenesis.

items.title: Additive genes underlie Mendelian inheritance and contribute to heterosis
items.corresponding_institution: National Technology Innovation Center for Saline-Alkali Tolerant Rice
items.abstract: Mendel proposed the laws of segregation and independent combination in his study. However, he focused on "dominant" characters but left "intermediate" ones. Using genotypic and phenotypic data for four representative genes, we reveal connections between the "intermediate" and "dominant" characters. We demonstrate that the fundamental inheritance patterns of these genes are additive effects on both component and compound traits. Additive effects involving more than two genes generate non-additive effects in hybrids. For compound traits such as grain yield, their inheritance depends on differential patterns of component traits in parents; only parents with optimal balances of reciprocal differences in component traits produce overdominant effects, which is important for hybrid breeding.

items.title: LRPPRC gene replacement therapy preserves cardiac function and prevents premature death in a mouse model of mitochondrial disease
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory for Genetics of rare ophthalmological, auditory and mitochondrial diseases, Imagine Institute, INSERM UMR 1163, Paris, France
items.abstract: Pathogenic variants in LRPPRC disrupt mitochondrial gene expression, causing severe and incurable mitochondrial disease with neurological involvement accompanied by hepatopathy or cardiomyopathy. The development for gene therapy for LRPPRC-linked disease is hindered by the large LRPPRC coding sequence exceeding AAV cargo capacity when combined with classical regulatory elements. Here, we engineered compact single rAAV9 vectors expressing human or mouse LRPPRC and administered them intravenously to heart and skeletal muscle-specific Lrpprc knockout mice. This approach restored cardiac LRPPRC expression, preserved oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) function, prevented cardiomyopathy and markedly extended survival. While skeletal muscle rescue was partial, the therapy effectively prevented fatal cardiac dysfunction. These findings provide the first in vivo proof-of-concept that AAV-mediated LRPPRC gene replacement can preserve OXPHOS function and prevent lethal cardiomyopathy, supporting its potential as a therapeutic strategy for mitochondrial disease linked to LRPPRC deficiency.

items.title: Empirical optimization of dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a for pooled screening in Yarrowia lipolytica
items.abstract: Yarrowia lipolytica is an important host for biotechnology and metabolic engineering, valued for its ability to accumulate lipids and produce a wide range of industrially relevant compounds. This creates a growing need for genome-scale tools that can accelerate the identification of genes underlying complex phenotypes. Although Cas9-based CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and activation (CRISPRa) tools are well established in Y. lipolytica, Cas12a offers a complementary platform with a T-rich PAM that can expand access to promoter regions and facilitate multiplexed regulation. Despite these advantages, Cas12a-based CRISPRi/a remains comparatively underdeveloped in Y. lipolytica, particularly for large-scale functional screening. Here, we establish and systematically benchmark dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a platforms for pooled screening in Y. lipolytica. We first compared two widely used effectors, dLbCas12a and denAsCas12a, across single-gene assays and a pooled CRISPRi library targeting nine essential or conditionally essential genes with 752 crRNAs. Both orthologs supported robust transcriptional repression, but their relative performance was crRNA- and condition-dependent, with dLbCas12a showing more consistent and stronger late-stage depletion across targets. dLbCas12a also enabled enrichment-based CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens, recovering expected drug-resistance and lipid-associated phenotypes. The broad design of the pooled library further enabled identification of crRNA features associated with CRISPRi efficacy. Highly active crRNAs were enriched near transcription start sites, with an effective targeting interval extending from approximately -260 to +50 bp. Intermediate GC content was associated with higher efficacy, while PAM identity showed a weaker but consistent effect, with TTTA and TTTT PAMs linked to stronger depletion than TTTC and TTTG PAMs. Spacer length showed the strongest association with CRISPRi efficacy, with 18-nt crRNAs consistently outperforming matched longer 20-, 23-, and 25-nt variants. Finally, we tested dHyperLbCas12a, an engineered LbCas12a variant with enhanced activity, and found that it produced substantially stronger CRISPRi and CRISPRa phenotypes than dLbCas12a. Together, these results establish Cas12a as a versatile platform for pooled CRISPRi/a screens in Y. lipolytica, identify practical crRNA prioritization rules for improved library performance, and highlight dHyperLbCas12a as a promising effector for future large-scale gain- and loss-of-function screens.

items.title: MAUDE-Py: A Python Implementation for Analyzing Sorting-Based Pooled CRISPR Screens
items.abstract: The Python programming language is gaining popularity in bioinformatics owing to its versatility in computing-heavy applications. An area of particular interest where computational power can be leveraged is analyzing and interpreting pooled CRISPR screens. Here, we replicate the core functionality of an existing platform, Mean Alterations Using Discrete Expression (MAUDE), in Python (MAUDE-Py) to analyze pooled CRISPR screens. Our tool complements the original R MAUDE software as a robust and user-friendly Python package that integrates with existing CRISPR analysis workflows. While preserving the core probabilistic framework of MAUDE, MAUDE-Py introduces notable enhancements. These enhancements include automated baseline calculations, a more robust null-sampling methodology for determining significance at both the gene and non-coding element levels, and an integrated visualization suite for displaying the analyzed results. Benchmarking MAUDE-Py against the original MAUDE on a series of datasets demonstrates a 2.09x to 4.19x speedup in execution time while achieving near-perfect consistency, confirming that our Python implementation is a highly accurate and viable alternative for such analyses.

items.title: Characterizing Multimodal Mutational Processes in Cancer Using MOTET
items.corresponding_institution: Section of Computational Biomedicine, Department of Medicine, Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA.
items.abstract: Mutational signatures are characteristic patterns of somatic alterations in cancer genomes. A single aberrant mechanism can simultaneously generate coordinated patterns of alterations across multiple mutation modalities, including single-base substitutions (SBSs), doublet-base substitutions (DBSs), and small insertions and deletions (IDs). However, these signatures are typically inferred separately and linked post hoc, obscuring their shared underlying mechanisms. To resolve this, we formally define a Mutational Process (MP) as a unified latent activity that induces coupled mutational signatures across these modalities. We developed MOTET, a Bayesian framework that jointly infers multimodal MPs. Applied to 2,583 whole genomes from the PCAWG cohort, MOTET recovers known MPs more accurately than standard post hoc correlation methods. MOTET also identifies a process linking an SBS37-related signature with a TG>CA-dominated DBS component and resolves canonical SBS12-like activity into two separate MPs with distinct tissue distributions. These results establish a paradigm for formally defining catalogs of MPs and demonstrate that integrating across modalities enhances the ability to discover new mutational patterns.

items.title: Graph-guided flow matching enables biologically informed prediction at single-cell resolution
items.corresponding_institution: TRON - Translational Oncology at the University Medical Center of the Johannes Gutenberg University gGmbH, Mainz, Germany
items.abstract: Perturb-seq enables systematic interrogation of massively parallel genetic perturbations at single-cell resolution, yet exhaustive characterization of the full perturbation space remains impractical. Here, we present Graph-guided Flow Matching (GFM), a generative framework that integrates biological knowledge graphs with latent flow matching to predict post-perturbation single-cell transcriptomes. Across multiple large-scale Perturb-seq datasets, GFM outperforms a strong linear baseline and current deep-learning models in predicting unseen single-gene perturbations, while training up to 30x faster and remaining robust with limited training data. GFM also demonstrates competitive performance in the two-gene perturbation prediction task when neither perturbed gene is observed during training. Ablation experiments show that combining flow matching with knowledge graphs enables accurate prediction of perturbation responses. Finally, GFM accurately calculates transcriptional consequences of HSP90AA1 inactivation and identifies target candidates unseen by the model in chronic myeloid leukemia. Our study establishes GFM as a biologically informed generative framework that predicts single-cell perturbation responses for prioritization of therapeutic targets.

items.title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
items.abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88). Its predicted variant effects agree with likely causal caQTLs (Spearman correlation = 0.52) but not with variants associated only through linkage, a traditionally challenging task. Overall, ModBERT establishes a framework for personal-genome language modeling, in which a model reads each individual's genetic and epigenetic sequence rather than a shared reference. This enables in silico dissection of variant and methylation effects on gene regulation and principled prioritization of candidates for experimental validation as population-scale long-read cohorts (e.g., 1KGP and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium) grow.

items.title: Spindle: Scalable Indexing of Spatial-Omics Data for Fast Querying
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has unlocked new avenues for biological discovery by jointly capturing gene expression and spatial context. ST datasets are typically stored as gene expression matrices paired with spatial coordinates, supporting queries based on expression levels at individual locations. However, characterizing how genes vary together requires representations of relationships between genes, such as covariance matrices computed over spatial neighborhoods. These gene--gene co-expression patterns capture coordinated biological variation and can reveal spatially localized gene programs. As datasets grow to atlas scale, efficiently searching for such patterns becomes a central computational bottleneck due to the combination of high dimensionality, extreme sparsity, and variability in gene expression across large numbers of spatial regions. Such searches require repeated access to second-order statistics, motivating a compact, searchable representation of spatial co-expression. We address this problem with Spindle, a platform-agnostic indexing algorithm for efficiently searching spatial gene co-expression patterns. Spindle exploits the approximate block-diagonal structure of gene--gene covariance matrices over spatial regions, in which covariances between blocks are small in magnitude, to selectively store informative components while compactly representing recurring covariance patterns. This yields a compressed yet searchable index suitable for atlas-scale spatial datasets. Across multiple real-world biological datasets (87,000--817,000 cells), Spindle indexes are 113--197 times smaller than the whole covariance matrices. A complete query, including query preprocessing, takes 2.8--28 ms on one CPU core, 5.1--16 times faster than a scan over the whole covariance matrices, and the tiles it returns recover a median of 81% of the exact near neighbors. In breast cancer, the regions retrieved by covariance search closely match the cell-type composition of the query (median cell-type composition difference 0.15, compared with 0.54 for random regions). Spindle supports both partial covariance queries and queries specified as gene lists, as well as retrieval across measurement platforms.

items.title: DynamicsPLM: A Dynamics-Enriched Small Protein Language Model for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
items.abstract: Predicting how mutations impact protein function and stability remains a key challenge in computational biology. Current state-of-the-art protein language models (PLMs) primarily scale parameter size on sequence corpora to capture evolutionary constraints but remain blind to the explicit physical dynamics of folded proteins. Conversely, models trained strictly on physical dynamics neglect critical evolutionary sequence statistics. In this paper, we bridge this gap by introducing DynamicsPLM, a highly parameter-efficient 35-million-parameter model that unifies evolutionary and biophysical representation learning. Utilizing a second-stage, multi-task continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins, we enrich a foundational sequence encoder with explicit residue-level and pairwise molecular dynamics heads while preserving its original evolutionary knowledge. At inference, DynamicsPLM computes zero-shot mutation effects from sequence alone by balancing an evolutionary plausibility score against a structural dynamics disruption score. Across the massive ProteinGym benchmark and natural variants of the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, DynamicsPLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among all models under 100M parameters, and matches or outperforms several billion-scale sequence-based models of its size. Our findings demonstrate that explicit structural-dynamics supervision provides a parameter-efficient alternative to raw scale. Availability: All codes including data preparation scripts, training and validation recipes, and experimental configurations for LoMuS are available at: https://github.com/kabir-ai2bio-lab/DynamicsPLM.

items.title: Phylospatial optimal transport for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data integration
items.abstract: The spatial organization of evolving cell populations in tumors influences how they progress and respond to treatment. Spatially resolved transcriptomics data may be used to examine the locations of these diverse cell states in tumor sections. However, these technologies often lack single-cell resolution and instead capture groups of cells in spatial spots, making it difficult to resolve cancer clones. In contrast, dissociated single-cell transcriptomics data are better suited for obtaining cell lineages, but do not capture the locations of the cells in the tissue. Here, we introduce SpOTr, an optimal transport approach that leverages the concordance between the evolutionary tree and the spatial distribution of cancer cells to integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data from tumors. SpOTr combines a spot deconvolution model with Fused Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, in which cells that are close in the tree are drawn to nearby spots. In simulations and in real spatial lineage tracing data, SpOTr recovered the spatial locations of clones better than methods that ignore the tree. In a human colorectal liver metastasis, SpOTr mapped copy number clones from dissociated cells to spatial spots, showing that it successfully maps the evolutionary history of tumors in space.

items.title: A statistical framework for identifying candidate genetic interactions from adaptive laboratory evolution data
items.abstract: Background Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) is widely used to improve microbial fitness under defined selective pressures. Mutations accumulated during ALE may interact epistatically, with the effect of one mutation depending on another. Understanding these interactions can help explain adaptive phenotypes and inform combinatorial strain engineering, but experimentally testing all mutation combinations is impractical. We developed a computational framework that uses gene-pair co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity patterns to identify candidates for experimental investigation of epistasis. Results We applied the framework to a curated compendium of 141 Escherichia coli ALE experiments from ALEdb, using the Fisher exact test and DISCOVER as complementary statistical screens. Testing and multiple-testing correction were performed separately within each experiment, method, and direction (co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity). At a 5% false discovery rate threshold, the Fisher exact test identified 74 significant gene pairs, comprising 36 co-occurrences and 38 mutual exclusivities. DISCOVER identified 5 significant pairs, all for mutual exclusivity and also significant under the Fisher exact test. These shared pairs suggested alternative adaptive routes involving temperature tolerance, glycerol utilization, and associations between RNA polymerase subunit genes. The two methods produced similar expected overlaps for Fisher-significant pairs, but the broader null distributions of DISCOVER yielded larger raw p-values. Of the 69 pairs significant only under the Fisher exact test, 60 arose in experiments with multiple strain labels or involved a gene with only one distinct mutation recorded across all affected endpoints (final samples from lineages evolved in parallel), highlighting the need to examine genetic backgrounds and mutation origins when interpreting the results. Power analysis indicated that the Fisher exact test required 70 independent endpoints for co-occurrence and 215 for mutual exclusivity to achieve 80% power under pre-specified scenarios. We implemented the framework as a reusable Nextflow pipeline that automates statistical screening of ALEdb and user-supplied mutation datasets. Conclusions By combining gene-pair screening with mutation-level interpretation, this reproducible framework narrows the search space for experimental investigation of epistasis and can contribute to combinatorial strain design. The power analysis provides sample-size benchmarks for planning future ALE experiments with adequate power to screen for candidate genetic interactions.

items.title: Neuronal Aralar/AGC1 deficiency impairs social behavior through dopaminergic and redox dysfunction and is rescued by β-hydroxybutyrate
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto Universitario de Biologia Molecular, (IUBM), and Centro de Biologia Molecular Severo Ochoa, Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, Madrid, Spain
items.abstract: Background: Pathogenic variants in SLC25A12/AGC1 (Aralar) have been linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the mechanisms connecting neuronal metabolic dysfunction to altered social behavior remain poorly understood. Aralar is a key component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, supporting neuronal oxidative metabolism and lactate utilization. Here, we investigated the consequences of postnatal neuronal Aralar deletion and the therapeutic potential of {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Methods: We generated neuron-specific Aralar knockout mice (Neu Aralar-KO) using CamKII-Cre, producing efficient recombination in cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. Behavioral, transcriptomic, neurochemical, morphometric, histological, and biochemical analyses were performed in adult mice. The effects of systemic BHB administration were assessed using behavioral, metabolic, oxidative stress, and transcriptomic endpoints. Results: Despite a 55-65% reduction of Aralar expression in forebrain regions, Neu Aralar-KO mice displayed normal growth, survival, brain structure, and myelination. Unexpectedly, loss of neuronal Aralar did not impair spatial memory, episodic memory, or reversal learning. In contrast, Neu Aralar-KO mice exhibited hyperactivity and a marked deficit in sociability, revealing an ASD-relevant behavioral phenotype. Morphological analysis showed significant remodeling of striatal dendritic spines without changes in spine density. Transcriptomic profiling identified 433 differentially expressed genes, the vast majority being upregulated, with enrichment of pathways related to neuropeptide signaling, synaptic transmission, membrane excitability, and behavior. Notably, genes involved in dopamine (DA) and glutamate handling, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulatory signaling, and ASD-associated pathways were strongly induced. Neurochemical analyses revealed preserved glutamate and GABA levels but reduced striatal DA content accompanied by an increased DOPAC/DA ratio, indicating enhanced DA degradation. DAergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) showed minimal recombination, suggesting that DA dysfunction arises through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Consistent with increased DA oxidative catabolism, Neu Aralar-KO striata displayed elevated lipid peroxidation, induction of glutathione-related pathways, upregulation of antioxidant genes, and astrocyte activation. Remarkably, BHB treatment restored sociability, normalized striatal metabolic alterations, reduced oxidative stress, and abolished genotype-dependent neurochemical abnormalities. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Aralar deficiency recapitulates a substantial fraction of the fasting/BHB-induced epigenetic transcriptional program. Conclusions: Postnatal neuronal Aralar deficiency uncouples social behavior from cognitive performance and drives ASD-like phenotypes through a mechanism linking neuronal metabolic dysfunction, oxidative stress, glial activation, and impaired DAergic homeostasis. The rescue of behavioral, metabolic, and redox abnormalities by BHB identifies restoration of metabolic homeostasis as a major therapeutic mechanism and highlights metabolic interventions as promising strategies for AGC1 deficiency and ASD-associated disorders involving neuronal metabolic dysfunction.

items.title: Neural dynamics track the approach to physical exhaustion
items.abstract: Physical exhaustion has long been described through its cardiorespiratory and metabolic cost, while the neural dynamics of its approach remain largely unexplored. Here we recorded high-density electroencephalography in 28 trained cyclists during a maximal incremental test to characterise how neural dynamics change towards exhaustion. As physiological strain rose, oscillatory power shifted to lower frequencies, neural activity became more regular and predictable, and functional coupling extended to longer timescales. Participant-specific models built on neural dynamics tracked proximity to exhaustion with accuracy comparable to cardiorespiratory measures. Over the final minutes, neural features remained informative while cardiorespiratory measures lost accuracy. Models trained across participants still tracked proximity to exhaustion, but less precisely. The approach to exhaustion thus follows a common neural path, tuned to each individual.

items.title: Zdhhc17/Hip14 functions in neurons to control behavior via DHHC-dependent and independent mechanisms
items.corresponding_institution: University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine
items.abstract: To navigate a complex sensory environment, animals filter out inconsequential sensory inputs and habituate to familiar stimuli. By establishing innate response thresholds and modifying them through habituation, animals can focus on key sensory stimuli while ignoring irrelevant ones. Huntingtin-interacting protein 14 (Hip14), also known as zDHHC17, is a palmitoyl acyltransferase (PAT) that regulates both of these sensory filtering processes. Larval zebrafish lacking Hip14 are hypersensitive to acoustic stimuli and cannot regulate their responses to repeated acoustic stimuli via habituation. Yet how Hip14 regulates these behaviors, and whether it does so through different mechanisms, is unknown. Prior work demonstrates that Hip14 is expressed throughout the nervous system, but where it functions to control these overlapping sensory functions remains unaddressed. We found that the catalytic (DHHC) domain, despite being a defining feature for PATs including Hip14, is not required for regulating acoustic startle sensitivity, but is sufficient to regulate habituation. We find, furthermore, that Hip14 function in either mechanosensory hair cells or neurons can restore normal startle sensitivity, whereas habituation is regulated exclusively by neuronal expression. Finally, we found that the Hip14 N-terminal ankyrin repeat domains are crucial for its control of behavior. Together, our study establishes that habituation and startle sensitivity are regulated through distinct circuit and molecular mechanisms and establishes a new in vivo catalytic-independent role for Hip14.

items.title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
items.abstract: Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

items.title: Satellite glial translatome reprograms to favor mitochondrial and vesicular signaling under pelvic pain conditions
items.corresponding_institution: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
items.abstract: Sensory satellite glial cells actively contribute to inflammatory and neuropathic pain, but their roles in pelvic pain remain unclear. This study examined how the active translating mRNAs in sensory SGCs change during pelvic pain symptoms using translating ribosome affinity purification followed by RNA sequencing (TRAP-seq) in a chronic pelvic pain (CPP) mouse model. Our data showed that SGCs exhibit sex-specific translatome patterns at baseline, which were reprogrammed in CPP conditions under the control of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (Eif4e). In CPP conditions, sensory SGCs exhibit increased translation of mitochondrial and vesicular genes and suppression of immune genes in both sexes; an anti-inflammatory cytokine profile was detected in female pelvic sensory ganglia. We are the first to characterize SGC translatome in pelvic pain conditions and to report sex differences in SGC translatome. Our data suggested that mitochondrial and vesicular gene translation in sensory SGCs may be important to afferent hypersensitivity.

items.title: Amyloidosis and tauopathy progressively disrupt near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits
items.abstract: Mechanistically distinct neurodegenerative diseases result in similar cognitive deficits, and pathology is often concentrated in a set of circuits known to be selectively vulnerable. Selective vulnerability is an intrinsic property of a circuit: in APP/PS1 mice, where plaques are global, functional disruptions are confined to circuits within the default mode network. What characterizes the dynamics of vulnerable circuits from those of spared circuits is unknown. We asked whether the distinguishing property is the proximity of population dynamics to criticality, a homeostatic set-point of network activity that determines computational capacity. We recorded single units simultaneously in three selectively vulnerable regions (retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and CA1 hippocampus) and in primary visual cortex of freely behaving young and old APP/PS1 and wild-type mice. Firing rate and spike-time variability differed by genotype inconsistently across regions and ages. In contrast, three measures from criticality theory each revealed deficits that emerged only with age and only in the vulnerable regions. No measure detected a progressive change in V1. Avalanche scaling is not fixed in neural activity, but varies along a scaling line as the network state changes. As a result, the lines generated by each genotype revealed a constitutive effect of the transgene in young animals, which inverted with age in amyloid-bearing animals, but only in vulnerable circuits. If the destabilization of near-critical dynamics directly reflects a circuit's functional capacity, the same signature should identify a mechanistically distinct degenerative disease. In a model of tauopathy (P301S/E4), CA1 dynamics were displaced from the control scaling line with the same age-dependent reversal observed in APP/PS1. Our results suggest a network-level principle of neurodegenerative diseases: molecularly unrelated pathologies converge on the loss of near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits.

items.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain
items.corresponding_institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School
items.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

items.title: Multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities support IFT-A-IFT-B coordination in vivo
items.abstract: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) depends on coordinated movement of IFT-A and IFT-B, yet how these assemblies remain coupled within dynamic ciliary trains is unclear. Here, we combine endogenous fluorescent knock-in tagging, quantitative in vivo FLIM-FRET, structural modeling, and targeted mutagenesis to define IFT organization in C. elegans and mammalian cells. FLIM-FRET mapping identifies proximity networks within IFT-B and places IFT144 near IFT172 and IFT88 in intact cilia. Loss of BBSome function is associated with weaker IFT-A-IFT-B proximity signals and divergent subcomplex transport dynamics, consistent with a contribution of the BBSome to IFT coordination in vivo. Split-GFP complementation places BBSome components near IFT-A and IFT-B, while structural modeling nominates complementary charged surfaces on the IFT46-IFT52 dimer and BBS7/BBS9. Charge-reversal mutations targeting these surfaces impair BBSome recruitment and functional rescue. Together, these findings support a model in which multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities contribute to IFT-A-IFT-B coordination during ciliary transport.

items.title: Longitudinal miRNA-mRNA Profiling Reveals Network Reorganization in Preeclampsia
items.abstract: Background: Preeclampsia (PE) is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity. Temporal dynamics of molecular dysregulation across pregnancy remain poorly understood. We performed longitudinal RNA sequencing of maternal whole blood to characterize miRNA-mRNA regulatory network evolution in PE. Methods: Whole-blood samples from early (M1: 10-18 weeks) and late pregnancy (M2: 32-38 weeks) were analyzed from 43 PE cases and 106 normotensive controls, including 109 paired samples (36 PE cases, 73 controls). Differential expression, temporal classification, pathway enrichment, and miRNA-mRNA network integration were performed. Placental expression support was assessed using internal RNA-seq and public databases. Key miRNA-mRNA interactions were experimentally validated in HTR-8/SVneo trophoblast cells. Results: PE exhibited marked temporal reorganization of miRNA-mRNA networks, with strongly opposing temporal effect sizes across overlapping miRNA and mRNA features (Spearman {rho} = -0.82, P < 0.0001). PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling showed biphasic reversal (NES = +1.46, FDR = 0.028 at M1; NES = -1.64, FDR = 0.025 at M2), and heme-metabolism programs showed progressive suppression (2.1-fold NES intensification; FDR < 0.05 at both timepoints). Network analysis identified 29 high-confidence biphasic miRNA-mRNA pairs, including convergent targeting of ADGRA2 by three miRNAs and HSD17B1 by three miRNAs. miR-101-3p overexpression reduced DEPP1 mRNA (~40%) and protein (~26%) in trophoblast cells (P < 0.01), supporting a FOXO-DEPP1 axis. Blood-derived pairs showed pathway convergence with placental VGLL3-centered programs (PI3K/AKT, FOXO, TGF-{beta}, trophoblast differentiation). Conclusions: PE is associated with predominantly stage-specific or biphasic miRNA-mRNA network reorganization, with PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 dynamic remodeling and progressive heme-metabolism suppression. These findings support gestational-age-specific biomarker development and identify regulatory axes, including miR-101-3p [->] DEPP1, for mechanistic investigation.

items.title: An oxidative mutational signature in normal tissues of a monoallelic MUTYH carrier
items.abstract: Biallelic loss of MUTYH causes MUTYH-associated polyposis (OMIM: 608456), characterized by the oxidative base-excision-repair mutational signature SBS18, but whether the roughly 1 in 100 individuals who carry a single pathogenic MUTYH allele acquire a mutational phenotype in normal tissue is unknown. Analysis of multi-tissue sequencing of 25 donors from the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network identified three heterozygous carriers of MUTYH p.Gly396Asp. One carrier showed SBS18 across multiple normal tissues, ranking first of 25 donors with three independent methods and remaining significant after adjustment for tissue, without a somatic, epigenetic or transcriptional second hit at the MUTYH locus. A single hypomorphic MUTYH allele can therefore leave a measurable oxidative mutational mark in healthy tissues, supporting tissue-level mutational readouts as an approach to cancer risk stratification within this common carrier state.

items.title: HieraPTM: From PTM Site Recognition to Functional Phosphosite Prediction through Hierarchical Context and Protein Mechanics
items.abstract: Protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate cellular signaling and protein function, making accurate site identification essential for understanding protein regulation. However, PTM site recognition and functional phosphosite prediction are largely modeled independently, limiting the transfer of large-scale recognition knowledge to functional prioritization. Here, we introduce HieraPTM-HieraFuncPhos, a cross-task hierarchical framework that separately models and conditionally integrates transferable PTM recognition representations and function-specific mechanical evidence. HieraPTM integrates local sequence patterns, protein language model representations, and three-dimensional structural information to recognize multiple PTM types. HieraFuncPhos transfers these representations through parameter-efficient adaptation and adaptively retrieves local and distal mechanical evidence conditioned on functional representations. At HSP90AA1 T36 and T115, the model reveals distinct mechanical response patterns consistent with published nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observations, suggesting that the framework not only prioritizes functional phosphosites but also provides biophysically grounded, testable hypotheses regarding site-specific regulation. HieraPTM achieved macro-averaged AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.9237 and 0.8425 across eight PTM tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on severely imbalanced external benchmarks. HieraFuncPhos achieved an AUROC of 0.8274 and an AUPRC of 0.8188, outperforming existing comparison methods. Together, this framework connects PTM site recognition, functional prioritization, and structure-informed hypotheses regarding potential regulatory processes.

items.title: Unsupervised Deep Learning for Cryo-EM/ET Particle Classification
items.abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is widely used to determine protein structures from purified samples. With cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET), it is possible to image thin sections of cells and directly visualize diverse proteins in their native environment. However, separating the massive mixture of different types of proteins inside cells remains challenging, especially without human intervention. In this work, we present an unsupervised deep learning framework for classifying cryo-EM/ET particle images that jointly optimizes for pose and structure through an autoencoder-based multi-stage pipeline. On single-particle cryo-EM datasets, our framework can capture the continuous variation in particle views and separate images of real particles from contamination. Using in silico mixtures of multiple types of proteins, we demonstrated our method's capability of separating the protein classes without supervision. Finally in a real cryo-ET dataset of algal chloroplast, our deep learning model successfully detected the four main protein complexes of photosynthesis on native thylakoid membranes. Taken together, these results demonstrate that our framework offers a scalable, annotation-free solution for robust structural discovery across diverse cryo-EM and cryo-ET applications.

items.title: ECMExplainer: a functional matrisome framework for decoding cellular stress states and aging trajectories
items.corresponding_institution: RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research
items.abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as both a hallmark of aging and a durable record of the cellular stress states that shape age-related tissue dysfunction. Despite its apparent role in aging and disease, translating matrisome gene expression into interpretable biological meaning remains an unresolved challenge. Here we introduce ECMExplainer, a framework that uses 180 matrisome gene-pair ratios, partitioned into 76 Assembly/Destruction and 104 Signaling/Signaling pairs to position fibroblast transcriptomes within a functional matrisome phenotype space defined by six reference fibroblast states spanning physiological and stress-associated conditions: Proliferating, Quiescence, Senescence, Fibrosis, Inflammation, and Hypoxia. Because each ratio records only which of the two genes is more highly expressed, it is largely insensitive to sequencing depth and batch offsets, allowing ECMExplainer to outperform magnitude-based classifiers on unseen data. Rather than assigning only a single phenotype label, ECMExplainer measures a sample's coordinate distance to each reference state, enabling quantitative mapping of matrisome state trajectories while giving biological meaning even to conditions that fall between or outside the training phenotypes. Across 20 independent fibroblast datasets, ECMExplainer uncovered conserved ECM signatures underlying diverse fibroblast states and showed that they capture multiple aging-related processes. Specifically, it identified FST/ITGA1 as a rapamycin-sensitive senescence-associated ratio, revealed a fibrosis-biased ECM trajectory in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome distinct from chronological aging, and distinguished successful from failed OSKM reprogramming using an ECM Aging Score without retraining. Together, these findings establish the matrisome as a compact and biologically interpretable carrier of cellular state information, and ECMExplainer as a quantitative foundation for interpreting aging, fibrosis and rejuvenation through the lens of the ECM.

items.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
items.abstract: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

items.title: Nucleus reuniens gates selective hippocampal-prefrontal interactions during NREM sleep
items.corresponding_institution: Pediatrics Division of Neurology, University of California Irvine, Irvine, CA, USA
items.abstract: Memory consolidation requires functional synchrony between the hippocampus (HC) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The nucleus reuniens (RE) is a structural and functional hub between HC and mPFC. Here, we used in vivo electrophysiology to monitor the hippocampal-thalamic-prefrontal network in rats during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. We identified ripple-like activity in the RE (120 Hz peak frequency, 45 ms oscillatory duration) that occurred most frequently during NREM sleep and was associated with robust recruitment of thalamic neural spiking. RE ripple activity was phase-locked to both hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWR) and mPFC ripples. Although ripples were independently detected in all three structures, we found that coupling between HC and mPFC ripples mainly involved co-occurring RE ripples. These results suggest RE ripples help organize when hippocampal activity engages prefrontal circuits during sleep, with potential implications for network mechanisms of memory consolidation.

items.title: Inactivation of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase reduces phosphatidylcholine amounts in the brain of infant mice
items.abstract: Hypophosphatasia is a rare disease caused by dysfunctions of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP). TNAP is expressed in numerous tissues, notably the brain, and patients with hypophosphatasia exhibit neurological symptoms, including epilepsy in the most severe forms of the disease. TNAP knockout (KO) mouse models have provided a wealth of information regarding TNAP functions. Specifically, metabolomic studies focusing on the aqueous fraction of the brain of TNAP KO mice identified numerous molecules whose amounts were altered as a direct or indirect consequence of TNAP inactivation. Among these molecules, several are involved either directly (e.g., vitamin B6) or indirectly (e.g., N-acetylaspartate) in lipid metabolism. In this study, we therefore extended these investigations by examining the consequences of TNAP inactivation on the brain lipidome. We used a targeted lipidomic approach, examining four main categories of lipids: fatty acids, neutral lipids, sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids, subdivided into 16 lipid classes and amounting to 296 lipid species. Eleven lipid species showed significantly reduced amounts in the brain of TNAP KO mice. All belonged to the phosphatidylcholine class. As phosphatidylcholines are major constituents of brain cell membranes, our results suggest that hypophosphatasia could be associated with alterations in membrane structure and functions, which could contribute to the neurodevelopmental disorders associated with the disease.

items.title: Microglial Stim1/Stim2 deletion reduces calcium signaling but promotes infarct expansion after ischemic stroke
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Virginia, Charlottesville
items.abstract: Microglia respond to ischemic stroke with calcium transients carried by calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels, gated by the endoplasmic reticulum sensors Stim1 and Stim2. Since CRAC signaling drives pro-inflammatory responses in immune cells, blocking it in microglia should protect the ischemic brain. We have examined this hypothesis in 15-month-old mice lacking Stim1 and Stim2 in microglia (Cx3cr1-CreERT2; Stim cKO). In vivo two-photon imaging confirmed that cKO microglia produced one-third smaller calcium transients during cortical spreading depolarizations. We then followed distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAo) with multiparametric MRI at 9.4 T. Six hours after occlusion, both the control and cKO genotypes demonstrated similar infarct size, edema, and diffusion, but lesion perfusion tended to be lower in cKO mice. Differences in tissue injury emerged later. Between 6 and 48 hours, the infarcts in control males did not grow, whereas infarcts in cKO males expanded 2.7-fold. At 48 hours, cKO males had 2.2-fold larger infarcts, while cKO females did not differ from controls. Moreover, cKO lesions showed a lower apparent diffusion coefficient, indicating more severe tissue injury. Neither hemispheric swelling nor cerebral arterial anatomy accounted for these differences. Contrary to our hypothesis, ablating microglial CRAC channels worsened stroke outcome. Microglial CRAC signaling may therefore protect threatened tissue in the first days after ischemia, possibly by sustaining its perfusion, and this role appears to outweigh its pro-inflammatory effects.

items.title: Multivalent mRNA tuberculosis vaccines protect against mycobacterial infection in zebrafish, mice and guinea pigs
items.abstract: Despite a century of BCG use, tuberculosis remains a leading cause of death from infectious diseases and more effective vaccines are urgently needed. Here we combined antigen discovery in zebrafish with mRNA vaccine technology to generate multivalent vaccine candidates, TUmRNA4, TUmRNA6 and TUmRNA9, encoding four, six, or nine Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, respectively. The vaccines were well tolerated, and induced robust antigen-specific cellular immune responses, including IFN{gamma} production and expansion of memory T-cell populations. In mice, TUmRNA4 and TUmRNA6 reduced pulmonary M. tuberculosis burden and lung pathology to levels comparable to BCG vaccination and TUmRNA6 enhanced BCG-mediated protection when used as a booster vaccine. In guinea pigs, TUmRNA9 reduced bacterial burden in the lungs, spleen, and lymph nodes and decreased pulmonary lesions. These findings demonstrate that protective antigens identified in zebrafish can be translated into effective multivalent mRNA vaccines and establish a framework for tuberculosis vaccine development across multiple preclinical models.

items.title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
items.abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.

items.title: mRNA-LNP vaccination induces microenvironment remodeling and generation of tissue-resident memory T cells in glioblastoma
items.abstract: Glioblastoma remains highly refractory to immunotherapy, in part because of a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment that limits effective T-cell responses. Although mRNA vaccines can induce anti-tumour immunity, how they reshape the glioblastoma immune ecosystem to support durable tumour control is not well understood. Here we use an immunocompetent EGFRvIII-driven syngeneic glioblastoma model and antigen-specific mRNA lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccination to define the cellular and spatial mechanisms underlying therapeutic response. In our model, vaccination induced durable EGFRvIII-specific humoral and cellular immunity, resulting in complete tumour eradication and long-term protection against intracranial rechallenge. Integrative analyses incorporating flow cytometry, tumour interstitial fluid profiling, multiplex immunostaining, spatial transcriptomics and ligand-receptor modelling demonstrated extensive remodelling of the tumour microenvironment following vaccination. Early tumour control was associated with expansion of pro-inflammatory and antigen-presenting myeloid populations, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration and activation, enhanced interferon-responsive signalling, and the formation of immune-supportive spatial niches enriched for antigen presentation and chemokine-mediated cellular communication. Vaccination promoted inflammatory chemokine relay networks centred on the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis, a pathway linked to tissue residency programming in the central nervous system. Functional depletion studies identified CD4 and CD8 T cells as essential mediators of therapeutic efficacy, while durable protection was maintained by tumour-specific brain-resident memory CD8 T cells that persisted despite peripheral lymphocyte depletion. Together, these findings identify T-cell-driven microenvironmental remodelling as a critical mechanism linking mRNA vaccination to the establishment of long-term brain-resident anti-tumour immunity in glioblastoma.

items.title: Single-cell Profiling of Airway-associated CD4+ T cells in Metal-induced Hypersensitivity
items.abstract: Omics-based approaches are increasingly used to identify unique molecular signatures that may serve as biomarkers for early disease detection and potential therapeutic targets. Chronic beryllium disease (CBD), resulting from beryllium-induced hypersensitivity, is characterized by the accumulation and expansion of pathogenic CD4+ T cells in the lungs, ultimately contributing to impaired pulmonary function. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on sorted viable bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cells from beryllium-exposed patients (n=2) and compared their transcriptional profiles with publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from healthy controls (n=10). We identified 11 distinct CD3-associated cell clusters comprising T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and regulatory T cells. Further analysis of CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients revealed increased expression of genes associated with T cell activation, immune regulation, and persistence, including IFNG, TNF, TNFAIP3, and CD74. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis further revealed upregulation of pathways associated with cellular activation, immune responses, and immune effector functions, whereas pathways related to metabolic processes were downregulated in beryllium samples compared with healthy controls. Overall, our findings identify distinct transcriptional signatures, including IFI27 and FABP4, in CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients, providing insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying beryllium-induced pulmonary inflammation and highlighting potential candidates for further investigation as disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

items.title: T cell receptors from CD8 regulatory T cells direct the development of natural intraepithelial lymphocytes
items.corresponding_institution: Washington University in St Louis School of Medicine, St Louis
items.abstract: CD8 regulatory T cells (CD8 Tregs) in mice have been identified by their expression of the surface receptor family Ly49 and the transcription factor Helios. To our surprise, many Ly49+ and Helios+ T cells express neither CD4 nor CD8, and many express only CD8. We found that CD8 Tregs in the spleen are linked to the CD8{beta}- natural intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) that reside in the small intestine. Blocking trafficking to the intestine increased splenic CD8 Treg frequency, and transferred splenic CD8 Tregs gave rise to natural IELs. Unexpectedly, Helios was dispensable for natural IEL development, arguing against its role as a shared lineage-determining transcription factor. Instead, we found that T cell receptors (TCRs) from splenic Ly49+ CD8 Tregs deterministically direct natural IEL development. Our findings suggest that CD8 Tregs may derive from the same TCR-directed developmental program that generates natural IELs and shed light on the origins of these immunoregulatory cells.

items.title: COVID-19 and Active Tuberculosis Exhibit Distinct Maturation-Associated Neutrophil Transcriptional Programs
items.abstract: Neutrophils can promote pathogen control or drive tissue-damaging inflammation, but the mechanisms that determine these divergent outcomes remain poorly defined. COVID-19 and active tuberculosis (TB) offer a purposeful comparison since both are pulmonary infections with substantial neutrophil involvement, yet differ in pathogen class, inflammatory duration, and the balance between neutrophil-associated host defense and pathology. We therefore tested whether their divergent neutrophil programs align with distinct maturation-associated transcriptional states. We integrated six publicly available whole-blood bulk RNA-sequencing datasets, comprising three COVID-19 and three active TB cohorts. A curated panel of 770 genes covered activation, degranulation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, chemotaxis, cell surface receptors, and maturation. Study-associated variation was reduced using ComBat-Seq, and differential expression relative to disease-appropriate controls was assessed with DESeq2. Most genes changed in the same direction in both diseases, but 348 (45.2%) differed significantly in response magnitude, with 159 genes showing a stronger response in COVID-19 and 189 in TB. COVID-19 samples showed reduced expression of the maturation markers CD10 (MME) and CD16 (FCGR3A), alongside elevated expression of granule-cargo and NET-associated genes, including MPO and ELANE, consistent with a greater contribution from immature, emergency granulopoiesis-derived neutrophil populations. In contrast, TB samples showed higher maturation-associated, receptor, oxidative, and recruitment responses, consistent with a relatively mature receptor-competent neutrophil transcriptional signature. Independent COVID-19 Ward and pulmonary TB cohorts showed directional agreement for maturation and NET-associated signatures (100% and 90% concordance, respectively), while chemotaxis and select receptor and degranulation genes showed weaker reproducibility indicating that maturation represents the most consistently reproduced axis of distinction between the two diseases. Together, these findings identify maturation-associated transcription as the most consistently reproduced axis distinguishing COVID-19 from TB. These signatures provide candidate biomarkers for future studies linking neutrophil states to clinical outcomes and informing host-directed therapeutic strategies that preserve antimicrobial function while limiting immunopathology.

items.title: Exploratory positional differences in observed CDRH2 lineage-state transitions following HIV-1 germline-targeting vaccination
items.abstract: Background: Germline-targeting HIV-1 vaccination recruits VRC01-class B-cell precursors, but the positional patterns of observed longitudinal B-cell receptor lineage-state changes remain incompletely described. We compared CDRH2 profiles between homologous and heterologous boosting regimens using published IAVI G002 data. Methods: Participant-specific Week-8 lineages were prospectively matched to Week-24 observations. Germline-to-nongermline changes in sampled lineage-modal residues were evaluated at seven IGHV1-2*02 CDRH2 positions using participant-balanced, mean-centered profiles and exact participant-label permutation inference. Sampling-depth and sorting-probe sensitivity analyses assessed observability. A separate participant-held-out benchmark evaluated antibody-language-model representations for predicting observed Week-24 lineage detection. Results: The CDRH2 analysis included 332 lineages, 15 participants, 2,179 eligible lineage-position observations, and 241 observed state changes. The regional profile statistic was 0.027066 (exact p = 0.001709; six-region adjusted q = 0.010256), with descriptive differences at V-relative positions 51, 54, and 55. Most eligible longitudinal observations had one assessable cell per visit. In seven Group-1 participants, Week-24 dual-probe sampling recovered 181 baseline lineages with eOD-GT8 and 143 with Cg28v2, including 60 detected by both probes. In a separate cohort of 2,739 lineages from 17 participants, IgBERT and AbLang-2 representations did not improve participant-balanced average precision over a four-feature biological baseline. Conclusions: Observed CDRH2 lineage-modal-state profiles differed between regimens in this exploratory secondary analysis. Sparse sampling, potentially probe-related ascertainment, and absent linked functional validation preclude inference about mutation timing, functional improvement, or causal booster effects.

items.title: Selective Elimination of HIV-1-Infected Macrophages by Targeted Activator of Cell Kill
items.corresponding_institution: University of Miami School of Medicine
items.abstract: In the pursuit of an HIV cure, elimination of persistent HIV reservoirs requires strategies that promote immune-mediated or cytopathic clearance of infected cells. While many such approaches are being developed against infected CD4+ T cells, HIV-infected macrophages are comparatively resistant to cell death and to several killing mechanisms being explored for T-cell reservoirs, highlighting the need for strategies that specifically eliminate this reservoir. Targeted Activator of Cell Kill (TACK), developed by Merck Pharmaceuticals, are non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-derived molecules designed to selectively kill HIV-1-infected cells by inducing premature activation of the viral protease. Here, we evaluated the TACK compounds Pyr01 and it?s inactive analog Pyr02, in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs). Pyr01 had minimal effects on uninfected MDM viability but potently targeted HIV-1-infected MDMs, with an EC?? of approximately 0.36 ?M. Pyr01 treatment produced a rapid and sustained reduction in extracellular virion-associated HIV-1 RNA and significantly decreased cell-associated viral RNA, whereas Pyr02 exhibited minimal activity. Immunofluorescence microscopy and live-cell imaging further demonstrated a marked loss of HIV-1-infected macrophages following Pyr01 treatment, consistent with selective elimination of infected cells. These findings identify Pyr01 as a specific mediator of HIV-infected macrophage death and establish premature viral protease activation as a strategy for overcoming the intrinsic resistance of macrophage reservoirs to clearance. Targeting this macrophage-specific barrier may complement approaches directed at CD4+ T-cell reservoirs and broaden the cellular reach of HIV cure strategies.

items.title: Dual cellular targeting of complement receptor 2 (CR2/CD21) synergistically suppresses autoreactive germinal center activity and autoimmunity in lupus
items.abstract: Pathogenic germinal center (GC) activity persists in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) because current B cell-targeting therapies do not consistently eliminate the resilient GC niche that sustains autoimmunity. Complement receptor 2 (CR2/CD21) presents a unique bicellular therapeutic target to impede GC-associated autoimmune disease. For B cells, it has been previously shown to lower the threshold for B cell activation, and for follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), it sustains the GC response. Using a CD21-blocking antibody in a spontaneous lupus-prone mouse model, we demonstrate that dual CD21 blockade on both B cells and FDCs synergistically inhibited GC B cell responses and suppressed autoantibody production, memory recall, and renal antibody deposition. Mechanistically, B cell-specific blockade impaired GC entry by limiting initial activation, whereas FDC-specific blockade disrupted GC architecture and curtailed ongoing responses. Further, dual blockade uniquely reshaped immunological memory by promoting accumulation of a CD21low/-CD38+ memory B cell subset with attenuated antibody-secreting cell (ASC) recall potential. These findings identify CD21 blockade as a precision immunomodulatory strategy capable of suppressing pathogenic humoral immunity without complete B cell depletion.

items.title: L-selectin shedding regulates post-infarction neutrophilia without altering myocardial injury or ventricular remodelling.
items.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) triggers rapid neutrophil mobilisation from the bone marrow (BM), resulting in systemic neutrophilia that is widely associated with myocardial injury. However, whether the magnitude of this response directly influences cardiac injury and subsequent ventricular remodelling remains unclear. Ectodomain shedding of L-selectin is a hallmark of neutrophil activation, although its contribution to neutrophil mobilisation following MI has not been established. Using mice expressing a non-cleavable L-selectin mutant (L(E)), we investigated the role of L-selectin shedding in post-MI neutrophilia. Under homeostatic conditions, WT and L(E) mice exhibited comparable BM neutrophil maturation and circulating neutrophil representation. Following permanent coronary ligation, however, L(E) mice exhibited markedly attenuated neutrophilia, associated with reduced circulating CXCL2 and decreased surface CXCR2 expression on BM neutrophils. Intravenous recombinant CXCL2 increased circulating neutrophil representation in WT but not L(E) mice, suggesting that impaired mobilisation cannot be explained solely by reduced ligand availability. Despite attenuated neutrophilia, myocardial neutrophil representation was comparable between genotypes at 24 hours post-MI. Circulating cardiac troponin I concentrations and MRI-quantified infarct size also showed no detectable differences. Longitudinal cardiac MRI at days 1, 14 and 28 revealed comparable ventricular structure and function, while histological scar size was similar at day 28. These findings identify L-selectin shedding as a regulator of post-MI neutrophilia and suggest that the magnitude of this systemic response can be dissociated from acute myocardial injury and subsequent ventricular remodelling.

items.title: Contact-phagy remodels ER-mitochondria contact sites
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Biochemistry II, Faculty of Medicine, Goethe University Frankfurt, Theodor-Stern-Kai 7, 60590 Frankfurt am Main, Germany; Buchmann Institute for Mo
items.abstract: Membrane contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and other organelles coordinate cellular organization, metabolism and stress responses, yet how these interfaces are selectively remodeled and removed remains poorly understood. Here we identify a selective autophagy pathway that targets defined ER-mitochondria contact-site (ERMCS) subdomains for turnover, a process we term Contact-phagy. The ER-resident chaperone SIGMAR1 forms a functional complex with the ER-phagy receptor CCPG1, and SIGMAR1-CCPG1 nanoclusters define ERMCS-associated sites of autophagy initiation.
