Contact-phagy is selectively engaged by metabolic and mitochondrial stress and promotes turnover of defined contact-site components without broadly affecting general ER-phagy, mitophagy or bulk autophagy. At these sites, SIGMAR1-CCPG1 function is coupled to mitochondrial fission: MFF promotes DRP1 recruitment to ERMCS, whereas loss of CCPG1 or SIGMAR1 causes abnormal persistence and clustering of DRP1 and MFF, accompanied by altered mitochondrial remodeling. Loss of CCPG1 further disrupts ER-mitochondria organization and mitochondrial function in pancreatic tissue, while pancreatic cancer cells depend on CCPG1 and SIGMAR1 for organelle integrity and bioenergetic capacity. Together, our findings establish Contact-phagy as a selective pathway for the turnover of defined organelle contact site subdomains and suggest a broader principle by which interorganelle interfaces are maintained.

items.title: AlphaScreen profiling of extracellular vesicle-associated platelet, immune, and vascular markers reveals disease-specific signatures in ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and long COVID
items.corresponding_institution: School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Catholic University of Valencia, Valencia, Spain
items.abstract: Introduction: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), fibromyalgia (FM), and long COVID (LC-19) are chronic diseases with overlapping clinical features and poorly understood pathophysiology. Increasing evidence suggests the involvement of immune dysregulation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered vascular physiology. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are key mediators of intercellular communication and are envisioned as sensors of homeostasis and disease. The aim of this study was to determine whether EV marker profiling could provide a basis for the differential diagnosis of ME/CFS, FM and LC-19 and/or patient stratification. Methods: EV-enriched plasma from ME/CFS, FM, cases co-diagnosed with ME/CFS and FM, LC-19 patients, and matched healthy controls (n = 10 per study group) were analyzed. EV concentration and size distribution were assessed by nanoparticle tracking analysis, followed by targeted profiling of EV-associated surface markers via AlphaScreen, including tetraspanins CD9 and CD63, platelet- (CD41/CD61), myeloid- (CD13), immune- (CD74 and CX3CR1), and renin-angiotensin system- associated ACE1 (also known as CD143), and ACE2 surface markers. Results: The studied disease groups presented distinct EV signatures. LC-19 samples exhibited the most pronounced and coordinated alterations, characterized by increased levels of CD9/CD74, CD9/CX3CR1, and CD9/ACE1-positive EVs, along with reduced overall particle concentrations. Notably, platelet-derived CD9/CD41/CD61-positive EVs were significantly elevated in both LC-19 and ME/CFS, as compared to healthy controls, indicating enhanced platelet activation. Immune-associated markers revealed differential pathway activation in LC-19, with CD74-positive EVs reflecting antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling, and CX3CR1-positive EVs indicating altered leukocyte trafficking and vascular interaction. Increased ACE1-positive EVs in LC-19 further suggested a shift toward pro-inflammatory renin-angiotensin signaling. Conclusion: Collectively, these findings support a disease-specific dysregulation of platelet, immune, and vascular pathways. The integrated EV signatures distinguish LC-19 from the related chronic conditions ME/CFS and FM, highlighting the potential of EV-based profiling for differential diagnosis. Our results provide a systems-level perspective on the differential pathophysiology of these disorders and identify EV-associated markers as candidate biomarkers with clinical value.

items.title: Repeated exposure to a conserved antigen drives dynamic clonal and epitope succession
items.abstract: Defining the dynamics of T cell memory formation with epitope-level resolution can inform vaccine design. Longitudinal T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination has enabled detailed tracking of T cell responses; however, connecting expanded clonotypes following antigen exposure to their cognate epitopes remains a challenge due to limited curated paired /{beta}TCR information. To fill this gap, we used TIRTL-seq to identify paired /{beta}TCRs from CD8+ T cell lineages associated with mRNA immunization in serial samples across 38 healthy donors over multiple rounds of vaccinations. Vaccine-associated paired /{beta}TCRs, identified based on their longitudinal kinetics, were grouped according to sequence similarity to infer their shared epitope specificities. We assigned epitope specificity to 1,109 clonotypes, recognizing 15 SARS-CoV-2 spike targets, identifying multiple previously undescribed responses, and confirming putative specificities experimentally. This approach uncovered a striking pattern of clonal succession in anti-spike T cell memory lineages resulting from repeated vaccination, characterized by a transition from low-avidity clones recognizing conserved coronavirus epitopes to high-avidity clones targeting epitopes unique to SARS-CoV-2. These results highlight the surprisingly dynamic responses underlying homologous boosting, suggest avenues for improving vaccine strategies, and pave the way for repertoire-based monitoring of antigen-specific T cell immunity.

items.title: Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments reveal modular architecture and expand functional coverage in bacteriophage proteins
items.corresponding_institution: Malopolska Centre of Biotechnology, Jagiellonian University, Krakow, Poland
items.abstract: Bacteriophage proteins evolve through extensive modular exchange, yet the sequence units underlying this process remain poorly defined. Classical domains are plausible evolutionary modules, but they incompletely annotate phage proteins and may not always coincide with the regions conserved across protein families. Here, we constructed 13,035 Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments (ECFs), grouped into 3,167 families, through large-scale HMM-HMM comparisons of proteins from 5,396 RefSeq phage genomes, without imposing predefined domain boundaries. ECFs overlapped substantially with ECOD and Pfam annotations but formed a heterogeneous spectrum comprising subdomains, domain-equivalent units, composite regions and fragments with no counterpart in either resource. Their relationships were frequently nested, indicating that conserved modules occur at multiple organisational scales. ECFs annotated 50% of phage representative proteins (at least doubling the coverage of either database), with the largest gains in structural and infection-related functions, a pattern replicated in independent metagenomic data. ECF families also showed function-dependent patterns of diversity and spatial segregation and provided functional associations for 23,925 protein families lacking detectable Pfam or ECOD domains. In receptor-binding proteins, ECFs subdivided established domains, delineated previously unannotated structural elements and recovered homologous regions where structural similarity was ambiguous. These results show that the evolutionary building blocks of phage proteins do not always coincide with classical domains, highlighting that evolutionary processes act across multiple scales. ECFs provide a complementary, sequence-derived framework for investigating how complex viral proteins are assembled, diversified and functionally organised.

items.title: Chimera: Cross-Species Single-Cell Generative Modeling of Expression Deployment Relative to Protein Conservation
items.abstract: A protein's sequence says what a gene could do in another species; the cells of that species say what it does there. Comparative genomics measures the first. Chimera measures the second, a gene's deployment, on the same genes and reports the difference. It aligns single-cell atlases across species in one generative model and returns, for every one-to-one ortholog, the evidence in the counts for a shared expression pattern, and {Delta}[a], the position of that evidence above or below what the protein's identity predicts. This difference is not sequence constraint under another name: across eight tissues, protein identity tracks dN/dS, whereas {Delta}[a] tracks neither. A gene therefore has two coordinates, not one, and the second can contradict the first: spermatocyte genes such as ZPBP2 keep their stage pattern on less conserved proteins, in eight held-out species, whereas conserved hepatocyte enzymes such as ALAS1 share their pattern but not their level. More broadly, genes of specialized cells sit above what their proteins predict in 23 of 24 cohorts, and approved drug targets do so more often than matched genes. Even among nearly identical proteins, where sequence can no longer tell genes apart, the count evidence still does. Nor does this rest on the model alone: independent data support the count evidence in liver and testis and, in a pre-specified test, {Delta}[a] in liver. With both coordinates, one can ask whether another species uses a gene as humans do, the premise of every animal model of a disease gene or drug target.

items.title: Single-AAV-mediated cardiomyocyte-specific adenine base editing ameliorates cardiac hypertrophy in vivo
items.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common inherited cardiac disorder, frequently accompanied by cardiac hypercontractility, diastolic dysfunction, heart failure and sudden cardiac death. The disease is predominantly caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins and current therapeutic strategies largely focus on symptom management. Adeno-associated virus-based (AAV) delivery of base editing tools has emerged as an alternative strategy that acts directly on the genetic cause of disease. However, canonical SpCas9-based editors are too large to package into a single-AAV vector which mandates dual-AAV approaches that require higher overall vector doses with elevated toxicity risk and increased manufacturing costs. Here, we report the development and application of a single vector approach for cardiomyocyte-specific adenine base editing to correct a Dutch founder mutation in MYBPC3 (c.2827C>T, p.Arg943Ter) that causes HCM. We systematically compared compact base editors in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) and selected the most efficient configuration, which reversed disease-associated hypercontractility in engineered human myocardium (EHM). To fit the editor/guide construct in a single-AAV vector, we screened a library of rationally designed small chimeric promoters and identified 6C2 to effectively drive expression in hiPSC-CMs and cardiac tissue of both mice and non-human primates (NHP) with exceptional specificity. Delivered in a single next-generation cardiotropic AAV capsid, we achieved therapeutic correction in an HCM mouse model at doses 20-fold below published dual-AAV cardiomyopathy base editing approaches. These results establish cardiomyocyte-specific, single vector-mediated base editing as a viable therapeutic strategy for inherited cardiomyopathies.

items.title: Genetic diversity of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium malariae and its association with infectivity of Anopheles coluzzii in the Mfou Health District, Central Region of Cameroon
items.corresponding_institution: Pasteur Center in Cameroon: Centre Pasteur du Cameroun
items.abstract: Background Malaria remains a major public health challenge in Cameroon, with sustained transmission particularly in forest-savannah transition zones. Although Plasmodium falciparum is the predominant malaria parasite, non-falciparum species such as P. malariae also contribute to the human infectious reservoir and to onward transmission. Parasite genetic diversity and multiplicity of infection (MOI) are recognized determinants of malaria transmission and may influence the prevalence and intensity of infection in mosquito vectors. However, whether parasite genetic diversity and MOI differentially influence the infectivity of P. falciparum and P. malariae to local Anopheles coluzzii populations remains poorly characterized. This knowledge gap is particularly relevant in the Mfou Health District, where malaria transmission persists and both P. falciparum and non-falciparum infections occur. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted between September 2022 and November 2023 in twelve primary schools in the Mfou Health District. Finger-prick blood samples were collected from children aged 3-17 years and examined by microscopy to identify Plasmodium infections and gametocyte carriers. Gametocyte-positive participants were enrolled in direct membrane feeding assays (DMFA) using locally reared Anopheles coluzzii. Blood samples were tested under two conditions: whole blood (WB) and replacement with naive AB serum. Mosquito infection outcomes were assessed at the oocyst (day 7) and sporozoite stages (day 14). Parasite species were confirmed by quantitative PCR (qPCR), and genetic diversity was assessed using seven microsatellite loci, together with msp1 and msp2 markers for P. falciparum and pmmsp1 for P. malariae. MOI and expected heterozygosity (He) were calculated, and their associations with mosquito infection prevalence and intensity were evaluated using generalized linear models. Results Among 2,807 children screened, 2,111 (75.2%) were infected with Plasmodium, and 388 (18.4%) carried gametocytes. A total of 169 children aged 4-13 years were selected for membrane feeding assays using Anopheles coluzzii, of whom 68% successfully infected mosquitoes. Among 10,872 dissected mosquitoes, 20.2% were infected at the oocyst stage, with both infection prevalence and intensity being higher in mosquitoes fed on AB serum-reconstituted blood than with whole blood. Sporozoite-stage infections were detected in 5.8% of mosquitoes, predominantly under AB serum conditions. Mosquito infection prevalence and intensity increased with gametocyte density, although submicroscopic gametocyte carriers were also infectious. P. falciparum exhibited high genetic diversity (MOI 2.4 {+/-} 0.8; He 0.72 {+/-} 0.07), while P. malariae showed limited diversity (MOI 0.11-0.21; He {approx} 0). Mixed-species and polyclonal infections were associated with enhanced infection outcomes. Moreover, the msp2 FC27 allelic family in P. falciparum and the 800-bp pmmsp1 allele in P. malariae were associated with oocyst development. Overall, parasite genetic diversity, multiplicity of infection, and species composition were positively associated with mosquito infectivity, with only minor seasonal variation observed. Conclusion Malaria transmission in Mfou is sustained by genetically diverse and multiclonal P. falciparum infections, with P. malariae also contributing to the human infectious reservoir. The association of parasite genetic diversity, MOI, and allele-specific factors with mosquito infectivity underscores the importance of addressing asymptomatic and multiclonal infections in malaria control strategies.

items.title: Algorithms for Designing Therapeutic Oligonucleotides on Pangenome Graphs
items.abstract: Designing therapeutic oligonucleotides that act reliably across human genetic diversity requires more than alignment to a single reference genome. Binding affinity of an siRNA or ASO to a usually complementary site in an mRNA target molecule is one main determinant of drug efficacy. Thus, variation in sub-populations can lead to failures in drug development if this variation reduces binding affinity. We provide a first methodological step towards principled, variant-aware design of therapeutic oligonucleotides. The genetic diversity in target genes, or specific regions thereof, is represented as a pangenome graph. We define individual or small sets of suitable therapeutic oligonucleotides by their ability to cover all paths in a directed acyclic graph within a bounded edit distance <= k. Edit distance is used as an accepted proxy to the commonly used binding affinity. We formalize the resulting computational problem and provide complexity results: NP-hardness of identifying such minimal sets even for k =0, and coNP-completeness of verifying the validity of a given set of oligonucleotides. Further, we propose algorithmic approaches operating on a product graph of an automaton (an Aho-Corasick DFA or an Ukkonen DFA) and the pangenome graph, as well as a dynamic programming-based lossless filter. We evaluate the approaches on gene-specific subgraphs of human pangenome graphs and demonstrate favorable performance compared to naive brute-force computation. Our results show that candidate target sites with a threshold of k <= 3 can be identified even for large, complex graphs where the brute-force computation did not complete within 24h. We observe that the dynamic programming-based lossless filter outperforms both product-graph approaches as well as brute-force baselines while maintaining an average approximation ratio < 1.5 across more than a hundred evaluated subgraphs. We also present examples where a small set of oligonucleotides constitutes a feasible solution where no single oligonucleotide with a threshold of k <= 2 covers all paths.

items.title: Dynamic rewiring of super-enhancers shapes condition-specific genome regulation
items.abstract: Enhancers and promoters communicate through three-dimensional chromatin contacts to control cell13 type-specific gene expression. While chromosome conformation capture has enabled genome-wide mapping of these contacts, and graph-based analyses of the resulting interaction networks have shown that super enhancers occupy highly connected positions. However, how the network positions of super enhancers and typical enhancers changes as cells transition between states remains unclear. In this study, enhancer-promoter networks from high-resolution Hi-C data were constructed, and network18 based approaches were applied to characterize the regulatory architecture and its remodeling during differentiation, using Hi-C and HiChIP datasets from three differentiation systems: PMA-induced K562 differentiation, cardiomyocyte differentiation of h9 cells, and differentiation of primary foreskin keratinocytes. The networks are modular, with the largest clusters consisting of promoters and both enhancer types. Super-enhancer constituents and typical enhancers occupy distinct topological positions. During differentiation, network structure is mainly reshaped by enhancer turnover rather than by enhancer reorganization. Among the persistent enhancers, super-enhancer constituents rewire more extensively than typical enhancers. Functionally, remodeled super-enhancers connect to promoters controlling cell type's identity-defining programs, whereas typical enhancers connect to promoters involved in general metabolic and stress-response loci. These results provide evidence that super-enhancers act as a sensitive, identity-focused layer of chromatin communication. The present study also providesquantitative, network-level evidence for how super-enhancers shape the architecture of chromatin communication.

items.title: Single-cell transfer RNA sequencing reveals principles of translational regulation
items.corresponding_institution: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, NY
items.abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) decode genetic instructions from messenger RNA (mRNA) into protein, yet their abundance and regulation across cell states remain largely undefined, as multimodal measures of cellular tRNAs have remained elusive. Here, we develop a massively parallel assay for single-cell translatome and RNA sequencing (sctRNA-seq), which profiles transcriptome-wide mRNA and tRNA abundance simultaneously and chart the tRNA composition of 364,841 cells. Through multimodal perturbation screening of protein-coding genes and tRNA loci, we reveal dynamics across the mRNA and tRNA transcriptomes, delineating distinct tRNA-linked modules regulated by metabolic and Pol III-mediated transcription. Further, we uncover a close correspondence between codon demand and tRNA-mediated anticodon composition during hematopoietic multilineage commitment and differentiation. Tri-modal profiling of mRNA, tRNA, and proteins from primary human T cells reveals tRNA-mediated regulation that partially explains the discordance between mRNA and protein levels, particularly for selenoproteins and transcription factors. Finally, we uncover a stress-responsive tRNA module defined by gene-internal promoter sequences. Together, our analyses resolve tRNAs as a previously undefined layer of translational control underlying cellular identity and cell-state transitions.

items.title: Aging drives senescence in visceral adipose to a greater extent than obesity, instigating multicellular common signaling patterns that impair organ function and drive inflammation
items.abstract: Abstract Obesity accelerates key hallmarks of biological aging in visceral adipose tissue (VAT), yet age-associated changes in cellular senescence against a background of sustained elevated adiposity remain poorly understood. To investigate these changes, we examined human omental VAT from younger (18-35 years), middle-aged (36-51 years), and older adults (52-75 years) with comparable BMI (40 {+/-}5 kg/m2) using a cross-sectional design. We integrated bulk and single- nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), Visium HD spatial transcriptomics, and three complementary computational approaches for senescent cell (SnC) identification. VAT from older adults exhibited increased expression of senescence-associated markers, including CDKN2A (p16INK4a) and CDKN1A (p21CIP1), as well as enhanced fibro-inflammatory and tissue-remodeling programs. snRNA-seq revealed a non-linear age-associated pattern, with relatively modest differences between younger and middle-aged adults and more pronounced senescence- associated changes in older adults. SnCs were increased primarily in adipose stem/progenitor cells and mesothelium, which also emerged as major intercellular communication hubs. CellChat analyses identified SnCs of multiple lineages converging on shared outgoing signaling programs, implicating inflammatory, extracellular matrix-remodeling, and adipogenic regulatory pathways, including IL-1, IL-6, TGF-{beta}, and WNT signaling. These predicted interactions were accompanied by transcriptional programs involving HIF1A, NF-{kappa}B, SMADs, PRRX1, and TP53 in SnCs, as well as consistent upregulation of KDM6B a histone demethylase activating gene expression. Collectively, our findings suggest that aging drives the senescence program to a greater extent than obesity, potentiating tissue dysfunction through coordinated intercellular signaling mechanisms.

items.title: Spatially enforced engagement of PD-1⁺ T cells with AXL⁺ cells reprograms the tumor microenvironment and overcomes anti-PD-1 resistance
items.corresponding_institution: The Shraga Segal Department of Microbiology, Immunology, and Genetics, Faculty of Health Sciences, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, 8410501 Beer-Sheva, Israe
items.abstract: Background: AXL overexpression promotes tumor-cell plasticity, local immune suppression, and resistance to PD-1 blockade. Conventional anti-AXL and anti-PD-1 antibodies combinations act independently and do not ensure physical proximity between PD-1+ T cells and AXL+ cells within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Methods: To address this limitation, we developed a non-tandem, tetravalent IgG bispecific antibody designed to simultaneously engage PD-1 and AXL (BiTE-AXL/PD-1). Its antitumor activity was evaluated using in vitro functional assays and humanized and immunocompetent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) models and compared with the combination of monospecific anti-AXL and anti-PD-1 antibodies. Spatial multiplex imaging was used to characterize treatment-associated changes in the tumor microenvironment of an anti-PD-1-resistant murine model. Results: BiTE-AXL/PD-1 enhanced T-cell activation, promoted AXL-dependent tumor-T-cell conjugation, and increased tumor-cell killing in vitro, outperforming the combination of the two monospecific antibodies. In humanized and immunocompetent HNSCC models, BiTE treatment significantly delayed tumor growth compared with the antibody combination and was well tolerated, with no overt toxicity. Spatial multiplex imaging revealed a shift from a fibroblast-dominated microenvironment characterized by exhausted CD8+ T cells toward dendritic-cell- and CD8+ T-cell-enriched niches associated with antitumor immune activity. Conclusion: BiTE-AXL/PD-1 promotes physical proximity between PD-1+ T cells and AXL+ cells, enhances antitumor immune responses, and remodels the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. These findings support PD-1/AXL bispecific targeting as a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome resistance to PD-1 blockade in HNSCC.

items.title: Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
items.corresponding_institution: Prescient Design - AI for Drug Discovery, Computational Science Center Of Excellence, Roche, Basel, Switzerland
items.abstract: Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies. Using this dataset, we benchmark six leading structure prediction models (AlphaFold-Multimer, Boltz-2, IntelliFold v2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1, and Protenix-v2) on their ability to discriminate binders from decoys. The best-performing model, Protenix-v2, achieves 72% pairwise accuracy over all pairs and 87% on the most confident half of predictions, and correctly identifies the true binder from a pool of 50 candidates in 29% of trials; this represents a substantial enrichment over random selection, yet remains far from reliable single-candidate identification. Structural consensus across models also discriminates binders from decoys, with pairwise accuracy reaching 73.1% when three or more models converge on a pose (DockQ>0.23, covering around 54.2% of pairs). Epitope localization remains unreliable: the best model contacts annotated epitope residues in only 62.8% of cases, indicating that binding discrimination does not establish accurate epitope localization. Our results suggest that current folding models provide useful but limited signal for antibody screening and should be complemented by orthogonal methods. We release POISK as a community resource for future benchmarking and model training.

items.title: CNVSIM: an interpretable cross-study copy-number reference atlas for cancer subtyping
items.abstract: Genome-wide copy-number variation (CNV) profiles provide a representation of structural changes in cancer genomes, but interpreting new profiles with respect to their underlying biology remains challenging. We developed CNVSIM, which organizes CNV profiles into root-specific reference spaces and defines subtypes with chromosome-scale and gene-level signatures. Applied to the Progenetix dataset, CNVSIM established 112 CNV-defined subtypes across 19 cancer roots, supported by 155,881 neoplastic analyses from diverse studies and assay platforms. In the context of diagnostic concepts, these subtypes distinguish genomic architectures and reveal associated differences in somatic mutation patterns, with selected associations supported across cohorts. In practice, CNVSIM enables new profiles to be projected onto the established reference and linked to corresponding reference analyses. Additionally, CNVSIM enables the identification of cancer cell lines with copy-number architectures similar to individual subtypes, while also revealing gaps in subtype and alteration coverage based on available data. Reference robustness was supported by subtype recovery after data reduction and assignment of 77.6% of held-out TCGA profiles using a reference reconstructed without TCGA.

items.title: A genome-guided multilocus sequence analysis scheme to detect and resolve diversity within the X-disease phytoplasma group (16SrIII)
items.abstract: Phytoplasmas of the X-disease group (16SrIII) cause economically important diseases of vegetables, forage and staple crops, fruit trees and ornamentals in South America, where they are diagnosed and classified only by 16S rRNA gene RFLP. Because this gene is highly conserved, strains that differ in host range, vectors and regulatory relevance cannot be distinguished. We developed a multilocus sequence analysis (MLSA) scheme for typing 16SrIII phytoplasmas, using genome data to select the markers and to define reference lineages. Five single-copy loci (tuf, secA, secY, mutM, cimH) were chosen from 16 curated genomes; primers matched all genomes in silico, and four of the five pairs did not amplify phytoplasmas of other groups co-occurring in the region (16SrI, 16SrVII, 16SrXIII). Genome comparisons resolved four lineages, including one restricted to South America that shared only 90.8-93.9% average nucleotide identity with the other lineages, despite > 98.8% 16S rRNA identity. The concatenated MLSA (2,870 nt) reproduced the genome-based lineages and assigned five Argentinian field isolates from weeds, fodder beet, cassava, plum and a native shrub. Identical 16SrIII-B RFLP patterns occurred in different lineages, and one 16SrIII-B isolate grouped within the 16SrIII-J clade, showing that subgroups are not reliable proxies for lineages. The South American lineage had the broadest host range, spanning six plant families. We also detected chimeric rRNA copies and sequencing artefacts that can cause misclassification. This MLSA provides a PCR-based tool to identify 16SrIII lineages in crops, weeds and insects, supporting epidemiological studies, disease management and phytosanitary decisions.

items.title: Accessibility-guided targeting of NRF2-responsive long noncoding RNA NMRAL2P alters a distinct gene expression program and reduces non-small cell lung cancer proliferation
items.corresponding_institution: University of Michigan Department of Biological Chemistry
items.abstract: Aberrant activation of the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 promotes non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) survival and therapy resistance, but downstream effectors beyond redox regulation remain incompletely defined. Transcriptome profiling of lung and NSCLC cells identified the pseudogene-derived long noncoding RNA LOC344887/NMRAL2P as consistently associated with NRF2 activity. The NMRAL2P locus produces three predominant, nuclear-localized isoforms whose expression depends on NRF2 across normal lung, lung adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous carcinoma cells. In-cell SHAPE-MaP identified accessible regions within NMRAL2P transcripts, guiding antisense gapmer design. NMRAL2P depletion inhibited NSCLC cell proliferation and increased sensitivity to cisplatin. Transcriptome analysis revealed that NMRAL2P depletion altered a restricted gene expression program involving cell adhesion and MAPK signaling, with responses distinct from those observed following NRF2 depletion. Core NRF2 antioxidant target genes were largely unaffected by NMRAL2P depletion. These findings support a model in which NRF2 induces NMRAL2P to sustain a distinct gene expression program that contributes to NSCLC proliferation and survival. NMRAL2P represents an RNA effector downstream of NRF2 that links oncogenic NRF2 activity to cellular functions beyond canonical antioxidant responses, providing a potential point of intervention in NRF2-active lung cancers and motivating further investigation of the mechanisms connecting this nuclear RNA to signaling pathways.

items.title: AGPAT2 Inflammatory Metabolic Reprogramming Mediates Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-associated Myocarditis via LPAR5-pyroptosis Axis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Cardiology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases
items.abstract: Objectives: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), especially programmed cell death protein-1 (PD1) inhibitors, are effective onco-therapeutic agents. However, ICI-associated myocarditis (ICIAM) greatly limits their clinical utility. Imbalance between 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferases (AGPAT2) and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) induced by inflammatory metabolic reprogramming (IMRP) might cause cardiovascular injury. This study aims to explore the link between AGPAT2 pathway and ICIAM as well as identifies diagnosis and treatment targets of ICIAM. Methods: ICIAM model was established by injecting anti-PD1 (PD1) in wild-type (WT) and AGPAT2 heterozygous knockout (AGPAT2+/-) mice. The pathogenic and regulating mechanisms of AGPAT2-LPA and its downstream signaling were examined in vitro and in vivo. A tumor-patient cohort was enrolled to observe the association between serum LPA and risk of ICIAM. Results: In the PD1-induced ICIAM model, myocardial IMRP occurred due to upstream immunity disorder, leading to downstream AGPAT2 degradation via lysosomal pathway and subsequent LPA accumulation. Knockout of AGPAT2 gene also promoted LPA accumulation. The accumulated LPA, by binding to its dominant receptor subtype 5 (LPAR5), triggered pyroptotic myocardial damage and resultant ICIAM. LPAR5 knockdown with siRNA or inhibition with TCLPA5-4 played the most significant rescue effect on myocardial pyroptosis, while stimulating LPAR5 with overdose LPA significantly increased myocardial pyroptosis. In ICI-treated patients, elevated serum LPA was associated with increased risk of ICIAM. Conclusions: IMRP-triggered dysfunction of AGPAT2-LPA-LPAR5-pyroptosis axis is involved in pathogenesis of ICIAM. Several elements in this axis may be the promising targets in diagnosis (LPA as a biomarker) and treatment (LPA or LPAR5 as therapeutics) of ICIAM.

items.title: Scalable recorders of cellular calcium dynamics and molecular interactions across time
items.abstract: Cellular processes are mediated by dynamic biochemical events in their native context, including changes in intracellular ion concentrations and transient interactions between molecules. Studying these processes across large cell populations requires recording their dynamics across time in single cells, simultaneously and at scale. Here, we introduce split-1POK, a split protein tape monomer whose two halves reconstitute when the domains fused to them interact. The reconstituted monomer is incorporated into the protein tape as it elongates across time in live cells, enabling scalable, spatiotemporally resolved endpoint readout under conventional light microscopy. Split-1POK provides a programmable scaffold for new recorders in the CytoSense family, our previously introduced framework (ref. 1) in which the same cytosol-localized monomer senses cellular activity and writes it along protein tape recorders. Unlike transcription-based activity recorders, which encode the signal through new gene expression, CytoSense recorders act on monomers post-synthesis, so the activity signal is sensed and written directly in the cytosol without passing through transcription- or translation-associated cascades. Fusing calmodulin and its binding peptide to split-1POK, we built TCaMP (Tape monomer-CalModulin-Peptide), a genetically encoded calcium recorder (GECR) that measures calcium dynamics on a single, analog intensity scale along a continuous time axis, providing quantitative comparison of calcium levels over time within the same cell. In cultured human cells, TCaMP records transient calcium dynamics from transmembrane entry, receptor activation, and intracellular store release, detecting stimulations as brief as ten minutes. With hour-scale kinetics over days, TCaMP complements fluorescent calcium indicators by trading sub-second temporal resolution for scalable, long-term recording. Fusing conditional dimerization pairs to split-1POK yields recorders of molecular interaction histories in response to external stimuli. Split-1POK thus brings scalable, spatiotemporally resolved recording to intracellular calcium dynamics and molecular interactions across time.

items.title: Improved long-read sequencing technology reveals full genome architecture of Malian Plasmodium falciparum field isolates
items.corresponding_institution: Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine
items.abstract: Understanding genome plasticity in malaria parasites and the diversity of their repetitive gene families requires high-quality reference genomes derived from parasites recently isolated from patients. However, generating such genomes in Plasmodium falciparum remains challenging owing to the parasite's extreme AT content, extensive repetitive regions, and the frequent occurrence of multiclonal infections in endemic settings. As a result, most available reference genomes are derived from laboratory-adapted strains, that have experienced prolonged in vitro maintenance, and that incompletely represent natural parasite diversity. We developed and optimized a de novo assembly strategy based on PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing and applied it to eight recently-isolated and cloned P. falciparum parasites from Mali. HiFi sequencing enabled highly accurate genome reconstruction, yielding assemblies with a mean of 18 contigs, 301 pseudogenes, and a frameshift rate of 0.04% following Liftoff annotation. Assemblies showed high structural integrity and near-complete chromosomes, including improved recovery of subtelomeric regions and multigene families, without requiring short-read correction. Despite overall conservation of chromosome organization, substantial variation was observed in chromosome-end architecture, subtelomeric structure, and telomeric repeat content among parasite genomes. Our approach simplifies the generation of high-quality P. falciparum genomes and reduces sequencing requirements fourfold. The resulting assemblies enabled characterization of natural variation in telomere plasticity and multicopy gene family diversity in field isolates. These findings establish PacBio HiFi sequencing as an effective and scalable strategy for producing highly contiguous and accurate de novo assemblies of P. falciparum, supporting the development of geographically-diverse, field-relevant malaria parasite reference genomes.

items.title: From Screening to Differential Diagnosis: Benchmarking 3D Facial Representations Across Craniofacial Conditions
items.abstract: Rare genetic disorders often present with highly heterogeneous physical features: some have distinctive craniofacial characteristics, whereas others produce subtler or more variable facial differences, making phenotype-based diagnosis challenging. Three-dimensional (3D) facial scanning is a noninvasive approach that captures facial shape and surface geometry, providing quantitative information on craniofacial morphology beyond conventional 2D photographs. Here, we investigated how well 3D facial representations support clinical tasks ranging from broad screening to fine-grained differential diagnosis without landmark registration, dense correspondence, or template fitting. We benchmarked four 3D models, including PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, and a geometric baseline, using 26,990 facial scans from 18,785 subjects across four prediction tasks. Across models, performance declined as greater diagnostic specificity was required. Broad affected-versus-unaffected screening achieved high performance (accuracy 0.893; AUC 0.956), although sensitivity analyses revealed substantial influences of cohort composition and demographic differences. Fine-grained syndrome diagnosis remained more challenging, with limited top-1 accuracy despite meaningful class-wise discrimination. Combining repeated scans improved patient-level diagnosis beyond differences in patient weighting. Prototype inference further improved diagnostic prioritization, placing the correct syndrome among the top five candidates for about 65\% of held-out patients across 49 diagnoses. Patient-to-patient retrieval identified phenotypically similar confirmed cases, while useful syndrome prototypes could be constructed from relatively few reference patients. Anatomical region-occlusion analysis revealed syndrome-dependent patterns of facial importance broadly consistent with clinically recognized craniofacial features, although overlapping facial phenotypes contributed to diagnostic confusion. Overall, these findings support the potential of 3D facial representations for diagnostic candidate prioritization and retrieval, while emphasizing the influence of cohort composition on screening performance and the challenges of distinguishing phenotypically similar genetic syndromes.

items.title: Nlrp6-dependent sentinel goblet cell functions dictate defensive responses during bacterial invasion of colonic crypts
items.abstract: The intestinal mucus layer serves as the primary physical barrier against microbial invasion, shielding the epithelium from luminal pathogens and inflammatory insults. This barrier is maintained by a heterogeneous population of goblet cells (GCs), which secrete regionally and organizationally distinct mucus layers. However, when this primary barrier is compromised, the burden of defense likely shifts to secondary mechanisms that remain incompletely defined. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the proposed role of microbe-sensing sentinel goblet cells (senGCs) as a secondary defensive mechanism that becomes critical when the primary mucus barrier fails, focusing on their capacity to mount localized secretory responses and preserve crypt sterility under challenge conditions. Using a GC specific Nlrp6 knockout model (Nlrp6{Delta}GC), we demonstrate that senGC deficiency leads to increased susceptibility to DSS induced colitis and Citrobacter rodentium infection, marked by exacerbated inflammation and enhanced crypt invasion respectively. Transcriptomic and immunolgical profiling revealed both common and sex-specific immune dysregulation, with especially female Nlrp6{Delta}GC mice exhibiting heightened mucosal pathogen burden, reduced Th17 expansion and increased CD8 T cell recruitment. The senGC-deficient mice also showed diminished baseline mucus secretion and accelerated GC loss during infection, suggesting a previously unrecognized mucus maintenance role for senGCs. Furthermore, infection induced expansion of Nlrp6 GCs in wild-type mice, enhancing MAMP-triggered mucus secretion, a response that is absent in Nlrp6{Delta}GC tissue. These findings confirm senGCs as an important regulator of epithelial protection by integrating GC-intrinsic microbial sensing with mucosal defense.

items.title: Pigmentation markers enable efficient co-CRISPR selection in the pantry moth Plodia interpunctella
items.abstract: CRISPR co-targeting (co-CRISPR) of pigment genes facilitates the identification and recovery of genome-edited individuals in model organisms. Using Plodia interpunctella, an emerging lepidopteran model, we characterized mutant phenotypes of eight genes involved in the melanin and ommochrome biosynthesis pathways (black, ebony, yellow, tan, vermilion, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase/cinnabar (kmo/cn), scarlet, and white) to evaluate their suitability as co-CRISPR markers. Disruption of black, ebony, and yellow altered larval sclerite, pupal cuticle, and adult wing coloration. All four ommochrome pathway genes studied contributed to larval cuticle and adult eye pigmentation, whereas only vermilion and kmo/cn disruption produced visible phenotypes in the adult wings. Sequencing revealed low apparent mosaicism in some yellow and tan G0 individuals, along with recurrent deletions at the yellow and tan target sites consistent with possible microhomology-mediated end joining repair. Using white or scarlet as co-CRISPR selection markers, we identified G0 individuals carrying a secondary mutation in the yellow gene with a positive predictive value of 100% by scoring its knockout phenotype. Extending this approach to six meiosis-related genes without visibly scorable phenotypes, selection based on the white mutant phenotype identified sequence-confirmed mutations at the corresponding gene-of-interest in 191 of 206 G0 individuals (93%). Together, these findings establish white and scarlet as effective co-CRISPR selection markers and provide a practical strategy for facilitating functional genetic studies in Plodia.

items.title: Cell atlases of schistosome human infective stages reveal larval tissue fates and innovations
items.abstract: Schistosomes infect over 250 million people, yet the cellular basis of their human-infective cercaria larva, that drives transmission and infection, remains poorly understood. We present single-cell atlases of Schistosoma mansoni cercariae, widely regarded as transcriptionally quiescent, and schistosomula, the first intra-mammalian stage. Twenty-two cercarial cell types either persist into schistosomula or are lost. The tail harbours several cercaria-specific innovations, including a novel tegument. Gene-age analysis supports the cercaria as the most recent addition to the life cycle and tail cells as younger than body cells. Persisting cell types undergo clear transcriptional transitions which give new insights into the dynamics of cercarial transformation into schistosomula. These findings link the recent origin of cercarial cell types to the evolution of active dispersal and transmission in digenean parasites.

items.title: Discovery of molecular glues for modulating MHC presentation of cancer neoantigens
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California, San Francisco, CA, USA; Department of Chemistry, U
items.abstract: Antigen presentation by MHC class I molecules is essential for cancer immunosurveillance, but many cancer-specific antigens fail to form complexes with Class I MHC and are poorly presented on the cell surface. In this study, we present a chemical strategy to overcome this limitation by identifying peptide MHC glues (PMGs) that promote the formation of peptide-MHC complexes with otherwise unpresentable cancer antigens. Crystal structures of these complexes show that our compounds stabilize antigen-MHC binding by making simultaneous interactions with the MHC protein and the antigen peptides. These findings reveal a new approach for chemically rewiring Class I MHC antigen presentation and accessing rare cancer antigens for therapeutic targeting.

items.title: Complex Spatial and Temporal Organization of Functional Brain Networks
items.abstract: Recent research exploring brain-behavior associations has relied on the language of complex systems to understand how stable behavioral individual differences emerge from brain function. At the same time, advances in neuroimaging have provided greater insight into both the topological and temporal properties of macroscale cortical networks. These new approaches offer a potential avenue for understanding how functional activity in the brain might behave in a manner that aligns with complex-systems interpretations of psychological traits. The present study used resting-state data from the Human Connectome project (N = 994) to explore associations between the spatial and temporal features of functional brain networks. Using an adaptive frequency approach to explore brain function at different timescales together with a family of methods from complex systems theory, we identified patterns of brain state organization reflecting a state-trait continuum, with more stable trait-like dynamics and greater functional coupling between networks in lower frequency oscillations. Additionally, we found evidence of greater coupling across timescales in brain networks associated with higher-order cognition. This research supports interpretations of brain organization as a spatiotemporal hierarchy and provides future avenues for exploring brain-behavior associations from a complex system perspective.

items.title: An expanded, phenotypically distinct tumor cell subset with low HPV mRNA increases recurrence risk
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA
items.abstract: Human papillomavirus-related (HPV+) cancers harbor a subset of tumor cells expressing certain senescence-related transcripts and reduced levels of HPV mRNAs. We aimed to define this HPV-low population's biologic traits and clinical significance via integrated analysis of recurrence-prone human HPV+ oropharyngeal cancers (OPCs) and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) of variable therapy sensitivity. Single-cell mRNA sequencing of PDXs and human tumors detected gene expression profiles in HPV-low cells indicating lack of senescence or terminal differentiation and intact tumorigenic capacity. HPV-low cells in cisplatin-refractory PDXs and particular human OPCs differentially upregulated multiple pathways linked to aggressive tumor biology, including RAS signaling, IL-6 signaling, and EMT. Predicted loss of cell-cell interactions among HPV-low cells reflected reduced epithelial identity, further supporting their more aggressive biology. Accordingly, the size of the pre-treatment HPV-low fraction had strong, independent association with recurrence risk. Genetic subclones within OPCs varied widely in content of HPV-low cells, which were enriched in particular lineages. Our findings uncover novel pro-tumor functions of HPV-low cells and support a central role for them in therapy resistance as well as potential utility as a clinical biomarker. Further elucidating mechanisms of cooperativity and plasticity between HPV-low and high states holds promise to reveal targets in treatment-refractory HPV+ malignancies.

items.title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

items.title: Recurrent astrocyte transcriptional states with spatial and functional specialization are induced by brain metastases independently of their primary tumor origin
items.abstract: Reactive astrocytes have emerged as important components of the brain metastasis niche, yet a state-resolved framework for metastasis-associated astrocyte biology is still lacking. Here, we integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics across syngeneic breast, lung and melanoma models of brain metastases to define a state-resolved astrocyte landscape. We identify recurrent tumor-associated astrocyte states shared across tumor origins, map their spatial distribution, and find that a subset, which we term AST-BrM, becomes selectively reprogrammed at the tumor-microenvironment interface, supporting niche-coupled organization rather than a diffuse brain-wide reactive response. AST-BrM defines distinct metastasis-associated astrocyte states at the peritumoral interface, distinguishes them from homeostatic-like astrocytes beyond generic inflammatory activation, and resolves into two therapeutically actionable programs: an AP-1-high axis and a STAT3+/HOPX+-associated axis. Genetic and pharmacologicall perturbations establish functional relevance, and an AP-1/c-FOS-driven signature is associated with clinical outcome. Together, these findings define conserved, spatially organized and actionable astrocyte programs that drive brain metastasis progression.

items.title: Optimizing Lumipulse plasma pTau217/Aβ42 ratio cutpoints in an Asian cohort with high cerebrovascular disease burden
items.corresponding_institution: Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore
items.abstract: The generalizability of FDA-cleared Lumipulse plasma pTau217 / A{beta}42 ratio cutpoints to Asian populations remains uncertain, especially in those with high burden of concomitant cerebrovascular disease (CeVD). We evaluated pTau217, A{beta}42 and their ratio in 205 Singapore-based participants with corresponding amyloid neuroimaging. In-house cutpoints were derived using a three-range strategy targeting 95% sensitivity and specificity. Plasma pTau217/A{beta}42 ratio outperformed pTau217 alone (area under the curve, 0.951 versus 0.925; p=0.004), with comparable performance across CeVD severities. Plasma ratio cutpoints achieved 98% negative predictive value, 88% positive predictive value, and 95% accuracy, classifying 10% as intermediate-risk. Using FDA-cleared cutpoints for our cohort retained 97% sensitivity and negative predictive value but yielded lower specificity (86%), positive predictive value (77%) and accuracy (85%), with 29% classified as intermediate-risk. Our findings support the need for population-specific validation of cutpoints from FDA-cleared blood biomarkers of brain amyloid pathology.

items.title: Tremor Morphology Toolkit: Waveform Modulation-Based Tremor Phenotyping
items.abstract: Clinicians typically characterize tremor by its frequency, amplitude, and body region affected. Other aspects also provide critical clues to the type of tremor and its underlying pathophysiology including tremor waveform morphology, consistency across cycles, and variability in amplitude and timing. We introduce the Tremor Morphology Toolkit (TMT), an eight-metric, waveform-derived panel that quantifies these features from upper-limb inertial signals. Using accelerometer and gyroscope recordings from 34 individuals with upper-extremity tremor across four standardized tasks (rest, outstretched, wing-beating, and kinetic), we computed: (i) rSHAPE, cycle-to-cycle shape consistency via pairwise similarity of normalized cycles; (ii) rSINE, sinusoidality, the mean correlation of each cycle with its best-fit sinusoid; (iii) rCVA, the coefficient of variation of cycle amplitude; (iv) rCVD, the coefficient of variation of cycle duration; (v) AWI, amplitude-warping index; (vi) DWI, duration-warping index; (vii) FreqVar, a spectral bandwidth indexing power-weighted frequency spread; and (viii) Amplitude Breathing indices, which quantify slow waxing and waning of tremor amplitude over time from fluctuations in the signal envelope, representing the time-varying amplitude of the tremor waveform. We detail algorithms, parameterizations, and implementation defaults to support reproducible use. TMT is designed to complement conventional frequency-amplitude measures by capturing tremor morphology and modulation in a simple, interpretable framework. It enables objective quantification of features often assessed qualitatively at the bedside, facilitates comparisons across recording conditions, and provides a foundation for validation against clinical labels and disease phenotypes. Future studies can integrate these parameters with electrophysiological measures to investigate mechanisms underlying tremor generation and modulation. HighlightsO_LIIntroducing Tremor Morphology Toolkit (TMT), an eight-metric framework for objective tremor characterization. C_LIO_LICorrelation analysis identified redundant and complementary relationships among tremor-shape features, with sinusoidal waveform characteristics (rSINE), cycle-to-cycle amplitude variability (rCVA), and tremor frequency variability (FreqVar) providing a concise, complementary set for characterizing tremor shape. C_LIO_LIExamination of the alignment between newly defined tremor-shape features and clinician perceptions found that clinicians relied more on envelope-based amplitude dynamics than on individual tremor cycles. C_LI

items.title: Statistical design of Path to Prevention platform trial in early neuronal alpha-synuclein disease
items.corresponding_institution: Berry Consultants, LLC, Austin, Texas 78746, United States
items.abstract: The Path to Prevention (P2P) platform trial is a first-in-class, phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled learning study. Its design expedites the assessment of investigational therapies for the treatment of early-stage Neuronal -Synuclein Disease (NSD), a biological disease continuum that encompasses and often precedes clinically manifest Parkinsons Disease. P2P is embedded within the Parkinsons Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a robust observational longitudinal cohort study on Parkinsons disease progression and a trial-facilitating enrollment framework. A regimen, comprised of an active investigational therapy and a matched placebo control, evaluates a therapeutic candidate within the P2P perpetual platform framework. Multiple regimens can be enrolled, enabling efficient testing of multiple therapeutics. A two-stage randomization scheme determines regimen sample size with 125 participants assigned to a regimens active therapy and a variable number to placebo control. The treated follow up period is a minimum of 96 weeks and a maximum of 144 weeks, with the last randomized participant followed for 96 weeks. As a pioneering interventional trial in early-stage NSD, P2P endpoint selection was critically informed by modeling and analysis of available PPMI data. In P2P, regimens will be evaluated for efficacy using two primary endpoints: 1) a biomarker outcome of Dopamine Transporter Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (DAT SPECT) imaging measured by the bilateral putamen Specific Binding Ratio (SBR) and 2) a clinical outcome measured by the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinsons Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III score. Each endpoint will be assessed separately using a longitudinal Bayesian mixed effects model, which compares the active treatment group to the shared placebo control group. The model uses regimen-specific controls at full weight and dynamically discounts controls from other regimens. Additionally, placebo control estimates are supplemented by non-randomized control data from the PPMI cohort. Clinical trial simulations, informed by longitudinal data from 275 P2P-eligible PPMI study participants (Age 60-81, 35% Female, 65% Male), were conducted to evaluate the design. Each regimen is well-powered to detect a 40% slowing in progression for both the clinical and biomarker primary endpoints when comparing active treatment to randomized control data. Supplementing the control estimation with non-randomized, P2P-eligible registry participant data increases power in the explored scenarios up to 4% for each endpoint. The embedded P2P platform trial is a powerful learning study that leverages statistical efficiencies from the platform trial design and established PPMI infrastructure and is poised to advance treatment development in early-stage NSD.

items.title: Path to Prevention Platform Trial in Early-Stage Neuronal Alpha-Synuclein Disease: Study Design
items.corresponding_institution: Berry Consultants, LLC, Austin, Texas 78746, United States
items.abstract: The development of biologically targeted therapeutics (BTTs) that slow Parkinsons disease progression has been hampered by a reliance on testing interventions in clinically defined populations with already advanced pathobiology. Publications on the biological definition and classification of neuronal -synuclein disease (NSD), and the development of the NSD integrated staging system (NSD-ISS), have generated a framework for identifying individuals with NSD prior to the emergence of a clinically defined syndrome. Path to Prevention (P2P) is a phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled platform trial designed to assess the safety and efficacy of interventions in an early-stage NSD population. The trial is embedded within the observational Parkinsons Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a structure that enables recruitment of participants from the PPMI cohort, leverages existing operational infrastructure, and utilizes data from non-P2P enrolled PPMI participants in the Bayesian statistical modeling. P2P will enroll participants at least 60 years of age with NSD Stage 2B (abnormal -synuclein, dopaminergic dysfunction, and prodromal signs or symptoms without functional impairment) without a clinically defined diagnosis of PD or a related disorder. As a platform trial, P2P will enable the testing of multiple interventions under a Master Protocol at approximately 35 sites across North America and Europe. Interventions are selected from industry-submitted applications based on biological relevance of the targets, and on the adequacy of the safety data appropriate to the target population. Each treatment regimen will have 125 participants on active treatment and at least 125 shared placebo control participants. Participants will remain on treatment for a maximum of 144 weeks or until 96 weeks since the randomization of the last participant. P2P has two primary endpoints, 1) rate of change in mean putamen specific binding ratio from baseline through follow-up and, 2) rate of change in the MDS-UPDRS Part III motor examination from baseline through follow-up or initiation of dopaminergic treatment. A range of secondary and exploratory biomarker-focused endpoints will be assessed. The protocol was developed with input from multiple stakeholders, including people with early-stage NSD, biopharmaceutical industry leaders, and regulatory authorities. P2P is the first trial to test biologically targeted assets in biologically defined prodromal participants utilizing an efficient platform design, which will provide the field with tools to expand therapeutic development, and enable intervention at earlier stages of neurodegeneration. P2P is scheduled to begin enrollment in December 2026 and is committed to data sharing and broad dissemination of learnings from the study.

items.title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Incident Solid Cancers Resolved by Histologic Subtype: A Prospective Cohort Study
items.corresponding_institution: The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center
items.abstract: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is a recognized precursor of myeloid malignancy and an independent cardiovascular risk factor, but its relationship with solid tumors is incompletely defined, particularly at histologic resolution. Here, we quantify the association between CHIP and incident cancer across hematologic and solid-organ sites, by clone size, mutation number, and histologic subtype in a prospective cohort of UK Biobank participants with baseline genetic sequencing and cancer ascertained by national registry linkage; those with pre-baseline cancer were excluded. Vanderbilt BioVU was used for replication. CHIP was associated with any incident cancer (HR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.18-1.27) and with all solid tumors combined (HR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.08-1.19). Among 17 endpoints, two survived multiple testing correction: lung adenocarcinoma (HR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.48-2.16) and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (HR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.37-3.81). Risk increased with clone size and multi-hit CHIP, most markedly for esophageal cancer (VAF [≥]30%: HR, 2.72), and the esophageal squamous association persisted in 5-year landmark analysis (HR, 2.57). In BioVU, CHIP was directionally associated with esophageal cancer and lung adenocarcinoma and its association with all solid tumors overall (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.17-1.32) was confirmed. These findings extend CHIP from a hematologic and cardiovascular risk marker to a risk marker of solid-organ cancer risk with histologic resolution and motivate clone-size-aware risk models and mechanistic studies.

items.title: The Complex Interplay Between Cancer and the Lung Microbiome
items.corresponding_institution: Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine
items.abstract: BackgroundThe lung fosters a diverse microbiome that may have a complex interplay with underlying diseases, such as lung cancer. However, existing literature has revealed diverse results, likely owing to small sample sizes and diverse sampling methods. In this context, we aim to characterize the lung microbiome and its association with malignancy via multiple sampling methods during lung resection. MethodsPatients undergoing lung resection for confirmed malignancy were prospectively included in the study. During the operation, a bronchial swab and a parenchymal biopsy of lung tissue were collected from the resected specimen and sent for analysis via 16S rRNA gene amplicon (V4) sequencing. An established bioinformatics pipeline was used to determine taxonomic identification and compare these results to clinical and tumor data. ResultsThere were 83 participants included, with 75 (90.4%) patients having primary lung tumors and 8 (9.6%) having metastatic lesions. Resections included lobectomy (69.9%), wedge (25.3%), and segmentectomy (4.8%). Lung microbiome composition differed by primary malignancy site (lung vs metastatic; p=0.014) and tumor mutations (TP53, p=0.040; KRAS, p=0.054). For primary lung cancer, there was no difference in microbiome composition by tumor histology. A near-significant association was noted for patients with prolonged air leaks and alpha diversity of the lung microbiome (p=0.070). ConclusionsIn this study, we demonstrate associations between the lung microbiome and underlying malignancy and tumor characteristics. Validation of these results may assist with diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic interventions in the operative and peri-operative management of lung cancer.

items.title: Shared additive- and variance-associated genetic architecture of cardiac structure and function
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Department of Medicine; Department of Genetics; Cardiovascular Institute, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsy
items.abstract: Cardiac remodeling underlies cardiomyopathy and heart failure, yet how common genetic effects are organized across the four chambers, and whether they influence phenotypic variability beyond additive genetic effects, remains unclear. We analyzed 22 cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes in up to 77,271 UK Biobank participants. Additive mapping identified 748 locus-trait associations across 239 regions. Multivariate fine-mapping revealed that 96% of signals showed effects across multiple cardiac chambers, while resolving independent signals with distinct anatomical profiles, including predominantly atrial and ventricular signals at RBM20. Fine-mapped signal sharing formed three robust communities corresponding broadly to atrial function, chamber remodeling and ventricular systolic function. Variance mapping identified 19 associations, 13 without a nearby additive signal. Individual variance loci and polygenic effects generalized to clinical echocardiographic phenotypes and outcomes in the Penn Medicine Biobank. These findings reveal cardiac common-variant architecture as broadly shared yet locally heterogeneous and identify phenotypic variability as a partly distinct genetic dimension.

items.title: Electric and Magnetic Source Imaging in Epilepsy: Anatomical Insights from Realistic Simulations
items.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms (p<0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls (p<0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods (p<0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources (p<0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI (p<0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE. Key pointsO_LIEEG and MEG exhibit complementary sensitivity profiles, with EEG detecting more spikes from gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms and MEG from sulcal walls. C_LIO_LIMSI provides more focal and precise source localization than ESI, particularly for tangentially oriented sources. C_LIO_LIDipole-based inverse method achieves higher localization accuracy than experimental dSPM and LCMV. C_LI

items.title: Circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) and short-term functional change in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS): exploratory evidence for systemic trophic-metabolic reserve.
items.corresponding_institution: MND Research Centre, Faculty of Medicine, Health and Human Sciences, Macquarie University
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibit heterogeneous functional decline, potentially influenced by systemic metabolic reserve. We investigate whether circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is associated with subsequent functional change in ALS. Serum IGF-1 was measured in 37 participants with ALS and 25 healthy controls. Baseline levels were compared between groups, and across disease-duration defined progression categories. Lagged regression assessed whether prior visit IGF-1 level predicted change in Revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) on the next visit, adjusting for inter-visit interval, body mass index, age and sex. Mixed-effects and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. Baseline IGF-1 did not differ significantly between controls and ALS (mean + SD: 107.3 + 54.3 vs 132.2 + 68.3 ng/mL, p = 0.12), or across progression categories (F(2, 34) = 0.13, p = 0.88). Across 48 intervals from 23 ALS participants, each 1-SD higher IGF-1 from prior visit was associated with 1.40-point less subsequent {Delta}ALSFRS-R decline (95% CI: 0.03 to 2.77, p = 0.045). Generalised estimating equations yielded a similar association ({beta} = 1.50, p = 0.030), whereas small-cluster robust inference showed wider uncertainty (p = 0.084). Repeated IGF-1 showed an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.69, and the lagged association remained positive in all 23 leave-one-participant-out analyses. The IGF-1-by-time interaction was not significant in a random-slope mixed model (p =0.254). Higher circulating IGF-1 may reflect systemic trophic-metabolic reserve associated with short-term functional preservation in ALS, but limited precision precludes definitive prognostic or causal conclusions.

items.title: Optimized phase-targeted auditory stimulation reduces nocturnal spikes in childhood epilepsies
items.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges, so called spikes, are often strongly activated during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in childhood epilepsies. In children with pronounced spike activation during NREM-sleep, spike burden can be associated with lifelong impaired cognitive functions. This spike activation is also related to alterations in sleep oscillations, specifically slow waves and spindles, which play essential roles in brain maintenance and maturation. These observations suggest that spikes may disrupt sleep-dependent brain processes that are critical for the development of cognitive functions. Phase-targeted auditory stimulation during NREM sleep delivers brief, non-arousing tones at specific phases of ongoing slow waves to modulate sleep oscillations. Recently, our group showed that isolated, less frequent, and thus less expected, tones engage widespread thalamocortical networks, whereas repetitive, regular trains of tones promote habituation and engage more local corticocortical networks. In this study, we use these contrasting stimulation patterns for a targeted modulation of sleep oscillations and examine their interaction with epileptic spikes. In an initial exploratory study (N = 10; age range: 7.3-16.2 years), we used a within-night block design to directly compare responses to the different stimulation patterns. Isolated tones delivered at long interstimulus intervals induced a transient increase in spike rate, whereas down-phase stimulation delivered in trains at short, regular intervals was associated with a significant reduction. We subsequently optimized the train-based paradigm and evaluated stimulation delivered throughout the night in a proof-of-concept study using a counterbalanced, between-night design (N = 5; age range: 4.4-10.7 years). Spike density decreased locally in all patients, providing convergent evidence for the effects observed in the exploratory study. With this mechanistically guided approach, we demonstrate that repetitive down-phase auditory stimulation of slow waves results in a local reduction of epileptic spikes. This framework may provide a rational basis for targeted interventions aimed at reducing spikes and related cognitive impairments.

items.title: Longitudinal Participation and Cognitive Score Interpretation in the J-TRC Webstudy
items.abstract: INTRODUCTIONWeb-based registries support remote cognitive assessment for Alzheimers disease research, but participant-driven reassessment raises questions about long-term data yield and interpretation of repeated scores. We evaluated data contribution, selective observation, and retest-dependent estimates of cognitive change in the Japanese Trial-Ready Cohort (J-TRC) Webstudy. METHODSWe analyzed over six years of J-TRC Webstudy data (launched October 2019; registrations through March 31, 2025; assessments through May 31, 2026). We examined data contribution, inactivity, reactivation, score-associated observation, first-exposure contrasts, and sensitivity to retest models and estimators. RESULTSAmong 14,912 registered accounts, 10,863 participants were eligible; 10,645 (98.0%) completed the Cognitive Function Instrument (CFI), 6,419 (59.1%) completed Cogstate, and 5,792 (53.3%) contributed assessments on multiple days. Among those with sufficient opportunity, 19.4% and 14.1% contributed data at or beyond three and five years. After 365 days without assessment, the estimated probability of resuming within two years was 7.2%. Worse prior cognitive scores were associated with lower odds of subsequent assessment (adjusted odds ratios per standard deviation: CFI, 0.952; Cogstate, 0.845). By assessment 12, returnee changes were +0.43 and +1.14 favorable baseline standard deviations (CFI, Cogstate), versus -0.06 and +0.08 in first-exposure contrasts. Marginal CFI time estimates differed under categorical versus flexible retest adjustment (+0.080 versus -0.227 standard deviations/year). DISCUSSIONHigh initial completion was accompanied by limited long-term data contribution. Subsequent assessment was associated with prior scores, and estimated time trends varied by retest model. Reporting assessment histories and testing model sensitivity are important for interpreting repeated online cognitive scores.

items.title: Cognitive Performance in Prodromal Neuronal α Synuclein Disease
authors: on behalf of the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative,
items.last_author: on behalf of the Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative,
items.abstract: ImportanceCognitive abnormalities may emerge during prodromal neuronal -synuclein disease (NSD), but their domain specificity and longitudinal course are uncertain. ObjectiveTo characterize baseline cognition and longitudinal change in prodromal NSD compared with healthy controls, NSD-negative genetic carriers, and sporadic Parkinson disease (PD). DesignLongitudinal cohort study using Parkinsons Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) data, with first visits from July 2010 through April 2026 and up to 4 years of follow-up. SettingMulticenter cohort. ParticipantsHealthy controls (HC; n=244), GBA1 or LRRK2 nonmanifesting carriers without NSD (n=323), prodromal NSD participants recruited through hyposmia or isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder cohorts (n=1640), and sporadic PD (n=824). ExposuresNSD status and clinical cohort. Main Outcomes and MeasuresCognitive summary scores for verbal memory, executive function, processing speed, language, and visuospatial function, and PPMI-defined mild cognitive impairment (MCI).
