MethodsTrio lrGS (Oxford Nanopore or PacBio HiFi) was performed, complemented by short-read genome sequencing (srGS) and mRNA sequencing (blood or fibroblast) of index cases, where available. Comprehensive variant analysis included small nucleotide variants, indels, SVs, and short tandem repeats. To identify the diagnostic yield of each method, we compared lrGS, srGS and ES re-analysis, and evaluated the additional value of RNA sequencing. ResultsWe established a diagnosis in 21 of 124 families (16.9%). Fourteen variants were retrospectively detectable in prior ES. Two cases with non-coding variants in SCN1A and RNU2-2 were detectable by both srGS and lrGS. Five SVs also required genome sequencing (5.6% of the total cohort), three of which could be detected, but not confidently resolved by srGS due to breakpoint complexity, repeat-mediated rearrangements, and large copy-neutral events: LrGS enabled accurate characterization of Alu-mediated CDKL5 and STXBP1 deletions and a MEF2C deletion with large inversion. A copy-neutral SCN1A inversion was well characterizable by both srGS and lrGS. One balanced translocation t(X;17) disrupting CDKL5 was resolved by lrGS (srGS unavailable). RNA sequencing confirmed pathogenicity of two SVs including t(X;17), the MEF2C deletion with inversion, and two CNVs. In addition, ZNF569 and ZNF570 emerged as candidate epilepsy genes from our cohort. DiscussionIn ES-negative DEE, the incremental diagnostic yield of genome sequencing was modest, while lrGS provided particular value for the structural resolution of complex rearrangements, especially those involving repetitive sequences. The finding that two-thirds of diagnoses were retrospectively detectable in prior ES highlights the substantial value of systematic reanalysis. Further gains from genome sequencing may increasingly depend on improved interpretation of non-coding variation and integration of long-read-specific information. Our findings indicate that complex SVs represent the class for which lrGS currently yields the most distinctive diagnostic information.

items.title: Transdiagnostic Psychiatric Polygenic Scores Reveal Pleiotropic Effects Across Medical and Laboratory Phenome
items.corresponding_institution: Radboud University Medical Center, Department of Human Genetics, Nijmegen, The Netherlands
items.abstract: BackgroundCurrent psychiatric diagnoses lack biological grounding. Using transdiagnostic psychiatric dimensions derived through data-driven genetic studies with large-scale clinical health records of multiple physiological and clinical outcomes, we can gain new insights into biological similarity and differences between such dimensions, informing nosological discourse. MethodsHere, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two healthcare biobanks. Genetic liabilities of individuals were estimated as polygenic scores for five first-order psychopathology factors (compulsive, thought, neurodevelopmental, substance use, internalizing disorders) and one second-order factor (hierarchical/p-factor). Phenome-wide and laboratory-wide association scans encompassed 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory metrics, meta-analyzed across sites. People with lived experience were involved in the design, preparation, interpretation and reporting of this work. OutcomesWe observed robust associations with up to 143 conditions (14 disease categories) for first- order factors and 221 conditions (15 categories) for the hierarchical factor (OR=0.75-1.94). Circulatory, digestive, and respiratory diseases were linked to neurodevelopmental, internalizing, and substance use liabilities. Metabolic conditions were negatively associated with thought and compulsive liabilities but positively associated with the remaining three factors. Laboratory results, particularly lipid and glucose metabolism markers, supported these differential findings. Immune markers also showed differential associations, with C- reactive protein and Complement C4 specifically linked to neurodevelopmental and thought factors, respectively. Similar trends emerged in the smaller African-like ancestry sample. InterpretationOverall, these findings support ongoing efforts to define biologically informed subtypes in psychiatry, such as immuno-metabolic profiles, which can facilitate patient stratification in clinical trials and support transdiagnostic precision psychiatry approaches. FundingThe work was supported by funding from the participating institutions. BFs and NRMs contributions were supported by the European Communitys Horizon 2020 Programme (H2020/2014-2020) under grant agreement No. 847879 (PRIME). NRM was also supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO) Innovation Programme (Vidi grant No. 09150172410043). Research reported in this publication was also supported by the National Institute of Mental Health of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number R01MH124851. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the funders. Research in Context Evidence before this studyWe searched PubMed from database inception to October 13, 2026, without date or language restrictions, using combinations of the terms "transdiagnostic", "cross-disorder", "genomic SEM", "polygenic score", "polygenic risk", "phenome-wide", "PheWAS", "laboratory", and "somatic". We considered original human genetic studies examining transdiagnostic psychiatric genetic liability and its associations with medical or laboratory phenotypes, excluding studies without relevant psychiatric genetic analyses. Previous studies demonstrated shared genetic liability across psychiatric disorders and phenome-wide associations of cross-disorder polygenic scores, although evidence was limited by ancestry representation, sample selection, and phenotypic ascertainment. Studies jointly examining multiple transdiagnostic psychiatric genetic dimensions across medical diagnoses and laboratory biomarkers remain limited. Added value of this studyUsing EHR-linked data from 121,411 individuals across two US biobanks, we examined six genetically defined transdiagnostic psychiatric factors in relation to 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory measures. We identified shared and distinct associations across psychiatric dimensions, particularly involving metabolic, immune, and cardiovascular systems. Findings showed broadly concordant directions of association across genetically inferred ancestry groups, although statistical power was limited in the smaller African-like ancestry cohort. Implications of all the available evidenceOur findings highlight the value of transdiagnostic genetic approaches for understanding shared and distinct physiological correlates of psychiatric liability beyond conventional diagnostic boundaries. These associations may inform future research into biologically informed psychiatric stratification and the integration of physical health considerations into psychiatric care, although their clinical utility requires further evaluation.

items.title: Genetic architecture and polygenic prediction of self-reported response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors in individuals with depression: a genome-wide meta-analysis
items.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h{superscript 2} = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (SLC17A6) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR=1.05, 95% CI 1.02-1.08, p=0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.

items.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pharmacy, College of Health Sciences and Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, Axum University, Axum, Ethiopia
items.abstract: BackgroundDespite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. MethodsWe pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohens d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. ResultsThree features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. ConclusionsThis study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.

items.title: Atrophy-related inflammation CSF markers predict clinical progression in genetic frontotemporal dementia
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognised as a key contributor to frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathophysiology, yet how inflammatory processes relate to neurodegeneration and clinical progression remains poorly defined. This study aimed to identify a multivariate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory signature covarying with brain atrophy, and to determine its relevance to clinical and cognitive outcomes in genetic FTD. We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR (R) + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments. A regularised canonical correlation analysis (rCCA) was used to derive a shared protein-brain covariance axis. Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope). The predictive value of the inflammation- and MRI-based profiles for cross-sectional CDR-SB, CDR slope, DSST and DSST slope were tested in linear models. Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals (CI) and bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2nd-level linear models; effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero. The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern. In symptomatic carriers, the MRI canonical variate was associated with CDR-SB ({beta}=3.80, CI: [0.64, 6.20]) at baseline, whereas the inflammatory protein canonical variate was predictive of CDR-SB slope ({beta}=0.24, CI: [0.02, 0.46]). Whereas both MRI ({beta}= -7.27, CI:[-14.20, -1.00]) and protein ({beta}= -7.83, CI:[-14.00, -2.16]) canonical variates were linked to DSST cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally. No significant associations were found in pre-symptomatic carriers or non-carrier controls. A data-driven CSF inflammatory signature, covarying with frontotemporal-insular atrophy, tracks with clinical severity and cognitive impairment in people with genetic FTD, highlighting inflammation as a candidate therapeutic target and progression biomarker in the earliest clinically manifest stages of disease.

items.title: Enrichment of Rare Exonic Variants in Cognitive Superagers from Centenarian Families
authors: Resilience/Resistance against Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring,
items.last_author: Resilience/Resistance against Alzheimer's Disease in Centenarians and Offspring,
items.abstract: While the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia increases with advanced age, a fraction of individuals maintains high levels of cognitive function at extreme ages. Here, we compared whole-exome sequencing variant frequency data for 136 centenarian and offspring cognitive superagers, whose episodic memory performance matches normative expectations for persons [~]30 years younger, 114 average-cognition controls, and the gnomAD population reference database. A rare variant allele frequency analysis identified 114 rare coding variants significantly enriched in cognitive superagers, of which the ten most significant variants were exceedingly rare missense variants residing in nine genes implicating neurovascular biology (LOX, CLEC4M, ZNG1F), immune regulation (HLA-B, HLA-DRB1, ITGAX, MUC4, MUC1), and neuronal structure (CEP131, two variants). Together, these findings support the study of an extreme phenotype as a tractable framework for prioritizing rare coding variation and nominating a set of candidate loci for functional follow-up to help elucidate protective genetic mechanisms in cognitive superagers.

items.title: Longitudinal Cerebrospinal Fluid Biomarker Changes Following Shunt Surgery in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus - Insights from the Gothenburg POiNT study
items.corresponding_institution: Hydrocephalus Research Unit, Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Institute of Neuroscience and Physiology, The Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, S
items.abstract: BackgroundThe underlying pathophysiology of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is incompletely understood and reliable predictors of shunt response are lacking. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may provide insights into disease mechanisms and help identify patients most likely to benefit from surgery. The aim of this study was to explore CSF biomarker dynamics following shunt surgery and their relationship with clinical outcome. MethodsThe POiNT (Prediction of Outcome in iNPH) was a prospective longitudinal study. One hundred and thirty-five patients with iNPH underwent standardized clinical assessment and lumbar CSF sampling 3.6 (SD 2.1) months before and 5.7 months (SD 2.4) after shunt surgery. CSF was analyzed for biomarkers of astrogliosis, axonal injury, amyloid, and tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the iNPH scale. Associations between baseline biomarker levels, postoperative biomarker changes, and clinical outcomes were evaluated using adjusted correlation and regression analyses. ResultsIn total, 69% (n=93) improved after shunt surgery. Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as A{beta}40 (1.93-fold change), and A{beta}42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001). In adjusted analyses, postoperative change in several biomarker levels were associated with degree of clinical improvement. However, baseline biomarker levels generally showed limited predictive value. Lower baseline monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP1) levels were associated with greater odds of overall clinical improvement but had a modest predictive performance (AUC 0.67). No baseline biomarker demonstrated strong discrimination of treatment response. ConclusionShunt surgery was associated with substantial changes in CSF biomarker concentrations, several of which correlated with the degree of clinical improvement. Although baseline levels did not predict clinical outcome, the observed biomarker changes may reflect biological responses to treatment, altered CSF dynamics, or both .iNPH. Future studies examining these processes relating to disease reversibility might help elucidate pathophysiological mechanisms in iNPH.

items.title: Cancer risk and survival outcomes in germline POT1 variant carriers
items.abstract: BackgroundThe prevalence of germline POT1 variants, spectrum of associated tumors, cancer risk and survival outcomes are incompletely described, and clinical management guidelines vary. We evaluated POT1 variant carriers in three biobanks and a clinical cohort to address these limitations. MethodsPrevalence, cancer spectrum and risk associated with germline POT1 pathogenic/likely pathogenic and additional functionally assessed variants were evaluated in Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n=51,172), Geisinger MyCode (MyCode; n=220,582), UK Biobank (UKBB; n=469,558) and a Penn Medicine clinical cohort. ResultsEstimated POT1 variant prevalence ranged from 1:1,279 to 1:2,902. Compared to non-carriers, cancer diagnoses were more frequent among POT1 variant carriers in PMBB (OR 3.41, 95%CI 1.81-6.43, p=1.88x10-4), MyCode (OR 2.23, 95%CI 1.31-3.79, p=0.003), and UKBB (OR 1.40, 95%CI 1.07-1.84, p=0.015). Cancer incidence increased beginning in the mid-30s, without evidence of increased mortality. Along with previously described cancer types, lung cancer was associated with POT1 variant carriers in two biobank cohorts. ConclusionPOT1 is a cancer susceptibility gene associated with a moderate (1.5-3.5-fold) increased cancer risk. Variants are relatively frequent and predispose to a broad tumor spectrum and increased incidence starting in the mid-30s, without increasing mortality. These findings expand understanding of POT1-associated disease and provide data to inform clinical management.

items.title: Sub-Threshold Stochastic Vibration Improves Fingertip Tactile Sensitivity in Stroke Survivors and Healthy Adults, with Source-Localized EEG Evidence for Cortical Network Reorganization in Healthy Adults
items.corresponding_institution: Neu(RAL)2: NeuRAL Systems and Rehabilitation and Assistive Technologies Laboratory, School of Physics, Engineering and Computer Science, University of Hertfords
items.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub-threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source-localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster-based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance-based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

items.title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
items.corresponding_institution: Barrow Neuro Analytics Center, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, AZ; Departments of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Barrow Neurological Institute, Phoenix, AZ
items.abstract: BackgroundWhite matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. MethodsWe developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). ResultsIn the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7-9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19-0.54) and for lesions of [≤]100 voxels (detection 77-87% vs. 14-63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p [≤] 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11-1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. ConclusionsTraining a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies. KEY POINTSO_LIA single nnU-Net trained across neurodegenerative, cerebral small vessel disease, and population-based cohorts and across 2D and 3D FLAIR outperformed SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg, with the largest gains in low-burden scans and small lesions. C_LIO_LIIn same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans, the models volume bias relative to acquisition-specific reference masks varied less across acquisitions, whereas comparator biases varied with acquisition. C_LIO_LIOnly WMH volume from the model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia beyond clinical covariates, highlighting the potential influence of segmentation algorithm choice on downstream clinical inference. C_LI

items.title: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
items.corresponding_institution: Medical College, Aga Khan University, Karachi, Pakistan; Byers Eye Institute, Stanford University School of Medicine, Palo Alto, United States
items.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCls) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Na"ive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and Fl-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and Fl-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications. HighlightsO_LIMultidomain feature engineering extracts 416 features from 16-channel EEG signals. C_LIO_LIMRMR reduces 416 EEG features to four discriminative features for classification. C_LIO_LIGaussian SVM achieves 95.48% accuracy for motor imagery classification. C_LIO_LIGaussian SVM achieves 92.50% accuracy for motor activity classification. C_LI

items.title: Histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscle and their associations with gait in older adults
items.abstract: Background/objectiveThere is a paucity of data about muscle morphology in aging adults. We quantified histologic features of the quadriceps muscle and examined their associations with gait function and physical activity in community-dwelling older adults. MethodsParticipants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Postmortem sections of the quadriceps muscles were examined by immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myosin heavy chain, and histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscles were derived through images quantifications and segmentations. In addition, brain sections were assessed for collection of Alzheimers disease and related dementias pathologies. Before death, participants physical activity was objectively measured through wearing an accelerometer sensor for 10 days, and gait function was quantified by walking 8 feet and turning 360{degrees} twice. Linear regressions and compositional analyses were used for analyzing data. ResultsPostmortem quadriceps was examined in 236 decedents (mean age at death was 91.7{+/-}6.0 years, and 71.6% (n=169) were females. On average, 44.7% (SD=19.5) of the muscle fibers were type I and 54.2% (SD=19.4) were type II, and 40.6% (SD=13.0) and 21.9% (12.9) of the quadriceps muscle area were composed of type I and II muscle fibers, respectively. In compositional analyses, male sex (estimate=0.303, SE=0.126, p=0.016) and more physical activity (estimate=0.118, SE=0.059, p=0.045) were associated with larger quadriceps muscle areas with type II muscle fibers, which were related to better gait (estimate=-0.049, SE=0.021, p=0.021). Quadriceps muscle composition explained an additional 3.2% of gaits variance beyond the 5.8% variance explained by Alzheimers disease and related dementias brain pathologies. ConclusionQuadriceps muscles having larger areas with type II muscle fibers were associated with more physical activity and better gait function in aging adults. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying these associations are critical for developing new therapies.

items.title: The phenomic landscape of rare gain- and loss-of-function variation
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Current large-scale phenome-wide association studies do not distinguish between genetic variants with distinct functional consequences, despite evidence that gain-of-function (GoF) and loss-of-function (LoF) variants can produce different phenotypes. Consequently, the phenotypic consequences of variants stratified by predicted GoF and LoF effects have not been systematically characterized at scale. Here, we systematically analyzed rare predicted GoF and LoF variants in 18,214 genes across 1,244 binary and 202 quantitative traits using whole-exome sequencing and electronic health records from the Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program, a phenotypically rich hospital-based biobank comprised of 50,067 participants, primarily representing African, Admixed American and European ancestries. We identified numerous established and previously unreported ancestry-specific and shared gene- and variant-level associations, many of which were supported by complementary evidence from both diagnostic phenotypes and clinical measurements. Proteomic evaluation of the previously unreported association between VNN1 LoF variants and body mass index in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis revealed reduced circulating vanin-1 levels with LoF variants, which in turn were associated with body composition and additional cardiometabolic phenotypes. Functional stratification of predicted GoF and LoF variants revealed gene-trait associations that were attenuated when these variants were combined, demonstrating that traditional aggregation of variants with different functional effects can obscure association signals. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating predicted functional consequences into association analyses and establish a comprehensive resource linking exome-wide predicted GoF and LoF variants to the human phenome across ancestry-specific and multi-ancestry analyses.

items.title: Unraveling the Lifespan Trajectory of White Matter Hypointensity on T1-weighted MR Images and Clinical Application in Various Brain Disorders
items.corresponding_institution: Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University
items.abstract: White matter hypointensity on T1-weighted MRI (T1-WMHypo), a putative marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, has been less systematically investigated than the widely studied T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) hyperintensity lesions. Here, we built the lifespan normative reference and assessed the clinical significance of T1-WMHypo across various brain disorders using a large multicenter dataset. We first established lifespan normative reference for T1-WMHypo volume by 34,148 healthy individuals (aged 4-85 years). Then, in 7,587 patients across 21 neurological and psychiatric disorders, normative reference-derived deviations revealed disease-specific patterns, with marked deviations in neurological diseases. Deviations of T1-WMHypo volume contributed to differential diagnosis, larger deviations correlated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, and poorer outcomes in various brain disorders. Elevated burden of T1-WMHypo volume predicted poor medication response in Parkinsons disease and accelerated disability progression in multiple sclerosis. These associations persisted after adjusting for conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity lesions. T1-WMHypo deviations provide an individualized marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, offering novel insights for precision medicine across development, aging and brain disorders.

items.title: DxToniaNet: A Neural Network for Estimating the Severity of Leg Dystonia in Children with Cerebral Palsy
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, USA
items.abstract: ImportanceLeg dystonia affects 50-80% of children with cerebral palsy (CP), but severity assessment remains subjective and time-consuming. Objective tools are urgently needed to quantify leg dystonia severity in clinical care and clinical trials. ObjectiveTo develop and validate a deep neural network (DxToniaNet) for leg dystonia severity estimation using 2D clinical video recordings. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsWe retrospectively analyzed video recordings of 298 children with cerebral palsy undergoing a seated hand open-close task as part of routine clinical care (Center 1: 193 videos, 720p/30fps; Center 2: 105 videos, 4K/60fps). Videos were rated for leg dystonia severity by a group of 7 experts using the Global Dystonia Rating Scale (GDRS) leg subscore (range 0-40) which has a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 4 points. Videos displaying leg dystonia (median expert GDRS score [≥]1) were used to develop and test a machine learning model (DxToniaNet) for estimating leg dystonia severity. Open-source software (OpenPose) estimated bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates, normalized for height and camera positioning, and 69 variance and amplitude features were calculated based on established expert-cited features of leg dystonia. A neural network, DxToniaNet, was developed, trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation on Center 1 videos before final testing on independent Center 2 videos. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s){square}Mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and accuracy in differentiating between videos with clinically meaningful differences in GDRS scores were calculated relative to experts median GDRS scores. ResultsWhen estimating experts leg GDRS scores in testing data, the proposed machine learning (ML) model yielded a MAE of 1.71 {+/-} 1.68 and RMSE of 2.21 {+/-} 0.34 (significantly less than the GDRS MCID of 4), and 90-94% accuracy in differentiating between videos with greater than a 4-point difference in the GDRS. Conclusions and RelevanceWe have demonstrated that DxToniaNet can accurately estimate leg dystonia severity compared to experts assessments with a small (clinically insignificant) error margin. Our methodology supports generalizability since DxToniaNet was developed and tested using independent videos datasets from different centers, recorded under different conditions. In the future, DxToniaNet may help facilitate standardized leg dystonia severity estimation in clinical care and clinical trials. Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan a deep learning model use clinically-acquired videos to accurately estimate experts leg dystonia severity assessments in children with cerebral palsy? FindingsAn automated deep learning model (DxToniaNet) trained and tested on clinically-acquired smartphone videos of 298 children with cerebral palsy estimates leg dystonia severity with 90-94% accuracy compared to experts assessments. MeaningDxToniaNet is an objective and free tool to estimate leg dystonia severity and may thus help facilitate standardized tracking of longitudinal treatment responses and clinical trial outcomes.

items.title: "Wow, this could be massive": Donor-Conceived Families Experience with Unexpected Recontact for Risk of Inherited Cardiac Conditions
items.abstract: IntroductionRecontacting families post-gamete donation, after a genetic diagnosis is made in the donor, can create complex challenges for healthcare providers and families. However, there is little literature that explores the family experience. This study aimed to explore the experiences of parents and donor-conceived young people navigating the recontact process and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants experiences in unexpectedly being recontacted and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A reflexive thematic analysis was performed. ResultsThirteen participants agreed to be interviewed, nine were parents and four were donor conceived young people. Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Out of the Blue, (2) A ripple effect on the family, (3) Calm after the storm, (4) Beneath the Ripples: the psychological impact. DiscussionInterviews provided insights into fertility services recontact and the predictive genetic testing process. From the themes, we conceptualize a ripple effect model. Findings highlight how cardiac genetics and fertility services are evolving, and the critical role of genetic counselors. The recontact process affects the entire family. However, most participants adapted and moved forward from this event.

items.title: Age and body-mass index account for part of the sex differences in cerebral venous thrombosis
items.abstract: BackgroundWomen with cerebral venous thrombosis are younger than men and more often present with headache, but these differences have not been adjusted for age or body-mass index, both of which differ by sex. MethodsSingle-center cohort of 219 consecutive adults with confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis admitted in Zurich in 2001-2021. Presentation, imaging and laboratory findings were compared between women and men, and every difference was re-estimated at equal age and body-mass index. Secondary analyses compared functional outcome, residual symptoms and return to work by sex, with an audit of incomplete follow-up. ResultsWomen (132, 60.3%) were younger (47.3 versus 54.9 years) and had a lower body-mass index (25.9 versus 27.8 kg/m{superscript 2}) than men. Headache (72.0% versus 57.5%) and cortical vein thrombosis (14.4% versus 5.7%) were more frequent in women, but neither association persisted after adjustment (odds ratios, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.54-2.54] and 2.05 [95% CI, 0.59-7.06]). Higher platelet counts (+56 x 10/L [95% CI, 26-86]) and elevated acute-phase markers without documented infection (59.1% versus 33.3%; odds ratio, 2.91 [95% CI, 1.44-5.87]) persisted after adjustment for age, body-mass index and calendar period. Among assessed patients (38% at 6 months), functional independence (86.3% versus 87.5%), residual headache, return to work and recanalization did not differ by sex. ConclusionsAt equal age and body-mass index, the female excess of headache and cortical vein involvement was no longer apparent, whereas a higher platelet count and a non-specific acute-phase response remained. Neither translated into a difference in outcome among assessed patients. Clinical Perspective What Is New?O_LIIn 219 consecutive adults with cerebral venous thrombosis, the female excess of headache and cortical vein thrombosis reported by the large registries was attenuated once age and body-mass index were accounted for, whereas higher platelet counts and more frequent elevation of acute-phase markers without infection in women persisted. C_LIO_LIWomen without a sex-specific risk factor resembled men in age and in the frequency of headache, which suggests that part of the female phenotype of cerebral venous thrombosis is a phenotype of young age and reproductive exposures. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LISex differences in presentation were not accompanied by differences in functional outcome, residual symptoms, return to work, or recanalization among the patients assessed, so sex alone does not identify patients who need a different follow-up. C_LI

items.title: Gene-based map of cardiovascular diseases
items.abstract: BackgroundRare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied. MethodsWe analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups. ResultsWe identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes. ConclusionsThese findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

items.title: Monocyte-to-lymphocyte and Platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Faculty of Medicine, Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt
items.abstract: BackgroundNeuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders (NMOSD) are a group of neuroinflammatory conditions that affect the nervous system. MLR and PLR are simple inflammatory biomarkers and are studied in many autoimmune and demyelinating diseases. In this study, we investigate the available evidence to determine whether MLR and PLR are higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy subjects. MethodsSystematic review and meta-analysis of studies measuring levels of PLR and/or MLR in both NMOSD patients and healthy controls were conducted. Mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were used to measure the difference in levels of MLR and PLR between patients and healthy subjects. ResultsFor MLR, the main meta-analysis yielded a pooled MD of 0.125 [-0.114; 0.363]. I2 was 83.8%. Subgroup meta-analysis of age- and sex-matched studies, demonstrated a pooled MD of 0.066 [0.012; 0.12]. For PLR, meta-analysis revealed a pooled MD of 23.99 [6.03; 41.96]. I2 was 82.3%. Subgroup analysis for age- and sex-matched studies for PLR, showed a pooled MD of 14 [-19.68; 47.68]. ConclusionThe main analysis suggests that MLR is not higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy controls. However, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies and leave-one-out analysis excluding the outlier study showed a statistically significant MLR increase in patients. PLR was found to exhibit a modest increase in NMOSD patients compared with healthy controls. Nonetheless, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies showed a statistically non-significant increase. Results should be interpreted cautiously. The available evidence is inconsistent and further research is needed.

items.title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
items.abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimers disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimers Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded diagnosis of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.

items.title: The contribution of Neanderthal ancestry to cancer risk
items.abstract: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated. Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry. Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk. Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal ([≥] 50% posterior inclusion probability). Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk. Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy. Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry. As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers. However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data. These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against. However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects. This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.
